title: 9.2 Multiplicity and the Morse index
search_title: Multiplicity and the Morse index
text: The coefficients of a sweepout do not determine the multiplicities of its varifold limit. Index estimates require their own hypotheses in addition to the existence and regularity theory. Definition 9.2.1 (Bumpy metrics and the index of a minimal cycle) . BE8BE104CF66 A smooth metric is bumpy if no smooth closed immersed minimal hypersurface admits a nonzero normal Jacobi field. For an embedded minimal cycle $V=\sum _ j m_ j|\Sigma _ j|$ with distinct disjoint components, define $\operatorname {index}(V)=\sum _ j\operatorname {index}(\Sigma _ j)$; the integers $m_ j$ do not multiply the index. Multiplicity one means that every $m_ j$ is one. This convention is used in [ MNIndex ] , Section 1. A disconnected hypersurface is allowed. Theorem 9.2.2 (Index equality under a critical-set multiplicity hypothesis) . 5CC6B5664356 Let $g$ be a smooth bumpy metric on a closed connected $M^{n+1}$ with $2\leq n\leq 6$. Use the $\mathbf F$-continuous sweepout convention of [ MNIndex ] . Let $\Pi $ be a homotopy class of $p$-sweepouts on a fixed finite $p$-dimensional simplicial complex, with $\mathbf L(\Pi )=\omega _ p(M,g)$, and let $\Phi _ i$ be a minimizing sequence in $\Pi $. Suppose that every embedded minimal cycle in its critical set has multiplicity one. Then that critical set contains an embedded minimal cycle $\Sigma $ satisfying \[  \operatorname {Area}_ g(\Sigma )=\omega _ p(M,g),\qquad \operatorname {index}(\Sigma )=p.  \] Source: [ MNIndex ] , Main Theorem 1.3, p. 5. The proof remains external. The multiplicity assumption concerns the whole indicated critical set, not merely one selected element; this theorem does not by itself prove multiplicity one.

title: 10.1 The Willmore energy and the catenoid estimate
search_title: The Willmore energy and the catenoid estimate
section: 10.1 The Willmore energy and the catenoid estimate
text: The same general min-max machinery can be applied to very different geometric families. The energy bound and topological detection must be supplied anew for each application. Definition 10.1.1 (Willmore energy and normalization) . 9E90E1906976 For a smooth immersed closed surface $\Sigma \subset S^3$ in the unit round sphere, set \[  \mathcal W(\Sigma )=\int _\Sigma (1+H_{\mathrm{av}}^2)\, dA, \qquad H_{\mathrm{av}}=(k_1+k_2)/2.  \] For a surface in $\mathbb R^3$ the corresponding energy is $\int _\Sigma H_{\mathrm{av}}^2\, dA$. The subscript distinguishes averaged mean curvature from the trace convention in Definition 7.1.1 . Source: [ MNWill ] , Definition 1.2, p. 685. Theorem 10.1.2 (The Willmore bound for embedded positive-genus surfaces) . 1EB4A795BBF2 A smooth connected closed embedded surface $\Sigma \subset S^3$ of genus at least one satisfies $\mathcal W(\Sigma )\geq 2\pi ^2$. Equality holds precisely for conformal images of the Clifford torus $S^1(1/\sqrt2)\times S^1(1/\sqrt2)$. Source: [ MNWill ] , Theorem A, p. 685. The proof is external. Its main bridge constructs a canonical family controlled by the Willmore energy and uses its topology to force a min-max lower bound; it is not a consequence of the Weyl asymptotic formula. Remark 10.1.3 (What the catenoid estimate supplies) . 1D4901862AD8 For a closed two-sided unstable embedded minimal surface in a three-manifold, the first negative direction for area produces nearby sheets with a quadratic area decrease. Ketover–Marques–Neves [ KMN ] , Section 2 and Theorem 2.4, control the cost of inserting and opening connecting necks, obtaining suitable families whose areas remain strictly below twice the central area. Their logarithmic neck estimate resolves the critical two-dimensional comparison. A complete formulation of the deformation and its topology is still an external dependency here. Applications must retain the particular sweepout class; the estimate is not a general theorem that all min-max limits have multiplicity one. Theorem 10.1.4 (One-parameter width in positive Ricci curvature) . 7A5ED0EFD787 Let $(M^{n+1},g)$ be smooth, closed, connected, and orientable, with $2\leq n\leq 6$ and $\operatorname {Ric}_ g>0$. Consider the classical Almgren–Pitts width of the integral fundamental class, using one-parameter integer-cycle sweepouts based at the zero cycle. This width is realized with multiplicity one by an orientable embedded minimal hypersurface of Morse index one. Source: [ KMN ] , Theorem 1.5; proof external. This is a fixed fundamental-class width. The source's Remark 1.6 cautions that allowing periodic families in other components of the mod-two cycle space changes the problem.

text: Theorem 10.1.2 (The Willmore bound for embedded positive-genus surfaces) . 1EB4A795BBF2 A smooth connected closed embedded surface $\Sigma \subset S^3$ of genus at least one satisfies $\mathcal W(\Sigma )\geq 2\pi ^2$. Equality holds precisely for conformal images of the Clifford torus $S^1(1/\sqrt2)\times S^1(1/\sqrt2)$. Source: [ MNWill ] , Theorem A, p. 685. The proof is external. Its main bridge constructs a canonical family controlled by the Willmore energy and uses its topology to force a min-max lower bound; it is not a consequence of the Weyl asymptotic formula.

title: Remark 10.1.3 (What the catenoid estimate supplies)
search_title: What the catenoid estimate supplies
section: 10.1 The Willmore energy and the catenoid estimate
text: Remark 10.1.3 (What the catenoid estimate supplies) . 1D4901862AD8 For a closed two-sided unstable embedded minimal surface in a three-manifold, the first negative direction for area produces nearby sheets with a quadratic area decrease. Ketover–Marques–Neves [ KMN ] , Section 2 and Theorem 2.4, control the cost of inserting and opening connecting necks, obtaining suitable families whose areas remain strictly below twice the central area. Their logarithmic neck estimate resolves the critical two-dimensional comparison. A complete formulation of the deformation and its topology is still an external dependency here. Applications must retain the particular sweepout class; the estimate is not a general theorem that all min-max limits have multiplicity one.

title: Theorem 10.1.4 (One-parameter width in positive Ricci curvature)
search_title: One-parameter width in positive Ricci curvature

text: Theorem 10.1.4 (One-parameter width in positive Ricci curvature) . 7A5ED0EFD787 Let $(M^{n+1},g)$ be smooth, closed, connected, and orientable, with $2\leq n\leq 6$ and $\operatorname {Ric}_ g>0$. Consider the classical Almgren–Pitts width of the integral fundamental class, using one-parameter integer-cycle sweepouts based at the zero cycle. This width is realized with multiplicity one by an orientable embedded minimal hypersurface of Morse index one. Source: [ KMN ] , Theorem 1.5; proof external. This is a fixed fundamental-class width. The source's Remark 1.6 cautions that allowing periodic families in other components of the mod-two cycle space changes the problem.

title: 10.2 Low widths of the round three-sphere
search_title: Low widths of the round three-sphere
section: 10.2 Low widths of the round three-sphere
text: The unit round metric gives concrete checks on both the normalization and the possible repetitions in the volume spectrum. The following records results from the supplied 2016 thesis, without presenting them as a complete list of presently known widths. Theorem 10.2.1 (Nurser's low-width results) . EDAAB3DCB932 For the mod-two volume spectrum of the unit round three-sphere, \[  \omega _1=\omega _2=\omega _3=\omega _4=4\pi ,\qquad \omega _5=\omega _6=\omega _7=2\pi ^2,  \] \[  2\pi ^2<\omega _9<8\pi ,\qquad \omega _{13}\leq 8\pi .  \] Source: [ Nurser ] , Theorem 8, p. 17. The proof uses explicit detecting families and Lusternik–Schnirelmann arguments, and is not included here. In particular, the final inequality is an upper bound, not a determination of $\omega _{13}$. No value of $\omega _8$ is asserted in this entry. Example 10.2.2 (The latitude family) . A2692E8AF721 In $S^3\subset \mathbb R^4$, the slice $\{ x_4=t\} $ has area $4\pi (1-t^2)$ for $-1<t<1$: it is a Euclidean two-sphere of radius $\sqrt{1-t^2}$. The maximal slice has area $4\pi $, and the endpoint slices collapse to points. The boundaries of the corresponding sublevel regions form the basic one-parameter sweepout. This calculation alone supplies the maximal area, not the lower bound for $\omega _1$ or the detection of a higher cup power. See [ Nurser ] , Sections 1.3.1 and 3.1–3.2.

title: 11.1 Constant mean curvature and constrained area
search_title: Constant mean curvature and constrained area
section: 11.1 Constant mean curvature and constrained area
text:
Finite-perimeter sets retain the enclosed region as well as its boundary. This is essential for the area-minus-volume functional, and connects the BV foundations with the CMC min-max construction of Zhou–Zhu [ ZZCMC ] . Definition 11.1.1 (The area-minus-volume functional) . 858933BEFE56 For a finite-perimeter set $\Omega $ in a smooth closed $(M^{n+1},g)$ and a prescribed number $c$, define \[  \mathcal A^ c(\Omega )=P(\Omega ;M)-c\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega ).  \] On a smooth boundary $\Sigma =\partial \Omega $ we use the outward unit normal and $H=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma 
u $. A CMC hypersurface has constant scalar $H$. Prescribing $c$ and finding a critical point of $\mathcal A^ c$ is a different problem from minimizing perimeter at a fixed volume. See [ ZZCMC ] , Introduction and Section 1. Proposition 11.1.2 (The smooth CMC Euler-Lagrange equation) . DEFFDC26B8E9 For a smooth compact region $\Omega \subset M$ with smooth boundary, a variation with boundary velocity $f
u $ satisfies \[  \delta \mathcal A^ c(f
u )=\int _{\partial \Omega }(H-c)f\, dA.  \] It is critical under all smooth variations if and only if $H=c$ everywhere. Proof Proposition 7.1.2 gives the area derivative $\int Hf$. The divergence theorem applied to an extension $X$ of $f
u $ gives the volume derivative $\int _\Omega \operatorname {div}_ M X=\int _{\partial \Omega }f$. Subtract $c$ times this derivative. Every smooth $f$ extends to a variation, so vanishing for all $f$ is equivalent to $H-c=0$. $\square$ Definition 11.1.3 (Almost embedded hypersurfaces) . D37CE32A4FFA An almost embedded hypersurface is a smooth immersion whose local sheets are embedded and, when they meet, lie on one side of each other: tangential touching is allowed but transverse crossing is excluded. This is the notion used in [ ZZCMC ] , following Theorem 0.1. It is weaker than embeddedness. The multiplicity of a parametrized sheet and the density at a touching point should not be confused. Theorem 11.1.4 (Prescribed positive constant mean curvature) . BEF02630A1D3 Let $M^{n+1}$ be a smooth closed connected Riemannian manifold with $2\leq n\leq 6$. For each $c>0$ there exists a nonempty smooth closed almost embedded hypersurface with constant mean curvature $c$, in the boundary orientation of the Zhou–Zhu construction. The min-max hypersurface has sheet multiplicity one. Source: [ ZZCMC ] , Theorem 0.1 and Remark 0.2, in the supplied arXiv v2 of August 11, 2017. Proof external. The conclusion permits touching; it does not assert global embeddedness or connectedness.

title: 11.2 Constant geodesic curvature networks
search_title: Constant geodesic curvature networks
text: The one-dimensional problem has a separate regularity theory. In particular, a hypersurface theorem in ambient dimensions three through seven cannot simply be applied with $n=1$. Theorem 11.2.1 (Curvature networks on a closed surface) . 1BE70B8F92FD Let $(S,g)$ be a smooth closed connected Riemannian surface and let $c>0$. There is a nontrivial integral one-varifold induced with multiplicity one by the boundary of a finite-perimeter set, and a finite set $F\subset S$, such that away from $F$ its boundary is an almost embedded curve of constant geodesic curvature $c$. At each point of $F$ the density is an integer and every tangent cone is a stationary geodesic network in the tangent plane, smooth away from the origin. Source: [ ZZNet ] , Theorem 1.1. Its proof is external. This result does not assert that the entire output is a smooth embedded closed curve.

title: 12.1 Allen-Cahn energy and minimal interfaces
search_title: Allen-Cahn energy and minimal interfaces
text: Allen–Cahn theory approaches geometric interfaces through functions. Chodosh's 2019 course notes, in the supplied revision dated June 29, 2023, give the basic analytic and variational setup [ ChAC ] . The following sections develop transition profiles, BV phase compactness, the perimeter lower bound, recovery sequences, gradient bounds, stability, and monotone-solution rigidity. The energy below is a diffuse-interface energy; its min-max levels are not identified with cycle-space widths without a comparison theorem. Definition 12.1.1 (The Allen-Cahn energy) . E4C01FDF2BAC Let $(M^{n+1},g)$ be a smooth closed manifold and $\varepsilon >0$. For $u\in H^1(M)\cap L^4(M)$ set \[  E_\varepsilon (u)=\int _ M\left(\frac\varepsilon 2|\nabla u|^2+\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon \right)dV_ g, \qquad W(s)=\frac14(1-s^2)^2.  \] We assign energy $+\infty $ outside this domain. The wells are $u=\pm 1$. The interface normalization is $c_ W=\int _{-1}^{1}\sqrt{2W(s)}\, ds=2\sqrt2/3$. Source: [ ChAC ] , Definition 2.1 and Section 2.2. Any comparison with area must keep this normalization. Proposition 12.1.2 (Equation and second variation of Allen-Cahn) . 6CA7B05E1A99 A smooth function is critical for $E_\varepsilon $ if and only if $\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u=W'(u)=u(u^2-1)$. At a smooth critical point its second variation in the direction $\phi $ is \[  Q_\varepsilon (\phi ,\phi )=\int _ M\left(\varepsilon |\nabla \phi |^2+\varepsilon ^{-1}W''(u)\phi ^2\right)dV_ g.  \] Compare [ ChAC ] , Section 2.1. Proof Differentiate the integrand at $u+t\phi $ once and integrate the gradient term by parts on the closed manifold. The first derivative is $\int _ M(-\varepsilon \Delta _ g u+\varepsilon ^{-1}W'(u))\phi $. Its vanishing for every smooth test function is exactly the equation. Differentiating a second time gives the displayed quadratic form. $\square$ Example 12.1.3 (A single transition layer) . 3C84C0DE867A For the potential in Definition 12.1.1 , $q(t)=\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$ satisfies $q''=W'(q)$, $q(\pm \infty )=\pm 1$, and $q'=\sqrt{2W(q)}$. Thus $u(t)=q(t/\varepsilon )$ solves the one-dimensional equation, and its energy per unit transverse area is \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\left(\tfrac 12|q'|^2+W(q)\right)dt =\int _{-1}^{1}\sqrt{2W(s)}\, ds=c_ W.  \] The substitution $s=q(t)$ proves the identity and explains why diffuse-interface energies must be divided by $c_ W$ when comparing with area. See [ ChAC ] , Section 2.2. Remark 12.1.4 (Multiplicity, curvature, and index in dimension three) . 7FD866591D17 The supplied Chodosh–Mantoulidis paper [ CM ] is arXiv:1803.02716v2, with a manuscript date of May 16, 2018. Its Sections 3–5 develop curvature estimates, separation of transition sheets, and the relationship between multiplicity and Jacobi fields for solutions with controlled energy and Morse index. Theorem 1.7 explains why a smooth limiting component with multiplicity, or a one-sided component, forces a positive Jacobi field (on the two-sided cover when needed). For bumpy metrics on closed three-manifolds this obstruction gives two-sided multiplicity-one components. The full convergence and index theorems, including their analytic hypotheses, remain external dependencies here. We do not infer any equality of Allen–Cahn and Almgren–Pitts widths from this source discussion.

title: 13.1 Obstacle problems and variational inequalities
search_title: Obstacle problems and variational inequalities
text: This chapter begins the obstacle-problem branch with a model variational formulation. The Sobolev and weak-solution background is developed in [ SimonPDE ] , Chapters 5–9. The classical free-boundary theory is developed in subsequent sections using [ Fig18 ] , with variational calculations and monotonicity proofs included and the deep regularity inputs identified. Definition 13.1.1 (The classical scalar obstacle problem) . C97A1383B3DD Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be bounded with Lipschitz boundary, $f\in L^2(U)$, and $g,\psi \in H^1(U)$. Assume the convex admissible set \[  K=\{ v\in H^1(U):v-g\in H^1_0(U),\  v\geq \psi \text{ almost everywhere}\}   \] is nonempty. The obstacle problem is to minimize $\mathcal E(v)=\frac12\int _ U|Dv|^2-\int _ Ufv$ over $K$. The inequality is a unilateral constraint. Existence is proved in Theorem 13.2.1 ; regularity requires additional assumptions. Proposition 13.1.2 (Variational inequality for the obstacle problem) . 422992397FE9 For $u\in K$, minimization of $\mathcal E$ over $K$ is equivalent to \[  \int _ U Du\cdot D(v-u)\geq \int _ U f(v-u)\qquad \text{for every }v\in K.  \] Proof If $u$ minimizes and $v\in K$, convexity gives $u+t(v-u)\in K$ for $0\leq t\leq 1$. Its energy has nonnegative right derivative at zero, which is exactly the inequality. Conversely, expand the quadratic energy: \[  \mathcal E(v)-\mathcal E(u) =\int _ U Du\cdot D(v-u)-\int _ U f(v-u)+\tfrac 12\int _ U|D(v-u)|^2.  \] Every term on the right after combining the first two is nonnegative under the stated inequality. Hence $u$ minimizes. $\square$ Remark 13.1.3 (Scope of the classical obstacle theory) . E2F2435B4E26 When $u$ and $\psi $ have continuous representatives, the contact set is $\{ u=\psi \} $ and the interior free boundary is $\partial \{ u>\psi \} \cap U$. The following sections develop existence, comparison, the reaction measure, quadratic blow-ups, and the Weiss and Monneau formulas. Theorem 13.3.1 , Theorem 13.3.14 , and Theorem 13.4.10 record precise external regularity inputs. Thin obstacles, variable-coefficient free-boundary regularity, and geometric obstacles require different hypotheses and remain future branches.

title: 14.1 Smooth mean curvature flow
search_title: Smooth mean curvature flow
text: Mean curvature flow is the evolution associated with the first variation of area. This introductory section fixes the sign and supplies a basic model. The subsequent sections develop evolution equations, comparison, Gaussian monotonicity, rescaling, and Brakke flow. Smooth identities and weak inequalities are stated separately. Definition 14.1.1 (Smooth mean curvature flow) . 3FFB3EED5409 A smooth family of immersions $F:\Sigma ^ n\times [0,T)\to M^{n+1}$ evolves by mean curvature flow if \[  (\partial _ tF)^\perp =\vec H.  \] Tangential velocity only changes the parametrization. With the convention of Definition 7.1.1 , a normal parametrization satisfies $\partial _ tF=-H\nu $. The vector $\vec H$ is the trace mean curvature vector, so there is no factor $1/n$ in this equation. The smooth first-variation background is [ ChMin ] , Section 7, and [ MM ] , Section 2. Proposition 14.1.2 (Area dissipation along a smooth closed flow) . C8E6BF7840BF For a smooth mean curvature flow of a compact hypersurface without boundary, \[  \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma _ t) =-\int _{\Sigma _ t}|\vec H|^2\, dA\leq 0.  \] Proof Apply Proposition 7.1.2 at each time with the variation velocity $\partial _ tF$. Its normal component is $\vec H$, and its tangential component has zero inner product with $\vec H$. The first variation is therefore the negative integral of $|\vec H|^2$. $\square$ Example 14.1.3 (Shrinking round spheres) . 2E074E821F62 For a round $S^ n_{R(t)}\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ with outward normal, $H=n/R(t)$, so the flow equation gives $R'=-n/R$. Consequently \[  R(t)^2=R(0)^2-2nt,\qquad 0\leq t<R(0)^2/(2n).  \] The sphere remains smooth on this interval and its radius tends to zero at its endpoint. This calculation checks the sign and time scaling of the convention; it makes no assertion about continuing an arbitrary flow through a singularity. Remark 14.1.4 (Planned weak flows and related variational problems) . D1D70B3B2945 Theorem 14.3.9 supplies the smooth existence and continuation statement, Proposition 14.3.8 gives avoidance, and Theorem 14.4.3 proves Gaussian monotonicity for a closed smooth flow. Definition 14.6.1 and Theorem 14.6.8 introduce one weak category and its compactness theorem. The distinction between weak flow and unit-regular flow is illustrated in Example 14.6.11 . Tangent-flow extraction, level-set comparison, and finer singularity theory still require further development. Related variational branches include Plateau problems, the free-boundary geometry introduced in Definition 7.17.1 , capillarity, and prescribed mean curvature.

title: 14.2 Convex flow and shrinking models
search_title: Convex flow and shrinking models
text:
A round sphere is a model for a flow singularity, but the theory must explain when such a model is forced and when other models can occur. The supplied papers of Huisken [ Hui86 ] and Chodosh–Choi–Mantoulidis–Schulze [ CCMS20 ] provide two entry points. Theorem 14.2.1 (Convex Euclidean hypersurfaces become round) . 7CECF8A8FAC9 Let $\Sigma _0^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a smooth, connected, closed, embedded, strictly convex hypersurface, with $n\geq 2$. Its mean curvature flow exists smoothly until a finite time $T$, contracts to a single point, and, after dilation about that point to keep the area fixed, converges smoothly to a round sphere as $t\uparrow T$. This is the Euclidean specialization of [ Hui86 ] , Theorem 1.1. The introduction of that article attributes the Euclidean result to Huisken's earlier work. In a curved ambient manifold, the theorem requires quantitative pinching relative to ambient curvature; mere convexity is not substituted for those hypotheses. The proof remains external. Definition 14.2.2 (Self-shrinkers) . F2183BE1F075 A smooth hypersurface $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ is a self-shrinker with center zero and scale one when \[  \vec H+ rac12 x^\perp =0.  \] Here $x^\perp $ is the normal projection of the position vector. The associated family is $\Sigma _ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$, evolving by mean curvature in its normal velocity. This normalization matches [ CCMS20 ] , Sections 1.2 and 2. Proposition 14.2.3 (Round shrinking cylinders) . B31B3405D469 For $1\leq k\leq n$, the cylinder $S^ k(\sqrt{2k})	imes \mathbb R^{n-k}\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ is a self-shrinker. A hyperplane through the origin is also a self-shrinker. Proof On the radius-$r$ cylinder, let $
u $ be the outward radial normal to the spherical factor. There are $k$ principal curvatures equal to $1/r$ and $n-k$ equal to zero. Our convention gives $\vec H=-(k/r)
u $ and $x^\perp =r

Differentiating the dilation $\sqrt{-t}$ shows that its normal velocity is exactly the rescaled mean curvature vector. $\square$ Proposition 14.2.4 (Gaussian area and the shrinker equation) . 12DACC1AA667 For a smooth closed hypersurface, put \[  F(\Sigma )=(4\pi )^{-n/2}\int _\Sigma e^{-|x|^2/4}\, dA.  \] For a smooth normal variation with velocity $X$, its first variation is \[  \delta F(X)=-(4\pi )^{-n/2}\int _\Sigma \left\langle \vec H+	frac 12x^\perp ,Xightangle e^{-|x|^2/4}\, dA.  \] Consequently the critical hypersurfaces for this functional satisfy the self-shrinker equation. Compare [ CCMS20 ] , Section 2. The noncompact compact-variation statement is Proposition 14.8.1 , and the Hessian with moving center and scale is Theorem 14.9.2 . Proof Since $X$ is normal, the pointwise first variation of area is $-\langle \vec H,Xangle dA$. The derivative of the Gaussian factor is $-	frac 12\langle x,Xangle e^{-|x|^2/4}$. Add these contributions and use $\langle x,Xangle =\langle x^\perp ,Xangle $. AAE9B0385275 The supplied version of [ CCMS20 ] is arXiv:2003.14344v1, dated March 31, 2020. It studies one-sided ancient flows and perturbations avoiding certain unstable singularity models. Its introduction explicitly retains possible obstructions involving higher multiplicity and noncylindrical models with cylindrical ends. We do not turn this version into an unconditional classification of all generic flow singularities. Definitions 14.6.1 , 14.4.6 , and 14.6.10 now provide the weak-flow, entropy, and regularity vocabulary. title: 6.2 Integral compactness and mod-two compatibility
search_title: Integral compactness and mod-two compatibility
text: Weak convergence of measures alone can lose the integer structure of a surface. First-variation bounds provide an additional geometric compactness principle. Compare the current compactness theorem in the currents chapter with the following varifold result. Theorem 6.2.1 (Allard compactness for integral varifolds) . 5A050AC47DEE Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$ be open, and let $V_ j$ be integral $m$-varifolds in $U$ with locally bounded first variation. Assume that for every relatively compact open $W\Subset U$, \[  \sup _ j\bigl (\| V_ j\| (W)+\| \delta V_ j\| (W)\bigr )<\infty .  \] Here $\| \delta V_ j\| $ is the total variation measure of the first-variation functional. A subsequence converges as varifolds to an integral $m$-varifold $V$ with locally bounded first variation. Integrality of the limit is the substantive additional conclusion beyond weak compactness of Radon measures. Source: [ Allard72 ] , Theorem 6.4; see also [ White09 ] , Section 3. The proof remains external. Definition 6.2.2 (The mod-two chain of an integral varifold) . 8706AD13DA84 For an integral varifold $V=V(S,\theta )$, let $[V]$ denote the rectifiable flat chain with coefficients in $\mathbb Z_2$ obtained by reducing the integer multiplicity $\theta $ modulo two. No orientation is required. Thus its density is $\theta \bmod 2$ at almost every point of $S$. Varifold convergence concerns measures on the Grassmann bundle, whereas flat convergence concerns chains; neither convergence is identified with the other by this definition. See [ White09 ] , Section 1. Theorem 6.2.3 (Compatibility of varifold and mod-two limits) . A428515E6D50 Suppose integral $m$-varifolds $V_ j$ in an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$ converge to $V$ as varifolds, with uniformly locally bounded first variations. If $\partial [V_ j]$ converges in the local flat topology, then $[V_ j]$ converges in that topology to $[V]$. In particular, the integral limit is provided by Theorem 6.2.1 , and the flat-chain limit agrees with its multiplicity modulo two. Source: [ White09 ] , Theorems 1.1 and 3.3, using the local conventions in Section 4. The boundary convergence assumption is retained. The proof remains external. Example 6.2.4 (Even multiplicity is invisible modulo two) . 58C720EC2E67 If $P$ is an $m$-plane, the integral varifold $2|P|$ has twice the weight of $|P|$, but $[2|P|]=0$. Consequently the mod-two chain alone does not determine the area or multiplicity of the varifold. This elementary example explains why the two forms of convergence in Theorem 6.2.3 carry different information; see [ White09 ] , Section 2, for examples involving sequences.

title: 7.3 Compactness with bounded area and index
search_title: Compactness with bounded area and index
section: 7.3 Compactness with bounded area and index
text: The Morse index measures the number of independent unstable directions, not the size of the second fundamental form. Its local consequence is particularly useful in compactness arguments. Lemma 7.3.1 (Disjoint unstable regions consume index) . 3E0AAA9F69FA Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth closed two-sided minimal hypersurface with index at most $I$. Among any $I+1$ open subsets of $\Sigma $ with pairwise disjoint closures, at least one is stable for normal variations compactly supported in that subset. Proof Otherwise choose nonzero smooth compactly supported functions $f_1,\ldots ,f_{I+1}$, one in each subset, with $Q(f_ i,f_ i)<0$. The disjoint supports make every cross term $Q(f_ i,f_ j)$ vanish for $i\ne j$. Hence \[  Q\left(\sum _ i a_ if_ i,\sum _ i a_ if_ i\right)=\sum _ i a_ i^2Q(f_ i,f_ i)<0  \] for every nonzero coefficient vector. The functions are linearly independent, producing an $(I+1)$-dimensional negative subspace, contrary to the index bound. This is the localization mechanism used in [ Sharp17 ] , Lemma 3.1. $\square$ Theorem 7.3.2 (Sharp compactness) . 780986CC98B2 Let $(M^{n+1},g)$ be smooth and closed, with $2\leq n\leq 6$. Let $\Sigma _ j$ be smooth, connected, closed, embedded minimal hypersurfaces satisfying \[  \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma _ j)\leq \Lambda ,\qquad \operatorname {index}(\Sigma _ j)\leq I  \] for fixed finite $\Lambda $ and integer $I\geq 0$. After a subsequence, $|\Sigma _ j|$ converges to $m|\Sigma |$ for a positive integer $m$ and a smooth closed embedded minimal hypersurface $\Sigma $, with area at most $\Lambda $ and index at most $I$. The convergence is smooth and graphical away from a set $Y\subset \Sigma $ of at most $I$ points. If $m=1$, it is smooth and graphical everywhere. If $m\geq 2$ and $\Sigma $ is two-sided, $\Sigma $ is stable. Source: [ Sharp17 ] , Theorem 2.3, pp. 321–322. The more detailed nullity conclusions are not needed here. The proof remains external. Remark 7.3.3 (Where regularity enters) . EFD6BFF7085F Lemma 7.3.1 limits the number of regions where stability can fail. It does not itself give a curvature estimate. Theorem 7.6.6 now states the smooth Euclidean curvature estimate explicitly. Theorem 7.6.5 and Proposition 7.6.3 explain how separated sheets imply stability of a limit. Sharp's argument uses the local stable-hypersurface estimates of Schoen–Simon [ SS81 ] ; the initial use is stated in [ Sharp17 ] , Theorem 2.1. For singular stable hypersurfaces, stability must be accompanied by the appropriate assumptions on the singular set. Theorem 7.11.4 now proves stability across finite punctures on an already smooth hypersurface, and Theorem 7.12.6 proves index persistence when the weak limit is already smooth and two-sided. These deductions do not supply the regularity of a singular support. Neither stability nor a bound on index alone asserts that an arbitrary stationary varifold is smooth.

title: 7.4 Sobolev and isoperimetric inequalities
search_title: Sobolev and isoperimetric inequalities
text: The area functional connects intrinsic analysis with the extrinsic mean curvature. Here $\vec H$ is the trace of the second fundamental form, rather than its average. Theorem 7.4.1 (Michael–Simon inequality in the smooth case) . A63DB2A4CACB Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^ N$ be a smooth embedded submanifold, with $n\geq 2$, and let $f\in C_ c^1(\Sigma \setminus \partial \Sigma )$ be nonnegative. There is a dimensional constant $C(n,N)$ such that \[  \left(\int _\Sigma f^{n/(n-1)}\, dA\right)^{(n-1)/n} \leq C(n,N)\int _\Sigma \bigl (|\nabla _\Sigma f|+|\vec H|f\bigr )\, dA.  \] The compact support is intrinsic and avoids the boundary. This is the smooth-submanifold specialization of [ MS73 ] , Example 1.6 and Theorem 2.1. We do not claim a sharp value of $C(n,N)$. The proof remains external. Theorem 7.4.2 (Sharp isoperimetry in codimension at most two) . ED2217821AC7 Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth compact embedded $n$-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb R^{n+2}$ with smooth boundary, where $n\geq 2$. If $\omega _ n$ is the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb R^ n$, then \[  \mathcal H^{n-1}(\partial \Sigma )+\int _\Sigma |\vec H|\, dA \geq n\omega _ n^{1/n}\mathcal H^ n(\Sigma )^{(n-1)/n}.  \] In particular, the curvature term vanishes when $\Sigma $ is minimal. The same inequality applies to submanifolds of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ by the isometric inclusion into $\mathbb R^{n+2}$. Source: [ Brendle19 ] , Corollary 2 in the supplied August 29, 2019 version. The proof remains external. This sharp constant is not asserted here in higher codimension. Example 7.4.3 (The flat ball fixes the normalization) . 35A87C0CF8FF For the radius-$R$ ball in an affine $n$-plane, $\vec H=0$, its $n$-volume is $\omega _ nR^ n$, and its boundary area is $n\omega _ nR^{n-1}$. Substitution gives equality in Theorem 7.4.2 . Both sides scale as $R^{n-1}$, as does the curvature integral because mean curvature scales as inverse length.

title: 9.3 Bumpy metrics, multiplicity, and abundance
search_title: Bumpy metrics, multiplicity, and abundance
text: In this section $M^{n+1}$ is closed. The width $\omega _ p$ always denotes the mod-two volume spectrum defined in Definition 9.1.2 ; it is not an arbitrary fixed homotopy-class width. Definition 9.3.1 (Bumpy metrics) . 3AFB2285C181 A smooth Riemannian metric is bumpy if every closed immersed minimal hypersurface has trivial kernel for its normal Jacobi operator. This includes finite covers; checking only embedded hypersurfaces is a weaker condition. See [ White17 ] , Theorem 2.1, and [ Zhou20 ] , Introduction. Theorem 9.3.2 (Generic bumpiness) . 826686D45D1C For a smooth closed manifold $M$, a Baire-generic smooth Riemannian metric has no closed immersed minimal submanifold with a nontrivial Jacobi field. Here generic means that the property holds on a residual set in the $C^\infty $ topology. This is [ White17 ] , Theorem 2.1 with the symmetry group taken to be trivial and $k=\infty $. The proof remains external. Theorem 9.3.3 (Multiplicity-one realization of the volume spectrum) . 0BB7ED8003DE Let $(M^{n+1},g)$ be a smooth closed connected orientable Riemannian manifold with $2\leq n\leq 6$ and a bumpy metric. For every positive integer $p$, there is a finite disjoint collection of smooth, connected, closed, embedded, two-sided minimal hypersurfaces $\Sigma _1,\ldots ,\Sigma _ q$ realizing \[  \omega _ p(M,g)=\sum _{i=1}^ q\operatorname {Area}_ g(\Sigma _ i),\qquad \sum _{i=1}^ q\operatorname {index}(\Sigma _ i)\leq p.  \] Each component occurs with multiplicity one. We state an orientable specialization of [ Zhou20 ] , Theorem A and Theorem 5.2, retaining its mod-two volume-spectrum setting. This is an existence statement about a realization of $\omega _ p$, not a claim about every critical varifold in an arbitrary min-max class. The proof uses prescribed-mean-curvature approximation and remains external. Theorem 9.3.4 (Infinitely many minimal hypersurfaces) . DD08D48E52FD Every smooth closed connected Riemannian manifold $M^{n+1}$ with $2\leq n\leq 6$ contains infinitely many geometrically distinct smooth closed embedded minimal hypersurfaces. Neither bumpiness nor positive Ricci curvature is required. Source: [ Song18 ] , Theorem 1, in the supplied June 22, 2018 version. The statement concerns distinct hypersurfaces, not repeated integer multiples of one surface. Its proof remains external. Theorem 9.3.5 (Equidistribution for generic metrics) . 5DAA3668FA8E Let $M^{n+1}$ be smooth, closed, and connected, with $2\leq n\leq 6$. For a $C^\infty $-generic metric $g$, there exists a sequence of smooth connected closed embedded minimal hypersurfaces $\Sigma _ j$ such that, for every $f\in C^\infty (M)$, \[  \lim _{q\to \infty } \frac{\sum _{j=1}^ q\int _{\Sigma _ j}f\, dA_ g}{\sum _{j=1}^ q\operatorname {Area}_ g(\Sigma _ j)} =\frac{1}{\operatorname {Vol}_ g(M)}\int _ M f\, dV_ g.  \] This uses the total area of the first $q$ surfaces as the denominator, rather than the unweighted average of their separately normalized area measures. Source: [ MNS19 ] , Main Theorem, equation (1), p. 422. The theorem provides a suitable sequence; it does not assert equidistribution for every choice of width realizers. The proof remains external.

text: Theorem 9.3.3 (Multiplicity-one realization of the volume spectrum) . 0BB7ED8003DE Let $(M^{n+1},g)$ be a smooth closed connected orientable Riemannian manifold with $2\leq n\leq 6$ and a bumpy metric. For every positive integer $p$, there is a finite disjoint collection of smooth, connected, closed, embedded, two-sided minimal hypersurfaces $\Sigma _1,\ldots ,\Sigma _ q$ realizing \[  \omega _ p(M,g)=\sum _{i=1}^ q\operatorname {Area}_ g(\Sigma _ i),\qquad \sum _{i=1}^ q\operatorname {index}(\Sigma _ i)\leq p.  \] Each component occurs with multiplicity one. We state an orientable specialization of [ Zhou20 ] , Theorem A and Theorem 5.2, retaining its mod-two volume-spectrum setting. This is an existence statement about a realization of $\omega _ p$, not a claim about every critical varifold in an arbitrary min-max class. The proof uses prescribed-mean-curvature approximation and remains external.

title: Theorem 9.3.4 (Infinitely many minimal hypersurfaces)
search_title: Infinitely many minimal hypersurfaces
text: Theorem 9.3.4 (Infinitely many minimal hypersurfaces) . DD08D48E52FD Every smooth closed connected Riemannian manifold $M^{n+1}$ with $2\leq n\leq 6$ contains infinitely many geometrically distinct smooth closed embedded minimal hypersurfaces. Neither bumpiness nor positive Ricci curvature is required. Source: [ Song18 ] , Theorem 1, in the supplied June 22, 2018 version. The statement concerns distinct hypersurfaces, not repeated integer multiples of one surface. Its proof remains external.

title: Theorem 9.3.5 (Equidistribution for generic metrics)
search_title: Equidistribution for generic metrics
text: Theorem 9.3.5 (Equidistribution for generic metrics) . 5DAA3668FA8E Let $M^{n+1}$ be smooth, closed, and connected, with $2\leq n\leq 6$. For a $C^\infty $-generic metric $g$, there exists a sequence of smooth connected closed embedded minimal hypersurfaces $\Sigma _ j$ such that, for every $f\in C^\infty (M)$, \[  \lim _{q\to \infty } \frac{\sum _{j=1}^ q\int _{\Sigma _ j}f\, dA_ g}{\sum _{j=1}^ q\operatorname {Area}_ g(\Sigma _ j)} =\frac{1}{\operatorname {Vol}_ g(M)}\int _ M f\, dV_ g.  \] This uses the total area of the first $q$ surfaces as the denominator, rather than the unweighted average of their separately normalized area measures. Source: [ MNS19 ] , Main Theorem, equation (1), p. 422. The theorem provides a suitable sequence; it does not assert equidistribution for every choice of width realizers. The proof remains external.

title: 15.1 Origins of geometric measure theory
search_title: Origins of geometric measure theory
text: These historical notes connect the mathematical definitions with the problems and people that shaped them. Personal recollections are attributed to their author; they are not used as substitutes for theorem statements. The principal first-person sources are Fleming's 2015 retrospective [ Fle15 ] , his 2016 account of De Giorgi [ Fle16 ] , and his 2007 memoir [ Fle07 ] . Remark 15.1.1 (1958–1960: compactness as a design principle) . 9EF132811524 Fleming recalls that he joined Brown in 1958 and worked with Federer during the academic year 1958–1959 on the paper Normal and integral currents , published in 1960. The objective was more specific than merely enlarging the class of smooth surfaces: generalized domains of integration had to retain enough geometric structure while admitting compactness for variational problems. This helps explain the simultaneous appearance of mass and boundary-mass bounds in the compactness theory. See [ Fle15 ] , Section 3, pp. 13–16, and [ Fle07 ] , Part I, Section 1. The corresponding definitions are in the currents chapter. Remark 15.1.2 (De Giorgi's boundary without smoothness) . E409AB8EC052 In his account of the 1950s, Fleming emphasizes De Giorgi's replacement of a smooth boundary by a reduced boundary carrying an approximate normal. A divergence theorem could then survive even when the topological boundary was unsuitable for classical differential geometry. The connection with distributional derivatives of characteristic functions brought the problem into the theory of functions of bounded variation. The modern formulation is Theorem 4.1.5 ; the historical account is [ Fle16 ] , Section 3, pp. 3–4. Fleming also stresses the influence of Caccoppoli's earlier work. Remark 15.1.3 (1969: a dimension threshold that surprised analysts) . AE10C8E9DF1A Fleming remembers being at Stanford in spring 1969 when news arrived that the higher-dimensional Bernstein assertion fails for entire minimal graphs over $\mathbb R^ m$ when $m\geq 8$. His recollection records Gilbarg's surprise that a PDE conclusion valid through seven variables could fail beyond that threshold. The geometric explanation passes through nonflat minimizing cones. The dimension here is the graph domain dimension, not the ambient dimension. See [ Fle15 ] , Section 7, p. 26, for both the anecdote and the chain from De Giorgi through Almgren and Simons. Compare the minimal graph equation in Proposition 7.2.1 . Theorem 7.8.6 supplies the two-dimensional geometric proof, while Theorem 7.9.10 explains the dimension restriction for stable cones with smooth links. Remark 15.1.4 (Different notions of a generalized surface) . A7B67D7E0642 The history did not produce a single universal replacement for a smooth surface. Fleming describes the influence of de Rham's currents, Whitney's geometric integration theory, and Young's generalized surfaces, before discussing Almgren's varifolds. Orientation and boundary make currents suited to one family of questions; measures recording tangent planes make varifolds suited to another. Allard's 1972 paper [ Allard72 ] developed first-variation, compactness, and regularity tools for the latter setting. See [ Fle15 ] , Sections 2 and 8. The modern compatibility theorem of White, Theorem 6.2.3 , shows how these viewpoints can interact without identifying their topologies.

title: 15.2 From one minimal hypersurface to many
search_title: From one minimal hypersurface to many
section: 15.2 From one minimal hypersurface to many
text: The following milestones refer to particular results and editions. Dates of supplied preprints are distinguished from dates of journal publication. Remark 15.2.1 (Existence, regularity, and the meaning of dimension) . 035643999D57 Pitts' 1981 monograph [ Pitts81 ] made discrete min-max and almost-minimizing constructions into a systematic existence theory. In the smooth closed setting, its original hypersurface range is $2\leq n\leq 5$, or ambient dimension $3\leq n+1\leq 6$. Schoen–Simon's stable regularity theory [ SS81 ] supplies the extension used in the modern ambient-dimension-seven statement. This is why the project records Pitts' original range separately from later realization theorems. Song's introduction [ Song18 ] gives a concise historical account of this distinction. Remark 15.2.2 (The volume spectrum and a sequence of geometric questions) . C5CCD5D00E73 The Weyl law [ LMN ] relates high-parameter widths to ambient volume. The next questions are different: whether there are infinitely many distinct hypersurfaces, whether they spread through the manifold, and whether a width is realized without multiplicity. The supplied sources record Song's 2018 preprint [ Song18 ] on infinitely many hypersurfaces for arbitrary closed metrics in dimensions three through seven; the 2019 article of Marques–Neves–Song [ MNS19 ] on equidistribution for generic metrics; and Zhou's 2020 article [ Zhou20 ] on multiplicity one for the volume spectrum of a bumpy metric. Theorems 9.3.4 , 9.3.5 , and 9.3.3 state these conclusions separately, with their distinct assumptions.

title: 7.5 Elliptic estimates for weak solutions
search_title: Elliptic estimates for weak solutions
text: The estimates below separate three levels of information: energy control, continuity with merely measurable coefficients, and higher regularity with continuous coefficients. They supply the analytic inputs used in the minimal graph and Jacobi-field sections. All balls in this section are Euclidean balls in $\mathbb R^ n$, with $n\geq 2$. Definition 7.5.1 (Sobolev spaces and weak derivatives) . 848E8C69703F For an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, $1\leq p<\infty $, and integer $k\geq 0$, the space $W^{k,p}(U)$ consists of functions whose distributional derivatives $D^\beta u$, $|\beta |\leq k$, belong to $L^ p(U)$. Its norm is $\sum _{|\beta |\leq k}\| D^\beta u\| _{L^ p(U)}$. A first weak derivative is characterized by $\int uD_ i\phi =-\int D_ i u\, \phi $ for all $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$. We write $H^1=W^{1,2}$, and $W^{1,p}_0(U)$ for the closure of $C_ c^\infty (U)$ in $W^{1,p}(U)$. The subscript $\mathrm{loc}$ requires the corresponding property on every relatively compact subdomain. See [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 5. Definition 7.5.2 (Uniform ellipticity and weak divergence equations) . 5454001B58EE Let $A:U\to \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be measurable and symmetric. We assume that constants $0<\lambda \leq \Lambda <\infty $ satisfy \[  \lambda |\xi |^2\leq A(x)\xi \cdot \xi \leq \Lambda |\xi |^2 \quad \text{for almost every }x\in U,\  \xi \in \mathbb R^ n.  \] A function $v\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ solves $\operatorname {div}(A Dv)=0$ weakly if $\int A Dv\cdot D\phi =0$ for all $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$. A weak subsolution of this equation satisfies $\int A Dv\cdot D\phi \leq 0$ for nonnegative test functions. No derivatives or continuity of $A$ are assumed. This is the homogeneous, symmetric, zero-lower-order-term case of [ SimonPDE ] , Chapters 6 and 17. Definition 7.5.3 (Hölder seminorms) . 9B57A69E7130 For $0<\alpha <1$, define \[  [f]_{\alpha ;U}=\sup _{x,y\in U,\  x\ne y}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha }.  \] The space $C^{k,\alpha }(U)$ consists of $C^ k$ functions with finite norm $\sum _{|\beta |\leq k}\| D^\beta f\| _{C^0(U)}+\sum _{|\beta |=k}[D^\beta f]_{\alpha ;U}$. Local versions are defined on relatively compact subdomains. On a ball of radius $R$, the scale-invariant combination for the $k$th derivative is $R^ k\| D^ kf\| _\infty +R^{k+\alpha }[D^ kf]_\alpha $. See [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 12. Lemma 7.5.4 (Caccioppoli energy estimate) . 494C2D3530AB If $v$ solves the equation in Definition 7.5.2 , $\eta \in C_ c^1(U)$, and $c\in \mathbb R$, then \[  \int \eta ^2|Dv|^2\leq 4(\Lambda /\lambda )^2\int |D\eta |^2|v-c|^2.  \] In particular, if $B_ R\subset U$ and $0<r<R$, then $\int _{B_ r}|Dv|^2\leq C(R-r)^{-2}\int _{B_ R}|v-c|^2$, with $C$ depending only on $\Lambda /\lambda $ and the cutoff choice. Proof By density we may test with $\eta ^2(v-c)$. Ellipticity and the operator-norm bound $|A|\leq \Lambda $ give \[  \lambda \int \eta ^2|Dv|^2 \leq 2\Lambda \int |\eta ||v-c||Dv||D\eta | \leq \frac\lambda 2\int \eta ^2|Dv|^2+ \frac{2\Lambda ^2}{\lambda }\int |v-c|^2|D\eta |^2.  \] Absorb the first term. A cutoff equal to one on $B_ r$ and with $|D\eta |\leq C/(R-r)$ gives the last assertion. Compare the energy-test method in [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 17. $\square$ Theorem 7.5.5 (Local boundedness of weak solutions) . C56302366B3D Let $v\in H^1(B_{2R}(a))$ solve the equation in Definition 7.5.2 . Then \[  \operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R(a)}|v| \leq C\left(R^{-n}\int _{B_{2R}(a)}|v|^2\right)^{1/2},  \] where $C=C(n,\Lambda /\lambda )$. This is [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 18, Theorem 2, p. 212, with zero forcing and lower-order terms. The local iteration proof is supplied below. Proof By Lemma 7.13.2 , $v_+$ and $(-v)_+$ are nonnegative weak subsolutions of the same zero-lower-order equation. Apply Theorem 7.13.5 to each. Their $L^2$ norms are at most that of $v$, and $|v|$ is their pointwise maximum. This gives the displayed estimate. The supporting argument uses truncated power tests, the external Sobolev gain, an integrability-improvement step and a convergent product of iteration constants; see Lemmas 7.13.3 and 7.13.4 . $\square$ Theorem 7.5.6 (Interior Harnack inequality) . 4D92018C184B If $v\in H^1(B_{2R}(a))$ is nonnegative and solves the equation in Definition 7.5.2 , then \[  \operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R(a)}v\leq C\operatorname *{ess\, inf}_{B_ R(a)}v, \qquad C=C(n,\Lambda /\lambda ).  \] The sign assumption is essential, and the estimate is on a smaller ball. This is the zero-lower-order-term specialization of [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 18, Theorem 1, p. 211. The proof remains external. Corollary 7.5.7 (Hölder continuity from oscillation decay) . 482FCE0EEBCC There are $\alpha =\alpha (n,\Lambda /\lambda )\in (0,1)$ and $C=C(n,\Lambda /\lambda )$ such that every weak solution on $B_{2R}(a)$ has a $C^{0,\alpha }$ representative on $B_ R(a)$ and \[  \| v\| _{C^0(B_ R(a))}+R^\alpha [v]_{\alpha ;B_ R(a)} \leq C\left(R^{-n}\int _{B_{2R}(a)}|v|^2\right)^{1/2}.  \] Proof Local boundedness first bounds $v$ on $B_{3R/2}(a)$. On any ball $B_{2s}$ compactly contained there, let $M$ and $m$ be its essential supremum and infimum. Apply Harnack to $M-v$ and $v-m$. Adding the resulting inequalities gives \[  \operatorname *{ess\, osc}_{B_ s}v\leq \frac{C_ H-1}{C_ H+1}\operatorname *{ess\, osc}_{B_{2s}}v,  \] where we may take $C_ H>1$. Iteration on concentric dyadic balls gives a bound $C(s/R)^\alpha $ for the oscillation, choosing a smaller exponent if necessary to have $\alpha <1$. The essential oscillations therefore define a unique continuous representative. Balls centered in $B_ R(a)$ of radius at most $R/4$, followed by the bound for pairs farther apart, give the stated seminorm estimate. This is the oscillation mechanism of De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory; see [ SimonPDE ] , Chapters 17–18. $\square$ Theorem 7.5.8 (Interior Schauder regularity) . 275ADD902409 Let $0<\alpha <1$, and let $a^{ij}=a^{ji}$, $b^ i$, and $c$ belong to $C^{0,\alpha }(B_1)$, with $\lambda I\leq (a^{ij})\leq \Lambda I$ and the sum of their $C^{0,\alpha }$ norms at most $K$. If $u\in C^2(B_1)\cap C^0(\overline{B_1})$ solves \[  a^{ij}D_{ij}u+b^ iD_ i u+cu=f,\qquad f\in C^{0,\alpha }(B_1),  \] then $u\in C^{2,\alpha }(B_{1/2})$ and \[  \| u\| _{C^{2,\alpha }(B_{1/2})}\leq C\bigl (\| u\| _{C^0(B_1)}+\| f\| _{C^{0,\alpha }(B_1)}\bigr ),  \] with $C=C(n,\alpha ,\lambda ,\Lambda ,K)$. The corresponding higher interior estimates hold when the coefficients and forcing have higher Hölder regularity. No sign assumption on $c$ is needed for this interior estimate. Sources: [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 12; [ ChMin ] , Appendix A, equation (A.2), printed p. 86. The proof remains external. Theorem 7.5.9 (Interior Sobolev estimate for the Laplacian) . B926EC268DB9 Let $1<p<\infty $ and $u\in W^{2,p}(B_1)$. Then \[  \| u\| _{W^{2,p}(B_{1/2})}\leq C(n,p) \bigl (\| u\| _{L^ p(B_1)}+\| \Delta u\| _{L^ p(B_1)}\bigr ).  \] This is the $k=0$ case of [ ChMin ] , Appendix A, equation (A.1), printed p. 86. It is an a priori estimate in the stated Sobolev class; neither endpoint $p=1,\infty $ is included. The proof remains external.

text:
The stability inequality, the linearized mean-curvature equation, and the separation of nearby sheets are different statements. This section develops their connections. We use the scalar convention $H=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma 
u $ from Definition 7.1.1 . Definition 7.6.1 (Stability on a noncompact hypersurface) . 35808222AC5B Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth two-sided minimal hypersurface in a smooth Riemannian manifold, possibly noncompact or with boundary. Put $q=|B|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )$ and $J=\Delta _\Sigma +q$. Stability means \[  Q(\phi ,\phi )=\int _\Sigma (|
abla \phi |^2-q\phi ^2)\, dA\geq 0 \quad 	ext{for all }\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\Sigma \setminus \partial \Sigma ).  \] Thus stability on an open subset only tests variations supported there. The compactly supported second-variation formula is the local version of Theorem 7.1.3 ; see [ ChMin ] , Theorem 23.4. Proposition 7.6.2 (Linearization of scalar mean curvature) . E4E4294F8594 Let $\Sigma $ be smooth, two-sided, and minimal. For a normal variation with velocity $f
u $, differentiating scalar mean curvature at $t=0$ gives \[  \left.\partial _ t H_{\Sigma _ t}ight|_{t=0}=-Jf.  \] The sign agrees with $Q(f,f)=-\int fJf$ and with the first variation $\delta A(f
u )=\int Hf$. Proof Take a two-parameter normal graph variation with initial velocities $f
u $ and $\phi 
u $, both compactly supported. Differentiate its first-variation identity in the other parameter. Terms differentiating the area form or normal component are multiplied by $H=0$, leaving $\int \phi \, \partial _ tH$. The mixed second derivative is the polarization of the second variation, $Q(f,\phi )=-\int \phi Jf$. Since $\phi $ is arbitrary, the identity follows pointwise. For a general smooth $f$, insert cutoffs near the point being tested. Compare [ ChMin ] , the proof of Proposition 33.3, pp. 80–81. $\square$ Proposition 7.6.3 (Positive Jacobi fields imply stability) . F531FEF8EC1D If $w>0$ is smooth on a two-sided minimal hypersurface and $Jw=0$, then for every compactly supported smooth $\phi $ in its interior, \[  Q(\phi ,\phi )=\int _\Sigma w^2\left|
abla \left( rac\phi wight)ight|^2dA\geq 0.  \] In particular the hypersurface is stable in the sense of Definition 7.6.1 . Proof Set $\eta =\phi /w$. Expanding $|
abla (w\eta )|^2$ and subtracting $q w^2\eta ^2$, the terms other than $w^2|
abla \eta |^2$ integrate to $\int 
abla w\cdot 
abla (w\eta ^2)-qw^2\eta ^2=-\int w\eta ^2(\Delta w+qw)=0$. There is no boundary term because $\eta $ has compact support. This identity makes explicit the positive-Jacobi-field argument of [ ChMin ] , Proposition 33.4. $\square$ Corollary 7.6.4 (The vertical angle makes a minimal graph stable) . 6FAB89AC045D For a smooth minimal graph in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ with upward normal $
u $, the function \[  w=\langle 
u ,e_{n+1}angle =(1+|Du|^2)^{-1/2}  \] is a positive Jacobi function. Hence the graph is stable under all compactly supported normal variations. Proof Vertical translations preserve minimality. Their normal speed is $w$; their tangential part differentiates the identically zero mean curvature and contributes zero. Proposition 7.6.2 therefore gives $Jw=0$. Apply Proposition 7.6.3 . This also follows from the minimizing property in Proposition 7.2.13 . $\square$ Theorem 7.6.5 (Separated sheets produce a positive Jacobi field) . BB7E1EEFDC4F Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth connected two-sided embedded minimal hypersurface in a smooth Riemannian manifold. Let $U_1\Subset U_2\Subset \cdots $ be connected relatively compact open subsets exhausting its interior, and fix $p\in U_1$. Suppose smooth functions $u_{1,j}<u_{2,j}$ on $U_ j$ define minimal normal graphs by the normal exponential map, with both functions converging to zero in $C^\infty $ on every compact subset of $\Sigma \setminus \partial \Sigma $. Then a subsequence of \[  v_ j= rac{u_{2,j}-u_{1,j}}{(u_{2,j}-u_{1,j})(p)}  \] converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to a function $v>0$ with $v(p)=1$ and $Jv=0$. Consequently the interior of $\Sigma $ is stable. This is the normal-graph formulation of [ ChMin ] , Proposition 33.3, including its stated Riemannian extension. The local proof below retains Harnack and Schauder estimates as external analytic inputs. The conclusion assumes two globally ordered sheets on the exhaustion, not merely a numerical multiplicity at one point. Proof By Lemma 7.10.3 , the positive gaps $w_ j=u_{2,j}-u_{1,j}$ solve linear equations $L_ jw_ j=0$, with smooth coefficients converging on compact subsets to those of $J$. Division by the positive value $w_ j(p)$ preserves the equation. Lemma 7.10.2 gives a subsequential smooth local limit $v>0$ with $v(p)=1$ and $Jv=0$. Proposition 7.6.3 then gives stability on the interior. The exhaustion hypothesis ensures that every compact set used in the Harnack and Schauder arguments is eventually in the domain of both graphs. No conclusion about extension across a singularity is needed for this theorem. $\square$ Theorem 7.6.6 (Stable curvature estimate in dimensions at most six) . 0B9CCB2E229B Let $2\leq n\leq 6$. Suppose $\Sigma ^ n$ is a smooth properly embedded two-sided minimal hypersurface without boundary in $B_{2R}^{n+1}(a)$, is stable for compactly supported normal variations there, and satisfies \[  \mathcal H^ n(\Sigma \cap B_{2R}(a))\leq \Lambda R^ n.  \] Then $\sup _{\Sigma \cap B_ R(a)}|B|\leq C(n,\Lambda )/R$. This is the smooth Euclidean specialization of Schoen–Simon [ SS81 ] , as stated in [ Sharp17 ] , Theorem 2.1, pp. 320–321. Applying that local estimate at points of $\Sigma \cap B_ R(a)$ gives the stated interior bound. Smoothness removes the singular-set hypothesis in that source; for singular hypersurfaces the hypothesis must be restored. The area bound and dimension restriction are retained. The proof remains external.

title: 6.3 Tangent cones and stratification
search_title: Tangent cones and stratification
text: A blow-up records the geometry visible at smaller and smaller scales. Compactness provides limits, monotonicity forces them to be cones, and stratification measures their translational symmetries. Throughout this section $V$ is a stationary integral $n$-varifold in an open $U\subset \mathbb R^{n+k}$, where $n,k\geq 1$. Definition 6.3.1 (Dilations of a varifold) . CC955C20A984 For $a\in U$ and $r>0$, set $\eta _{a,r}(x)=(x-a)/r$. The dilated varifold $V_{a,r}=(\eta _{a,r})_\# V$ is defined on $\eta _{a,r}(U)$ by \[  \int \varphi (y,S)\, dV_{a,r}(y,S) =r^{-n}\int \varphi ((x-a)/r,S)\, dV(x,S).  \] The factor $r^{-n}$ is the tangential Jacobian of the dilation. This is not the unweighted pushforward of the measure on the Grassmann bundle. See [ Minter ] , Section 1, p. 11. Proposition 6.3.2 (Mass and stationarity under dilation) . 989EAE3823D1 For every ball with $B_{rR}(a)\subset U$, \[  \| V_{a,r}\| (B_ R(0))=r^{-n}\| V\| (B_{rR}(a)).  \] Moreover $V_{a,r}$ is stationary and integral, and $\Theta ^ n(\| V_{a,r}\| ,0)=\Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a)$. Proof The mass identity follows by testing the definition with approximations to the indicator of $B_ R$. If $Y$ is a compactly supported vector field in the dilated domain, put $X(x)=Y((x-a)/r)$. Then $\delta V_{a,r}(Y)=r^{1-n}\delta V(X)=0$. Rectifiable sets and integer multiplicities are preserved by the dilation. Divide the mass identity by $\omega _ n R^ n$ and send $R$ to zero to obtain the density identity. $\square$ Proposition 6.3.3 (Upper semicontinuity of stationary density) . 04D4F1210FAB If stationary integral varifolds $V_ j$ converge to $V$ in $U$ and $a_ j\to a\in U$, then \[  \limsup _ j\Theta ^ n(\| V_ j\| ,a_ j)\leq \Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a).  \] In particular the density of a fixed stationary integral varifold is upper semicontinuous in the center. Compare [ Minter ] , Lemma 0.6. Proof Fix $s>0$ with $\overline{B_ s(a)}\subset U$ and $\| V\| (\partial B_ s(a))=0$. For $0<\varepsilon <s$ and all large $j$, $B_{s-\varepsilon }(a_ j)\subset B_ s(a)$. Monotonicity bounds the density at $a_ j$ by $\| V_ j\| (B_ s(a))/(\omega _ n(s-\varepsilon )^ n)$. At the chosen continuity radius the numerator converges to $\| V\| (B_ s(a))$. Take the upper limit, then let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, and finally let $s\downarrow 0$ through continuity radii. Only countably many radii can fail the boundary-mass condition. $\square$ Corollary 6.3.4 (Density at every support point) . 3A22ED5AAEBA For every $a\in \operatorname {spt}\| V\| $, $\Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a)\geq 1$. Proof Integrality gives positive integer density at $\| V\| $-almost every point. Every ball about a support point has positive weight, so choose such points tending to $a$. Proposition 6.3.3 , applied to the constant sequence $V$, gives the lower bound. This conclusion uses both integrality and stationarity. $\square$ Definition 6.3.5 (Regular and singular points) . 9EC8D9CF963C A support point $a$ is regular if in some neighborhood $V=q|\Sigma |$, where $\Sigma $ is a smooth embedded $n$-submanifold without boundary there and $q$ is a positive integer. The remaining support points form $\operatorname {sing}V$; the regular set is $\operatorname {reg}V$. Locally constant multiplicity is included in regularity, so a multiple plane is regular. Transverse crossings are singular for this definition. For stationary integral varifolds this agrees with the smooth-support definition using Theorem 6.5.3 ; see [ Minter ] , Lemma 0.7 and Definitions 0.8–0.9. Theorem 6.3.6 (Existence and structure of tangent cones) . 4897B19C7602 Let $a\in \operatorname {spt}\| V\| $. For every sequence $r_ j\downarrow 0$, a subsequence of $V_{a,r_ j}$ converges locally as varifolds on $\mathbb R^{n+k}$ to a nonzero stationary integral $n$-varifold $C$. The limit is a cone: \[  (\eta _{0,s})_\# C=C\quad (s>0),\qquad \| C\| (B_ R(0))=\omega _ n R^ n\Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a)\quad (R>0).  \] Such limits are called tangent cones; their set is denoted $\operatorname {Tan}(V,a)$. No uniqueness is asserted. Sources: [ Minter ] , Section 1, Lemmas 1.1–1.2 and Definition 1.3. The compactness input remains external; the conical-structure deduction follows below. Proof Choose $r_0>0$ with $\overline{B_{r_0}(a)}\subset U$. For fixed $R$ and all sufficiently large $j$, scaling and stationary monotonicity give \[  \| V_{a,r_ j}\| (B_ R)=r_ j^{-n}\| V\| (B_{r_ jR}(a)) \leq R^ n r_0^{-n}\| V\| (B_{r_0}(a)).  \] The dilates are integral and stationary by Proposition 6.3.2 ; hence their first variations vanish on every fixed compact set for large $j$. Allard compactness, Theorem 6.2.1 , on an exhaustion and a diagonal subsequence give a stationary integral limit $C$ on all of $\mathbb R^{n+k}$. Stationarity also follows directly from Lemma 6.7.1 . At any radius $R$ with $\| C\| (\partial B_ R)=0$, weak convergence and scaling imply \[  \| C\| (B_ R)=\lim _ j r_ j^{-n}\| V\| (B_{r_ jR}(a)) =\omega _ nR^ n\Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a).  \] Only countably many radii fail this continuity condition. Approximating any radius from below by continuity radii and using continuity from below of open-ball masses proves the identity for every $R>0$. Theorem 6.7.4 now proves dilation invariance, including the tangent-plane distribution. Corollary 6.3.4 gives $\Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a)\geq 1$, so the limit is nonzero. The construction uses subsequences and supplies no uniqueness statement. $\square$ Definition 6.3.7 (The spine of a stationary cone) . 19F77FBF48A6 For a nonzero stationary integral cone $C$ in $\mathbb R^{n+k}$, its spine is the set of translation symmetries \[  S(C)=\{ y\in \mathbb R^{n+k}:(\eta _{y,1})_\# C=C\} .  \] Translation acts on the entire varifold, including multiplicity. See [ Minter ] , Definition 1.4. Theorem 6.3.8 (Spine structure and splitting) . 2C1BC96081EA The spine of a nonzero stationary integral $n$-cone is a linear subspace of dimension $d\leq n$, and \[  S(C)=\{ y:\Theta ^ n(\| C\| ,y)=\Theta ^ n(\| C\| ,0)\} .  \] The vertex has maximal density. After an orthogonal change of coordinates, $C=C_0\times \mathbb R^ d$, where $C_0$ is a stationary integral $(n-d)$-cone; for $d=n$, $C_0$ is a positive integer multiple of the origin. Source: [ Minter ] , Lemma 1.5. Proof Proposition 6.9.4 identifies the maximal-density set with a linear spine of dimension at most $n$. If $d=0$, take $C_0=C$. If $1\leq d<n$, Proposition 6.9.7 gives the stationary integral transverse cone, using rectifiable coarea as its recorded external input. If $d=n$, Corollary 6.9.8 gives a positive integer multiple of the spine, with transverse factor $q\delta _0$. These statements identify the weight, tangent planes, multiplicity, and first variation of each factor. $\square$ Definition 6.3.9 (Singular strata) . AA22661A81D0 For $0\leq j\leq n$, define \[  \mathcal S^ j(V)=\{ a\in \operatorname {sing}V: \dim S(C)\leq j\text{ for every }C\in \operatorname {Tan}(V,a)\} .  \] Thus $\mathcal S^0\subset \cdots \subset \mathcal S^ n=\operatorname {sing}V$. The quantifier is over every tangent cone, without assuming tangent-cone uniqueness. A point with a planar tangent cone of higher multiplicity can lie in the top stratum. See [ Minter ] , Definition 1.6. Theorem 6.3.10 (Dimension bound for the strata) . 20B7E5509A93 For every stationary integral $n$-varifold and $0\leq j\leq n$, \[  \dim _{\mathcal H}\mathcal S^ j(V)\leq j.  \] This is the qualitative stratification theorem stated in [ Minter ] , Theorem 1.7, p. 17. Its covering proof is given below. The estimate alone does not remove the top stratum or give the codimension-seven bound available under stronger minimizing or stability hypotheses. Proof Fix $\beta >0$ and choose $\delta >0$ small enough for Proposition 6.10.3 in ambient dimension $n+k$ and plane dimension $j$. Proposition 6.10.5 , proved by tangent-cone compactness and density upper semicontinuity, decomposes $\mathcal S^ j(V)$ into countably many sets with one-sided $\delta $ approximation by $j$-planes at all sufficiently small scales. Each piece has zero $\mathcal H^{j+\beta }$ outer measure by the covering proposition. Countable subadditivity gives the same conclusion for the stratum. Since $\beta >0$ is arbitrary, its Hausdorff dimension is at most $j$. This proves a dimension bound; it does not prove finite $\mathcal H^ j$ measure, rectifiability, or uniqueness of tangent cones. $\square$ Example 6.3.11 (Crossing planes remain stationary) . BFB7F867B030 Let $P_1,P_2$ be distinct $n$-dimensional hyperplanes in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ through the origin. The varifold $|P_1|+|P_2|$ is stationary by linearity and Proposition 6.1.4 . Its singular set and spine are $P_1\cap P_2$, of dimension $n-1$. The density is two on the intersection and one elsewhere on the support. Thus stationarity and integrality allow a large singular set. Compare [ Minter ] , Sections 0–1.

For fixed $R$ and all sufficiently large $j$, scaling and stationary monotonicity give \[  \| V_{a,r_ j}\| (B_ R)=r_ j^{-n}\| V\| (B_{r_ jR}(a)) \leq R^ n r_0^{-n}\| V\| (B_{r_0}(a)).  \] The dilates are integral and stationary by Proposition 6.3.2 ; hence their first variations vanish on every fixed compact set for large $j$. Allard compactness, Theorem 6.2.1 , on an exhaustion and a diagonal subsequence give a stationary integral limit $C$ on all of $\mathbb R^{n+k}$. Stationarity also follows directly from Lemma 6.7.1 . At any radius $R$ with $\| C\| (\partial B_ R)=0$, weak convergence and scaling imply \[  \| C\| (B_ R)=\lim _ j r_ j^{-n}\| V\| (B_{r_ jR}(a)) =\omega _ nR^ n\Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a).  \] Only countably many radii fail this continuity condition. Approximating any radius from below by continuity radii and using continuity from below of open-ball masses proves the identity for every $R>0$. Theorem 6.7.4 now proves dilation invariance, including the tangent-plane distribution. Corollary 6.3.4 gives $\Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a)\geq 1$, so the limit is nonzero. The construction uses subsequences and supplies no uniqueness statement. $\square$

title: Definition 6.3.7 (The spine of a stationary cone)
search_title: The spine of a stationary cone
text: Definition 6.3.7 (The spine of a stationary cone) . 19F77FBF48A6 For a nonzero stationary integral cone $C$ in $\mathbb R^{n+k}$, its spine is the set of translation symmetries \[  S(C)=\{ y\in \mathbb R^{n+k}:(\eta _{y,1})_\# C=C\} .  \] Translation acts on the entire varifold, including multiplicity. See [ Minter ] , Definition 1.4.

title: Theorem 6.3.8 (Spine structure and splitting)
search_title: Spine structure and splitting
text: Theorem 6.3.8 (Spine structure and splitting) . 2C1BC96081EA The spine of a nonzero stationary integral $n$-cone is a linear subspace of dimension $d\leq n$, and \[  S(C)=\{ y:\Theta ^ n(\| C\| ,y)=\Theta ^ n(\| C\| ,0)\} .  \] The vertex has maximal density. After an orthogonal change of coordinates, $C=C_0\times \mathbb R^ d$, where $C_0$ is a stationary integral $(n-d)$-cone; for $d=n$, $C_0$ is a positive integer multiple of the origin. Source: [ Minter ] , Lemma 1.5. Proof Proposition 6.9.4 identifies the maximal-density set with a linear spine of dimension at most $n$. If $d=0$, take $C_0=C$. If $1\leq d<n$, Proposition 6.9.7 gives the stationary integral transverse cone, using rectifiable coarea as its recorded external input. If $d=n$, Corollary 6.9.8 gives a positive integer multiple of the spine, with transverse factor $q\delta _0$. These statements identify the weight, tangent planes, multiplicity, and first variation of each factor. $\square$

title: Definition 6.3.9 (Singular strata)
search_title: Singular strata
text: Definition 6.3.9 (Singular strata) . AA22661A81D0 For $0\leq j\leq n$, define \[  \mathcal S^ j(V)=\{ a\in \operatorname {sing}V: \dim S(C)\leq j\text{ for every }C\in \operatorname {Tan}(V,a)\} .  \] Thus $\mathcal S^0\subset \cdots \subset \mathcal S^ n=\operatorname {sing}V$. The quantifier is over every tangent cone, without assuming tangent-cone uniqueness. A point with a planar tangent cone of higher multiplicity can lie in the top stratum. See [ Minter ] , Definition 1.6.

title: Theorem 6.3.10 (Dimension bound for the strata)
search_title: Dimension bound for the strata
text: Theorem 6.3.10 (Dimension bound for the strata) . 20B7E5509A93 For every stationary integral $n$-varifold and $0\leq j\leq n$, \[  \dim _{\mathcal H}\mathcal S^ j(V)\leq j.  \] This is the qualitative stratification theorem stated in [ Minter ] , Theorem 1.7, p. 17. Its covering proof is given below. The estimate alone does not remove the top stratum or give the codimension-seven bound available under stronger minimizing or stability hypotheses. Proof Fix $\beta >0$ and choose $\delta >0$ small enough for Proposition 6.10.3 in ambient dimension $n+k$ and plane dimension $j$. Proposition 6.10.5 , proved by tangent-cone compactness and density upper semicontinuity, decomposes $\mathcal S^ j(V)$ into countably many sets with one-sided $\delta $ approximation by $j$-planes at all sufficiently small scales. Each piece has zero $\mathcal H^{j+\beta }$ outer measure by the covering proposition. Countable subadditivity gives the same conclusion for the stratum. Since $\beta >0$ is arbitrary, its Hausdorff dimension is at most $j$. This proves a dimension bound; it does not prove finite $\mathcal H^ j$ measure, rectifiability, or uniqueness of tangent cones. $\square$

title: Example 6.3.11 (Crossing planes remain stationary)
search_title: Crossing planes remain stationary
text: Example 6.3.11 (Crossing planes remain stationary) . BFB7F867B030 Let $P_1,P_2$ be distinct $n$-dimensional hyperplanes in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ through the origin. The varifold $|P_1|+|P_2|$ is stationary by linearity and Proposition 6.1.4 . Its singular set and spine are $P_1\cap P_2$, of dimension $n-1$. The density is two on the intersection and one elsewhere on the support. Thus stationarity and integrality allow a large singular set. Compare [ Minter ] , Sections 0–1.

title: 6.4 Excess and Allard regularity
search_title: Excess and Allard regularity
text: Being close to a plane has several meanings. Height excess measures distance from the plane, tilt excess measures tangent directions, and a mass-ratio bound controls multiplicity. These quantities cannot be substituted for one another without a theorem. Definition 6.4.1 (Height and tilt excess) . 2C463D5AB6FB Let $V$ be an $n$-varifold in $B_ R(a)\subset \mathbb R^{n+k}$ and $P$ a linear $n$-plane. With $\pi _ S$ denoting orthogonal projection onto $S$, set \[  E_ h(V,a,R,P)^2=R^{-n-2}\int _{B_ R(a)}\operatorname {dist}(x,a+P)^2\, d\| V\| (x),  \] \[  E_ t(V,a,R,P)^2=R^{-n}\int _{G_ n(B_ R(a))}|\pi _ S-\pi _ P|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2\, dV(x,S).  \] Here $|\cdot |_{\mathrm{HS}}$ is the Hilbert–Schmidt norm. These are dimensionless quantities; our tilt normalization is fixed by this formula and need not equal another author's scalar-normal convention. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 5, and [ Minter ] , Sections 2–3. Proposition 6.4.2 (Excess is invariant under simultaneous rescaling) . 0938FA23F7B1 For $V_{a,R}$ as in Definition 6.3.1 , \[  E_ h(V,a,R,P)=E_ h(V_{a,R},0,1,P),\qquad E_ t(V,a,R,P)=E_ t(V_{a,R},0,1,P).  \] If the first variation is entirely represented by a mean-curvature field $H\in L^ p(\| V\| )$, its rescaled field is $H_ R(y)=R H(a+Ry)$, and \[  \left(\int _{B_1}|H_ R|^ p\, d\| V_{a,R}\| \right)^{1/p} =R^{1-n/p}\left(\int _{B_ R(a)}|H|^ p\, d\| V\| \right)^{1/p}.  \] Proof The mass factor is $R^{-n}$, distances scale by $R^{-1}$, and planes are unchanged. Substitute into the excess definitions. For the curvature formula, use the first-variation scaling from Proposition 6.3.2 and the identity $\delta V(X)=-\int H\cdot X\, d\| V\| $. The last equality is then a change of variables. $\square$ Theorem 6.4.3 (Allard regularity with supercritical mean curvature) . AB385BD66E1E Fix $n,k\geq 1$ and $n<p<\infty $. There are $\varepsilon >0$ and $\gamma \in (0,1)$, depending only on $n,k,p$, with the following property. Let $V$ be an integral $n$-varifold in an open neighborhood of $\overline{B_ R(a)}\subset \mathbb R^{n+k}$, with $a\in \operatorname {spt}\| V\| $, and suppose its first variation in $B_ R(a)$ has no singular part: \[  \delta V(X)=-\int H\cdot X\, d\| V\| \quad (X\in C_ c^1(B_ R(a);\mathbb R^{n+k})).  \] Assume $H\in L^ p(\| V\| \llcorner B_ R(a))$ and \[  \frac{\| V\| (B_ R(a))}{\omega _ n R^ n}\leq 1+\varepsilon , \qquad R^{1-n/p}\left(\int _{B_ R(a)}|H|^ p\, d\| V\| \right)^{1/p}\leq \varepsilon .  \] Then in $B_{\gamma R}(a)$ the support of $V$ is a single $C^{1,1-n/p}$ graph over an $n$-plane, and $V$ has multiplicity one there. This is the integral-varifold specialization of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 5, hypotheses (5.1) and Theorem 5.2, pp. 145–146, following [ Allard72 ] . The source's density-lower-bound hypothesis is supplied here by integrality almost everywhere. The proof, including affine approximation and excess decay, remains external. General bounded first variation with a singular boundary term does not satisfy the stated hypothesis. Corollary 6.4.4 (Density one forces a regular point) . B253B69E9E98 If $V$ is stationary and integral and $\Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a)=1$, then $a$ is regular with multiplicity one. In particular one multiplicity-one planar tangent cone is enough to imply regularity and uniqueness of the tangent cone at $a$. Proof At a sufficiently small radius the mass ratio is at most $1+\varepsilon $, while the mean-curvature term is zero. Theorem 6.4.3 gives a $C^{1,\alpha }$ single graph. The stationary graph equation and elliptic bootstrapping make this graph smooth; this stationary consequence is also recorded in [ Minter ] , Corollary 3.2. A multiplicity-one planar tangent cone has density one by Theorem 6.3.6 . At a smooth point every blow-up is the ordinary tangent plane with its multiplicity. $\square$ Theorem 6.4.5 (A density gap above one) . 5DBE38E6CA27 There is $\delta =\delta (n,k)>0$ such that every support point $a$ of a stationary integral $n$-varifold in $\mathbb R^{n+k}$ with $\Theta ^ n(\| V\| ,a)<1+\delta $ is regular with multiplicity one. Equivalently, every singular point has density at least $1+\delta $. This is [ Minter ] , Corollary 3.2, pp. 44–45. Its Allard regularity input remains external. Proof Let $\varepsilon =\varepsilon (n,k,2n)$ be the mass tolerance in Theorem 6.4.3 , and take $\delta =\varepsilon /2$. At a point with density less than $1+\delta $, the mass ratio is less than $1+\varepsilon $ at all sufficiently small radii. Stationarity gives $H=0$, so the curvature hypothesis holds with $p=2n>n$. Allard regularity gives a multiplicity-one $C^{1,1/2}$ graph near the point. The stationary graph equation and elliptic bootstrapping make it smooth, as in Corollary 6.4.4 . Thus the gap is a local consequence of the already stated Allard theorem. $\square$ Example 6.4.6 (Zero excess does not specify multiplicity) . 2D4CD27BD1E5 For $V=q|P|$ with integer $q\geq 2$, both excesses relative to $P$ vanish at every scale centered on $P$, but the mass ratio and density are $q$. Thus zero height and tilt excess do not imply a single sheet with multiplicity one. This varifold is nevertheless regular under Definition 6.3.5 ; high multiplicity and singular support are different issues.
