Proof Apply Theorem 7.15.3 with $c=0$. Its proof gives the Gauss–Codazzi commutation explicitly, so no external curvature-commutation input is needed for the evolution identities below. $\square$ Proposition 14.3.4 (Curvature evolution under mean curvature flow) . 04E6931281D3 Along a smooth Euclidean hypersurface flow, \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta )A_ i{}^ j=|A|^2A_ i{}^ j, \qquad (\partial _ t-\Delta )H=|A|^2H,  \] \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta )|A|^2=-2|
abla A|^2+2|A|^4.  \] The mixed-index equation differs from the equation for $h_{ij}$, because the metric evolves. See [ HP99 ] , Section 3, and [ Hui90 ] , p. 286. Proof Put $f=-H$ in Proposition 14.3.2 . Theorem 14.3.3 gives \[  \partial _ th_{ij}=\Delta h_{ij}+|A|^2h_{ij}-2Hh_ i{}^ kh_{kj}.  \] Since $\partial _ tg^{ij}=2Hh^{ij}$, raising an index cancels the last term. Trace the resulting mixed-index equation to obtain the equation for $H$. Finally $|A|^2=\operatorname {tr}(A^2)$, so the product rule and metric compatibility give $\Delta \operatorname {tr}(A^2)=2\operatorname {tr}(A\Delta A)+2|
abla A|^2$. Taking its time derivative proves the last identity. $\square$ Corollary 14.3.5 (Preservation of nonnegative mean curvature) . 96E8050C4C5A Let a smooth flow have compact connected parameter manifold without boundary and a continuous choice of normal. If $H\geq 0$ initially, then $H\geq 0$ at every later smooth time. If initially $H$ is not identically zero, then $H>0$ for every positive smooth time. Proof On each compact time interval contained in the smooth existence interval, $|A|^2$ is bounded. Apply the weak and strong parabolic maximum principles to $\partial _ tH=\Delta H+|A|^2H$, multiplying by $e^{-Ct}$ when needed to make the zeroth-order coefficient nonpositive. Connectedness is used for the strict conclusion. This is an application of the scalar maximum principle, as in [ Hui90 ] , Section 4; it does not assert preservation of every curvature pinching condition. $\square$ Proposition 14.3.6 (Position and squared-distance equations) . F339F20D3177 For a normal parametrization of a smooth Euclidean mean curvature flow and a fixed $a\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$, \[  \partial _ tF=\Delta _{\Sigma _ t}F,\qquad (\partial _ t-\Delta _{\Sigma _ t})|F-a|^2=-2n.  \] Every fixed linear coordinate of $F$ solves the scalar heat equation for the evolving metric. Proof The normal component of $D_ ie_ j$ is $-h_{ij}
u $. Tracing after removing the tangential Christoffel term gives $\Delta F=-H
u =\partial _ tF$. The product rule gives $\Delta |F-a|^2=2\langle F-a,\Delta Fangle +2|
abla F|^2$. An orthonormal tangent frame yields $|
abla F|^2=n$, proving the second identity. Compare the Euclidean identities underlying [ Hui90 ] , Sections 1–2. $\square$ Corollary 14.3.7 (Confinement and finite lifetime) . 785D6B9AC5DE If a nonempty smooth closed flow starts inside $\overline{B_{R_0}(a)}$, then at every smooth time \[  \max _{\Sigma _ t}|x-a|^2\leq R_0^2-2nt.  \] Consequently its smooth maximal existence time is at most $R_0^2/(2n)$. Each linear coordinate also stays between its initial minimum and maximum, so the flow stays in the convex hull of its initial image. Proof Apply the maximum principle to $|F-a|^2+2nt$ and, separately, to each linear coordinate in Proposition 14.3.6 . A nonempty immersed positive-dimensional hypersurface cannot have negative squared distance or consist of the single point $a$. Intersecting the preserved half-spaces gives the convex-hull assertion. $\square$ Proposition 14.3.8 (Avoidance for two closed hypersurface flows) . 7F1B08626B76 Let $F_ i:M_ i^ n	imes [0,T)	o \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $i=1,2$, be smooth mean curvature flows of compact manifolds without boundary. If their initial images are disjoint, then their distance is nondecreasing on $[0,T)$. In particular their images remain disjoint while both flows are smooth. Proof Use normal parametrizations. Until a possible first contact, choose a pair realizing the positive minimum of $|F_1(p,t)-F_2(q,t)|^2$, and write $d=F_1-F_2$. The first derivative test makes $d$ normal to both tangent spaces. Since both are hypersurfaces, the tangent spaces coincide with $d^\perp $. Choose matching orthonormal tangent vectors $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ at the pair, and vary the two points simultaneously along geodesics with these initial velocities. The first derivatives of $d$ cancel. Summing the second derivative test yields \[  0\leq 2\langle d,\vec H_1-\vec H_2angle =\partial _ t|F_1-F_2|^2.  \] On compact time intervals the minimum is locally Lipschitz; its derivative at almost every time is bounded below by the least time derivative among its minimizing pairs. Hence the squared distance cannot decrease. Its initial positive value rules out first contact. This is the closest-pair argument illustrated for curves in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Theorem 2.2; the common-tangent-space step explains the hypersurface hypothesis here. $\square$ Theorem 14.3.9 (Short-time existence and the curvature continuation criterion) . 8302053CCFCA A smooth closed immersed hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ admits a smooth mean curvature flow on a nonempty time interval. There is a finite maximal smooth time $T>0$, and \[  \limsup _{t\uparrow T}\max _{\Sigma _ t}|A|=\infty .  \] Equivalently, a uniform bound for $|A|$ up to a finite endpoint permits smooth extension beyond it. Short-time existence is the mean-curvature specialization of [ HP99 ] , Theorem 3.1 and its subsequent example, pp. 51–52. The maximal-time and continuation statement is [ Hui90 ] , Theorem 1.1, p. 286. The parabolic existence and derivative-estimate proofs remain external. This theorem does not furnish a continuation through a curvature singularity in the smooth category. Proposition 14.3.10 (Curvature ODE bound and a lower singularity rate) . E31D01359511 For a smooth closed flow, put $U(t)=\max _{\Sigma _ t}|A|^2$. If $t\geq s$ and $2U(s)(t-s)<1$, then \[  U(t)\leq  rac{U(s)}{1-2U(s)(t-s)}.  \] If $T$ is the finite maximal smooth time, then \[  U(s)\geq  rac{1}{2(T-s)}\quad (0\leq s<T).  \] Thus the second inequality is a lower blow-up rate, not a Type I upper bound. Compare [ Hui90 ] , Lemma 1.2. Proof At a maximum, Proposition 14.3.4 gives the upper differential inequality $U'\leq 2U^2$, valid almost everywhere on compact smooth time intervals. Compare with the solution $y'=2y^2$, $y(s)=U(s)$, to obtain the first estimate. If $2U(s)(T-s)<1$, the same estimate bounds curvature up to $T$, contradicting Theorem 14.3.9 . This proves the second assertion without presuming that the blow-up has a particular model. $\square$ Definition 14.3.11 (Type I and Type II finite-time singularities) . 9ABDA62436F0 For a closed flow with finite maximal smooth time $T$, the singularity is Type I if \[  \sup _{0\leq t<T}(T-t)\max _{\Sigma _ t}|A|^2<\infty .  \] Otherwise it is Type II. This is a global classification of the rate at the first singular time, and does not by itself specify the model at every singular point. Compare the upper-rate assumption (2) in [ Hui90 ] , p. 286, and the rescaling discussion in [ HP99 ] , Section 4. Proposition 14.3.12 (Parabolic rescaling) . F012BE46BD79 Fix $\lambda >0$ and $(x_0,t_0)$. Whenever the original time is defined, set \[  \widetilde F(p,s)=\lambda  igl (F(p,t_0+\lambda ^{-2}s)-x_0 igr ).  \] Then $\widetilde F$ is again mean curvature flow. Its area and curvature satisfy \[  d\widetilde\mu =\lambda ^ n d\mu ,\qquad |\widetilde A|=\lambda ^{-1}|A|,\qquad \widetilde H=\lambda ^{-1}H.  \] In particular $(T-t)|A|^2$ is unchanged by the corresponding change of space and time scales. See [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 6. Proof Spatial dilation changes the induced metric to $\lambda ^2g$ and the covariant second fundamental form to $\lambda h$. Consequently the shape operator scales by $\lambda ^{-1}$, and the area element by $\lambda ^ n$. Differentiating the displayed parametrization in $s$ gives $\lambda ^{-1}\partial _ tF=\lambda ^{-1}\vec H$, which is the new mean curvature vector. The time-to-endpoint scales by $\lambda ^2$, proving the last claim. $\square$ Proposition 14.3.13 (The graphical mean curvature equation) . D2D2F8698415 The family of graphs $F(x,t)=(x,u(x,t))$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ moves by mean curvature in its normal velocity precisely when \[  \partial _ tu=\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}\, \operatorname {div}\left( rac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}ight) =\left(\delta _{ij}- rac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}ight)u_{ij}.  \] On a region with $|Du|\leq L$, the spatial coefficient eigenvalues lie between $(1+L^2)^{-1}$ and $1$. The parametrization need not have purely normal velocity. See [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 3.1, p. 8. Proof The upward normal is $
u =(-Du,1)/\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$, so the normal speed is $u_ t/\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$. With our scalar convention, $H=-\operatorname {div}(Du/\sqrt{1+|Du|^2})$. Equating normal speed with $-H$ proves the divergence expression; expanding it gives the second expression. Its eigenvalues were computed in Proposition 7.2.4 . $\square$ Proposition 14.3.14 (Comparison for graphical flows) . 07334621E069 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$ be bounded with smooth boundary. Suppose $u_1,u_2$ are smooth solutions of Proposition 14.3.13 on $\overline\Omega 	imes [0,T]$. If $u_1\leq u_2$ on $\overline\Omega 	imes \{ 0\} $ and on $\partial \Omega 	imes [0,T]$, then $u_1\leq u_2$ throughout the cylinder. Proof Write $w=u_2-u_1$ and $a^{ij}(p)=\delta _{ij}-p_ ip_ j/(1+|p|^2)$. Subtracting the equations gives \[  w_ t=a^{ij}(Du_2)w_{ij}+b^ kw_ k, \qquad b^ k=\int _0^1\partial _{p_ k}a^{ij}(Du_1+	heta Dw)\, d	heta \, (u_1)_{ij}.  \] The smoothness and compactness assumptions bound the gradients and $b$, giving uniform parabolicity. The parabolic maximum principle implies $w\geq 0$. This states explicitly the boundary and regularity conditions for the comparison argument in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 3.1, pp. 8–9. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.3.3 (Euclidean Simons identity)
search_title: Euclidean Simons identity
text: Theorem 14.3.3 (Euclidean Simons identity) . 18C726B29E0F For a smooth Euclidean hypersurface with the convention in Definition 14.3.1 , \[  \Delta h_{ij}=\nabla _ i\nabla _ jH+Hh_ i{}^ kh_{kj}-|A|^2h_{ij}.  \] This is the Euclidean specialization of [ HP99 ] , Corollary 2.2, p. 49. The formula is valid without a minimality or convexity hypothesis. Proof Apply Theorem 7.15.3 with $c=0$. Its proof gives the Gauss–Codazzi commutation explicitly, so no external curvature-commutation input is needed for the evolution identities below. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.3.4 (Curvature evolution under mean curvature flow)
search_title: Curvature evolution under mean curvature flow
text: Proposition 14.3.4 (Curvature evolution under mean curvature flow) . 04E6931281D3 Along a smooth Euclidean hypersurface flow, \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta )A_ i{}^ j=|A|^2A_ i{}^ j, \qquad (\partial _ t-\Delta )H=|A|^2H,  \] \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta )|A|^2=-2|\nabla A|^2+2|A|^4.  \] The mixed-index equation differs from the equation for $h_{ij}$, because the metric evolves. See [ HP99 ] , Section 3, and [ Hui90 ] , p. 286. Proof Put $f=-H$ in Proposition 14.3.2 . Theorem 14.3.3 gives \[  \partial _ th_{ij}=\Delta h_{ij}+|A|^2h_{ij}-2Hh_ i{}^ kh_{kj}.  \] Since $\partial _ tg^{ij}=2Hh^{ij}$, raising an index cancels the last term. Trace the resulting mixed-index equation to obtain the equation for $H$. Finally $|A|^2=\operatorname {tr}(A^2)$, so the product rule and metric compatibility give $\Delta \operatorname {tr}(A^2)=2\operatorname {tr}(A\Delta A)+2|\nabla A|^2$. Taking its time derivative proves the last identity. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.3.5 (Preservation of nonnegative mean curvature)
search_title: Preservation of nonnegative mean curvature
text: Corollary 14.3.5 (Preservation of nonnegative mean curvature) . 96E8050C4C5A Let a smooth flow have compact connected parameter manifold without boundary and a continuous choice of normal. If $H\geq 0$ initially, then $H\geq 0$ at every later smooth time. If initially $H$ is not identically zero, then $H>0$ for every positive smooth time. Proof On each compact time interval contained in the smooth existence interval, $|A|^2$ is bounded. Apply the weak and strong parabolic maximum principles to $\partial _ tH=\Delta H+|A|^2H$, multiplying by $e^{-Ct}$ when needed to make the zeroth-order coefficient nonpositive. Connectedness is used for the strict conclusion. This is an application of the scalar maximum principle, as in [ Hui90 ] , Section 4; it does not assert preservation of every curvature pinching condition. $\square$

Proof The normal component of $D_ ie_ j$ is $-h_{ij}
u $. Tracing after removing the tangential Christoffel term gives $\Delta F=-H
u =\partial _ tF$. The product rule gives $\Delta |F-a|^2=2\langle F-a,\Delta Fangle +2|

title: Corollary 14.3.7 (Confinement and finite lifetime)
search_title: Confinement and finite lifetime
text: Corollary 14.3.7 (Confinement and finite lifetime) . 785D6B9AC5DE If a nonempty smooth closed flow starts inside $\overline{B_{R_0}(a)}$, then at every smooth time \[  \max _{\Sigma _ t}|x-a|^2\leq R_0^2-2nt.  \] Consequently its smooth maximal existence time is at most $R_0^2/(2n)$. Each linear coordinate also stays between its initial minimum and maximum, so the flow stays in the convex hull of its initial image. Proof Apply the maximum principle to $|F-a|^2+2nt$ and, separately, to each linear coordinate in Proposition 14.3.6 . A nonempty immersed positive-dimensional hypersurface cannot have negative squared distance or consist of the single point $a$. Intersecting the preserved half-spaces gives the convex-hull assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.3.8 (Avoidance for two closed hypersurface flows)
search_title: Avoidance for two closed hypersurface flows
text: Proposition 14.3.8 (Avoidance for two closed hypersurface flows) . 7F1B08626B76 Let $F_ i:M_ i^ n\times [0,T)\to \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $i=1,2$, be smooth mean curvature flows of compact manifolds without boundary. If their initial images are disjoint, then their distance is nondecreasing on $[0,T)$. In particular their images remain disjoint while both flows are smooth. Proof Use normal parametrizations. Until a possible first contact, choose a pair realizing the positive minimum of $|F_1(p,t)-F_2(q,t)|^2$, and write $d=F_1-F_2$. The first derivative test makes $d$ normal to both tangent spaces. Since both are hypersurfaces, the tangent spaces coincide with $d^\perp $. Choose matching orthonormal tangent vectors $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ at the pair, and vary the two points simultaneously along geodesics with these initial velocities. The first derivatives of $d$ cancel. Summing the second derivative test yields \[  0\leq 2\langle d,\vec H_1-\vec H_2\rangle =\partial _ t|F_1-F_2|^2.  \] On compact time intervals the minimum is locally Lipschitz; its derivative at almost every time is bounded below by the least time derivative among its minimizing pairs. Hence the squared distance cannot decrease. Its initial positive value rules out first contact. This is the closest-pair argument illustrated for curves in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Theorem 2.2; the common-tangent-space step explains the hypersurface hypothesis here. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.3.9 (Short-time existence and the curvature continuation criterion)
search_title: Short-time existence and the curvature continuation criterion
text: Theorem 14.3.9 (Short-time existence and the curvature continuation criterion) . 8302053CCFCA A smooth closed immersed hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ admits a smooth mean curvature flow on a nonempty time interval. There is a finite maximal smooth time $T>0$, and \[  \limsup _{t\uparrow T}\max _{\Sigma _ t}|A|=\infty .  \] Equivalently, a uniform bound for $|A|$ up to a finite endpoint permits smooth extension beyond it. Short-time existence is the mean-curvature specialization of [ HP99 ] , Theorem 3.1 and its subsequent example, pp. 51–52. The maximal-time and continuation statement is [ Hui90 ] , Theorem 1.1, p. 286. The parabolic existence and derivative-estimate proofs remain external. This theorem does not furnish a continuation through a curvature singularity in the smooth category.

title: Proposition 14.3.10 (Curvature ODE bound and a lower singularity rate)
search_title: Curvature ODE bound and a lower singularity rate
text: Proposition 14.3.10 (Curvature ODE bound and a lower singularity rate) . E31D01359511 For a smooth closed flow, put $U(t)=\max _{\Sigma _ t}|A|^2$. If $t\geq s$ and $2U(s)(t-s)<1$, then \[  U(t)\leq \frac{U(s)}{1-2U(s)(t-s)}.  \] If $T$ is the finite maximal smooth time, then \[  U(s)\geq \frac{1}{2(T-s)}\quad (0\leq s<T).  \] Thus the second inequality is a lower blow-up rate, not a Type I upper bound. Compare [ Hui90 ] , Lemma 1.2. Proof At a maximum, Proposition 14.3.4 gives the upper differential inequality $U'\leq 2U^2$, valid almost everywhere on compact smooth time intervals. Compare with the solution $y'=2y^2$, $y(s)=U(s)$, to obtain the first estimate. If $2U(s)(T-s)<1$, the same estimate bounds curvature up to $T$, contradicting Theorem 14.3.9 . This proves the second assertion without presuming that the blow-up has a particular model. $\square$

title: Definition 14.3.11 (Type I and Type II finite-time singularities)
search_title: Type I and Type II finite-time singularities
text: Definition 14.3.11 (Type I and Type II finite-time singularities) . 9ABDA62436F0 For a closed flow with finite maximal smooth time $T$, the singularity is Type I if \[  \sup _{0\leq t<T}(T-t)\max _{\Sigma _ t}|A|^2<\infty .  \] Otherwise it is Type II. This is a global classification of the rate at the first singular time, and does not by itself specify the model at every singular point. Compare the upper-rate assumption (2) in [ Hui90 ] , p. 286, and the rescaling discussion in [ HP99 ] , Section 4.

Differentiating the displayed parametrization in $s$ gives $\lambda ^{-1}\partial _ tF=\lambda ^{-1}\vec H$, which is the new mean curvature vector. The time-to-endpoint scales by $\lambda ^2$, proving the last claim. $\square$

title: 14.4 Huisken monotonicity and entropy
search_title: Huisken monotonicity and entropy
text:
The Gaussian integral measures area near a spacetime point at the parabolic scale. Its dissipation identifies self-similar models, while taking the supremum over centers and scales gives entropy. We first prove the identities for smooth closed Euclidean flows, so every integration by parts has no boundary term. Noncompact and weak formulations need additional hypotheses and are stated separately. The main source is [ Hui90 ] , Section 3, with the normalization converted to that of Definition 14.2.2 . Proposition 14.4.1 (Transport of a test function along a closed flow) . C7F71E4E8F61 Let $\Sigma _ t$ be a smooth closed mean curvature flow in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, and let $\phi (x,t)$ be smooth in an ambient neighborhood of its spacetime track. Then \[   rac{d}{dt}\int _{\Sigma _ t}\phi \, d\mu _ t =\int _{\Sigma _ t}\left(\partial _ t\phi +
abla \phi \cdot \vec H-\phi |\vec H|^2ight)d\mu _ t.  \] Here $\partial _ t\phi $ is the ambient partial derivative, with the spatial point held fixed. Proof Choose a normal parametrization. The chain rule gives $ rac{d}{dt}\phi (F(p,t),t)=\partial _ t\phi +
abla \phi \cdot \vec H$, and Proposition 14.3.2 gives $\partial _ t d\mu =-|\vec H|^2d\mu $. Adding the two contributions proves the formula. A tangential velocity adds a tangential divergence, whose integral vanishes on a closed hypersurface. Compare [ WhiMCF15 ] , Sections 6 and 9. $\square$ Definition 14.4.2 (Backward Gaussian kernel) . E0C369653A50 For a spacetime center $(x_0,t_0)$ and $t<t_0$, define \[  ho _{x_0,t_0}(x,t)=(4\pi (t_0-t))^{-n/2} \exp \left(- rac{|x-x_0|^2}{4(t_0-t)}ight).  \] The normalization uses the dimension $n$ of the evolving hypersurface, not the ambient dimension $n+1$. In particular its integral over an affine $n$-plane through $x_0$ is one. See [ Hui90 ] , p. 288. Theorem 14.4.3 (Huisken's monotonicity identity for closed smooth flows) . 09F92AB39467 For a smooth closed Euclidean mean curvature flow and a fixed $(x_0,t_0)$, at every flow time $t<t_0$, \[   rac{d}{dt}\int _{\Sigma _ t}ho _{x_0,t_0}\, d\mu _ t =-\int _{\Sigma _ t}\left|\vec H+  rac{(x-x_0)^\perp }{2(t_0-t)}ight|^2ho _{x_0,t_0}\, d\mu _ t.  \] This is [ Hui90 ] , Theorem 3.1, pp. 288–289. The square uses the vector mean curvature, so the sign agrees with $\vec H=-H
u $. Proof Write $y=x-x_0$, $	au =t_0-t$, and $ho =ho _{x_0,t_0}$. Direct differentiation gives \[  \partial _ tho =ho \left( rac n{2	au }- rac{|y|^2}{4	au ^2}ight), \qquad 
abla ho =- rac{y}{2	au }ho .  \] The integrand in Proposition 14.4.1 is consequently \[  ho \left( rac n{2	au }- rac{|y|^2}{4	au ^2} - rac{\langle y,\vec Hangle }{2	au }-|\vec H|^2ight).  \] Since $\operatorname {div}_{\Sigma _ t}y^ T=n+\langle y,\vec Hangle $, the product rule gives \[  \operatorname {div}_{\Sigma _ t}\left(ho  rac{y^ T}{2	au }ight) =ho \left( rac n{2	au }+ rac{\langle y,\vec Hangle }{2	au } - rac{|y^ T|^2}{4	au ^2}ight).  \] Subtract this divergence from the previous integrand. The remaining expression is $-ho |\vec H+y^\perp /(2	au )|^2$. The divergence integrates to zero because the time slice is compact and without boundary. $\square$ Corollary 14.4.4 (Gaussian density at an endpoint) . EDEB2CF33691 Suppose a smooth closed flow is defined on $[a,t_0)$. For every $x_0\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$ the finite limit \[  \Theta (\mathcal M,x_0,t_0)= \lim _{t\uparrow t_0}\int _{\Sigma _ t}ho _{x_0,t_0}\, d\mu _ t  \] exists and is nonnegative. Equivalently, the Gaussian ratio at scale $r$ is the integral on $\Sigma _{t_0-r^2}$ with variance $r^2$, and these ratios are nondecreasing as $r$ increases within the available time interval. Proof Theorem 14.4.3 makes the integral nonincreasing in time and bounded below by zero. At any fixed earlier time it is finite because the time slice is compact. This yields a finite one-sided limit even when the flow is singular at $t_0$. Replacing $t$ by $t_0-r^2$ reverses the order of the parameter. This is the smooth-flow density construction used in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10.2. $\square$ Proposition 14.4.5 (Gaussian density at a smooth embedded point) . EB49673FA9F0 If a closed embedded flow is smooth through time $t_0$ and $x_0\in \Sigma _{t_0}$, then $\Theta (\mathcal M,x_0,t_0)=1$. If $x_0
otin \Sigma _{t_0}$, the density is zero. These assertions concern a single embedded sheet with unit multiplicity. Proof Near a point on $\Sigma _{t_0}$, use a smooth graphical representation over its tangent plane. At time $t_0-r^2$, dilating by $r^{-1}$ about $x_0$ makes the graph converge smoothly on each bounded set to that plane: the spatial graph error is quadratic and the time displacement is $O(r^2)$. Its Gaussian integral converges to the plane integral, one. On the fixed graphical neighborhood the rescaled area elements are uniformly bounded and the Gaussian tails are uniformly integrable. Outside that neighborhood a fixed positive distance from $x_0$ gives an exponentially small term, since the total areas stay bounded near $t_0$. If $x_0$ is off the final slice, compactness and smooth dependence in time give a positive distance from all nearby slices, so the entire integral tends to zero. Compare [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10.2. $\square$ Definition 14.4.6 (Gaussian area at arbitrary center and scale, and entropy) . 19F04507562E For a Radon measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, put \[  F_{x_0,s}(\mu )=(4\pi s)^{-n/2}\int e^{-|x-x_0|^2/(4s)}\, d\mu (x), \qquad s>0,  \] \[  \lambda (\mu )=\sup _{x_0\in \mathbb R^{n+1},\  s>0}F_{x_0,s}(\mu ).  \] The value may be infinite. For a hypersurface, use its area measure; for an integral varifold, use its weight measure, including multiplicity. The functional in Proposition 14.2.4 is $F_{0,1}$. Sources: [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10, and [ CCMS20 ] , Section 2. Proposition 14.4.7 (Entropy is invariant under translations and dilations) . C2244E09A64A Let $D(x)=b+ax$, $a>0$, and define the geometric dilation of an $n$-dimensional measure by $\mu '=a^ nD_\# \mu $. Then \[  F_{x_0,s}(\mu ')=F_{(x_0-b)/a,s/a^2}(\mu ), \qquad \lambda (\mu ')=\lambda (\mu ).  \] Thus the measure scaling includes the tangential area factor, as in Definition 6.3.1 . Proof Substitute $x=b+ay$ into the defining integral. The factor $a^ n$ combines with $(4\pi s)^{-n/2}$ to give $(4\pi s/a^2)^{-n/2}$. The change $(x_0,s)\mapsto ((x_0-b)/a,s/a^2)$ is a bijection on the set of centers and positive scales, so taking suprema proves the entropy identity. $\square$ Proposition 14.4.8 (Entropy is nonincreasing along a closed smooth flow) . 01983F7EAFC3 If $t_1<t_2$ are smooth times of a closed Euclidean mean curvature flow, then \[  \lambda (\Sigma _{t_2})\leq \lambda (\Sigma _{t_1}).  \] The supremum in the entropy definition need not be attained for this argument. Proof Fix $x_0$ and $s>0$ and apply Theorem 14.4.3 with terminal time $t_2+s$. It gives \[  F_{x_0,s}(\Sigma _{t_2})\leq F_{x_0,s+t_2-t_1}(\Sigma _{t_1})\leq \lambda (\Sigma _{t_1}).  \] Take the supremum over $x_0,s$. This is the entropy consequence discussed in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10. $\square$ Proposition 14.4.9 (Entropy and uniform Euclidean area growth) . 9867B85F190C If $\lambda (\mu )\leq \Lambda $, then for every $x\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$ and $r>0$, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\leq e^{1/4}(4\pi )^{n/2}\Lambda r^ n.  \] Conversely, if $\mu (B_ r(x))\leq Kr^ n$ for every center and radius, then $\lambda (\mu )\leq C(n)K$. The uniformity in the center is part of the hypothesis. Proof In $B_ r(x)$ the exponential in $F_{x,r^2}$ is at least $e^{-1/4}$, proving the first inequality. Conversely fix a scale $s=r^2$. Bound the contribution of $B_ r(x)$ by $(4\pi )^{-n/2}K$. On the annulus $2^ jr\leq |y-x|<2^{j+1}r$, the exponential is at most $e^{-4^ j/4}$ and the mass is at most $K(2^{j+1}r)^ n$. Thus the whole integral is bounded by \[  (4\pi )^{-n/2}K\left(1+\sum _{j=0}^\infty 2^{(j+1)n}e^{-4^ j/4}ight).  \] The sum converges independently of $x,r$. Compare the bounded-area-ratio class used in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10.1. $\square$ Example 14.4.10 (A plane records its multiplicity in entropy) . 73E4373C1387 For an affine $n$-plane $P$ with integer multiplicity $q\geq 1$, \[  F_{x_0,s}(q\mathcal H^ n\llcorner P) =q\exp \left(- rac{\operatorname {dist}(x_0,P)^2}{4s}ight), \qquad \lambda (q|P|)=q.  \] To check this, split $x-x_0$ into orthogonal tangential and normal components and integrate the tangential Gaussian. The supremum is attained by choosing $x_0\in P$. Small support excess therefore does not make the entropy close to one when multiplicity is large; compare Example 6.4.6 .

text: Definition 14.4.2 (Backward Gaussian kernel) . E0C369653A50 For a spacetime center $(x_0,t_0)$ and $t<t_0$, define \[  \rho _{x_0,t_0}(x,t)=(4\pi (t_0-t))^{-n/2} \exp \left(-\frac{|x-x_0|^2}{4(t_0-t)}\right).  \] The normalization uses the dimension $n$ of the evolving hypersurface, not the ambient dimension $n+1$. In particular its integral over an affine $n$-plane through $x_0$ is one. See [ Hui90 ] , p. 288.

title: Theorem 14.4.3 (Huisken's monotonicity identity for closed smooth flows)
search_title: Huisken's monotonicity identity for closed smooth flows
text: Theorem 14.4.3 (Huisken's monotonicity identity for closed smooth flows) . 09F92AB39467 For a smooth closed Euclidean mean curvature flow and a fixed $(x_0,t_0)$, at every flow time $t<t_0$, \[  \frac{d}{dt}\int _{\Sigma _ t}\rho _{x_0,t_0}\, d\mu _ t =-\int _{\Sigma _ t}\left|\vec H+ \frac{(x-x_0)^\perp }{2(t_0-t)}\right|^2\rho _{x_0,t_0}\, d\mu _ t.  \] This is [ Hui90 ] , Theorem 3.1, pp. 288–289. The square uses the vector mean curvature, so the sign agrees with $\vec H=-H\nu $. Proof Write $y=x-x_0$, $\tau =t_0-t$, and $\rho =\rho _{x_0,t_0}$. Direct differentiation gives \[  \partial _ t\rho =\rho \left(\frac n{2\tau }-\frac{|y|^2}{4\tau ^2}\right), \qquad \nabla \rho =-\frac{y}{2\tau }\rho .  \] The integrand in Proposition 14.4.1 is consequently \[  \rho \left(\frac n{2\tau }-\frac{|y|^2}{4\tau ^2} -\frac{\langle y,\vec H\rangle }{2\tau }-|\vec H|^2\right).  \] Since $\operatorname {div}_{\Sigma _ t}y^ T=n+\langle y,\vec H\rangle $, the product rule gives \[  \operatorname {div}_{\Sigma _ t}\left(\rho \frac{y^ T}{2\tau }\right) =\rho \left(\frac n{2\tau }+\frac{\langle y,\vec H\rangle }{2\tau } -\frac{|y^ T|^2}{4\tau ^2}\right).  \] Subtract this divergence from the previous integrand. The remaining expression is $-\rho |\vec H+y^\perp /(2\tau )|^2$. The divergence integrates to zero because the time slice is compact and without boundary. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.4.4 (Gaussian density at an endpoint)
search_title: Gaussian density at an endpoint
text: Corollary 14.4.4 (Gaussian density at an endpoint) . EDEB2CF33691 Suppose a smooth closed flow is defined on $[a,t_0)$. For every $x_0\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$ the finite limit \[  \Theta (\mathcal M,x_0,t_0)= \lim _{t\uparrow t_0}\int _{\Sigma _ t}\rho _{x_0,t_0}\, d\mu _ t  \] exists and is nonnegative. Equivalently, the Gaussian ratio at scale $r$ is the integral on $\Sigma _{t_0-r^2}$ with variance $r^2$, and these ratios are nondecreasing as $r$ increases within the available time interval. Proof Theorem 14.4.3 makes the integral nonincreasing in time and bounded below by zero. At any fixed earlier time it is finite because the time slice is compact. This yields a finite one-sided limit even when the flow is singular at $t_0$. Replacing $t$ by $t_0-r^2$ reverses the order of the parameter. This is the smooth-flow density construction used in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10.2. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.4.5 (Gaussian density at a smooth embedded point)
search_title: Gaussian density at a smooth embedded point
text: Proposition 14.4.5 (Gaussian density at a smooth embedded point) . EB49673FA9F0 If a closed embedded flow is smooth through time $t_0$ and $x_0\in \Sigma _{t_0}$, then $\Theta (\mathcal M,x_0,t_0)=1$. If $x_0\notin \Sigma _{t_0}$, the density is zero. These assertions concern a single embedded sheet with unit multiplicity. Proof Near a point on $\Sigma _{t_0}$, use a smooth graphical representation over its tangent plane. At time $t_0-r^2$, dilating by $r^{-1}$ about $x_0$ makes the graph converge smoothly on each bounded set to that plane: the spatial graph error is quadratic and the time displacement is $O(r^2)$. Its Gaussian integral converges to the plane integral, one. On the fixed graphical neighborhood the rescaled area elements are uniformly bounded and the Gaussian tails are uniformly integrable. Outside that neighborhood a fixed positive distance from $x_0$ gives an exponentially small term, since the total areas stay bounded near $t_0$. If $x_0$ is off the final slice, compactness and smooth dependence in time give a positive distance from all nearby slices, so the entire integral tends to zero. Compare [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10.2. $\square$

title: Definition 14.4.6 (Gaussian area at arbitrary center and scale, and entropy)
search_title: Gaussian area at arbitrary center and scale, and entropy
text: Definition 14.4.6 (Gaussian area at arbitrary center and scale, and entropy) . 19F04507562E For a Radon measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, put \[  F_{x_0,s}(\mu )=(4\pi s)^{-n/2}\int e^{-|x-x_0|^2/(4s)}\, d\mu (x), \qquad s>0,  \] \[  \lambda (\mu )=\sup _{x_0\in \mathbb R^{n+1},\  s>0}F_{x_0,s}(\mu ).  \] The value may be infinite. For a hypersurface, use its area measure; for an integral varifold, use its weight measure, including multiplicity. The functional in Proposition 14.2.4 is $F_{0,1}$. Sources: [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10, and [ CCMS20 ] , Section 2.

title: Proposition 14.4.7 (Entropy is invariant under translations and dilations)
search_title: Entropy is invariant under translations and dilations
text: Proposition 14.4.7 (Entropy is invariant under translations and dilations) . C2244E09A64A Let $D(x)=b+ax$, $a>0$, and define the geometric dilation of an $n$-dimensional measure by $\mu '=a^ nD_\# \mu $. Then \[  F_{x_0,s}(\mu ')=F_{(x_0-b)/a,s/a^2}(\mu ), \qquad \lambda (\mu ')=\lambda (\mu ).  \] Thus the measure scaling includes the tangential area factor, as in Definition 6.3.1 . Proof Substitute $x=b+ay$ into the defining integral. The factor $a^ n$ combines with $(4\pi s)^{-n/2}$ to give $(4\pi s/a^2)^{-n/2}$. The change $(x_0,s)\mapsto ((x_0-b)/a,s/a^2)$ is a bijection on the set of centers and positive scales, so taking suprema proves the entropy identity. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.4.8 (Entropy is nonincreasing along a closed smooth flow)
search_title: Entropy is nonincreasing along a closed smooth flow
text: Proposition 14.4.8 (Entropy is nonincreasing along a closed smooth flow) . 01983F7EAFC3 If $t_1<t_2$ are smooth times of a closed Euclidean mean curvature flow, then \[  \lambda (\Sigma _{t_2})\leq \lambda (\Sigma _{t_1}).  \] The supremum in the entropy definition need not be attained for this argument. Proof Fix $x_0$ and $s>0$ and apply Theorem 14.4.3 with terminal time $t_2+s$. It gives \[  F_{x_0,s}(\Sigma _{t_2})\leq F_{x_0,s+t_2-t_1}(\Sigma _{t_1})\leq \lambda (\Sigma _{t_1}).  \] Take the supremum over $x_0,s$. This is the entropy consequence discussed in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.4.9 (Entropy and uniform Euclidean area growth)
search_title: Entropy and uniform Euclidean area growth
text: Proposition 14.4.9 (Entropy and uniform Euclidean area growth) . 9867B85F190C If $\lambda (\mu )\leq \Lambda $, then for every $x\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$ and $r>0$, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\leq e^{1/4}(4\pi )^{n/2}\Lambda r^ n.  \] Conversely, if $\mu (B_ r(x))\leq Kr^ n$ for every center and radius, then $\lambda (\mu )\leq C(n)K$. The uniformity in the center is part of the hypothesis. Proof In $B_ r(x)$ the exponential in $F_{x,r^2}$ is at least $e^{-1/4}$, proving the first inequality. Conversely fix a scale $s=r^2$. Bound the contribution of $B_ r(x)$ by $(4\pi )^{-n/2}K$. On the annulus $2^ jr\leq |y-x|<2^{j+1}r$, the exponential is at most $e^{-4^ j/4}$ and the mass is at most $K(2^{j+1}r)^ n$. Thus the whole integral is bounded by \[  (4\pi )^{-n/2}K\left(1+\sum _{j=0}^\infty 2^{(j+1)n}e^{-4^ j/4}\right).  \] The sum converges independently of $x,r$. Compare the bounded-area-ratio class used in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 10.1. $\square$

title: Example 14.4.10 (A plane records its multiplicity in entropy)
search_title: A plane records its multiplicity in entropy
text: Example 14.4.10 (A plane records its multiplicity in entropy) . 73E4373C1387 For an affine $n$-plane $P$ with integer multiplicity $q\geq 1$, \[  F_{x_0,s}(q\mathcal H^ n\llcorner P) =q\exp \left(-\frac{\operatorname {dist}(x_0,P)^2}{4s}\right), \qquad \lambda (q|P|)=q.  \] To check this, split $x-x_0$ into orthogonal tangential and normal components and integrate the tangential Gaussian. The supremum is attained by choosing $x_0\in P$. Small support excess therefore does not make the entropy close to one when multiplicity is large; compare Example 6.4.6 .

title: 14.5 Rescaled flow and self-similar models
search_title: Rescaled flow and self-similar models
text: Logarithmic time converts a finite-time singularity into a long-time problem. This is a change of variables before it is a compactness theorem. We retain the scale-one shrinker convention $\vec H+x^\perp /2=0$ throughout. Proposition 14.5.1 (Logarithmic rescaling at a finite time) . F139BDB06172 Fix a point $x_0$ and a time $T$ later than the times under consideration. Set \[  \tau =-\log (T-t),\qquad \widetilde F(p,\tau )=(T-t)^{-1/2}(F(p,t)-x_0).  \] Then the normal velocity of the rescaled hypersurfaces is \[  (\partial _\tau \widetilde F)^\perp = \vec H_{\widetilde\Sigma _\tau }+\tfrac 12\widetilde F^\perp .  \] If the original flow is Type I at $T$, its rescaled curvature is uniformly bounded. This last assertion supplies a curvature bound, not a claim of convergence or uniqueness of a limiting shrinker. Proof Since $dt/d\tau =T-t$ and $(T-t)^{-1/2}=e^{\tau /2}$, differentiation yields $\partial _\tau \widetilde F=\widetilde F/2+(T-t)^{1/2}\vec H$. The second term is the mean curvature vector of the dilated hypersurface. Project normally to get the equation. Proposition 14.3.12 gives $|\widetilde A|^2=(T-t)|A|^2$, proving the curvature assertion. Huisken [ Hui90 ] , Section 2, uses instead $(2(T-t))^{-1/2}$ and $-\frac12\log (T-t)$; his rescaled equation has coefficient one instead of $1/2$. $\square$ Proposition 14.5.2 (Gaussian area dissipates along rescaled flow) . 714B0C7286EF For a smooth closed rescaled flow satisfying Proposition 14.5.1 , \[  \frac{d}{d\tau }F_{0,1}(\widetilde\Sigma _\tau ) =-(4\pi )^{-n/2}\int _{\widetilde\Sigma _\tau } \left|\vec H+\tfrac 12x^\perp \right|^2e^{-|x|^2/4}\, d\mu .  \] Consequently, if the rescaled flow exists for all $\tau \geq \tau _0$, then the time integral of the nonnegative expression on the right, with its minus sign removed, is finite. Proof Insert the rescaled normal velocity in Proposition 14.2.4 . Tangential velocity contributes only a divergence. Integrate in $\tau $ and use $F_{0,1}\geq 0$. This is [ Hui90 ] , Corollary 3.2, after converting the Gaussian normalization. $\square$ Corollary 14.5.3 (Times with small Gaussian dissipation) . E1D33EF33BA1 Under the long-time hypothesis in Proposition 14.5.2 , there are $\tau _ j\to \infty $ such that \[  \int _{\widetilde\Sigma _{\tau _ j}} \left|\vec H+\tfrac 12x^\perp \right|^2e^{-|x|^2/4}\, d\mu \longrightarrow 0.  \] If, in addition, these slices converge smoothly with multiplicity one on compact subsets to a smooth hypersurface $\Sigma _\infty $, then $\Sigma _\infty $ satisfies the self-shrinker equation. The compactness assumption is separate from the dissipation conclusion. Proof A nonnegative integrable function on $[\tau _0,\infty )$ has a sequence of times tending to infinity at which it tends to zero. For the second assertion, multiply the integrand by a nonnegative compactly supported ambient cutoff. Smooth convergence permits passage to the limit in this localized integral, which is bounded above by the full dissipation. The limit integral is zero for every cutoff; continuity and the positive Gaussian weight force $\vec H+x^\perp /2=0$ on $\Sigma _\infty $. No assertion about mass escaping to infinity or uniqueness follows from this local argument. Compare [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 6. $\square$ Proposition 14.5.4 (Equality in monotonicity gives self-similar motion) . 5900E7823B75 Suppose a smooth closed flow has constant Gaussian integral centered at $(x_0,T)$ on a time interval $(a,b)\subset (-\infty ,T)$. Then throughout that interval \[  \vec H+\frac{(x-x_0)^\perp }{2(T-t)}=0.  \] Equivalently, the images $(T-t)^{-1/2}(\Sigma _ t-x_0)$ are independent of time and form a self-shrinker in the project's scale-one normalization. Proof Theorem 14.4.3 gives zero integral of a continuous nonnegative function at each time, and hence the displayed pointwise equation. By Proposition 14.5.1 , the rescaled velocity is tangent everywhere. A time-dependent tangential vector field on the compact parameter manifold can be removed by reparametrization, so the rescaled images are constant. The equation then reads $\vec H+x^\perp /2=0$. Conversely that equation makes the monotonicity integrand zero. $\square$ Definition 14.5.5 (Translators and self-expanders) . 2B1C5447089D A smooth hypersurface is a translator with velocity $v\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$ if $\vec H=v^\perp $. Its translates $\Sigma _ t=\Sigma +tv$ have normal velocity $\vec H$. A scale-one self-expander satisfies $\vec H-x^\perp /2=0$; its expanding family is $\Sigma _ t=\sqrt t\, \Sigma $, $t>0$. These are exact solution classes, not automatic classifications of Type II singularities. Compare the translating models discussed in [ HP99 ] , Section 4, and [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 9.3. Example 14.5.6 (The grim reaper and its cylindrical products) . 652E4AB4233E The graphs \[  u(x,t)=-\log (\cos x)+t,\qquad -\pi /2<x<\pi /2,  \] give a translating curve-shortening flow. Indeed $u_ t=1$, $u_ x=\tan x$, and $u_{xx}=\sec ^2x$, so $u_ t=u_{xx}/(1+u_ x^2)$. Taking the product with $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ gives a translating hypersurface flow in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ with the same scalar graphical equation. Its slope is unbounded near the boundary of the graph domain, even though the complete translating hypersurface has no boundary there. The intrinsic length to either end diverges because $\sqrt{1+u_ x^2}=1/\cos x$. Compare the translator discussion in [ HP99 ] , Section 4.

title: 14.6 Brakke flows and loss of mass

section: 14.6 Brakke flows and loss of mass
text:
A weak flow records time-dependent area measures and an inequality expressing dissipation. It may lose mass abruptly. We use an integrated, boundaryless formulation, stating the integrability and time-interval requirements explicitly. This makes the difference from the smooth identity in Proposition 14.4.1 visible. Sources are [ WhiMCF15 ] , Section 9, and [ CCMS20 ] , Sections 2.4–2.6. Definition 14.6.1 (Integral Brakke flow without boundary) . E7CE50A27004 Let $U\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open and $I$ an interval. An integral Brakke flow in the formulation used here is a weakly measurable family of Radon measures $(\mu _ t)_{t\in I}$ with the following properties. For almost every $t$, $\mu _ t=\| V_ t\| $ for an integral $n$-varifold, and its first variation has no singular part: \[  \delta V_ t(X)=-\int \vec H_ t\cdot X\, d\mu _ t, \qquad \vec H_ t\perp T_ xV_ t\quad \mu _ t	ext{-almost everywhere}.  \] On each compact $K\subset U$ and compact interval $[a,b]\subset I$ we require uniform local mass bounds and \[  \sup _{t\in [a,b]}\mu _ t(K)<\infty , \qquad \int _ a^ b\int _ K|\vec H_ t|^2\, d\mu _ t\, dt<\infty .  \] For every such $[a,b]$ and every nonnegative $\phi \in C_ c^1(U	imes [a,b])$, \[  \mu _ b(\phi (\cdot ,b))-\mu _ a(\phi (\cdot ,a)) \leq \int _ a^ b\int \left(\partial _ t\phi +
abla \phi \cdot \vec H_ t -\phi |\vec H_ t|^2ight)d\mu _ t\, dt.  \] Here $\mu _ t(f)=\int f\, d\mu _ t$. The integral inequality is imposed on every subinterval, not only at almost every pair of endpoints. The mass and curvature bounds are listed as part of the working formulation; compare [ WhiMCF15 ] , Definition 9.1 and Corollary 9.4–Theorem 9.5. Prescribed boundary terms are not included in this definition. Proposition 14.6.2 (A smooth closed flow is a Brakke flow) . 8F7B94661BFD The area measures of a smooth closed embedded mean curvature flow satisfy Definition 14.6.1 . Its integrated inequality holds with equality. Proof Each smooth time slice gives a multiplicity-one integral varifold, whose first variation is $-\int \vec H\cdot X$. Smoothness on the compact parameter manifold and a compact time interval gives both local mass and curvature bounds. Integrate Proposition 14.4.1 from $a$ to $b$. The same argument is local for test functions supported away from a boundary. $\square$ Example 14.6.3 (A plane that suddenly disappears) . DE579F937CAC Let $P$ be an affine $n$-plane, let $q\geq 1$ be an integer, and fix a time $t_*$. Set $\mu _ t=q\mathcal H^ n\llcorner P$ for $t<t_*$ and $\mu _ t=0$ for $t\geq t_*$. This is an integral Brakke flow. To verify the inequality, note that $\vec H=0$ whenever the measure is nonzero. On an interval crossing $t_*$, the time integral of $\partial _ t\phi $ is \[  q\int _ P\phi (x,t_*)\, d\mathcal H^ n-q\int _ P\phi (x,a)\, d\mathcal H^ n,  \] while the difference of the endpoint measures is just the negative second term. Nonnegativity of $\phi $ gives the required inequality. On intervals not crossing $t_*$ it is an equality. Thus the Brakke inequality alone permits disappearance even though curvature was zero. Compare [ WhiMCF15 ] , Remark 9.2. Proposition 14.6.4 (A shrinking spatial cutoff) . B62A11A57299 Suppose $\overline{B_ R(a)}\subset U$ and $s\leq t$ are flow times. Put \[  q(x,t)= igl (R^2-|x-a|^2-2n(t-s) igr )_+, \qquad \phi (x,t)=q(x,t)^3.  \] Then $t\mapsto \mu _ t(\phi (\cdot ,t))$ is nonincreasing for $t\geq s$. In particular, for $0<r<R$ and $0\leq t-s\leq (R^2-r^2)/(4n)$, \[  \mu _ t(B_ r(a))\leq \left( rac{2R^2}{R^2-r^2}ight)^3\mu _ s(B_ R(a)).  \] This is a cubic-cutoff version of the local mass estimate in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Theorem 9.3. Proof The cube of the positive part is $C^2$, with compact spatial support in $U$ for $t\geq s$. On the region where $q>0$, and for any $n$-plane $S$, \[  \partial _ t\phi =-6nq^2,\qquad \operatorname {tr}_ S D^2\phi =6q|
abla ^ Sq|^2-6nq^2.  \] Thus $\partial _ t\phi -\operatorname {tr}_ SD^2\phi \leq 0$, also across $q=0$. The first-variation identity with $X=
abla \phi $ gives $\int 
abla \phi \cdot \vec H_ t\, d\mu _ t=-\int \operatorname {tr}_{T_ xV_ t}D^2\phi \, d\mu _ t$ at almost every time. Insert this in the integrated Brakke inequality and discard $-\phi |\vec H|^2$. This proves monotonicity. On $B_ r(a)$ at the stated times, $q\geq (R^2-r^2)/2$, whereas initially $\phi \leq R^6$. These two bounds give the displayed mass estimate. $\square$ Proposition 14.6.5 (Local curvature energy from the Brakke inequality) . 420AE237E649 Let $\eta \in C_ c^1(U)$ and $[a,b]\subset I$. Then \[  \int _ a^ b\int \eta ^2|\vec H_ t|^2\, d\mu _ t\, dt \leq 2\mu _ a(\eta ^2)-2\mu _ b(\eta ^2) +4\int _ a^ b\int |D\eta |^2\, d\mu _ t\, dt.  \] The last integral is controlled by local mass bounds on the support of $\eta $. This is the energy estimate of [ WhiMCF15 ] , Theorem 9.5, written with a squared cutoff. Proof Use the time-independent test function $\phi =\eta ^2$. Young's inequality gives $2\eta 
abla \eta \cdot \vec H\leq  rac12\eta ^2|\vec H|^2+2|
abla \eta |^2$. Move the remaining negative curvature term to the other side of the Brakke inequality and multiply by two. In particular a cutoff equal to one on a compact set bounds the spacetime curvature energy there. $\square$ Proposition 14.6.6 (One-sided limits of localized mass) . A93E660E56E8 For $\eta \in C_ c^1(U)$ and a compact time interval $[a,b]\subset I$, there is $C<\infty $ such that \[  t\longmapsto \mu _ t(\eta ^2)-Ct  \] is nonincreasing on $[a,b]$. Consequently its left and right limits exist at interior times, and \[  \lim _{s\uparrow t}\mu _ s(\eta ^2)\geq \mu _ t(\eta ^2) \geq \lim _{s\downarrow t}\mu _ s(\eta ^2).  \] These inequalities allow downward jumps. They are not continuity in time. Compare [ WhiMCF15 ] , Theorems 9.6–9.7. Proof Complete the square in the time-independent Brakke integrand: \[  -\eta ^2|\vec H|^2+2\eta 
abla \eta \cdot \vec H =-|\eta \vec H-
abla \eta |^2+|
abla \eta |^2\leq |
abla \eta |^2.  \] Let $M$ bound $\mu _ t(\operatorname {spt}\eta )$ on the interval, and take $C=M\| D\eta \| _\infty ^2$. The integrated inequality between arbitrary times gives the monotonicity. The one-sided conclusions follow from elementary properties of a monotone real function. $\square$ Definition 14.6.7 (Convergence of integral Brakke flows) . 70B180C0E800 We say $\mathcal M_ j=(\mu ^ j_ t)$ converges to $\mathcal M=(\mu _ t)$ on a common space-time domain if $\mu ^ j_ tightharpoonup \mu _ t$ as Radon measures at every time, and for almost every time one can pass to a further subsequence, possibly depending on the time, for which the associated integral varifolds converge to the varifold of the limiting flow. This is the convention of [ CCMS20 ] , Section 2.6. The time-dependent subsequence in the second clause is not a single subsequence with varifold convergence at every time. Theorem 14.6.8 (Compactness of integral Brakke flows) . 30AF4D42548B Let $\mathcal M_ j$ be integral Brakke flows on $U	imes [a,b]$. Suppose for every compact $K\subset U$, \[  \sup _ j\sup _{t\in [a,b]}\mu _ t^ j(K)<\infty .  \] Then a subsequence converges to an integral Brakke flow in the sense of Definition 14.6.7 . Source: [ WhiMCF15 ] , Theorem 9.8, pp. 23–24; compare [ CCMS20 ] , Section 2.6. The proof combines the localized mass monotonicity, curvature energy bounds, varifold compactness, and lower semicontinuity of the Brakke functional. That proof remains external. This is weak compactness and does not assert smooth convergence. Theorem 14.6.9 (Gaussian monotonicity for Brakke flows) . 7B8AE5E95CE9 Let $\mathcal M$ be an integral Brakke flow on $\mathbb R^{n+1}	imes I$. Assume that on each compact time interval its measures have a uniform entropy bound. For $[a,b]\subset I$ and any $t_0>b$, \[  \int ho _{x_0,t_0}(x,b)\, d\mu _ b- \int ho _{x_0,t_0}(x,a)\, d\mu _ a \leq -\int _ a^ b\int \left|\vec H_ t+  rac{(x-x_0)^\perp }{2(t_0-t)}ight|^2ho _{x_0,t_0}\, d\mu _ t\, dt.  \] The Gaussian ratios and density are then defined as in Corollary 14.4.4 . Entropy is nonincreasing. The entropy bound supplies spatial tail control for using a Gaussian in place of compactly supported test functions; compare Proposition 14.4.9 . This is a two-sided neighborhood in time. It is an additional property, not part of Definition 14.6.1 . See [ CCMS20 ] , Section 2.6. At $(x,t_*)$ with $x\in P$, every backward Gaussian ratio is one, so the Gaussian density is one. Nevertheless every two-sided spacetime neighborhood meets the vanished part of the flow. text: Definition 14.6.1 (Integral Brakke flow without boundary) . E7CE50A27004 Let $U\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open and $I$ an interval. An integral Brakke flow in the formulation used here is a weakly measurable family of Radon measures $(\mu _ t)_{t\in I}$ with the following properties. For almost every $t$, $\mu _ t=\| V_ t\| $ for an integral $n$-varifold, and its first variation has no singular part: \[  \delta V_ t(X)=-\int \vec H_ t\cdot X\, d\mu _ t, \qquad \vec H_ t\perp T_ xV_ t\quad \mu _ t\text{-almost everywhere}.  \] On each compact $K\subset U$ and compact interval $[a,b]\subset I$ we require uniform local mass bounds and \[  \sup _{t\in [a,b]}\mu _ t(K)<\infty , \qquad \int _ a^ b\int _ K|\vec H_ t|^2\, d\mu _ t\, dt<\infty .  \] For every such $[a,b]$ and every nonnegative $\phi \in C_ c^1(U\times [a,b])$, \[  \mu _ b(\phi (\cdot ,b))-\mu _ a(\phi (\cdot ,a)) \leq \int _ a^ b\int \left(\partial _ t\phi +\nabla \phi \cdot \vec H_ t -\phi |\vec H_ t|^2\right)d\mu _ t\, dt.  \] Here $\mu _ t(f)=\int f\, d\mu _ t$. The integral inequality is imposed on every subinterval, not only at almost every pair of endpoints. The mass and curvature bounds are listed as part of the working formulation; compare [ WhiMCF15 ] , Definition 9.1 and Corollary 9.4–Theorem 9.5. Prescribed boundary terms are not included in this definition.

title: Proposition 14.6.2 (A smooth closed flow is a Brakke flow)

text: Proposition 14.6.2 (A smooth closed flow is a Brakke flow) . 8F7B94661BFD The area measures of a smooth closed embedded mean curvature flow satisfy Definition 14.6.1 . Its integrated inequality holds with equality. Proof Each smooth time slice gives a multiplicity-one integral varifold, whose first variation is $-\int \vec H\cdot X$. Smoothness on the compact parameter manifold and a compact time interval gives both local mass and curvature bounds. Integrate Proposition 14.4.1 from $a$ to $b$. The same argument is local for test functions supported away from a boundary. $\square$

title: Example 14.6.3 (A plane that suddenly disappears)

section: 14.6 Brakke flows and loss of mass
text: Example 14.6.3 (A plane that suddenly disappears) . DE579F937CAC Let $P$ be an affine $n$-plane, let $q\geq 1$ be an integer, and fix a time $t_*$. Set $\mu _ t=q\mathcal H^ n\llcorner P$ for $t<t_*$ and $\mu _ t=0$ for $t\geq t_*$. This is an integral Brakke flow. To verify the inequality, note that $\vec H=0$ whenever the measure is nonzero. On an interval crossing $t_*$, the time integral of $\partial _ t\phi $ is \[  q\int _ P\phi (x,t_*)\, d\mathcal H^ n-q\int _ P\phi (x,a)\, d\mathcal H^ n,  \] while the difference of the endpoint measures is just the negative second term. Nonnegativity of $\phi $ gives the required inequality. On intervals not crossing $t_*$ it is an equality. Thus the Brakke inequality alone permits disappearance even though curvature was zero. Compare [ WhiMCF15 ] , Remark 9.2.

Proposition 14.6.4 (A shrinking spatial cutoff) . B62A11A57299 Suppose $\overline{B_ R(a)}\subset U$ and $s\leq t$ are flow times. Put \[  q(x,t)= igl (R^2-|x-a|^2-2n(t-s) igr )_+, \qquad \phi (x,t)=q(x,t)^3.  \] Then $t\mapsto \mu _ t(\phi (\cdot ,t))$ is nonincreasing for $t\geq s$. In particular, for $0<r<R$ and $0\leq t-s\leq (R^2-r^2)/(4n)$, \[  \mu _ t(B_ r(a))\leq \left( rac{2R^2}{R^2-r^2}ight)^3\mu _ s(B_ R(a)).  \] This is a cubic-cutoff version of the local mass estimate in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Theorem 9.3. Proof The cube of the positive part is $C^2$, with compact spatial support in $U$ for $t\geq s$. On the region where $q>0$, and for any $n$-plane $S$, \[  \partial _ t\phi =-6nq^2,\qquad \operatorname {tr}_ S D^2\phi =6q|
abla ^ Sq|^2-6nq^2.  \] Thus $\partial _ t\phi -\operatorname {tr}_ SD^2\phi \leq 0$, also across $q=0$. The first-variation identity with $X=
abla \phi $ gives $\int 
abla \phi \cdot \vec H_ t\, d\mu _ t=-\int \operatorname {tr}_{T_ xV_ t}D^2\phi \, d\mu _ t$ at almost every time. Insert this in the integrated Brakke inequality and discard $-\phi |\vec H|^2$. This proves monotonicity. On $B_ r(a)$ at the stated times, $q\geq (R^2-r^2)/2$, whereas initially $\phi \leq R^6$. These two bounds give the displayed mass estimate. $\square$

text: Proposition 14.6.5 (Local curvature energy from the Brakke inequality) . 420AE237E649 Let $\eta \in C_ c^1(U)$ and $[a,b]\subset I$. Then \[  \int _ a^ b\int \eta ^2|\vec H_ t|^2\, d\mu _ t\, dt \leq 2\mu _ a(\eta ^2)-2\mu _ b(\eta ^2) +4\int _ a^ b\int |D\eta |^2\, d\mu _ t\, dt.  \] The last integral is controlled by local mass bounds on the support of $\eta $. This is the energy estimate of [ WhiMCF15 ] , Theorem 9.5, written with a squared cutoff. Proof Use the time-independent test function $\phi =\eta ^2$. In particular a cutoff equal to one on a compact set bounds the spacetime curvature energy there. $\square$

title: 4.2 BV approximation and compactness
search_title: BV approximation and compactness
text: We now develop the analytic compactness behind finite-perimeter minimization. Here $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is open, and $Du$ denotes the distributional vector measure of Definition 4.1.1 . The basic reference is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2, pp. 52–56. The proofs below spell out the mollification and compactness steps needed in the direct method. Proposition 4.2.1 (Lower semicontinuity of total variation) . 41DD93923E24 If $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, then for every open $W\subset U$, \[  |Du|(W)\leq \liminf _ j|Du_ j|(W),  \] using the variational definition even when its value is infinite. In particular, uniform local variation bounds force $u\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Proof For $X\in C_ c^1(W;\mathbb R^ n)$ with $|X|\leq 1$, local $L^1$ convergence gives $\int u\operatorname {div}X=\lim _ j\int u_ j\operatorname {div}X\leq \liminf _ j|Du_ j|(W)$. Take the supremum over $X$. This is the general-function form of Proposition 4.1.3 , and the lower-semicontinuity step in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 2.6. $\square$ Proposition 4.2.2 (Multiplication by a smooth cutoff) . 770E0596E45F If $u\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and $\eta \in C_ c^1(U)$, then the function $\eta u$, extended by zero outside $U$, belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^ n)$ and \[  D(\eta u)=\eta Du+uD\eta \, \mathcal L^ n, \qquad |D(\eta u)|(\mathbb R^ n) \leq \int |\eta |\, d|Du|+\int |u||D\eta |\, dx.  \] The compact support of the cutoff prevents a boundary measure from appearing at $\partial U$. Proof For a compactly supported test field $X$, use $\eta \operatorname {div}X=\operatorname {div}(\eta X)-D\eta \cdot X$. The defining identity for $Du$ then gives the asserted vector measure. Its total variation is bounded by the sum of the total variations of the two terms. Both are finite on the compact support, and $\eta u$ is integrable. Compare the product estimate in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, the proof of Lemma 2.8. $\square$ Lemma 4.2.3 (Mollification and the variation bound) . 33DD11902347 Let $u\in BV(\mathbb R^ n)$ and let $\rho \in C_ c^\infty (B_1)$ be nonnegative with integral one. Put $\rho _\varepsilon (x)=\varepsilon ^{-n}\rho (x/\varepsilon )$ and $u_\varepsilon =\rho _\varepsilon *u$. Then $u_\varepsilon \to u$ in $L^1(\mathbb R^ n)$ and \[  Du_\varepsilon (x)=\int \rho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, dDu(y), \qquad |Du_\varepsilon (x)|\leq \int \rho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, d|Du|(y).  \] In particular, $\int |Du_\varepsilon |\leq |Du|(\mathbb R^ n)$, and for a Borel set $A$, $\int _ A|Du_\varepsilon |\leq |Du|(A_\varepsilon )$, where $A_\varepsilon =\{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,A)<\varepsilon \} $. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Lemma 2.5. Proof Convolution is an approximate identity on $L^1$, giving the first convergence. Distributional differentiation commutes with convolution: test against a compactly supported smooth function, use Fubini, and then apply the defining integration-by-parts identity for $Du$. The triangle inequality for integration against a vector measure gives the pointwise bound. Integrate it and use Fubini again. The kernel has total integral one, and it vanishes when $|x-y|\geq \varepsilon $, which proves the two integral bounds. $\square$ Definition 4.2.4 (Strict convergence in BV) . D0AFF720A2E2 A sequence $u_ j\in BV(U)$ converges strictly to $u\in BV(U)$ if \[  \| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(U)}\to 0, \qquad |Du_ j|(U)\to |Du|(U).  \] This does not mean $|D(u_ j-u)|(U)\to 0$. In particular, convergence of the total variations is different from convergence in the full BV norm. The terminology describes the approximation property in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Lemma 2.5; the local Radon-measure version there requires localization. Corollary 4.2.5 (Global mollification is strict approximation) . C86A997AF569 The mollifications in Lemma 4.2.3 converge strictly to $u$ in $BV(\mathbb R^ n)$. Proof The lemma gives the $L^1$ convergence and the upper bound $\limsup \int |Du_\varepsilon |\leq |Du|(\mathbb R^ n)$. Proposition 4.2.1 gives the reverse lower bound. Both together yield convergence of the total variations. On a general domain, arbitrary zero extension can create a boundary jump; the whole-space hypothesis is part of this statement. $\square$ Proposition 4.2.6 (Translation estimate for BV functions) . D525EB5675E7 For $u\in BV(\mathbb R^ n)$ and $h\in \mathbb R^ n$, \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ n}|u(x+h)-u(x)|\, dx \leq |h|\, |Du|(\mathbb R^ n).  \] Consequently, with the mollifier from Lemma 4.2.3 , \[  \| u_\varepsilon -u\| _{L^1}\leq \varepsilon \left(\int |z|\rho (z)\, dz\right)|Du|(\mathbb R^ n).  \] Proof For the smooth function $u_\delta $, the fundamental theorem of calculus along $x+th$, followed by Fubini, gives \[  \int |u_\delta (x+h)-u_\delta (x)|\, dx \leq |h|\int _0^1\int |Du_\delta (x+th)|\, dx\, dt \leq |h||Du|(\mathbb R^ n).  \] Pass to the limit $\delta \downarrow 0$ in $L^1$. Average the translation estimate against $\rho _\varepsilon (h)$ to get the second inequality. This supplies a quantitative form of the smoothing step in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 2.6. $\square$ Theorem 4.2.7 (Local compactness of BV functions) . C33FE0726B69 Suppose $u_ j\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and for every relatively compact open $W\subset U$, \[  \sup _ j\left(\| u_ j\| _{L^1(W)}+|Du_ j|(W)\right)<\infty .  \] Then a subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ to a function $u\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. The lower-semicontinuity conclusion of Proposition 4.2.1 holds on every open subset. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 2.6, pp. 54–55. Proof First suppose the functions are globally BV, supported in one compact set $K$, and have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norm and total variation. For fixed $\varepsilon >0$, their convolutions with $\rho _\varepsilon $ have common compact support in $K+\overline{B_\varepsilon }$ and uniform bounds for their values and first derivatives, obtained from the $L^1$ bound and the suprema of $\rho _\varepsilon $ and $D\rho _\varepsilon $. Arzelà–Ascoli therefore makes these convolutions precompact in $L^1$. Proposition 4.2.6 bounds the $L^1$ distance from each function to its convolution by $C\varepsilon $, uniformly in $j$. For each prescribed tolerance, the convolutions have a finite $L^1$ net, which becomes a finite net for the original functions with twice the error after choosing $\varepsilon $ small. Hence the original sequence is precompact in $L^1$. For the local statement, choose an exhaustion $W_ k\Subset U$ and cutoffs $\eta _ k\in C_ c^1(U)$ equal to one on $W_ k$. Proposition 4.2.2 gives uniform whole-space BV bounds for $\eta _ ku_ j$, with a common compact support for each $k$. Extract subsequences successively and then take a diagonal subsequence. The limits agree on overlaps because they are limits in $L^1$, and therefore define $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Proposition 4.2.1 gives local finite variation and the asserted bounds. $\square$ Corollary 4.2.8 (Compactness of finite-perimeter sets) . 8CF44F9AEC71 Let $E_ j$ be measurable sets with uniformly bounded perimeter on every relatively compact open subset of $U$. Then a subsequence satisfies $\chi _{E_ j}\to \chi _ E$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ for a set $E$ of locally finite perimeter. If all $E_ j$ lie almost everywhere in one compact set $K\subset \mathbb R^ n$ and have uniformly bounded total perimeter, the convergence is in $L^1(\mathbb R^ n)$, the limit also lies in $K$ almost everywhere, and the volumes converge. Proof On a relatively compact $W$, the characteristic functions have $L^1$ norm at most $\mathcal L^ n(W)$, so Theorem 4.2.7 applies. A further subsequence converges almost everywhere on an exhaustion; since every value is zero or one, its limit is a characteristic function. Proposition 4.1.3 gives the perimeter bound. With common compact support, use the whole-space compactness argument in the theorem. Global $L^1$ convergence implies convergence of the integrals and hence of the volumes. $\square$ Proposition 4.2.9 (Weak convergence of the derivative measures) . CC9026172A99 If $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and their variations are uniformly bounded on relatively compact open sets, then $Du_ j\rightharpoonup Du$ as vector Radon measures locally in $U$. Convergence of the variation measures $|Du_ j|$ to $|Du|$ is not asserted. Proof Testing with a smooth compactly supported vector field $X$ gives $\int X\cdot dDu_ j=-\int u_ j\operatorname {div}X\to -\int u\operatorname {div}X$. A continuous compactly supported field can be approximated uniformly by smooth ones supported in a fixed relatively compact neighborhood. The variation bound controls the error uniformly in $j$, proving weak convergence against every continuous test field. This is the distributional-measure argument of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2. $\square$ Example 4.2.10 (Variation control without function control is insufficient) . BD09D0B6392E On a bounded nonempty open set, the constants $u_ j=j$ have $|Du_ j|=0$, but no subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The local $L^1$ hypothesis in Theorem 4.2.7 cannot be omitted. For characteristic functions this hypothesis is automatic locally, which explains the simpler assumptions in Corollary 4.2.8 . Example 4.2.11 (Strict convergence need not be BV-norm convergence) . 3214264E8308 In one dimension let $u=\chi _{(0,1)}$ and let $u_\varepsilon $ be its nonnegative smooth mollifications. Then $u_\varepsilon \to u$ strictly by Corollary 4.2.5 , and $|Du|(\mathbb R)=2$. But $Du=\delta _0-\delta _1$ is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure, whereas $Du_\varepsilon $ is absolutely continuous. Hence these derivative measures are mutually singular and \[  |D(u_\varepsilon -u)|(\mathbb R)=\int |Du_\varepsilon |\, dx+2\longrightarrow 4.  \] Thus the stronger BV norm does not tend to zero. This example also distinguishes weak convergence of vector measures from convergence of their total variation norms.

text: Proposition 4.2.2 (Multiplication by a smooth cutoff) . 770E0596E45F If $u\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and $\eta \in C_ c^1(U)$, then the function $\eta u$, extended by zero outside $U$, belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^ n)$ and \[  D(\eta u)=\eta Du+uD\eta \, \mathcal L^ n, \qquad |D(\eta u)|(\mathbb R^ n) \leq \int |\eta |\, d|Du|+\int |u||D\eta |\, dx.  \] The compact support of the cutoff prevents a boundary measure from appearing at $\partial U$. Proof For a compactly supported test field $X$, use $\eta \operatorname {div}X=\operatorname {div}(\eta X)-D\eta \cdot X$. The defining identity for $Du$ then gives the asserted vector measure. Its total variation is bounded by the sum of the total variations of the two terms. Both are finite on the compact support, and $\eta u$ is integrable. Compare the product estimate in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, the proof of Lemma 2.8. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.2.3 (Mollification and the variation bound)
search_title: Mollification and the variation bound
text: Lemma 4.2.3 (Mollification and the variation bound) . 33DD11902347 Let $u\in BV(\mathbb R^ n)$ and let $\rho \in C_ c^\infty (B_1)$ be nonnegative with integral one. Put $\rho _\varepsilon (x)=\varepsilon ^{-n}\rho (x/\varepsilon )$ and $u_\varepsilon =\rho _\varepsilon *u$. Then $u_\varepsilon \to u$ in $L^1(\mathbb R^ n)$ and \[  Du_\varepsilon (x)=\int \rho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, dDu(y), \qquad |Du_\varepsilon (x)|\leq \int \rho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, d|Du|(y).  \] In particular, $\int |Du_\varepsilon |\leq |Du|(\mathbb R^ n)$, and for a Borel set $A$, $\int _ A|Du_\varepsilon |\leq |Du|(A_\varepsilon )$, where $A_\varepsilon =\{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,A)<\varepsilon \} $. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Lemma 2.5. Proof Convolution is an approximate identity on $L^1$, giving the first convergence. Distributional differentiation commutes with convolution: test against a compactly supported smooth function, use Fubini, and then apply the defining integration-by-parts identity for $Du$. The triangle inequality for integration against a vector measure gives the pointwise bound. Integrate it and use Fubini again. The kernel has total integral one, and it vanishes when $|x-y|\geq \varepsilon $, which proves the two integral bounds. $\square$

title: Definition 4.2.4 (Strict convergence in BV)
search_title: Strict convergence in BV
text: Definition 4.2.4 (Strict convergence in BV) . D0AFF720A2E2 A sequence $u_ j\in BV(U)$ converges strictly to $u\in BV(U)$ if \[  \| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(U)}\to 0, \qquad |Du_ j|(U)\to |Du|(U).  \] This does not mean $|D(u_ j-u)|(U)\to 0$. In particular, convergence of the total variations is different from convergence in the full BV norm. The terminology describes the approximation property in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Lemma 2.5; the local Radon-measure version there requires localization.

title: Corollary 4.2.5 (Global mollification is strict approximation)
search_title: Global mollification is strict approximation
text: Corollary 4.2.5 (Global mollification is strict approximation) . C86A997AF569 The mollifications in Lemma 4.2.3 converge strictly to $u$ in $BV(\mathbb R^ n)$. Proof The lemma gives the $L^1$ convergence and the upper bound $\limsup \int |Du_\varepsilon |\leq |Du|(\mathbb R^ n)$. Proposition 4.2.1 gives the reverse lower bound. Both together yield convergence of the total variations. On a general domain, arbitrary zero extension can create a boundary jump; the whole-space hypothesis is part of this statement. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.2.6 (Translation estimate for BV functions)
search_title: Translation estimate for BV functions
text: Proposition 4.2.6 (Translation estimate for BV functions) . D525EB5675E7 For $u\in BV(\mathbb R^ n)$ and $h\in \mathbb R^ n$, \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ n}|u(x+h)-u(x)|\, dx \leq |h|\, |Du|(\mathbb R^ n).  \] Consequently, with the mollifier from Lemma 4.2.3 , \[  \| u_\varepsilon -u\| _{L^1}\leq \varepsilon \left(\int |z|\rho (z)\, dz\right)|Du|(\mathbb R^ n).  \] Proof For the smooth function $u_\delta $, the fundamental theorem of calculus along $x+th$, followed by Fubini, gives \[  \int |u_\delta (x+h)-u_\delta (x)|\, dx \leq |h|\int _0^1\int |Du_\delta (x+th)|\, dx\, dt \leq |h||Du|(\mathbb R^ n).  \] Pass to the limit $\delta \downarrow 0$ in $L^1$. Average the translation estimate against $\rho _\varepsilon (h)$ to get the second inequality. This supplies a quantitative form of the smoothing step in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 2.6. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.2.7 (Local compactness of BV functions)
search_title: Local compactness of BV functions
text: Theorem 4.2.7 (Local compactness of BV functions) . C33FE0726B69 Suppose $u_ j\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and for every relatively compact open $W\subset U$, \[  \sup _ j\left(\| u_ j\| _{L^1(W)}+|Du_ j|(W)\right)<\infty .  \] Then a subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ to a function $u\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. The lower-semicontinuity conclusion of Proposition 4.2.1 holds on every open subset. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 2.6, pp. 54–55. Proof First suppose the functions are globally BV, supported in one compact set $K$, and have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norm and total variation. For fixed $\varepsilon >0$, their convolutions with $\rho _\varepsilon $ have common compact support in $K+\overline{B_\varepsilon }$ and uniform bounds for their values and first derivatives, obtained from the $L^1$ bound and the suprema of $\rho _\varepsilon $ and $D\rho _\varepsilon $. Arzelà–Ascoli therefore makes these convolutions precompact in $L^1$. Proposition 4.2.6 bounds the $L^1$ distance from each function to its convolution by $C\varepsilon $, uniformly in $j$. For each prescribed tolerance, the convolutions have a finite $L^1$ net, which becomes a finite net for the original functions with twice the error after choosing $\varepsilon $ small. Hence the original sequence is precompact in $L^1$. For the local statement, choose an exhaustion $W_ k\Subset U$ and cutoffs $\eta _ k\in C_ c^1(U)$ equal to one on $W_ k$. Proposition 4.2.2 gives uniform whole-space BV bounds for $\eta _ ku_ j$, with a common compact support for each $k$. Extract subsequences successively and then take a diagonal subsequence. The limits agree on overlaps because they are limits in $L^1$, and therefore define $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Proposition 4.2.1 gives local finite variation and the asserted bounds. $\square$

title: Corollary 4.2.8 (Compactness of finite-perimeter sets)
search_title: Compactness of finite-perimeter sets
text: Corollary 4.2.8 (Compactness of finite-perimeter sets) . 8CF44F9AEC71 Let $E_ j$ be measurable sets with uniformly bounded perimeter on every relatively compact open subset of $U$. Then a subsequence satisfies $\chi _{E_ j}\to \chi _ E$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ for a set $E$ of locally finite perimeter. If all $E_ j$ lie almost everywhere in one compact set $K\subset \mathbb R^ n$ and have uniformly bounded total perimeter, the convergence is in $L^1(\mathbb R^ n)$, the limit also lies in $K$ almost everywhere, and the volumes converge. Proof On a relatively compact $W$, the characteristic functions have $L^1$ norm at most $\mathcal L^ n(W)$, so Theorem 4.2.7 applies. A further subsequence converges almost everywhere on an exhaustion; since every value is zero or one, its limit is a characteristic function. Proposition 4.1.3 gives the perimeter bound. With common compact support, use the whole-space compactness argument in the theorem. Global $L^1$ convergence implies convergence of the integrals and hence of the volumes. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.2.9 (Weak convergence of the derivative measures)
search_title: Weak convergence of the derivative measures
text: Proposition 4.2.9 (Weak convergence of the derivative measures) . CC9026172A99 If $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and their variations are uniformly bounded on relatively compact open sets, then $Du_ j\rightharpoonup Du$ as vector Radon measures locally in $U$. Convergence of the variation measures $|Du_ j|$ to $|Du|$ is not asserted. Proof Testing with a smooth compactly supported vector field $X$ gives $\int X\cdot dDu_ j=-\int u_ j\operatorname {div}X\to -\int u\operatorname {div}X$. A continuous compactly supported field can be approximated uniformly by smooth ones supported in a fixed relatively compact neighborhood. The variation bound controls the error uniformly in $j$, proving weak convergence against every continuous test field. This is the distributional-measure argument of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2. $\square$

title: Example 4.2.10 (Variation control without function control is insufficient)
search_title: Variation control without function control is insufficient
text: Example 4.2.10 (Variation control without function control is insufficient) . BD09D0B6392E On a bounded nonempty open set, the constants $u_ j=j$ have $|Du_ j|=0$, but no subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The local $L^1$ hypothesis in Theorem 4.2.7 cannot be omitted. For characteristic functions this hypothesis is automatic locally, which explains the simpler assumptions in Corollary 4.2.8 .

title: Example 4.2.11 (Strict convergence need not be BV-norm convergence)
search_title: Strict convergence need not be BV-norm convergence
text: Example 4.2.11 (Strict convergence need not be BV-norm convergence) . 3214264E8308 In one dimension let $u=\chi _{(0,1)}$ and let $u_\varepsilon $ be its nonnegative smooth mollifications. Then $u_\varepsilon \to u$ strictly by Corollary 4.2.5 , and $|Du|(\mathbb R)=2$. But $Du=\delta _0-\delta _1$ is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure, whereas $Du_\varepsilon $ is absolutely continuous. Hence these derivative measures are mutually singular and \[  |D(u_\varepsilon -u)|(\mathbb R)=\int |Du_\varepsilon |\, dx+2\longrightarrow 4.  \] Thus the stronger BV norm does not tend to zero. This example also distinguishes weak convergence of vector measures from convergence of their total variation norms.

title: 4.3 Perimeter blow-ups and the direct method
search_title: Perimeter blow-ups and the direct method
section: 4.3 Perimeter blow-ups and the direct method
text:
Compactness and lower semicontinuity establish existence before smoothness is known. The reduced-boundary blow-up identifies the local geometric object, but by itself does not make every topological boundary point regular. In this section $n\geq 2$. Definition 4.3.1 (Measure-theoretic interior and exterior) . A0CDC4480E37 For a measurable set $E\subset \mathbb R^ n$, define \[  E^{(1)}=\left\{ x:\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{|E\cap B_ r(x)|}{|B_ r(x)|}=1ight\} , \qquad E^{(0)}=\left\{ x:\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{|E\cap B_ r(x)|}{|B_ r(x)|}=0ight\} .  \] The essential boundary is $\partial ^ eE=\mathbb R^ n\setminus (E^{(0)}\cup E^{(1)})$. These definitions are unchanged by a Lebesgue-null modification of $E$. They differ from the topological interior, exterior, and boundary, which depend on the chosen representative. Compare the measure-density framework of [ Sim18 ] , Chapters 1 and 3. Theorem 4.3.2 (Half-space blow-up at a reduced-boundary point) . DA28F4FE0B6B Let $E$ have locally finite perimeter in $U$, and let $x\in \partial ^*E\cap U$. With outward normal $
u _ E(x)$, set $E_{x,r}=(E-x)/r$. As $r\downarrow 0$, \[  \chi _{E_{x,r}}\longrightarrow \chi _{\{ y:y\cdot 
u _ E(x)<0\} } \quad 	ext{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n),  \] and the perimeter measures converge locally to $\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner 
u _ E(x)^\perp $. In particular, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{|E\cap B_ r(x)|}{\omega _ nr^ n}= rac12, \qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{P(E;B_ r(x))}{\omega _{n-1}r^{n-1}}=1.  \] This is the blow-up conclusion in the proof of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, especially equations (9)–(13), pp. 98–100, with the project's outward-normal convention. The substantial blow-up and density argument remains external. The convergence holds as $r\downarrow 0$, not merely for one selected subsequence. Example 4.3.3 (A null modification can change the whole topological boundary) . 9BC8B81C327D The set $E=\mathbb Q^ n$ is null and dense, and its complement is also dense. Thus its topological boundary is all of $\mathbb R^ n$, while $\chi _ E=0$ almost everywhere, $P(E;U)=0$, $E^{(0)}=\mathbb R^ n$, and its reduced and essential boundaries are empty. Perimeter measures are therefore attached to measurable sets modulo null sets, not to arbitrary topological representatives. Proposition 4.3.4 (Existence with a fixed volume in a compact container) . D065989825F9 Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be compact and $v\geq 0$. Suppose there is at least one measurable $E\subset K$ almost everywhere with $|E|=v$ and finite total perimeter. Then the infimum of $P(E;\mathbb R^ n)$ over this class is attained. No regularity of $K$ is needed for this existence statement, and no smoothness of the minimizing boundary is concluded. Proof Choose a minimizing sequence with bounded total perimeter. All its characteristic functions are supported in $K$ and have fixed $L^1$ norm $v$. Corollary 4.2.8 gives a globally $L^1$-convergent subsequence whose limit remains supported in $K$ and has volume $v$. Proposition 4.1.3 shows that this limit attains the infimum. This is a direct application of the BV compactness theorem in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2. $\square$ Proposition 4.3.5 (A local direct method with a bulk term) . 8128DEB47531 Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be bounded and open, let $K\Subset U$ be compact, let $E_0$ have finite perimeter in $U$, and let $g\in L^1(U)$. Then \[  \mathcal J_ g(E)=P(E;U)-\int _{E\cap U}g(x)\, dx  \] attains its infimum among measurable sets $E$ with $\chi _ E=\chi _{E_0}$ almost everywhere on $U\setminus K$. The compactly contained set of allowed changes is part of the boundary-data formulation. This extends the constant bulk term in Definition 11.1.1 . Proof The functional is bounded below by $-\| g\| _{L^1(U)}$, and $E_0$ is an admissible finite-energy competitor. A minimizing sequence therefore has uniformly bounded perimeter. Corollary 4.2.8 gives a subsequence converging locally in $L^1$ and, after a further extraction, almost everywhere. The limit agrees with $E_0$ on $U\setminus K$. Dominated convergence, using $|g\chi _ E|\leq |g|$, shows convergence of the bulk integrals. Perimeter lower semicontinuity then proves attainment. The argument uses no trace-continuity assertion at $\partial U$, because every competitor is fixed outside $K$. $\square$ Proposition 4.3.6 (The Euler equation on a smooth minimizing interface) . FCE1DA6B5E31 Suppose $g\in C^1(U)$ and $E$ minimizes the functional in Proposition 4.3.5 . On any open region $W\subset \operatorname {int}K$ where $E$ is represented by a domain with smooth boundary, that boundary satisfies \[  H=g  \] with respect to the outward unit normal and the trace convention $H=\operatorname {div}_{\partial E}
u $. This is an interior conclusion; it makes no assertion about contact with the container or about singular points. Proof Use the flow of a smooth vector field compactly supported in $W$ to vary $E$. Both positive and negative variation times are admissible. If $f=X\cdot 
u $ is the normal speed, the first variation of perimeter is $\int _{\partial E}Hf\, dA$, while the transport formula for the bulk integral gives $\int _{\partial E}gf\, dA$. Minimality makes their difference zero. Every compactly supported smooth normal speed on the interface can be extended to an ambient field, so $H-g=0$ there. Compare Proposition 11.1.2 for constant $g$. $\square$
