title: 5.3 Operations on currents
search_title: Operations on currents
text: Pushforwards, restrictions, and homotopies turn geometric constructions into identities with quantitative mass bounds. Throughout this section, $m$ is the current dimension and $N$ is the ambient Euclidean dimension. We retain the comass convention of Definition 5.1.3 . The main source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 2, pp. 159–169; its initial Euclidean norm on forms must be distinguished from comass for nonrectifiable currents. Definition 5.3.1 (Support and normal currents) . F9AA0927D6D3 The support $\operatorname {spt}T$ of a current in $U$ is the complement, relative to $U$, of the largest open set on which it vanishes on all test forms. A current is locally normal if $T$ and $\partial T$ have finite mass on every relatively compact open subset of $U$. It is normal with finite mass if $\mathbf M(T)+\mathbf M(\partial T)<\infty $. Normality is an analytic condition; it does not require integer multiplicities or rectifiability. Every locally integral current is locally normal. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Sections 2–3, and [ Fed69 ] , Section 4.1. Theorem 5.3.2 (Representation of currents with locally finite mass) . E73216D55EF5 If $T$ has locally finite mass in $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, there are a Radon measure $\| T\| $ and a measurable $m$-vector field $\xi $ such that \[  T(\omega )=\int _ U\langle \omega ,\xi \rangle \, d\| T\| , \qquad |\xi |_{\mathrm{mass}}=1\quad \| T\| \text{-almost everywhere}, \qquad \mathbf M_ W(T)=\| T\| (W).  \] Here $|\cdot |_{\mathrm{mass}}$ is the norm on $m$-vectors dual to comass. The field $\xi $ need not be simple. The current extends uniquely to compactly supported continuous forms, and its integral representation also defines evaluation on bounded Borel forms with compact support. This is the vector-measure representation theorem, obtained from Riesz representation and polar decomposition. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, equations (2.8)–(2.10), with the norm convention changed by duality as explained in Remark 2.7. The representation theorem remains an external dependency. Proposition 5.3.3 (Weak compactness from local mass bounds) . AA1586653736 Suppose $T_ j$ are $m$-currents in $U$ and $\sup _ j\mathbf M_ W(T_ j)<\infty $ for every $W\Subset U$. A subsequence converges weakly to an $m$-current with locally finite mass. If also $\sup _ j\mathbf M_ W(\partial T_ j)<\infty $ for every such $W$, the limit is locally normal. This conclusion does not by itself preserve integer rectifiability; that is the additional content of Theorem 5.1.6 . Compare [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 2.17, p. 162. Proof On an exhaustion of $U$ by relatively compact open sets, the coordinate measures in Theorem 5.3.2 have uniformly bounded total variation. Weak-star compactness of finite vector measures, the separability of continuous compactly supported test functions, and a diagonal choice give a subsequence converging on all compactly supported continuous forms. The limits on overlapping sets agree, hence define a current on $U$. Mass lower semicontinuity gives its local mass bound. Boundary commutes with weak convergence by Proposition 5.1.2 ; applying mass lower semicontinuity once more bounds the boundary mass. The functional-analytic weak-star compactness theorem is used here as an external input. $\square$ Definition 5.3.4 (Restriction and contraction by a differential) . D80FDA4F9AB7 For a locally finite-mass current and a Borel set $E\subset U$, define \[  (T\llcorner E)(\omega )=\int _ E\langle \omega ,\xi \rangle \, d\| T\| .  \] More generally $T\llcorner u$ inserts a locally bounded Borel scalar function $u$ into this integral. For smooth $u$ and $m\geq 1$, the $(m-1)$-current $T\llcorner du$ is defined by \[  (T\llcorner du)(\eta )=T(du\wedge \eta ).  \] The order $du\wedge \eta $ fixes the sign used below. Restricting a normal current to an arbitrary Borel set need not give a normal current. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, equations (2.11)–(2.12) and Section 4. Proposition 5.3.5 (Boundary of a smooth scalar restriction) . C518F9F87741 For a locally normal $m$-current, $m\geq 1$, and smooth $u$, \[  \partial (T\llcorner u)=(\partial T)\llcorner u-T\llcorner du.  \] In particular multiplication by a smooth compactly supported function produces a normal current of finite mass, with \[  \mathbf M\bigl (\partial (T\llcorner u)\bigr ) \leq \int |u|\, d\| \partial T\| +\int |Du|\, d\| T\| .  \] Proof For a test $(m-1)$-form $\eta $, expand $d(u\eta )=du\wedge \eta +u\, d\eta $ and apply $T$. This gives the identity. If $\| \eta \| _*\leq 1$, then $\| du\wedge \eta \| _*\leq |Du|$: on a unit simple $m$-vector this is the norm bound for contraction by $Du$. The mass estimates follow by integration and taking the supremum. Compare [ Sim18 ] , the computation on p. 170. $\square$ Definition 5.3.6 (Smooth pushforward and properness) . 6D60EECBFF25 Let $f:U\to V$ be smooth and proper on $\operatorname {spt}T$: for every compact $K\subset V$, the set $f^{-1}(K)\cap \operatorname {spt}T$ is compact in $U$. Define \[  f_\# T(\omega )=T(\chi f^*\omega ),  \] where $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$ equals one on a neighborhood of $\operatorname {spt}T\cap f^{-1}(\operatorname {spt}\omega )$. Different choices give the same value because their difference vanishes near the part of the current being tested. In particular compact support of $T$ guarantees properness. See [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.29), p. 164. Proposition 5.3.7 (Pushforward, boundary, and composition) . 738450753968 For smooth maps with the required properness, \[  \partial (f_\# T)=f_\# (\partial T),\qquad (g\circ f)_\# T=g_\# (f_\# T),\qquad \operatorname {spt}(f_\# T)\subset f(\operatorname {spt}T).  \] The image on the right is relatively closed under the properness hypothesis. It can be strictly larger than the support of the pushforward because of cancellation. Proof The first two identities follow from $d(f^*\eta )=f^*(d\eta )$ and $(g\circ f)^*=f^*g^*$. In the boundary calculation, derivatives of the auxiliary cutoff vanish near $\operatorname {spt}T\cap f^{-1}(\operatorname {spt}\eta )$, and the remaining terms vanish where the test form does. To prove the support inclusion, a test form supported off $f(\operatorname {spt}T)$ pulls back to zero near the support of $T$. Properness makes that image closed: a convergent sequence of image points lies in a compact target neighborhood, whose inverse image on the support is compact. See [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.31). $\square$ Proposition 5.3.8 (Mass bound for a pushforward) . 126C4418F9FD Let $T$ have locally finite mass and let $f$ be as in Definition 5.3.6 . title: Definition 5.3.1 (Support and normal currents)
search_title: Support and normal currents
text: Definition 5.3.1 (Support and normal currents) . F9AA0927D6D3 The support $\operatorname {spt}T$ of a current in $U$ is the complement, relative to $U$, of the largest open set on which it vanishes on all test forms. A current is locally normal if $T$ and $\partial T$ have finite mass on every relatively compact open subset of $U$. It is normal with finite mass if $\mathbf M(T)+\mathbf M(\partial T)<\infty $. Normality is an analytic condition; it does not require integer multiplicities or rectifiability. Every locally integral current is locally normal. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Sections 2–3, and [ Fed69 ] , Section 4.1.

title: Theorem 5.3.2 (Representation of currents with locally finite mass)
search_title: Representation of currents with locally finite mass
text: Theorem 5.3.2 (Representation of currents with locally finite mass) . E73216D55EF5 If $T$ has locally finite mass in $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, there are a Radon measure $\| T\| $ and a measurable $m$-vector field $\xi $ such that \[  T(\omega )=\int _ U\langle \omega ,\xi \rangle \, d\| T\| , \qquad |\xi |_{\mathrm{mass}}=1\quad \| T\| \text{-almost everywhere}, \qquad \mathbf M_ W(T)=\| T\| (W).  \] Here $|\cdot |_{\mathrm{mass}}$ is the norm on $m$-vectors dual to comass. The field $\xi $ need not be simple. The current extends uniquely to compactly supported continuous forms, and its integral representation also defines evaluation on bounded Borel forms with compact support. This is the vector-measure representation theorem, obtained from Riesz representation and polar decomposition. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, equations (2.8)–(2.10), with the norm convention changed by duality as explained in Remark 2.7. The representation theorem remains an external dependency.

title: Proposition 5.3.3 (Weak compactness from local mass bounds)
search_title: Weak compactness from local mass bounds
text: Proposition 5.3.3 (Weak compactness from local mass bounds) . AA1586653736 Suppose $T_ j$ are $m$-currents in $U$ and $\sup _ j\mathbf M_ W(T_ j)<\infty $ for every $W\Subset U$. A subsequence converges weakly to an $m$-current with locally finite mass. If also $\sup _ j\mathbf M_ W(\partial T_ j)<\infty $ for every such $W$, the limit is locally normal. This conclusion does not by itself preserve integer rectifiability; that is the additional content of Theorem 5.1.6 . Compare [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 2.17, p. 162. Proof On an exhaustion of $U$ by relatively compact open sets, the coordinate measures in Theorem 5.3.2 have uniformly bounded total variation. Weak-star compactness of finite vector measures, the separability of continuous compactly supported test functions, and a diagonal choice give a subsequence converging on all compactly supported continuous forms. The limits on overlapping sets agree, hence define a current on $U$. Mass lower semicontinuity gives its local mass bound. Boundary commutes with weak convergence by Proposition 5.1.2 ; applying mass lower semicontinuity once more bounds the boundary mass. The functional-analytic weak-star compactness theorem is used here as an external input. $\square$

title: Definition 5.3.4 (Restriction and contraction by a differential)

text: Definition 5.3.4 (Restriction and contraction by a differential) . D80FDA4F9AB7 For a locally finite-mass current and a Borel set $E\subset U$, define \[  (T\llcorner E)(\omega )=\int _ E\langle \omega ,\xi \rangle \, d\| T\| .  \] More generally $T\llcorner u$ inserts a locally bounded Borel scalar function $u$ into this integral. title: Proposition 5.3.5 (Boundary of a smooth scalar restriction)

text: Proposition 5.3.5 (Boundary of a smooth scalar restriction) . C518F9F87741 For a locally normal $m$-current, $m\geq 1$, and smooth $u$, \[  \partial (T\llcorner u)=(\partial T)\llcorner u-T\llcorner du.  \] In particular multiplication by a smooth compactly supported function produces a normal current of finite mass, with \[  \mathbf M\bigl (\partial (T\llcorner u)\bigr ) \leq \int |u|\, d\| \partial T\| +\int |Du|\, d\| T\| .  \] Proof For a test $(m-1)$-form $\eta $, expand $d(u\eta )=du\wedge \eta +u\, d\eta $ and apply $T$. This gives the identity. If $\| \eta \| _*\leq 1$, then $\| du\wedge \eta \| _*\leq |Du|$: on a unit simple $m$-vector this is the norm bound for contraction by $Du$. The mass estimates follow by integration and taking the supremum. Compare [ Sim18 ] , the computation on p. 170. $\square$

title: Definition 5.3.6 (Smooth pushforward and properness)

text: Definition 5.3.6 (Smooth pushforward and properness) . 6D60EECBFF25 Let $f:U\to V$ be smooth and proper on $\operatorname {spt}T$: for every compact $K\subset V$, the set $f^{-1}(K)\cap \operatorname {spt}T$ is compact in $U$. Define \[  f_\# T(\omega )=T(\chi f^*\omega ),  \] where $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$ equals one on a neighborhood of $\operatorname {spt}T\cap f^{-1}(\operatorname {spt}\omega )$. title: Proposition 5.3.7 (Pushforward, boundary, and composition)

Insert these two currents as the filling and residual in the homotopy formula. For general polar vectors the estimate follows by duality with comass, just as in Proposition 5.3.8 . $\square$

title: Proposition 5.3.19 (Cone identity and mass estimate)
search_title: Cone identity and mass estimate
text: Proposition 5.3.19 (Cone identity and mass estimate) . FE4C86C4A57D For $m\geq 1$ and $T$ as above, \[  \partial C_ aT=T-C_ a(\partial T),\qquad \mathbf M(C_ aT)\leq \frac{R}{m+1}\mathbf M(T) \quad \text{if }\operatorname {spt}T\subset \overline B_ R(a).  \] If $T$ is integral, then so is $C_ aT$. In particular an integral cycle of positive dimension supported in a ball has an integral filling in the same ball, with the displayed mass bound. Proof In the homotopy formula, $g$ is the identity and $f$ is constant. A constant map sends every positive-dimensional current to zero, so the boundary identity follows. The differential sends the interval direction to $x-a$ and spatial $m$-vectors to $t^ m$ times themselves. Thus the mass is at most $\int _0^1 Rt^ m\mathbf M(T)\, dt=R\mathbf M(T)/(m+1)$. The interval product is integral when $T$ is, and its smooth pushforward remains integral by Theorem 5.3.9 . Convexity of the ball controls the support. $\square$

text: Example 5.3.20 (The zero-dimensional augmentation condition) . A3DF20FFB628 For $T=\sum _{i=1}^ k a_ i\delta _{p_ i}$ with integer coefficients, the cone is a sum of oriented segments and \[  \partial C_ aT=T-\left(\sum _ i a_ i\right)\delta _ a.  \] Thus a zero-dimensional current has a compactly supported one-current filling when $\sum _ i a_ i=0$. title: 5.4 Slicing and the Plateau direct method
search_title: Slicing and the Plateau direct method
section: 5.4 Slicing and the Plateau direct method
text:
Restricting a current to a sublevel set creates a new boundary on the level set. Slicing identifies this boundary for almost every level and estimates its mass. The statements below use real-valued Lipschitz slicing functions and integer coefficients, following [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 4, pp. 180–185. Definition 5.4.1 (Slice by a scalar function) . 4F695BB95218 Let $T$ be a locally normal $m$-current, $m\geq 1$, and let $f:U	o \mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Its lower slice, initially defined as a distributional current, is \[  \langle T,f,tangle =\partial (T\llcorner \{ f<t\} )-(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} .  \] This formula alone does not give finite mass at every level. The almost-everywhere mass and rectifiability statements are the content of the slicing theorem. The boundary sign is fixed by restricting to $\{ f<t\} $; compare [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.6)–(4.7). Theorem 5.4.2 (Slicing of integral currents) . 0E99E4802BCA Let $T=\llbracket M,	heta ,	au rbracket $ be locally integral in $U$, and let $f:U	o \mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. For almost every $t$, the slice $\langle T,f,tangle $ is a locally integral $(m-1)$-current supported in $\operatorname {spt}T\cap f^{-1}(t)$; the restriction $T\llcorner \{ f<t\} $ is locally integral as well. For a Borel set $E\subset U$, \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\| \langle T,f,tangle \| (E)\, dt =\int _ E|
abla ^ M f|\, d\| T\| .  \] In particular, if $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, this is at most $L\| T\| (E)$. On the rectifiable part of $M\cap f^{-1}(t)$ where $
abla ^ M f
e 0$, the slice carries multiplicity $	heta $ and orientation $	au \mathbin {\lrcorner }(
abla ^ M f/|
abla ^ M f|)$, where $\langle 	au \mathbin {\lrcorner }v,\eta angle =\langle 	au ,v\wedge \eta angle $. Sources: [ Sim18 ] , Definition 4.4 and Lemma 4.5, pp. 181–183. The rectifiable coarea formula gives the mass identity. Identifying this geometric slice with the distributional boundary in Definition 5.4.1 , including a single exceptional null set for all test forms, is a further argument whose proof remains external. All conclusions concerning a slice are almost-everywhere in the level. Proposition 5.4.3 (Boundary and slicing have opposite signs) . 90329BDB0E5A If $m\geq 2$, then at almost every level for a locally integral current, \[  \partial \langle T,f,tangle =-\langle \partial T,f,tangle .  \] If $m=1$, the slice is a zero-current and its boundary is zero by convention. See [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.5(3). Proof Apply $\partial $ to the definition of the slice. The boundary-squared term vanishes, leaving $-\partial ((\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} )$. Apply the same definition to $\partial T$ and use $\partial ^2T=0$ to identify it with the negative slice of $\partial T$. The almost-everywhere qualification ensures the finite-mass and integral conclusions for both slices. $\square$ Proposition 5.4.4 (Choosing a radius with controlled cutting boundary) . 73C4D018ADAF Let $T$ be locally integral near $\overline B_ R(a)$ and let $0<r<R$. For almost every $s\in (r,R)$, \[  \partial (T\llcorner B_ s(a)) =(\partial T)\llcorner B_ s(a)+\langle T,|x-a|,sangle .  \] There is such an $s$ for which \[  \mathbf M igl (\langle T,|x-a|,sangle  igr ) \leq  rac{\| T\| (B_ R(a)\setminus \overline B_ r(a))}{R-r}.  \] Consequently the boundary mass of the restricted current is at most this quantity plus $\| \partial T\| (B_ R(a))$. Proof The distance function is one-Lipschitz. Apply the slicing theorem over the annulus and integrate over $s\in (r,R)$. The integral of the slice masses is no larger than the numerator, so some good level has mass no larger than their average. The restriction-boundary formula is the definition of the slice, and the boundary-mass estimate follows by the triangle inequality. A good level is chosen from the full-measure set where all slicing conclusions hold. $\square$ Example 5.4.5 (The slice of an oriented rectangle) . A2CEDE0295D2 Let $T$ be integration over $[0,1]^2$ with orientation $e_1\wedge e_2$, and set $f(x,y)=x$. For $0<t<1$, $\langle T,f,tangle $ is the vertical segment $\{ t\} 	imes [0,1]$ oriented toward increasing $y$. Indeed $(e_1\wedge e_2)\mathbin {\lrcorner }e_1=e_2$. Its boundary is $\delta _{(t,1)}-\delta _{(t,0)}$. The slice of the oriented boundary of the rectangle has the opposite sign, directly illustrating Proposition 5.4.3 . Definition 5.4.6 (The integral Plateau problem in a compact container) . 959193546633 Fix $1\leq m<N$, a compact set $K\subset \mathbb R^ N$, and an integral $(m-1)$-current $Z$ of finite mass. The admissible class consists of integral $m$-currents $T$ with finite mass, $\operatorname {spt}T\subset K$, and $\partial T=Z$. The Plateau problem minimizes $\mathbf M(T)$ in this class. We assume the class is nonempty when asserting existence; in particular $\partial Z=0$ is necessary. No parametrization, connectedness, or genus is fixed by this definition. Compare the compactness approach in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Sections 3 and 7. Theorem 5.4.7 (Existence of a mass-minimizing integral filling) . 5D2EEA517377 If the class in Definition 5.4.6 is nonempty, its mass infimum is attained by an integral current supported in $K$. Proof Choose one admissible current to bound the infimum from above, then take a minimizing sequence with bounded masses. Its boundary is always $Z$, so the boundary masses are uniformly bounded. Federer–Fleming compactness, Theorem 5.1.6 , gives a weakly convergent subsequence with an integral limit supported in $K$. Boundary continuity gives $\partial T=Z$. Mass lower semicontinuity shows that its mass is no larger than the infimum, while admissibility gives the opposite inequality. Thus it attains the infimum. This is the direct-method consequence of the compactness theorem in [ Sim18 ] , Section 3; regularity of the minimizer is a separate problem. $\square$ Corollary 5.4.8 (Compact boundaries have Euclidean minimizers) . 2DDDF8908CF1 Let $1\leq m<N$, and let $Z$ be a compactly supported integral $(m-1)$-current of finite mass. If $m\geq 2$, assume $\partial Z=0$; if $m=1$, assume the total signed multiplicity of $Z$ is zero. Then there is a compactly supported integral $m$-current minimizing mass among all compactly supported integral fillings of $Z$ in $\mathbb R^ N$. Proof Choose a closed ball containing the support of $Z$. Proposition 5.3.19 , or Example 5.3.20 when $m=1$, supplies a filling in that ball. The nearest-point projection $p$ to a closed Euclidean ball is one-Lipschitz and fixes $Z$. Every compactly supported integral filling $S$ therefore projects to another filling $p_\# S$ in the ball, with no larger mass, by Theorem 5.3.9 . Thus the infimum in the ball is the full compactly supported infimum. Apply Theorem 5.4.7 in this fixed container. The use of compact supports makes properness automatic for the projection. $\square$

title: 11.3 Volume constraints and CMC stability
search_title: Volume constraints and CMC stability
text:
Stationarity and stability depend on which variations are allowed. We distinguish critical points of area minus a prescribed multiple of volume from critical points of area on a fixed-volume class. The second-variation form is the same at a CMC hypersurface, but its domain of test functions is different. Sources are [ ZZCMC ] , equations (1.2)–(1.3) and Definition 2.1, and the smooth variation calculations in [ HP99 ] and [ ChMin ] , Section 23. Definition 11.3.1 (Infinitesimal volume-preserving variations) . 69AD8C3A2E1D Let $\Omega $ be a smooth compact region in a Riemannian manifold, with nonempty smooth boundary $\Sigma $ and outward normal $
u $. A normal speed $f\in C^\infty (\Sigma )$ preserves volume to first order when \[  \int _\Sigma f\, dA=0.  \] An exactly volume-preserving variation instead satisfies $\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega _ t)=\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega )$ for all sufficiently small $t$. The integral condition is its linearization by Proposition 11.1.2 . Unless stated otherwise, we constrain the total volume of the region, not a separate volume for every boundary component. Compare [ ZZCMC ] , Introduction, with its unrestricted $\mathcal A^ c$ variations. Proposition 11.3.2 (Realizing a zero-mean speed with an exact volume constraint) . 35ECF4C2F5DD Every smooth $f$ with $\int _\Sigma f=0$ is the initial normal speed of a smooth exactly volume-preserving variation of $\Omega $. Proof Use the normal tubular neighborhood of the compact embedded boundary. For small $(t,s)$, let $\Omega _{t,s}$ have boundary the normal graph of $tf+s$ over $\Sigma $. Its volume is a smooth function $V(t,s)$, with \[  \partial _ tV(0,0)=\int _\Sigma f=0,\qquad \partial _ sV(0,0)=\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )>0.  \] The implicit function theorem gives a smooth $s(t)$ with $s(0)=0$ and $V(t,s(t))=V(0,0)$. Differentiating gives $s'(0)=0$, so the initial speed is $f$. Tubular coordinates and the inverse function theorem ensure that these small normal graphs bound the corresponding smoothly varied regions. This argument uses only the first-volume-variation formula. $\square$ Proposition 11.3.3 (Fixed-volume stationarity characterizes constant mean curvature) . AC0FE2421EEA A smooth compact boundary $\Sigma =\partial \Omega $ is stationary for area under all exactly volume-preserving variations if and only if its outward scalar mean curvature is one constant on all of $\Sigma $. Proof By the preceding proposition, stationarity gives $\int _\Sigma Hf=0$ for every smooth zero-mean function. Set $\overline H=\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )^{-1}\int _\Sigma H$ and choose $f=H-\overline H$. Then $0=\int H(H-\overline H)=\int (H-\overline H)^2$, so $H=\overline H$ everywhere. Conversely constant $H=c$ gives $\delta A=c\int f=0$ along every volume-preserving variation. This also shows why imposing only the total volume gives the same constant across different components: the admissible speeds allow exchange of volume between them. $\square$ Proposition 11.3.4 (Riemannian normal variation of mean curvature) . 2DBE30F27E50 Let a smooth two-sided hypersurface in a Riemannian manifold vary with normal velocity $f
u $ at the time under consideration. With $H=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma

This derives the formula independently of the second variation. $\square$ Proposition 11.3.5 (Second variation of area minus volume) . 0C2679767FF6 If a smooth compact boundary has $H=c$, the second derivative of $\mathcal A^ c=A-cV$ along a variation with initial normal speed $f$ is \[  Q(f,f)=\int _\Sigma \left(|
abla f|^2- (|A|^2+\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u ))f^2ight)dA.  \] Along an exactly volume-preserving variation, this is also the second derivative of area. The formula is [ ZZCMC ] , equation (1.3), p. 6. Proof Differentiate $\delta \mathcal A^ c=\int (H-c)f\, dA$. At the critical hypersurface, the derivatives of the speed and the area element are multiplied by $H-c=0$. The remaining term is $\int f\dot H$. Proposition 11.3.4 and integration by parts give $Q(f,f)$. A tangential component of the initial velocity only differentiates the identically zero function $H-c$, so the result depends on the normal speed. If volume is constant along the variation, the second derivatives of $A$ and $A-cV$ coincide. $\square$ Definition 11.3.6 (Strong and volume-constrained CMC stability) . 067C762778A0 A closed CMC boundary is strongly stable if $Q(f,f)\geq 0$ for every smooth $f$. It is volume-constrained stable, also called weakly stable in this setting, if the inequality holds for all $f$ with $\int _\Sigma f=0$. The latter condition is equivalent to nonnegative second variation along exactly volume-preserving paths by Proposition 11.3.2 . The stable $c$-hypersurfaces of [ ZZCMC ] , Definition 2.1, use unrestricted compactly supported tests on their open domain, hence the strong notion there. Their local curvature estimates cannot be applied by silently replacing strong stability by a global volume constraint. Proposition 11.3.7 (One scalar constraint changes index by at most one) . 93851119AB24 Let $\operatorname {ind}(Q)$ be the maximal dimension of a negative-definite subspace of smooth functions on a closed CMC boundary, and let $\operatorname {ind}_0(Q)$ use only zero-mean functions. Then \[  \operatorname {ind}_0(Q)\leq \operatorname {ind}(Q) \leq \operatorname {ind}_0(Q)+1.  \] In particular volume-constrained stability implies unrestricted index at most one. The converse implication from index one to volume-constrained stability does not follow from this dimension estimate. Proof Every negative subspace in the constrained space is also negative in the full space. Conversely a finite-dimensional negative subspace $E$ intersects the kernel of the linear functional $f\mapsto \int f$ in dimension at least $\dim E-1$. The quadratic form remains negative on that intersection. Taking the supremum over $E$ proves the bounds; the argument also applies to unbounded index. This is linear algebra for the second-variation form, not an assertion about which eigenfunction has nonzero mean. $\square$ Proposition 11.3.8 (The sharp Poincare inequality on a round sphere) . 4AF6DFFAC5BC On the round sphere $S_ R^ n$, $n\geq 2$, every smooth $f$ of zero mean satisfies \[  \int _{S_ R^ n}|
abla f|^2\, dA\geq  rac n{R^2}\int _{S_ R^ n}f^2\, dA.  \] The constant is sharp, since restrictions of ambient linear coordinate functions attain equality. Proof The spectral theorem for the Laplace operator on a compact connected manifold gives a positive first eigenvalue $\lambda _1$ and a smooth zero-mean eigenfunction $u$, with $-\Delta u=\lambda _1u$. Integrate Bochner's identity and use $\operatorname {Ric}_{S_ R^ n}=(n-1)R^{-2}g$ and $|
abla ^2u|^2\geq (\Delta u)^2/n$: \[  0=\int \left(|

abla u|^2ight) \geq (n-1)\left( rac1{R^2}- rac{\lambda _1}{n}ight) \int |
abla u|^2.  \] Hence $\lambda _1\geq n/R^2$. Directly differentiating the coordinate functions on the sphere gives $\Delta x_ i=-nx_ i/R^2$, so equality is attained. The Rayleigh characterization of $\lambda _1$ gives the inequality for every zero-mean $f$. The compact spectral theorem and Bochner identity are the external analytic and differential-geometric inputs to this calculation. $\square$ Example 11.3.9 (A round sphere is weakly stable but strongly unstable) . 62447F464A27 The boundary of a Euclidean ball of radius $R$ has $H=n/R$, $|A|^2=n/R^2$, and \[  Q(f,f)=\int _{S_ R^ n}\left(|
abla f|^2- rac n{R^2}f^2ight)dA.  \] For $n\geq 2$, Proposition 11.3.8 proves volume-constrained stability. The constant function gives $Q(1,1)=-nR^{-2}\operatorname {Area}(S_ R^ n)<0$, so the sphere is not strongly stable and its unrestricted index is exactly one by Proposition 11.3.7 . Coordinate-function speeds have zero quadratic form; they are the normal speeds of translations. This elementary model distinguishes the two notions of stability used in CMC problems. Proposition 11.3.10 (Strong instability under nonnegative Ricci curvature) . 6BAA97140F05 In an ambient manifold with $\operatorname {Ric}_ M\geq 0$, every nonempty closed two-sided CMC hypersurface with $c
e 0$ is unstable for unrestricted $\mathcal A^ c$ variations. Proof The pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $|A|^2\geq H^2/n=c^2/n$. Therefore $Q(1,1)=-\int (|A|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u ))<0$. The constant speed changes volume, so it is not a permitted test for volume-constrained stability. This is the CMC counterpart of Corollary 7.1.5 . $\square$ Proposition 11.3.11 (Volume stability forces connectedness when the potential is positive) . 9C857ED1F719 Suppose a smooth compact CMC boundary is volume-constrained stable and $q=|A|^2+\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u )>0$ on every component. Then it is connected. In particular this applies to a volume-constrained stable boundary with $c
e 0$ in nonnegative Ricci curvature. Proof If there are two components $\Sigma _1,\Sigma _2$, choose a smooth function constant $a

title: Definition 11.3.1 (Infinitesimal volume-preserving variations)
search_title: Infinitesimal volume-preserving variations
text: Definition 11.3.1 (Infinitesimal volume-preserving variations) . 69AD8C3A2E1D Let $\Omega $ be a smooth compact region in a Riemannian manifold, with nonempty smooth boundary $\Sigma $ and outward normal $\nu $. A normal speed $f\in C^\infty (\Sigma )$ preserves volume to first order when \[  \int _\Sigma f\, dA=0.  \] An exactly volume-preserving variation instead satisfies $\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega _ t)=\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega )$ for all sufficiently small $t$. The integral condition is its linearization by Proposition 11.1.2 . Unless stated otherwise, we constrain the total volume of the region, not a separate volume for every boundary component. Compare [ ZZCMC ] , Introduction, with its unrestricted $\mathcal A^ c$ variations.

title: Proposition 11.3.2 (Realizing a zero-mean speed with an exact volume constraint)
search_title: Realizing a zero-mean speed with an exact volume constraint
text: Proposition 11.3.2 (Realizing a zero-mean speed with an exact volume constraint) . 35ECF4C2F5DD Every smooth $f$ with $\int _\Sigma f=0$ is the initial normal speed of a smooth exactly volume-preserving variation of $\Omega $. Proof Use the normal tubular neighborhood of the compact embedded boundary. For small $(t,s)$, let $\Omega _{t,s}$ have boundary the normal graph of $tf+s$ over $\Sigma $. Its volume is a smooth function $V(t,s)$, with \[  \partial _ tV(0,0)=\int _\Sigma f=0,\qquad \partial _ sV(0,0)=\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )>0.  \] The implicit function theorem gives a smooth $s(t)$ with $s(0)=0$ and $V(t,s(t))=V(0,0)$. Differentiating gives $s'(0)=0$, so the initial speed is $f$. Tubular coordinates and the inverse function theorem ensure that these small normal graphs bound the corresponding smoothly varied regions. This argument uses only the first-volume-variation formula. $\square$

title: Proposition 11.3.3 (Fixed-volume stationarity characterizes constant mean curvature)
search_title: Fixed-volume stationarity characterizes constant mean curvature
text: Proposition 11.3.3 (Fixed-volume stationarity characterizes constant mean curvature) . AC0FE2421EEA A smooth compact boundary $\Sigma =\partial \Omega $ is stationary for area under all exactly volume-preserving variations if and only if its outward scalar mean curvature is one constant on all of $\Sigma $. Proof By the preceding proposition, stationarity gives $\int _\Sigma Hf=0$ for every smooth zero-mean function. Set $\overline H=\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )^{-1}\int _\Sigma H$ and choose $f=H-\overline H$. Then $0=\int H(H-\overline H)=\int (H-\overline H)^2$, so $H=\overline H$ everywhere. Conversely constant $H=c$ gives $\delta A=c\int f=0$ along every volume-preserving variation. This also shows why imposing only the total volume gives the same constant across different components: the admissible speeds allow exchange of volume between them. $\square$

title: Proposition 11.3.5 (Second variation of area minus volume)

text:
Proposition 11.3.5 (Second variation of area minus volume) . 0C2679767FF6 If a smooth compact boundary has $H=c$, the second derivative of $\mathcal A^ c=A-cV$ along a variation with initial normal speed $f$ is \[  Q(f,f)=\int _\Sigma \left(|

title: Definition 11.3.6 (Strong and volume-constrained CMC stability)
search_title: Strong and volume-constrained CMC stability
text: Definition 11.3.6 (Strong and volume-constrained CMC stability) . 067C762778A0 A closed CMC boundary is strongly stable if $Q(f,f)\geq 0$ for every smooth $f$. It is volume-constrained stable, also called weakly stable in this setting, if the inequality holds for all $f$ with $\int _\Sigma f=0$. The latter condition is equivalent to nonnegative second variation along exactly volume-preserving paths by Proposition 11.3.2 . The stable $c$-hypersurfaces of [ ZZCMC ] , Definition 2.1, use unrestricted compactly supported tests on their open domain, hence the strong notion there. Their local curvature estimates cannot be applied by silently replacing strong stability by a global volume constraint.

title: Proposition 11.3.7 (One scalar constraint changes index by at most one)
search_title: One scalar constraint changes index by at most one
text: Proposition 11.3.7 (One scalar constraint changes index by at most one) . 93851119AB24 Let $\operatorname {ind}(Q)$ be the maximal dimension of a negative-definite subspace of smooth functions on a closed CMC boundary, and let $\operatorname {ind}_0(Q)$ use only zero-mean functions. Then \[  \operatorname {ind}_0(Q)\leq \operatorname {ind}(Q) \leq \operatorname {ind}_0(Q)+1.  \] In particular volume-constrained stability implies unrestricted index at most one. The converse implication from index one to volume-constrained stability does not follow from this dimension estimate. Proof Every negative subspace in the constrained space is also negative in the full space. Conversely a finite-dimensional negative subspace $E$ intersects the kernel of the linear functional $f\mapsto \int f$ in dimension at least $\dim E-1$. The quadratic form remains negative on that intersection. Taking the supremum over $E$ proves the bounds; the argument also applies to unbounded index. This is linear algebra for the second-variation form, not an assertion about which eigenfunction has nonzero mean. $\square$

title: Example 11.3.9 (A round sphere is weakly stable but strongly unstable)

text: Example 11.3.9 (A round sphere is weakly stable but strongly unstable) . 62447F464A27 The boundary of a Euclidean ball of radius $R$ has $H=n/R$, $|A|^2=n/R^2$, and \[  Q(f,f)=\int _{S_ R^ n}\left(|\nabla f|^2-\frac n{R^2}f^2\right)dA.  \] For $n\geq 2$, Proposition 11.3.8 proves volume-constrained stability. title: 7.7 Stability and scalar curvature

In dimension three the Gauss equation rewrites the Jacobi potential in terms of scalar curvature and the intrinsic Gaussian curvature. Stability then has topological consequences. The arguments follow [ ChMin ] , Section 24, with closedness, orientability, and the convention $R_\Sigma =2K_\Sigma $ stated explicitly. Proposition 7.7.1 (The traced Gauss equation) . 3E7688AA201F For a smooth two-sided hypersurface $\Sigma ^ n\subset M^{n+1}$, \[  R_ M=R_\Sigma +2\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u )+|A|^2-H^2.  \] Here scalar curvature is twice the sum of sectional curvatures over unordered orthonormal pairs, and $H$ is the sum of principal curvatures. This is [ ChMin ] , Lemma 24.2, pp. 61–62. Proof At a point diagonalize the scalar second fundamental form in an orthonormal frame $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$, with principal curvatures $\kappa _ i$. The Gauss equation on each tangent two-plane is $K_\Sigma (e_ i,e_ j)=K_ M(e_ i,e_ j)+\kappa _ i\kappa _ j$. It follows by inserting $
abla ^ M_ XY=
abla ^\Sigma _ XY-h(X,Y)
u $ in the curvature definition and taking the tangential component. Sum over $i
e j$. The extrinsic sum is $H^2-|A|^2$, and the omitted ambient two-planes containing $
u $ contribute $2\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u )$. Rearranging proves the identity. $\square$ Corollary 7.7.2 (The Jacobi potential on a minimal surface) . 522E4EE726E6 For a two-sided minimal surface $\Sigma ^2\subset M^3$, \[  q=|A|^2+\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u ) = rac12(R_ M+|A|^2)-K_\Sigma .  \] Consequently its stability inequality is equivalent to \[   rac12\int _\Sigma (R_ M+|A|^2)\phi ^2 \leq \int _\Sigma  igl (|
abla \phi |^2+K_\Sigma \phi ^2 igr )  \] for every compactly supported smooth test function in the interior. Proof Put $H=0$ and $R_\Sigma =2K_\Sigma $ in Proposition 7.7.1 , solve for $q$, and substitute in Definition 7.6.1 . The factor two relates scalar and Gaussian curvature on a surface. $\square$ Theorem 7.7.3 (Topology and area of a stable surface in positive scalar curvature) . 478117A3A30D Let $\Sigma $ be a nonempty smooth closed connected orientable two-sided stable minimal surface in a Riemannian three-manifold. If $R_ M>0$ along $\Sigma $, then $\Sigma $ has genus zero. If moreover $R_ M\geq \sigma >0$ there, then \[  \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\leq  rac{8\pi }{\sigma }.  \] The genus conclusion is the closed orientable form of [ ChMin ] , Theorem 24.3, attributed there to Schoen–Yau. Both the closedness and the orientability hypotheses enter the proof. Proof The constant test function is admissible because $\Sigma $ is closed. Corollary 7.7.2 and Gauss–Bonnet give \[  0<\int _\Sigma (R_ M+|A|^2) \leq 2\int _\Sigma K_\Sigma =4\pi \chi (\Sigma )=8\pi (1-g).  \] Thus the nonnegative integer $g$ is zero. The same inequality with $R_ M\geq \sigma $ gives $\sigma \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\leq 8\pi $. Gauss–Bonnet and the classification of closed orientable surfaces are the topological inputs. This argument applies to an immersion as well, using its induced metric and global normal. $\square$ Proposition 7.7.4 (Rigidity of a stable torus under nonnegative scalar curvature) . EBC1C1900387 Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth closed two-sided stable minimal torus in $M^3$, and suppose $R_ M\geq 0$ along $\Sigma $. Then, along $\Sigma $, \[  A=0,\qquad R_ M=0,\qquad \operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u )=0,\qquad K_\Sigma =0.  \] In particular the induced metric is flat. No splitting of an ambient neighborhood is asserted. Proof The constant stability test and $\chi (\Sigma )=0$ give $\int (R_ M+|A|^2)\leq 0$. Nonnegativity and continuity force $R_ M=|A|=0$. The traced Gauss equation then gives $q=\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )=-K_\Sigma $, and Gauss–Bonnet gives $Q(1,1)=-\int q=0$. For arbitrary smooth $\psi $, stability of $1+s\psi $ for both signs of small $s$ forces $Q(1,\psi )=0$. Thus $\int q\psi =0$ for every $\psi $, so $q=0$ pointwise. Hence $K_\Sigma =0$ as well. This is the equality argument in the preceding stability calculation; the polarization step is needed to obtain pointwise Ricci and Gaussian curvature conclusions. $\square$ Example 7.7.5 (A flat stable torus) . 785CBF422ACB In the flat product $\mathbb T^2	imes \mathbb S^1$, each slice $\mathbb T^2	imes \{ t\} $ is two-sided and totally geodesic, with $q=0$. Hence $Q(\phi ,\phi )=\int |
abla \phi |^2\geq 0$. This realizes the zero-scalar-curvature case of Proposition 7.7.4 ; replacing positive scalar curvature by nonnegative scalar curvature does not force a sphere. Example 7.7.6 (Why orientability is a separate hypothesis) . 1FEFF0FF3A61 Give $\mathbb {RP}^2$ the metric induced from the unit round sphere and consider $M=\mathbb {RP}^2	imes \mathbb S^1$ with the product metric. A slice $\mathbb {RP}^2	imes \{ t\} $ is a closed two-sided totally geodesic minimal surface. The product direction gives a global unit normal with $\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )=0$, so the slice is stable. The ambient scalar curvature equals $2$, but the slice is not orientable and is not a sphere. This is the possibility noted in the footnote to [ ChMin ] , Theorem 24.3. Two-sidedness alone implies orientability only when the ambient manifold is oriented.

title: Example 7.7.6 (Why orientability is a separate hypothesis)
search_title: Why orientability is a separate hypothesis
text: Example 7.7.6 (Why orientability is a separate hypothesis) . 1FEFF0FF3A61 Give $\mathbb {RP}^2$ the metric induced from the unit round sphere and consider $M=\mathbb {RP}^2\times \mathbb S^1$ with the product metric. A slice $\mathbb {RP}^2\times \{ t\} $ is a closed two-sided totally geodesic minimal surface. The product direction gives a global unit normal with $\operatorname {Ric}(\nu ,\nu )=0$, so the slice is stable. The ambient scalar curvature equals $2$, but the slice is not orientable and is not a sphere. This is the possibility noted in the footnote to [ ChMin ] , Theorem 24.3. Two-sidedness alone implies orientability only when the ambient manifold is oriented.

title: 7.8 Logarithmic cutoffs and the Bernstein theorem
search_title: Logarithmic cutoffs and the Bernstein theorem
section: 7.8 Logarithmic cutoffs and the Bernstein theorem
text:
The following proof of the two-dimensional Bernstein theorem separates its ingredients: stability, quadratic area growth, and cutoffs of arbitrarily small Dirichlet energy. Properness supplies compact support for cutoffs defined by ambient distance. We follow [ ChMin ] , Corollary 18.2 and Section 25, pp. 51 and 62–64. Definition 7.8.1 (Exhausting cutoffs with vanishing Dirichlet energy) . 428ADAED15DA A smooth manifold without boundary has the cutoff property used here if there are compactly supported locally Lipschitz functions $\eta _ j$ such that \[  0\leq \eta _ j\leq 1,\qquad \eta _ j\longrightarrow 1	ext{ pointwise}, \qquad \int |
abla \eta _ j|^2\longrightarrow 0.  \] Only this explicit analytic property is needed below. It is often expressed through capacity or parabolicity, but those broader equivalences are not assumed here. The logarithmic cutoffs in [ ChMin ] , the proof of Theorem 25.1, provide a geometric example. Proposition 7.8.2 (A nonnegative stability potential vanishes under small-energy cutoffs) . 58F6D1EE7150 Suppose a smooth manifold has the cutoff property in Definition 7.8.1 , and let $q\geq 0$ be a continuous function satisfying \[  \int q\phi ^2\leq \int |
abla \phi |^2 \quad 	ext{for every }\phi \in C_ c^\infty .  \] Then $q=0$ everywhere. In particular, a two-sided stable minimal hypersurface in Euclidean space with this cutoff property is totally geodesic. Proof Compactly supported locally Lipschitz tests are admissible by approximation in $W^{1,2}$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of their support; $q$ is bounded there, so the potential integral also converges. Use $\eta _ j$ as a test and apply Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative functions $q\eta _ j^2$. This gives $\int q\leq \liminf _ j\int |
abla \eta _ j|^2=0$. Continuity yields pointwise vanishing. For a Euclidean minimal hypersurface the stability potential is $q=|A|^2$. $\square$ Proposition 7.8.3 (Quadratic area growth gives logarithmic cutoffs) . 80D85FC586A0 Let $F:\Sigma ^2	o \mathbb R^ N$ be a proper smooth immersion of a surface without boundary. Suppose for some $a$ and $C<\infty $, \[  \operatorname {Area} igl (F^{-1}(B_ R(a)) igr )\leq CR^2 \quad (R\geq 1).  \] Area is computed in the induced metric, including multiplicity of the immersion. Then $\Sigma $ has the cutoff property of Definition 7.8.1 . Proof Write $ho =|F-a|$ and take $R=2^ k$, $k\geq 1$. Define $\eta _ R$ to be one for $ho \leq R$, zero for $ho \geq R^2$, and $\log (R^2/ho )/\log R$ in between. Properness makes its support compact. Since $|
abla _\Sigma ho |\leq 1$, almost everywhere on the annulus, \[  |
abla \eta _ R|^2\leq  rac{1}{ho ^2(\log R)^2}.  \] Decompose $R<ho <R^2$ into the $k$ dyadic annuli $2^ j<ho <2^{j+1}$, $j=k,\ldots ,2k-1$. On each, the integral of $ho ^{-2}$ is at most $2^{-2j}C2^{2j+2}=4C$. Hence $\int |
abla \eta _ R|^2\leq 4Ck/(k\log 2)^2	o 0$. The functions take values between zero and one and converge pointwise to one. This is the logarithmic cutoff argument in [ ChMin ] , pp. 63–64, with the squared-gradient estimate explicit. $\square$ Theorem 7.8.4 (Stable Bernstein with quadratic area growth) . A5EAD6B995B6 Let $F:\Sigma ^2	o \mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty complete connected proper smooth two-sided minimal immersion without boundary. If it is stable and its induced area satisfies the quadratic growth bound in Proposition 7.8.3 , then its image is an affine plane. Proof The logarithmic cutoffs and Proposition 7.8.2 give $A=0$. The global unit normal therefore has zero derivative and is constant on connected $\Sigma $. The image lies in an affine plane and is open in that plane because $F$ is an immersion of the same dimension. Properness makes the image closed, so it is the entire plane. This is the stability-and-growth argument used for graphs in [ ChMin ] , Theorem 25.1. The growth and properness hypotheses are part of this version; no classification of all complete stable immersions in higher dimensions is claimed. $\square$ Proposition 7.8.5 (Uniform area growth for an entire minimal graph) . 2D3AB8786897 If $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^ n)$ solves the scalar minimal surface equation, its graph $\Gamma $ satisfies, for every ambient center $a$ and radius $R>0$, \[  \mathcal H^ n(\Gamma \cap B_ R(a)) \leq (n+1)\omega _{n+1}R^ n.  \] No global gradient bound is assumed. This gives an explicit constant in [ ChMin ] , Corollary 18.2, p. 51. Proof The vector field $N(x,z)=(-Du(x),1)/\sqrt{1+|Du(x)|^2}$ is globally defined, has length one, and is divergence free. It is the outward normal to the subgraph $\Omega =\{ z<u(x)\} $. For almost every radius, the graph meets the sphere transversely, and the divergence theorem on the bounded region $\Omega \cap B_ R(a)$ gives \[  0=\mathcal H^ n(\Gamma \cap B_ R(a)) +\int _{\Omega \cap \partial B_ R(a)}N\cdot 
u _{B_ R}\, d\mathcal H^ n.  \] The absolute value of the second term is no larger than the area of the entire sphere, $(n+1)\omega _{n+1}R^ n$. The divergence theorem applies to this piecewise smooth boundary; its codimension-two corner has zero boundary area. Classical graph bootstrapping supplies smoothness when using Sard's theorem for the transverse radii. Approximation by good radii increasing to an arbitrary $R$ proves the estimate for every ball. This is also the flux form of the graph calibration in Proposition 7.2.13 . $\square$ Theorem 7.8.6 (Bernstein's theorem for an entire graph over the plane) . 1087ACBCE404 Every $C^2$ solution $u:\mathbb R^2	o \mathbb R$ of the scalar minimal surface equation is affine. Proof Its graph is smooth by Proposition 7.2.7 , two-sided and stable by Corollary 7.6.4 , and has quadratic area growth by Proposition 7.8.5 . An entire graph is proper: the inverse image of an ambient compact set is closed and has bounded horizontal coordinates. Its induced metric is complete, since it dominates the Euclidean metric on the base and is uniformly comparable to it on each compact subset. Theorem 7.8.4 makes the image an affine plane. A plane that is a graph over all of $\mathbb R^2$ is the graph of an affine function. This is the geometric proof of [ ChMin ] , Theorem 25.1, pp. 62–64. $\square$ Example 7.8.7 (A stable graph need not be an entire graph) . 729C4A9152CC The nonflat Scherk graph in Example 7.2.14 is stable by its positive vertical Jacobi function. Its domain is a square, so it does not satisfy Bernstein's entire-domain hypothesis. It is also not proper as that graph in $\mathbb R^3$: along $x=y\uparrow \pi /2$ its height stays zero and its points approach a finite point outside the graph. Thus pulling back ambient distance cutoffs does not automatically produce compactly supported functions on this incomplete graph. No contradiction with Theorem 7.8.4 follows.

title: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones

section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text:
Cone stability combines a spherical operator with a one-dimensional Hardy inequality. Here $n\geq 2$ is the cone dimension; its link has dimension $n-1$ and lies in the unit sphere $\mathbb S^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$. We assume a smooth closed connected embedded two-sided link, so the cone is smooth away from its vertex. These hypotheses exclude more general cones with singular links. Sources are [ ChMin ] , Section 26, pp. 64–68, and the Simons identities in [ HP99 ] , Section 2. Definition 7.9.1 (The cone over a spherical hypersurface) . 016DAF7407ED For a link $L\subset \mathbb S^ n$ as above, set \[  C^*(L)=\{ rp:r>0,\  p\in L\} ,\qquad C(L)=C^*(L)\cup \{ 0\} .  \] The normal $
u _ L$ to $L$ within the sphere extends to the cone by $
u _ C(rp)=
u _ L(p)$. The point $0$ is not included in the smooth domain $C^*(L)$. This is the cone parametrization used in [ ChMin ] , Section 26. Proposition 7.9.2 (Metric, curvature, and Laplacian of a cone) . F3105662B738 Under $F(r,p)=rp$, \[  g_ C=dr^2+r^2g_ L,\qquad dA_ C=r^{n-1}dr\, dA_ L, \qquad H_ C=r^{-1}H_ L,\qquad |A_ C|^2=r^{-2}|A_ L|^2,  \] \[  \Delta _ C v=\partial _{rr}v+ rac{n-1}{r}\partial _ rv+r^{-2}\Delta _ Lv.  \] In particular $C^*(L)$ is minimal precisely when $L$ is minimal in the unit sphere. Proof The radial vector is $p$ and an angular coordinate vector is $r\partial _ ip$. They are orthogonal and have the displayed metric. The normal is independent of $r$, so the radial principal curvature is zero; angular principal curvatures are those of the spherical link divided by $r$. The Euclidean derivative of $
u _ L$ in a link direction has no radial component, because $\langle 
u _ L,pangle =\langle 
u _ L,\partial _ ipangle =0$. This gives the mean-curvature and norm formulas. The determinant of the metric is $r^{2(n-1)}\det g_ L$; the coordinate divergence formula for the Laplacian yields the last identity. Compare [ ChMin ] , the calculation preceding Proposition 26.1. $\square$ Definition 7.9.3 (Stability away from a cone vertex) . 7D56079904BC For a minimal link $L$, the cone is stable away from its vertex if \[  Q_ C(\phi ,\phi )=\int _{C^*(L)} \left(|
abla _ C\phi |^2-|A_ C|^2\phi ^2ight)dA_ C\geq 0 \quad (\phi \in C_ c^\infty (C^*(L))).  \] Thus every test is supported in an annulus with positive inner radius. This definition does not assert regularity at the vertex or area minimization among integral-current or finite-perimeter competitors. It is the test class in [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1. Lemma 7.9.4 (The sharp radial Hardy inequality) . B401AC1A32A6 Let $n\geq 2$ and $a=(n-2)/2$. For $\eta \in C_ c^\infty ((0,\infty ))$, \[  \int _0^\infty |\eta '|^2r^{n-1}dr \geq a^2\int _0^\infty \eta ^2r^{n-3}dr.  \] The constant $a^2$ is sharp, including the value zero when $n=2$, and equality holds only for $\eta =0$ in this compactly supported class. Proof Put $t=\log r$ and $\psi (t)=r^ a\eta (r)$. Direct substitution gives \[  \int _0^\infty  igl (|\eta '|^2r^{n-1}-a^2\eta ^2r^{n-3} igr )dr =\int _{\mathbb R}|\psi '|^2dt, \qquad \int _0^\infty \eta ^2r^{n-3}dr=\int _{\mathbb R}\psi ^2dt.  \] The cross term integrates to zero because $\psi $ is compactly supported. A zero right side makes $\psi $ constant and thus zero. To prove sharpness, fix a nonzero $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ and use $\psi _ T(t)=\chi (t/T)$. Its derivative-energy to $L^2$-norm ratio is $T^{-2}\int |\chi '|^2/\int \chi ^2	o 0$. This is the logarithmic substitution underlying [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1, pp. 64–65. $\square$ Definition 7.9.5 (The spherical link Rayleigh quotient) . C3BBE589F9AC For a smooth minimal link define \[  \lambda _0(L)=\inf _{0
e \psi \in C^\infty (L)}  rac{\int _ L(|
abla \psi |^2-|A_ L|^2\psi ^2)\, dA_ L}{\int _ L\psi ^2\, dA_ L}.  \] This is the lowest Rayleigh value of $-\Delta _ L-|A_ L|^2$. It omits the ambient Ricci term $n-1$ that appears in the Jacobi operator for $L$ as a hypersurface of $\mathbb S^ n$. Consequently it is not that spherical hypersurface's full stability eigenvalue. See [ ChMin ] , Section 26, p. 64. Proposition 7.9.6 (The spectral criterion for cone stability) . 2C4122B9D586 The cone $C^*(L)$ is stable in Definition 7.9.3 if and only if \[  \lambda _0(L)\geq - rac{(n-2)^2}{4}.  \] This is [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1, attributed there to Simons. Proof Write $a=(n-2)/2$, $t=\log r$, and $v(t,p)=r^ a\phi (r,p)$. The cone metric and the same integration by parts as in Lemma 7.9.4 give the exact identity \[  Q_ C(\phi ,\phi )=\int _{\mathbb R}\int _ L \left(|\partial _ tv|^2+|
abla _ Lv|^2+(a^2-|A_ L|^2)v^2ight)dA_ Ldt.  \] If $\lambda _0\geq -a^2$, the angular part plus $a^2v^2$ has nonnegative integral at each fixed $t$, proving stability. Conversely, if a smooth $\psi $ has Rayleigh quotient below $-a^2$, choose $v(t,p)=\chi (t/T)\psi (p)$, with nonzero smooth compactly supported $\chi $. After division by $\int \chi (t/T)^2dt$, the positive time-derivative term is $T^{-2}\int |\chi '|^2/\int \chi ^2$ times $\int _ L\psi ^2$. For large $T$ the total form is negative. This contradicts stability and proves necessity without assuming that the Rayleigh infimum is attained. $\square$ Example 7.9.7 (Product-sphere links and the dimension-seven threshold) . BD8080CF7EC4 Let $p,q\geq 1$, set $n=p+q+1$, and put \[  L=\mathbb S^ p\left(\sqrt{ rac p{p+q}}ight) 	imes \mathbb S^ q\left(\sqrt{ rac q{p+q}}ight)\subset \mathbb S^ n.  \] Writing its radii as $a,b$, a unit normal is $
u (x,y)=(bx/a,-ay/b)$. Its principal curvatures are $b/a$ with multiplicity $p$ and $-a/b$ with multiplicity $q$. Hence $H_ L=0$ and $|A_ L|^2=p+q=n-1$. The Rayleigh quotient is minimized by constants, so $\lambda _0=-(n-1)$. Proposition 7.9.6 shows that its cone is stable away from zero exactly when $n-1\leq (n-2)^2/4$, or $n\geq 7$ in this family. This is a stability calculation, not a classification of which product cones minimize area. For equal factors with $p=q\geq 3$, Theorem 4.5.8 proves the stronger finite-perimeter minimizing property. Compare the cone examples in [ ChMin ] , Sections 13, 17, and 26. Theorem 7.9.8 (Simons identity for a minimal spherical hypersurface) . 8B46D4CA80AE Let $L^ d\subset \mathbb S^{d+1}$ be a smooth two-sided minimal hypersurface of the unit sphere. Its scalar second fundamental form satisfies \[  \Delta _ L h=(d-|A|^2)h,\qquad  rac12\Delta _ L|A|^2=|
abla A|^2+d|A|^2-|A|^4.  \] Here $\Delta _ Lh$ is the rough covariant Laplacian. These are the constant-curvature, minimal specializations of [ HP99 ] , Corollary 2.2, p. 49; the corresponding norm inequality is [ ChMin ] , Lemma 26.5. Proof The Gauss and Codazzi equations follow by decomposing the ambient covariant derivative into its tangential and normal parts. In the unit sphere they give $K_ L(e_ i,e_ k)=1+\kappa _ i\kappa _ k$ in a principal frame and $
abla _ kh_{ij}=
abla _ ih_{kj}$. The latter holds because the normal component of the ambient curvature on three tangent vectors is zero. Tracing Codazzi and using $H=0$ gives $\sum _ k
abla _ kh_{kj}=0$. At a chosen point use a geodesic orthonormal frame diagonalizing $h$. Commutation on a covariant two-tensor gives \[  \Delta h_{ij}=\sum _ k igl ((
abla _ k
abla _ i-
abla _ i
abla _ k)h igr )_{kj},  \] \[   igl ((
abla _ k
abla _ i-
abla _ i
abla _ k)h igr )(e_ k,e_ j) =-h(R^ L(e_ k,e_ i)e_ k,e_ j)-h(e_ k,R^ L(e_ k,e_ i)e_ j).  \] The diagonal component is therefore \[  \Delta h_{ii}=\sum _ k(1+\kappa _ i\kappa _ k)(\kappa _ i-\kappa _ k) =d\kappa _ i-\kappa _ i|A|^2,  \] since $\sum _ k\kappa _ k=0$. The off-diagonal components are zero at this point by the same Gauss equation in a principal frame. This proves the tensor identity. Take its inner product with $h$ and apply the product rule to $|A|^2$ to obtain the second identity. The curvature sign is the one fixed in Proposition 11.3.4 . $\square$ Proposition 7.9.9 (An upper bound for the nonflat link Rayleigh value) . 40C07F2B543A For a smooth closed minimal link $L^{n-1}$ with $A_ L$ not identically zero, \[  \lambda _0(L)\leq -(n-1).  \] Proof Integrate the spherical Simons identity to get \[  \int _ L|
abla A|^2-\int _ L|A|^4 =-(n-1)\int _ L|A|^2.  \] The Lipschitz function $w=|A|$ satisfies $|
abla w|\leq |
abla A|$ almost everywhere. Use $w$ in the Rayleigh quotient by smooth approximation, for example $w_\varepsilon =\sqrt{|A|^2+\varepsilon ^2}$ and passage in $W^{1,2}$. Its denominator tends to the positive number $\int |A|^2$, and its numerator is no larger in the limit than the left side above. This proves the bound. The approximation avoids dividing by $|A|$ at its zero set. Compare [ ChMin ] , the proof of Corollary 26.6, pp. 67–68. $\square$ Theorem 7.9.10 (Stable cones with smooth links are flat in dimensions at most six) . 0574E4F9C647 Let $2\leq n\leq 6$ and let $L^{n-1}\subset \mathbb S^ n$ be a smooth closed connected embedded two-sided minimal hypersurface. If $C^*(L)$ is stable away from its vertex, then $L$ is a great sphere and $C(L)$ is a hyperplane. This is the smooth-link version of the dimension bound in [ ChMin ] , Corollary 26.6. Proof If $A_ L$ is not identically zero, the previous proposition and the stability criterion give \[  - rac{(n-2)^2}{4}\leq \lambda _0(L)\leq -(n-1),  \] which is impossible for $2\leq n\leq 6$. Hence $A_ L=0$. Its spherical unit normal has zero Euclidean derivative in every tangent direction, so it is constant on connected $L$. Thus $L$ lies in the equator orthogonal to that normal. It is open in that equator by equality of dimensions, and closed by compactness; hence it is the entire great sphere. The hypotheses include smoothness of the link. Extending this statement to cones with additional singularities requires a separate regularity or dimension-reduction argument. $\square$

u _ L$ in a link direction has no radial component, because $\langle 
u _ L,pangle =\langle 
u _ L,\partial _ ipangle =0$. This gives the mean-curvature and norm formulas. The determinant of the metric is $r^{2(n-1)}\det g_ L$; the coordinate divergence formula for the Laplacian yields the last identity. Compare [ ChMin ] , the calculation preceding Proposition 26.1. $\square$

title: Definition 7.9.3 (Stability away from a cone vertex)
search_title: Stability away from a cone vertex
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Definition 7.9.3 (Stability away from a cone vertex) . 7D56079904BC For a minimal link $L$, the cone is stable away from its vertex if \[  Q_ C(\phi ,\phi )=\int _{C^*(L)} \left(|\nabla _ C\phi |^2-|A_ C|^2\phi ^2\right)dA_ C\geq 0 \quad (\phi \in C_ c^\infty (C^*(L))).  \] Thus every test is supported in an annulus with positive inner radius. This definition does not assert regularity at the vertex or area minimization among integral-current or finite-perimeter competitors. It is the test class in [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1.

title: Lemma 7.9.4 (The sharp radial Hardy inequality)
search_title: The sharp radial Hardy inequality
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Lemma 7.9.4 (The sharp radial Hardy inequality) . B401AC1A32A6 Let $n\geq 2$ and $a=(n-2)/2$. For $\eta \in C_ c^\infty ((0,\infty ))$, \[  \int _0^\infty |\eta '|^2r^{n-1}dr \geq a^2\int _0^\infty \eta ^2r^{n-3}dr.  \] The constant $a^2$ is sharp, including the value zero when $n=2$, and equality holds only for $\eta =0$ in this compactly supported class. Proof Put $t=\log r$ and $\psi (t)=r^ a\eta (r)$. Direct substitution gives \[  \int _0^\infty \bigl (|\eta '|^2r^{n-1}-a^2\eta ^2r^{n-3}\bigr )dr =\int _{\mathbb R}|\psi '|^2dt, \qquad \int _0^\infty \eta ^2r^{n-3}dr=\int _{\mathbb R}\psi ^2dt.  \] The cross term integrates to zero because $\psi $ is compactly supported. A zero right side makes $\psi $ constant and thus zero. To prove sharpness, fix a nonzero $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ and use $\psi _ T(t)=\chi (t/T)$. Its derivative-energy to $L^2$-norm ratio is $T^{-2}\int |\chi '|^2/\int \chi ^2\to 0$. This is the logarithmic substitution underlying [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1, pp. 64–65. $\square$

title: Definition 7.9.5 (The spherical link Rayleigh quotient)
search_title: The spherical link Rayleigh quotient
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Definition 7.9.5 (The spherical link Rayleigh quotient) . C3BBE589F9AC For a smooth minimal link define \[  \lambda _0(L)=\inf _{0\ne \psi \in C^\infty (L)} \frac{\int _ L(|\nabla \psi |^2-|A_ L|^2\psi ^2)\, dA_ L}{\int _ L\psi ^2\, dA_ L}.  \] This is the lowest Rayleigh value of $-\Delta _ L-|A_ L|^2$. It omits the ambient Ricci term $n-1$ that appears in the Jacobi operator for $L$ as a hypersurface of $\mathbb S^ n$. Consequently it is not that spherical hypersurface's full stability eigenvalue. See [ ChMin ] , Section 26, p. 64.

title: Proposition 7.9.6 (The spectral criterion for cone stability)
search_title: The spectral criterion for cone stability
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Proposition 7.9.6 (The spectral criterion for cone stability) . 2C4122B9D586 The cone $C^*(L)$ is stable in Definition 7.9.3 if and only if \[  \lambda _0(L)\geq -\frac{(n-2)^2}{4}.  \] This is [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1, attributed there to Simons. Proof Write $a=(n-2)/2$, $t=\log r$, and $v(t,p)=r^ a\phi (r,p)$. The cone metric and the same integration by parts as in Lemma 7.9.4 give the exact identity \[  Q_ C(\phi ,\phi )=\int _{\mathbb R}\int _ L \left(|\partial _ tv|^2+|\nabla _ Lv|^2+(a^2-|A_ L|^2)v^2\right)dA_ Ldt.  \] If $\lambda _0\geq -a^2$, the angular part plus $a^2v^2$ has nonnegative integral at each fixed $t$, proving stability. Conversely, if a smooth $\psi $ has Rayleigh quotient below $-a^2$, choose $v(t,p)=\chi (t/T)\psi (p)$, with nonzero smooth compactly supported $\chi $. After division by $\int \chi (t/T)^2dt$, the positive time-derivative term is $T^{-2}\int |\chi '|^2/\int \chi ^2$ times $\int _ L\psi ^2$. For large $T$ the total form is negative. This contradicts stability and proves necessity without assuming that the Rayleigh infimum is attained. $\square$

title: Example 7.9.7 (Product-sphere links and the dimension-seven threshold)
search_title: Product-sphere links and the dimension-seven threshold
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Example 7.9.7 (Product-sphere links and the dimension-seven threshold) . BD8080CF7EC4 Let $p,q\geq 1$, set $n=p+q+1$, and put \[  L=\mathbb S^ p\left(\sqrt{\frac p{p+q}}\right) \times \mathbb S^ q\left(\sqrt{\frac q{p+q}}\right)\subset \mathbb S^ n.  \] Writing its radii as $a,b$, a unit normal is $\nu (x,y)=(bx/a,-ay/b)$. Its principal curvatures are $b/a$ with multiplicity $p$ and $-a/b$ with multiplicity $q$. Hence $H_ L=0$ and $|A_ L|^2=p+q=n-1$. The Rayleigh quotient is minimized by constants, so $\lambda _0=-(n-1)$. Proposition 7.9.6 shows that its cone is stable away from zero exactly when $n-1\leq (n-2)^2/4$, or $n\geq 7$ in this family. This is a stability calculation, not a classification of which product cones minimize area. For equal factors with $p=q\geq 3$, Theorem 4.5.8 proves the stronger finite-perimeter minimizing property. Compare the cone examples in [ ChMin ] , Sections 13, 17, and 26.

title: Theorem 7.9.8 (Simons identity for a minimal spherical hypersurface)

Theorem 7.9.8 (Simons identity for a minimal spherical hypersurface) . 8B46D4CA80AE Let $L^ d\subset \mathbb S^{d+1}$ be a smooth two-sided minimal hypersurface of the unit sphere. Its scalar second fundamental form satisfies \[  \Delta _ L h=(d-|A|^2)h,\qquad  rac12\Delta _ L|A|^2=|
abla A|^2+d|A|^2-|A|^4.  \] Here $\Delta _ Lh$ is the rough covariant Laplacian. These are the constant-curvature, minimal specializations of [ HP99 ] , Corollary 2.2, p. 49; the corresponding norm inequality is [ ChMin ] , Lemma 26.5. Proof The Gauss and Codazzi equations follow by decomposing the ambient covariant derivative into its tangential and normal parts. In the unit sphere they give $K_ L(e_ i,e_ k)=1+\kappa _ i\kappa _ k$ in a principal frame and $
abla _ kh_{ij}=
abla _ ih_{kj}$. The latter holds because the normal component of the ambient curvature on three tangent vectors is zero. Tracing Codazzi and using $H=0$ gives $\sum _ k
abla _ kh_{kj}=0$. At a chosen point use a geodesic orthonormal frame diagonalizing $h$. Commutation on a covariant two-tensor gives \[  \Delta h_{ij}=\sum _ k igl ((
abla _ k
abla _ i-
abla _ i
abla _ k)h igr )_{kj},  \] \[   igl ((
abla _ k
abla _ i-
abla _ i
abla _ k)h igr )(e_ k,e_ j) =-h(R^ L(e_ k,e_ i)e_ k,e_ j)-h(e_ k,R^ L(e_ k,e_ i)e_ j).  \] The diagonal component is therefore \[  \Delta h_{ii}=\sum _ k(1+\kappa _ i\kappa _ k)(\kappa _ i-\kappa _ k) =d\kappa _ i-\kappa _ i|A|^2,  \] since $\sum _ k\kappa _ k=0$. The off-diagonal components are zero at this point by the same Gauss equation in a principal frame. This proves the tensor identity. Take its inner product with $h$ and apply the product rule to $|A|^2$ to obtain the second identity. The curvature sign is the one fixed in Proposition 11.3.4 . $\square$

title: Proposition 7.9.9 (An upper bound for the nonflat link Rayleigh value)
search_title: An upper bound for the nonflat link Rayleigh value
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text:
Proposition 7.9.9 (An upper bound for the nonflat link Rayleigh value) . 40C07F2B543A For a smooth closed minimal link $L^{n-1}$ with $A_ L$ not identically zero, \[  \lambda _0(L)\leq -(n-1).  \] Proof Integrate the spherical Simons identity to get \[  \int _ L|
abla A|^2-\int _ L|A|^4 =-(n-1)\int _ L|A|^2.  \] The Lipschitz function $w=|A|$ satisfies $|
abla w|\leq |
abla A|$ almost everywhere. Use $w$ in the Rayleigh quotient by smooth approximation, for example $w_\varepsilon =\sqrt{|A|^2+\varepsilon ^2}$ and passage in $W^{1,2}$. Its denominator tends to the positive number $\int |A|^2$, and its numerator is no larger in the limit than the left side above. This proves the bound. The approximation avoids dividing by $|A|$ at its zero set. Compare [ ChMin ] , the proof of Corollary 26.6, pp. 67–68. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.9.10 (Stable cones with smooth links are flat in dimensions at most six)
search_title: Stable cones with smooth links are flat in dimensions at most six
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Theorem 7.9.10 (Stable cones with smooth links are flat in dimensions at most six) . 0574E4F9C647 Let $2\leq n\leq 6$ and let $L^{n-1}\subset \mathbb S^ n$ be a smooth closed connected embedded two-sided minimal hypersurface. If $C^*(L)$ is stable away from its vertex, then $L$ is a great sphere and $C(L)$ is a hyperplane. This is the smooth-link version of the dimension bound in [ ChMin ] , Corollary 26.6. Proof If $A_ L$ is not identically zero, the previous proposition and the stability criterion give \[  -\frac{(n-2)^2}{4}\leq \lambda _0(L)\leq -(n-1),  \] which is impossible for $2\leq n\leq 6$. Hence $A_ L=0$. Its spherical unit normal has zero Euclidean derivative in every tangent direction, so it is constant on connected $L$. Thus $L$ lies in the equator orthogonal to that normal. It is open in that equator by equality of dimensions, and closed by compactness; hence it is the entire great sphere. The hypotheses include smoothness of the link. Extending this statement to cones with additional singularities requires a separate regularity or dimension-reduction argument. $\square$

title: 3.3 Tangential Jacobians and weighted coarea
search_title: Tangential Jacobians and weighted coarea
text: Integration along fibers is used both to cut currents and to select level sets of controlled perimeter. The relevant derivative on a rectifiable set is tangential; ambient differentiability at almost every ambient point does not by itself define a derivative on that set. We follow [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Section 2, pp. 92–94. Proposition 3.3.1 (Weighted Euclidean area formula) . 82E9244AC74A Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.2.2 , let $h:V\to [0,\infty ]$ be measurable. Then \[  \int _ V h(x)J_ mDf(x)\, dx =\int _{\mathbb R^ n}\sum _{x\in f^{-1}(y)}h(x)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y).  \] The sum means integration against counting measure, and both sides may be infinite. If $h$ is signed, the same identity holds when the left side with $|h|$ is finite. Proof For $h=\chi _ A$ this is the area formula. Additivity gives the identity for nonnegative simple functions; monotone convergence gives the general nonnegative case. Apply it to the positive and negative parts for the signed statement. This is the extension in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, equation (2.5), specialized to a Euclidean domain. Integrability with the Jacobian, rather than unweighted integrability alone, is the relevant condition. $\square$ Definition 3.3.2 (Tangential differential and coarea Jacobian) . 72A60FF7DFA9 Let $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ N$ be countably $m$-rectifiable, $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable, and of locally finite $\mathcal H^ m$ measure. Let $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz, where $1\leq k<m$. On countably many $C^1$ manifold pieces covering $M$ up to a null set, differentiate the restrictions of $f$ in manifold charts. Their differentials agree on overlaps almost everywhere, defining \[  d^ Mf_ x:T_ xM\to \mathbb R^ k,\qquad J^ M_ kf(x)=\sqrt{\det \bigl (d^ Mf_ x(d^ Mf_ x)^*\bigr )}.  \] Set the Jacobian to zero on the exceptional null set. If $k=1$, the tangential gradient represents the differential and $J^ M_1f=|\nabla ^ Mf|$. The existence of the manifold decomposition and the almost-everywhere independence are rectifiability results recorded in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Definition 2.1 and equations (2.2), (2.7); their proofs remain external here. At a point where the ambient differential exists, the tangential differential is its restriction to $T_ xM$. Theorem 3.3.3 (Coarea on a rectifiable set) . 6D91F1CCF988 With $M,f,m,k$ as in Definition 3.3.2 , for every $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable $A\subset M$, \[  \int _ A J^ M_ k f\, d\mathcal H^ m =\int _{\mathbb R^ k}\mathcal H^{m-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(y))\, dy.  \] The fiber measure is measurable and the equality allows infinite values. For almost every $y$, the fiber $M\cap f^{-1}(y)$ is countably $(m-k)$-rectifiable and has locally finite $\mathcal H^{m-k}$ measure in $U$. The coarea and rectifiability assertions are [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, equation (2.8) and Remark 2.10(2), pp. 93–94. Their proofs use manifold decomposition, the manifold coarea theorem, and approximation of Lipschitz maps; those arguments remain external. Local finiteness of the fibers follows from the formula on a countable compact exhaustion and local Lipschitz bounds, which bound $J^ M_ kf$ there. Corollary 3.3.4 (Weighted rectifiable coarea) . F478D1BCB783 For nonnegative measurable $g$ on $M$, \[  \int _ M gJ^ M_ kf\, d\mathcal H^ m =\int _{\mathbb R^ k}\left(\int _{M\cap f^{-1}(y)}g\, d\mathcal H^{m-k}\right)dy.  \] The identity also holds for signed $g$ with $\int _ M|g|J^ M_ kf<\infty $. In particular, if $C=\{ x:J^ M_ kf(x)=0\} $, then $\mathcal H^{m-k}(C\cap f^{-1}(y))=0$ for almost every $y$; no assertion that $f(C)$ has measure zero is made. Proof Approximate a nonnegative function by increasing simple functions and apply Theorem 3.3.3 and monotone convergence on both sides. Positive and negative parts give the signed statement. Set $g=\chi _ C$ for the last assertion. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, equation (2.9). $\square$ Proposition 3.3.5 (Selecting a radial slice of controlled area) . 579B93950659 Let $m\geq 2$, let $M$ satisfy the rectifiability and local-finiteness hypotheses above, and suppose $\overline{B_ b(a)}\subset U$, $0<a_0<b$. Then \[  \int _{a_0}^ b\mathcal H^{m-1}(M\cap \partial B_ r(a))\, dr \leq \mathcal H^ m(M\cap (B_ b(a)\setminus \overline{B_{a_0}(a)})).  \] Consequently, for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a radius $r\in (a_0,b)$, outside any prescribed Lebesgue-null exceptional set, such that the slice measure is at most the right side divided by $b-a_0$, plus $\varepsilon $. Proof Apply weighted coarea to the distance $\rho (x)=|x-a|$ with the annulus indicator. Its tangential gradient has norm at most one. The average bound implies the existence assertion; otherwise integrating the strict opposite inequality outside the exceptional set would contradict the bound. The exceptional-set clause lets this selection be combined with the almost-everywhere conclusions of the current slicing theorem, Theorem 5.4.2 . $\square$ Example 3.3.6 (Projection recovers Fubini) . 33937AFF00CD On $M=\mathbb R^ m$, let $f(x_1,\ldots ,x_ m)=(x_1,\ldots ,x_ k)$. Then $d^ Mf(d^ Mf)^*=I_ k$ and $J^ M_ kf=1$. The fibers are affine copies of $\mathbb R^{m-k}$, so weighted coarea becomes Fubini–Tonelli. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Remark 7.4(2). Example 3.3.7 (An ambient exceptional set can contain the whole surface) . 4C93F9F0300B For $M=\mathbb R^ m\times \{ 0\} \subset \mathbb R^{m+1}$ and $f(x,z)=|z|$, the ambient function is Lipschitz but is not differentiable at any point of $M$. Its restriction to $M$ is constant and its tangential gradient is zero everywhere. Thus assigning an arbitrary ambient derivative on the ambient Lebesgue-null exceptional set is not a definition of the tangential derivative. Differentiation in manifold charts is essential.

title: 4.4 BV coarea and level-set calculus
search_title: BV coarea and level-set calculus
text:
Throughout this section $n\geq 2$. A BV function packages a family of finite-perimeter superlevel sets. The coarea identity makes this precise and turns approximation of functions into approximation of interfaces. We follow [ Giu84 ] , Theorems 1.23–1.24, pp. 20–23, with the superlevel convention $E_ t=\{ u>t\} $ instead of the source's sublevel convention. Perimeter does not require the set to have finite volume. Lemma 4.4.1 (Layer cake and the distance between level sets) . 9CC91C075013 For real numbers $a,b$, \[  a=\int _{\mathbb R}(\chi _{\{ a>t\} }-\chi _{\{ 0>t\} })\, dt, \qquad |a-b|=\int _{\mathbb R}|\chi _{\{ a>t\} }-\chi _{\{ b>t\} }|\, dt.  \] Consequently, for measurable finite-valued functions $u,v$ on an open set $W$, \[  \| u-v\| _{L^1(W)} =\int _{\mathbb R}|(\{ u>t\} \mathbin {	riangle }\{ v>t\} )\cap W|\, dt,  \] including infinite values. Proof The indicators in the first formula differ only on the interval between $0$ and $a$, with the appropriate sign. The absolute difference in the second is the indicator of the interval between $a$ and $b$, up to its endpoints. Integrate the pointwise identity using Tonelli. This is the level-set identity used in [ Giu84 ] , the proof of Theorem 1.23, pp. 20–21. $\square$ Proposition 4.4.2 (Coarea for smooth superlevel sets) . 309A29065003 If $u\in C^\infty (U)$ and $W\subset U$ is open, then \[  \int _ W|
abla u|\, dx=\int _{\mathbb R}P(\{ u>t\} ;W)\, dt.  \] For every regular value $t$, the superlevel boundary inside $U$ is the smooth level hypersurface, and its outward normal is $-
abla u/|
abla u|$. Proof At a regular value, the implicit function theorem and the local divergence theorem give $P(\{ u>t\} ;W)=\mathcal H^{n-1}(W\cap \{ u=t\} )$. The outward normal points toward decreasing $u$. Sard's theorem excludes the nonregular values up to a null set. Apply Theorem 3.2.4 with $f=u$, whose coarea Jacobian is $|
abla u|$. Exhaustion handles noncompact $W$ and possibly infinite integrals. Compare the smooth step in [ Giu84 ] , Theorem 1.23. $\square$ Lemma 4.4.3 (Almost-everywhere convergence of superlevel sets) . 14EFA42D4221 If $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1(U)$, there is a subsequence such that \[  |(\{ u_ j>t\} \mathbin {	riangle }\{ u>t\} )\cap U|\longrightarrow 0 \quad 	ext{for almost every }t\in \mathbb R.  \] The same conclusion holds locally when the convergence is in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, with a single exceptional null set for a countable exhaustion. Proof Choose a subsequence with $\sum _ j\| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(U)}<\infty $. The layer-cake identity and Tonelli show that for almost every $t$ the sum of the displayed symmetric-difference measures is finite; hence its terms tend to zero. For local convergence choose a diagonal subsequence whose errors are summable on each set of a countable relatively compact exhaustion. The union of its exceptional sets is still null. See [ Giu84 ] , p. 21. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.4 (Whole-space BV coarea) . 0D1F3CCF1E8C For $u\in BV(\mathbb R^ n)$, \[  |Du|(\mathbb R^ n)=\int _{\mathbb R}P(E_ t;\mathbb R^ n)\, dt, \qquad E_ t=\{ u>t\} .  \] In particular almost every $E_ t$ has finite perimeter. Its volume may be infinite, especially when $t<0$. Proof For a compactly supported smooth vector field $X$, the signed layer-cake representation gives \[  \int u\operatorname {div}X =\int _{\mathbb R}\int _{E_ t}\operatorname {div}X\, dx\, dt,  \] because the baseline term integrates to zero. Fubini is justified before this cancellation by the bound $|u||\operatorname {div}X|$ on the compact support. If $|X|\leq 1$, the right side is at most $\int P(E_ t)dt$. Taking the supremum proves one inequality. Measurability of $t\mapsto P(E_ t;W)$ for an open $W$ follows by taking the supremum over a countable dense family of compactly supported $C^1$ test fields in the variational definition. For the reverse inequality, let $u_ j$ be smooth mollifications converging strictly as in Corollary 4.2.5 . By Lemma 4.4.3 , pass to a subsequence whose superlevel sets converge in symmetric difference for almost every $t$. Perimeter lower semicontinuity, Fatou, and smooth coarea give \[  \int P(E_ t)\, dt\leq \liminf _ j\int P(\{ u_ j>t\} )\, dt =\lim _ j\int |
abla u_ j|=|Du|(\mathbb R^ n).  \] This proves the identity. The argument is the approximation proof of [ Giu84 ] , Theorem 1.23, with strict approximation supplied here. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.5 (Local and weighted BV coarea) . 37A9B9679336 If $u\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, then almost every $E_ t=\{ u>t\} $ has locally finite perimeter in $U$, and for every Borel $A\subset U$, \[  |Du|(A)=\int _{\mathbb R}|D\chi _{E_ t}|(A)\, dt.  \] Equivalently, for every nonnegative Borel function $g$, \[  \int _ Ug\, d|Du| =\int _{\mathbb R}\int _ Ug\, d|D\chi _{E_ t}|\, dt.  \] The exceptional levels can be fixed once for a countable exhaustion of $U$.
