u (A)=\int |D\chi _{E_ t}|(A)dt$ a finite Borel measure. To justify this measure construction, measurability is known for open $A$ by the countable test-field description; regular approximation and the monotone-class theorem extend it to Borel sets, and Tonelli gives countable additivity. Values at the exceptional levels are set to zero. For an open ball $B$ with $|Du|(\partial B)=0$, apply the layer-cake test argument with fields supported in $B$ to obtain $|Du|(B)\leq 
u (B)$. The mollification and Fatou argument localized to $B$ gives \[  
u (B)\leq \liminf _ j\int _ B|
abla u_ j| \leq \lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}|Du|(B_\varepsilon ) =|Du|(\overline B)=|Du|(B).  \] Here $B_\varepsilon $ is the $\varepsilon $ neighborhood and the middle estimate is Lemma 4.2.3 . At each center only countably many radii have positive boundary mass. Approximation from below by the other radii gives equality on every ball; finite Radon measures agreeing on all balls agree on Borel sets. Thus $
u =|Du|$. For local $u$, choose a compactly supported smooth cutoff equal to one near any prescribed relatively compact open set. Proposition 4.2.2 gives a whole-space BV function agreeing with $u$ there. Its level sets and derivative measures therefore agree locally with those of $u$. A countable exhaustion proves the stated identity and the common exceptional-set assertion throughout $U$. Increasing simple functions and monotone convergence give the weighted version. This local form refines [ Giu84 ] , Theorem 1.23. $\square$ Proposition 4.4.6 (Lipschitz composition preserves local BV) . 9979CFE006F3 Let $u\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and let $F:\mathbb R	o \mathbb R$ have Lipschitz constant $L$. Then $F(u)\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and \[  |D(F(u))|\leq L|Du|  \] as measures. If $u\in BV(U)$ and $F(0)=0$, then $F(u)\in BV(U)$ as well. Proof First let $F$ be smooth with $|F'|\leq L$. Mollify a cutoff of $u$ that agrees with it near a ball $B\Subset U$ with $|Du|(\partial B)=0$. The smooth chain rule gives $|
abla F(u_ j)|\leq L|
abla u_ j|$, and Lipschitz continuity gives $F(u_ j)	o F(u)$ in $L^1(B)$. Lower semicontinuity and the localized mollification bound yield $|D(F(u))|(B)\leq L|Du|(B)$. Approximate radii to obtain this bound on every relatively compact ball. Integrating these ball inequalities against a nonnegative smooth function of the center, dividing by the ball volume, and shrinking the radius yields the inequality on smooth test functions. Radon measure regularity gives the measure inequality. For general $F$, convolve it on the real line. For $0<s<b-a$, its superlevel set is $\{ u>a+s\} $; outside this interval the superlevel set is either all of $U$ or empty, up to the endpoint levels. These two sets have zero relative perimeter. CCE6F12929C4 If $u,v\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, then their maximum and minimum are locally BV and \[  |D\max \{ u,v\} |+|D\min \{ u,v\} |\leq |Du|+|Dv|  \] as measures. Proof For smooth $u,v$, approximate the maximum and minimum by \[  M_\delta = rac{u+v+\sqrt{(u-v)^2+\delta ^2}}2, \qquad m_\delta = rac{u+v-\sqrt{(u-v)^2+\delta ^2}}2.  \] Their gradients are complementary convex combinations of $
abla u,
abla v$, so $|
abla M_\delta |+|
abla m_\delta |\leq |
abla u|+|
abla v|$. Let $\delta \downarrow 0$ using local $L^1$ convergence and lower semicontinuity. title: Lemma 4.4.1 (Layer cake and the distance between level sets)
search_title: Layer cake and the distance between level sets
text: Lemma 4.4.1 (Layer cake and the distance between level sets) . 9CC91C075013 For real numbers $a,b$, \[  a=\int _{\mathbb R}(\chi _{\{ a>t\} }-\chi _{\{ 0>t\} })\, dt, \qquad |a-b|=\int _{\mathbb R}|\chi _{\{ a>t\} }-\chi _{\{ b>t\} }|\, dt.  \] Consequently, for measurable finite-valued functions $u,v$ on an open set $W$, \[  \| u-v\| _{L^1(W)} =\int _{\mathbb R}|(\{ u>t\} \mathbin {\triangle }\{ v>t\} )\cap W|\, dt,  \] including infinite values. Proof The indicators in the first formula differ only on the interval between $0$ and $a$, with the appropriate sign. The absolute difference in the second is the indicator of the interval between $a$ and $b$, up to its endpoints. Integrate the pointwise identity using Tonelli. This is the level-set identity used in [ Giu84 ] , the proof of Theorem 1.23, pp. 20–21. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.4.2 (Coarea for smooth superlevel sets)

text:
Proposition 4.4.2 (Coarea for smooth superlevel sets) . 309A29065003 If $u\in C^\infty (U)$ and $W\subset U$ is open, then \[  \int _ W|
abla u|\, dx=\int _{\mathbb R}P(\{ u>t\} ;W)\, dt.  \] For every regular value $t$, the superlevel boundary inside $U$ is the smooth level hypersurface, and its outward normal is $-
abla u/|
abla u|$. Proof At a regular value, the implicit function theorem and the local divergence theorem give $P(\{ u>t\} ;W)=\mathcal H^{n-1}(W\cap \{ u=t\} )$. The outward normal points toward decreasing $u$. Sard's theorem excludes the nonregular values up to a null set. Apply Theorem 3.2.4 with $f=u$, whose coarea Jacobian is $|
abla u|$. Exhaustion handles noncompact $W$ and possibly infinite integrals. Compare the smooth step in [ Giu84 ] , Theorem 1.23. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.4.3 (Almost-everywhere convergence of superlevel sets)
search_title: Almost-everywhere convergence of superlevel sets
text: Lemma 4.4.3 (Almost-everywhere convergence of superlevel sets) . 14EFA42D4221 If $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1(U)$, there is a subsequence such that \[  |(\{ u_ j>t\} \mathbin {\triangle }\{ u>t\} )\cap U|\longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{for almost every }t\in \mathbb R.  \] The same conclusion holds locally when the convergence is in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, with a single exceptional null set for a countable exhaustion. Proof Choose a subsequence with $\sum _ j\| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(U)}<\infty $. The layer-cake identity and Tonelli show that for almost every $t$ the sum of the displayed symmetric-difference measures is finite; hence its terms tend to zero. For local convergence choose a diagonal subsequence whose errors are summable on each set of a countable relatively compact exhaustion. The union of its exceptional sets is still null. See [ Giu84 ] , p. 21. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.4.4 (Whole-space BV coarea)
search_title: Whole-space BV coarea
text: Theorem 4.4.4 (Whole-space BV coarea) . 0D1F3CCF1E8C For $u\in BV(\mathbb R^ n)$, \[  |Du|(\mathbb R^ n)=\int _{\mathbb R}P(E_ t;\mathbb R^ n)\, dt, \qquad E_ t=\{ u>t\} .  \] In particular almost every $E_ t$ has finite perimeter. Its volume may be infinite, especially when $t<0$. Proof For a compactly supported smooth vector field $X$, the signed layer-cake representation gives \[  \int u\operatorname {div}X =\int _{\mathbb R}\int _{E_ t}\operatorname {div}X\, dx\, dt,  \] because the baseline term integrates to zero. Fubini is justified before this cancellation by the bound $|u||\operatorname {div}X|$ on the compact support. If $|X|\leq 1$, the right side is at most $\int P(E_ t)dt$. Taking the supremum proves one inequality. Measurability of $t\mapsto P(E_ t;W)$ for an open $W$ follows by taking the supremum over a countable dense family of compactly supported $C^1$ test fields in the variational definition. For the reverse inequality, let $u_ j$ be smooth mollifications converging strictly as in Corollary 4.2.5 . By Lemma 4.4.3 , pass to a subsequence whose superlevel sets converge in symmetric difference for almost every $t$. Perimeter lower semicontinuity, Fatou, and smooth coarea give \[  \int P(E_ t)\, dt\leq \liminf _ j\int P(\{ u_ j>t\} )\, dt =\lim _ j\int |\nabla u_ j|=|Du|(\mathbb R^ n).  \] This proves the identity. The argument is the approximation proof of [ Giu84 ] , Theorem 1.23, with strict approximation supplied here. $\square$

title: 6.5 Smooth support and multiplicity
search_title: Smooth support and multiplicity
text:
Stationarity constrains both geometry and multiplicity. On a connected smooth support it forces constant multiplicity and minimality. Without stationarity a density can vary, and its derivative contributes to first variation. The main source is [ Minter ] , Lemma 0.7 and its proof, pp. 8–9. Lemma 6.5.1 (A distributionally constant function is constant) . CB1D1F5465B7 Let $W\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be connected and open, and let $h\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(W)$. If \[  \int _ W h\, \partial _ i\phi \, dx=0 \quad (\phi \in C_ c^\infty (W),\  i=1,\ldots ,m),  \] then $h$ is equal almost everywhere to one constant. Proof On a ball compactly contained in $W$, mollification gives smooth functions whose derivatives vanish on smaller concentric balls. Each mollification is constant on each such smaller ball. Its $L^1$ convergence shows that the limiting function is almost everywhere constant there as well: the constants converge, as seen by taking their averages. Overlapping balls have the same constant. Any two points of a connected open subset of Euclidean space can be joined by a finite chain of overlapping balls, so the local constants agree. This supplies the distributional step in [ Minter ] , Lemma 0.7. $\square$ Proposition 6.5.2 (Tangential stationarity forces constant density) . 5832EF0DAF5B Let $M$ be a connected $C^2$ Riemannian manifold without boundary and let $	heta \in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(M)$. If \[  \int _ M	heta \operatorname {div}_ M Y\, dA=0 \quad 	ext{for all compactly supported }C^1	ext{ tangent fields }Y,  \] then $	heta $ is constant almost everywhere. Proof In coordinates with volume element $\sqrt{g}\, dx$, the divergence is $\operatorname {div}_ M Y=(\sqrt g)^{-1}\partial _ i(\sqrt gY^ i)$. Choose $Y^ i=\phi /\sqrt g$ for one component and zero for the others. The hypothesis becomes $\int 	heta \partial _ i\phi \, dx=0$. Lemma 6.5.1 gives a constant on each connected chart. Constants agree on overlaps and hence throughout connected $M$. The volume factor must be included in this coordinate argument; it is absorbed into the chosen test field. Compare [ Minter ] , the second stage of the proof of Lemma 0.7. $\square$ Theorem 6.5.3 (Constancy on a smooth connected support) . B43FE7AAC565 Let $V$ be a stationary integral $m$-varifold in $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$. Suppose its support is contained in a connected, relatively closed, embedded $C^2$ $m$-submanifold $M\subset U$ without boundary in $U$. Then \[  V=q|M|\quad 	ext{in }U  \] for an integer $q\geq 0$. If $V
e 0$, then $q\geq 1$, $M$ is minimal, and $\operatorname {spt}\| V\| =M$ in $U$. This is the local smooth-support constancy theorem of [ Minter ] , Lemma 0.7, with the connected portion and ambient open set specified. Proof Integrality gives a representation on a rectifiable set with integer density. title: Lemma 6.5.1 (A distributionally constant function is constant)
search_title: A distributionally constant function is constant
text: Lemma 6.5.1 (A distributionally constant function is constant) . CB1D1F5465B7 Let $W\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be connected and open, and let $h\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(W)$. If \[  \int _ W h\, \partial _ i\phi \, dx=0 \quad (\phi \in C_ c^\infty (W),\  i=1,\ldots ,m),  \] then $h$ is equal almost everywhere to one constant. Proof On a ball compactly contained in $W$, mollification gives smooth functions whose derivatives vanish on smaller concentric balls. Each mollification is constant on each such smaller ball. Its $L^1$ convergence shows that the limiting function is almost everywhere constant there as well: the constants converge, as seen by taking their averages. Overlapping balls have the same constant. Any two points of a connected open subset of Euclidean space can be joined by a finite chain of overlapping balls, so the local constants agree. This supplies the distributional step in [ Minter ] , Lemma 0.7. $\square$

title: Proposition 6.5.2 (Tangential stationarity forces constant density)

text: Proposition 6.5.2 (Tangential stationarity forces constant density) . 5832EF0DAF5B Let $M$ be a connected $C^2$ Riemannian manifold without boundary and let $\theta \in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(M)$. If \[  \int _ M\theta \operatorname {div}_ M Y\, dA=0 \quad \text{for all compactly supported }C^1\text{ tangent fields }Y,  \] then $\theta $ is constant almost everywhere. title: 13.2 Obstacle existence, comparison, and reaction
search_title: Obstacle existence, comparison, and reaction
text: We use the admissible set and the sign convention of Definition 13.1.1 : the energy is $\mathcal E_ f(v)=\frac12\int _ U|Dv|^2-\int _ Ufv$, with a lower obstacle. The direct method and one-sided variations already yield existence, comparison, and a reaction measure. The zero-forcing version is developed in [ Fig18 ] , Sections 2–3, pp. 2–5; the proofs below retain an $L^2$ forcing term. Theorem 13.2.1 (Existence and uniqueness for the scalar obstacle problem) . A38AB8D7E124 Under the hypotheses of Definition 13.1.1 , there is a unique minimizer $u\in K$ of $\mathcal E_ f$. Uniqueness is as an $H^1$ function, hence up to almost-everywhere equality. No regularity of its free boundary is part of this assertion. Proof Fix $v_0\in K$ and write $v=v_0+w$, $w\in H^1_0(U)$. Poincare and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[  \mathcal E_ f(v)\geq \tfrac 14\| Dw\| _2^2-C,  \] where $C$ depends on $v_0,f,U$. Thus a minimizing sequence is bounded in $H^1$. Pass to a weakly convergent subsequence. The affine space $g+H^1_0(U)$ is weakly closed. The obstacle constraint is also weakly closed: for every nonnegative $\eta \in L^2(U)$, the inequalities $\int (v_ j-\psi )\eta \geq 0$ pass to the limit and imply $v\geq \psi $ almost everywhere. The squared gradient norm is weakly lower semicontinuous and the forcing term is weakly continuous, so the limit minimizes. If $u_1,u_2$ minimize, their midpoint is admissible. The parallelogram identity shows that its energy is the average energy minus $\frac18\| D(u_1-u_2)\| _2^2$. Thus the gradients agree. Since $u_1-u_2\in H^1_0(U)$, Poincare gives equality of the functions. This extends the proof of [ Fig18 ] , Proposition 2.1, to the stated forcing class. $\square$ Proposition 13.2.2 (The energy gap controls distance to the minimizer) . 96ECD731A7B8 For the minimizer $u$ and any $v\in K$, \[  \mathcal E_ f(v)-\mathcal E_ f(u)\geq \frac12\| D(v-u)\| _{L^2(U)}^2.  \] In particular every minimizing sequence converges strongly to $u$ in $H^1(U)$. Proof Expand the quadratic energy as in Proposition 13.1.2 . Its linear part is nonnegative by the variational inequality, leaving the displayed bound. Poincare controls the $L^2$ norm of $v-u$, since the boundary traces agree. Thus convergence of energies to the minimum implies strong convergence without taking a further subsequence. $\square$ Proposition 13.2.3 (Stability with respect to forcing) . 7F60F782DF82 Keep $U,g,\psi $ fixed and let $u_ i$ minimize with forcing $f_ i\in L^2(U)$. Then \[  \| D(u_1-u_2)\| _2\leq \| f_1-f_2\| _{H^{-1}(U)},  \] where the dual norm uses $\| D\phi \| _2$ on $H^1_0(U)$. Proof Use $u_2$ as the competitor for $u_1$ and $u_1$ for $u_2$ in the two variational inequalities. After addition and rearrangement, \[  \| D(u_1-u_2)\| _2^2\leq \int _ U(f_1-f_2)(u_1-u_2).  \] The difference belongs to $H^1_0(U)$. Apply the dual-norm bound and divide by its gradient norm when this norm is nonzero. The zero case is immediate. $\square$ Proposition 13.2.4 (Comparison for ordered data) . 72D49D22E1E5 On the same bounded Lipschitz domain, suppose $\psi _1\leq \psi _2$ almost everywhere, the boundary traces satisfy $\operatorname {Tr}g_1\leq \operatorname {Tr}g_2$, and $f_1\leq f_2$ almost everywhere. Assume both admissible classes are nonempty. Then their minimizers satisfy $u_1\leq u_2$ almost everywhere. Proof Sobolev truncation and the ordered traces give $w=(u_1-u_2)^+\in H^1_0(U)$. The functions $u_1-w=\min \{ u_1,u_2\} $ and $u_2+w=\max \{ u_1,u_2\} $ are admissible in the first and second problems respectively. The obstacle ordering is needed for the first assertion. Their variational inequalities imply \[  \int _ U|Dw|^2 =\int _ U(Du_1-Du_2)\cdot Dw \leq \int _ U(f_1-f_2)w\leq 0.  \] Poincare gives $w=0$. The Sobolev positive-part chain rule and compatibility of traces with Lipschitz truncation are the functional-analytic inputs, with background in [ SimonPDE ] , Chapters 5–9. $\square$ Proposition 13.2.5 (The nonnegative reaction measure) . 0005FEBA4E50 For a minimizer $u$, the distribution \[  \lambda =-\Delta u-f  \] is a nonnegative Radon measure in $U$. In particular $-\Delta u\geq f$ distributionally. The assertion is local finiteness on compact subsets, not necessarily finite mass on all of $U$. Proof If $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$ is nonnegative, $u+t\phi $ is admissible for $t\geq 0$. The variational inequality gives $\langle \lambda ,\phi \rangle =\int Du\cdot D\phi -\int f\phi \geq 0$. A positive distribution has order zero locally: for test functions supported in a compact $K$, choose a smooth nonnegative cutoff $\eta $ equal to one near $K$. Positivity applied to $\| \phi \| _\infty \eta \pm \phi $ bounds $|\langle \lambda ,\phi \rangle |$ by $\| \phi \| _\infty \langle \lambda ,\eta \rangle $. Extension to continuous test functions and the Riesz representation theorem give a nonnegative Radon measure. This is the forced version of [ Fig18 ] , Proposition 3.1. $\square$ Proposition 13.2.6 (The equation away from contact) . 4D161C1BC5E0 Suppose additionally that $u$ and $\psi $ have continuous representatives. On the open set $O=\{ u>\psi \} $, \[  -\Delta u=f,  \] and the reaction measure vanishes. Consequently its support in $U$ is contained in the contact set $\{ u=\psi \} $. Proof A smooth test function compactly supported in $O$ has support on which $u-\psi $ has a positive minimum. Thus both $u+t\phi $ and $u-t\phi $ are admissible for sufficiently small $t>0$. Their variational inequalities give equality in the weak equation. Since the reaction vanishes on every such test function, it vanishes as a measure on $O$. The contact set is relatively closed by continuity. Compare [ Fig18 ] , Corollary 3.4. Without a continuous representative, a statement involving pointwise contact sets requires additional care. $\square$ Proposition 13.2.7 (The minimizer is the least admissible supersolution) . EE25177AE75F If $v\in K$ satisfies \[  \int _ U Dv\cdot D\phi \geq \int _ U f\phi \quad \text{for every nonnegative }\phi \in H^1_0(U),  \] then the minimizer $u$ satisfies $u\leq v$ almost everywhere. Proof The variational inequality with $u+\phi $ shows that $u$ itself is an admissible supersolution. Set $w=(u-v)^+\in H^1_0(U)$. The competitor $\min \{ u,v\} =u-w$ lies in $K$, so the variational inequality gives $\int Du\cdot Dw\leq \int fw$. The supersolution inequality gives the reverse bound for $Dv$. Subtraction yields $\int |Dw|^2\leq 0$, and Poincare gives the result. This is an order characterization within the stated common boundary class, not an assertion about arbitrary boundary data. $\square$ Proposition 13.2.8 (Subtracting the obstacle and fixing the forcing sign) . 5294DE479829 Assume $\psi \in C^2(U)$ and put $v=u-\psi $. Locally the new obstacle is zero, and differences of energies between competitors with the same boundary values are those of \[  \mathcal J_ a(v)=\int \left(\tfrac 12|Dv|^2+av\right), \qquad a=-f-\Delta \psi .  \] On the noncontact region, whenever Proposition 13.2.6 applies, $\Delta v=a$. The normalized model $a=1$ therefore has a positive linear term in its energy. Proof Expand $|D(\psi +v)|^2$ and compare two competitors whose difference $w$ lies in $H^1_0$ on a relatively compact subdomain. The cross term is $\int D\psi \cdot Dw=-\int (\Delta \psi )w$. Together with $-\int fw$ this gives $\int aw$. The remaining terms depending only on $\psi $ cancel. The equation follows by subtracting $\Delta \psi $ from $\Delta u=-f$. This is the sign convention behind [ Fig18 ] , Section 5; that source begins with $f=0$ and chooses $-\Delta \psi =1$. $\square$

title: 13.3 Obstacle regularity and quadratic blow-ups
search_title: Obstacle regularity and quadratic blow-ups
text: The classical scalar obstacle problem has two distinct regularity questions: regularity of the minimizing function, and regularity of the boundary of its positivity set. The first is optimally $C^{1,1}$ for a $C^{1,1}$ obstacle. The free boundary can still have singular points. We use [ Fig18 ] , Sections 4–7, and state the deep regularity inputs separately from the subsequent elementary arguments. Theorem 13.3.1 (Interior optimal regularity for a smooth obstacle problem) . B6DAB91F1A68 Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, $n\geq 2$, be bounded with $C^1$ boundary. Suppose $\psi \in C^{1,1}(\overline U)$ and $g\in C^1(\overline U)$, with $g\geq \psi $ on $\partial U$. The minimizer of $\frac12\int _ U|Du|^2$ in the class of Definition 13.1.1 belongs to $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. This is [ Fig18 ] , Theorem 4.1, pp. 5–7, under the smooth-data setup of Section 2. Its proof combines quadratic growth from the contact set with interior harmonic estimates; that full regularity argument remains external here. The conclusion is interior and does not assert $C^2$ regularity or a smooth free boundary. Nonemptiness follows from the competitor $\max \{ g,\psi \} $. Lemma 13.3.2 (The Hessian vanishes almost everywhere on contact) . 44A7D8EEBA4E If $v\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and $v\geq 0$, then \[  Dv=0\text{ on }\{ v=0\} ,\qquad D^2v=0\text{ almost everywhere on }\{ v=0\} .  \] Proof Every contact point is a local minimum of the differentiable function, so its gradient is zero. The gradient is locally Lipschitz and hence differentiable almost everywhere by Theorem 3.1.2 . At almost every contact point $x$, the contact set also has Lebesgue density one by Corollary 2.5.7 . At such a point, for any unit vector $e$ there are contact points $y_ r$ with $|y_ r-(x+re)|=o(r)$: otherwise a sequence of missing balls of radius comparable to $r$ would contradict density one at $x$. Lipschitz continuity of $Dv$ and $Dv(y_ r)=Dv(x)=0$ imply $Dv(x+re)=o(r)$. Differentiability of $Dv$ then gives $D^2v(x)e=0$ in every direction. This proves the claim and supplies the contact-set step in [ Fig18 ] , Section 5, footnote 1. $\square$ Proposition 13.3.3 (The strong equation and complementarity) . 171E528F6D01 Suppose a minimizer $u$ and its obstacle $\psi $ are $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Put $v=u-\psi \geq 0$ and $a=-f-\Delta \psi $, with derivatives interpreted almost everywhere. Then \[  \Delta v=a\chi _{\{ v>0\} },\qquad \lambda =a\chi _{\{ v=0\} }\, dx\geq 0.  \] In particular $a\geq 0$ almost everywhere on contact. This statement assumes the displayed regularity; it does not infer it for arbitrary $L^2$ forcing. Proof On $\{ v>0\} $ use the noncontact equation. On $\{ v=0\} $ the preceding lemma gives $\Delta v=0$ almost everywhere. Because $v$ is $C^{1,1}$ locally, its distributional Laplacian has no singular part. Thus the two identities hold distributionally as well. Finally $\lambda =-\Delta u-f=a-\Delta v$ is nonnegative by Proposition 13.2.5 . Compare [ Fig18 ] , equation (5.1). $\square$ Definition 13.3.4 (The normalized classical obstacle equation) . 93AD2E417FD0 In this and the following section a normalized obstacle solution is a function $u\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ open and $n\geq 2$, satisfying \[  u\geq 0,\qquad \Delta u=\chi _{\{ u>0\} }\quad \text{almost everywhere in }U.  \] Its contact set is $\Lambda =\{ u=0\} $, its positivity set is $O=\{ u>0\} $, and its interior free boundary is $\Gamma =\partial O\cap U$. This is [ Fig18 ] , equation (5.2), after subtracting an obstacle with Laplacian $-1$ in the zero-forcing problem. Proposition 13.3.5 (The normalized equation is a variational obstacle equation) . 8273D1F0942D On every bounded Lipschitz $B\Subset U$, a normalized obstacle solution minimizes \[  \mathcal J(v)=\int _ B\left(\tfrac 12|Dv|^2+v\right)  \] among nonnegative $H^1(B)$ functions with $v-u\in H^1_0(B)$. Conversely a local minimizer in this class that is $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ satisfies the normalized equation. Proof For any competitor, integration by parts gives \[  \int _ B Du\cdot D(v-u)+\int _ B(v-u) =\int _ B(1-\Delta u)(v-u)=\int _{B\cap \Lambda }v\geq 0.  \] The variational inequality therefore proves minimality. Conversely, apply Proposition 13.3.3 with obstacle zero and forcing $f=-1$. This connects the normalized equation to the preceding variational theory without changing its sign convention. $\square$ Example 13.3.6 (The half-parabola model) . 7DB8F77B9F40 For a unit vector $e$, the function $h_ e(x)=\frac12((x\cdot e)^+)^2$ is $C^{1,1}$ and solves the normalized equation in all of $\mathbb R^ n$. Its gradient is $(x\cdot e)^+e$ and its Hessian is $e\otimes e$ on the positive half-space and zero on the negative half-space. The gradient is continuous across the interface, so the Laplacian has no surface measure. Its free boundary is a hyperplane, and it is generally not $C^2$ there. This is the regular model in [ Fig18 ] , Section 7.1. Example 13.3.7 (Quadratic models with thin contact sets) . C310C087055D Let $A$ be a symmetric nonnegative $n\times n$ matrix with $\operatorname {tr}A=1$. Then $p_ A(x)=\frac12x\cdot Ax$ solves the normalized equation: its contact set is $\ker A$, which has Lebesgue measure zero, and $\Delta p_ A=1$ everywhere. Its free boundary is exactly $\ker A$, of dimension between zero and $n-1$. For example, $|x|^2/(2n)$ has an isolated contact point, while $x_1^2/2$ has a hyperplane contact set with positivity on both sides. These differ from the half-parabola despite the last model having the same free-boundary hyperplane. See [ Fig18 ] , Section 7.2. Proposition 13.3.8 (Quadratic upper growth at the free boundary) . 5F4BD3841B73 Let $u$ solve the normalized equation, let $x_0\in \Gamma $, and suppose $\overline{B_ r(x_0)}\subset U$. If $Du$ has Lipschitz constant $L$ on this ball, then \[  0\leq \sup _{B_ r(x_0)}u\leq \frac L2r^2.  \] Proof Continuity and nonnegativity give $u(x_0)=0$ and $Du(x_0)=0$. Along the segment from $x_0$ to $x$, integrate $Du$ and use $|Du(x_0+t(x-x_0))|\leq Lt|x-x_0|$. This gives $u(x)\leq L|x-x_0|^2/2$. This is the Taylor estimate of [ Fig18 ] , Lemma 6.1. $\square$ Proposition 13.3.9 (Quadratic nondegeneracy) . 8279B7503355 If $u$ solves the normalized equation, $x_0\in \overline O\cap U$, and $\overline{B_ r(x_0)}\subset U$, then \[  \sup _{B_ r(x_0)}u\geq \frac{r^2}{2n}.  \] Proof First suppose $x_0\in O$. The function $h(x)=u(x)-|x-x_0|^2/(2n)$ is harmonic on $O\cap B_ r(x_0)$ and is positive at $x_0$. On the portion of its boundary inside $B_ r$, it is nonpositive, because that portion is in contact. The maximum principle on the component containing $x_0$ therefore puts a positive maximum on the spherical part of the boundary. There $u>r^2/(2n)$. Continuity equates the supremum over the open ball with the maximum over its closure. For $x_0\in \Gamma $, take $x_ j\in O$ tending to $x_0$ and $r_ j=r-|x_ j-x_0|>0$. The preceding bound on $B_{r_ j}(x_ j)\subset B_ r(x_0)$ gives $\sup _{B_ r(x_0)}u\geq r_ j^2/(2n)$. Send $j$ to infinity. This is [ Fig18 ] , Proposition 6.2; the maximum principle can be applied on an arbitrary bounded component because $h$ is continuous on its closure. $\square$ Definition 13.3.10 (Quadratic rescaling and obstacle blow-ups) . 02791D94E898 For $x_0\in \Gamma $ and $r>0$, set \[  u_{x_0,r}(x)=\frac{u(x_0+rx)}{r^2},\qquad x\in (U-x_0)/r.  \] A blow-up at $x_0$ is a limit of such functions along radii decreasing to zero, in $C^1$ on every compact set. This normalization is dictated by the upper and lower quadratic growth bounds; see [ Fig18 ] , equation (7.1). Theorem 13.3.11 (Compactness and nontriviality of obstacle blow-ups) . CD7780B6E0B3 Let $u$ be a normalized obstacle solution and $x_0\in \Gamma $. Every sequence $r_ j\downarrow 0$ has a subsequence for which $u_{x_0,r_ j}\to u_0$ in $C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n)$. The limit is a nonzero global normalized obstacle solution, with $0\in \partial \{ u_0>0\} $, $u_0(0)=|Du_0(0)|=0$, and a global bound on the Lipschitz constant of its gradient. No homogeneity or classification is assumed in this compactness statement. Proof Choose a fixed ball about $x_0$ on which $Du$ is Lipschitz with constant $L$. Scaling gives $D^2u_{x_0,r}(x)=D^2u(x_0+rx)$ almost everywhere, so the same gradient Lipschitz constant works on every fixed ball once $r$ is small. The values and gradients vanish at zero and are consequently bounded on fixed balls. Arzela–Ascoli and a diagonal subsequence give $C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence and a $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ limit with the bound $L$. Each rescaling satisfies $\Delta u_{x_0,r}=\chi _{\{ u_{x_0,r}>0\} }$. Where $u_0>0$, uniform convergence makes the approximants positive locally, so $\Delta u_0=1$ there. On its contact set the Hessian vanishes almost everywhere by Lemma 13.3.2 . Since the limit has a bounded weak Hessian, these two conclusions give the normalized equation on the whole space. This does not assume convergence of the characteristic functions on the limiting contact set. Nondegeneracy and convergence on every $\overline{B_ s}$ give $\sup _{B_ s}u_0\geq s^2/(2n)$. Thus the limit is nontrivial and zero remains on its free boundary. This expands the compactness discussion in [ Fig18 ] , pp. 10–11. $\square$ Definition 13.3.12 (Regular free-boundary points) . E00124214AB7 A point $x_0\in \Gamma $ is regular if some blow-up is $h_ e$ from Example 13.3.6 for a unit vector $e$. The definition initially requires only one sequence of radii. See [ Fig18 ] , Definition 7.1. Definition 13.3.13 (Singular free-boundary points) . E44AFB608CAD A point $x_0\in \Gamma $ is singular if some blow-up is $p_ A$ from Example 13.3.7 . Write $\Sigma $ for the set of these points. The definition alone does not establish uniqueness of $A$ or rule out other blow-up types. See [ Fig18 ] , Definition 7.2. Theorem 13.3.14 (The classical regular–singular dichotomy) . 02EBA4F86CC8 For a normalized classical obstacle solution, every interior free-boundary point belongs to exactly one of the regular and singular classes above. Near each regular point the free boundary is a real-analytic hypersurface consisting only of regular points. Consequently the regular set is relatively open in $\Gamma $ and $\Sigma $ is relatively closed. This is the classification and regular-point conclusion of [ Fig18 ] , Theorem 7.3, pp. 13–16, attributed there to Caffarelli. Its semiconvexity, classification, and free-boundary improvement arguments remain external. It applies to the constant-coefficient normalized classical obstacle equation, not automatically to thin obstacles, variable forcing, or geometric obstacles.

title: 13.4 Weiss and Monneau monotonicity
search_title: Weiss and Monneau monotonicity
text:
Monotonicity identifies the homogeneity of blow-ups and removes subsequence ambiguity at singular points. Throughout this section $u$ is a normalized obstacle solution as in Definition 13.3.4 , the chosen free-boundary point has been translated to zero, and $\overline{B_ R}\subset U$. We follow [ Fig18 ] , Section 8, pp. 17–19. Derivative identities are stated almost everywhere in the radius, with local absolute continuity supplying monotonicity at every radius. Definition 13.4.1 (The Weiss energy) . E7030A133549 For $0<r<R$, define \[  W(r,u)=r^{-n-2}\int _{B_ r}(|Du|^2+2u)\, dx -2r^{-n-3}\int _{\partial B_ r}u^2\, d\mathcal H^{n-1}.  \] The coefficient $2$ in the bulk term corresponds to the equation $\Delta u=1$ on positivity, and the boundary coefficient corresponds to quadratic scaling. Direct change of variables gives $W(r,u)=W(1,u_{0,r})$. This is [ Fig18 ] , Proposition 8.2. Theorem 13.4.2 (Weiss monotonicity and its exact derivative) . F5304A899D2C Let $u$ be a normalized obstacle solution with $0\in \Gamma $ and $\overline{B_ R}\subset U$. The function $r\mapsto W(r,u)$ is locally absolutely continuous and \[   rac{d}{dr}W(r,u) = rac{2}{r^{n+2}}\int _{\partial B_ r} \left(\partial _
u u- rac{2u}{r}ight)^2\, d\mathcal H^{n-1} \geq 0  \] for almost every $r$. It has a finite limit $W(0+,u)$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Proof Write $u_ r(x)=r^{-2}u(rx)$. On a compact interval of positive radii, the $C^{1,1}$ bounds justify differentiation under the fixed-ball integrals and integration by parts for almost every radius. In particular $W(1,u_ r)$ is absolutely continuous and \[   rac{d}{dr}W(1,u_ r) =2\int _{B_1}(1-\Delta u_ r)\partial _ ru_ r +2\int _{\partial B_1}(\partial _
u u_ r-2u_ r)\partial _ ru_ r.  \] The interior integrand vanishes: where $u_ r>0$ the first factor is zero, while on contact both $u_ r$ and $Du_ r$ vanish and $\partial _ ru_ r=r^{-1}(x\cdot Du_ r-2u_ r)=0$. On $\partial B_1$ this last identity becomes $r^{-1}(\partial _
u u_ r-2u_ r)$. Hence \[   rac{d}{dr}W(1,u_ r)= rac2r\int _{\partial B_1}(\partial _
u u_ r-2u_ r)^2.  \] Scaling the surface integral gives the displayed formula. Quadratic upper growth and $|Du(x)|\leq L|x|$ bound both terms in $W$ uniformly at small radii, so its monotone limit is finite. This is the computation in [ Fig18 ] , Proposition 8.2, with its regularity justification and scaling factors explicit. $\square$ Corollary 13.4.3 (Equality in Weiss monotonicity) . A3D7C291127B For $u$ as in Theorem 13.4.2 , the Weiss energy is constant on an interval $(a,b)\subset (0,R)$ if and only if \[  x\cdot Du(x)=2u(x)\quad (a<|x|<b).  \] Equivalently, along every ray the quotient $u(r\omega )/r^2$ is constant while $a<r<b$. Constancy on $(0,b)$ means that $u$ is homogeneous of degree two in $B_ b$. Proof If the energy is constant, the nonnegative derivative formula makes $x\cdot Du-2u$ vanish on almost every sphere in the annulus. Coarea and continuity make it vanish everywhere there. Along a ray, $ rac d{dr}(r^{-2}u(r\omega ))=r^{-3}(r\omega \cdot Du-2u)$, which proves the homogeneity assertion. Conversely that identity makes the derivative of $W$ zero almost everywhere; absolute continuity makes $W$ constant. This gives the equality case of Theorem 13.4.2 . $\square$ Proposition 13.4.4 (Every obstacle blow-up is quadratic homogeneous) . 55AC4AED0949 Every blow-up $u_0$ in Theorem 13.3.11 satisfies \[  u_0(tx)=t^2u_0(x)\quad (t>0),\qquad W(s,u_0)=W(0+,u)\quad (s>0).  \] Proof If $u_{r_ j}	o u_0$ in $C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then for any fixed $s>0$ the bulk and boundary integrals converge, giving $W(s,u_0)=\lim _ jW(s,u_{r_ j})=\lim _ jW(sr_ j,u)=W(0+,u)$. The limit is a normalized obstacle solution, so the equality case on every interval of radii proves global degree-two homogeneity. This uses no classification of homogeneous solutions. $\square$ Proposition 13.4.5 (Weiss energies of the two model families) . D998F7CCB961 For the quadratic polynomials $p_ A$ and half-parabolas $h_ e$, \[  W(r,p_ A)= rac{\omega _ n}{2(n+2)},\qquad W(r,h_ e)= rac{\omega _ n}{4(n+2)} \quad (r>0).  \] Thus the limiting Weiss energy distinguishes regular and singular points once the dichotomy theorem is applied. Proof Both models are degree-two homogeneous and satisfy $u\Delta u=u$ almost everywhere. E7030A133549 For $0<r<R$, define \[  W(r,u)=r^{-n-2}\int _{B_ r}(|Du|^2+2u)\, dx -2r^{-n-3}\int _{\partial B_ r}u^2\, d\mathcal H^{n-1}.  \] The coefficient $2$ in the bulk term corresponds to the equation $\Delta u=1$ on positivity, and the boundary coefficient corresponds to quadratic scaling. Theorem 13.4.2 (Weiss monotonicity and its exact derivative) . F5304A899D2C Let $u$ be a normalized obstacle solution with $0\in \Gamma $ and $\overline{B_ R}\subset U$. The function $r\mapsto W(r,u)$ is locally absolutely continuous and \[   rac{d}{dr}W(r,u) = rac{2}{r^{n+2}}\int _{\partial B_ r} \left(\partial _
u u- rac{2u}{r}ight)^2\, d\mathcal H^{n-1} \geq 0  \] for almost every $r$. It has a finite limit $W(0+,u)$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Proof Write $u_ r(x)=r^{-2}u(rx)$. On a compact interval of positive radii, the $C^{1,1}$ bounds justify differentiation under the fixed-ball integrals and integration by parts for almost every radius. In particular $W(1,u_ r)$ is absolutely continuous and \[   rac{d}{dr}W(1,u_ r) =2\int _{B_1}(1-\Delta u_ r)\partial _ ru_ r +2\int _{\partial B_1}(\partial _
u u_ r-2u_ r)\partial _ ru_ r.  \] The interior integrand vanishes: where $u_ r>0$ the first factor is zero, while on contact both $u_ r$ and $Du_ r$ vanish and $\partial _ ru_ r=r^{-1}(x\cdot Du_ r-2u_ r)=0$. On $\partial B_1$ this last identity becomes $r^{-1}(\partial _
u u_ r-2u_ r)$. Hence \[   rac{d}{dr}W(1,u_ r)= rac2r\int _{\partial B_1}(\partial _
u u_ r-2u_ r)^2.  \] Scaling the surface integral gives the displayed formula. Quadratic upper growth and $|Du(x)|\leq L|x|$ bound both terms in $W$ uniformly at small radii, so its monotone limit is finite. title: Corollary 13.4.3 (Equality in Weiss monotonicity)
search_title: Equality in Weiss monotonicity
text: Corollary 13.4.3 (Equality in Weiss monotonicity) . A3D7C291127B For $u$ as in Theorem 13.4.2 , the Weiss energy is constant on an interval $(a,b)\subset (0,R)$ if and only if \[  x\cdot Du(x)=2u(x)\quad (a<|x|<b).  \] Equivalently, along every ray the quotient $u(r\omega )/r^2$ is constant while $a<r<b$. Constancy on $(0,b)$ means that $u$ is homogeneous of degree two in $B_ b$. Proof If the energy is constant, the nonnegative derivative formula makes $x\cdot Du-2u$ vanish on almost every sphere in the annulus. Coarea and continuity make it vanish everywhere there. Along a ray, $\frac d{dr}(r^{-2}u(r\omega ))=r^{-3}(r\omega \cdot Du-2u)$, which proves the homogeneity assertion. Conversely that identity makes the derivative of $W$ zero almost everywhere; absolute continuity makes $W$ constant. This gives the equality case of Theorem 13.4.2 . $\square$

title: Proposition 13.4.4 (Every obstacle blow-up is quadratic homogeneous)

text: Proposition 13.4.4 (Every obstacle blow-up is quadratic homogeneous) . 55AC4AED0949 Every blow-up $u_0$ in Theorem 13.3.11 satisfies \[  u_0(tx)=t^2u_0(x)\quad (t>0),\qquad W(s,u_0)=W(0+,u)\quad (s>0).  \] Proof If $u_{r_ j}\to u_0$ in $C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then for any fixed $s>0$ the bulk and boundary integrals converge, giving $W(s,u_0)=\lim _ jW(s,u_{r_ j})=\lim _ jW(sr_ j,u)=W(0+,u)$. The limit is a normalized obstacle solution, so the equality case on every interval of radii proves global degree-two homogeneity. This uses no classification of homogeneous solutions. $\square$

text: Theorem 13.4.8 (Uniqueness and continuity of singular blow-ups) . 3BC351E89BC9 At each singular point $x_0$ of a normalized obstacle solution there is one quadratic model $p_{x_0}$ such that \[  u_{x_0,r}\longrightarrow p_{x_0}\quad \text{in }C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n) \quad \text{as }r\downarrow 0.  \] Its matrix depends continuously on $x_0$ within the singular set, and uniformly continuously on compact subsets of that set. title: 12.2 Transition profiles and phase-field energy
search_title: Transition profiles and phase-field energy
text: We separate the elementary energy identities from the later convergence of interfaces. The reference is [ ChAC ] , Sections 2–3, in the June 29, 2023 revision. Throughout, $W(s)=(1-s^2)^2/4$ and $c_ W=2\sqrt2/3$, as in Definition 12.1.1 . The Laplacian has the sign $\Delta =\operatorname {div}\nabla $. Definition 12.2.1 (Local diffuse-interface energy) . CF4888DCD29F For a bounded open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, $n\geq 1$, and $u\in H^1(U)\cap L^4(U)$, define the energy measure and its mass by \[  d\mu _\varepsilon ^ u=\left(\frac\varepsilon 2|Du|^2+\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon \right)dx, \qquad E_\varepsilon (u;A)=\mu _\varepsilon ^ u(A)  \] for Borel $A\subset U$. As a functional on $L^1(U)$, $E_\varepsilon (u;U)=+\infty $ outside this Sobolev domain. No boundary value is prescribed by this definition. This is the localized form of [ ChAC ] , Definition 2.1. Proposition 12.2.2 (Truncation to the two wells decreases energy) . A13F5CC7640E Let $T(s)=\max \{ -1,\min \{ s,1\} \} $. For finite-energy $u$ on $U$, \[  E_\varepsilon (T(u);A)\leq E_\varepsilon (u;A)  \] for every Borel $A\subset U$. If a prescribed Sobolev trace already takes values in $[-1,1]$, truncation preserves that trace. Proof The Sobolev chain rule gives $|D(T(u))|\leq |Du|$ almost everywhere. The potential is unchanged where $|u|\leq 1$, and becomes zero where $|u|>1$. Thus both energy terms decrease pointwise. Trace compatibility with Lipschitz composition gives the final assertion. This is a useful variational consequence of the potential chosen in [ ChAC ] , Definition 2.1; it does not require the Euler equation. $\square$ Proposition 12.2.3 (Maximum bound for smooth critical points) . D9C3CB6B8ECD A smooth solution of $\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u=u(u^2-1)$ on a closed Riemannian manifold satisfies $-1\leq u\leq 1$. The same conclusion holds for $u\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\overline U)$ on a bounded Euclidean domain when its boundary values lie in $[-1,1]$. Proof A maximum larger than one must occur at an interior point, where $\Delta _ g u\leq 0$, while $u(u^2-1)>0$. This contradicts the equation. At a minimum below minus one the two signs are reversed, giving the other bound. Compactness supplies the extrema; connectedness is unnecessary. This proves [ ChAC ] , Exercise 2.1(b), and the stated boundary version. $\square$ Proposition 12.2.4 (Zero energy and connected components) . C2E265EAC5A8 On a connected bounded open Euclidean domain, a finite-energy function has zero energy if and only if it equals $+1$ or $-1$ almost everywhere. On a closed manifold the same assertion holds on each connected component; different components may choose different signs. Proof Both integrands are nonnegative. Zero energy implies $Du=0$ and $W(u)=0$ almost everywhere. A Sobolev function with zero weak gradient is constant on each connected component: mollification makes it constant on interior balls, and overlapping balls propagate the constant. The zeros of $W$ are precisely $\pm 1$. Conversely either constant has zero energy. The argument in coordinate charts proves the manifold statement. The connectedness qualification refines the observation following Exercise 2.1 in [ ChAC ] . $\square$ Lemma 12.2.5 (The one-dimensional Hamiltonian) . 9904DDC4B1C1 If $u\in C^2(I)$ solves $\varepsilon ^2u''=W'(u)$ on an interval, then \[  \frac{\varepsilon ^2}{2}(u')^2-W(u)  \] is constant on $I$. Proof Its derivative is $u'(\varepsilon ^2u''-W'(u))=0$. The identity is the conservation law in [ ChAC ] , Section 2.2. It applies to solutions of the ODE, whereas the energy inequalities below apply to arbitrary competitors. $\square$ Theorem 12.2.6 (Classification of finite-energy entire transition profiles) . E6898370A6C4 Let $u\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ solve $\varepsilon ^2u''=W'(u)$. Its total one-dimensional energy is finite if and only if it is one of \[  u\equiv \pm 1,\qquad u(t)=\pm \tanh \left(\frac{t-t_0}{\varepsilon \sqrt2}\right), \quad t_0\in \mathbb R.  \] Every nonconstant profile in this list has energy $c_ W$. Proof Finiteness gives points $t_ j\to \infty $ at which both $(u'(t_ j))^2$ and $W(u(t_ j))$ tend to zero. Lemma 12.2.5 therefore has constant zero, so $\varepsilon |u'|=\sqrt{2W(u)}$. If $u$ reaches either well, its derivative there is zero; uniqueness for the smooth second-order ODE makes it constant. Otherwise it stays in one of $(-\infty ,-1)$, $(-1,1)$, or $(1,\infty )$ and $u'$ never vanishes. In the middle interval, separation of variables gives exactly the two translated hyperbolic-tangent families. In either exterior interval, choose the time direction in which $|u|$ increases. The time to reach infinity is finite, because $\int _ a^\infty (s^2-1)^{-1}ds<\infty $ for $a>1$. This contradicts an entire solution. Finally the equipartition identity and substitution $s=u(t)$ give energy $\int _{-1}^1\sqrt{2W(s)}ds=c_ W$ for the nonconstant profiles; the constants have zero energy. This supplies the details of [ ChAC ] , Lemma 2.3. $\square$ Definition 12.2.7 (The phase primitive) . B4E1EE0417C5 Set \[  \Phi (t)=\int _0^ t\sqrt{2W(s)}\, ds =\frac1{\sqrt2}\int _0^ t|1-s^2|\, ds.  \] It is odd, continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, and maps $\mathbb R$ onto $\mathbb R$. Its inverse is continuous. In particular $\Phi (\pm 1)=\pm c_ W/2$ and $|\Phi (t)|\leq C(1+|t|^3)$. Strict increase follows because its derivative vanishes only at two points. This is the primitive in [ ChAC ] , Section 3.1. Lemma 12.2.8 (The Sobolev primitive and Modica's energy inequality) . EFCBE4321CEF If $U$ is bounded and $u\in H^1(U)\cap L^4(U)$, then $\Phi (u)\in W^{1,1}(U)$ and \[  D\Phi (u)=\sqrt{2W(u)}Du,\qquad |D\Phi (u)|\leq \frac\varepsilon 2|Du|^2+\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon \quad \text{almost everywhere}.  \] Consequently $|D\Phi (u)|(A)\leq E_\varepsilon (u;A)$ for every Borel $A\subset U$. Proof The cubic growth gives $\Phi (u)\in L^1$. Truncate $u$ to $[-k,k]$ and apply the Lipschitz Sobolev chain rule to the corresponding bounded-range primitive. The gradients converge in $L^1$, since they are bounded by $C(1+|u|^2)|Du|$, which is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz and $u\in L^4$. The functions converge in $L^1$ by the cubic bound. Passing to weak derivatives proves the chain rule. Finally apply $2ab\leq a^2+b^2$ with $a=\sqrt{\varepsilon /2}|Du|$ and $b=\sqrt{W(u)/\varepsilon }$. This proves [ ChAC ] , equation (3.1), including its Sobolev justification. It is an energy inequality, not the pointwise gradient estimate for entire solutions also associated with Modica's name. $\square$ Proposition 12.2.9 (A sharp bound for a one-dimensional transition) . FE09C7FC0E55 For $u\in H^1(a,b)$, using its continuous representative, \[  \int _ a^ b\left(\frac\varepsilon 2|u'|^2+\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon \right)dt \geq |\Phi (u(b))-\Phi (u(a))|.  \] Equality holds exactly when $\varepsilon |u'|=\sqrt{2W(u)}$ almost everywhere and $\Phi (u)$ is monotone. For an entire finite-energy function with limits $-1$ and $+1$, the analogous bound is $c_ W$ and is attained by the increasing profile in Theorem 12.2.6 . Proof Integrate Lemma 12.2.8 , then use the fundamental theorem for the absolutely continuous function $\Phi (u)$. Equality in the first inequality requires $a=b$ in the square inequality, and equality between total variation and endpoint difference requires a derivative of constant sign almost everywhere. These are exactly the stated conditions. On the whole line, apply the bound on $(-R,R)$ and let $R\to \infty $. This makes the transition cost from [ ChAC ] , Exercise 2.3, explicit for competitors as well as solutions. $\square$ Definition 12.2.10 (Energy discrepancy) . F6D965E6AFE8 For a finite-energy function on $U$, its discrepancy is the signed measure \[  d\xi _\varepsilon ^ u= \left(\frac\varepsilon 2|Du|^2-\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon \right)dx.  \] It compares gradient and potential energy. Vanishing is equipartition; no sign is asserted for a general function. This notation isolates the two terms appearing in [ ChAC ] , Sections 2.2 and 3.1. Proposition 12.2.11 (The energy defect controls discrepancy) . 1B56A14C4675 Let $E=E_\varepsilon (u;U)$ and $D=E-\int _ U|D\Phi (u)|$. Then \[  D=\int _ U\left(\sqrt{\frac\varepsilon 2}|Du|-\sqrt{\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon }\right)^2dx, \qquad |\xi _\varepsilon ^ u|(U)\leq \sqrt{2ED}.  \] In particular $D\geq 0$, and $D=0$ is equivalent to equality of the two energy densities almost everywhere. Proof With $a,b$ as in Lemma 12.2.8 , the defect is $\int (a-b)^2$. The discrepancy density is $(a-b)(a+b)$. Cauchy–Schwarz and $(a+b)^2\leq 2(a^2+b^2)$ prove the bound. This quantitative refinement of the square inequality will turn convergence of total energy into equipartition. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.2.3 (Maximum bound for smooth critical points)
search_title: Maximum bound for smooth critical points
text: Proposition 12.2.3 (Maximum bound for smooth critical points) . D9C3CB6B8ECD A smooth solution of $\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u=u(u^2-1)$ on a closed Riemannian manifold satisfies $-1\leq u\leq 1$. The same conclusion holds for $u\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\overline U)$ on a bounded Euclidean domain when its boundary values lie in $[-1,1]$. Proof A maximum larger than one must occur at an interior point, where $\Delta _ g u\leq 0$, while $u(u^2-1)>0$. This contradicts the equation. At a minimum below minus one the two signs are reversed, giving the other bound. Compactness supplies the extrema; connectedness is unnecessary. This proves [ ChAC ] , Exercise 2.1(b), and the stated boundary version. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.2.4 (Zero energy and connected components)
search_title: Zero energy and connected components
text: Proposition 12.2.4 (Zero energy and connected components) . C2E265EAC5A8 On a connected bounded open Euclidean domain, a finite-energy function has zero energy if and only if it equals $+1$ or $-1$ almost everywhere. On a closed manifold the same assertion holds on each connected component; different components may choose different signs. Proof Both integrands are nonnegative. Zero energy implies $Du=0$ and $W(u)=0$ almost everywhere. A Sobolev function with zero weak gradient is constant on each connected component: mollification makes it constant on interior balls, and overlapping balls propagate the constant. The zeros of $W$ are precisely $\pm 1$. Conversely either constant has zero energy. The argument in coordinate charts proves the manifold statement. The connectedness qualification refines the observation following Exercise 2.1 in [ ChAC ] . $\square$

title: Lemma 12.2.5 (The one-dimensional Hamiltonian)
search_title: The one-dimensional Hamiltonian
text: Lemma 12.2.5 (The one-dimensional Hamiltonian) . 9904DDC4B1C1 If $u\in C^2(I)$ solves $\varepsilon ^2u''=W'(u)$ on an interval, then \[  \frac{\varepsilon ^2}{2}(u')^2-W(u)  \] is constant on $I$. Proof Its derivative is $u'(\varepsilon ^2u''-W'(u))=0$. The identity is the conservation law in [ ChAC ] , Section 2.2. It applies to solutions of the ODE, whereas the energy inequalities below apply to arbitrary competitors. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.2.6 (Classification of finite-energy entire transition profiles)
search_title: Classification of finite-energy entire transition profiles
text: Theorem 12.2.6 (Classification of finite-energy entire transition profiles) . E6898370A6C4 Let $u\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ solve $\varepsilon ^2u''=W'(u)$. Its total one-dimensional energy is finite if and only if it is one of \[  u\equiv \pm 1,\qquad u(t)=\pm \tanh \left(\frac{t-t_0}{\varepsilon \sqrt2}\right), \quad t_0\in \mathbb R.  \] Every nonconstant profile in this list has energy $c_ W$. Proof Finiteness gives points $t_ j\to \infty $ at which both $(u'(t_ j))^2$ and $W(u(t_ j))$ tend to zero. Lemma 12.2.5 therefore has constant zero, so $\varepsilon |u'|=\sqrt{2W(u)}$. If $u$ reaches either well, its derivative there is zero; uniqueness for the smooth second-order ODE makes it constant. Otherwise it stays in one of $(-\infty ,-1)$, $(-1,1)$, or $(1,\infty )$ and $u'$ never vanishes. In the middle interval, separation of variables gives exactly the two translated hyperbolic-tangent families. In either exterior interval, choose the time direction in which $|u|$ increases. The time to reach infinity is finite, because $\int _ a^\infty (s^2-1)^{-1}ds<\infty $ for $a>1$. This contradicts an entire solution. Finally the equipartition identity and substitution $s=u(t)$ give energy $\int _{-1}^1\sqrt{2W(s)}ds=c_ W$ for the nonconstant profiles; the constants have zero energy. This supplies the details of [ ChAC ] , Lemma 2.3. $\square$

title: Definition 12.2.7 (The phase primitive)
search_title: The phase primitive
text: Definition 12.2.7 (The phase primitive) . B4E1EE0417C5 Set \[  \Phi (t)=\int _0^ t\sqrt{2W(s)}\, ds =\frac1{\sqrt2}\int _0^ t|1-s^2|\, ds.  \] It is odd, continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, and maps $\mathbb R$ onto $\mathbb R$. Its inverse is continuous. In particular $\Phi (\pm 1)=\pm c_ W/2$ and $|\Phi (t)|\leq C(1+|t|^3)$. Strict increase follows because its derivative vanishes only at two points. This is the primitive in [ ChAC ] , Section 3.1.

title: Lemma 12.2.8 (The Sobolev primitive and Modica's energy inequality)
search_title: The Sobolev primitive and Modica's energy inequality
text: Lemma 12.2.8 (The Sobolev primitive and Modica's energy inequality) . EFCBE4321CEF If $U$ is bounded and $u\in H^1(U)\cap L^4(U)$, then $\Phi (u)\in W^{1,1}(U)$ and \[  D\Phi (u)=\sqrt{2W(u)}Du,\qquad |D\Phi (u)|\leq \frac\varepsilon 2|Du|^2+\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon \quad \text{almost everywhere}.  \] Consequently $|D\Phi (u)|(A)\leq E_\varepsilon (u;A)$ for every Borel $A\subset U$. Proof The cubic growth gives $\Phi (u)\in L^1$. Truncate $u$ to $[-k,k]$ and apply the Lipschitz Sobolev chain rule to the corresponding bounded-range primitive. The gradients converge in $L^1$, since they are bounded by $C(1+|u|^2)|Du|$, which is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz and $u\in L^4$. The functions converge in $L^1$ by the cubic bound. Passing to weak derivatives proves the chain rule. Finally apply $2ab\leq a^2+b^2$ with $a=\sqrt{\varepsilon /2}|Du|$ and $b=\sqrt{W(u)/\varepsilon }$. This proves [ ChAC ] , equation (3.1), including its Sobolev justification. It is an energy inequality, not the pointwise gradient estimate for entire solutions also associated with Modica's name. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.2.9 (A sharp bound for a one-dimensional transition)
search_title: A sharp bound for a one-dimensional transition
text: Proposition 12.2.9 (A sharp bound for a one-dimensional transition) . FE09C7FC0E55 For $u\in H^1(a,b)$, using its continuous representative, \[  \int _ a^ b\left(\frac\varepsilon 2|u'|^2+\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon \right)dt \geq |\Phi (u(b))-\Phi (u(a))|.  \] Equality holds exactly when $\varepsilon |u'|=\sqrt{2W(u)}$ almost everywhere and $\Phi (u)$ is monotone. For an entire finite-energy function with limits $-1$ and $+1$, the analogous bound is $c_ W$ and is attained by the increasing profile in Theorem 12.2.6 . Proof Integrate Lemma 12.2.8 , then use the fundamental theorem for the absolutely continuous function $\Phi (u)$. Equality in the first inequality requires $a=b$ in the square inequality, and equality between total variation and endpoint difference requires a derivative of constant sign almost everywhere. These are exactly the stated conditions. On the whole line, apply the bound on $(-R,R)$ and let $R\to \infty $. This makes the transition cost from [ ChAC ] , Exercise 2.3, explicit for competitors as well as solutions. $\square$

title: Definition 12.2.10 (Energy discrepancy)
search_title: Energy discrepancy
text: Definition 12.2.10 (Energy discrepancy) . F6D965E6AFE8 For a finite-energy function on $U$, its discrepancy is the signed measure \[  d\xi _\varepsilon ^ u= \left(\frac\varepsilon 2|Du|^2-\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon \right)dx.  \] It compares gradient and potential energy. Vanishing is equipartition; no sign is asserted for a general function. This notation isolates the two terms appearing in [ ChAC ] , Sections 2.2 and 3.1.

title: Proposition 12.2.11 (The energy defect controls discrepancy)
search_title: The energy defect controls discrepancy
text: Proposition 12.2.11 (The energy defect controls discrepancy) . 1B56A14C4675 Let $E=E_\varepsilon (u;U)$ and $D=E-\int _ U|D\Phi (u)|$. Then \[  D=\int _ U\left(\sqrt{\frac\varepsilon 2}|Du|-\sqrt{\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon }\right)^2dx, \qquad |\xi _\varepsilon ^ u|(U)\leq \sqrt{2ED}.  \] In particular $D\geq 0$, and $D=0$ is equivalent to equality of the two energy densities almost everywhere. Proof With $a,b$ as in Lemma 12.2.8 , the defect is $\int (a-b)^2$. The discrepancy density is $(a-b)(a+b)$. Cauchy–Schwarz and $(a+b)^2\leq 2(a^2+b^2)$ prove the bound. This quantitative refinement of the square inequality will turn convergence of total energy into equipartition. $\square$

title: 12.3 Phase compactness and the perimeter lower bound
search_title: Phase compactness and the perimeter lower bound
section: 12.3 Phase compactness and the perimeter lower bound
text: The energy bound alone forces two phases and a finite-perimeter interface; no Euler equation is needed. We give the details of [ ChAC ] , Proposition 3.5 and Exercise 3.1, using the BV compactness already established in Theorem 4.2.7 . Throughout this section $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is bounded and open. Lemma 12.3.1 (Quartic coercivity and concentration at the wells) . F41C9F46FACF For every real $s$, \[  W(s)\geq \frac18|s|^4-\frac14, \qquad \operatorname {dist}(s,\{ -1,1\} )^2\leq 4W(s).  \] Thus if $E_\varepsilon (u;U)\leq C$, then \[  \int _ U|u|^4\leq 8C\varepsilon +2|U|, \qquad \int _ U\operatorname {dist}(u,\{ -1,1\} )^2\leq 4C\varepsilon .  \] In particular the measure where the distance from the wells exceeds $\delta >0$ is at most $4C\varepsilon /\delta ^2$. Proof Subtracting $|s|^4/8-1/4$ from $W(s)$ gives $(s^2-2)^2/8$. Also $4W(s)=(|s|-1)^2(|s|+1)^2\geq (|s|-1)^2$. Integrate and use $\int W(u)\leq C\varepsilon $; Chebyshev's inequality gives the last statement. These are the coercivity and well-concentration estimates used in [ ChAC ] , pp. 8–9. $\square$ Proposition 12.3.2 (Binary phases and perimeter normalization) . AC8E360762C1 For a measurable set $E\subset U$, write $u_ E=2\chi _ E-1$. Then $u_ E\in BV(U)$ if and only if $E$ has finite perimeter in $U$, and \[  Du_ E=2D\chi _ E,\qquad |Du_ E|=2|D\chi _ E|, \qquad D\Phi (u_ E)=c_ WD\chi _ E.  \] For two measurable sets, $\| u_ E-u_ F\| _{L^1(U)}=2|E\triangle F|$. Proof Differentiate the affine expressions in distributions; the constant function has zero derivative relative to $U$. Since $\Phi (u_ E)=c_ W\chi _ E-c_ W/2$, the last derivative identity follows. The distance identity is pointwise. This is the two-phase specialization of Example 4.4.12 ; in particular $|D\Phi (u_ E)|=(c_ W/2)|Du_ E|$, retaining the factor two in [ ChAC ] , Proposition 3.5. $\square$ Theorem 12.3.3 (Compactness of bounded diffuse-interface energy) . 95CAAB2DF3CE Let $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ and $u_ j\in H^1(U)\cap L^4(U)$ satisfy $\sup _ j E_{\varepsilon _ j}(u_ j;U)<\infty $. A subsequence converges in $L^ p(U)$ for every $1\leq p<4$ to $u_ E=2\chi _ E-1$, where $E$ has finite perimeter in $U$. Along this subsequence $\Phi (u_ j)\to \Phi (u_ E)$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and \[  c_ W P(E;U)\leq \liminf _ j E_{\varepsilon _ j}(u_ j;U).  \] No boundary regularity or boundary trace condition is assumed. Proof Lemma 12.3.1 bounds $u_ j$ in $L^4(U)$. The cubic growth of $\Phi $ bounds $\Phi (u_ j)$ in $L^1(U)$, and Lemma 12.2.8 bounds their total variations. BV compactness and a diagonal almost-everywhere extraction give $\Phi (u_ j)\to v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and almost everywhere. Continuity of $\Phi ^{-1}$ gives $u_ j\to u_0=\Phi ^{-1}(v)$ almost everywhere. Fatou and $\int W(u_ j)\to 0$ show $u_0\in \{ -1,1\} $ almost everywhere. The $L^4$ bound gives uniform integrability on the finite-measure set $U$. More explicitly, $\int _ A|u_ j|\leq C|A|^{3/4}$, and truncation at a large value makes the remaining tails uniformly small. Dominated convergence for the bounded truncations then gives $L^1(U)$ convergence. Interpolation between this convergence and the uniform $L^4$ bound gives convergence in every $L^ p$, $p<4$. Write $u_0=u_ E$. Lower semicontinuity of variation applied to $\Phi (u_ j)$ gives $c_ WP(E;U)\leq \liminf _ j\int _ U|D\Phi (u_ j)|\leq \liminf _ jE_{\varepsilon _ j}(u_ j;U)$. Here the lower-semicontinuity theorem permits local $L^1$ convergence even when the variation is measured on all of $U$. The finite volume gives $u_ E\in L^1(U)$, so $E$ has finite relative perimeter. This fills out [ ChAC ] , Proposition 3.5; quartic coercivity upgrades the local convergence there to global convergence on bounded $U$. $\square$ Theorem 12.3.4 (The perimeter lower bound for a prescribed limit) . D022437E926D Suppose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ and $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1(U)$. Then \[  \liminf _ j E_{\varepsilon _ j}(u_ j;U)\geq \begin{cases}  c_ WP(E;U),& u=2\chi _ E-1\text{ a.e.},\  E\text{ of finite perimeter},\\  +\infty ,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] If the energies are uniformly bounded and $u=u_ E$, the localized bound $c_ WP(E;A)\leq \liminf _ j E_{\varepsilon _ j}(u_ j;A)$ holds for every open $A\subset U$. Proof If the liminf is finite, select a subsequence attaining it with bounded energy and apply Theorem 12.3.3 . Its phase limit must be the prescribed $L^1$ limit. This proves the global assertion, including infinite perimeter. For any fixed open $A$, restrict the sequence to $A$ and repeat the same argument for its energy liminf; $A$ is bounded and the prescribed convergence restricts to it. The subsequence used to prove the inequality may depend on $A$, but the inequality concerns the original sequence. This is the liminf conclusion of [ ChAC ] , Proposition 3.5. $\square$ Proposition 12.3.5 (The limiting energy measure dominates perimeter) . 0AB8B0DD0379 Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 12.3.3 , with $u_ j\to u_ E$ in $L^1(U)$. If a subsequence of the energy measures converges weakly on compactly supported continuous tests in $U$ to $\mu $, then \[  \mu \geq c_ W|D\chi _ E|  \] as Radon measures on $U$. Proof Pass further to the primitive-convergent subsequence in Theorem 12.3.3 ; this preserves $\mu $ and $u_ E$. For $X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ n)$, integration by parts and the pointwise energy inequality give \[  \left|\int _ U\Phi (u_ j)\operatorname {div}X\right| \leq \int _ U|X|\, d\mu _{\varepsilon _ j}^{u_ j}.  \] Pass to the limit. The resulting bound says that the vector measure $D\Phi (u_ E)$ has total variation at most $\mu $, by the dual characterization of total variation with localized test fields. Proposition 12.3.2 identifies this variation as $c_ W|D\chi _ E|$. Equality is an additional assertion and need not hold. $\square$ Corollary 12.3.6 (Energy convergence forces equipartition) . 194D96DE584A Suppose $u_ j\to u_ E$ in $L^1(U)$, $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, and $E_{\varepsilon _ j}(u_ j;U)\to c_ WP(E;U)<\infty $. Then \[  \int _ U|D\Phi (u_ j)|\to c_ WP(E;U),\qquad |\xi _{\varepsilon _ j}^{u_ j}|(U)\to 0.  \] Each of the gradient and potential energies tends to $c_ WP(E;U)/2$. Proof For every subsequence, bounded energy gives a further subsequence whose primitives converge locally to $\Phi (u_ E)$. Lower semicontinuity gives the lower bound $c_ WP(E;U)$ for their variations, while the energy inequality gives the matching upper bound. The subsequence criterion therefore gives convergence along the whole sequence. Its energy defect tends to zero. Proposition 12.2.11 makes the total variation of discrepancy tend to zero. Since the sum of the two energies converges to $c_ WP(E;U)$ and their difference tends to zero, each converges to half the sum. $\square$ Example 12.3.7 (Two disappearing layers can retain energy) . D80927740693 Let $U=(-1,1)$, $a_\varepsilon =\sqrt\varepsilon $, and \[  u_\varepsilon (x)=q\left(\frac{a_\varepsilon -|x|}\varepsilon \right), \qquad q(t)=\tanh (t/\sqrt2).  \] These $H^1$ functions converge to $-1$ in $L^1(U)$, but their energy measures converge to $2c_ W\delta _0$. Indeed, on each half interval the change of variables $t=(a_\varepsilon -|x|)/\varepsilon $ gives energy tending to $\int _{\mathbb R}(q')^2=c_ W$. Outside any neighborhood of zero the energy tends to zero by exponential decay. The positive-phase interval has length $2a_\varepsilon \to 0$, and pointwise convergence holds away from zero, proving the phase convergence by bounded convergence. The limiting phase has perimeter zero. These are competitors, not claimed solutions of the Euler equation; the example explains why a phase limit alone does not record all interface multiplicity.

title: 12.4 Recovery layers and variational limits
search_title: Recovery layers and variational limits
text:
The lower bound becomes sharp by placing the one-dimensional profile along an interface. We develop the construction behind [ ChAC ] , Proposition 3.6, first for smooth interfaces and then for compactly contained finite-perimeter sets. The general relative-boundary approximation is recorded separately as an external input. Throughout, $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is bounded and open and $n\geq 2$. We write $q(t)=	anh (t/\sqrt2)$ for the profile of Example 12.1.3 . Proposition 12.4.1 (A flat layer and its limiting energy measure) . FB823D886F0F Let $e\in \mathbb S^{n-1}$, $b\in \mathbb R$, and $u_\varepsilon (x)=q((x\cdot e-b)/\varepsilon )$ on $\mathbb R^ n$, where $q(t)=	anh (t/\sqrt2)$. This is a smooth Allen–Cahn solution, and locally \[  u_\varepsilon 	o 2\chi _{\{ x\cdot e>b\} }-1,\qquad \mu _\varepsilon ^{u_\varepsilon }ightharpoonup c_ W\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner \{ x\cdot e=b\} .  \] The phase convergence is in every finite $L^ p$ on bounded sets. Proof The chain rule and $q''=W'(q)$ give the equation. The phase convergence follows pointwise off the hyperplane and then by bounded convergence. Write $x=y+(b+\varepsilon t)e$ with $y\in e^\perp $. Equipartition gives energy density $\varepsilon ^{-1}(q'(t))^2$. For a continuous compactly supported test function $\zeta $, Fubini gives \[  \int \zeta \, d\mu _\varepsilon =\int _{e^\perp }\int _{\mathbb R} \zeta (y+(b+\varepsilon t)e)(q'(t))^2\, dt\, d\mathcal H^{n-1}(y).  \] Its integrand is dominated by an integrable function using the bounded transverse projection of the support and $\int (q')^2=c_ W$. title: 12.5 Gradient bounds and diffuse monotonicity

text:
The energy inequality for arbitrary competitors in Lemma 12.2.8 differs from the pointwise gradient estimate for entire solutions. We now prove the latter and derive the exact energy-ratio identity. The source is [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 1, pp. 27–28. We use $W(s)=(1-s^2)^2/4$ and initially set $\varepsilon =1$. Lemma 12.5.1 (Uniform estimates for bounded entire solutions) . 43AE37D12C79 If $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^ n)$, $|u|\leq 1$, and $\Delta u=W'(u)$, then $u$ is smooth. For every integer $k\geq 1$, $\sup _{\mathbb R^ n}|D^ ku|\leq C(n,k)$. Translates of any such sequence of solutions have a subsequence converging smoothly on compact sets to another solution with values in $[-1,1]$. Proof On each ball of radius two, both $u$ and $W'(u)$ are uniformly bounded. The interior Laplacian estimate of Theorem 7.5.9 , with $p>n$, gives a uniform $W^{2,p}$ bound on a smaller ball. Sobolev embedding gives a uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound for some $\alpha >0$. The polynomial right-hand side then has controlled Hölder derivatives, and Theorem 7.5.8 and its higher-order versions bootstrap to every order on smaller balls. Translation invariance makes the constants independent of the center. Arzelà–Ascoli and a diagonal exhaustion give the asserted compactness. For $n=1$ the same estimates follow directly from $u''=W'(u)$ and boundedness on intervals. This is the elliptic input in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.6 and Problem 1(d); the underlying elliptic estimates remain the previously recorded external inputs. $\square$ Lemma 12.5.2 (A bounded function has arbitrarily small gradient somewhere) . 4E4A8609F931 If $v\in C^2(\mathbb R^ n)$ is bounded, then $\inf _{\mathbb R^ n}|Dv|=0$. Proof Otherwise $|Dv|\geq a>0$. The vector field $X=Dv/|Dv|$ is continuously differentiable and bounded. Its integral curves exist for all forward time: bounded speed prevents escape to infinity in finite time, and local ODE continuation applies on compact sets. Along a curve $\gamma $, $ rac d{dt}v(\gamma (t))=|Dv(\gamma (t))|\geq a$, contradicting boundedness. This proves the elementary step in [ ChAC ] , Problem 1(a). $\square$ Lemma 12.5.3 (The differential inequality for the gradient defect) . 21D87AED7971 For a smooth solution of $\Delta u=W'(u)$, put $P=|Du|^2/2-W(u)$. On the open set $\{ |Du|>0\} $, \[  \Delta P- rac{2W'(u)}{|Du|^2}Du\cdot DP \geq  rac{|DP|^2}{|Du|^2}\geq 0.  \] Proof Differentiation and the Euclidean Bochner identity give $\Delta P=|D^2u|^2-(W'(u))^2$ and $DP=D^2u\, Du-W'(u)Du$. Hence \[  |D^2u|^2\geq  rac{|D^2u\, Du|^2}{|Du|^2} = rac{|DP|^2+2W'(u)Du\cdot DP}{|Du|^2}+(W'(u))^2.  \] Subtract the last square. This is [ ChAC ] , Problem 1(b), with $P$ equal to one-half of the defect used there. The drift coefficients are locally bounded where the gradient is nonzero. $\square$ Theorem 12.5.4 (Modica's pointwise gradient estimate) . 667E950C291A Every $C^2$ entire solution $u:\mathbb R^ n	o [-1,1]$ of $\Delta u=W'(u)$ satisfies \[   rac12|Du|^2\leq W(u).  \] Proof By Lemma 12.5.1 , $S=\sup P$ is finite. Suppose $S>0$, choose $x_ j$ with $P(x_ j)	o S$, and pass to a smooth local limit $v$ of $u(x+x_ j)$. Then $P_ v\leq S$ everywhere and $P_ v(0)=S$. In particular $Dv(0)
e 0$. On the connected component $O$ of $\{ |Dv|>0\} $ containing zero, Lemma 12.5.3 and the strong maximum principle make $P_ v$ constant, equal to $S$. The principle applies locally to the elliptic operator with the displayed drift and no zero-order term; connectedness propagates constancy through $O$. On this component $|Dv|^2=2(W(v)+S)\geq 2S$. A finite boundary point of $O$ would retain this lower bound by continuity and would still lie in the same open regular component, a contradiction. Thus $O$ is both open and closed in $\mathbb R^ n$, so it is all of $\mathbb R^ n$. This contradicts Lemma 12.5.2 . Therefore $S\leq 0$. This supplies the attained and unattained supremum arguments requested in [ ChAC ] , Problem 1(c)–(d). $\square$ Corollary 12.5.5 (Nonpositive discrepancy at arbitrary diffuse scale) . 4EB15D8DC6CD If $u:\mathbb R^ n	o [-1,1]$ solves $\varepsilon ^2\Delta u=W'(u)$, then \[   rac\varepsilon 2|Du|^2- rac{W(u)}\varepsilon \leq 0.  \] Thus the discrepancy measure of Definition 12.2.10 is nonpositive. Proof Apply Theorem 12.5.4 to $v(y)=u(\varepsilon y)$ and divide the resulting inequality by $\varepsilon $. The entire-domain hypothesis is retained by this rescaling. $\square$ Example 12.5.6 (A local solution need not satisfy Modica's bound) . 46CB1D1432FA The initial-value problem $u''=u^3-u$, $u(0)=0$, $u'(0)=2$ has a smooth solution on a neighborhood of zero, with $|u|<1$ after restricting the interval. At zero its defect is $P(0)=2-1/4=7/4>0$. Thus boundedness on a small domain and the Euler equation alone do not imply Theorem 12.5.4 . This also distinguishes the pointwise estimate from the energy inequality, which remains valid for this function. Theorem 12.5.7 (Rigidity in the pointwise gradient estimate) . F85802FCEEC5 Under the hypotheses of Theorem 12.5.4 , equality at one point holds if and only if either $u\equiv \pm 1$ or \[  u(x)=	anh \left( rac{e\cdot x-b}{\sqrt2}ight) \quad 	ext{for some }e\in \mathbb S^{n-1},\  b\in \mathbb R.  \] Proof By the ordered contact principle of Lemma 12.7.2 , a nonconstant solution has $-1<u<1$ everywhere. At an equality point $P=0$, $W(u)>0$ and hence $Du
e 0$. The strong maximum principle used above makes $P=0$ on that regular component. A finite boundary point of the component would have $Du=0$ and $P=0$, forcing $W(u)=0$, impossible for this nonconstant solution. Thus $P=0$ throughout space. Let $q(t)=	anh (t/\sqrt2)$ and $f=q^{-1}(u)$. Since $q'>0$ and $(q')^2=2W(q)$, the equality gives $|Df|=1$. The equation for $u=q(f)$ gives $q'\Delta f=0$, so $f$ is harmonic. Bochner's identity now gives $0=\Delta |Df|^2=2|D^2f|^2$. Therefore $f=e\cdot x-b$ with $|e|=1$. Conversely the displayed layers and constant wells satisfy equality directly. This proves [ ChAC ] , Problem 1(e), including the constant-well alternatives. $\square$ Definition 12.5.8 (The diffuse stress-energy tensor) . We use $(\operatorname {div}T)_ j=\sum _ iD_ iT_{ij}$ and $T:DX=\sum _{i,j}T_{ij}D_ iX_ j$. It provides the integration-by-parts identity behind [ ChAC ] , Problem 1(f). Compact support removes the boundary term. The conclusion uses the Euler equation, not just an energy bound. $\square$ Theorem 12.5.10 (The exact diffuse energy-ratio identity) . E77581190B89 Let $u$ be a smooth Allen–Cahn solution with parameter $\varepsilon >0$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B_ R(a)}$. For $0<r<R$, write $E(r)=E_\varepsilon (u;B_ r(a))$. Then \[   rac d{dr} igl (r^{1-n}E(r) igr ) =r^{-n}\int _{B_ r(a)}\left( rac{W(u)}\varepsilon - rac\varepsilon 2|Du|^2ight)dx +\varepsilon r^{1-n}\int _{\partial B_ r(a)}(\partial _
u u)^2\, d\mathcal H^{n-1}.  \] Proof Translate $a$ to zero. Conservation of $T$ implies $\operatorname {div}(Tx)=\operatorname {tr}T=ne_\varepsilon -\varepsilon |Du|^2$. On the sphere, $x=r
u $, so $(Tx)\cdot 
u =r(e_\varepsilon -\varepsilon (\partial _
u u)^2)$. The divergence theorem and $E'(r)=\int _{\partial B_ r}e_\varepsilon $ give \[  rE'(r)=(n-2)E(r)+2\int _{B_ r} rac{W(u)}\varepsilon +\varepsilon r\int _{\partial B_ r}(\partial _
u u)^2.  \] Differentiate $r^{1-n}E(r)$ and combine terms to obtain the formula. Smoothness justifies it for every $r>0$ under consideration. In particular, for $R\geq r>0$, \[  E_\varepsilon (u;B_ R(a))\geq (R/r)^{n-1}E_\varepsilon (u;B_ r(a)).  \] Proof Corollary 12.5.5 makes the bulk term in Theorem 12.5.10 nonnegative; the boundary term is a square. title: Lemma 12.5.1 (Uniform estimates for bounded entire solutions)
search_title: Uniform estimates for bounded entire solutions
text: Lemma 12.5.1 (Uniform estimates for bounded entire solutions) . 43AE37D12C79 If $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^ n)$, $|u|\leq 1$, and $\Delta u=W'(u)$, then $u$ is smooth. For every integer $k\geq 1$, $\sup _{\mathbb R^ n}|D^ ku|\leq C(n,k)$. Translates of any such sequence of solutions have a subsequence converging smoothly on compact sets to another solution with values in $[-1,1]$. Proof On each ball of radius two, both $u$ and $W'(u)$ are uniformly bounded. The interior Laplacian estimate of Theorem 7.5.9 , with $p>n$, gives a uniform $W^{2,p}$ bound on a smaller ball. Sobolev embedding gives a uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound for some $\alpha >0$. The polynomial right-hand side then has controlled Hölder derivatives, and Theorem 7.5.8 and its higher-order versions bootstrap to every order on smaller balls. Translation invariance makes the constants independent of the center. Arzelà–Ascoli and a diagonal exhaustion give the asserted compactness. For $n=1$ the same estimates follow directly from $u''=W'(u)$ and boundedness on intervals. This is the elliptic input in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.6 and Problem 1(d); the underlying elliptic estimates remain the previously recorded external inputs. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.5.2 (A bounded function has arbitrarily small gradient somewhere)
search_title: A bounded function has arbitrarily small gradient somewhere
text: Lemma 12.5.2 (A bounded function has arbitrarily small gradient somewhere) . 4E4A8609F931 If $v\in C^2(\mathbb R^ n)$ is bounded, then $\inf _{\mathbb R^ n}|Dv|=0$. Proof Otherwise $|Dv|\geq a>0$. The vector field $X=Dv/|Dv|$ is continuously differentiable and bounded. Its integral curves exist for all forward time: bounded speed prevents escape to infinity in finite time, and local ODE continuation applies on compact sets. Along a curve $\gamma $, $\frac d{dt}v(\gamma (t))=|Dv(\gamma (t))|\geq a$, contradicting boundedness. This proves the elementary step in [ ChAC ] , Problem 1(a). $\square$

title: Lemma 12.5.3 (The differential inequality for the gradient defect)
search_title: The differential inequality for the gradient defect
text: Lemma 12.5.3 (The differential inequality for the gradient defect) . 21D87AED7971 For a smooth solution of $\Delta u=W'(u)$, put $P=|Du|^2/2-W(u)$. On the open set $\{ |Du|>0\} $, \[  \Delta P-\frac{2W'(u)}{|Du|^2}Du\cdot DP \geq \frac{|DP|^2}{|Du|^2}\geq 0.  \] Proof Differentiation and the Euclidean Bochner identity give $\Delta P=|D^2u|^2-(W'(u))^2$ and $DP=D^2u\, Du-W'(u)Du$. Hence \[  |D^2u|^2\geq \frac{|D^2u\, Du|^2}{|Du|^2} =\frac{|DP|^2+2W'(u)Du\cdot DP}{|Du|^2}+(W'(u))^2.  \] Subtract the last square. This is [ ChAC ] , Problem 1(b), with $P$ equal to one-half of the defect used there. The drift coefficients are locally bounded where the gradient is nonzero. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.5.4 (Modica's pointwise gradient estimate)
search_title: Modica's pointwise gradient estimate
text: Theorem 12.5.4 (Modica's pointwise gradient estimate) . 667E950C291A Every $C^2$ entire solution $u:\mathbb R^ n\to [-1,1]$ of $\Delta u=W'(u)$ satisfies \[  \frac12|Du|^2\leq W(u).  \] Proof By Lemma 12.5.1 , $S=\sup P$ is finite. Suppose $S>0$, choose $x_ j$ with $P(x_ j)\to S$, and pass to a smooth local limit $v$ of $u(x+x_ j)$. Then $P_ v\leq S$ everywhere and $P_ v(0)=S$. In particular $Dv(0)\ne 0$. On the connected component $O$ of $\{ |Dv|>0\} $ containing zero, Lemma 12.5.3 and the strong maximum principle make $P_ v$ constant, equal to $S$. The principle applies locally to the elliptic operator with the displayed drift and no zero-order term; connectedness propagates constancy through $O$. On this component $|Dv|^2=2(W(v)+S)\geq 2S$. A finite boundary point of $O$ would retain this lower bound by continuity and would still lie in the same open regular component, a contradiction. Thus $O$ is both open and closed in $\mathbb R^ n$, so it is all of $\mathbb R^ n$. This contradicts Lemma 12.5.2 . Therefore $S\leq 0$. This supplies the attained and unattained supremum arguments requested in [ ChAC ] , Problem 1(c)–(d). $\square$

title: Corollary 12.5.5 (Nonpositive discrepancy at arbitrary diffuse scale)

text: Corollary 12.5.5 (Nonpositive discrepancy at arbitrary diffuse scale) . 4EB15D8DC6CD If $u:\mathbb R^ n\to [-1,1]$ solves $\varepsilon ^2\Delta u=W'(u)$, then \[  \frac\varepsilon 2|Du|^2-\frac{W(u)}\varepsilon \leq 0.  \] Thus the discrepancy measure of Definition 12.2.10 is nonpositive. Proof Apply Theorem 12.5.4 to $v(y)=u(\varepsilon y)$ and divide the resulting inequality by $\varepsilon $. The entire-domain hypothesis is retained by this rescaling. $\square$

title: Example 12.5.6 (A local solution need not satisfy Modica's bound)

text: Example 12.5.6 (A local solution need not satisfy Modica's bound) . 46CB1D1432FA The initial-value problem $u''=u^3-u$, $u(0)=0$, $u'(0)=2$ has a smooth solution on a neighborhood of zero, with $|u|<1$ after restricting the interval. This also distinguishes the pointwise estimate from the energy inequality, which remains valid for this function.
