title: 12.6 Stability and level-set geometry
search_title: Stability and level-set geometry
text:
A positive linearized solution, the geometry of regular level sets, and a growth bound give different routes to rigidity. We develop [ ChAC ] , Proposition 4.1 and Sections 5.1–5.4. Elliptic estimates and unique continuation are identified where used; the local computations do not replace those analytic inputs. Definition 12.6.1 (Local Allen-Cahn stability) . A8339114053E A smooth solution of $\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u=W'(u)$ on an open Riemannian manifold is stable if \[  Q_\varepsilon (\phi )=\int \left(\varepsilon |
abla \phi |^2+ \varepsilon ^{-1}W''(u)\phi ^2ight)dV_ g\geq 0 \quad 	ext{for every }\phi \in C_ c^\infty .  \] On a closed manifold all smooth tests are allowed. Compactly supported $H^1$ tests are also admissible by approximation, since the potential is bounded on their common compact support. This is the local form of Proposition 12.1.2 , as used in [ ChAC ] , Section 5.1. Proposition 12.6.2 (A positive linearized solution gives stability) . 4615C9B9B66E Let $u$ be a smooth Allen–Cahn solution. If $v>0$ is smooth and satisfies $\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g v=W''(u)v$, then for every compactly supported smooth $\phi $, \[  Q_\varepsilon (\phi )=\varepsilon \int v^2 \left|
abla \left( rac\phi vight)ight|^2dV_ g\geq 0.  \] Proof Write $\phi =v\eta $ and expand its gradient. The terms other than $v^2|
abla \eta |^2$ integrate to $\int \langle 
abla v,
abla (v\eta ^2)angle + \varepsilon ^{-2}W''(u)v^2\eta ^2=0$ by the equation for $v$. There is no boundary term because $\eta $ is compactly supported and $v$ stays positive there. Multiply by $\varepsilon $. This is the same ground-state mechanism as Proposition 7.6.3 , applied to the Allen–Cahn operator; compare [ ChAC ] , Lemma 5.6. $\square$ Corollary 12.6.3 (Monotone entire solutions are stable) . B2558F130634 If a smooth Euclidean Allen–Cahn solution has $\partial _ eu>0$ everywhere for one fixed unit vector $e$, it is stable for compactly supported variations. In particular every planar heteroclinic is stable. Proof Differentiate the equation in the constant direction $e$. The positive function $v=\partial _ eu$ satisfies the linearized equation, so Proposition 12.6.2 applies. A planar heteroclinic has a strictly positive derivative in its transition direction. This proves [ ChAC ] , Lemma 5.6 without imposing the additional limits needed for the minimizing theorem below. $\square$ Lemma 12.6.4 (The gradient defect and regular level geometry) . 78EF88634BFA Let $u$ be smooth, $w=|
abla u|$, and $
u =
abla u/w$ on the regular set $O=\{ w>0\} $. If $A$ is the second fundamental form of a regular level set with normal $
u $, then on $O$, \[  |

abla 
u |^2 =w^2|A|^2+|
abla _{\{ u=\mathrm{constant}\} }w|^2\geq 0.  \] Also $w$ is locally Lipschitz and $|
abla w|\leq |
abla ^2u|$ almost everywhere on the whole manifold. Proof Differentiate $
abla u=w
u $. The derivatives of the unit vector are perpendicular to it, so the squared norm gives $|
abla ^2u|^2=|
abla w|^2+w^2|
abla 
u |^2$. In a frame tangent to the level set, the tangential derivatives of $
u $ are its second fundamental form. Symmetry of the Hessian gives, for tangent $X$, $w\langle

u 
u ,Xangle =Xw$, so the remaining normal-direction contribution is $w^{-2}|
abla _{\{ u=\mathrm{constant}\} }w|^2$. The norm of a smooth vector field is locally Lipschitz. The usual norm chain rule gives the inequality where $w>0$; on its zero set the weak derivative of $w$ vanishes almost everywhere. Thus the a.e. inequality holds globally. This proves the identities behind [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.5(b),(c),(f). $\square$ Theorem 12.6.5 (The geometric stability inequality) . E4E01C8AC073 For a stable smooth Allen–Cahn solution on a Riemannian manifold and every $\eta \in C_ c^\infty $, \[  \int \left(|
abla ^2u|^2-|
abla |
abla u||^2+ \operatorname {Ric}(
abla u,
abla u)ight)\eta ^2 \leq \int |
abla u|^2|
abla \eta |^2.  \] Proof Put $w=|
abla u|$. Bochner and the equation give \[  	frac 12\Delta _ g w^2=|
abla ^2u|^2+ \varepsilon ^{-2}W''(u)w^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
abla u,
abla u).  \] The compactly supported $H^1$ test $\eta w$ is admissible in stability. Expanding $|
abla (\eta w)|^2$, use $w
abla w=	frac 12
abla w^2$ to integrate the cross term by parts. After division by $\varepsilon $, the potential term cancels the same term in the Bochner formula. The result is exactly the asserted inequality. All products are locally integrable; the norm test can equivalently be approximated by $\eta \sqrt{w^2+\delta ^2}$ and then $\delta \downarrow 0$. This proves [ ChAC ] , Proposition 4.1 and Exercise 4.2, with the test-function justification explicit. $\square$ Corollary 12.6.6 (Stable phases on a closed positive-Ricci manifold) . 674165351C6D On a connected closed Riemannian manifold with positive Ricci curvature, the only smooth stable Allen–Cahn solutions are $u\equiv +1$ and $u\equiv -1$, for every $\varepsilon >0$. Proof Use $\eta =1$ in Theorem 12.6.5 . The Hessian defect is nonnegative by Lemma 12.6.4 ; positivity of Ricci therefore forces $
abla u=0$. Connectedness makes $u$ constant, and the equation permits only $-1,0,1$. The value zero is unstable because $W''(0)=-1$ and the constant test gives $Q_\varepsilon (1)=-\varepsilon ^{-1}\operatorname {Vol}(M)<0$. At the wells $W''(\pm 1)=2$, so stability is immediate. This is the closed-manifold form of [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.3(b). $\square$ Proposition 12.6.7 (Quadratic gradient growth makes the level geometry flat) . 72E89BE7D42F Let $u:\mathbb R^ n	o [-1,1]$, $n\geq 2$, be a stable solution with $\varepsilon =1$. Suppose \[  \int _{B_ R}|Du|^2\leq CR^2\quad (R\geq 1).  \] Then $|D^2u|^2-|D|Du||^2=0$ on $\{ |Du|>0\} $. Consequently the unit gradient direction is constant on each connected regular component, and its level sets there have zero second fundamental form. Proof For $R=2^ k$, use the logarithmic cutoff $\eta _ R=1$ on $B_ R$, $\eta _ R=\log (R^2/|x|)/\log R$ on $B_{R^2}\setminus B_ R$, and zero outside. Compactly supported Lipschitz tests follow by approximation. The geometric stability inequality bounds the nonnegative defect integral against $\eta _ R^2$ by \[   rac1{(\log R)^2}\int _{B_{R^2}\setminus B_ R}|x|^{-2}|Du|^2 \leq  rac{4Ck}{(k\log 2)^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] The estimate sums over $k$ dyadic annuli, using the gradient-growth assumption on the enclosing ball. Fatou gives zero defect almost everywhere; continuity on the regular set gives zero everywhere there. Lemma 12.6.4 gives $D
u =0$, and connectedness makes its value constant. This is the weighted logarithmic-cutoff argument in [ ChAC ] , Section 5.4, and parallels Proposition 7.8.3 . $\square$ Lemma 12.6.8 (From zero level defect to a one-dimensional solution) . B7BCF88ADDC6 Let $u:\mathbb R^ n	o [-1,1]$ be a nonconstant smooth solution with $\varepsilon =1$. If the defect in Lemma 12.6.4 vanishes on its regular set, then $u(x)=f(e\cdot x)$ for a unit vector $e$ and a smooth function $f:\mathbb R	o [-1,1]$. Proof Choose a connected regular component. There the unit gradient is one constant vector $e$. For each constant $a\perp e$, the function $v=\partial _ a u$ vanishes on this nonempty open component and satisfies $\Delta v=W''(u)v$ on all of $\mathbb R^ n$. Unique continuation for this scalar linear elliptic equation gives $v=0$ everywhere. This unique-continuation theorem is an external analytic input, as in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.5(d); it is not proved by the preceding energy estimate. Choosing a basis of $e^\perp $ shows that $u$ is constant on every affine hyperplane perpendicular to $e$, hence has the asserted form. $\square$ Lemma 12.6.9 (Bounded stable one-dimensional profiles) . AF0A25D74045 A bounded $C^2$ solution $f:\mathbb R	o [-1,1]$ of $f''=W'(f)$ is stable on $\mathbb R$ if and only if it is a constant well or a translated, possibly reversed heteroclinic. If a solution $u(x)=f(e\cdot x)$ is stable on $\mathbb R^ n$, then $f$ is stable on $\mathbb R$. Proof For the second assertion rotate $e$ to the last coordinate and test with $\phi (t)\eta (y/R)$, where $\phi $ is compactly supported and $\eta 
ot\equiv 0$ is a fixed compactly supported transverse cutoff. Divide the stability inequality by $\int \eta (y/R)^2$. The transverse gradient contribution tends to zero like $R^{-2}$, giving the one-dimensional stability inequality. The case $n=1$ needs no reduction. The constant zero is unstable by testing with $\phi (t/L)$ and taking $L$ large: its negative potential term is of order $L$ and the gradient term of order $L^{-1}$. A nonconstant solution cannot attain $\pm 1$ or attain $0$ with zero derivative, by ODE uniqueness. If it has a turning point with value $a\in (-1,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $, its conserved Hamiltonian gives a periodic orbit between $-|a|$ and $|a|$. Indeed $f'^2=2(W(f)-W(a))$, positive between the two turning values, and the separated travel-time integrals are finite because their endpoint roots are simple. Let $(s,t)$ lie between successive extrema of this periodic orbit, and extend $h=f'$ on $[s,t]$ by zero. Then $h\in H^1_ c(\mathbb R)$, $h(s)=h(t)=0$, and integration of its linearized equation gives $Q(h)=0$. Nonnegative quadratic forms obey $Q(h,\zeta )=0$ for all compact tests, by applying stability to $h+	au \zeta $ for both signs of $	au $. But integration by parts gives $Q(h,\zeta )=h'(t)\zeta (t)-h'(s)\zeta (s)$, and $h'=f''=W'(f)
e 0$ at either extremum. Choosing a test supported near just one endpoint contradicts this identity. Thus a nonconstant stable profile has no turning point. It is strictly monotone and bounded, so it has distinct limits at both ends. Uniform derivative bounds and convergence of translates show that these limits are equilibria in $\{ -1,0,1\} $, with derivative tending to zero. Conservation of the Hamiltonian requires equal potential values at the two ends; the only distinct pair is $-1,+1$. Separation of variables now gives the heteroclinic. Conversely constant wells are stable, and heteroclinics are stable by their positive translation derivative and Proposition 12.6.2 . This resolves the ODE step in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.5(e). $\square$ Theorem 12.6.10 (Stable rigidity under quadratic gradient growth) . 1AB5B72578D5 Under the hypotheses of Proposition 12.6.7 , either $u\equiv \pm 1$ or \[  u(x)=	anh \left( rac{e\cdot x-b}{\sqrt2}ight), \qquad |e|=1.  \] In particular this conclusion holds for stable solutions on $\mathbb R^3$ with $E_1(u;B_ R)\leq CR^2$ for $R\geq 1$. Proof A constant solution is one of the two wells or zero, and zero is unstable as in Lemma 12.6.9 . For a nonconstant solution, Proposition 12.6.7 and Lemma 12.6.8 reduce it to one dimension. Stability passes to the profile, and Lemma 12.6.9 classifies it. The energy bound in the three-dimensional case implies $\int _{B_ R}|Du|^2\leq 2CR^2$. This proves the version of [ ChAC ] , Theorem 5.10 and Section 5.4, with constant wells included and the unique-continuation dependency explicit. $\square$ Corollary 12.6.11 (Classification of bounded stable solutions in the plane) . B1BFB391165D Every stable solution $u:\mathbb R^2	o [-1,1]$ of $\Delta u=W'(u)$ is a constant well or a planar heteroclinic. Therefore every bounded strictly monotone entire solution in the plane is a heteroclinic. Proof Lemma 12.5.1 gives a uniform gradient bound, so $\int _{B_ R}|Du|^2\leq CR^2$. Apply Theorem 12.6.10 . Strict monotonicity gives stability by Corollary 12.6.3 and excludes constant solutions. This is the two-dimensional classification of [ ChAC ] , Theorem 5.9 and Section 5.3, using the stated analytic dependencies. $\square$

title: Definition 12.6.1 (Local Allen-Cahn stability)

A8339114053E A smooth solution of $\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u=W'(u)$ on an open Riemannian manifold is stable if \[  Q_\varepsilon (\phi )=\int \left(\varepsilon |\nabla \phi |^2+ \varepsilon ^{-1}W''(u)\phi ^2\right)dV_ g\geq 0 \quad \text{for every }\phi \in C_ c^\infty .  \] On a closed manifold all smooth tests are allowed. In particular every planar heteroclinic is stable. Proof Differentiate the equation in the constant direction $e$. title: Corollary 12.6.6 (Stable phases on a closed positive-Ricci manifold)

text: Corollary 12.6.6 (Stable phases on a closed positive-Ricci manifold) . 674165351C6D On a connected closed Riemannian manifold with positive Ricci curvature, the only smooth stable Allen–Cahn solutions are $u\equiv +1$ and $u\equiv -1$, for every $\varepsilon >0$. Proof Use $\eta =1$ in Theorem 12.6.5 . The Hessian defect is nonnegative by Lemma 12.6.4 ; positivity of Ricci therefore forces $\nabla u=0$. title: Proposition 12.6.7 (Quadratic gradient growth makes the level geometry flat)
search_title: Quadratic gradient growth makes the level geometry flat
text: Proposition 12.6.7 (Quadratic gradient growth makes the level geometry flat) . 72E89BE7D42F Let $u:\mathbb R^ n\to [-1,1]$, $n\geq 2$, be a stable solution with $\varepsilon =1$. Suppose \[  \int _{B_ R}|Du|^2\leq CR^2\quad (R\geq 1).  \] Then $|D^2u|^2-|D|Du||^2=0$ on $\{ |Du|>0\} $. Consequently the unit gradient direction is constant on each connected regular component, and its level sets there have zero second fundamental form. Proof For $R=2^ k$, use the logarithmic cutoff $\eta _ R=1$ on $B_ R$, $\eta _ R=\log (R^2/|x|)/\log R$ on $B_{R^2}\setminus B_ R$, and zero outside. Compactly supported Lipschitz tests follow by approximation. The geometric stability inequality bounds the nonnegative defect integral against $\eta _ R^2$ by \[  \frac1{(\log R)^2}\int _{B_{R^2}\setminus B_ R}|x|^{-2}|Du|^2 \leq \frac{4Ck}{(k\log 2)^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] The estimate sums over $k$ dyadic annuli, using the gradient-growth assumption on the enclosing ball. Fatou gives zero defect almost everywhere; continuity on the regular set gives zero everywhere there. Lemma 12.6.4 gives $D\nu =0$, and connectedness makes its value constant. This is the weighted logarithmic-cutoff argument in [ ChAC ] , Section 5.4, and parallels Proposition 7.8.3 . $\square$

title: Lemma 12.6.8 (From zero level defect to a one-dimensional solution)
search_title: From zero level defect to a one-dimensional solution
text: Lemma 12.6.8 (From zero level defect to a one-dimensional solution) . B7BCF88ADDC6 Let $u:\mathbb R^ n\to [-1,1]$ be a nonconstant smooth solution with $\varepsilon =1$. If the defect in Lemma 12.6.4 vanishes on its regular set, then $u(x)=f(e\cdot x)$ for a unit vector $e$ and a smooth function $f:\mathbb R\to [-1,1]$. Proof Choose a connected regular component. There the unit gradient is one constant vector $e$. For each constant $a\perp e$, the function $v=\partial _ a u$ vanishes on this nonempty open component and satisfies $\Delta v=W''(u)v$ on all of $\mathbb R^ n$. Unique continuation for this scalar linear elliptic equation gives $v=0$ everywhere. This unique-continuation theorem is an external analytic input, as in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.5(d); it is not proved by the preceding energy estimate. Choosing a basis of $e^\perp $ shows that $u$ is constant on every affine hyperplane perpendicular to $e$, hence has the asserted form. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.6.9 (Bounded stable one-dimensional profiles)

text: Lemma 12.6.9 (Bounded stable one-dimensional profiles) . AF0A25D74045 A bounded $C^2$ solution $f:\mathbb R\to [-1,1]$ of $f''=W'(f)$ is stable on $\mathbb R$ if and only if it is a constant well or a translated, possibly reversed heteroclinic. If a solution $u(x)=f(e\cdot x)$ is stable on $\mathbb R^ n$, then $f$ is stable on $\mathbb R$. Proof For the second assertion rotate $e$ to the last coordinate and test with $\phi (t)\eta (y/R)$, where $\phi $ is compactly supported and $\eta \not\equiv 0$ is a fixed compactly supported transverse cutoff. Divide the stability inequality by $\int \eta (y/R)^2$. The transverse gradient contribution tends to zero like $R^{-2}$, giving the one-dimensional stability inequality. The case $n=1$ needs no reduction. The constant zero is unstable by testing with $\phi (t/L)$ and taking $L$ large: its negative potential term is of order $L$ and the gradient term of order $L^{-1}$. A nonconstant solution cannot attain $\pm 1$ or attain $0$ with zero derivative, by ODE uniqueness. If it has a turning point with value $a\in (-1,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $, its conserved Hamiltonian gives a periodic orbit between $-|a|$ and $|a|$. Indeed $f'^2=2(W(f)-W(a))$, positive between the two turning values, and the separated travel-time integrals are finite because their endpoint roots are simple. Let $(s,t)$ lie between successive extrema of this periodic orbit, and extend $h=f'$ on $[s,t]$ by zero. Then $h\in H^1_ c(\mathbb R)$, $h(s)=h(t)=0$, and integration of its linearized equation gives $Q(h)=0$. Nonnegative quadratic forms obey $Q(h,\zeta )=0$ for all compact tests, by applying stability to $h+\tau \zeta $ for both signs of $\tau $. But integration by parts gives $Q(h,\zeta )=h'(t)\zeta (t)-h'(s)\zeta (s)$, and $h'=f''=W'(f)\ne 0$ at either extremum. Choosing a test supported near just one endpoint contradicts this identity. Thus a nonconstant stable profile has no turning point. It is strictly monotone and bounded, so it has distinct limits at both ends. Uniform derivative bounds and convergence of translates show that these limits are equilibria in $\{ -1,0,1\} $, with derivative tending to zero. Conservation of the Hamiltonian requires equal potential values at the two ends; the only distinct pair is $-1,+1$. Separation of variables now gives the heteroclinic. Conversely constant wells are stable, and heteroclinics are stable by their positive translation derivative and Proposition 12.6.2 . This resolves the ODE step in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.5(e). $\square$

title: 12.7 Monotone solutions and minimizing properties
search_title: Monotone solutions and minimizing properties
text: Stability is a second-variation condition. A minimizing property compares finite changes and needs an additional argument. Here $\varepsilon =1$, $W(s)=(1-s^2)^2/4$, and $n\geq 2$. We develop the sliding proof in [ ChAC ] , Section 5.1, pp. 17–18. Definition 12.7.1 (Minimization on bounded balls) . D868C40CBC37 A smooth entire function $u$ minimizes the Allen–Cahn energy on bounded balls if, for every Euclidean ball $B$ and every $v\in H^1(B)\cap L^4(B)$ with $v-u\in H^1_0(B)$, \[  E_1(u;B)\leq E_1(v;B).  \] In particular it minimizes against every perturbation supported in a compact subset of space. This comparison is stronger than the nonnegativity of its quadratic second variation. It is the minimizing property used in [ ChAC ] , Proposition 5.8. Lemma 12.7.2 (Strong contact for ordered solutions) . 8A218837EB6A Let $u,v$ be smooth solutions of $\Delta u=W'(u)$ and $\Delta v=W'(v)$ on a connected open set. If $u\leq v$ and equality holds at one interior point, then $u=v$ throughout the set. Proof The function $w=v-u\geq 0$ solves $\Delta w=c(x)w$, where $c(x)=\int _0^1W''(u+t(v-u))dt$ is locally bounded. On a relatively compact ball choose $C\geq \max \{ 0,\sup c\} $. Then $z=-w\leq 0$ satisfies $(\Delta -C)z=(C-c)w\geq 0$. At a zero of $w$, $z$ attains the nonnegative maximum zero. The strong maximum principle, whose zero-order coefficient is now nonpositive, makes $z=0$ on that ball. Thus the zero set of $w$ is open as well as closed; connectedness finishes the proof. This proves [ ChAC ] , Lemma 5.7, without assuming an incorrect sign for $W''$. $\square$ Theorem 12.7.3 (A bounded Dirichlet minimizer on a ball) . 37A7AE57FF5D Let $B$ be a bounded ball and $g\in C^\infty (\overline B)$ with $-1<g<1$ on $\partial B$. There exists a minimizer of $E_1(v;B)$ over $v\in H^1(B)\cap L^4(B)$ with $v-g\in H^1_0(B)$. One can choose it smooth in $B$, continuous on $\overline B$, with $-1<v<1$ everywhere on $\overline B$. No uniqueness is asserted. Proof The class is nonempty, and its infimum is finite and nonnegative. A minimizing sequence has bounded gradient energy and, by quartic coercivity, bounded $L^4$ norm. It is therefore bounded in $H^1(B)$. Weak compactness and Rellich compactness on the ball give a subsequence converging weakly in $H^1$, strongly in $L^2$, and almost everywhere. The affine zero-trace class is weakly closed. Fatou gives lower semicontinuity of the nonnegative potential and finite $L^4$ norm of the limit; weak lower semicontinuity handles the gradient. Thus a minimizer exists. Truncation to $[-1,1]$ preserves the boundary data and cannot increase energy, so choose a bounded minimizer. Compactly supported variations give $\Delta v=W'(v)$ weakly. Interior elliptic regularity makes it smooth. Boundary regularity for the Poisson equation on the smooth ball with bounded forcing and smooth boundary data gives continuity on $\overline B$ and the prescribed boundary values. These are external elliptic and compactness inputs, not consequences of weak convergence alone. Comparison with the constant solutions $\pm 1$ via Lemma 12.7.2 gives strict inequalities in the interior; a constant well would contradict the boundary data. Together with the strict boundary inequalities this proves the assertion. This fills in the existence step of [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.2(a). $\square$ Lemma 12.7.4 (Uniform limits of monotone translates on compact sets) . CCDEB635E7C2 Suppose $u$ is continuously differentiable on $\mathbb R^ n$, $\partial _{x_ n}u>0$, and $u(x',t)\to \pm 1$ as $t\to \pm \infty $ for every $x'$. Then $u(x+se_ n)\to \pm 1$ uniformly on every compact subset as $s\to \pm \infty $. Proof For integer $s\to +\infty $, these continuous functions increase pointwise on a compact set to the continuous constant one. Dini's theorem gives uniform convergence. Monotonicity bounds intermediate real parameters between consecutive integers. Apply the decreasing version at minus infinity. This justifies the compact uniform convergence used in [ ChAC ] , Proposition 5.8. $\square$ Theorem 12.7.5 (Monotonicity with saturated ends gives minimization) . D96A7C9B599C Let $u:\mathbb R^ n\to (-1,1)$ be a smooth solution of $\Delta u=W'(u)$ with \[  \partial _{x_ n}u>0,\qquad \lim _{t\to \pm \infty }u(x',t)=\pm 1 \quad \text{for every }x'\in \mathbb R^{n-1}.  \] Then $u$ minimizes energy on bounded balls in the sense of Definition 12.7.1 . Proof Fix a ball $B$ and choose the minimizer $v$ with boundary data $u$ from Theorem 12.7.3 . Compactness of $\overline B$ and strict bounds give $\max v<1$ and $\min v>-1$. By Lemma 12.7.4 , $u_ s(x)=u(x+se_ n)$ satisfies $u_ s\geq v$ on $\overline B$ for sufficiently large positive $s$. Let $s_*\geq 0$ be the infimum of the parameters $s\geq 0$ with this property. Monotonicity makes the admissible parameters an upper interval, and continuity gives $u_{s_*}\geq v$. If $s_*>0$, strict ordering on $\partial B$ follows from $u_{s_*}>u=v$ there. Unless equality occurs somewhere in $B$, compactness gives a positive gap on $\overline B$, permitting a slightly smaller shift, a contradiction. Interior contact forces $u_{s_*}=v$ on $B$ by Lemma 12.7.2 , again contradicting the strict boundary ordering. Hence $s_*=0$ and $u\geq v$. Start instead with large negative translates, which lie below $v$, and move them upward toward shift zero. The same argument, with the ordering reversed, yields $u\leq v$. Thus $u=v$ on $B$, and it attains the Dirichlet minimum. Since the ball was arbitrary, the claimed property holds. This proves [ ChAC ] , Proposition 5.8; the two limiting phases are a separate hypothesis from stability. $\square$ Proposition 12.7.6 (Area-order energy bound for bounded minimizers) . 92B0918DB383 If a smooth entire solution $u:\mathbb R^ n\to [-1,1]$ minimizes energy on bounded balls, then \[  E_1(u;B_ R(a))\leq C(n)R^{n-1}\quad (R>0)  \] for every center $a$. Proof Lemma 12.5.1 gives a universal gradient bound. For $R\geq 2$, choose a radial cutoff $\eta $ equal to zero on $B_{R-1}(a)$ and one near $\partial B_ R(a)$, with $|D\eta |\leq C$. The competitor $v=1+\eta (u-1)$ has the same trace, takes values in $[-1,1]$, and has bounded gradient. It equals a zero-energy well in the inner ball, so its energy is at most a fixed constant times the volume of the width-one annulus, at most $C(n)R^{n-1}$. Minimality gives the same bound for $u$. For $R<2$, the bounded energy density gives $E_1(u;B_ R(a))\leq CR^ n\leq 2CR^{n-1}$. This proves [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.4. In dimension three the bound meets the growth hypothesis of Theorem 12.6.10 , since minimization implies stability by second variation. $\square$ Proposition 12.7.7 (Limits at the ends of a monotone solution) . D8F9E0D25BDD Suppose $u:\mathbb R^ n\to (-1,1)$, $n\geq 2$, is a smooth Allen–Cahn solution with $\partial _{x_ n}u>0$. Then \[  u(x+te_ n)\longrightarrow u_\pm (x')\quad \text{in }C^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n) \quad \text{as }t\to \pm \infty .  \] The functions $u_\pm :\mathbb R^{n-1}\to [-1,1]$ solve the Allen–Cahn equation and are stable in dimension $n-1$. Their classification is a separate lower-dimensional problem. Proof Bounded monotonicity gives pointwise limits, and a fixed shift in $x_ n$ does not change either limit, so they depend only on $x'$. Lemma 12.5.1 gives smooth local precompactness of the translates. Every subsequential limit must equal the same pointwise limit. The subsequence criterion therefore gives full smooth local convergence, and the equation passes to the limit. Each translate is stable by Corollary 12.6.3 . Smooth convergence passes stability to $u_\pm $, regarded as functions on $\mathbb R^ n$. To obtain stability on $\mathbb R^{n-1}$, test with $\phi (x')\eta (x_ n/R)$, divide by the one-dimensional cutoff's squared integral, and let $R\to \infty $. Its gradient-to-mass ratio tends to zero like $R^{-2}$, leaving exactly the lower-dimensional quadratic form. This proves the end-limit assertion in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.8, without assuming the ends are already the two wells. $\square$ Proposition 12.7.8 (Energy comparison with a monotone end limit) . ED5A458AE4FC For $u$ as in Proposition 12.7.7 and any ball $B_ R(a)\subset \mathbb R^ n$, \[  E_1(u;B_ R(a))\leq E_1(u_+;B_ R(a))+C(n)R^{n-1},  \] where $u_+(x')$ is regarded as a function on $\mathbb R^ n$ independent of $x_ n$. Proof Write $u_ t(x)=u(x+te_ n)$. Differentiate the energy on the fixed ball and use the equation to cancel its interior first variation: \[  \frac d{dt}E_1(u_ t;B_ R(a)) =\int _{\partial B_ R(a)}\partial _ tu_ t\, \partial _\nu u_ t.  \] The uniform gradient estimate and $\partial _ tu_ t>0$ bound this below by $-C(n)\int _{\partial B_ R(a)}\partial _ tu_ t$. Integrate from zero to $T$ and let $T\to \infty $, using smooth convergence on the closed ball. Since $0\leq u_+-u\leq 2$, the resulting boundary integral is bounded by a constant times the sphere area. This proves the energy-transport calculation in [ ChAC ] , Section 5.5, p. 22. $\square$ Theorem 12.7.9 (Monotone bounded solutions in three dimensions) . DB82FE46F8E6 Let $u:\mathbb R^3\to [-1,1]$ solve $\Delta u=W'(u)$ smoothly and satisfy $\partial _{x_3}u>0$. Then \[  u(x)=\tanh \left(\frac{e\cdot x-b}{\sqrt2}\right) \quad \text{with }|e|=1,\  e\cdot e_3>0.  \] No prescribed limit as $x_3\to \pm \infty $ is assumed. Proof Strict monotonicity and boundedness give $-1<u<1$ and stability. The upper end limit is a bounded stable solution on $\mathbb R^2$ by Proposition 12.7.7 . Corollary 12.6.11 makes it a constant well or a planar heteroclinic. Regarded on $\mathbb R^3$, either has energy in $B_ R$ at most $c_ W\pi R^2$: for a layer, slice in its transition direction, bound each transverse disk area by $\pi R^2$, and integrate its one-dimensional density of total mass $c_ W$. Proposition 12.7.8 now gives $E_1(u;B_ R)\leq CR^2$. Theorem 12.6.10 applies. The constant alternatives are excluded by strict monotonicity, which also forces the displayed direction to have positive third component. This is the argument of [ ChAC ] , Theorem 5.3 and Section 5.5, with the end-limit stability and growth steps separated. $\square$

If $u\leq v$ and equality holds at one interior point, then $u=v$ throughout the set. Then $z=-w\leq 0$ satisfies $(\Delta -C)z=(C-c)w\geq 0$. At a zero of $w$, $z$ attains the nonnegative maximum zero. The strong maximum principle, whose zero-order coefficient is now nonpositive, makes $z=0$ on that ball. Thus the zero set of $w$ is open as well as closed; connectedness finishes the proof. This proves [ ChAC ] , Lemma 5.7, without assuming an incorrect sign for $W''$. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.7.3 (A bounded Dirichlet minimizer on a ball)
search_title: A bounded Dirichlet minimizer on a ball
text: Theorem 12.7.3 (A bounded Dirichlet minimizer on a ball) . 37A7AE57FF5D Let $B$ be a bounded ball and $g\in C^\infty (\overline B)$ with $-1<g<1$ on $\partial B$. There exists a minimizer of $E_1(v;B)$ over $v\in H^1(B)\cap L^4(B)$ with $v-g\in H^1_0(B)$. One can choose it smooth in $B$, continuous on $\overline B$, with $-1<v<1$ everywhere on $\overline B$. No uniqueness is asserted. Proof The class is nonempty, and its infimum is finite and nonnegative. A minimizing sequence has bounded gradient energy and, by quartic coercivity, bounded $L^4$ norm. It is therefore bounded in $H^1(B)$. Weak compactness and Rellich compactness on the ball give a subsequence converging weakly in $H^1$, strongly in $L^2$, and almost everywhere. The affine zero-trace class is weakly closed. Fatou gives lower semicontinuity of the nonnegative potential and finite $L^4$ norm of the limit; weak lower semicontinuity handles the gradient. Thus a minimizer exists. Truncation to $[-1,1]$ preserves the boundary data and cannot increase energy, so choose a bounded minimizer. Compactly supported variations give $\Delta v=W'(v)$ weakly. Interior elliptic regularity makes it smooth. Boundary regularity for the Poisson equation on the smooth ball with bounded forcing and smooth boundary data gives continuity on $\overline B$ and the prescribed boundary values. These are external elliptic and compactness inputs, not consequences of weak convergence alone. Comparison with the constant solutions $\pm 1$ via Lemma 12.7.2 gives strict inequalities in the interior; a constant well would contradict the boundary data. Together with the strict boundary inequalities this proves the assertion. This fills in the existence step of [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.2(a). $\square$

title: Lemma 12.7.4 (Uniform limits of monotone translates on compact sets)
search_title: Uniform limits of monotone translates on compact sets
text: Lemma 12.7.4 (Uniform limits of monotone translates on compact sets) . CCDEB635E7C2 Suppose $u$ is continuously differentiable on $\mathbb R^ n$, $\partial _{x_ n}u>0$, and $u(x',t)\to \pm 1$ as $t\to \pm \infty $ for every $x'$. Then $u(x+se_ n)\to \pm 1$ uniformly on every compact subset as $s\to \pm \infty $. Proof For integer $s\to +\infty $, these continuous functions increase pointwise on a compact set to the continuous constant one. Dini's theorem gives uniform convergence. Monotonicity bounds intermediate real parameters between consecutive integers. Apply the decreasing version at minus infinity. This justifies the compact uniform convergence used in [ ChAC ] , Proposition 5.8. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.7.5 (Monotonicity with saturated ends gives minimization)
search_title: Monotonicity with saturated ends gives minimization
text: Theorem 12.7.5 (Monotonicity with saturated ends gives minimization) . D96A7C9B599C Let $u:\mathbb R^ n\to (-1,1)$ be a smooth solution of $\Delta u=W'(u)$ with \[  \partial _{x_ n}u>0,\qquad \lim _{t\to \pm \infty }u(x',t)=\pm 1 \quad \text{for every }x'\in \mathbb R^{n-1}.  \] Then $u$ minimizes energy on bounded balls in the sense of Definition 12.7.1 . Proof Fix a ball $B$ and choose the minimizer $v$ with boundary data $u$ from Theorem 12.7.3 . Compactness of $\overline B$ and strict bounds give $\max v<1$ and $\min v>-1$. By Lemma 12.7.4 , $u_ s(x)=u(x+se_ n)$ satisfies $u_ s\geq v$ on $\overline B$ for sufficiently large positive $s$. Let $s_*\geq 0$ be the infimum of the parameters $s\geq 0$ with this property. Monotonicity makes the admissible parameters an upper interval, and continuity gives $u_{s_*}\geq v$. If $s_*>0$, strict ordering on $\partial B$ follows from $u_{s_*}>u=v$ there. Unless equality occurs somewhere in $B$, compactness gives a positive gap on $\overline B$, permitting a slightly smaller shift, a contradiction. Interior contact forces $u_{s_*}=v$ on $B$ by Lemma 12.7.2 , again contradicting the strict boundary ordering. Hence $s_*=0$ and $u\geq v$. Start instead with large negative translates, which lie below $v$, and move them upward toward shift zero. The same argument, with the ordering reversed, yields $u\leq v$. Thus $u=v$ on $B$, and it attains the Dirichlet minimum. Since the ball was arbitrary, the claimed property holds. This proves [ ChAC ] , Proposition 5.8; the two limiting phases are a separate hypothesis from stability. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.7.6 (Area-order energy bound for bounded minimizers)
search_title: Area-order energy bound for bounded minimizers
text: Proposition 12.7.6 (Area-order energy bound for bounded minimizers) . 92B0918DB383 If a smooth entire solution $u:\mathbb R^ n\to [-1,1]$ minimizes energy on bounded balls, then \[  E_1(u;B_ R(a))\leq C(n)R^{n-1}\quad (R>0)  \] for every center $a$. Proof Lemma 12.5.1 gives a universal gradient bound. For $R\geq 2$, choose a radial cutoff $\eta $ equal to zero on $B_{R-1}(a)$ and one near $\partial B_ R(a)$, with $|D\eta |\leq C$. The competitor $v=1+\eta (u-1)$ has the same trace, takes values in $[-1,1]$, and has bounded gradient. It equals a zero-energy well in the inner ball, so its energy is at most a fixed constant times the volume of the width-one annulus, at most $C(n)R^{n-1}$. Minimality gives the same bound for $u$. For $R<2$, the bounded energy density gives $E_1(u;B_ R(a))\leq CR^ n\leq 2CR^{n-1}$. This proves [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.4. In dimension three the bound meets the growth hypothesis of Theorem 12.6.10 , since minimization implies stability by second variation. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.7.7 (Limits at the ends of a monotone solution)
search_title: Limits at the ends of a monotone solution
text: Proposition 12.7.7 (Limits at the ends of a monotone solution) . D8F9E0D25BDD Suppose $u:\mathbb R^ n\to (-1,1)$, $n\geq 2$, is a smooth Allen–Cahn solution with $\partial _{x_ n}u>0$. Then \[  u(x+te_ n)\longrightarrow u_\pm (x')\quad \text{in }C^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n) \quad \text{as }t\to \pm \infty .  \] The functions $u_\pm :\mathbb R^{n-1}\to [-1,1]$ solve the Allen–Cahn equation and are stable in dimension $n-1$. Their classification is a separate lower-dimensional problem. Proof Bounded monotonicity gives pointwise limits, and a fixed shift in $x_ n$ does not change either limit, so they depend only on $x'$. Lemma 12.5.1 gives smooth local precompactness of the translates. Every subsequential limit must equal the same pointwise limit. The subsequence criterion therefore gives full smooth local convergence, and the equation passes to the limit. Each translate is stable by Corollary 12.6.3 . Smooth convergence passes stability to $u_\pm $, regarded as functions on $\mathbb R^ n$. To obtain stability on $\mathbb R^{n-1}$, test with $\phi (x')\eta (x_ n/R)$, divide by the one-dimensional cutoff's squared integral, and let $R\to \infty $. Its gradient-to-mass ratio tends to zero like $R^{-2}$, leaving exactly the lower-dimensional quadratic form. This proves the end-limit assertion in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 5.8, without assuming the ends are already the two wells. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.7.8 (Energy comparison with a monotone end limit)
search_title: Energy comparison with a monotone end limit
text: Proposition 12.7.8 (Energy comparison with a monotone end limit) . ED5A458AE4FC For $u$ as in Proposition 12.7.7 and any ball $B_ R(a)\subset \mathbb R^ n$, \[  E_1(u;B_ R(a))\leq E_1(u_+;B_ R(a))+C(n)R^{n-1},  \] where $u_+(x')$ is regarded as a function on $\mathbb R^ n$ independent of $x_ n$. Proof Write $u_ t(x)=u(x+te_ n)$. Differentiate the energy on the fixed ball and use the equation to cancel its interior first variation: \[  \frac d{dt}E_1(u_ t;B_ R(a)) =\int _{\partial B_ R(a)}\partial _ tu_ t\, \partial _\nu u_ t.  \] The uniform gradient estimate and $\partial _ tu_ t>0$ bound this below by $-C(n)\int _{\partial B_ R(a)}\partial _ tu_ t$. Integrate from zero to $T$ and let $T\to \infty $, using smooth convergence on the closed ball. Since $0\leq u_+-u\leq 2$, the resulting boundary integral is bounded by a constant times the sphere area. This proves the energy-transport calculation in [ ChAC ] , Section 5.5, p. 22. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.7.9 (Monotone bounded solutions in three dimensions)
search_title: Monotone bounded solutions in three dimensions
text: Theorem 12.7.9 (Monotone bounded solutions in three dimensions) . DB82FE46F8E6 Let $u:\mathbb R^3\to [-1,1]$ solve $\Delta u=W'(u)$ smoothly and satisfy $\partial _{x_3}u>0$. Then \[  u(x)=\tanh \left(\frac{e\cdot x-b}{\sqrt2}\right) \quad \text{with }|e|=1,\  e\cdot e_3>0.  \] No prescribed limit as $x_3\to \pm \infty $ is assumed. Proof Strict monotonicity and boundedness give $-1<u<1$ and stability. The upper end limit is a bounded stable solution on $\mathbb R^2$ by Proposition 12.7.7 . Corollary 12.6.11 makes it a constant well or a planar heteroclinic. Regarded on $\mathbb R^3$, either has energy in $B_ R$ at most $c_ W\pi R^2$: for a layer, slice in its transition direction, bound each transverse disk area by $\pi R^2$, and integrate its one-dimensional density of total mass $c_ W$. Proposition 12.7.8 now gives $E_1(u;B_ R)\leq CR^2$. Theorem 12.6.10 applies. The constant alternatives are excluded by strict monotonicity, which also forces the displayed direction to have positive third component. This is the argument of [ ChAC ] , Theorem 5.3 and Section 5.5, with the end-limit stability and growth steps separated. $\square$

title: 6.6 Radial variation and exact monotonicity
search_title: Radial variation and exact monotonicity
text: Throughout this section $1\leq m<N$, $V$ is an $m$-varifold in an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, and $\mu =\| V\| $. Balls are open. The calculations develop [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, equations (3.3)–(3.6), pp. 240–241, including the endpoint convention needed for general varifolds. Definition 6.6.1 (Mass ratio and radial tilt) . 7577F97C39D0 For $\overline{B_ R(a)}\subset U$, put \[  f_ a(r)=r^{-m}\mu (B_ r(a)),\qquad T_ a(x,S)=\frac{|\pi _{S^\perp }(x-a)|^2}{|x-a|^{m+2}}\quad (x\ne a),  \] and set $T_ a(a,S)=0$. The normalized mass ratio is $f_ a(r)/\omega _ m$. Radial tilt vanishes when the displacement $x-a$ lies in the plane recorded by the varifold; this does not require that the varifold be rectifiable. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, (3.3)–(3.6), pp. 240–241. Lemma 6.6.2 (Divergence of a radial test field) . FF971C87180B Write $r=|x-a|$. If $X(x)=\gamma (r)(x-a)$ is $C^1$, then for $r>0$ \[  \operatorname {div}_ S X=m\gamma (r)+r\gamma '(r) -\frac{\gamma '(r)}r|\pi _{S^\perp }(x-a)|^2.  \] At $a$, if $\gamma $ is constant near zero, the divergence is $m\gamma (0)$. Proof For a unit vector $e\in S$, differentiation gives $\langle D_ eX,e\rangle =\gamma +\gamma '\langle x-a,e\rangle ^2/r$. Sum over an orthonormal basis of $S$ and use $|\pi _ S(x-a)|^2=r^2-|\pi _{S^\perp }(x-a)|^2$. The value at the center follows directly from the linear field there. $\square$ Proposition 6.6.3 (Exact stationary annular identity) . A2E5563F6D93 If $V$ is stationary and $0<\sigma <\rho <R$, then \[  f_ a(\rho )-f_ a(\sigma ) =\int _{G_ m(B_\rho (a)\setminus B_\sigma (a))}T_ a(x,S)\, dV(x,S).  \] The annulus includes its inner sphere and excludes its outer sphere. No assumption about the mass of either sphere is imposed. Proof First suppose both spheres have zero $\mu $ mass. Use the radial cutoff \[  \gamma (r)=\begin{cases}  \sigma ^{-m}-\rho ^{-m},& 0\leq r\leq \sigma ,\\  r^{-m}-\rho ^{-m},& \sigma <r<\rho ,\\  0,& r\geq \rho . \end{cases}  \] Smooth the two corners, keeping the derivative uniformly bounded and the support in a fixed compact subset of $U$. Away from the two spheres the fields and their derivatives converge. Dominated convergence in first variation is therefore valid. Lemma 6.6.2 gives \[  0=m\sigma ^{-m}\mu (B_\sigma )-m\rho ^{-m}\mu (B_\rho ) +m\int _{G_ m(B_\rho \setminus B_\sigma )}T_ a\, dV.  \] For arbitrary radii choose continuity radii $\sigma _ j\uparrow \sigma $ and $\rho _ j\uparrow \rho $, with $\sigma _ j<\rho _ j$. Such choices exist because disjoint positive-mass spheres are at most countable in a compact ball. Open-ball masses converge from below. The annular indicators converge to that of $\{ \sigma \leq |x-a|<\rho \} $; the integrands are bounded on a common annulus separated from $a$. Dominated convergence proves the identity, including both endpoint conventions. $\square$ Corollary 6.6.4 (Density defect and absence of atoms) . 4EA95AAE7E1A For stationary $V$, $\mu (\{ a\} )=0$ and \[  f_ a(\rho )-\omega _ m\Theta ^ m(\mu ,a) =\int _{G_ m(B_\rho (a))}T_ a\, dV<\infty \qquad (0<\rho <R).  \] Proof Theorem 6.1.5 bounds $\mu (B_ r(a))$ by $Cr^ m$ for small $r$, which excludes an atom since $m\geq 1$. In Proposition 6.6.3 send $\sigma \downarrow 0$. The left side converges by the definition of density, and monotone convergence applies on the right. The omitted fiber over $a$ has zero mass. $\square$ Corollary 6.6.5 (Equality and quantitative radial tilt) . E28E9DD8CC63 If $0<\sigma <\rho <R$, then $f_ a(\rho )=f_ a(\sigma )$ precisely when $x-a\in S$ for $V$-almost every $(x,S)$ with $\sigma \leq |x-a|<\rho $. Moreover \[  \int _{G_ m(B_\rho \setminus B_\sigma )}|\pi _{S^\perp }(x-a)|^2\, dV \leq \rho ^{m+2}\bigl (f_ a(\rho )-f_ a(\sigma )\bigr ).  \] Proof The integrand in Proposition 6.6.3 is nonnegative and its denominator is positive on the annulus. An integral of such a function vanishes exactly when the numerator vanishes almost everywhere. Multiplication by the upper bound $|x-a|^{m+2}\leq \rho ^{m+2}$ gives the estimate. This controls radial tilt, not distance from a fixed plane. $\square$ Example 6.6.6 (A stationary varifold with zero density on its support) . 9198A856EB15 Fix an $m$-plane $P\subset \mathbb R^ N$, $m<N$. The general varifold $V=\mathcal L^ N\otimes \delta _ P$ is stationary, has full support, and has zero $m$-density at every point. Proof In coordinates adapted to $P$, first variation is the integral over $\mathbb R^ N$ of $\sum _{i=1}^ m\partial _ iX_ i$, which vanishes by Fubini and compact support. Its normalized mass ratio is $(\omega _ N/\omega _ m)r^{N-m}$, tending to zero. Its weight is not $m$-rectifiable. Thus Corollary 6.3.4 cannot be extended to arbitrary stationary varifolds. $\square$ Example 6.6.7 (A stationary varifold that charges a sphere) . 2B91CC016F24 In $\mathbb R^2$ put $e_\theta =(\cos \theta ,\sin \theta )$ and define a general $1$-varifold by \[  V(\varphi )=\int _0^{2\pi }\varphi (e_\theta ,T_{e_\theta }S^1)\, d\theta +\int _0^{2\pi }\int _1^\infty \varphi (r e_\theta ,\mathbb R e_\theta )\, dr\, d\theta .  \] It is stationary, $\| V\| (S^1)=2\pi $, and \[  \| V\| (B_ r(0))=\begin{cases} 0,& 0<r\leq 1,\\ 2\pi r,& r>1.\end{cases}  \] Consequently the mass ratio of a general stationary varifold need not be continuous or absolutely continuous in radius. Proof Both terms define locally finite nonnegative measures on the Grassmann bundle. Integration by parts along the circle gives first variation $\int _0^{2\pi }X(e_\theta )\cdot e_\theta \, d\theta $. Along each outward ray it gives $-X(e_\theta )\cdot e_\theta $, so their sum vanishes. The ray endpoints have zero length measure. For $r>1$ their total mass in the ball is $2\pi (r-1)$, in addition to the circle mass. For $r\leq 1$ the open ball contains neither term. Outside the circle the weight has planar density $1/|x|$, so this is not a rectifiable $1$-varifold. The circle supplies exactly the radial-tilt jump in Proposition 6.6.3 . $\square$ Proposition 6.6.8 (No stationary varifold supported in a compact interior set) . 2C80FDE3480E If $V$ is stationary in $U$ and $\operatorname {spt}\| V\| $ is compactly contained in $U$, then $V=0$. Proof Choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood of the support and multiply it by $x-a$ for any fixed $a$. Its tangential divergence is $m$ on the support. Stationarity gives $0=m\| V\| (U)$, so the weight and hence the varifold vanish. The compact-containment assumption rules out boundary terms at $\partial U$. $\square$

title: 6.7 Conical structure and convergence of supports

section: 6.7 Conical structure and convergence of supports
text:
This section supplies the homogeneity argument in tangent-cone construction and separates weak measure convergence from convergence of supports. The source for the cone argument is [ Minter ] , Lemmas 1.1–1.2, pp. 11–12. Integral compactness remains the external input in Theorem 6.2.1 . Lemma 6.7.1 (Stationarity is closed under varifold convergence) . 30C4784016ED If stationary $m$-varifolds $V_ j$ converge weakly to $V$ in $U$, then $V$ is stationary in $U$. Proof For $X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N)$ the function $(x,S)\mapsto \operatorname {div}_ S X(x)$ is continuous and compactly supported on the Grassmann bundle. Thus $\delta V(X)=\lim _ j\delta V_ j(X)=0$. This assertion alone does not guarantee that an arbitrary limit is integral; integrality uses Theorem 6.2.1 under its hypotheses. $\square$ Lemma 6.7.2 (The weight determines a rectifiable varifold) . FE7578F66513 Two rectifiable $m$-varifolds with the same weight are equal as measures on the Grassmann bundle. Proof Write their weights as $	heta _ i\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M_ i$ with positive densities. Equality of the weights implies that $M_1$ and $M_2$ differ by an $\mathcal H^ m$-null set, after discarding null subsets. Their approximate tangent planes therefore agree almost everywhere by the rectifiable tangent characterization, Theorem 3.1.4 . Their Radon–Nikodym densities also agree. Substitute into Definition 6.1.2 for every compactly supported continuous test function. The positivity of the densities and rectifiability are essential to this argument. $\square$ Proposition 6.7.3 (Radial tangency gives homogeneous weight) . A324E62A87A7 Let $C$ be a stationary $m$-varifold on all of $\mathbb R^ N$, with $x\in S$ for $C$-almost every $(x,S)$. Its weight $
u $ satisfies \[  s^{-m}\int \phi (x/s)\, d
u (x)=\int \phi (x)\, d
u (x)\qquad (s>0)  \] for every $\phi \in C_ c^1(\mathbb R^ N)$. In particular $
u (sA)=s^ m
u (A)$ for every Borel set $A$. Proof Test stationarity with $X(x)=\phi (x)x$. Radial tangency gives $\int (m\phi +x\cdot D\phi )\, d
u =0$. The derivative of $F(s)=s^{-m}\int \phi (x/s)\, d

Proof Write their weights as $\theta _ i\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M_ i$ with positive densities. text: Here $V$ is an $m$-varifold in $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, $1\leq m<N$, with weight $\mu $. Assume throughout that \[  \delta V(X)=-\int H\cdot X\, d\mu ,\qquad |H|\leq \Lambda \quad \mu \text{-almost everywhere},  \] for compactly supported $C^1$ fields, with $\Lambda \geq 0$. In particular the first variation has no singular boundary part. These are sufficient hypotheses for [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, (3.4)–(3.5), p. 241. No rectifiability is required unless stated. Proposition 6.8.1 (Annular identity with mean-curvature error) . 11614439894F Let $\overline{B_ R(a)}\subset U$ and $0<\sigma <\rho <R$. With $f_ a,T_ a$ as in Definition 6.6.1 , define \[  \gamma _{\sigma ,\rho }(r)=\begin{cases}  \max \{ r,\sigma \} ^{-m}-\rho ^{-m},& r<\rho ,\\ 0,& r\geq \rho . \end{cases}  \] Then \[  f_ a(\rho )-f_ a(\sigma ) =\int _{G_ m(B_\rho (a)\setminus B_\sigma (a))}T_ a\, dV +\frac1m\int \gamma _{\sigma ,\rho }(|x-a|)H(x)\cdot (x-a)\, d\mu .  \] In particular \[  f_ a(\rho )-f_ a(\sigma )\geq -\Lambda \int _\sigma ^\rho f_ a(t)\, dt.  \] Proof Use the cutoff and divergence computation in the proof of Proposition 6.6.3 . First variation is now $-\int \gamma H\cdot (x-a)\, d\mu $, giving the stated sign after rearrangement. Approximate arbitrary radii from below through continuity radii as before; the bounded curvature and local finiteness justify dominated convergence for the extra term. The layer-cake formula \[  \gamma _{\sigma ,\rho }(r)=\int _\sigma ^\rho m t^{-m-1}\boldsymbol 1_{\{ r<t\} }\, dt  \] shows, by Tonelli, that the magnitude of a negative curvature contribution is at most \[  \Lambda \int _\sigma ^\rho t^{-m-1} \int _{B_ t(a)}|x-a|\, d\mu \, dt \leq \Lambda \int _\sigma ^\rho f_ a(t)\, dt.  \] The radial-tilt term is nonnegative. No differentiability of the ball-mass function was used. $\square$ Lemma 6.8.2 (An integrating factor for a measure differential inequality) . 8BCD68460FB3 Let $f$ be a locally bounded, left-continuous function of locally bounded variation on an interval $I$. If for every $s<t$ in $I$, \[  f(t)-f(s)\geq -\Lambda \int _ s^ t f(r)\, dr,  \] then $e^{\Lambda t}f(t)$ is nondecreasing. Proof Fix $t_0\in I$ and put $g(t)=f(t)+\Lambda \int _{t_0}^ t f(r)\, dr$. The hypothesis says $g$ is nondecreasing, so its distributional derivative is a nonnegative Radon measure. The product rule for a smooth factor and a BV function gives \[  D(e^{\Lambda t}f)=e^{\Lambda t}(Df+\Lambda f\, dt) =e^{\Lambda t}Dg\geq 0.  \] For completeness this product rule follows by writing the distributional derivative against a compactly supported smooth test and expanding the derivative of its product with $e^{\Lambda t}$. A function with nonnegative distributional derivative has a nondecreasing representative, as is seen by mollification. Left continuity selects that representative at every interior point, including jumps, and proves the claimed pointwise conclusion. $\square$ Theorem 6.8.3 (Exponential monotonicity for bounded mean curvature) . 6871F1D8A0BA Let $V$ be an $m$-varifold in $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, $1\leq m<N$, with $\mu =\| V\| $. Suppose $\delta V(X)=-\int H\cdot X\, d\mu $ for all $X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N)$ and $|H|\leq \Lambda $ almost everywhere, where $\Lambda \geq 0$. If $\overline{B_ R(a)}\subset U$, then \[  r\longmapsto e^{\Lambda r}\frac{\mu (B_ r(a))}{\omega _ m r^ m}  \] is nondecreasing for $0<r<R$. The density $\Theta ^ m(\mu ,a)$ exists, is finite and nonnegative, and $\mu (\{ a\} )=0$. This is the bounded-mean-curvature case of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, (3.5), p. 241. Proof The function $r\mapsto \mu (B_ r(a))$ is nondecreasing and left-continuous. Therefore $f_ a$ is locally bounded and of locally bounded variation away from zero. Proposition 6.8.1 and Lemma 6.8.2 give exponential monotonicity. Its nonnegative ratios have a finite limit at zero, bounded above by any fixed-radius value. Since $e^{\Lambda r}\to 1$, that limit is the usual density after division by $\omega _ m$. The resulting small-ball bound $\mu (B_ r(a))\leq Cr^ m$ excludes atoms. $\square$ Corollary 6.8.4 (Density and mass lower bounds with bounded curvature) . CECE32EC9E60 If $V$ is also integral, then for every $a\in \operatorname {spt}\mu $, \[  \Theta ^ m(\mu ,a)\geq 1,\qquad \mu (B_ r(a))\geq e^{-\Lambda r}\omega _ m r^ m  \] whenever $\overline{B_ r(a)}\subset U$. Proof First density is upper semicontinuous in the center. Indeed, for $a_ j\to a$ and $0<\varepsilon <s$, the inclusion $B_{s-\varepsilon }(a_ j)\subset B_ s(a)$ and exponential monotonicity give \[  \Theta ^ m(\mu ,a_ j)\leq e^{\Lambda (s-\varepsilon )}\frac{\mu (B_ s(a))}{\omega _ m(s-\varepsilon )^ m}  \] for large $j$. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, then $s\downarrow 0$. Integrality supplies density at least one almost everywhere. Choose such points approaching any support point; upper semicontinuity gives the same lower bound there. Finally compare the corrected ratio at $r$ with its limit at zero. This proof parallels Corollary 6.3.4 and specifies the curvature correction. $\square$ Example 6.8.5 (Why a disk is not a zero-curvature test case) . FD22E871D957 A flat unit $m$-disk in an $m$-plane of $\mathbb R^ N$, viewed as a varifold on all of $\mathbb R^ N$, has a boundary contribution to first variation. It does not satisfy the hypotheses of this section with $H=0$. Proof The divergence theorem gives $\delta V(X)=\int _{\partial D}X\cdot \nu \, d\mathcal H^{m-1}$, where $\nu $ is the outward conormal; for $m=1$ this is the signed endpoint sum. This measure is singular with respect to the disk's $m$-dimensional weight. The centered ratio $\| V\| (B_ r)/r^ m$ equals $\omega _ m$ for $r\leq 1$ and $\omega _ m r^{-m}$ for $r>1$, so it decreases beyond the boundary. Vanishing classical curvature in the interior cannot remove that boundary term. $\square$

Let $C$ be a nonzero stationary integral $m$-cone on $\mathbb R^ N$, where $1\leq m<N$, and write $\mu =\| C\| $ and $\Theta (y)=\Theta ^ m(\mu ,y)$. We develop the argument of [ Minter ] , Lemma 1.5, pp. 13–15. A cone is invariant under dilations as a varifold, including the tangential Jacobian and the recorded planes. Proposition 6.9.1 (Density under scaling and at infinity) . 135F8E55ADD3 For every $y\in \mathbb R^ N$ and $s>0$, \[  \Theta (sy)=\Theta (y),\qquad \lim _{R	o \infty } rac{\mu (B_ R(y))}{\omega _ mR^ m}=\Theta (0).  \] Consequently $\Theta (y)\leq \Theta (0)$ for every $y$. Proof Homogeneity gives $\mu (B_ r(sy))=s^ m\mu (B_{r/s}(y))$. Divide by $\omega _ mr^ m$ and let $r\downarrow 0$. For $R>|y|$, the inclusions \[  B_{R-|y|}(0)\subset B_ R(y)\subset B_{R+|y|}(0)  \] and $\mu (B_ t(0))=\omega _ mt^ m\Theta (0)$ squeeze the ratio at $y$ between $\Theta (0)(1-|y|/R)^ m$ and $\Theta (0)(1+|y|/R)^ m$. Let $R	o \infty $. Stationary monotonicity, Theorem 6.1.5 , bounds the density at $y$ by this limit. $\square$ Proposition 6.9.2 (Maximal density gives another cone vertex) . 53B7945861D9 For $y\in \mathbb R^ N$, $\Theta (y)=\Theta (0)$ if and only if $C$ is invariant under every homothety $h_{y,s}(x)=y+s(x-y)$, $s>0$. Proof If the densities agree, the nondecreasing mass ratio centered at $y$ has equal limits at zero and infinity by Proposition 6.9.1 . It is therefore constant. Translate the origin to $y$ and apply Theorem 6.7.4 ; using reciprocal scale gives precisely the stated homotheties. Conversely these homotheties make every centered ratio at $y$ constant, so its zero and infinite scale limits coincide, again by Proposition 6.9.1 . $\square$ Lemma 6.9.3 (Two vertices generate a line of translations) . A06E3D122AB7 If a varifold is invariant under $h_{0,s}$ and $h_{y,s}$ for every $s>0$, then it is invariant under $	au _{ty}(x)=x+ty$ for every real $t$. Proof The composition $h_{y,s}\circ h_{0,1/s}$ equals $x\mapsto x+(1-s)y$. Varifold pushforwards compose: the scalar tangential Jacobians multiply, and here $s^ m s^{-m}=1$. Thus every translation with $t<1$ preserves the varifold. The inverse of a preserving translation also preserves it, supplying all remaining values of $t$. This is an identity of full varifolds, not just their supports. $\square$ Proposition 6.9.4 (The spine is the linear set of maximal density) . 6C0B9465DCAB The spine from Definition 6.3.7 satisfies \[  S(C)=\{ y:\Theta (y)=\Theta (0)\} .  \] It is a closed linear subspace of dimension at most $m$. Proof A preserving translation gives $\mu (B_ r(y))=\mu (B_ r(0))$, hence equality of densities. The reverse implication follows from Proposition 6.9.2 and Lemma 6.9.3 . Preserving translations are closed under addition and inverses; the lemma gives all real multiples of any one of them. They form a linear subspace. Closedness also follows from continuity of translations against compactly supported continuous tests, with all supports in a common compact set when the translation vectors converge. Write $d=\dim S(C)$. The mass $b=\mu (B_1(0))$ is positive, by conical homogeneity and nonzeroness. A lattice in $S(C)$ with separation three has at least $c_ dR^ d$ points in $B_ R(0)$ for large $R$ if $d>0$. The unit balls at these points are disjoint, each has mass $b$, and all lie in $B_{R+1}(0)$. Thus $c_ dbR^ d\leq b(R+1)^ m$, forcing $d\leq m$. The case $d=0$ needs no estimate. $\square$ Lemma 6.9.5 (Factoring a translation-invariant Radon measure) . 5E59E735DDCC Let $L$ be a $d$-dimensional linear subspace, $d\geq 1$. If a Radon measure $\mu $ on $L^\perp 	imes L$ is invariant under translations in $L$, there is a unique Radon measure $

title: Proposition 6.9.1 (Density under scaling and at infinity)
search_title: Density under scaling and at infinity
section: 6.9 Spines and products of stationary cones
text: Proposition 6.9.1 (Density under scaling and at infinity) . 135F8E55ADD3 For every $y\in \mathbb R^ N$ and $s>0$, \[  \Theta (sy)=\Theta (y),\qquad \lim _{R\to \infty }\frac{\mu (B_ R(y))}{\omega _ mR^ m}=\Theta (0).  \] Consequently $\Theta (y)\leq \Theta (0)$ for every $y$. Proof Homogeneity gives $\mu (B_ r(sy))=s^ m\mu (B_{r/s}(y))$. Divide by $\omega _ mr^ m$ and let $r\downarrow 0$. For $R>|y|$, the inclusions \[  B_{R-|y|}(0)\subset B_ R(y)\subset B_{R+|y|}(0)  \] and $\mu (B_ t(0))=\omega _ mt^ m\Theta (0)$ squeeze the ratio at $y$ between $\Theta (0)(1-|y|/R)^ m$ and $\Theta (0)(1+|y|/R)^ m$. Let $R\to \infty $. Stationary monotonicity, Theorem 6.1.5 , bounds the density at $y$ by this limit. $\square$

title: Proposition 6.9.2 (Maximal density gives another cone vertex)
search_title: Maximal density gives another cone vertex
section: 6.9 Spines and products of stationary cones
text: Proposition 6.9.2 (Maximal density gives another cone vertex) . 53B7945861D9 For $y\in \mathbb R^ N$, $\Theta (y)=\Theta (0)$ if and only if $C$ is invariant under every homothety $h_{y,s}(x)=y+s(x-y)$, $s>0$. Proof If the densities agree, the nondecreasing mass ratio centered at $y$ has equal limits at zero and infinity by Proposition 6.9.1 . It is therefore constant. Translate the origin to $y$ and apply Theorem 6.7.4 ; using reciprocal scale gives precisely the stated homotheties. Conversely these homotheties make every centered ratio at $y$ constant, so its zero and infinite scale limits coincide, again by Proposition 6.9.1 . $\square$

title: Lemma 6.9.3 (Two vertices generate a line of translations)
search_title: Two vertices generate a line of translations
section: 6.9 Spines and products of stationary cones
text: Lemma 6.9.3 (Two vertices generate a line of translations) . A06E3D122AB7 If a varifold is invariant under $h_{0,s}$ and $h_{y,s}$ for every $s>0$, then it is invariant under $\tau _{ty}(x)=x+ty$ for every real $t$. Proof The composition $h_{y,s}\circ h_{0,1/s}$ equals $x\mapsto x+(1-s)y$. Varifold pushforwards compose: the scalar tangential Jacobians multiply, and here $s^ m s^{-m}=1$. Thus every translation with $t<1$ preserves the varifold. The inverse of a preserving translation also preserves it, supplying all remaining values of $t$. This is an identity of full varifolds, not just their supports. $\square$

title: Proposition 6.9.4 (The spine is the linear set of maximal density)
search_title: The spine is the linear set of maximal density
section: 6.9 Spines and products of stationary cones
text: Proposition 6.9.4 (The spine is the linear set of maximal density) . 6C0B9465DCAB The spine from Definition 6.3.7 satisfies \[  S(C)=\{ y:\Theta (y)=\Theta (0)\} .  \] It is a closed linear subspace of dimension at most $m$. Proof A preserving translation gives $\mu (B_ r(y))=\mu (B_ r(0))$, hence equality of densities. The reverse implication follows from Proposition 6.9.2 and Lemma 6.9.3 . Preserving translations are closed under addition and inverses; the lemma gives all real multiples of any one of them. They form a linear subspace. Closedness also follows from continuity of translations against compactly supported continuous tests, with all supports in a common compact set when the translation vectors converge. Write $d=\dim S(C)$. The mass $b=\mu (B_1(0))$ is positive, by conical homogeneity and nonzeroness. A lattice in $S(C)$ with separation three has at least $c_ dR^ d$ points in $B_ R(0)$ for large $R$ if $d>0$. The unit balls at these points are disjoint, each has mass $b$, and all lie in $B_{R+1}(0)$. Thus $c_ dbR^ d\leq b(R+1)^ m$, forcing $d\leq m$. The case $d=0$ needs no estimate. $\square$

title: 6.10 Covering arguments for singular strata
search_title: Covering arguments for singular strata
text: Let $V$ be a stationary integral $m$-varifold in $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, $1\leq m<N$. Write $\Theta (x)=\Theta ^ m(\| V\| ,x)$ and use the strata $\mathcal S^ j(V)$ of Definition 6.3.9 . The argument below expands [ Minter ] , Theorem 1.7 and its proof, pp. 17–19 and 22–24. It uses every possible tangent cone through the definition of the strata, but never assumes tangent-cone uniqueness. Definition 6.10.1 (One-sided approximation by planes) . 90B2A5CC707F A set $A\subset \mathbb R^ N$ has the $(j,\delta ,r_0)$ approximation property if for every $a\in A$ and $0<r\leq r_0$ there is a $j$-dimensional linear subspace $L=L(a,r)$ such that \[  A\cap B_ r(a)\subset \{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,a+L)<\delta r\} .  \] Here $0\leq j<N$ and $\delta ,r_0>0$. The plane may depend on both center and scale; no converse approximation of the plane by $A$ is required. Compare [ Minter ] , p. 19. Lemma 6.10.2 (Refining a cover near a plane) . F04616F157C3 There is $C_ N\geq 1$ such that, if $0<\delta <1/16$ and $A$ has the $(j,\delta ,r_0)$ approximation property, each $A\cap B_ r(a)$, $a\in A$, $r\leq r_0$, can be covered by at most $C_ N\delta ^{-j}$ balls of radius $8\delta r$ whose centers belong to $A\cap B_ r(a)$. Proof Project orthogonally onto the approximating plane $a+L$. The projected points lie in its $j$-ball of radius $r$. A cubical grid covers this ball by at most $C_ N\delta ^{-j}$ cells of diameter at most $\delta r$. For each cell whose inverse image meets $A\cap B_ r(a)$, select one point of that intersection. Two points over the same cell have projected distance at most $\delta r$ and normal components of length less than $\delta r$ each; their distance is less than $3\delta r$. The balls of radius $8\delta r$ at the selected points therefore cover the set. If $j=0$, the projection is a single point and one such ball suffices. Centers remain in $A$, which allows iteration of the approximation hypothesis. $\square$ Proposition 6.10.3 (Small one-sided approximation bounds Hausdorff dimension) . EBCF2E3FB28D For every $\beta >0$ there is $\delta _*(N,j,\beta )>0$ such that any set with the $(j,\delta ,r_0)$ approximation property, $0<\delta <\delta _*$, has \[  \mathcal H^{j+\beta }(A)=0.  \] No measurability or closedness assumption on $A$ is needed for this outer-measure conclusion. Proof Set $s=j+\beta $ and $\vartheta =8\delta $. Choose $\delta _*<1/16$ so small that $C_ N\delta ^{-j}\vartheta ^ s<1/2$ whenever $0<\delta <\delta _*$. This is possible because the expression is $C_ N8^ s\delta ^\beta $. First suppose $A$ is bounded. Total boundedness supplies a finite cover by balls of a fixed radius $r<r_0$ with centers in $A$. Let the sum of their diameter-to-the-$s$ powers be $T$. Apply Lemma 6.10.2 to every ball and iterate. Each new center still lies in $A$ and each radius is smaller than $r_0$. At the $k$th stage all radii are $\vartheta ^ kr$ and the sum of diameter-to-the-$s$ powers is at most $2^{-k}T$. These are arbitrarily fine covers with cost tending to zero, so $\mathcal H^ s(A)=0$, regardless of its normalization constant. For unbounded $A$, apply the argument to $A\cap B_\ell (0)$, which inherits the same property, and take a countable union. $\square$ Lemma 6.10.4 (Nearly maximal density concentrates near a spine) . B01C74EE7C25 For $a\in \mathcal S^ j(V)$ and $\delta >0$, there is $\varepsilon >0$ with $\overline{B_{2\varepsilon }(a)}\subset U$ such that for each $0<r\leq \varepsilon $ some $j$-plane $L=L(a,r)$ satisfies \[  \{ y\in B_ r(a):\Theta (y)\geq \Theta (a)-\varepsilon \}  \subset \{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,a+L)<\delta r\} .  \] Proof If the assertion fails, choose $\varepsilon _ i\downarrow 0$ and $r_ i\leq \varepsilon _ i$ for which no $j$-plane works. Theorem 6.3.6 gives a subsequence of $V_{a,r_ i}$ converging locally to a tangent cone $C$. Its spine has dimension at most $j$ by the definition of $\mathcal S^ j$. Choose a $j$-plane $L$ containing this spine. Failure for this particular plane gives points $z_ i\in B_1(0)$ with \[  \Theta ^ m(\| V_{a,r_ i}\| ,z_ i)\geq \Theta (a)-\varepsilon _ i, \qquad \operatorname {dist}(z_ i,L)\geq \delta .  \] Pass to $z_ i\to z\in \overline{B_1(0)}$. Density upper semicontinuity, Proposition 6.3.3 , gives $\Theta ^ m(\| C\| ,z)\geq \Theta (a)=\Theta ^ m(\| C\| ,0)$. Proposition 6.9.4 forces $z\in S(C)\subset L$, contradicting the distance bound. Convergence is on all compact subsets of $\mathbb R^ N$, so a limit with $|z|=1$ causes no boundary problem. $\square$ Proposition 6.10.5 (Decomposing a stratum by scale and density) . BD5246D88700 For every fixed $\delta >0$, $\mathcal S^ j(V)$ is a countable union of sets, each having the $(j,\delta ,1/i)$ approximation property for some positive integer $i$. Proof Let $E_ i$ consist of points $a\in \mathcal S^ j(V)$ for which the conclusion of Lemma 6.10.4 holds with tolerance and scale $\varepsilon =1/i$, and $\overline{B_{2/i}(a)}\subset U$. Every stratum point belongs to some $E_ i$: decreasing the tolerance and allowed scale preserves the conclusion. Subdivide into \[  E_{i,q}=\{ a\in E_ i:(q-1)/i<\Theta (a)\leq q/i\} ,\qquad q=1,2,\ldots .  \] Densities are finite and at least one at support points, so these sets cover the stratum. If $a,y\in E_{i,q}$, then $\Theta (y)>\Theta (a)-1/i$. Thus the concentration conclusion at $a$, for any $r\leq 1/i$, applies to every $y\in E_{i,q}\cap B_ r(a)$. This is precisely the desired approximation property. $\square$ Corollary 6.10.6 (The zero stratum is countable) . A98914D9EBD1 The set $\mathcal S^0(V)$ is at most countable. Proof Use Proposition 6.10.5 with a fixed $0<\delta <1$. A piece with the $(0,\delta ,r_0)$ property has no distinct points $a,b$ with $d=|a-b|<r_0$: choose $d<r\leq r_0$ also satisfying $\delta r<d$. The property at $a$ would give $b\in B_{\delta r}(a)$, a contradiction. Each piece is therefore $r_0$-separated and has finitely many points in each bounded region. It is countable, as is the union of pieces. No local finiteness of the entire zero stratum is asserted. $\square$ Definition 6.10.7 (Flat singular points) . 8E5306B184C0 A singular point of $V$ is called flat if at least one tangent cone there is a positive-integer multiple of an $m$-plane. The point is still required to be singular according to Definition 6.3.5 ; a regular multiple plane is not a flat singular point. This terminology follows [ Minter ] , p. 20. Corollary 6.10.8 (Flat singular points form the top stratum difference) . 3C81F5ADA4BE The flat singular points are exactly $\mathcal S^ m(V)\setminus \mathcal S^{m-1}(V)$. At each such point the density is an integer $q\geq 2$. Proof Failure of membership in $\mathcal S^{m-1}$ means some tangent cone has spine dimension $m$, since Proposition 6.9.4 bounds it above by $m$. Corollary 6.9.8 identifies that cone as $q|P|$. Conversely a multiple plane has spine dimension $m$. The tangent-cone mass formula, Theorem 6.3.6 , identifies the density at the original point as $q$. If $q=1$, Corollary 6.4.4 makes the point regular, a contradiction. $\square$ Corollary 6.10.9 (The singular set below density two) . 5CC0A191C3F4 One has \[  \dim _{\mathcal H}\{ a\in \operatorname {sing}V:\Theta (a)<2\} \leq m-1.  \] For $m=1$ this set is at most countable. Proof Corollary 6.10.8 excludes the top stratum difference under the density bound. The set is therefore contained in $\mathcal S^{m-1}(V)$. Apply Theorem 6.3.10 ; for $m=1$ use the stronger conclusion of Corollary 6.10.6 . This does not assert regularity merely from density less than two. $\square$

Convergence is on all compact subsets of $\mathbb R^ N$, so a limit with $|z|=1$ causes no boundary problem. $\square$

title: Proposition 6.10.5 (Decomposing a stratum by scale and density)
search_title: Decomposing a stratum by scale and density
text: Proposition 6.10.5 (Decomposing a stratum by scale and density) . BD5246D88700 For every fixed $\delta >0$, $\mathcal S^ j(V)$ is a countable union of sets, each having the $(j,\delta ,1/i)$ approximation property for some positive integer $i$. Proof Let $E_ i$ consist of points $a\in \mathcal S^ j(V)$ for which the conclusion of Lemma 6.10.4 holds with tolerance and scale $\varepsilon =1/i$, and $\overline{B_{2/i}(a)}\subset U$. Every stratum point belongs to some $E_ i$: decreasing the tolerance and allowed scale preserves the conclusion. Subdivide into \[  E_{i,q}=\{ a\in E_ i:(q-1)/i<\Theta (a)\leq q/i\} ,\qquad q=1,2,\ldots .  \] Densities are finite and at least one at support points, so these sets cover the stratum. If $a,y\in E_{i,q}$, then $\Theta (y)>\Theta (a)-1/i$. Thus the concentration conclusion at $a$, for any $r\leq 1/i$, applies to every $y\in E_{i,q}\cap B_ r(a)$. This is precisely the desired approximation property. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.10.6 (The zero stratum is countable)
search_title: The zero stratum is countable
text: Corollary 6.10.6 (The zero stratum is countable) . A98914D9EBD1 The set $\mathcal S^0(V)$ is at most countable. Proof Use Proposition 6.10.5 with a fixed $0<\delta <1$. A piece with the $(0,\delta ,r_0)$ property has no distinct points $a,b$ with $d=|a-b|<r_0$: choose $d<r\leq r_0$ also satisfying $\delta r<d$. The property at $a$ would give $b\in B_{\delta r}(a)$, a contradiction. Each piece is therefore $r_0$-separated and has finitely many points in each bounded region. It is countable, as is the union of pieces. No local finiteness of the entire zero stratum is asserted. $\square$

title: Definition 6.10.7 (Flat singular points)
search_title: Flat singular points
text: Definition 6.10.7 (Flat singular points) . 8E5306B184C0 A singular point of $V$ is called flat if at least one tangent cone there is a positive-integer multiple of an $m$-plane. The point is still required to be singular according to Definition 6.3.5 ; a regular multiple plane is not a flat singular point. This terminology follows [ Minter ] , p. 20.

title: Corollary 6.10.8 (Flat singular points form the top stratum difference)
search_title: Flat singular points form the top stratum difference
text: Corollary 6.10.8 (Flat singular points form the top stratum difference) . 3C81F5ADA4BE The flat singular points are exactly $\mathcal S^ m(V)\setminus \mathcal S^{m-1}(V)$. At each such point the density is an integer $q\geq 2$. Proof Failure of membership in $\mathcal S^{m-1}$ means some tangent cone has spine dimension $m$, since Proposition 6.9.4 bounds it above by $m$. Corollary 6.9.8 identifies that cone as $q|P|$. Conversely a multiple plane has spine dimension $m$. The tangent-cone mass formula, Theorem 6.3.6 , identifies the density at the original point as $q$. If $q=1$, Corollary 6.4.4 makes the point regular, a contradiction. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.10.9 (The singular set below density two)

title: 6.11 Balanced junctions and flat singular examples
search_title: Balanced junctions and flat singular examples
section: 6.11 Balanced junctions and flat singular examples
text: One-dimensional cones provide explicit singular models, and products turn them into higher-dimensional junctions. We expand the examples following [ Minter ] , Lemma 1.5, pp. 15–16, and distinguish flat singular points from regular points of high multiplicity. Definition 6.11.1 (A finite weighted ray cone) . 479485EBDA40 For distinct unit vectors $v_1,\ldots ,v_ k\in S^{N-1}$ and positive integers $q_1,\ldots ,q_ k$, define \[  C=\sum _{i=1}^ k q_ i|R_{v_ i}|,\qquad R_{v_ i}=\{ t v_ i:t\geq 0\} .  \] Each ray records its line $\mathbb R v_ i$ and length measure. The vertex itself has zero weight. This is an integral $1$-cone; stationarity imposes the additional balance condition below. See [ Minter ] , p. 15. Proposition 6.11.2 (First variation and density of a ray junction) . F9B23C2936BA For the cone of Definition 6.11.1 , \[  \delta C(X)=-X(0)\cdot \sum _{i=1}^ kq_ iv_ i.  \] Thus $C$ is stationary if and only if $\sum _ iq_ iv_ i=0$. Its vertex density is $\frac12\sum _ iq_ i$, and its density at a nonzero point of $R_{v_ i}$ is $q_ i$. Proof On one ray, tangential divergence is $\frac d{dt}(X(tv_ i)\cdot v_ i)$. Integration from zero to infinity gives $-X(0)\cdot v_ i$ by compact support. Arbitrary values of $X(0)$ prove the equivalence. The centered ball has mass $r\sum _ iq_ i$ and $\omega _1=2$. Near a nonzero point of one ray, all other finitely many rays are absent, so the local density is its multiplicity. $\square$ Lemma 6.11.3 (Polar measure of a one-dimensional cone) . D981C02BEF95 If $C$ is a stationary $1$-cone on $\mathbb R^ N$ with weight $\mu $, there is a finite measure $\sigma $ on $S^{N-1}$ such that \[  \int \phi (x)\, d\mu (x)=\int _{S^{N-1}}\int _0^\infty \phi (tv)\, dt\, d\sigma (v)  \] for every nonnegative Borel function $\phi $. Moreover $\Theta ^1(\mu ,v)=\sigma (\{ v\} )$ for every unit vector $v$. Proof There is no atom at zero by Corollary 6.6.4 . Define $\sigma (A)=\mu (\{ tv:0<t<1,\  v\in A\} )$ for Borel $A\subset S^{N-1}$. Homogeneity gives the corresponding truncated-sector mass $r\sigma (A)$ for every $r>0$. Centered spheres have zero mass because $\mu (B_ r(0))$ is a constant times $r$. Subtracting truncated sectors proves that the mass of a polar rectangle $(a,b)\times A$ is $(b-a)\sigma (A)$. Uniqueness of measures on rectangles proves the formula. For $0<r<1/2$, the part of the ray through $v$ inside $B_ r(v)$ has length $2r$. Conversely, if $tu\in B_ r(v)$, then $1-r<t<1+r$ and $|u-v|<2r$. Hence \[  2r\sigma (\{ v\} )\leq \mu (B_ r(v)) \leq 2r\sigma (\{ u:|u-v|<2r\} ).  \] Divide by $2r$ and let $r\downarrow 0$; finiteness of $\sigma $ gives the claimed density. $\square$ Theorem 6.11.4 (Classification of stationary integral one-dimensional cones) . BC1EE471EB15 Every nonzero stationary integral $1$-cone in $\mathbb R^ N$, $N\geq 2$, is a finite weighted ray cone in the sense of Definition 6.11.1 , with $\sum _ iq_ iv_ i=0$. In particular its density at the vertex is a positive half-integer. This is the one-dimensional assertion in [ Minter ] , p. 15. Proof Use the polar measure $\sigma $ from Lemma 6.11.3 . Density is constant along each ray by Proposition 6.9.1 . Integrality makes the density a positive integer at $\mu $-almost every point. The polar formula and the lemma therefore show that $\sigma (\{ v\} )$ is a positive integer for $\sigma $-almost every $v$. Thus $\sigma $ is supported on atoms of integer mass at least one. Its finiteness implies that only finitely many such atoms occur, say $\sigma =\sum _ iq_ i\delta _{v_ i}$. The polar formula identifies the weight of $C$ with that of the corresponding weighted rays. Both are rectifiable; Lemma 6.7.2 identifies the full varifolds. Proposition 6.11.2 gives the balance condition and density formula. The balance condition rules out a total weight of one; total weight two consists of two opposite unit-weight rays and is a line. $\square$ Corollary 6.11.5 (Density of cones with a codimension-one spine) . 5872374C9915 If a nonzero stationary integral $m$-cone has spine dimension exactly $m-1$, then its density at the vertex belongs to \[  \{ 3/2,2,5/2,3,\ldots \} .  \] It is a finite union, with positive integer multiplicities, of $m$-dimensional half-planes meeting along the spine and satisfying the transverse ray balance. Proof For $m>1$, Theorem 6.3.8 expresses the cone as the product of its spine and a stationary integral $1$-cone. For $m=1$ use the cone itself. Apply Theorem 6.11.4 . Each product ray is an $m$-dimensional half-plane and contributes $q_ i\omega _ mr^ m/2$ to a centered ball, so the density is $\sum _ iq_ i/2$. Total weight two would give a full $m$-plane with spine dimension $m$, contrary to the hypothesis; total weight one is unbalanced. Thus the total weight is at least three. $\square$ Example 6.11.6 (The triple junction and its products) . 9A121EC9BA8B Three unit-multiplicity planar rays with angles $120$ degrees form a stationary integral $1$-cone $Y$ of density $3/2$. For $m\geq 1$, $Y\times \mathbb R^{m-1}$ is a stationary integral $m$-cone in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$. Its spine and singular set are both $\{ 0\} \times \mathbb R^{m-1}$, and its density there is $3/2$. Proof The three unit direction vectors sum to zero, so Proposition 6.11.2 gives stationarity. Product integration preserves stationarity: the transverse divergence integrates to zero by stationarity of $Y$, while coordinate derivatives along the Euclidean factor integrate to zero by compact support. Away from the common axis the support is a single smooth multiplicity-one half-plane interior. On the axis three half-planes meet and the support is not a smooth manifold. Their three half-ball masses give density $3/2$ there and density one elsewhere. Proposition 6.9.4 identifies the axis as the spine. All tangent cones at axis points equal this same cone, so these points lie in $\mathcal S^{m-1}$ and, for $m\geq 2$, in no lower stratum. $\square$ Example 6.11.7 (A nonplanar cone with a smooth disconnected link) . 86409CB74347 In $\mathbb R^4=\mathbb R^2\times \mathbb R^2$, let $P=\mathbb R^2\times \{ 0\} $ and $Q=\{ 0\} \times \mathbb R^2$. The cone $C=|P|+|Q|$ is stationary and integral, has spine $\{ 0\} $, and has density two at zero. Its link is two disjoint great circles in $S^3$, with no junction points. Proof Both planes are stationary and meet only at zero. Density is one at nonzero support points and two at zero, so Proposition 6.9.4 gives the asserted spine. Their intersections with $S^3$ are disjoint smooth great circles. Thus nonplanarity of a two-dimensional cone does not, in arbitrary codimension, force a junction in its link. This example specifies the limitation of arguments based only on the presence of junctions. $\square$ Example 6.11.8 (A flat singular point from two smooth minimal graphs) . 67A305ACFB42 Let $\Omega =(-\pi /2,\pi /2)^2$ and \[  u(x,y)=\log (\cos y)-\log (\cos x).  \] In $\Omega \times \mathbb R$, the sum of the varifolds of the graph of $u$ and the plane $z=0$ is stationary and integral. The origin is a flat singular point with density two and a unique tangent cone equal to twice the horizontal plane. Proof Here $u_ x=\tan x$, $u_ y=-\tan y$, $u_{xx}=\sec ^2x$, $u_{yy}=-\sec ^2y$, and $u_{xy}=0$. The minimal graph equation in two variables is \[  (1+u_ y^2)u_{xx}-2u_ xu_ yu_{xy}+(1+u_ x^2)u_{yy}=0,  \] which these derivatives satisfy. Thus both smooth graphs are stationary for compactly supported variations in the indicated open cylinder. At zero, $u=0$ and $Du=0$, so the tangent cone of their sum is twice the horizontal plane; smoothness makes this blow-up unique. The support is not a single smooth surface near zero. If it were, its horizontal tangent plane would make it a graph on a smaller neighborhood by the inverse function theorem. But the support contains both the zero graph and nonzero values of $u$ arbitrarily close to zero, giving two heights over some base points. This contradiction proves singularity. The graphs cross along $y=\pm x$; this is not one-sided contact prohibited by the strong maximum principle. It also differs from a regular multiplicity-two plane, which has only one geometric sheet as a set. $\square$
