title: 5.5 Calibrated currents and mass comparison
search_title: Calibrated currents and mass comparison
text: The smooth comparison of Proposition 7.2.12 extends to currents and gives useful equality and convergence statements. Here $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$ is open, $1\leq m\leq N$, and $\omega $ is a smooth closed $m$-form with comass at most one. The motivating source is [ ChMin ] , Section 16, p. 46; current evaluation and mass use the conventions of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, and Definition 5.1.3 . Definition 5.5.1 (A current calibrated by a form) . 5E8055ACA3A7 A compactly supported real $m$-current $T$ of finite mass in $U$ is calibrated by $\omega $ if \[  T(\omega )=\mathbf M(T).  \] Evaluation uses a smooth cutoff equal to one near the support of $T$. For a locally integer rectifiable current, the local calibration condition is $\langle \omega (x),\tau _ T(x)\rangle =1$ for $\| T\| $-almost every $x$. No global finite mass is required for this local condition. Compare Definition 7.2.11 and [ ChMin ] , Theorem 16.2. Lemma 5.5.2 (The calibration defect and equality condition) . 0A0C249D90DB For a compactly supported integer rectifiable current $T$ of finite mass, \[  \mathbf M(T)-T(\omega ) =\int \bigl (1-\langle \omega ,\tau _ T\rangle \bigr )\, d\| T\| \geq 0.  \] Equality holds exactly when the local calibration condition holds almost everywhere. Proof Use the oriented rectifiable representation and mass formula in Definition 5.1.5 . Its unit tangent vector is simple, so the comass bound gives $\langle \omega ,\tau _ T\rangle \leq 1$. The difference is the integral of a nonnegative function, and it vanishes if and only if that function vanishes almost everywhere. The sign of the orientation is part of the condition. $\square$ Theorem 5.5.3 (Calibrated currents minimize in their compact homology class) . 249A6CDC9F2C Let $T$ be a compactly supported finite-mass real $m$-current calibrated by $\omega $ in $U$. If $S$ is another compactly supported finite-mass real $m$-current and $S-T=\partial R$ for a compactly supported $(m+1)$-current $R$ in $U$, then \[  \mathbf M(S)-\mathbf M(T)=\mathbf M(S)-S(\omega )\geq 0.  \] If $S$ is integer rectifiable, equality holds precisely when $S$ is also calibrated. This is the current form of the argument in [ ChMin ] , Theorem 16.2, p. 46. Proof Choose a cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ equal to one on a neighborhood of all three compact supports. Since $d\omega =0$, \[  S(\omega )-T(\omega )=\partial R(\chi \omega ) =R(d\chi \wedge \omega +\chi d\omega )=0.  \] The mass definition gives $S(\omega )\leq \mathbf M(S)$, since the cutoff form has comass at most one. Substitute $T(\omega )=\mathbf M(T)$; Lemma 5.5.2 gives the equality statement. The filling is required to stay inside $U$. $\square$ Corollary 5.5.4 (Fixed-boundary minimization in Euclidean space) . 060B7E4721DF Suppose $\omega $ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^ N$. A compactly supported calibrated finite-mass $m$-current $T$, $m\geq 1$, minimizes mass among all compactly supported finite-mass real $m$-currents $S$ with $\partial S=\partial T$. Proof The difference $Z=S-T$ is a compactly supported normal cycle: its mass is finite and its boundary is zero. Proposition 5.3.19 gives a compactly supported filling $R=C_ aZ$ with $\partial R=Z$. Apply Theorem 5.5.3 . If $S,T$ are integral, this filling is integral too. No corresponding filling inside an arbitrary nonconvex open subset is inferred from this argument. $\square$ Proposition 5.5.5 (Weak limits of calibrated currents retain mass) . 4C4FD4B0981B Let $T_ j$ be calibrated finite-mass real $m$-currents with supports in a common compact $K\subset U$, and suppose $T_ j\rightharpoonup T$. Then $T$ is calibrated, is supported in $K$, and \[  \mathbf M(T_ j)\longrightarrow \mathbf M(T).  \] This conclusion does not by itself prove integrality of $T$. Proof A fixed cutoff equal to one near $K$ gives $\mathbf M(T_ j)=T_ j(\omega )\to T(\omega )$, a finite limit. Tests outside $K$ show $\operatorname {spt}T\subset K$. Mass lower semicontinuity and the comass inequality give \[  \mathbf M(T)\leq \liminf _ j\mathbf M(T_ j)=T(\omega )\leq \mathbf M(T).  \] Thus all terms agree. The finite mass of $T$ follows from the first inequality; the last evaluation is justified by that finite mass. Integrality requires an additional closure theorem, such as Theorem 5.1.6 with its boundary-mass hypothesis. $\square$ Proposition 5.5.6 (Stationarity away from the boundary of a calibrated current) . C4108F50C678 Let $T$ be a compactly supported calibrated integral $m$-current in $U$, and let $V_ T$ be its rectifiable varifold obtained by forgetting orientation and retaining the positive integer multiplicity. Then $V_ T$ is stationary in $U\setminus \operatorname {spt}\partial T$. Proof Take a smooth vector field $X$ compactly supported away from $\operatorname {spt}\partial T$, with flow $F_ t$. For small $t$, the trace of this flow on the compact support stays inside $U$. The homotopy formula, Proposition 5.3.13 , shows that $(F_ t)_\# T-T$ is a compactly supported boundary in $U$. The term involving $\partial T$ vanishes because the flow is constant on a neighborhood of that boundary, so its derivative in the time direction is zero there. Theorem 5.5.3 gives $\mathbf M((F_ t)_\# T)\geq \mathbf M(T)$ for both signs of $t$. A diffeomorphism causes no overlap cancellation; the area formula expresses this mass as $\int J_ m(F_ t|S)\, dV_ T(x,S)$. Differentiating at zero gives $\int \operatorname {div}_ S X\, dV_ T=0$. Bounded derivatives of the flow on a compact set justify differentiation under the finite measure. Smooth fields are dense in compactly supported $C^1$ fields, giving stationarity in the stated domain. $\square$ Example 5.5.7 (Why the homology condition matters) . 1B4F98280302 In the flat torus $M=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^{m+1}$, the oriented slice $\Sigma =(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^ m\times \{ 0\} $ is calibrated by $\omega =dx_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dx_ m$. It has empty boundary and positive area, while the zero chain has the same boundary. These two cycles are not homologous. Proof The angular one-forms are globally defined and closed; their wedge has comass one and restricts to the positive volume form of the slice. Hence $\int _\Sigma \omega =1$. If $\Sigma $ were a boundary, Stokes' theorem and $d\omega =0$ would force that integral to be zero. Thus the calibration theorem does not compare this cycle to zero in its homology class. In contrast, Corollary 5.5.4 uses a filling available in Euclidean space. $\square$

title: Definition 5.5.1 (A current calibrated by a form)
search_title: A current calibrated by a form
text: Definition 5.5.1 (A current calibrated by a form) . 5E8055ACA3A7 A compactly supported real $m$-current $T$ of finite mass in $U$ is calibrated by $\omega $ if \[  T(\omega )=\mathbf M(T).  \] Evaluation uses a smooth cutoff equal to one near the support of $T$. For a locally integer rectifiable current, the local calibration condition is $\langle \omega (x),\tau _ T(x)\rangle =1$ for $\| T\| $-almost every $x$. No global finite mass is required for this local condition. Compare Definition 7.2.11 and [ ChMin ] , Theorem 16.2.

title: Lemma 5.5.2 (The calibration defect and equality condition)
search_title: The calibration defect and equality condition
text: Lemma 5.5.2 (The calibration defect and equality condition) . 0A0C249D90DB For a compactly supported integer rectifiable current $T$ of finite mass, \[  \mathbf M(T)-T(\omega ) =\int \bigl (1-\langle \omega ,\tau _ T\rangle \bigr )\, d\| T\| \geq 0.  \] Equality holds exactly when the local calibration condition holds almost everywhere. Proof Use the oriented rectifiable representation and mass formula in Definition 5.1.5 . Its unit tangent vector is simple, so the comass bound gives $\langle \omega ,\tau _ T\rangle \leq 1$. The difference is the integral of a nonnegative function, and it vanishes if and only if that function vanishes almost everywhere. The sign of the orientation is part of the condition. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.5.3 (Calibrated currents minimize in their compact homology class)
search_title: Calibrated currents minimize in their compact homology class
text: Theorem 5.5.3 (Calibrated currents minimize in their compact homology class) . 249A6CDC9F2C Let $T$ be a compactly supported finite-mass real $m$-current calibrated by $\omega $ in $U$. If $S$ is another compactly supported finite-mass real $m$-current and $S-T=\partial R$ for a compactly supported $(m+1)$-current $R$ in $U$, then \[  \mathbf M(S)-\mathbf M(T)=\mathbf M(S)-S(\omega )\geq 0.  \] If $S$ is integer rectifiable, equality holds precisely when $S$ is also calibrated. This is the current form of the argument in [ ChMin ] , Theorem 16.2, p. 46. Proof Choose a cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ equal to one on a neighborhood of all three compact supports. Since $d\omega =0$, \[  S(\omega )-T(\omega )=\partial R(\chi \omega ) =R(d\chi \wedge \omega +\chi d\omega )=0.  \] The mass definition gives $S(\omega )\leq \mathbf M(S)$, since the cutoff form has comass at most one. Substitute $T(\omega )=\mathbf M(T)$; Lemma 5.5.2 gives the equality statement. The filling is required to stay inside $U$. $\square$

title: Corollary 5.5.4 (Fixed-boundary minimization in Euclidean space)
search_title: Fixed-boundary minimization in Euclidean space
text: Corollary 5.5.4 (Fixed-boundary minimization in Euclidean space) . 060B7E4721DF Suppose $\omega $ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^ N$. A compactly supported calibrated finite-mass $m$-current $T$, $m\geq 1$, minimizes mass among all compactly supported finite-mass real $m$-currents $S$ with $\partial S=\partial T$. Proof The difference $Z=S-T$ is a compactly supported normal cycle: its mass is finite and its boundary is zero. Proposition 5.3.19 gives a compactly supported filling $R=C_ aZ$ with $\partial R=Z$. Apply Theorem 5.5.3 . If $S,T$ are integral, this filling is integral too. No corresponding filling inside an arbitrary nonconvex open subset is inferred from this argument. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.5.5 (Weak limits of calibrated currents retain mass)
search_title: Weak limits of calibrated currents retain mass
text: Proposition 5.5.5 (Weak limits of calibrated currents retain mass) . 4C4FD4B0981B Let $T_ j$ be calibrated finite-mass real $m$-currents with supports in a common compact $K\subset U$, and suppose $T_ j\rightharpoonup T$. Then $T$ is calibrated, is supported in $K$, and \[  \mathbf M(T_ j)\longrightarrow \mathbf M(T).  \] This conclusion does not by itself prove integrality of $T$. Proof A fixed cutoff equal to one near $K$ gives $\mathbf M(T_ j)=T_ j(\omega )\to T(\omega )$, a finite limit. Tests outside $K$ show $\operatorname {spt}T\subset K$. Mass lower semicontinuity and the comass inequality give \[  \mathbf M(T)\leq \liminf _ j\mathbf M(T_ j)=T(\omega )\leq \mathbf M(T).  \] Thus all terms agree. The finite mass of $T$ follows from the first inequality; the last evaluation is justified by that finite mass. Integrality requires an additional closure theorem, such as Theorem 5.1.6 with its boundary-mass hypothesis. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.5.6 (Stationarity away from the boundary of a calibrated current)
search_title: Stationarity away from the boundary of a calibrated current
text: Proposition 5.5.6 (Stationarity away from the boundary of a calibrated current) . C4108F50C678 Let $T$ be a compactly supported calibrated integral $m$-current in $U$, and let $V_ T$ be its rectifiable varifold obtained by forgetting orientation and retaining the positive integer multiplicity. Then $V_ T$ is stationary in $U\setminus \operatorname {spt}\partial T$. Proof Take a smooth vector field $X$ compactly supported away from $\operatorname {spt}\partial T$, with flow $F_ t$. For small $t$, the trace of this flow on the compact support stays inside $U$. The homotopy formula, Proposition 5.3.13 , shows that $(F_ t)_\# T-T$ is a compactly supported boundary in $U$. The term involving $\partial T$ vanishes because the flow is constant on a neighborhood of that boundary, so its derivative in the time direction is zero there. Theorem 5.5.3 gives $\mathbf M((F_ t)_\# T)\geq \mathbf M(T)$ for both signs of $t$. A diffeomorphism causes no overlap cancellation; the area formula expresses this mass as $\int J_ m(F_ t|S)\, dV_ T(x,S)$. Differentiating at zero gives $\int \operatorname {div}_ S X\, dV_ T=0$. Bounded derivatives of the flow on a compact set justify differentiation under the finite measure. Smooth fields are dense in compactly supported $C^1$ fields, giving stationarity in the stated domain. $\square$

title: 5.6 Complex curves and singular calibrated minimizers
search_title: Complex curves and singular calibrated minimizers
section: 5.6 Complex curves and singular calibrated minimizers
text: Complex curves supply explicit mass-minimizing currents with singularities in higher codimension. We prove the complex-dimension-one calibration directly, following [ ChMin ] , Example 16.5, p. 46, and develop the cusp mentioned in [ Minter ] , p. 20. No higher-dimensional Wirtinger inequality or general classification of singular complex varieties is used. Lemma 5.6.1 (The Euclidean complex two-form has comass one) . 7DF03FA4481E On $\mathbb C^ k=\mathbb R^{2k}$ with its standard complex structure $J$, let \[  \omega =\sum _{j=1}^ k dx_ j\wedge dy_ j.  \] Then $d\omega =0$, $\| \omega \| _*=1$, and for an orthonormal pair $(v,w)$, \[  \omega (v,w)=1\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad w=Jv.  \] Thus equality selects complex lines with their complex orientation. Proof The coefficients are constant, so the form is closed. Direct calculation gives $\omega (v,w)=\langle Jv,w\rangle $. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds its absolute value by one; the value one occurs at $(v,Jv)$, since $J$ is orthogonal and $v\perp Jv$. Equality with positive sign in Cauchy–Schwarz is exactly $w=Jv$. This is the two-dimensional calculation in [ ChMin ] , Example 16.5. $\square$ Proposition 5.6.2 (Area and orientation of a holomorphic parametrization) . CFFF3E4138B6 Let $F:D\subset \mathbb C\to \mathbb C^ k$ be holomorphic, and write the domain coordinate as $z=s+it$. Then \[  F_ t=JF_ s,\qquad J_2DF=|F'(z)|^2, \qquad F^*\omega =|F'(z)|^2\, ds\wedge dt.  \] At every point with $F'\ne 0$, the oriented tangent plane is a positively oriented complex line. Proof The Cauchy–Riemann equations give the first identity componentwise. The two derivative vectors are orthogonal and have equal length $|F'|$, so their Gram determinant is $|F'|^4$. The area Jacobian is its square root. Lemma 5.6.1 gives $\omega (F_ s,F_ t)=|F_ s|^2$. At a critical point both sides vanish, so the formulas remain valid there. $\square$ Proposition 5.6.3 (Holomorphic disks give calibrated integral currents) . BDA9EE059317 Let $D\subset \mathbb C$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, and suppose $F$ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $\overline D$. Orient $D$ by $ds\wedge dt$ and put $T=F_\# \llbracket D\rrbracket $. Then $T$ is a compactly supported integral current, \[  \partial T=F_\# \llbracket \partial D\rrbracket , \qquad \mathbf M(T)=T(\omega )=\int _ D|F'|^2\, ds\, dt.  \] It minimizes mass among compactly supported finite-mass real two-currents in $\mathbb C^ k$ with the same boundary. The formula counts multiplicity if $F$ is not injective. Proof The map is smooth and Lipschitz on a neighborhood of the compact closure; Theorem 5.3.9 gives integrality and the boundary formula. The pushforward representation gives $\mathbf M(T)\leq \int _ DJ_2DF$. Proposition 5.6.2 gives $T(\omega )=\int _ DJ_2DF$, whereas the comass bound gives $T(\omega )\leq \mathbf M(T)$. Equality follows, showing in particular that orientation cancellation cannot reduce the mass. Corollary 5.5.4 gives the minimizing property. Compactly supported cutoff forms justify each evaluation. $\square$ Example 5.6.4 (The complex cusp as an integral minimizer) . 94391B08C348 For $D=\{ z\in \mathbb C:|z|<1\} $ and $F(z)=(z^2,z^3)$, the current $T=F_\# \llbracket D\rrbracket $ is calibrated and mass minimizing with its prescribed outer boundary. The map is injective, is an immersion away from zero, and has area Jacobian \[  J_2DF(z)=4|z|^2+9|z|^4.  \] Its image satisfies $w^2=v^3$ in coordinates $(v,w)\in \mathbb C^2$. The origin is not asserted to be a smooth complex submanifold point. Proof If two nonzero parameters have the same image, their ratio has both square and cube equal to one, so the parameters agree. Zero has only the zero preimage. The derivative $(2z,3z^2)$ vanishes exactly at zero. Its squared norm gives the displayed Jacobian by Proposition 5.6.2 ; Proposition 5.6.3 supplies integrality and minimization. The boundary is the smooth embedded outer curve $F(\partial D)$, since the derivative is nonzero there. The algebraic equation follows by substitution. Compare the cusp example of [ Minter ] , p. 20; the parameter convention here interchanges the source's two coordinates. $\square$ Proposition 5.6.5 (Exact density of the calibrated cusp) . 213862B49C97 Let $V$ be the rectifiable varifold associated to the cusp current in Example 5.6.4 . For $0<r<\sqrt2$, let $R\in (0,1)$ solve $R^4+R^6=r^2$. Then \[  \| V\| (B_ r(0))=2\pi R^4+3\pi R^6, \qquad \frac{\| V\| (B_ r(0))}{\pi r^2} =\frac{2+3R^2}{1+R^2}.  \] In particular $\Theta ^2(\| V\| ,0)=2$. Proof The norm squared of $F(z)$ is $|z|^4+|z|^6$, strictly increasing in $|z|$. Thus the preimage of the ambient ball is the parameter disk of radius $R$. Injectivity and the area formula give \[  \| V\| (B_ r(0))=2\pi \int _0^ R(4t^2+9t^4)t\, dt =2\pi R^4+3\pi R^6.  \] Divide by $\pi (R^4+R^6)$ and let $R\downarrow 0$. The critical point contributes no area atom. $\square$ Proposition 5.6.6 (The cusp has a unique double-plane tangent) . C6197AF07C02 For the cusp varifold $V$, the full family of dilations $V_{0,r}$ converges as $r\downarrow 0$ to $2|P|$, where $P=\mathbb C\times \{ 0\} \subset \mathbb C^2$. Proof In the dilation integral make the substitution $z=\sqrt r\, \zeta $. The position is then $(\zeta ^2,\sqrt r\, \zeta ^3)$, the plane away from zero is the complex span of $(2\zeta ,3\sqrt r\, \zeta ^2)$, and the rescaled area factor is \[  4|\zeta |^2+9r|\zeta |^4.  \] For a continuous Grassmann-bundle test supported over $B_ A(0)$, the contributing parameters satisfy $|\zeta |\leq \sqrt A$, because the first coordinate is $\zeta ^2$. On this fixed bounded disk the area factors are uniformly bounded for $r\leq 1$. Except at the zero parameter the planes converge to $P$, so dominated convergence gives the limit integral with position $(\zeta ^2,0)$ and factor $4|\zeta |^2$. The planar area formula for $\zeta \mapsto \zeta ^2$ identifies this with twice the integral over $P$; every nonzero image point has two preimages. The calculation holds along the full limit $r\downarrow 0$, proving uniqueness as a varifold. $\square$ Corollary 5.6.7 (A singular calibrated surface with a flat tangent) . 44CA40B3EEB1 The cusp varifold is stationary away from its outer boundary, smooth at every nonzero interior point, and singular at zero. Its origin is a flat singular point of density two with a unique tangent cone. Thus higher-codimension mass minimization permits this type of flat singularity. Proof Stationarity follows from Proposition 5.5.6 . Injectivity and immersion give smoothness locally away from zero. If the support were a smooth embedded surface near zero, Proposition 5.6.6 would make its tangent plane horizontal, so it would be a single graph over $P$ on a smaller neighborhood. For each sufficiently small nonzero $v$, however, the two parameters solving $z^2=v$ give opposite nonzero values of $w=z^3$. Both points lie in that neighborhood, contradicting the graph property. Propositions 5.6.5 and 5.6.6 give the stated density and tangent. This is a concrete example under Definition 6.10.7 , not a classification of all flat singularities. $\square$

title: 4.5 Subcalibrations and minimizing Simons cones
search_title: Subcalibrations and minimizing Simons cones
text:
The signed-divergence method proves perimeter minimization even when a divergence-free calibration is unavailable. We use outward normals, so $D\chi _ E=-
u _ E|D\chi _ E|$. The model calculation is [ ChMin ] , Theorem 17.1 and Exercise 17.1, pp. 48–50. We include perturbations on both sides of the cone and justify the field at its singular point. The comparison class here consists of sets of locally finite perimeter. Lemma 4.5.1 (Locality of perimeter under compact perturbations) . 3BAFA27CC6BD Suppose $E,F$ have locally finite perimeter in $U\subset \mathbb R^ D$ and $\chi _ E=\chi _ F$ almost everywhere on $U\setminus K$, where $K\Subset U$ is compact. Then their distributional derivatives and perimeter measures agree on $U\setminus K$. If $K\subset W\Subset U$ is open and $\phi \in C_ c^1(W)$ equals one near $K$, then \[  P(F;W)-P(E;W)=\int \phi \, d(|D\chi _ F|-|D\chi _ E|).  \] Proof Tests supported outside $K$ have identical integrals against the two characteristic functions, hence identical distributional derivatives there. Uniqueness of the representing vector measure and its total variation gives equality of the perimeter measures on that open set. The signed difference is therefore supported in $K$. Since the measures are finite on $\overline W$, integration against $\phi $ agrees with their total difference on $W$. $\square$ Lemma 4.5.2 (Removing one singular point from a flux identity) . E2985F310128 Let $D\geq 2$, $a\in U$, and let $X$ be bounded and $C^1$ on $U\setminus \{ a\} $, with its classical divergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Give $X(a)$ any bounded value. For every locally finite-perimeter set $F$ and $\phi \in C_ c^1(U)$, \[  \int _ F igl (\phi \operatorname {div}X+D\phi \cdot X igr )\, dx =\int _{\partial ^*F}\phi X\cdot 
u _ F\, d\mathcal H^{D-1}.  \] Proof Let $\eta _\varepsilon $ be zero on $B_\varepsilon (a)$, one outside $B_{2\varepsilon }(a)$, with $|D\eta _\varepsilon |\leq C/\varepsilon $. Apply Theorem 4.1.5 to the compactly supported $C^1$ field $\eta _\varepsilon \phi X$. The extra bulk term has magnitude at most $C\varepsilon ^{-1}\mathcal L^ D(B_{2\varepsilon })=O(\varepsilon ^{D-1})$, tending to zero. All other bulk terms converge by boundedness and the assumed integrability of the divergence. De Giorgi's representation implies that $|D\chi _ F|$ has no point atoms when $D\geq 2$. Dominated convergence therefore also applies to the boundary flux. This proves the formula without a point-supported divergence term. $\square$ Definition 4.5.3 (A signed subcalibration for a perimeter set) . 97A353BE0D4C For a locally finite-perimeter set $E\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ D$, $D\geq 2$, a signed subcalibration is a field $X$ that is $C^1$ in $U$ or satisfies Lemma 4.5.2 at one exceptional point, and obeys \[  |X|\leq 1,\qquad X\cdot 
u _ E=1\quad |D\chi _ E|	ext{-almost everywhere},  \] \[  \operatorname {div}X\leq 0	ext{ almost everywhere in }E, \qquad \operatorname {div}X\geq 0	ext{ almost everywhere in }U\setminus E.  \] The boundary condition saturates the flux bound. Unlike a calibration arising from a closed form, the divergence may be nonzero. The sign convention agrees with the outward field in [ ChMin ] , Section 17, pp. 49–50. Proposition 4.5.4 (The exact perimeter-gap identity) . 1F6565B8CB14 Let $X$ be a signed subcalibration for $E$, and let $F$ have locally finite perimeter with $\chi _ F=\chi _ E$ almost everywhere outside a compact $K\Subset U$. For every open $K\subset W\Subset U$, \[  P(F;W)-P(E;W) =\int _ W(\chi _ F-\chi _ E)\operatorname {div}X\, dx +\int _{\partial ^*F\cap W}(1-X\cdot 
u _ F)\, d\mathcal H^{D-1}.  \] Both terms on the right are nonnegative. Proof Choose $0\leq \phi \leq 1$ compactly supported in $W$ and equal to one near $K$. Subtract the flux identities for $F$ and $E$, using Lemma 4.5.2 if necessary. The term $(\chi _ F-\chi _ E)D\phi \cdot X$ is zero. The difference of boundary flux measures is supported in $K$, by the equality of vector derivatives in Lemma 4.5.1 . Thus the cutoffs can be removed from the difference, giving \[  \int _{\partial ^*F\cap W}X\cdot 
u _ F\, d\mathcal H^{D-1} -\int _{\partial ^*E\cap W}X\cdot 
u _ E\, d\mathcal H^{D-1} =\int _ W(\chi _ F-\chi _ E)\operatorname {div}X.  \] The second boundary integral equals $P(E;W)$ by the saturated flux. Subtract the first from $P(F;W)$ to obtain the identity. The bulk term is nonnegative separately on $F\setminus E$ and $E\setminus F$ by the divergence signs. The boundary term is nonnegative because $|X|\leq 1$. $\square$ Corollary 4.5.5 (Perimeter minimality and strictness from a subcalibration) . E4164B83C461 A set admitting a signed subcalibration minimizes perimeter under every compactly supported perturbation by a set of locally finite perimeter. u _{E_ k}(x,y)= rac{(x,-y)}{\sqrt{|x|^2+|y|^2}}.  \] Its link is $L=\mathbb S^{k-1}(1/\sqrt2)	imes \mathbb S^{k-1}(1/\sqrt2)$, and \[  P(E_ k;B_ R(0))= rac{\mathcal H^{2k-2}(L)}{2k-1}R^{2k-1}.  \] Proof The function $|x|^2-|y|^2$ has nonzero gradient on $C_ k\setminus \{ 0\} $, giving a smooth boundary there and the displayed outward normal. title: Lemma 4.5.1 (Locality of perimeter under compact perturbations)

text: Lemma 4.5.1 (Locality of perimeter under compact perturbations) . 3BAFA27CC6BD Suppose $E,F$ have locally finite perimeter in $U\subset \mathbb R^ D$ and $\chi _ E=\chi _ F$ almost everywhere on $U\setminus K$, where $K\Subset U$ is compact. Then their distributional derivatives and perimeter measures agree on $U\setminus K$. If $K\subset W\Subset U$ is open and $\phi \in C_ c^1(W)$ equals one near $K$, then \[  P(F;W)-P(E;W)=\int \phi \, d(|D\chi _ F|-|D\chi _ E|).  \] Proof Tests supported outside $K$ have identical integrals against the two characteristic functions, hence identical distributional derivatives there. Uniqueness of the representing vector measure and its total variation gives equality of the perimeter measures on that open set. The signed difference is therefore supported in $K$. Since the measures are finite on $\overline W$, integration against $\phi $ agrees with their total difference on $W$. $\square$

E2985F310128 Let $D\geq 2$, $a\in U$, and let $X$ be bounded and $C^1$ on $U\setminus \{ a\} $, with its classical divergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Give $X(a)$ any bounded value. title: Definition 4.5.3 (A signed subcalibration for a perimeter set)

text: Definition 4.5.3 (A signed subcalibration for a perimeter set) . 97A353BE0D4C For a locally finite-perimeter set $E\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ D$, $D\geq 2$, a signed subcalibration is a field $X$ that is $C^1$ in $U$ or satisfies Lemma 4.5.2 at one exceptional point, and obeys \[  |X|\leq 1,\qquad X\cdot \nu _ E=1\quad |D\chi _ E|\text{-almost everywhere},  \] \[  \operatorname {div}X\leq 0\text{ almost everywhere in }E, \qquad \operatorname {div}X\geq 0\text{ almost everywhere in }U\setminus E.  \] The boundary condition saturates the flux bound. Proposition 4.5.4 (The exact perimeter-gap identity) . 1F6565B8CB14 Let $X$ be a signed subcalibration for $E$, and let $F$ have locally finite perimeter with $\chi _ F=\chi _ E$ almost everywhere outside a compact $K\Subset U$. For every open $K\subset W\Subset U$, \[  P(F;W)-P(E;W) =\int _ W(\chi _ F-\chi _ E)\operatorname {div}X\, dx +\int _{\partial ^*F\cap W}(1-X\cdot 
u _ F)\, d\mathcal H^{D-1}.  \] Both terms on the right are nonnegative. Proof Choose $0\leq \phi \leq 1$ compactly supported in $W$ and equal to one near $K$. Subtract the flux identities for $F$ and $E$, using Lemma 4.5.2 if necessary. The term $(\chi _ F-\chi _ E)D\phi \cdot X$ is zero. The difference of boundary flux measures is supported in $K$, by the equality of vector derivatives in Lemma 4.5.1 . Thus the cutoffs can be removed from the difference, giving \[  \int _{\partial ^*F\cap W}X\cdot 
u _ F\, d\mathcal H^{D-1} -\int _{\partial ^*E\cap W}X\cdot 
u _ E\, d\mathcal H^{D-1} =\int _ W(\chi _ F-\chi _ E)\operatorname {div}X.  \] The second boundary integral equals $P(E;W)$ by the saturated flux. Subtract the first from $P(F;W)$ to obtain the identity. The bulk term is nonnegative separately on $F\setminus E$ and $E\setminus F$ by the divergence signs. The boundary term is nonnegative because $|X|\leq 1$. $\square$

title: 14.7 Gaussian calculus on self-shrinkers

text:
We develop the weighted identities behind the variation theory of self-shrinkers. The primary reference is [ CM12 ] , Section 3.3, pp. 772–775. All integrals on immersed hypersurfaces are taken on the parameter manifold with its induced area measure, so multiplicity is retained. Write $[u]=\int _\Sigma uho \, dA$, where $ho =(4\pi )^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/4}$. Our scalar convention is $\vec H=-H
u $ and $H=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma 
u $. Definition 14.7.1 (Gaussian drift and polynomial area growth) . 0745A084E5F8 On a smooth immersed $n$-hypersurface $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\geq 1$, define \[  \mathcal D u=\Delta _\Sigma u-	frac 12\langle x^ T,
abla _\Sigma uangle .  \] Polynomial area growth means that $\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma \cap B_ R(0))\leq C(1+R)^ d$ for all $R\geq 1$, for some finite $C,d$. The intersection here means the inverse image under the immersion. This condition controls Gaussian tails; properness separately makes ambient radial cutoffs compactly supported. See [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.8 and the hypotheses of Lemma 3.25. Lemma 14.7.2 (Weighted integration by parts with compact support) . 895D966424D5 On a smooth boundaryless immersed hypersurface, if $u\in C_ c^1(\Sigma )$ and $v\in C^2(\Sigma )$, then \[  \mathcal Dv=ho ^{-1}\operatorname {div}_\Sigma (ho 
abla v), \qquad [u\mathcal Dv]=-[\langle

abla v)$; it has compact support and its integral is zero by the divergence theorem. This proves the identity, which is [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.8. $\square$ Lemma 14.7.3 (Global weighted integration by parts) . F4CA20B83C44 Suppose $\Sigma $ is a connected complete smooth immersed hypersurface without boundary, and $u,v\in C^2(\Sigma )$ satisfy \[  [\, |u
abla v|+|
abla u||
abla v|+|u\mathcal Dv|\, ]<\infty .  \] Then $[u\mathcal Dv]=-[\langle 
abla u,
abla vangle ]$. If these conditions also hold with $u,v$ interchanged, then $[u\mathcal Dv]=[v\mathcal Du]$. Proof Take intrinsic distance cutoffs $0\leq \eta _ j\leq 1$, equal to one on the intrinsic ball of radius $j$ about a fixed point, zero outside radius $j+1$, and with $|
abla \eta _ j|\leq 1$ almost everywhere. Completeness makes their supports compact. The compact-support identity extends to these Lipschitz tests by local smooth approximation. Apply it to $\eta _ ju$ and $v$: \[  [\eta _ ju\mathcal Dv]=-[\eta _ j\langle 
abla u,
abla vangle ] -[u\langle 
abla \eta _ j,
abla vangle ].  \] Dominated convergence applies to the first two terms. The last tends to zero since its absolute value is at most the tail integral of $|u
abla v|ho $. Interchanging the functions gives symmetry. These are the integrability requirements in [ CM12 ] , Corollary 3.10; completeness alone does not remove them. $\square$ Lemma 14.7.4 (Gaussian moments from area growth) . 3D797C21D18F If a smooth immersed hypersurface has polynomial area growth, then for every $a>0$ and $q\geq 0$, \[  \int _\Sigma (1+|x|)^ q e^{-a|x|^2}\, dA<\infty .  \] The integral over $\{ |x|>R\} $ tends to zero as $R	o \infty $. Proof The part inside $B_1$ has finite area by hypothesis. On $B_{j+1}\setminus B_ j$, the integral is bounded by $C(j+2)^{q+d}e^{-aj^2}$. This series converges: the quadratic exponential eventually dominates any polynomial. Its tails tend to zero. This also justifies differentiating Gaussian integrals in center and positive scale on compact parameter sets, since each derivative is bounded by a polynomial times $e^{-a|x|^2}$ for some $a>0$. $\square$ Proposition 14.7.5 (Coordinate and radial drift identities) . 89901739599A On any smooth immersed self-shrinker $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, \[  \mathcal D x_ i=-	frac 12x_ i,\qquad \mathcal D|x|^2=2n-|x|^2,\qquad |
abla |x|^2|^2=4|x^ T|^2.  \] These are pointwise identities and require no growth hypothesis. Proof The immersion satisfies $\Delta _\Sigma x=\vec H=-x^\perp /2$. The drift subtracts $x^ T/2$, giving $\mathcal Dx=-x/2$. The product rule for $\mathcal D$ and $\sum _ i|
abla x_ i|^2=n$ give the radial identity. Finally $
abla |x|^2=2x^ T$. Compare [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.20. $\square$ Proposition 14.7.6 (Gaussian center, radius, and mixed moments) . 9410BE875CB7 Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a connected complete smooth immersed self-shrinker without boundary and with polynomial area growth. Then \[  [x]=0,\qquad [|x|^2]=2n[1],\qquad [x|x|^2]=0.  \] For every constant vector $v\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$, \[  [\langle x,vangle ^2]=2[|v^ T|^2].  \] Proof All products of the coordinate functions, $|x|^2$, their first derivatives, and their drift derivatives that occur here are polynomially bounded. Symmetry with $u=x_ i$, $v=|x|^2$ gives \[  -	frac 12[x_ i|x|^2]=[|x|^2\mathcal Dx_ i] =[x_ i\mathcal D|x|^2]=-[x_ i|x|^2],  \] so this mixed moment is zero. These are the identities of [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.25. $\square$ Proposition 14.7.7 (The fourth moment and the scale variance) . 2AA75BC1A69D Let $\Sigma $ satisfy the hypotheses of Proposition 14.7.6 and be two-sided, with $H=\langle x,
u angle /2$. Then \[  [|x|^4]=4n(n+2)[1]-16[H^2], \qquad \left[\left(	frac {|x|^2}{4}-	frac n2ight)^2ight] =	frac n2[1]-[H^2].  \] In particular $[H^2]\leq n[1]/2$. Proof Integration by parts with $u=v=|x|^2$ is justified as above and gives \[  2n[|x|^2]-[|x|^4]=-4[|x^ T|^2] =-4[|x|^2]+16[H^2].  \] Insert $[|x|^2]=2n[1]$ to obtain the first formula. Expand the square and substitute both moment identities to get the second. Its left side is nonnegative. This is [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.25 and Corollary 3.34. $\square$ Corollary 14.7.8 (A radial constraint for closed shrinkers) . CF7BD7C076CF A connected smooth closed embedded self-shrinker $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ satisfies \[  \min _\Sigma |x|\leq \sqrt{2n}\leq \max _\Sigma |x|.  \] If it lies entirely in $\overline B_{\sqrt{2n}}$ or entirely in its exterior $\{ |x|\geq \sqrt{2n}\} $, it is the round sphere of radius $\sqrt{2n}$ centered at zero. Proof The positive weighted measure and $[|x|^2-2n]=0$ force both inequalities. Under either one-sided radial condition, the continuous integrand has one sign and zero integral, so $|x|^2=2n$ everywhere. The inclusion in the sphere is a local diffeomorphism because both manifolds have dimension $n$ and the immersion has full rank. The image is open, and compactness makes it closed. The sphere is connected for $n\geq 1$, so the image is the whole sphere. Embeddedness identifies it with the round sphere rather than a covering parametrization. $\square$

title: Definition 14.7.1 (Gaussian drift and polynomial area growth)
search_title: Gaussian drift and polynomial area growth
text: Definition 14.7.1 (Gaussian drift and polynomial area growth) . 0745A084E5F8 On a smooth immersed $n$-hypersurface $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\geq 1$, define \[  \mathcal D u=\Delta _\Sigma u-\tfrac 12\langle x^ T,\nabla _\Sigma u\rangle .  \] Polynomial area growth means that $\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma \cap B_ R(0))\leq C(1+R)^ d$ for all $R\geq 1$, for some finite $C,d$. The intersection here means the inverse image under the immersion. This condition controls Gaussian tails; properness separately makes ambient radial cutoffs compactly supported. See [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.8 and the hypotheses of Lemma 3.25.

title: Lemma 14.7.2 (Weighted integration by parts with compact support)

text:
Lemma 14.7.2 (Weighted integration by parts with compact support) . 895D966424D5 On a smooth boundaryless immersed hypersurface, if $u\in C_ c^1(\Sigma )$ and $v\in C^2(\Sigma )$, then \[  \mathcal Dv=ho ^{-1}\operatorname {div}_\Sigma (ho 
abla v), \qquad [u\mathcal Dv]=-[\langle 
abla u,
abla vangle ].  \] Neither the shrinker equation nor finite total Gaussian area is needed. Proof The tangential derivative of $\log ho $ is $-x^ T/2$. Expand the divergence using the product rule. Integrate $\operatorname {div}_\Sigma (uho 
abla v)$; it has compact support and its integral is zero by the divergence theorem. This proves the identity, which is [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.8. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.7.3 (Global weighted integration by parts)

text:
Lemma 14.7.3 (Global weighted integration by parts) . F4CA20B83C44 Suppose $\Sigma $ is a connected complete smooth immersed hypersurface without boundary, and $u,v\in C^2(\Sigma )$ satisfy \[  [\, |u
abla v|+|
abla u||
abla v|+|u\mathcal Dv|\, ]<\infty .  \] Then $[u\mathcal Dv]=-[\langle 
abla u,
abla vangle ]$. If these conditions also hold with $u,v$ interchanged, then $[u\mathcal Dv]=[v\mathcal Du]$. Proof Take intrinsic distance cutoffs $0\leq \eta _ j\leq 1$, equal to one on the intrinsic ball of radius $j$ about a fixed point, zero outside radius $j+1$, and with $|
abla \eta _ j|\leq 1$ almost everywhere. Completeness makes their supports compact. The compact-support identity extends to these Lipschitz tests by local smooth approximation. Apply it to $\eta _ ju$ and $v$: \[  [\eta _ ju\mathcal Dv]=-[\eta _ j\langle 
abla u,
abla vangle ] -[u\langle 
abla \eta _ j,
abla vangle ].  \] Dominated convergence applies to the first two terms. The last tends to zero since its absolute value is at most the tail integral of $|u

title: Lemma 14.7.4 (Gaussian moments from area growth)
search_title: Gaussian moments from area growth
text: Lemma 14.7.4 (Gaussian moments from area growth) . 3D797C21D18F If a smooth immersed hypersurface has polynomial area growth, then for every $a>0$ and $q\geq 0$, \[  \int _\Sigma (1+|x|)^ q e^{-a|x|^2}\, dA<\infty .  \] The integral over $\{ |x|>R\} $ tends to zero as $R\to \infty $. Proof The part inside $B_1$ has finite area by hypothesis. On $B_{j+1}\setminus B_ j$, the integral is bounded by $C(j+2)^{q+d}e^{-aj^2}$. This series converges: the quadratic exponential eventually dominates any polynomial. Its tails tend to zero. This also justifies differentiating Gaussian integrals in center and positive scale on compact parameter sets, since each derivative is bounded by a polynomial times $e^{-a|x|^2}$ for some $a>0$. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.7.5 (Coordinate and radial drift identities)
search_title: Coordinate and radial drift identities
text:
Proposition 14.7.5 (Coordinate and radial drift identities) . 89901739599A On any smooth immersed self-shrinker $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, \[  \mathcal D x_ i=-	frac 12x_ i,\qquad \mathcal D|x|^2=2n-|x|^2,\qquad |
abla |x|^2|^2=4|x^ T|^2.  \] These are pointwise identities and require no growth hypothesis. Proof The immersion satisfies $\Delta _\Sigma x=\vec H=-x^\perp /2$. The drift subtracts $x^ T/2$, giving $\mathcal Dx=-x/2$. The product rule for $\mathcal D$ and $\sum _ i|
abla x_ i|^2=n$ give the radial identity. Finally $
abla |x|^2=2x^ T$. Compare [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.20. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.7.6 (Gaussian center, radius, and mixed moments)
search_title: Gaussian center, radius, and mixed moments
text: Proposition 14.7.6 (Gaussian center, radius, and mixed moments) . 9410BE875CB7 Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a connected complete smooth immersed self-shrinker without boundary and with polynomial area growth. Then \[  [x]=0,\qquad [|x|^2]=2n[1],\qquad [x|x|^2]=0.  \] For every constant vector $v\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$, \[  [\langle x,v\rangle ^2]=2[|v^ T|^2].  \] Proof All products of the coordinate functions, $|x|^2$, their first derivatives, and their drift derivatives that occur here are polynomially bounded. Lemma 14.7.4 therefore verifies each hypothesis of Lemma 14.7.3 . Apply that lemma with $u=1$ and $v=x_ i$ or $|x|^2$ to obtain the first two identities from Proposition 14.7.5 . Symmetry with $u=x_ i$, $v=|x|^2$ gives \[  -\tfrac 12[x_ i|x|^2]=[|x|^2\mathcal Dx_ i] =[x_ i\mathcal D|x|^2]=-[x_ i|x|^2],  \] so this mixed moment is zero. Finally, setting $u=v=\langle x,v\rangle $ in integration by parts gives $-\tfrac 12[\langle x,v\rangle ^2]=-[|v^ T|^2]$. These are the identities of [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.25. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.7.7 (The fourth moment and the scale variance)
search_title: The fourth moment and the scale variance
text: Proposition 14.7.7 (The fourth moment and the scale variance) . 2AA75BC1A69D Let $\Sigma $ satisfy the hypotheses of Proposition 14.7.6 and be two-sided, with $H=\langle x,\nu \rangle /2$. Then \[  [|x|^4]=4n(n+2)[1]-16[H^2], \qquad \left[\left(\tfrac {|x|^2}{4}-\tfrac n2\right)^2\right] =\tfrac n2[1]-[H^2].  \] In particular $[H^2]\leq n[1]/2$. Proof Integration by parts with $u=v=|x|^2$ is justified as above and gives \[  2n[|x|^2]-[|x|^4]=-4[|x^ T|^2] =-4[|x|^2]+16[H^2].  \] Insert $[|x|^2]=2n[1]$ to obtain the first formula. Expand the square and substitute both moment identities to get the second. Its left side is nonnegative. This is [ CM12 ] , Lemma 3.25 and Corollary 3.34. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.7.8 (A radial constraint for closed shrinkers)
search_title: A radial constraint for closed shrinkers
text: Corollary 14.7.8 (A radial constraint for closed shrinkers) . CF7BD7C076CF A connected smooth closed embedded self-shrinker $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ satisfies \[  \min _\Sigma |x|\leq \sqrt{2n}\leq \max _\Sigma |x|.  \] If it lies entirely in $\overline B_{\sqrt{2n}}$ or entirely in its exterior $\{ |x|\geq \sqrt{2n}\} $, it is the round sphere of radius $\sqrt{2n}$ centered at zero. Proof The positive weighted measure and $[|x|^2-2n]=0$ force both inequalities. Under either one-sided radial condition, the continuous integrand has one sign and zero integral, so $|x|^2=2n$ everywhere. The inclusion in the sphere is a local diffeomorphism because both manifolds have dimension $n$ and the immersion has full rank. The image is open, and compactness makes it closed. The sphere is connected for $n\geq 1$, so the image is the whole sphere. Embeddedness identifies it with the round sphere rather than a covering parametrization. $\square$

title: 14.8 Gaussian second variation and symmetry modes

section: 14.8 Gaussian second variation and symmetry modes
text:
The shrinker equation is the Euler–Lagrange equation of Gaussian area, but its Hessian differs from the ordinary minimal-surface Jacobi form. We use the scalar convention $H=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma 
u $ and $\Phi =H-\langle x,
u angle /2$. Thus $\Phi =0$ is Definition 14.2.2 . Sources are [ CM12 ] , Sections 4–5, and [ CCMS20 ] , Section 3.1. The notation $[u]=\int uho \, dA$ and $\mathcal D$ is that of Definition 14.7.1 . Proposition 14.8.1 (Compact variations of noncompact Gaussian area) . E8BEBA69F77A Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth two-sided boundaryless immersed hypersurface with $F(\Sigma )=[1]<\infty $. For a smooth variation supported on a compact subset of its parameter manifold, with initial normal velocity $f
u $, \[  F'(0)=[f\Phi ].  \] Consequently it is critical for all such variations exactly when it is a self-shrinker. Proof The changing part of the integral is compact. There $dA'=fH\, dA$ and $ho '=-(f/2)\langle x,
u angle ho $, by Proposition 14.3.2 . The product rule proves the formula. Tests with arbitrary compactly supported $f$ imply $\Phi =0$ by continuity. No boundary term at infinity is taken; the integrand is unchanged there. This extends Proposition 14.2.4 to the stated noncompact setting. $\square$ Definition 14.8.2 (The Gaussian Jacobi operator) . 9EB35742B3AF For a smooth two-sided self-shrinker, define \[  Lf=\mathcal Df+(|A|^2+	frac 12)f, \qquad Q(f,g)=[\langle 
abla f,
abla gangle -(|A|^2+	frac 12)fg]  \] for compactly supported smooth functions. Write $Q(f)=Q(f,f)$. The sign convention is that a negative value of $Q$ decreases centered Gaussian area to second order. See [ CM12 ] , (4.13), and [ CCMS20 ] , (3.1). The drift operator $\mathcal D$ and the Jacobi operator $L$ are different operators. Proposition 14.8.3 (Linearizing the shrinker equation) . 3AED5B2D47FB For a normal variation $f
u $ of a smooth two-sided hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, \[  \Phi '= -\left(\Delta -	frac 12\langle x^ T,
abla \cdot angle +|A|^2+	frac 12ight)f.  \] At a self-shrinker this is $-Lf$. A tangential velocity $Y$ adds $Y(\Phi )$, which vanishes at a self-shrinker. Proof Proposition 7.6.2 gives $H'=-\Delta f-|A|^2f$. Since $
u '=-
abla f$, \[  (\langle x,
u angle )'=f-\langle x^ T,
abla fangle .  \] Subtract half this identity from the first one. Tangential variations differentiate the scalar function by reparametrization. This also explains the signs in [ CM12 ] , (4.10). $\square$ Theorem 14.8.4 (Second variation with fixed center and scale) . 81208FDD5A9C Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth two-sided boundaryless immersed self-shrinker with finite Gaussian area. For every smooth compactly supported variation with initial normal velocity $f
u $, \[  F''(0)=-[fLf]=Q(f).  \] Moreover $-[fLg]=Q(f,g)=-[gLf]$ for compactly supported smooth $f,g$. This is the fixed-center case of [ CM12 ] , Theorem 4.14, and [ CCMS20 ] , Section 3.1. Proof Differentiate Proposition 14.8.1 . At a shrinker the factors multiplying $\Phi $ vanish, including any acceleration contribution, so the derivative is $[f\Phi ']=-[fLf]$. Proposition 14.8.3 gives the operator; Lemma 14.7.2 gives $Q$ and its bilinear symmetry. This is formal self-adjointness on compact tests; it does not specify a self-adjoint domain or a discrete spectrum on an arbitrary noncompact surface. $\square$ Proposition 14.8.5 (Translation and dilation modes) . B2A315CA544B On a smooth two-sided self-shrinker, for each constant vector $v$ put $a_ v=\langle v,
u angle $. Then \[  La_ v=	frac 12a_ v,\qquad LH=H.  \] These pointwise identities do not require compactness. A mode is an eigenfunction only when it is nonzero and belongs to the domain under consideration. Compare [ CM12 ] , Theorem 5.2. Proof Translate the immersion to $x+sv$. Its scalar curvature and normal are unchanged, so its residual is $\Phi _ s=-s a_ v/2$. The normal velocity is $a_ v$; its tangential component contributes zero because $\Phi =0$. Linearization therefore yields $-La_ v=-a_ v/2$. For the dilation $x_ s=(1+s)x$, scalar curvature is $H/(1+s)$ and the normal is unchanged. Thus $\Phi _ s=H((1+s)^{-1}-(1+s))$, with derivative $-2H$. The normal velocity is $\langle x,
u angle =2H$. Linearization gives $-L(2H)=-2H$. These arguments are local calculations and do not assert convergence of noncompact integrals. $\square$ Proposition 14.8.6 (Rotations give Jacobi fields) . 3E301015DE84 If $K$ is a skew-symmetric linear map of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ and $\Sigma $ is a smooth two-sided self-shrinker, then \[  L\langle Kx,
u angle =0.  \] Proof The orthogonal maps $e^{sK}$ preserve both mean curvature and the radial Gaussian weight. Thus $e^{sK}\Sigma $ has identically zero shrinker residual for every $s$. Its normal velocity is $\langle Kx,
u angle $. Proposition 14.8.3 gives the conclusion. If the rotation preserves $\Sigma $, this function can be identically zero. This construction gives an integrable symmetry field; it does not say that every element of the kernel integrates to a family of shrinkers. $\square$ Corollary 14.8.7 (Orthogonality of the geometric modes on a closed shrinker) . 21CF7F379644 On a smooth closed two-sided self-shrinker, \[  [H\langle v,
u angle ]=0  \] for every constant vector $v$. Nonzero rotation modes are likewise orthogonal to $H$ and all translation modes. Proof All smooth functions are compactly supported on a closed manifold. The bilinear symmetry in Theorem 14.8.4 gives $[uLw]=[wLu]$. Apply the pointwise equations of Propositions 14.8.5 and 14.8.6 . Distinct eigenvalues $1,1/2,0$ force the respective inner products to be zero. $\square$ Theorem 14.8.8 (Every finite-Gaussian-area proper shrinker is unstable at fixed center) . 64BCB21D3A98 Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a nonempty smooth complete properly immersed two-sided self-shrinker without boundary and with $F(\Sigma )<\infty $. There is $f\in C_ c^\infty (\Sigma )$ with $Q(f)<0$. Thus no such shrinker is stable for Gaussian area with its center and scale fixed. This explains the distinction preceding [ CM12 ] , Section 4.3. Proof Choose smooth radial cutoffs $0\leq \eta _ R\leq 1$ equal to one on $B_ R$, zero outside $B_{2R}$, with $|
abla _\Sigma \eta _ R|\leq C/R$. They are smooth at zero by being constant there, and properness makes their support compact on the parameter manifold. Dropping the nonpositive curvature term gives \[  Q(\eta _ R)\leq  rac{C^2}{R^2}[1]-	frac 12[\eta _ R^2].  \] Dominated convergence yields $[\eta _ R^2]	o [1]>0$. Hence the right side is negative for large $R$. This does not require a global integral bound for $|A|^2$: its contribution is finite on each compact support and only improves the inequality. The conclusion concerns fixed center and scale, unlike Definition 14.9.3 . $\square$

title: 14.9 Center and scale in shrinker stability

section: 14.9 Center and scale in shrinker stability
text:
Allowing the Gaussian center and scale to vary changes the stability question. We keep this finite-dimensional adjustment explicit. The source is [ CM12 ] , Theorem 4.14, Lemma 4.23, and Sections 5–6 and 11.1. Write $[u]=\int _\Sigma u(4\pi )^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/4}\, dA$ and use $L$ from Definition 14.8.2 . Proposition 14.9.1 (First variation with a moving Gaussian center and scale) . 9DB971431D60 Let $\Sigma _ s$ be a smooth compactly supported variation of a smooth two-sided properly immersed boundaryless hypersurface with polynomial area growth. Let the center and scale satisfy $c_0=0$, $t_0=1$, $c'_0=y$, $t'_0=h$, and let the initial normal speed be $f$. For \[  F_{c,t}(\Sigma )=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\int _\Sigma e^{-|x-c|^2/(4t)}\, dA  \] we have \[  \left. rac{d}{ds}ight|_0 F_{c_ s,t_ s}(\Sigma _ s) =[f\Phi +h\alpha + eta ],\qquad \alpha =	frac {|x|^2}{4}-	frac n2,\quad  eta =	frac {\langle x,yangle }{2}.  \] If $\Sigma $ is also a complete connected self-shrinker, this derivative is zero. Proof Differentiate the area factor and the logarithm of the Gaussian density. The shape terms give $f\Phi $ by Proposition 14.8.1 ; differentiating the scale gives $h\alpha $, and differentiating the center gives $ eta $. Outside the changing compact set, Gaussian moments from Lemma 14.7.4 dominate the parameter derivatives uniformly near $s=0$. At a shrinker, $\Phi =0$, $[\alpha ]=0$ and $[ eta ]=0$ by Proposition 14.7.6 . This is the normalized first-variation formula underlying [ CM12 ] , Sections 3–4. $\square$ Theorem 14.9.2 (The simultaneous shape, center, and scale Hessian) . 85B891A44BBE Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a connected complete smooth properly immersed two-sided self-shrinker without boundary and with polynomial area growth. For a smooth compactly supported shape variation with initial normal speed $f$, and center/scale derivatives $y\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$ and $h\in \mathbb R$ at $(c,t)=(0,1)$, \[  \left. rac{d^2}{ds^2}ight|_0 F_{c_ s,t_ s}(\Sigma _ s) =Q(f)+2h[fH]-h^2[H^2]+[f a_ y]-	frac 12[a_ y^2], \qquad a_ y=\langle y,
u angle .  \] Here $[u]=\int _\Sigma u(4\pi )^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/4}\, dA$, $Q$ is Definition 14.8.2 , and $h=t'_0$ is the derivative of the Gaussian time scale. This is [ CM12 ] , Theorem 4.14, pp. 777–778. Proof At a critical point the second derivative depends only on initial velocities: differences in accelerations are paired with the vanishing first variation. We may therefore use linear center and scale paths and a normal parametrization to compute. At $s=0$, differentiating the general versions of the three factors in Proposition 14.9.1 gives \[  \Phi '=-Lf+hH+	frac 12a_ y,\quad \alpha '=fH- eta -	frac h2(|x|^2-n),\quad  eta '=	frac 12fa_ y-	frac 12|y|^2-h eta .  \] For example $\Phi _ s=H_ s-\langle x_ s-c_ s,
u _ sangle /(2t_ s)$ and $\alpha _ s=|x_ s-c_ s|^2/(4t_ s^2)-n/(2t_ s)$. At the shrinker the logarithmic derivative of the weighted area element is $h\alpha + eta $. The product rule consequently yields \[  F''=\left[-fLf+2hfH+fa_ y-	frac {h^2}{2}(|x|^2-n) -2h eta -	frac 12|y|^2+(h\alpha + eta )^2ight].  \] Now $[ eta ]=[\alpha  eta ]=0$ by Proposition 14.7.6 . Proposition 14.7.7 gives $[\alpha ^2]=n[1]/2-[H^2]$, while $[|x|^2]=2n[1]$. Thus the quadratic scale terms reduce to $-h^2[H^2]$. Finally $[ eta ^2]=[|y^ T|^2]/2$, again by the moment identities, so the center terms reduce to $-[a_ y^2]/2$. All differentiations outside compact shape support involve only polynomial Gaussian moments, already integrable by the stated growth hypothesis. $\square$ Definition 14.9.3 (F-stability and its quantifiers) . 1D2681AB2F92 A shrinker satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 14.9.2 is $F$-stable if, for every $f\in C_ c^\infty (\Sigma )$, there exist a center derivative $y$ and a scale derivative $h$ for which that second variation is nonnegative. It is $F$-unstable if some such $f$ makes the second variation negative for every $y,h$. This is [ CM12 ] , Section 4.3. Fixing $y=h=0$ instead gives the different question in Theorem 14.8.8 . Entropy uses the supremum over all centers and positive scales, Definition 14.4.6 ; local $F$-stability does not by definition settle that global supremum problem. text: Proposition 14.9.1 (First variation with a moving Gaussian center and scale) . 9DB971431D60 Let $\Sigma _ s$ be a smooth compactly supported variation of a smooth two-sided properly immersed boundaryless hypersurface with polynomial area growth. Let the center and scale satisfy $c_0=0$, $t_0=1$, $c'_0=y$, $t'_0=h$, and let the initial normal speed be $f$. For \[  F_{c,t}(\Sigma )=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\int _\Sigma e^{-|x-c|^2/(4t)}\, dA  \] we have \[  \left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_0 F_{c_ s,t_ s}(\Sigma _ s) =[f\Phi +h\alpha +\beta ],\qquad \alpha =\tfrac {|x|^2}{4}-\tfrac n2,\quad \beta =\tfrac {\langle x,y\rangle }{2}.  \] If $\Sigma $ is also a complete connected self-shrinker, this derivative is zero. Proof Differentiate the area factor and the logarithm of the Gaussian density. The shape terms give $f\Phi $ by Proposition 14.8.1 ; differentiating the scale gives $h\alpha $, and differentiating the center gives $\beta $. text: Theorem 14.9.2 (The simultaneous shape, center, and scale Hessian) . 85B891A44BBE Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a connected complete smooth properly immersed two-sided self-shrinker without boundary and with polynomial area growth. For a smooth compactly supported shape variation with initial normal speed $f$, and center/scale derivatives $y\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$ and $h\in \mathbb R$ at $(c,t)=(0,1)$, \[  \left.\frac{d^2}{ds^2}\right|_0 F_{c_ s,t_ s}(\Sigma _ s) =Q(f)+2h[fH]-h^2[H^2]+[f a_ y]-\tfrac 12[a_ y^2], \qquad a_ y=\langle y,\nu \rangle .  \] Here $[u]=\int _\Sigma u(4\pi )^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/4}\, dA$, $Q$ is Definition 14.8.2 , and $h=t'_0$ is the derivative of the Gaussian time scale. This is [ CM12 ] , Theorem 4.14, pp. 777–778. Proof At a critical point the second derivative depends only on initial velocities: differences in accelerations are paired with the vanishing first variation. section: 14.10 Gaussian tails and convergence of entropy
text:
Local convergence of measures controls compact tests. Gaussian integrals need tail control, and entropy adds a supremum over a noncompact parameter space. We separate these steps. Use $F_{c,t}$ and $\lambda $ from Definition 14.4.6 , with dimension $n\geq 1$, and write $ho _{c,t}(x)=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x-c|^2/(4t)}$. The area-growth estimates extend the argument of [ CM12 ] , Lemma 7.28, pp. 788–789, to Radon measures. Proposition 14.10.1 (Lower semicontinuity of Gaussian area and entropy) . 7E46AD688EDF If nonnegative Radon measures $\mu _ j$ on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ converge locally weakly to $\mu $, then for every $c$ and $t>0$, \[  F_{c,t}(\mu )\leq \liminf _ j F_{c,t}(\mu _ j),\qquad \lambda (\mu )\leq \liminf _ j\lambda (\mu _ j).  \] The values may be infinite, and no uniform growth bound is required. Proof Choose compactly supported continuous cutoffs $0\leq \chi _ R\leq 1$ increasing to one. Local weak convergence gives $\int \chi _ Rho _{c,t}\, d\mu =\lim _ j\int \chi _ Rho _{c,t}\, d\mu _ j\leq \liminf _ jF_{c,t}(\mu _ j)$. Monotone convergence in $R$ proves the first inequality. The same argument bounds each $F_{c,t}(\mu )$ by $\liminf _ j\lambda (\mu _ j)$; take the supremum in $c,t$. This last step does not interchange a limit and a supremum as an equality. $\square$ Lemma 14.10.2 (Uniform polynomial Gaussian tails) . 52A6BD047625 Suppose $\lambda (\mu )\leq \Lambda $. Fix $q\geq 0$, $A\geq 0$ and $0<a\leq b<\infty $. Then \[  \sup _{|c|\leq A,\  a\leq t\leq b} \int _{|x|>R}(1+|x|)^ qho _{c,t}(x)\, d\mu (x)\longrightarrow 0  \] as $R	o \infty $, uniformly over all such measures. More precisely, for $R\geq 2A+2$ the integral is at most \[  C(n,a)\Lambda \sum _{j=\lfloor Rfloor }^{\infty } (j+2)^{n+q}\exp \left(- rac{(j-A)^2}{4b}ight).  \] Proof Proposition 14.4.9 bounds $\mu (B_{j+1}(0))$ by $C(n)\Lambda (j+1)^ n$. In the annulus $j\leq |x|<j+1$, the polynomial factor is at most $(j+2)^ q$, $|x-c|\geq j-A$, and the prefactor is at most $(4\pi a)^{-n/2}$. Sum these bounds. The series converges, with tails tending to zero independently of the measure and parameters. The same estimate with the bounded inner ball included gives uniform finite polynomial Gaussian moments. This is the annular method of [ CM12 ] , (7.31)–(7.32). $\square$ Theorem 14.10.3 (Gaussian convergence on compact parameter sets) . 951933FB16BD Suppose nonnegative Radon measures $\mu _ jightharpoonup \mu $ locally in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ and $\lambda (\mu _ j)\leq \Lambda $. Then \[  F_{c,t}(\mu _ j)\longrightarrow F_{c,t}(\mu )  \] uniformly for $(c,t)$ in every compact subset of $\mathbb R^{n+1}	imes (0,\infty )$. In particular the conclusion applies to the weight measures of locally convergent varifolds with uniformly bounded entropy. This uses the Gaussian tail estimates associated with [ CM12 ] , Lemma 7.28. Proof Proposition 14.10.1 gives $\lambda (\mu )\leq \Lambda $. For fixed $(c,t)$, insert a cutoff on $B_ R$; local weak convergence handles the cutoff Gaussian, while Lemma 14.10.2 makes both omitted tails uniformly small. This proves pointwise convergence. On $|c|\leq A$, $a\leq t\leq b$, the parameter derivatives of the kernel are \[  
abla _ cho _{c,t}= rac{x-c}{2t}ho _{c,t},\qquad \partial _ tho _{c,t}=\left( rac{|x-c|^2}{4t^2}- rac n{2t}ight)ho _{c,t}.  \] The moment bounds give a uniform bound for their integrals on a slightly larger compact parameter box. Differentiation under the integral follows by the same domination. Thus all $F_{c,t}(\mu _ j)$ and the limit function have a common Lipschitz constant there. Approximate the compact parameter set by a finite net: pointwise convergence on the net and the common Lipschitz bound give uniform convergence. No control of parameters with $t	o 0$, $t	o \infty $, or $|c|	o \infty $ is asserted. $\square$ Example 14.10.4 (Entropy can drop when a plane escapes to infinity) . 939147F750E3 Let $P_ h=\{ x_{n+1}=h\} $ and $\mu _ j=\mathcal H^ n\llcorner P_0+\mathcal H^ n\llcorner P_ j$. Then $\mu _ jightharpoonup \mathcal H^ n\llcorner P_0$ locally, while $\lambda (\mu _ j)=2$ and $\lambda (P_0)=1$. Thus entropy is not upper semicontinuous even with a common entropy bound and a fixed component. Proof The second plane eventually misses every compact set. If the center has last coordinate $a$, Example 14.4.10 gives \[  F_{c,t}(\mu _ j)=e^{-a^2/(4t)}+e^{-(a-j)^2/(4t)}\leq 2.  \] For fixed $j,c$ this tends to two as $t	o \infty $, proving the entropy value. At each fixed finite center and scale, the second term tends to zero as $j	o \infty $, in agreement with Theorem 14.10.3 . The optimizing scales are not confined to a compact parameter set. $\square$ Proposition 14.10.5 (Entropy controls the Gaussian second moment) . 572E84F0FD10 For every nonnegative Radon measure with finite entropy, \[  \int |x|^2ho _{c,t}(x)\, d\mu (x) \leq 2\lambda (\mu ) igl (|c|^2+C_ n t igr ),\qquad t>0.  \] Here $C_ n$ depends only on the dimension. This is the measure version of [ CM12 ] , Lemma 7.28. Proof Apply the geometric translation and dilation $z=(x-c)/\sqrt t$ from Proposition 14.4.7 , including the factor $t^{-n/2}$ in the transformed measure $\widetilde\mu $. The integral becomes $\int |c+\sqrt t z|^2ho _{0,1}(z)\, d\widetilde\mu $. The inequality $|c+\sqrt t z|^2\leq 2|c|^2+2t|z|^2$ bounds its first part by $2|c|^2\lambda (\mu )$. The area bound and unit annular sum in Lemma 14.10.2 bound the second moment of $\widetilde\mu $ by $C_ n\lambda (\widetilde\mu )=C_ n\lambda (\mu )$. $\square$ Proposition 14.10.6 (Entropy is unchanged by a Euclidean product) . 510CE72B5070 Let $\mu $ be a nonnegative Radon measure on $\mathbb R^{m+1}$ with Gaussian normalization of dimension $m\geq 1$. For $k\geq 1$, give $\mu 	imes \mathcal L^ k$ the normalization of dimension $m+k$. Then \[  F^{m+k}_{(c,b),t}(\mu 	imes \mathcal L^ k)=F^ m_{c,t}(\mu ), \qquad \lambda _{m+k}(\mu 	imes \mathcal L^ k)=\lambda _ m(\mu ).  \] Proof The nonnegative product Gaussian factors. Tonelli's theorem and $\int _{\mathbb R^ k}(4\pi t)^{-k/2}e^{-|z-b|^2/(4t)}\, dz=1$ give the first equality, even when the other factor is infinite. Taking suprema gives the second. Translation of the Gaussian center in a product direction has no effect; this will matter in Proposition 14.11.6 . $\square$ Proposition 14.10.7 (Small-scale Gaussian limits on a proper embedded hypersurface) . EC6BCD371796 Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be smooth, properly embedded, without boundary, and with polynomial area growth. Then \[  \lim _{t\downarrow 0}F_{c,t}(\Sigma )=  egin{cases} 1,& c\in \Sigma ,\ 0,& c
otin \Sigma .\end{cases}  \] In particular $\lambda (\Sigma )\geq 1$ when $\Sigma $ is nonempty. This is the local statement in [ CM12 ] , Lemma 7.2(3), with properness explicit. Proof At $c\in \Sigma $, represent a neighborhood as one smooth graph over its tangent plane, with graph value and derivative zero at $c$. Rescaling by $t^{-1/2}$ gives convergence to that plane on bounded sets. In a fixed small graph neighborhood the area Jacobian is bounded and the tangential Gaussian dominates an integrable Gaussian on the tangent plane; hence its integral tends to one by dominated convergence. Proper embeddedness allows this neighborhood to exclude all other sheets. Outside a fixed ambient ball of radius $\delta $ about $c$, for $0<t\leq t_*$ the Gaussian contribution is bounded by \[  (4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-\delta ^2/(8t)} \int _\Sigma e^{-|x-c|^2/(8t_*)}\, dA,  \] which tends to zero; the last integral is finite by polynomial area growth. If $c
otin \Sigma $, properness makes $\Sigma $ closed, so its distance from $c$ is positive and the same estimate applies to the whole surface. This is the static counterpart of Proposition 14.4.5 ; multiplicity or nonproper accumulation would change the argument. $\square$

text: Theorem 14.10.3 (Gaussian convergence on compact parameter sets) . 951933FB16BD Suppose nonnegative Radon measures $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu $ locally in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ and $\lambda (\mu _ j)\leq \Lambda $. Then \[  F_{c,t}(\mu _ j)\longrightarrow F_{c,t}(\mu )  \] uniformly for $(c,t)$ in every compact subset of $\mathbb R^{n+1}\times (0,\infty )$. In particular the conclusion applies to the weight measures of locally convergent varifolds with uniformly bounded entropy. This uses the Gaussian tail estimates associated with [ CM12 ] , Lemma 7.28. Proof Proposition 14.10.1 gives $\lambda (\mu )\leq \Lambda $. For fixed $(c,t)$, insert a cutoff on $B_ R$; local weak convergence handles the cutoff Gaussian, while Lemma 14.10.2 makes both omitted tails uniformly small. This proves pointwise convergence. On $|c|\leq A$, $a\leq t\leq b$, the parameter derivatives of the kernel are \[  \nabla _ c\rho _{c,t}=\frac{x-c}{2t}\rho _{c,t},\qquad \partial _ t\rho _{c,t}=\left(\frac{|x-c|^2}{4t^2}-\frac n{2t}\right)\rho _{c,t}.  \] The moment bounds give a uniform bound for their integrals on a slightly larger compact parameter box. text: Example 14.10.4 (Entropy can drop when a plane escapes to infinity) . 939147F750E3 Let $P_ h=\{ x_{n+1}=h\} $ and $\mu _ j=\mathcal H^ n\llcorner P_0+\mathcal H^ n\llcorner P_ j$. Then $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mathcal H^ n\llcorner P_0$ locally, while $\lambda (\mu _ j)=2$ and $\lambda (P_0)=1$. Thus entropy is not upper semicontinuous even with a common entropy bound and a fixed component. Proof The second plane eventually misses every compact set. text: Proposition 14.10.5 (Entropy controls the Gaussian second moment) . 572E84F0FD10 For every nonnegative Radon measure with finite entropy, \[  \int |x|^2\rho _{c,t}(x)\, d\mu (x) \leq 2\lambda (\mu )\bigl (|c|^2+C_ n t\bigr ),\qquad t>0.  \] Here $C_ n$ depends only on the dimension. This is the measure version of [ CM12 ] , Lemma 7.28. Proof Apply the geometric translation and dilation $z=(x-c)/\sqrt t$ from Proposition 14.4.7 , including the factor $t^{-n/2}$ in the transformed measure $\widetilde\mu $. The integral becomes $\int |c+\sqrt t z|^2\rho _{0,1}(z)\, d\widetilde\mu $. The inequality $|c+\sqrt t z|^2\leq 2|c|^2+2t|z|^2$ bounds its first part by $2|c|^2\lambda (\mu )$. For $k\geq 1$, give $\mu \times \mathcal L^ k$ the normalization of dimension $m+k$. Then \[  F^{m+k}_{(c,b),t}(\mu \times \mathcal L^ k)=F^ m_{c,t}(\mu ), \qquad \lambda _{m+k}(\mu \times \mathcal L^ k)=\lambda _ m(\mu ).  \] Proof The nonnegative product Gaussian factors. text: Proposition 14.10.7 (Small-scale Gaussian limits on a proper embedded hypersurface) . EC6BCD371796 Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be smooth, properly embedded, without boundary, and with polynomial area growth. Then \[  \lim _{t\downarrow 0}F_{c,t}(\Sigma )= \begin{cases} 1,& c\in \Sigma ,\\ 0,& c\notin \Sigma .\end{cases}  \] In particular $\lambda (\Sigma )\geq 1$ when $\Sigma $ is nonempty. This is the local statement in [ CM12 ] , Lemma 7.2(3), with properness explicit. Proof At $c\in \Sigma $, represent a neighborhood as one smooth graph over its tangent plane, with graph value and derivative zero at $c$. Rescaling by $t^{-1/2}$ gives convergence to that plane on bounded sets. In a fixed small graph neighborhood the area Jacobian is bounded and the tangential Gaussian dominates an integrable Gaussian on the tangent plane; hence its integral tends to one by dominated convergence. Proper embeddedness allows this neighborhood to exclude all other sheets. Outside a fixed ambient ball of radius $\delta $ about $c$, for $0<t\leq t_*$ the Gaussian contribution is bounded by \[  (4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-\delta ^2/(8t)} \int _\Sigma e^{-|x-c|^2/(8t_*)}\, dA,  \] which tends to zero; the last integral is finite by polynomial area growth. If $c\notin \Sigma $, properness makes $\Sigma $ closed, so its distance from $c$ is positive and the same estimate applies to the whole surface. This is the static counterpart of Proposition 14.4.5 ; multiplicity or nonproper accumulation would change the argument. $\square$

For every $\varepsilon >0$ there is $\delta >0$ such that \[  \sup _{|c|+|\log t|\geq \varepsilon }F_{c,t}(\Sigma ) \leq \lambda (\Sigma )-\delta .  \] This is the uniform, rather than merely pointwise, conclusion of [ CM12 ] , Lemma 7.10. In particular $\lambda (\Sigma )>1$. Proof Choose a closed Euclidean parameter ball of radius $r_0>0$ about $(0,1)$, small enough to lie in the quadratic-deficit neighborhood and in $\{ |c|+|\log t|<\varepsilon \} $. Its boundary has deficit at least $\gamma r_0^2$. For any target outside $\{ |c|+|\log t|<\varepsilon \} $, the continuous path $(sc,1+(t-1)s^2)$ starts at the center and ends outside this ball. It crosses the boundary at some $s_0\in (0,1]$. Its scale remains positive, and Proposition 14.11.2 makes the Gaussian area nonincreasing after that crossing. Thus every target has deficit at least $\delta =\gamma r_0^2$. Choose a point $p\in \Sigma $ and let $t\downarrow 0$. The parameters $(p,t)$ eventually satisfy the excluded-neighborhood condition. Proposition 14.10.7 gives $F_{p,t}\to 1$, so $1\leq \lambda (\Sigma )-\delta $. This proves strict entropy greater than one without a separate classification theorem. $\square$

section: 11.4 Minkowski identities and Euclidean CMC rigidity
text:
The volume constraint admits a particularly useful test function built from the support function. We derive the integral identities and then identify an exactly volume-preserving path producing that test. The rigidity theorem is due to Barbosa and do Carmo; [ Wen91 ] , pp. 375–379, gives an elementary parallel-surface proof. Our convention is $A=D
u $ and $H=\operatorname {tr}A$, so an outward sphere has $H=n/R$. Wente's scalar mean curvature is $-H/n$ in this notation. Definition 11.4.1 (Support function and tangential position) . 752F687F8B39 For a smooth oriented hypersurface $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, with position vector $x$ relative to a fixed origin and unit normal $
u $, its support function and tangential position field are \[  u=\langle x,
u angle ,\qquad x^ T=x-u
u .  \] Neither $u$ nor $x^ T$ requires star-shapedness; $u$ may change sign. The variation used in [ Wen91 ] , pp. 377–378, combines normal displacement with dilation and thus involves $u$. Lemma 11.4.2 (Tangential position and the first Minkowski identity) . D97C63B72CB5 For the notation of Definition 11.4.1 , \[  
abla _\Sigma x^ T=I-uA,\qquad \operatorname {div}_\Sigma x^ T=n-Hu.  \] If $\Sigma $ is compact without boundary, then $\int _\Sigma Hu\, dA=n\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )$. This is the integral identity underlying [ Wen91 ] , equation (10) and its appendix. Proof For a tangent vector $v$, differentiate $x-u
u $ in Euclidean space and project tangentially. The derivative of $x$ is $v$, the term $v(u)
u $ has zero tangential projection, and the remaining term is $-uAv$. Taking the trace gives the divergence formula. The divergence theorem on the closed hypersurface gives the integral identity. No sign condition on $u$ or on the principal curvatures enters this argument. $\square$ Lemma 11.4.3 (The first Newton tensor has zero divergence) . 56A52E4D2856 On a Euclidean hypersurface put $P_1=HI-A$. Then \[  \operatorname {div}_\Sigma P_1=0,\qquad \operatorname {tr}P_1=(n-1)H,\qquad \operatorname {tr}(P_1A)=H^2-|A|^2.  \] Here $H$ need not be constant. Proof The Euclidean Codazzi equation $
abla _ i h_{jk}=
abla _ j h_{ik}$ follows by commuting ambient derivatives of the normal and using zero ambient curvature. Contracting the first and third indices gives $

title: 11.5 Constrained Jacobi fields and spectral tests
search_title: Constrained Jacobi fields and spectral tests
section: 11.5 Constrained Jacobi fields and spectral tests
text:
A scalar constraint changes the equation defining the nullspace as well as the allowed test functions. We work on a smooth closed connected two-sided CMC boundary $\Sigma =\partial \Omega $ in a Riemannian manifold and put \[  q=|A|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u ),\qquad J=\Delta _\Sigma +q,\qquad Q(f,g)=\int _\Sigma (\langle 
abla f,
abla gangle -qfg)\, dA.  \] The source is [ BdCE88 ] , Section 2, pp. 125–129. The scalar mean curvature in that paper is the negative of our $H/n$; its normalized Ricci tensor is multiplied by $n$ in the potential, giving the usual Ricci tensor used here. Definition 11.5.1 (The constrained Jacobi nullspace) . B49559F552E6 Let $\mathcal Z=\{ f\in C^\infty (\Sigma ):\int _\Sigma f\, dA=0\} $. A constrained Jacobi speed is an $f\in \mathcal Z$ for which $Q(f,g)=0$ for every $g\in \mathcal Z$. An ordinary Jacobi speed instead satisfies $Jf=0$, with no mean condition built into that equation. This is the distinction in [ BdCE88 ] , Definition 2.8, Proposition 2.9 and Remark 2.11. Being a null vector of a bilinear form is stronger than merely satisfying $Q(f,f)=0$ when the form is indefinite. Proposition 11.5.2 (The constrained Jacobi equation has a constant right-hand side) . 2927E9BDF88B For $f\in \mathcal Z$, the constrained Jacobi condition is equivalent to \[  Jf=b\quad \hbox{on }\Sigma  \] for some real constant $b$. Moreover $b=\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )^{-1}\int _\Sigma qf\, dA$. This is [ BdCE88 ] , Proposition 2.9. Proof Integration by parts gives $Q(f,g)=-\int gJf$. If $Jf=b$, the latter expression vanishes for all $g$ of zero mean. Conversely let $b$ be the average of the smooth function $Jf$ and take $g=Jf-b\in \mathcal Z$. The nullspace condition gives $0=-\int (Jf-b)Jf=-\int (Jf-b)^2$, hence $Jf=b$ everywhere. Integrating the equation and using $\int \Delta f=0$ gives the formula for $b$. If $q$ is constant, then $b=0$ since $f$ has zero mean; for variable $q$ that deduction is unavailable. $\square$ Lemma 11.5.3 (Zero quadratic form and stability) . 758BCB624841 Suppose $Q\geq 0$ on $\mathcal Z$. For $f\in \mathcal Z$, the condition $Q(f,f)=0$ is then equivalent to the constrained Jacobi condition. Without stability, the implication from zero quadratic form need not hold. Proof For every $g\in \mathcal Z$ and $t\in \mathbb R$, \[  0\leq Q(f+tg,f+tg)=2tQ(f,g)+t^2Q(g,g)  \] when $Q(f,f)=0$. A nonzero linear coefficient would make the expression negative for a sufficiently small $t$ of one sign. Thus $Q(f,g)=0$ for every $g$. The converse follows by taking $g=f$. For an indefinite form, $B((a,b),(a,b))=a^2-b^2$ has $B((1,1),(1,1))=0$ but $B((1,1),(1,0))=1$. This algebraic example explains why the stability assumption cannot be removed from the inference. $\square$ Proposition 11.5.4 (Tangents to fixed-volume CMC families) . 8A682F667B82 Let $\Sigma _ t$ be a smooth family of closed CMC boundaries with constant enclosed volume, and write $H_{\Sigma _ t}=c(t)$. Its initial normal speed $f$ satisfies \[  \int _{\Sigma _0}f\, dA=0,\qquad Jf=-c'(0).  \] It is therefore a constrained Jacobi speed. This identifies the geometric meaning of the constant in [ BdCE88 ] , equation (2.10). Proof Differentiate volume and use the transport formula to obtain zero mean. Proposition 11.3.4 gives the derivative of mean curvature for a normal variation as $-Jf$. A tangential component of velocity contributes the tangential derivative of $H_{\Sigma _0}$, which vanishes because it is constant. Thus $c'(0)=-Jf$ at every point, and Proposition 11.5.2 applies. This is a necessary condition for an actual CMC family; it does not assert that every constrained Jacobi field integrates to such a family. $\square$ Proposition 11.5.5 (Killing fields give zero-mean Jacobi speeds on boundaries) . AABDDC64A629 Let $K$ be a smooth ambient Killing field defined on a neighborhood of the compact region $\Omega $. Then $f=\langle K,
u angle $ on its CMC boundary satisfies $Jf=0$ and $\int _\Sigma f=0$. Hence it belongs to the constrained Jacobi nullspace. The function can be identically zero if $K$ is everywhere tangent to $\Sigma $. Compare [ BdCE88 ] , Proposition 2.12 and the following paragraph. Proof The local flow of $K$ consists of isometries, so it preserves the constant mean-curvature value of $\Sigma $. The normal-variation formula, with zero tangential derivative of $H$, gives $Jf=0$. Tracing the Killing equation gives $\operatorname {div}K=0$ in the ambient manifold. The divergence theorem on $\Omega $ therefore gives $\int _\Sigma f=0$. The boundary hypothesis matters for this last step; an arbitrary two-sided hypersurface need not bound an available region on which $K$ is defined. $\square$ Proposition 11.5.6 (The constant-potential stability criterion) . DFACAFB09577 Suppose $q$ is constant on the closed connected hypersurface and let $\lambda _1>0$ be the first positive eigenvalue of $-\Delta _\Sigma $. Then \[  \Sigma 	ext{ is volume-constrained stable}\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad q\leq \lambda _1.  \] If $q>0$ and an ambient Killing field has a nonzero normal speed on $\Sigma $, with the hypotheses of Proposition 11.5.5 , this is equivalent to $q=\lambda _1$. This is the precise nontrivial-mode setting of [ BdCE88 ] , Proposition 2.13 and its preceding paragraph. Proof The Rayleigh characterization of the first eigenvalue gives $\int |
abla f|^2\geq \lambda _1\int f^2$ for every zero-mean smooth $f$. Thus $q\leq \lambda _1$ implies nonnegativity of $Q$. If $q>\lambda _1$, a first eigenfunction gives $Q(f,f)=(\lambda _1-q)\int f^2<0$. Existence and smoothness of this eigenfunction use the compact Laplace spectral theorem. For a nonzero Killing normal speed, $Jf=0$ gives $-\Delta f=qf$, and $f$ has zero mean. Hence $q$ is a positive eigenvalue and $q\geq \lambda _1$. Combining the inequalities gives the last equivalence. Without such a mode, equality is not part of the general criterion. $\square$ Proposition 11.5.7 (Index and nullity for a constant potential) . 8A971915C319 Under the hypotheses of Proposition 11.5.6 , let the eigenvalues of $-\Delta $ be $0=\lambda _0<\lambda _1\leq \lambda _2\leq \cdots $, counted with multiplicity. The constrained index is the number of $\lambda _ j<q$ with $j\geq 1$. Its constrained nullspace is the span of the eigenfunctions with $\lambda _ j=q$, $j\geq 1$. If $q>0$, the unrestricted index is the constrained index plus one. Proof Use the external compact spectral theorem to expand $f=\sum _ j a_ j\phi _ j$ in an orthonormal Laplace eigenbasis, with $\phi _0$ constant. The second-variation form is diagonal: \[  Q(f,f)=\sum _ j(\lambda _ j-q)a_ j^2.  \] For smooth $f$ this follows from integration by parts and the spectral expansion of the Dirichlet energy. Zero mean removes exactly $a_0$. The negative eigenspace gives a negative subspace of the asserted dimension; any larger subspace intersects its orthogonal complement and hence contains a vector with nonnegative quadratic form. Proposition 11.5.2 gives $Jf=0$ in the constant-potential case, so the constrained nullspace consists exactly of the eigenmodes with eigenvalue $q$. Finally the constant mode is negative precisely when $q>0$. The discreteness and divergence of the Laplace spectrum ensure finiteness of these counts. $\square$
