Then $f=\langle K,\nu \rangle $ on its CMC boundary satisfies $Jf=0$ and $\int _\Sigma f=0$. Hence it belongs to the constrained Jacobi nullspace. The function can be identically zero if $K$ is everywhere tangent to $\Sigma $. Compare [ BdCE88 ] , Proposition 2.12 and the following paragraph. Proof The local flow of $K$ consists of isometries, so it preserves the constant mean-curvature value of $\Sigma $. The normal-variation formula, with zero tangential derivative of $H$, gives $Jf=0$. Tracing the Killing equation gives $\operatorname {div}K=0$ in the ambient manifold. The divergence theorem on $\Omega $ therefore gives $\int _\Sigma f=0$. The boundary hypothesis matters for this last step; an arbitrary two-sided hypersurface need not bound an available region on which $K$ is defined. $\square$

title: Proposition 11.5.6 (The constant-potential stability criterion)
search_title: The constant-potential stability criterion
section: 11.5 Constrained Jacobi fields and spectral tests
text: Proposition 11.5.6 (The constant-potential stability criterion) . DFACAFB09577 Suppose $q$ is constant on the closed connected hypersurface and let $\lambda _1>0$ be the first positive eigenvalue of $-\Delta _\Sigma $. Then \[  \Sigma \text{ is volume-constrained stable}\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad q\leq \lambda _1.  \] If $q>0$ and an ambient Killing field has a nonzero normal speed on $\Sigma $, with the hypotheses of Proposition 11.5.5 , this is equivalent to $q=\lambda _1$. This is the precise nontrivial-mode setting of [ BdCE88 ] , Proposition 2.13 and its preceding paragraph. Proof The Rayleigh characterization of the first eigenvalue gives $\int |\nabla f|^2\geq \lambda _1\int f^2$ for every zero-mean smooth $f$. Thus $q\leq \lambda _1$ implies nonnegativity of $Q$. If $q>\lambda _1$, a first eigenfunction gives $Q(f,f)=(\lambda _1-q)\int f^2<0$. Existence and smoothness of this eigenfunction use the compact Laplace spectral theorem. For a nonzero Killing normal speed, $Jf=0$ gives $-\Delta f=qf$, and $f$ has zero mean. Hence $q$ is a positive eigenvalue and $q\geq \lambda _1$. Combining the inequalities gives the last equivalence. Without such a mode, equality is not part of the general criterion. $\square$

title: Proposition 11.5.7 (Index and nullity for a constant potential)
search_title: Index and nullity for a constant potential
section: 11.5 Constrained Jacobi fields and spectral tests
text: Proposition 11.5.7 (Index and nullity for a constant potential) . 8A971915C319 Under the hypotheses of Proposition 11.5.6 , let the eigenvalues of $-\Delta $ be $0=\lambda _0<\lambda _1\leq \lambda _2\leq \cdots $, counted with multiplicity. The constrained index is the number of $\lambda _ j<q$ with $j\geq 1$. Its constrained nullspace is the span of the eigenfunctions with $\lambda _ j=q$, $j\geq 1$. If $q>0$, the unrestricted index is the constrained index plus one. Proof Use the external compact spectral theorem to expand $f=\sum _ j a_ j\phi _ j$ in an orthonormal Laplace eigenbasis, with $\phi _0$ constant. The second-variation form is diagonal: \[  Q(f,f)=\sum _ j(\lambda _ j-q)a_ j^2.  \] For smooth $f$ this follows from integration by parts and the spectral expansion of the Dirichlet energy. Zero mean removes exactly $a_0$. The negative eigenspace gives a negative subspace of the asserted dimension; any larger subspace intersects its orthogonal complement and hence contains a vector with nonnegative quadratic form. Proposition 11.5.2 gives $Jf=0$ in the constant-potential case, so the constrained nullspace consists exactly of the eigenmodes with eigenvalue $q$. Finally the constant mode is negative precisely when $q>0$. The discreteness and divergence of the Laplace spectrum ensure finiteness of these counts. $\square$

The scalar constraint makes geodesic spheres stable even when their unrestricted second variation has a negative direction. We develop this explicitly in space forms and prove the spherical rigidity argument of [ BdCE88 ] , Section 3, pp. 129–131. All hypersurfaces here have dimension $n\geq 2$. We use unaveraged $H=\operatorname {tr}(D
u )$ and the stability convention in Definition 11.3.6 . Proposition 11.6.1 (Geometry of a space-form geodesic sphere) . 7ED8B4A1932C In the simply connected complete space form of sectional curvature $c$, let $\Sigma _ r$ be a geodesic sphere of radius $r>0$, with $r<\pi /\sqrt c$ when $c>0$. Set \[  s_ c(r)= egin{cases} \sin (\sqrt c\, r)/\sqrt c,& c>0,\  r,& c=0,\  \sinh (\sqrt{-c}\, r)/\sqrt{-c},& c<0.\end{cases}  \] With the normal pointing away from the center, its induced metric is $s_ c(r)^2g_{S^ n}$ and \[  A= rac{s_ c'}{s_ c}I,\qquad H=n rac{s_ c'}{s_ c},\qquad q=|A|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )= rac n{s_ c^2}.  \] These formulas make explicit the quantities in [ BdCE88 ] , Lemma 3.4. Proof A perpendicular Jacobi field along a unit radial geodesic with initial data $Y(0)=0$, $Y'(0)=v$ satisfies $Y''+cY=0$ after parallel transport. Thus $Y(r)=s_ c(r)v$, giving the polar metric $dr^2+s_ c(r)^2g_{S^ n}$ before the antipode in the positive-curvature case. Taking one half of the radial derivative of the tangential metric gives $A=(s_ c'/s_ c)I$. Also $\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )=nc$. The identity $(s_ c')^2+cs_ c^2=1$ follows either from the displayed formulas or by differentiating it and using $s_ c''+cs_ c=0$ and the initial data. Therefore $q=n((s_ c'/s_ c)^2+c)=n/s_ c^2$. $\square$ Theorem 11.6.2 (Stability and unrestricted index of geodesic spheres) . CC7BA2BA9BC5 For $n\geq 2$, every geodesic sphere in Proposition 11.6.1 is stable for the enclosed-volume constraint and has unrestricted index exactly one. This is the stability assertion of [ BdCE88 ] , Lemma 3.4, together with its index consequence. Proof The induced sphere has radius $s_ c(r)$, so Proposition 11.3.8 gives first positive eigenvalue $n/s_ c(r)^2=q$. Proposition 11.5.6 proves constrained stability. The constant function gives $Q(1,1)=-q\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma _ r)<0$. Proposition 11.3.7 then bounds the unrestricted index above by one, proving equality. The exact-volume realization proposition identifies the mean-zero calculation with the geometric variation problem. $\square$ Proposition 11.6.3 (Nullity of a geodesic sphere) . 4DBCEFBB183C The constrained Jacobi nullspace of $\Sigma _ r$ has dimension $n+1$ and consists of the first spherical harmonics for its round induced metric. The unrestricted Jacobi nullspace is the same space. Proof The potential is the positive constant $q=n/s_ c(r)^2$. By Proposition 11.5.7 , the nullspace is the Laplace eigenspace with that eigenvalue. The standard spherical harmonic decomposition, used here as an external spectral input, gives eigenvalues $\ell (\ell +n-1)/s_ c(r)^2$, $\ell =0,1,\ldots $, with the $\ell =1$ eigenspace consisting of restrictions of linear functions on the intrinsic round-sphere model. It has dimension $n+1$ and zero mean. The constant mode has eigenvalue zero, so it adds no Jacobi fields in the unrestricted space. This computation concerns infinitesimal nullity and does not assert uniqueness of a nonlinear CMC deformation. $\square$ Lemma 11.6.4 (Position and normal equations in the unit sphere) . 1562412D4BBC Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset S^{n+1}\subset \mathbb R^{n+2}$ be a smooth two-sided CMC hypersurface with position $x$ and unit normal $
u $ tangent to $S^{n+1}$. Then \[  \Delta x=-nx-H
u ,\qquad \Delta

u ,vangle $ and constant $v\in \mathbb R^{n+2}$, these imply \[  Jg_ v=|A|^2g_ v-Hf_ v,\qquad Jf_ v=nf_ v-Hg_ v, \qquad J=\Delta +|A|^2+n.  \] Compare [ BdCE88 ] , Lemma 3.3, after converting its mean-curvature convention. Proof Choose an orthonormal tangent frame geodesic at the point in question. In the ambient Euclidean space, \[  D_{e_ i}e_ j=
abla ^\Sigma _{e_ i}e_ j-h_{ij}

u -Hx$, using Codazzi in constant curvature. Since $H$ is constant, the gradient vanishes. Pairing the vector equations with $v$ and adding the potential $|A|^2+n$ gives the claimed Jacobi formulas. The ambient position and hypersurface normal are perpendicular, both of unit length. $\square$ Proposition 11.6.5 (Spherical coordinate tests and the summed defect) . 70DBFEAC8FA7 For a closed hypersurface in Lemma 11.6.4 , put $D=|A|^2-H^2/n$ and \[  u_ v=g_ v+ rac Hn f_ v.  \] Then $\int _\Sigma u_ v=0$ and $Ju_ v=Dg_ v$. If $v_1,\ldots ,v_{n+2}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^{n+2}$, then \[  \sum _{i=1}^{n+2}Q(u_{v_ i},u_{v_ i})=-\int _\Sigma D\, dA.  \] This is the spherical test family in [ BdCE88 ] , proof of Theorem 1.2, pp. 130–131. Proof The position equation gives $u_ v=-\Delta g_ v/n$, hence zero integral. The two Jacobi equations give \[  Ju_ v=(|A|^2-H^2/n)g_ v+(-H+H)f_ v=Dg_ v.  \] Therefore $Q(u_ v,u_ v)=-\int D(g_ v^2+(H/n)f_ vg_ v)$. Summing over the basis uses $\sum _ i g_{v_ i}^2=|x|^2=1$ and $\sum _ i f_{v_ i}g_{v_ i}=\langle 
u ,xangle =0$. These pointwise identities give the integral formula. Each summand is an admissible volume-constrained test, whether or not it vanishes identically. $\square$ Theorem 11.6.6 (Volume-stable CMC boundaries in a round sphere) . 9679240B53E6 For $n\geq 2$, a smooth closed connected embedded two-sided CMC boundary in the unit sphere $S^{n+1}$ is volume-constrained stable if and only if it is a geodesic sphere, including an equator. This is the positive-curvature case of [ BdCE88 ] , Theorem 1.2. Proof Set $D=|A|^2-H^2/n$. Under stability, every summand in Proposition 11.6.5 is nonnegative, whereas their sum is $-\int D\leq 0$. It follows that $D=0$ everywhere, hence $A=\kappa I$ with the constant $\kappa =H/n$. In $\mathbb R^{n+2}$, \[  D_ v(
u -\kappa x)=Av-\kappa v=0  \] for every tangent vector $v$. Connectedness therefore gives a constant vector $a=
u -\kappa x$, with $|a|^2=1+\kappa ^2$ and $\langle x,aangle =-\kappa $. The intersection of the unit sphere with this affine hyperplane is a connected geodesic sphere: its offset has absolute value $|\kappa |/\sqrt{1+\kappa ^2}<1$. The hypersurface image is open in that intersection by equality of tangent dimensions and closed by compactness, hence equals it. The converse is Theorem 11.6.2 . When $\kappa =0$, the hyperplane passes through the origin and the geodesic sphere is an equator. Uniform rescaling gives the corresponding result for every positive ambient constant curvature. $\square$ Example 11.6.7 (An equator separates two notions of minimal stability) . 8B1EF7479D38 An equator $S^ n\subset S^{n+1}$ is minimal, has $A=0$, and is stable for the enclosed-volume constraint but unstable for unrestricted area variations. Its unrestricted index is one. This example is emphasized in [ BdCE88 ] , Remark 3.5. Proof At geodesic radius $\pi /2$ the space-form formula gives $H=0$ and $q=n$ because the ambient normal Ricci curvature is $n$. Thus $Q(f,f)=\int (|
abla f|^2-nf^2)$. The sharp spherical Poincare inequality makes this nonnegative for zero-mean $f$, while $Q(1,1)<0$. The index statement follows as above. In particular the minimal equation $H=0$ does not remove the distinction between testing all normal speeds and testing only those that preserve enclosed volume. $\square$ Example 11.6.8 (Product tori have many volume-preserving unstable directions) . B95481624243 Let $p,q\geq 1$, $n=p+q$, $r,s>0$, and $r^2+s^2=1$. The product \[  \Sigma =S^ p(r)	imes S^ q(s)\subset S^{n+1}  \] is a closed embedded CMC hypersurface. Its constrained index is at least $n+2$, and its unrestricted index is at least $n+3$. This supplies explicit unstable tests consistent with Theorem 11.6.6 . Proof At $(x,y)$ take $
u =((s/r)x,-(r/s)y)$. It is unit and perpendicular both to the position and to the product tangent space. Differentiating gives principal curvatures $s/r$ in the $p$ first-factor directions and $-r/s$ in the $q$ other directions. Hence $H=ps/r-qr/s$ is constant and \[  |A|^2+n= rac p{r^2}+ rac q{s^2}.  \] Each of the $p+1$ first-factor coordinate functions has zero mean and Laplace eigenvalue $p/r^2$, so its quadratic form is $-(q/s^2)\int f^2$. Each of the $q+1$ second-factor coordinates has eigenvalue $q/s^2$ and quadratic form $-(p/r^2)\int f^2$. Coordinate functions in this combined space are mutually orthogonal, and the second-variation form is diagonal on it, including when the two eigenvalues coincide. Thus they span a negative-definite mean-zero space of dimension $p+q+2=n+2$. The constant function is orthogonal to it and gives another negative direction. The coordinate eigenvalue formula follows directly by tracing the Euclidean second fundamental form of each round factor; no full product spectral decomposition is needed. $\square$

title: 8.3 Continuity and concentration in cycle families
search_title: Continuity and concentration in cycle families
section: 8.3 Continuity and concentration in cycle families
text: The admissibility condition in Definition 9.1.1 is uniform in the parameter and the center of the ball. We prove sufficient conditions and construct a flat-continuous family that fails it. Except for the final counterexample about dimension zero, $M^{n+1}$ is smooth, closed and connected, $n\geq 1$, and cycles are integral mod-two boundaries as in Definition 8.1.1 . The primary source is [ LMN ] , Section 2.6 and Lemma 2.7, pp. 941–942. Lemma 8.3.1 (Compact families of nonatomic measures have uniform small-ball control) . 9C1A64CA147E Let $Y$ be a compact metric space and let $\mathcal K$ be a weakly compact family of finite nonnegative Radon measures on $Y$. Suppose every member of $\mathcal K$ has no atoms. Then \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\sup _{\mu \in \mathcal K,\, y\in Y}\mu (B_ r(y))=0.  \] The total masses are uniformly bounded. Proof Evaluation against the constant function one is continuous, so weak compactness bounds the total masses. On a compact metric space the weak topology on bounded sets of nonnegative measures is metrizable, by testing a countable dense subset of $C(Y)$. If the assertion failed, there would be $\varepsilon >0$, $r_ j\downarrow 0$, $y_ j\in Y$, and $\mu _ j\in \mathcal K$ with $\mu _ j(B_{r_ j}(y_ j))\geq \varepsilon $. Pass to a subsequence with $y_ j\to y$ and $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu \in \mathcal K$. For every $\rho >0$, the small balls eventually lie in $\overline B_\rho (y)$. The closed-set inequality for weak convergence gives \[  \varepsilon \leq \limsup _ j\mu _ j(\overline B_\rho (y))\leq \mu (\overline B_\rho (y)).  \] Let $\rho \downarrow 0$. Continuity from above for the finite measure gives $\mu (\{ y\} )\geq \varepsilon $, a contradiction. The closed-set inequality used here is the Portmanteau theorem, an external elementary weak-convergence fact. It is essential that the limiting measure belongs to the nonatomic family. $\square$ Proposition 8.3.2 (Compact F-continuous cycle families are admissible analytically) . EBBABF0F3388 Let $X$ be a compact metric parameter space and let $\Phi :X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2)$ be $\mathbf F$-continuous, with $n\geq 1$. Then $\Phi $ has bounded maximal mass and no concentration of mass. No cohomological detection is implied by this assertion. The topology is that of Definition 8.1.1 , from [ MNIndex ] , Section 2. Proof The associated varifold map $x\mapsto |\Phi (x)|$ is weakly continuous by the definition of $\mathbf F$. Testing a continuous function on $M$ as a function independent of the tangent plane gives weak continuity of the weight map $x\mapsto \| \Phi (x)\| $. Its image is a compact family of finite measures. Each weight is that of a rectifiable $n$-cycle; since $n\geq 1$, it gives zero mass to every singleton. Lemma 8.3.1 gives both conclusions. In particular the varifold term controls a feature that the flat distance alone need not control. $\square$ Proposition 8.3.3 (Mass-continuous families have no concentration) . E324C500C6C8 Let $X$ be compact and let $\Phi :X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2)$ be continuous in the mass norm, with $n\geq 1$. Then its maximal mass is bounded and it has no concentration of mass. This is the closed-manifold, positive-dimensional case of [ LMN ] , Lemma 2.7. Proof The image is compact in the mass metric. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose finitely many cycles $T_1,\ldots ,T_ N$ so every $\Phi (x)$ is within mass distance $\varepsilon /2$ of one of them. Each fixed weight is finite and nonatomic, so Lemma 8.3.1 , applied to this finite family, gives $r>0$ such that $\| T_ i\| (B_ r(y))<\varepsilon /2$ for all $i,y$. The local mass triangle inequality gives \[  \| \Phi (x)\| (B_ r(y)) \leq \| T_ i\| (B_ r(y))+\mathbf M(\Phi (x)-T_ i)<\varepsilon .  \] Thus the small-ball estimate is uniform. The global triangle inequality with the same finite covering bounds all masses. Also $\mathcal F(T-S)\leq \mathbf M(T-S)$, so the family is flat-continuous. Set $\Phi =0$ on $[1/2,1]$ and at zero. A constant family whose value is the mod-two boundary of a nontrivial short arc in a circle is a counterexample to such a zero-dimensional extension of Proposition 8.3.3 . Proof The boundary consists of its two distinct endpoints, each with unit mass. The constant family is continuous in every cycle topology, but every ball centered at one endpoint has mass at least one. Thus the small-ball supremum never tends to zero. The nonatomic step in the positive-dimensional proof is exactly what fails. All volume-spectrum statements in this project retain $n\geq 1$. $\square$

text: Lemma 8.3.1 (Compact families of nonatomic measures have uniform small-ball control) . 9C1A64CA147E Let $Y$ be a compact metric space and let $\mathcal K$ be a weakly compact family of finite nonnegative Radon measures on $Y$. Suppose every member of $\mathcal K$ has no atoms. Then \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\sup _{\mu \in \mathcal K,\, y\in Y}\mu (B_ r(y))=0.  \] The total masses are uniformly bounded. Proof Evaluation against the constant function one is continuous, so weak compactness bounds the total masses. On a compact metric space the weak topology on bounded sets of nonnegative measures is metrizable, by testing a countable dense subset of $C(Y)$. If the assertion failed, there would be $\varepsilon >0$, $r_ j\downarrow 0$, $y_ j\in Y$, and $\mu _ j\in \mathcal K$ with $\mu _ j(B_{r_ j}(y_ j))\geq \varepsilon $. Pass to a subsequence with $y_ j\to y$ and $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu \in \mathcal K$. For every $\rho >0$, the small balls eventually lie in $\overline B_\rho (y)$. The closed-set inequality for weak convergence gives \[  \varepsilon \leq \limsup _ j\mu _ j(\overline B_\rho (y))\leq \mu (\overline B_\rho (y)).  \] Let $\rho \downarrow 0$. Continuity from above for the finite measure gives $\mu (\{ y\} )\geq \varepsilon $, a contradiction. The closed-set inequality used here is the Portmanteau theorem, an external elementary weak-convergence fact. It is essential that the limiting measure belongs to the nonatomic family. $\square$

EBBABF0F3388 Let $X$ be a compact metric parameter space and let $\Phi :X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2)$ be $\mathbf F$-continuous, with $n\geq 1$. Then $\Phi $ has bounded maximal mass and no concentration of mass. No cohomological detection is implied by this assertion. The topology is that of Definition 8.1.1 , from [ MNIndex ] , Section 2. title: 8.4 Detecting classes and parameter-space arguments
search_title: Detecting classes and parameter-space arguments
text: Let $M^{n+1}$ be smooth, closed and connected, $n\geq 1$. We use the mod-two boundary component, the class $\bar\lambda \in H^1(\mathcal Z_ n^0;\mathbb Z_2)$, and admissibility of Definition 9.1.2 . Almgren's identification of the detecting class remains external. The arguments below use ordinary singular cohomology with $\mathbb Z_2$ coefficients and its cellular computation for finite complexes. Sources are [ LMN ] , Sections 2.5–2.6, and [ MNIndex ] , Section 5. Lemma 8.4.1 (Pulling back a detecting family) . E0E6244C817A Let $\Phi :X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0$ be an admissible family on a finite cubical complex, and let $f:Y\to X$ be continuous with $Y$ another finite cubical complex. Then $\Phi \circ f$ is flat-continuous, has no concentration, and has maximal mass at most that of $\Phi $. It is a $p$-sweepout exactly when \[  f^*(\Phi ^*\bar\lambda ^ p)\ne 0.  \] Proof Continuity follows by composition. Every slice of the composite is a slice of the original family, so its maximal mass and every uniform small-ball supremum are bounded by those of $\Phi $. Naturality of cohomological pullback gives $(\Phi \circ f)^*(\bar\lambda ^ p)=f^*(\Phi ^*\bar\lambda ^ p)$. This proves the exact detection criterion; the geometric bounds alone do not imply it. $\square$ Proposition 8.4.2 (A parameter-dimension obstruction) . DB13365CEAA2 A $p$-sweepout on a finite cubical complex $X$ requires $\dim X\geq p$. Having dimension at least $p$ is not sufficient for a family to be a $p$-sweepout. Proof The cellular cochain groups above $\dim X$ vanish, and cellular cohomology agrees with singular cohomology. Hence $H^ p(X;\mathbb Z_2)=0$ when $p>\dim X$, contradicting detection. Conversely a constant family has zero pullback in every positive cohomological degree, regardless of the dimension of its parameter space. The cellular comparison theorem is the external algebraic-topology input. $\square$ Proposition 8.4.3 (The p-skeleton retains a p-sweepout) . 61F934F4A7A0 If $\Phi :X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0$ is an admissible $p$-sweepout on a finite cubical complex, its restriction to the $p$-skeleton $X^{(p)}$ is an admissible $p$-sweepout with no larger maximal mass. Proof Let $i:X^{(p)}\hookrightarrow X$ be inclusion. The relative cellular cochain complex for $(X,X^{(p)})$ has no cochains in degrees at most $p$, so $H^ p(X,X^{(p)};\mathbb Z_2)=0$. The long exact sequence of the pair therefore makes $i^*:H^ p(X;\mathbb Z_2)\to H^ p(X^{(p)};\mathbb Z_2)$ injective. Thus the nonzero class $\Phi ^*\bar\lambda ^ p$ remains nonzero on the skeleton. Lemma 8.4.1 gives the analytic admissibility and mass bound. This reduces the parameter dimension of a detecting family without making a claim about the index of a limiting hypersurface. $\square$ Proposition 8.4.4 (Detection is invariant under flat homotopy) . F4C1074C9761 Suppose $\Phi _0,\Phi _1:X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0$ are flat-homotopic and both independently satisfy the bounded-mass and no-concentration conditions. Then $\Phi _0$ is a $p$-sweepout if and only if $\Phi _1$ is. The homotopy itself need not satisfy a uniform no-concentration estimate for this cohomological conclusion. Compare [ LMN ] , Section 2.6. Proof A homotopy into the cycle space with its flat topology induces the same pullback on singular cohomology at its two endpoints. Thus $\Phi _0^*\bar\lambda ^ p=\Phi _1^*\bar\lambda ^ p$. Nonvanishing is equivalent, and the separately assumed analytic conditions make each endpoint admissible. This argument cannot be used to infer no concentration for an endpoint from flat homotopy alone; Example 8.3.5 explains the missing control. $\square$ Proposition 8.4.5 (A detecting fixed class bounds the spectral infimum) . 46EEAF367871 Let $X$ have a finite cubical structure and let $\Phi :X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0$ be an $\mathbf F$-continuous $p$-sweepout. Let $\Pi $ be its flat-homotopy class among $\mathbf F$-continuous maps on $X$, as in Definition 8.1.2 , using a triangulation when expressing $X$ as a simplicial complex. Then \[  \omega _ p(M,g)\leq \mathbf L(\Pi ).  \] There is no assertion of equality for an arbitrary such class. Proof Every $\Psi \in \Pi $ has bounded maximal mass and no concentration by Proposition 8.3.2 . It detects the same cup power as $\Phi $ by Proposition 8.4.4 . Thus every competitor in the infimum defining $\mathbf L(\Pi )$ is also a competitor for $\omega _ p$, whose infimum allows other domains and classes as well. This inclusion of competitor sets gives the inequality. Triangulation changes neither the underlying space nor its cohomology or maps; no interpolation between different cycle topologies is used in this comparison. $\square$ Example 8.4.6 (The same slices can lose detection after reparametrization) . EDF55A1658FD Let $\Phi :S^1\to \mathcal Z_ n^0$ be an admissible one-sweepout, with $S^1$ given a finite cubical structure. The family $\Psi (z)=\Phi (z^2)$ has the same image, the same maximal mass and the same small-ball suprema, but is not a one-sweepout. Proof The degree-two map $f(z)=z^2$ is surjective, so the sets of slices are identical. On $H^1(S^1;\mathbb Z_2)$ its pullback is multiplication by two, hence zero. Therefore $\Psi ^*\bar\lambda =f^*(\Phi ^*\bar\lambda )=0$. The elementary degree computation can be seen by traversing the oriented circle twice and reducing the resulting homology class modulo two. It shows why covering the same geometric slices does not preserve the topological obstruction. $\square$ Lemma 8.4.7 (Cup-product vanishing on an open cover) . F7855903756E Let $X$ be a finite complex, let $U_1,\ldots ,U_ N$ be open subsets covering $X$, and let $\alpha _ i\in H^{d_ i}(X;\mathbb Z_2)$ with $d_ i\geq 1$. If $\alpha _ i|_{U_ i}=0$ for every $i$, then $\alpha _1\smile \cdots \smile \alpha _ N=0$. This is the topological step behind the localization argument described in [ LMN ] , pp. 935–937. Proof The long exact sequence of $(X,U_ i)$ lifts $\alpha _ i$ to a class $\widetilde\alpha _ i\in H^{d_ i}(X,U_ i;\mathbb Z_2)$. The relative cup product for open, hence excisive, pairs places the product of these lifts in \[  H^{d_1+\cdots +d_ N}(X,U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_ N;\mathbb Z_2).  \] Its image in absolute cohomology is the desired product by naturality. Since the union is $X$, the relative group is zero. The long exact sequence and relative cup product are the explicit external algebraic-topology inputs; this argument supplies the deduction from them. $\square$ Proposition 8.4.8 (A common parameter above several cost thresholds) . D6C9F6556AEA Let $\beta \in H^1(X;\mathbb Z_2)$ on a finite complex satisfy $\beta ^ p\ne 0$. Suppose $p_ i\geq 1$ and $\sum _{i=1}^ N p_ i\leq p$. Let $c_ i:X\to [0,\infty )$ be continuous, let $a_ i>0$, and assume $\beta ^{p_ i}$ restricts to zero on $U_ i=\{ c_ i<a_ i\} $. Then some $x\in X$ satisfies $c_ i(x)\geq a_ i$ for every $i$. If $F(x)\geq \sum _ i c_ i(x)$ for all $x$, then $\sup _ XF\geq \sum _ i a_ i$. Proof If the $U_ i$ covered $X$, Lemma 8.4.7 would give $\beta ^{\sum _ i p_ i}=0$. Multiplying by the remaining cup power, or using this equality directly if the sum is $p$, would give $\beta ^ p=0$, a contradiction. Thus a point lies outside every $U_ i$ and satisfies all thresholds. The bound for $F$ follows at that point. Applying this abstract lemma to cycle masses in subdomains requires additional work: those costs need not be continuous in the flat topology, and restriction need not give finite-mass relative boundaries. These are precisely the issues recorded in [ LMN ] , p. 937; their geometric resolution is not proved by the present topological lemma. $\square$

Multiplying by the remaining cup power, or using this equality directly if the sum is $p$, would give $\beta ^ p=0$, a contradiction. Thus a point lies outside every $U_ i$ and satisfies all thresholds. The bound for $F$ follows at that point. section: 9.4 Metric comparison and uniform Weyl asymptotics
text: Throughout, $M^{n+1}$ is smooth, closed and connected, $n\geq 1$, and $\omega _ p$ is the mod-two volume spectrum of Definition 9.1.2 . We compare smooth Riemannian metrics on the same manifold. The normalized metric estimate follows the argument in [ MNS19 ] , Lemma 1, p. 425. The Weyl theorem itself, Theorem 9.1.5 , remains external. Lemma 9.4.1 (Mass and flat norms under metric comparison) . EFEF93C848C0 If $a^2g\leq h\leq b^2g$ as quadratic forms, where $0<a\leq b$, then every rectifiable mod-two $k$-chain $T$ satisfies \[  a^ k\mathbf M_ g(T)\leq \mathbf M_ h(T)\leq b^ k\mathbf M_ g(T).  \] For the flat norm of an $n$-chain, \[  \min \{ a^ n,a^{n+1}\} \mathcal F_ g(T) \leq \mathcal F_ h(T) \leq \max \{ b^ n,b^{n+1}\} \mathcal F_ g(T).  \] In particular the two flat topologies agree. Proof On an approximate tangent $k$-plane the eigenvalues of $h$ relative to $g$ lie in $[a^2,b^2]$. The square root of their product, the area-density ratio, lies in $[a^ k,b^ k]$. Integrate against the rectifiable multiplicity to obtain the mass bounds, also on every measurable subset. For each flat decomposition $T=R+\partial S$, with $R$ of dimension $n$ and $S$ of dimension $n+1$, apply the upper mass bounds to the two terms and take the infimum. This gives the upper flat bound. Interchanging the two metrics gives the lower bound. Smooth uniformly equivalent metrics have the same rectifiable and finite-mass chain classes, so these infima use the same decompositions. $\square$ Proposition 9.4.2 (Sweepout admissibility is independent of a smooth metric) . 2F345F35724A An admissible $p$-sweepout for one smooth metric on $M$ is admissible for every other smooth metric on $M$, with the same detecting cohomology class. Proof Compactness of $M$ gives comparison constants $a,b$ as in Lemma 9.4.1 . The same underlying cycle group has the same flat topology, boundary component and distinguished nonzero degree-one class under the identity map. Flat continuity and cohomological detection are therefore unchanged. Maximal mass remains bounded by the mass inequality. Distances satisfy $d_ h\geq a d_ g$, so $B_ r^ h(y)\subset B_{r/a}^ g(y)$, and the localized mass inequality gives \[  \| \Phi (x)\| _ h(B_ r^ h(y)) \leq b^ n\| \Phi (x)\| _ g(B_{r/a}^ g(y)).  \] Taking the supremum and then $r\downarrow 0$ proves no concentration for $h$. The reverse comparison proves equivalence. $\square$ Proposition 9.4.3 (Bilateral metric bounds for every width) . 5B976BBC1CB5 If $a^2g\leq h\leq b^2g$, then for every $p\geq 1$, \[  a^ n\omega _ p(M,g)\leq \omega _ p(M,h)\leq b^ n\omega _ p(M,g).  \] This is the metric comparison used in [ MNS19 ] , proof of Lemma 1. Proof Proposition 9.4.2 identifies the two sets of competitors. Apply the $n$-mass comparison to every slice of each family, take the supremum in the parameter, and then take the infimum over families. This proves both bounds. In particular $g\leq h$ implies $\omega _ p(M,g)\leq \omega _ p(M,h)$. Taking $a=b$ recovers the scaling formula of Lemma 9.1.4 . $\square$ Proposition 9.4.4 (Diffeomorphism invariance of the spectrum) . 278B1E4F1245 If $F:M\to M$ is a smooth diffeomorphism and $g$ is smooth, then \[  \omega _ p(M,F^*g)=\omega _ p(M,g)\quad (p\geq 1).  \] No orientation assumption on $F$ is required for mod-two coefficients. Proof The map $F:(M,F^*g)\to (M,g)$ is an isometry. Its pushforward on mod-two chains preserves boundary, masses, flat norms, and metric-ball mass estimates. Thus it gives a bijection of the admissible families. Its induced homeomorphism of the boundary-cycle component preserves the unique nonzero degree-one generator and hence all of its cup powers. Corresponding families have identical maximal masses, so their infima agree. The pushforward uses mod-two multiplicities and therefore does not require a choice of ambient orientation. $\square$ Theorem 9.4.5 (Uniform Lipschitz control of normalized widths) . D72F5ECF16F3 Let $M^{n+1}$ be smooth, closed and connected, with $n\geq 1$. Fix a smooth metric $g_0$ on $M$ and $0<A\leq B$. There is $K=K(M,g_0,A,B,n)$ such that all smooth metrics $g,h$ with $Ag_0\leq g,h\leq Bg_0$ satisfy \[  \left|p^{-1/(n+1)}\omega _ p(M,g)-p^{-1/(n+1)}\omega _ p(M,h)\right| \leq K\| g-h\| _{C^0(g_0)}  \] for every $p\geq 1$. Here the norm is $\sup _{x,v:\, g_0(v,v)=1}|(g-h)(v,v)|$. This is the smooth-metric form of [ MNS19 ] , Lemma 1. Proof Write $\varepsilon =\| g-h\| _{C^0(g_0)}$. Since $g\geq Ag_0$, we have $h\leq (1+\varepsilon /A)g$. Proposition 9.4.3 gives \[  \omega _ p(h)-\omega _ p(g) \leq \left((1+\varepsilon /A)^{n/2}-1\right)\omega _ p(g) \leq \left((1+\varepsilon /A)^{n/2}-1\right)B^{n/2}\omega _ p(g_0).  \] The norm is at most $2B$ on this band. The derivative of $t\mapsto (1+t)^{n/2}$ is bounded on $[0,2B/A]$, so the parenthesis is at most a constant times $\varepsilon $. Reverse $g,h$ for the other inequality. Finally Theorem 9.1.5 bounds $p^{-1/(n+1)}\omega _ p(g_0)$ for large $p$. The finitely many smaller widths are finite and bounded by a sufficiently large one using Lemma 9.1.3 . This gives a bound uniform in all $p$. This last step uses the external Weyl theorem; the source instead invokes the external Gromov–Guth growth bound, [ LMN ] , Theorem 2.8. $\square$ Theorem 9.4.6 (The Weyl limit is uniform on compact metric families) . 9EA7E95DFE3F Let $\mathcal G$ be a $C^0$-compact set of smooth Riemannian metrics on the fixed closed connected $M^{n+1}$, $n\geq 1$. Then \[  \lim _{p\to \infty }\sup _{g\in \mathcal G} \left|p^{-1/(n+1)}\omega _ p(M,g) -a(n)\operatorname {Vol}(M,g)^{n/(n+1)}\right|=0.  \] This is a local uniformity consequence of the pointwise Weyl law in [ LMN ] , Theorem 1.1, and the estimate of [ MNS19 ] , Lemma 1. Proof Fix $g_0$. Compactness and positive definiteness give common constants $A,B>0$ with $Ag_0\leq g\leq Bg_0$ for every $g\in \mathcal G$. Indeed the smallest and largest relative eigenvalues vary continuously with the metric in $C^0$, and their extrema over $M$ and the compact family are positive and finite. The functions $W_ p(g)=p^{-1/(n+1)}\omega _ p(M,g)$ have a common Lipschitz constant by Theorem 9.4.5 . The candidate limit $W(g)=a(n)\operatorname {Vol}(M,g)^{n/(n+1)}$ is continuous: the volume density is the square root of the metric determinant, uniformly bounded above and below on this band. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose a finite sufficiently fine $C^0$ net $g_1,\ldots ,g_ N$ in $\mathcal G$ so both the common Lipschitz error and the uniform-continuity error for $W$ are below $\varepsilon /3$. The pointwise external Weyl law makes $|W_ p(g_ i)-W(g_ i)|<\varepsilon /3$ for all net points once $p$ is large. The triangle inequality then bounds $|W_ p(g)-W(g)|$ by $\varepsilon $ for every $g\in \mathcal G$. No claim about nonsmooth limiting metrics or derivatives is made. $\square$ Proposition 9.4.7 (Volume normalization removes constant scaling) . 1F28B96B56ED For each $p\geq 1$, the quantity \[  \mathcal W_ p(g)=\frac{\omega _ p(M,g)}{\operatorname {Vol}(M,g)^{n/(n+1)}}  \] is unchanged by constant metric scaling $g\mapsto r^2g$ and by pullback under a diffeomorphism. It is continuous in the $C^0$ topology on smooth metrics. Moreover $p^{-1/(n+1)}\mathcal W_ p(g)\to a(n)$ uniformly on every $C^0$-compact family of smooth metrics. Proof Lemma 9.1.4 multiplies the numerator and denominator by the same factor $r^ n$. Diffeomorphisms preserve volume under pullback, and Proposition 9.4.4 handles the numerator. Theorem 9.4.5 gives continuity of the numerator for fixed $p$ on each uniform metric band; the determinant formula gives continuity and positivity of the denominator. On a compact family that denominator is bounded away from zero. Divide the uniform estimate in Theorem 9.4.6 by it to obtain the final assertion. This normalized quantity still depends on the shape of the metric; scaling invariance is not a statement that volume determines a finite width. $\square$ Proposition 9.4.8 (First variation with respect to the ambient metric) . 3129F5895E82 Let $g_ t$ be a smooth family of metrics with $g_0=g$ and $\dot g_0=h$. For a fixed smooth closed immersed $n$-dimensional hypersurface $\Sigma $, \[  \left.\frac d{dt}\right|_0\operatorname {Area}_{g_ t}(\Sigma ) =\frac12\int _\Sigma \operatorname {tr}_{T\Sigma ,g}h\, dA_ g, \qquad \left.\frac d{dt}\right|_0\operatorname {Vol}(M,g_ t) =\frac12\int _ M\operatorname {tr}_ g h\, dV_ g.  \] For $g_ t=e^{2tf}g$, these become $n\int _\Sigma f\, dA_ g$ and $(n+1)\int _ M f\, dV_ g$. The hypersurface formula is the metric derivative appearing in [ MNS19 ] , Lemma 2, p. 426. Proof In fixed local coordinates on $\Sigma $, let $G(t)$ be the induced metric matrix. The determinant identity gives \[  \frac d{dt}\sqrt{\det G(t)}\Big|_0 =\frac12\sqrt{\det G(0)}\operatorname {tr}(G(0)^{-1}\dot G(0)).  \] The trace is precisely the restriction of $h$ to the tangent space, traced with its induced metric. A partition of unity and compactness permit differentiation under the integral. The same calculation in ambient coordinates proves the volume formula. For the conformal variation, $h=2fg$ has tangential trace $2nf$ and ambient trace $2(n+1)f$. The calculation is local and does not need orientability of the hypersurface. $\square$ Proposition 9.4.9 (Width differentiation along an assumed smooth realizing family) . 557132487616 Suppose $g_ t$ is smooth for $t$ near zero and there are finitely many smoothly varying closed embedded $g_ t$-minimal hypersurfaces $\Sigma _ i(t)$ and fixed positive integers $m_ i$ such that \[  \omega _ p(M,g_ t)=\sum _ i m_ i\operatorname {Area}_{g_ t}(\Sigma _ i(t))  \] throughout that interval. Then the width is differentiable at zero and \[  \left.\frac d{dt}\right|_0\omega _ p(M,g_ t) =\frac12\sum _ i m_ i\int _{\Sigma _ i(0)}\operatorname {tr}_{T\Sigma _ i(0),g_0}\dot g_0\, dA_{g_0}.  \] The existence of such a smooth realizing family is an assumption here. The generic-family derivative representation in [ MNS19 ] , Lemma 2, is a separate theorem with additional regularity, transversality and dimension hypotheses. Proof Differentiate each area as a function of both the metric and the immersion. Its metric contribution is Proposition 9.4.8 . Its immersion contribution at fixed $g_0$ is the first variation of the closed minimal hypersurface and vanishes, for every variation field, whether or not the normal bundle is trivial. The finite weighted sum is therefore differentiable with the displayed derivative. By the assumed identity on an entire interval this derivative equals that of the width. An equality at a single time would not justify this step, and pointwise existence of a minimizing varifold would not give a smooth family. $\square$ Example 9.4.10 (Uniform Weyl convergence does not justify differentiating its limit) . 09F3DF8E7EC5 Uniform convergence, even with a common Lipschitz bound, does not imply convergence of derivatives at a point where all the functions and their limit are differentiable. Consequently Theorem 9.4.6 alone cannot supply a derivative formula for widths or equidistribution of individual realizing hypersurfaces. Proof On $[-1,1]$ take $f_ j(t)=\sin (jt)/j$. Then $\| f_ j\| _\infty \leq 1/j$, so $f_ j\to 0$ uniformly, and $|f_ j'(t)|=|\cos (jt)|\leq 1$. Nevertheless $f_ j'(0)=1$ for every $j$, whereas the derivative of the limit is zero. This is an elementary logical obstruction to exchanging a limit and differentiation; it does not assert that these particular functions are width functions. The additional geometric and nonsmooth variational arguments in [ MNS19 ] , Lemmas 2–3, are not replaced by uniform convergence. $\square$

section: 8.5 Compact critical sets and deformation topologies
text: The continuous pull-tight argument in [ MNIndex ] , Section 2.8, separates compactness, descent, and preservation of the homotopy class. Throughout this section $M^{n+1}$ is smooth, closed and connected, $n\geq 1$. All cycles have mod-two coefficients and lie in the boundary component of Definition 8.1.1 . Varifolds need not be rectifiable. Definition 8.5.1 (A mass cap and its stationary subset) . 7FF786CD9267 For $C>0$ let $K_ C$ be the space of all nonnegative $n$-varifolds $V$ on $M$ with $\| V\| (M)\leq C$, equipped with the bounded-Lipschitz metric $\mathbf F_ V$ on $G_ n(M)$. Write \[  S_ C=\{ V\in K_ C:\delta V(X)=0\text{ for every smooth vector field }X\} .  \] Thus $0\in S_ C$. This compact ambient space, rather than a space restricted to integral varifolds, is used in [ LiAP ] , Section 4.2. The first variation is $\delta V(X)=\int \operatorname {div}_ P X\, dV(x,P)$. Lemma 8.5.2 (Compactness and joint continuity of first variation) . 6FFDB2ED1D18 The spaces $K_ C$ and $S_ C$ of Definition 8.5.1 are compact and metrizable. If $V_ j\to V$ weakly in $K_ C$ and $X_ j\to X$ in $C^1$, then $\delta V_ j(X_ j)\to \delta V(X)$. Proof The Grassmann bundle of a closed manifold is compact and metrizable. Weak compactness of bounded positive measures on a compact space, with the Riesz representation theorem, makes $K_ C$ compact. The bounded-Lipschitz metric induces this weak topology. FA1671BEBE2B Let $X$ be a finite simplicial complex, $\Pi $ a class in Definition 8.1.2 , and $\Phi _ i\in \Pi $ a minimizing sequence with $L=\mathbf L(\Pi )<\infty $. Proof For a continuous test function $f$ on $G_ n(M)$, pushforward integrates \[  f(\varphi _ j(x),D\varphi _ j(P))J_ P\varphi _ j(x)  \] against $V_ j$. These functions converge uniformly to the corresponding expression for $\varphi $. Uniform mass bounds and weak convergence give the first assertion. For the flat part, split the difference into $(\varphi _ j)_\# (T_ j-T)$ and $(\varphi _ j)_\# T-\varphi _\# T$. A uniform Lipschitz bound gives a uniform flat-norm operator bound for the first term: push forward a decomposition $T_ j-T=A+\partial B$ and bound the masses in dimensions $n$ and $n+1$. For the second, join the sufficiently close maps by the short ambient geodesic homotopy $h_ j$. Its time derivative is bounded by a constant times $\sup d(\varphi _ j,\varphi )$, and its spatial derivative is uniformly bounded. Using a pair of tori ensures that every cycle lies in the boundary component; an individual coordinate torus would not have that property. $\square$

title: 8.6 Continuous descending fields and mass-decreasing flows

section: 8.6 Continuous descending fields and mass-decreasing flows
text: We give a continuous deformation underlying [ MNIndex ] , Section 2.8, and the outline in [ LiAP ] , Section 4.2. Fix a smooth closed connected $M^{n+1}$, $n\geq 1$, a mass bound $C>0$, and $K_ C,S_ C$ from Definition 8.5.1 . Smooth norms are fixed using a finite atlas or a background connection. The construction below uses a uniformly summable selection of fields, so a locally finite partition of unity is unnecessary. Lemma 8.6.1 (A negative first variation persists on a neighborhood) . FEE57F22C3EB For every $V\in K_ C\setminus S_ C$ there are a smooth vector field $X_ V$, a number $b_ V>0$, and an open neighborhood \[  U_ V=\{ W\in K_ C:\delta W(X_ V)<-b_ V\}   \] of $V$, disjoint from $S_ C$. Proof Nonstationarity gives a smooth field with nonzero first variation. Change its sign if necessary to make the variation negative, and choose $b_ V$ strictly between zero and $-\delta V(X_ V)$. Continuity from Lemma 8.5.2 makes $U_ V$ open. A stationary varifold has zero first variation on this field, so cannot belong to $U_ V$. $\square$ Lemma 8.6.2 (A continuous selection of smooth descending fields) . ED073D8BA201 There is a map $V\mapsto Y_ V$ from $K_ C$ to smooth vector fields, continuous in every $C^ k$ norm and uniformly bounded in each such norm, with $Y_ V=0$ for $V\in S_ C$ and $\delta V(Y_ V)<0$ for $V\notin S_ C$. Proof The open subspace $K_ C\setminus S_ C$ is second countable, so the cover in Lemma 8.6.1 has a countable subcover $U_ i$, with associated fields $X_ i$. If this subspace is empty use $Y=0$. Otherwise, repeating sets if the cover is finite, define \[  \chi _ i(V)=\frac{d(V,K_ C\setminus U_ i)}{1+d(V,K_ C\setminus U_ i)},\qquad B_ i=\max \{ 1,\| X_ i\| _{C^0},\ldots ,\| X_ i\| _{C^ i}\} ,\qquad Y_ V=\sum _{i=1}^\infty 2^{-i}\chi _ i(V)X_ i/B_ i.  \] The complements are nonempty because they contain zero. Each $\chi _ i$ is continuous, vanishes off $U_ i$, and is positive on $U_ i$. For any fixed $k$, the tail starting at $i\geq k$ is bounded in $C^ k$ by the summable series $\sum 2^{-i}$. Thus the series converges uniformly in every $C^ k$ norm and defines a spatially smooth field; uniform convergence of the continuous finite sums proves continuity of the selection and uniform bounds. On $S_ C$ every coefficient vanishes. For other $V$, all terms in $\delta V(Y_ V)$ are nonpositive and at least one is strictly negative. Passing first variation through the sum is justified by its $C^1$ convergence and the bound in Lemma 8.5.2 . $\square$ Lemma 8.6.3 (A continuous stationarity defect) . 3E3D48604A0F For the selection in Lemma 8.6.2 , set $a(V)=-\delta V(Y_ V)$. Then $a$ is continuous and nonnegative on $K_ C$, and its zero set is exactly $S_ C$. On any nonempty set $\{ V:d(V,S_ C)\geq \eta \} $ with $\eta >0$, it has a strictly positive minimum. Proof Joint continuity of first variation and $C^1$ continuity of $Y$ give continuity of $a$. Its sign and zero set follow from the selection. The set a positive distance from $S_ C$ is compact and contains no zero of $a$, so the extreme value theorem gives a positive minimum. This defect is auxiliary and depends on the chosen fields; it is not being identified with a norm of generalized mean curvature. $\square$ Lemma 8.6.4 (Uniform Taylor control along the selected flows) . CC858385ED7D Let $\varphi _ t^ V$ be the flow of the fixed field $Y_ V$ and let $A_ V(t)=\|  (\varphi _ t^ V)_\# V\| (M)$. There is $B\geq 1$, independent of $V\in K_ C$, such that for $0\leq t\leq 1$, \[  A'_ V(0)=-a(V),\qquad |A''_ V(t)|\leq B,\qquad A'_ V(t)\leq -a(V)+Bt.  \] Proof Smooth ODE flow existence and dependence on a vector field in smooth norms are the differential-equation inputs. The fields are complete since $M$ is compact, and have uniform bounds in every smooth norm. Consequently their flows and the needed spatial and time derivatives are uniformly bounded for $0\leq t\leq 1$. The rectifiable plane Jacobian, defined for every $P\in G_ n(M)$ regardless of rectifiability of $V$, gives \[  A_ V(t)=\int _{G_ n(M)}J_ P\varphi _ t^ V(x)\, dV(x,P).  \] The first derivative at zero is the first-variation formula. The second time derivative of the Jacobian is bounded uniformly on $K_ C\times [0,1]\times G_ n(M)$: it is a continuous expression in the flow derivatives, and the flow differential stays invertible with a uniform inverse bound on this interval. Integrating this bound against mass at most $C$ gives $|A''_ V|\leq B$, after enlarging $B$ to at least one. Integration in time yields the last inequality. $\square$ Proposition 8.6.5 (A continuous time choice with a positive mass drop) . 8B58860B5F4F Fix $0<\tau _0\leq 1$ and put \[  \tau (V)=\min \{ \tau _0,a(V)/(2B)\} ,\qquad D(V)=\tfrac 12 a(V)\tau (V),\qquad \mathscr H(s,V)=(\varphi _{s\tau (V)}^ V)_\# V.  \] Then $\mathscr H:[0,1]\times K_ C\to K_ C$ is continuous, fixes every stationary varifold, starts at the identity, and has nonincreasing mass in $s$. At its endpoint, \[  \| \mathscr H(1,V)\| (M)\leq \| V\| (M)-D(V).  \] The continuous function $D$ vanishes exactly on $S_ C$. Proof For $0\leq t\leq \tau (V)$, Lemma 8.6.4 gives $A'_ V(t)\leq -a(V)/2$. Integrate from zero to $s\tau (V)$ to obtain monotonicity and the endpoint estimate. For stationary $V$, both the field and the chosen time are zero. For nonstationary $V$, both $a$ and $\tau $ are positive, so $D>0$. Continuity of the fields and times gives $C^1$ continuity of the diffeomorphisms in $(s,V)$. Lemma 8.5.5 gives continuity of $\mathscr H$. Its mass bound shows it stays in $K_ C$. $\square$ Corollary 8.6.6 (Uniform loss away from stationary varifolds) . D31BFD6C3534 For every $\eta >0$ such that $K_\eta =\{ V\in K_ C:d(V,S_ C)\geq \eta \} $ is nonempty, there is $d_\eta >0$ with \[  \| \mathscr H(1,V)\| (M)\leq \| V\| (M)-d_\eta \quad (V\in K_\eta ).  \] In particular, if the mass losses of a sequence tend to zero, every convergent subsequence of the original varifolds has stationary limit. Proof Take $d_\eta =\min _{K_\eta }D>0$ using compactness and positivity from Proposition 8.6.5 . If $V_ j\to V$ and the actual losses tend to zero, the bound $0\leq D(V_ j)\leq \| V_ j\| (M)-\| \mathscr H(1,V_ j)\| (M)$ implies $D(V)=0$. Thus $V\in S_ C$. A fixed deformation and its fixed positive defect are used here; arbitrarily small losses for a changing sequence of unrelated deformations would not yield this conclusion. $\square$ Lemma 8.6.7 (Uniform closeness to the identity) . 52267311276E The choice of $\tau _0$ in Proposition 8.6.5 can make the deformation arbitrarily close to the identity in $\mathbf F_ V$, uniformly on $[0,1]\times K_ C$. For every integral mod-two cycle $T$ with mass at most $C$, the corresponding diffeomorphisms also satisfy \[  \mathcal F((\varphi _ t^{|T|})_\# T-T)\leq A t\mathbf M(T),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1,  \] with $A$ independent of $T$. Proof Uniform smooth bounds give $d(\varphi _ t(x),x)\leq A_1t$, displacement of the tangent plane at most $A_1t$, and $|J_ P\varphi _ t-1|\leq A_1t$, with a fixed smooth metric on $G_ n(M)$. For a test function of absolute value and Lipschitz constant at most one, subtract the pushforward and original integrals to bound their difference by $A_2Ct$. Taking the supremum gives the varifold estimate. For cycles, use the external mod-two homotopy formula for $h(u,x)=\varphi _ u^{|T|}(x)$ on $[0,t]\times M$. Its time derivative is uniformly bounded and its spatial derivatives are bounded, hence the swept $(n+1)$-chain has mass at most $At\mathbf M(T)$. Its boundary is the required difference because $\partial T=0$. Taking $t\leq \tau _0$ makes the sum of the two bounds arbitrarily small. No mass-distance bound follows from this argument; Example 8.5.6 rules one out in general. $\square$ Theorem 8.6.8 (A continuous pull-tight homotopy on boundary cycles) . 90DB4B31CDD9 Let $M^{n+1}$ be smooth, closed and connected, $n\geq 1$, and let $C,\varepsilon >0$. On the mass-at-most-$C$ part of $\mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2)$ there is a jointly $\mathbf F$-continuous homotopy $H(s,T)$ which starts at $T$, fixes $T$ whenever $|T|$ is stationary, has nonincreasing mass in $s$, and satisfies \[  \mathbf M(H(1,T))\leq \mathbf M(T)-D(|T|),\qquad \mathbf F(H(s,T),T)\leq \varepsilon ,  \] where $D$ is continuous on $K_ C$ and positive precisely off $S_ C$. This proves the continuous deformation stated in [ MNIndex ] , Section 2.8, from the current operations and ODE inputs specified above. Proof Choose $\tau _0$ using Lemma 8.6.7 and define $H(s,T)=(\varphi _{s\tau (|T|)}^{|T|})_\# T$. Diffeomorphic pushforward preserves integral mod-two cycles and commutes with boundary. In particular if $T=\partial U$, its image is the boundary of the image of $U$, so remains in the boundary component. The Jacobian formula with no cancellation identifies $|H(s,T)|=\mathscr H(s,|T|)$. Proposition 8.6.5 supplies mass monotonicity, the drop, and the fixed-point properties. Lemma 8.6.7 supplies the distance estimate. Finally $\mathbf F$ convergence of cycles gives weak convergence of their varifolds, hence $C^1$ convergence of the selected diffeomorphisms. Lemma 8.5.5 proves joint $\mathbf F$ continuity. No discrete mass-fineness assertion is used or proved. $\square$

Integrating this bound against mass at most $C$ gives $|A''_ V|\leq B$, after enlarging $B$ to at least one. Integration in time yields the last inequality. $\square$

text: Proposition 8.6.5 (A continuous time choice with a positive mass drop) . 8B58860B5F4F Fix $0<\tau _0\leq 1$ and put \[  \tau (V)=\min \{ \tau _0,a(V)/(2B)\} ,\qquad D(V)=\tfrac 12 a(V)\tau (V),\qquad \mathscr H(s,V)=(\varphi _{s\tau (V)}^ V)_\# V.  \] Then $\mathscr H:[0,1]\times K_ C\to K_ C$ is continuous, fixes every stationary varifold, starts at the identity, and has nonincreasing mass in $s$. At its endpoint, \[  \| \mathscr H(1,V)\| (M)\leq \| V\| (M)-D(V).  \] The continuous function $D$ vanishes exactly on $S_ C$. Proof For $0\leq t\leq \tau (V)$, Lemma 8.6.4 gives $A'_ V(t)\leq -a(V)/2$. Integrate from zero to $s\tau (V)$ to obtain monotonicity and the endpoint estimate. For stationary $V$, both the field and the chosen time are zero. For nonstationary $V$, both $a$ and $\tau $ are positive, so $D>0$. Continuity of the fields and times gives $C^1$ continuity of the diffeomorphisms in $(s,V)$. Lemma 8.5.5 gives continuity of $\mathscr H$. Its mass bound shows it stays in $K_ C$. $\square$

text: Corollary 8.6.6 (Uniform loss away from stationary varifolds) . D31BFD6C3534 For every $\eta >0$ such that $K_\eta =\{ V\in K_ C:d(V,S_ C)\geq \eta \} $ is nonempty, there is $d_\eta >0$ with \[  \| \mathscr H(1,V)\| (M)\leq \| V\| (M)-d_\eta \quad (V\in K_\eta ).  \] In particular, if the mass losses of a sequence tend to zero, every convergent subsequence of the original varifolds has stationary limit. Proof Take $d_\eta =\min _{K_\eta }D>0$ using compactness and positivity from Proposition 8.6.5 . If $V_ j\to V$ and the actual losses tend to zero, the bound $0\leq D(V_ j)\leq \| V_ j\| (M)-\| \mathscr H(1,V_ j)\| (M)$ implies $D(V)=0$. Thus $V\in S_ C$. A fixed deformation and its fixed positive defect are used here; arbitrarily small losses for a changing sequence of unrelated deformations would not yield this conclusion. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.6.7 (Uniform closeness to the identity)

section: 8.6 Continuous descending fields and mass-decreasing flows
text: Lemma 8.6.7 (Uniform closeness to the identity) . 52267311276E The choice of $\tau _0$ in Proposition 8.6.5 can make the deformation arbitrarily close to the identity in $\mathbf F_ V$, uniformly on $[0,1]\times K_ C$. For every integral mod-two cycle $T$ with mass at most $C$, the corresponding diffeomorphisms also satisfy \[  \mathcal F((\varphi _ t^{|T|})_\# T-T)\leq A t\mathbf M(T),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1,  \] with $A$ independent of $T$. Proof Uniform smooth bounds give $d(\varphi _ t(x),x)\leq A_1t$, displacement of the tangent plane at most $A_1t$, and $|J_ P\varphi _ t-1|\leq A_1t$, with a fixed smooth metric on $G_ n(M)$. For a test function of absolute value and Lipschitz constant at most one, subtract the pushforward and original integrals to bound their difference by $A_2Ct$. Taking the supremum gives the varifold estimate. For cycles, use the external mod-two homotopy formula for $h(u,x)=\varphi _ u^{|T|}(x)$ on $[0,t]\times M$. Its time derivative is uniformly bounded and its spatial derivatives are bounded, hence the swept $(n+1)$-chain has mass at most $At\mathbf M(T)$. Its boundary is the required difference because $\partial T=0$. Taking $t\leq \tau _0$ makes the sum of the two bounds arbitrarily small. No mass-distance bound follows from this argument; Example 8.5.6 rules one out in general. $\square$

title: Theorem 8.6.8 (A continuous pull-tight homotopy on boundary cycles)

section: 8.6 Continuous descending fields and mass-decreasing flows
text: Theorem 8.6.8 (A continuous pull-tight homotopy on boundary cycles) . 90DB4B31CDD9 Let $M^{n+1}$ be smooth, closed and connected, $n\geq 1$, and let $C,\varepsilon >0$. On the mass-at-most-$C$ part of $\mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2)$ there is a jointly $\mathbf F$-continuous homotopy $H(s,T)$ which starts at $T$, fixes $T$ whenever $|T|$ is stationary, has nonincreasing mass in $s$, and satisfies \[  \mathbf M(H(1,T))\leq \mathbf M(T)-D(|T|),\qquad \mathbf F(H(s,T),T)\leq \varepsilon ,  \] where $D$ is continuous on $K_ C$ and positive precisely off $S_ C$. This proves the continuous deformation stated in [ MNIndex ] , Section 2.8, from the current operations and ODE inputs specified above. Proof Choose $\tau _0$ using Lemma 8.6.7 and define $H(s,T)=(\varphi _{s\tau (|T|)}^{|T|})_\# T$. Diffeomorphic pushforward preserves integral mod-two cycles and commutes with boundary. In particular if $T=\partial U$, its image is the boundary of the image of $U$, so remains in the boundary component. The Jacobian formula with no cancellation identifies $|H(s,T)|=\mathscr H(s,|T|)$. Proposition 8.6.5 supplies mass monotonicity, the drop, and the fixed-point properties. Lemma 8.6.7 supplies the distance estimate. Finally $\mathbf F$ convergence of cycles gives weak convergence of their varifolds, hence $C^1$ convergence of the selected diffeomorphisms. Lemma 8.5.5 proves joint $\mathbf F$ continuity. No discrete mass-fineness assertion is used or proved. $\square$

title: 8.7 Pulled-tight sequences and the limits of stationarity
search_title: Pulled-tight sequences and the limits of stationarity
section: 8.7 Pulled-tight sequences and the limits of stationarity
text: The preceding deformation now acts on whole minimizing sequences. The compactness argument proves stationarity without assuming rectifiability of an arbitrary weak varifold limit. Almost-minimizing selection and replacement regularity remain further steps. Definition 8.7.1 (A pulled-tight minimizing sequence) . FB67EB71A6E8 For a fixed flat-homotopy class $\Pi $ of $\mathbf F$-continuous maps on a finite simplicial complex, a minimizing sequence is called pulled-tight if every member of its critical set is stationary. This is [ MNIndex ] , Definition 2.9. The terminology records stationarity, not smoothness, multiplicity one or index control. Theorem 8.7.2 (Pull-tight preserves the width and decreases the critical set) . CD1277EA8D53 Let $M^{n+1}$ be smooth, closed and connected, $n\geq 1$, and let $\Phi _ i\in \Pi $ be a minimizing sequence in the mod-two boundary-cycle setting of Definition 8.1.2 , with finite width $L$. There is a minimizing sequence $\Psi _ i\in \Pi $ such that \[  \mathcal C(\Psi _ i)\subset \mathcal C(\Phi _ i)\cap \{ V:\delta V=0\} .  \] Moreover $\Psi _ i$ may be chosen uniformly as close to $\Phi _ i$ in $\mathbf F$ as prescribed. This is the continuous pull-tight conclusion of [ MNIndex ] , Section 2.8; the discrete version discussed in [ LiAP ] , Section 4.2, additionally requires interpolation. Proof Choose $C>\sup _{i,x}\mathbf M(\Phi _ i(x))$, finite because the maximal masses converge. Use one fixed homotopy from Theorem 8.6.8 and set $\Psi _ i(x)=H(1,\Phi _ i(x))$. The composition is $\mathbf F$-continuous and the homotopy $H(s,\Phi _ i(x))$ is flat-continuous, so $\Psi _ i\in \Pi $. By the definition of the width and mass decrease, \[  L\leq \max _ x\mathbf M(\Psi _ i(x))\leq \max _ x\mathbf M(\Phi _ i(x))\longrightarrow L.  \] Let $W$ be critical for the new sequence, represented by $|\Psi _{i_ j}(x_ j)|\to W$ with masses tending to $L$. Pass to a subsequence with $V_ j=|\Phi _{i_ j}(x_ j)|\to V$ in $K_ C$. The old masses lie between the new masses and the old maximal masses, so they also tend to $L$. Thus $V\in \mathcal C(\Phi _ i)$ and the mass losses tend to zero. Corollary 8.6.6 gives $V\in S_ C$. Continuity of the varifold deformation then gives \[  W=\lim _ j\mathscr H(1,V_ j)=\mathscr H(1,V)=V.  \] This proves both stationarity and inclusion in the original critical set. The prescribed closeness follows from the same homotopy, without letting its positive defect vary with $i$. $\square$ Corollary 8.7.3 (Positive width produces a nonzero stationary varifold) . CB49E43C32FF Under the hypotheses of Theorem 8.7.2 , if $L>0$, there is a nonzero stationary $n$-varifold on $M$ of mass $L$ in the critical set of the original minimizing sequence. Proof The pulled-tight sequence has a nonempty critical set by Lemma 8.5.3 . Choose a member. Theorem 8.7.2 makes it stationary and a member of the original critical set; Lemma 8.5.3 gives mass $L>0$. This proof yields neither integrality nor regularity. Those stronger conclusions require additional variational selection, as in the external Theorem 8.2.3 . $\square$ Proposition 8.7.4 (Near-maximal slices of a pulled-tight sequence approach stationarity) . E310F2DBD8F7 For a pulled-tight minimizing sequence with finite width $L$, every $\eta >0$ admits $\delta >0$ and $i_0$ such that \[  i\geq i_0,\quad \mathbf M(\Phi _ i(x))\geq L-\delta \quad \Longrightarrow \quad d(|\Phi _ i(x)|,S_ C)<\eta ,  \] where $C$ bounds all masses. No rate in terms of $L-\mathbf M(\Phi _ i(x))$ is asserted. Proof The open $\eta $-neighborhood of $S_ C$ contains the critical set because the sequence is pulled-tight. Apply Lemma 8.5.4 to this neighborhood. The compactness argument supplies qualitative thresholds, with no quantitative lower bound on the auxiliary defect from first variation alone. $\square$ Example 8.7.5 (A diffuse stationary varifold on a compact manifold) . D95BB0100791 For $n\geq 1$ on the unit flat torus $M=\mathbb R^{n+1}/\mathbb Z^{n+1}$, let $P$ be the parallel plane spanned by the first $n$ coordinate fields. The varifold defined by \[  \int f\, dV=\int _ M f(x,P)\, d\operatorname {Vol}_{n+1}(x)  \] is stationary, has positive finite mass, and is not $n$-rectifiable. Proof For a smooth periodic vector field $X$, its first variation is $\int _ M\sum _{i=1}^ n\partial _ iX_ i\, dx=0$ by integration over each periodic coordinate. Its weight is ambient volume. Any countably $n$-rectifiable set has zero $(n+1)$-dimensional volume: each bounded piece of a Lipschitz image of a subset of $\mathbb R^ n$ has zero ambient volume by the elementary dimension estimate, and countable unions retain this property. Thus ambient volume cannot be carried by such a set. This example shows why the compact mass cap in the deformation argument cannot silently be treated as a compact space of integral varifolds. $\square$ Example 8.7.6 (Stationary integral varifolds can have crossings) . ADB5C190FC3B On the unit flat $(n+1)$-torus, $n\geq 1$, the varifold sum of the coordinate tori $\{ x_1=0\} $ and $\{ x_2=0\} $ is integral and stationary. Its support is not a smooth embedded hypersurface near their intersection. Proof Both tori are closed and totally geodesic, hence stationary, and first variation is linear in the varifold. Their intersection has dimension $n-1$ and zero $n$-dimensional measure, so adding them gives an integral varifold with multiplicity one away from the intersection. At an intersection point its tangent cone is the sum of two distinct transverse $n$-planes. The support therefore cannot be locally a single smooth hypersurface, nor a disjoint collection of embedded hypersurfaces. Integrality and stationarity alone cannot replace the almost-minimizing and replacement arguments in Remark 8.2.4 . $\square$

title: 7.10 Positive solutions and limits of normal graphs
search_title: Positive solutions and limits of normal graphs
section: 7.10 Positive solutions and limits of normal graphs
text:
This section supplies the analytic steps behind separated-sheet convergence in [ ChMin ] , Section 33, pp. 79–82. We retain Harnack and Schauder estimates as external inputs and prove the normalization, linearization and compactness deductions. The scalar mean-curvature convention is $H=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma 
u $, so its derivative at a minimal hypersurface is $-J$. Theorem 7.10.1 (Harnack with bounded lower-order coefficients) . C122EB493E51 Let $n\geq 1$, $R>0$, and let $A=(a^{ij})$ be symmetric and measurable on $B_{2R}\subset \mathbb R^ n$, with $\lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I$ for $0<\lambda \leq \Lambda $. Let $b,c$ be bounded measurable coefficients. If $u\in H^1(B_{2R})$ is nonnegative and solves \[  \operatorname {div}(A Du)+b\cdot Du+cu=0  \] weakly, then \[  \operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R}u\leq C\operatorname *{ess\, inf}_{B_ R}u,  \] where $C$ depends on $n,\lambda ,\Lambda ,R\| b\| _\infty ,R^2\| c\| _\infty $. No sign assumption on $c$ is required for this inequality for nonnegative solutions. The Harnack estimate is an external analytic input from [ ChMin ] , Appendix B, p. 87, and [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 18. The nonnegativity and interior margin, implicit in the shorthand appendix statement, are explicit here. Lemma 7.10.2 (Compactness after normalizing a positive solution) . A22B04D02BB2 Let $\Sigma $ be a connected smooth manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, exhausted by connected relatively compact open sets $U_ j$, and fix $p\in U_1$. Let $L_ j$ be smooth second-order operators on $U_ j$ whose coefficients converge in $C^\infty $ on every compact subset to those of a locally uniformly elliptic operator $L$. Assume their principal coefficients are symmetric. If $v_ j>0$, $L_ jv_ j=0$, and $v_ j(p)=1$, then a subsequence converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to $v>0$ with $Lv=0$ and $v(p)=1$. Proof On a coordinate chart write $L_ j=a_ j^{ab}\partial _{ab}+b_ j^ a\partial _ a+c_ j$. Rewriting its principal part as $\partial _ a(a_ j^{ab}\partial _ b)$ changes the drift to $b_ j^ b-\partial _ a a_ j^{ab}$. Smooth coefficient convergence supplies uniform ellipticity and bounds for this drift and the potential on every fixed compact chart. Theorem 7.10.1 therefore applies uniformly there. Given a compact set $K\subset \Sigma $, use connectedness to join $p$ to finitely many coordinate balls covering $K$ by a finite chain of overlapping smaller balls inside a larger relatively compact open set. For all sufficiently large $j$ these balls lie in $U_ j$. Iterating Harnack along the chain gives $C_ K^{-1}\leq v_ j\leq C_ K$ on $K$. Interior Schauder estimates, including the higher estimates in Theorem 7.5.8 , give uniform bounds for all derivatives on smaller charts. Arzela–Ascoli and a diagonal subsequence yield smooth local convergence. The positive lower bounds and normalization pass to the limit, and coefficient convergence gives $Lv=0$. Neither the Harnack iteration proof nor Schauder theory is being reproved here. $\square$ Lemma 7.10.3 (The equation for the gap between minimal normal graphs) . B17410FAAB18 Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth two-sided minimal hypersurface in a smooth Riemannian manifold, with $n\geq 1$. Suppose $u_{1,j},u_{2,j}$ define minimal normal graphs on an exhaustion and converge to zero smoothly on compact subsets. There are linear operators $L_ j$, locally uniformly elliptic for large $j$, such that \[  L_ j(u_{2,j}-u_{1,j})=0,\qquad L_ j\longrightarrow J=\Delta _\Sigma +|B|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )  \] in the smooth coefficient topology on compact subsets. Proof Pull scalar mean curvature of the graph back to $\Sigma $ and denote the resulting operator by $\mathcal H(u)$. In a normal coordinate tube $F(x,s)=\exp _ x(s
u )$, the induced metric and graph normal depend smoothly on $(x,u,Du)$. Tracing the second fundamental form shows that $\mathcal H$ is quasilinear of order two. More explicitly, its coefficient of $\partial _{ab}u$ is \[  -g_ u^{ab}\langle \partial _ sF,
u _ uangle .  \] The inner product is positive for small $C^1$ graphs; hence the negative of the linearization is elliptic. The remaining coefficients of the linearization depend smoothly on $(x,u,Du,D^2u)$ and the ambient metric. For $w_ j=u_{2,j}-u_{1,j}$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  0=\mathcal H(u_{2,j})-\mathcal H(u_{1,j}) =\int _0^1 D\mathcal H(u_{1,j}+tw_ j)[w_ j],dt.  \] Set $L_ j=-\int _0^1D\mathcal H(u_{1,j}+tw_ j)\, dt$. On each compact set all interpolating graphs tend smoothly to zero, so the coefficients converge smoothly to $-D\mathcal H(0)=J$ by Proposition 7.6.2 . This also gives uniform local ellipticity. This is the operator Taylor expansion in [ ChMin ] , Proposition 33.3, with its sign fixed by the stated scalar convention. $\square$ Corollary 7.10.4 (Comparable sheet gaps on compact subsets) . 747E58F53F15 Under the hypotheses of Theorem 7.6.5 , write $w_ j=u_{2,j}-u_{1,j}>0$. For every compact $K$ in the interior there is $C_ K\geq 1$ such that, for all large $j$, \[  C_ K^{-1}\leq w_ j(x)/w_ j(p)\leq C_ K\qquad (x\in K).  \] If a normalized subsequence tends to $v$ and $q$ is another interior point, normalization at $q$ instead gives the limit $v/v(q)$. Proof Apply the Harnack-chain step of Lemma 7.10.2 to the operators from Lemma 7.10.3 . This gives the bounds without a priori control on the rate at which the unnormalized gap tends to zero. For the last assertion divide $w_ j(x)/w_ j(p)$ by $w_ j(q)/w_ j(p)$; the denominator converges to the positive number $v(q)$. $\square$ Proposition 7.10.5 (Positive supersolutions and the quadratic form) . 8E562438D97E Let $(\Sigma ,g)$ be smooth, let $q$ be smooth, and set $J=\Delta +q$ and $Q(\phi )=\int (|
abla \phi |^2-q\phi ^2)$. For every smooth $w>0$ and compactly supported smooth interior test $\phi $, \[  Q(\phi )=\int w^2|
abla (\phi /w)|^2+\int  rac{-Jw}{w}\phi ^2.  \] In particular $Jw\leq 0$ implies $Q\geq 0$ on such tests. This extends the positive-solution identity used in [ ChMin ] , Proposition 33.4. Proof Write $\phi =w\eta $. Expand $|
abla (w\eta )|^2$ and group the terms other than $w^2|
abla \eta |^2$ as $
abla w\cdot 
abla (w\eta ^2)-qw^2\eta ^2$. Their integral is $-\int w\eta ^2(\Delta w+qw)$ by integration by parts. Substitution of $\eta =\phi /w$ proves the identity. Compact support removes boundary terms, and $w$ has a positive minimum on the support, so every expression is well defined. $\square$ Proposition 7.10.6 (A positive Jacobi field on a closed manifold has simple kernel) . 3A7A095E3DA2 Let $\Sigma $ be smooth, connected and closed, and let $q$ be smooth. If $w>0$ satisfies $(\Delta +q)w=0$, then the smooth kernel of $J=\Delta +q$ consists exactly of the constant multiples of $w$. Proof For any $Jf=0$, integration by parts gives $Q(f)=-\int fJf=0$. Proposition 7.10.5 , applied on the compact manifold with no boundary, gives $0=\int w^2|
abla (f/w)|^2$. Thus $f/w$ is constant by connectedness. Conversely every constant multiple of $w$ lies in the kernel. Closedness is essential to this integration argument; no corresponding assertion for all solutions on a noncompact manifold is made. $\square$ Proposition 7.10.7 (Accumulating minimal normal graphs force degeneracy) . 8A40075C4DD7 Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth closed two-sided embedded minimal hypersurface, $n\geq 1$. Suppose nonzero smooth functions $u_ j	o 0$ in $C^\infty (\Sigma )$ define minimal normal graphs. Then $J$ has a nonzero smooth kernel element. Consequently, if $\ker J=0$, the zero graph is isolated among minimal normal graphs in the smooth topology. The functions $u_ j$ need not have a common sign. Compare the nullity mechanism in [ Sharp17 ] , Theorem 2.3 and its discussion. Proof Apply the averaged linearization of Lemma 7.10.3 with $u_{1,j}=0$ and $u_{2,j}=u_ j$, and set $v_ j=u_ j/\| u_ j\| _{C^0}$. Then $L_ jv_ j=0$, $L_ j	o J$ smoothly and $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}=1$. A finite covering of the closed hypersurface and interior Schauder estimates yield uniform bounds in every $C^ k$ norm. A subsequence converges smoothly to $v$ with $Jv=0$ and $\| v\| _{C^0}=1$. If the zero graph were not isolated in the metrizable smooth topology, a sequence of distinct minimal graphs converging smoothly to zero would contradict the trivial-kernel assumption. This is local isolation of normal graphs, not a global finiteness theorem for minimal hypersurfaces. $\square$

C122EB493E51 Let $n\geq 1$, $R>0$, and let $A=(a^{ij})$ be symmetric and measurable on $B_{2R}\subset \mathbb R^ n$, with $\lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I$ for $0<\lambda \leq \Lambda $. If $u\in H^1(B_{2R})$ is nonnegative and solves \[  \operatorname {div}(A Du)+b\cdot Du+cu=0  \] weakly, then \[  \operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R}u\leq C\operatorname *{ess\, inf}_{B_ R}u,  \] where $C$ depends on $n,\lambda ,\Lambda ,R\| b\| _\infty ,R^2\| c\| _\infty $. No sign assumption on $c$ is required for this inequality for nonnegative solutions. The Harnack estimate is an external analytic input from [ ChMin ] , Appendix B, p. 87, and [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 18. title: Lemma 7.10.2 (Compactness after normalizing a positive solution)

section: 7.10 Positive solutions and limits of normal graphs
text: Lemma 7.10.2 (Compactness after normalizing a positive solution) . A22B04D02BB2 Let $\Sigma $ be a connected smooth manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, exhausted by connected relatively compact open sets $U_ j$, and fix $p\in U_1$. Let $L_ j$ be smooth second-order operators on $U_ j$ whose coefficients converge in $C^\infty $ on every compact subset to those of a locally uniformly elliptic operator $L$. Assume their principal coefficients are symmetric. If $v_ j>0$, $L_ jv_ j=0$, and $v_ j(p)=1$, then a subsequence converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to $v>0$ with $Lv=0$ and $v(p)=1$. Proof On a coordinate chart write $L_ j=a_ j^{ab}\partial _{ab}+b_ j^ a\partial _ a+c_ j$. Rewriting its principal part as $\partial _ a(a_ j^{ab}\partial _ b)$ changes the drift to $b_ j^ b-\partial _ a a_ j^{ab}$. Smooth coefficient convergence supplies uniform ellipticity and bounds for this drift and the potential on every fixed compact chart. Theorem 7.10.1 therefore applies uniformly there. Given a compact set $K\subset \Sigma $, use connectedness to join $p$ to finitely many coordinate balls covering $K$ by a finite chain of overlapping smaller balls inside a larger relatively compact open set. For all sufficiently large $j$ these balls lie in $U_ j$. Iterating Harnack along the chain gives $C_ K^{-1}\leq v_ j\leq C_ K$ on $K$. Interior Schauder estimates, including the higher estimates in Theorem 7.5.8 , give uniform bounds for all derivatives on smaller charts. Arzela–Ascoli and a diagonal subsequence yield smooth local convergence. The positive lower bounds and normalization pass to the limit, and coefficient convergence gives $Lv=0$. Neither the Harnack iteration proof nor Schauder theory is being reproved here. $\square$

Lemma 7.10.3 (The equation for the gap between minimal normal graphs) . B17410FAAB18 Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth two-sided minimal hypersurface in a smooth Riemannian manifold, with $n\geq 1$. Suppose $u_{1,j},u_{2,j}$ define minimal normal graphs on an exhaustion and converge to zero smoothly on compact subsets. There are linear operators $L_ j$, locally uniformly elliptic for large $j$, such that \[  L_ j(u_{2,j}-u_{1,j})=0,\qquad L_ j\longrightarrow J=\Delta _\Sigma +|B|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )  \] in the smooth coefficient topology on compact subsets. Proof Pull scalar mean curvature of the graph back to $\Sigma $ and denote the resulting operator by $\mathcal H(u)$. In a normal coordinate tube $F(x,s)=\exp _ x(s
u )$, the induced metric and graph normal depend smoothly on $(x,u,Du)$. Tracing the second fundamental form shows that $\mathcal H$ is quasilinear of order two. More explicitly, its coefficient of $\partial _{ab}u$ is \[  -g_ u^{ab}\langle \partial _ sF,
u _ uangle .  \] The inner product is positive for small $C^1$ graphs; hence the negative of the linearization is elliptic. The remaining coefficients of the linearization depend smoothly on $(x,u,Du,D^2u)$ and the ambient metric. For $w_ j=u_{2,j}-u_{1,j}$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  0=\mathcal H(u_{2,j})-\mathcal H(u_{1,j}) =\int _0^1 D\mathcal H(u_{1,j}+tw_ j)[w_ j],dt.  \] Set $L_ j=-\int _0^1D\mathcal H(u_{1,j}+tw_ j)\, dt$. On each compact set all interpolating graphs tend smoothly to zero, so the coefficients converge smoothly to $-D\mathcal H(0)=J$ by Proposition 7.6.2 . This also gives uniform local ellipticity. This is the operator Taylor expansion in [ ChMin ] , Proposition 33.3, with its sign fixed by the stated scalar convention. $\square$

text: Corollary 7.10.4 (Comparable sheet gaps on compact subsets) . 747E58F53F15 Under the hypotheses of Theorem 7.6.5 , write $w_ j=u_{2,j}-u_{1,j}>0$. For every compact $K$ in the interior there is $C_ K\geq 1$ such that, for all large $j$, \[  C_ K^{-1}\leq w_ j(x)/w_ j(p)\leq C_ K\qquad (x\in K).  \] If a normalized subsequence tends to $v$ and $q$ is another interior point, normalization at $q$ instead gives the limit $v/v(q)$. Proof Apply the Harnack-chain step of Lemma 7.10.2 to the operators from Lemma 7.10.3 . This gives the bounds without a priori control on the rate at which the unnormalized gap tends to zero. title: Proposition 7.10.6 (A positive Jacobi field on a closed manifold has simple kernel)
search_title: A positive Jacobi field on a closed manifold has simple kernel
section: 7.10 Positive solutions and limits of normal graphs
text: Proposition 7.10.6 (A positive Jacobi field on a closed manifold has simple kernel) . 3A7A095E3DA2 Let $\Sigma $ be smooth, connected and closed, and let $q$ be smooth. If $w>0$ satisfies $(\Delta +q)w=0$, then the smooth kernel of $J=\Delta +q$ consists exactly of the constant multiples of $w$. Proof For any $Jf=0$, integration by parts gives $Q(f)=-\int fJf=0$. Proposition 7.10.5 , applied on the compact manifold with no boundary, gives $0=\int w^2|\nabla (f/w)|^2$. Thus $f/w$ is constant by connectedness. Conversely every constant multiple of $w$ lies in the kernel. Closedness is essential to this integration argument; no corresponding assertion for all solutions on a noncompact manifold is made. $\square$

title: Proposition 7.10.7 (Accumulating minimal normal graphs force degeneracy)
search_title: Accumulating minimal normal graphs force degeneracy
section: 7.10 Positive solutions and limits of normal graphs
text: Proposition 7.10.7 (Accumulating minimal normal graphs force degeneracy) . 8A40075C4DD7 Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth closed two-sided embedded minimal hypersurface, $n\geq 1$. Suppose nonzero smooth functions $u_ j\to 0$ in $C^\infty (\Sigma )$ define minimal normal graphs. Then $J$ has a nonzero smooth kernel element. Consequently, if $\ker J=0$, the zero graph is isolated among minimal normal graphs in the smooth topology. The functions $u_ j$ need not have a common sign. Compare the nullity mechanism in [ Sharp17 ] , Theorem 2.3 and its discussion. Proof Apply the averaged linearization of Lemma 7.10.3 with $u_{1,j}=0$ and $u_{2,j}=u_ j$, and set $v_ j=u_ j/\| u_ j\| _{C^0}$. Then $L_ jv_ j=0$, $L_ j\to J$ smoothly and $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}=1$. A finite covering of the closed hypersurface and interior Schauder estimates yield uniform bounds in every $C^ k$ norm. A subsequence converges smoothly to $v$ with $Jv=0$ and $\| v\| _{C^0}=1$. If the zero graph were not isolated in the metrizable smooth topology, a sequence of distinct minimal graphs converging smoothly to zero would contradict the trivial-kernel assumption. This is local isolation of normal graphs, not a global finiteness theorem for minimal hypersurfaces. $\square$

title: 7.11 Small-capacity punctures and removable stability
