text:
The cutoffs here shrink around a missing point, in contrast with the large-radius cutoffs used in Bernstein arguments. We work on an already smooth manifold with a locally bounded potential; removal of a singularity of the hypersurface itself is a different regularity problem. The geometric source is [ ChMin ] , Lemma 33.5, pp. 81–82, and the cutoff discussion in [ Sharp17 ] , p. 324. Definition 7.11.1 (Local cutoffs avoiding a closed set) . B8E027663FF9 A closed measure-zero subset $E$ of a smooth manifold $\Sigma $ has the cutoff property used here if, for every compact $K\subset \Sigma $, there are locally Lipschitz functions $0\leq \eta _ j\leq 1$ on a neighborhood of $K$, vanishing on an open neighborhood of $E\cap K$, such that $\eta _ j	o 1$ almost everywhere on $K$ and $\int _ K|
abla \eta _ j|^2	o 0$. The property must hold also on larger compact neighborhoods containing the support of any test function. This explicit local zero-capacity condition is all that is used below; broader equivalences for capacity are not assumed. Compare the cutoff mechanism in [ ChMin ] , Lemma 33.5. Lemma 7.11.2 (A point has cutoffs of arbitrarily small energy in dimension at least two) . 4E098CFF9186 On a smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with $n\geq 2$, a single interior point has the property in Definition 7.11.1 . The cutoffs can equal one outside a shrinking coordinate ball. Their Dirichlet energies are $O(\varepsilon ^{n-2})$ for $n>2$ and $O(1/|\log \varepsilon |)$ for $n=2$. Proof Use normal coordinates centered at the point, where the metric and volume density are uniformly comparable with their Euclidean counterparts in a fixed small ball. For $n>2$, take a radial cutoff zero for $r\leq \varepsilon $, one for $r\geq 2\varepsilon $, and with derivative bounded by $2/\varepsilon $. Its energy is at most $C\varepsilon ^{-2}\varepsilon ^ n$. For $n=2$ and $0<\varepsilon <1$, take zero for $r\leq \varepsilon ^2$, one for $r\geq \varepsilon $, and \[  \eta _\varepsilon (r)= rac{\log (r/\varepsilon ^2)}{\log (1/\varepsilon )} \quad (\varepsilon ^2<r<\varepsilon ).  \] Its energy is bounded by \[   rac{C}{\log (1/\varepsilon )^2}\int _{\varepsilon ^2}^{\varepsilon } rac{dr}{r} = rac{C}{\log (1/\varepsilon )}.  \] Extend each cutoff by one outside the chart. They are locally Lipschitz, vanish near the point, and converge to one away from it. A point has zero Riemannian volume, so the almost-everywhere requirement follows. The estimates are the small-radius logarithmic cutoff argument of [ ChMin ] , Lemma 33.5. $\square$ Lemma 7.11.3 (Finite unions and approximation of test functions) . 04A378869597 Finite sets on a smooth manifold of dimension at least two have the cutoff property. More generally, if a closed set $E$ has that property, every $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\Sigma )$ can be approximated in $H^1$ by functions $\phi _ j\in C_ c^\infty (\Sigma \setminus E)$ whose supports lie in a fixed compact set. For any locally bounded $q$, the quadratic forms $\int (|
abla \phi _ j|^2-q\phi _ j^2)$ converge to the form of $\phi $. Proof For finitely many points take the product of their cutoffs. Each factor lies in $[0,1]$, so for $N$ factors its squared gradient is at most $N$ times the sum of the squared gradients. Pointwise convergence off the finite set and vanishing energy follow from Lemma 7.11.2 . For a general $E$, choose a compact neighborhood $K$ of $\operatorname {spt}\phi $ and cutoffs there. The functions $\phi \eta _ j$ vanish near $E$ on their support and \[  
abla (\phi \eta _ j-\phi )=(\eta _ j-1)
abla \phi +\phi 
abla \eta _ j.  \] Dominated convergence controls the first term and the $L^2$ error, while the vanishing energy controls the second term. Smooth approximation of each compactly supported Lipschitz function inside the open set $\Sigma \setminus E$, with error tending to zero in $H^1$, gives the required smooth sequence. The supports can remain in one fixed compact neighborhood. Since $q$ is bounded there, $H^1$ convergence also gives convergence of the potential term, by $L^2$ convergence and Cauchy–Schwarz. $\square$ Theorem 7.11.4 (Stability extends across sets with the cutoff property) . 04F4CF70F97D Let $\Sigma $ be smooth, $q\in L^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(\Sigma )$, and let $E\subset \Sigma $ be closed with the property in Definition 7.11.1 . If \[  \int _\Sigma (|
abla \phi |^2-q\phi ^2)\geq 0 \quad 	ext{for all }\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\Sigma \setminus E),  \] then the same inequality holds for all $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\Sigma )$. In particular, on a smooth two-sided minimal hypersurface of dimension at least two, stability away from finitely many points implies stability everywhere. This supplies the smooth-manifold cutoff deduction in [ ChMin ] , Lemma 33.5, and [ Sharp17 ] , p. 324. Proof Approximate an arbitrary compactly supported smooth test by Lemma 7.11.3 . Each approximant has nonnegative quadratic form, and the forms converge, so the limiting form is nonnegative. For a smooth minimal hypersurface the Jacobi potential $q=|B|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )$ is bounded on compact subsets. Finite sets satisfy the cutoff property in dimension at least two, so the general result applies. This proof does not require extending a positive Jacobi function across the missing points, nor does it prove that an initially singular hypersurface becomes smooth. $\square$ Example 7.11.5 (Removing a point can change stability in dimension one) . CEDADA80CB0B On $(-1,1)$ the quadratic form \[  Q(f)=\int _{-1}^1\left(|f'|^2- rac{\pi ^2}{2}f^2ight)  \] is nonnegative on $C_ c^\infty ((-1,1)\setminus \{ 0\} )$ but negative on some $C_ c^\infty (-1,1)$ test. Proof On each unit-length half-interval the positive sine function solves $w''+\pi ^2w=0$. Applying Proposition 7.10.5 with potential $\pi ^2$ gives $\int |f'|^2\geq \pi ^2\int f^2$ for compactly supported tests there. Splitting a test supported away from zero into its two halves proves nonnegativity for the displayed smaller potential. On the full interval, $f(x)=\cos (\pi x/2)$ belongs to $H_0^1(-1,1)$ and has $\int |f'|^2=(\pi ^2/4)\int f^2$, so $Q(f)<0$. Smooth compactly supported approximations in $H_0^1$ retain strict negativity. Thus the dimension restriction in point-capacity removal cannot be discarded. $\square$ Corollary 7.11.6 (Ordered sheets away from finitely many points imply global stability) . 7D9C1F01B117 Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth connected closed two-sided embedded minimal hypersurface, $n\geq 2$, and let $P\subset \Sigma $ be finite. Suppose on an exhaustion of $\Sigma \setminus P$ there are two globally ordered minimal normal graphs whose functions converge smoothly to zero on compact subsets. Then $\Sigma $ is stable. In particular this configuration is impossible if the ambient Ricci curvature is strictly positive along $\Sigma $. Proof A connected manifold of dimension at least two remains connected after finitely many points are removed: a path meeting those points can be rerouted in small punctured coordinate balls. Theorem 7.6.5 therefore gives a positive Jacobi function on $\Sigma \setminus P$, and Proposition 7.6.3 gives stability there. Theorem 7.11.4 extends it across $P$. If the ambient Ricci curvature is positive, the global test one instead gives \[  Q(1)=-\int _\Sigma  igl (|B|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u ) igr )\, dA<0,  \] contradicting stability. The existence of globally ordered normal sheets and a smooth two-sided limit are hypotheses; numerical multiplicity alone has not established them here. $\square$

title: 7.12 Localization of index and weak convergence of variations

section: 7.12 Localization of index and weak convergence of variations
text:
Negative directions persist only when their entire quadratic form remains negative definite. This section separates that finite-dimensional fact from regularity of a weak limit. Sources are [ Sharp17 ] , pp. 324–327, and the second-variation framework of the preceding chapters. Definition 7.12.1 (Compactly supported index) . 74B73BFDE4B7 For a smooth manifold $\Sigma $ and locally bounded real potential $q$, set $Q(f,h)=\int (\langle 
abla f,
abla hangle -qfh)$ on compactly supported smooth interior functions. Its index is the supremum of the dimensions of vector spaces on which $Q$ is negative definite, allowing the value infinity. Stability means index zero. For a two-sided minimal hypersurface use $q=|B|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )$. This compact-support convention extends the index used in [ Sharp17 ] , Section 3, to noncompact domains. Proposition 7.12.2 (Finite index gives stability outside a compact set) . E86FC1854BD4 If the quadratic form in Definition 7.12.1 has finite index, there is a compact subset $K\subset \Sigma $ such that $Q(f,f)\geq 0$ for every $f\in C_ c^\infty (\Sigma \setminus K)$. Proof If no such $K$ existed, choose a negative test $f_1$, then a negative test $f_2$ outside a compact neighborhood of its support, and continue outside compact neighborhoods of all preceding supports. This produces arbitrarily many nonzero negative tests with pairwise disjoint supports. Every cross term vanishes, so their span is negative definite. They are linearly independent, contradicting finite index. This is the same disjoint-support mechanism as Lemma 7.3.1 ; it uses no curvature estimate and asserts no geometry of the ends. $\square$ Proposition 7.12.3 (Finite index gives a stable punctured neighborhood) . 7034A7DD4402 Let $p$ be an interior point of a smooth manifold, and let $Q$ be a quadratic form as in Definition 7.12.1 on a punctured neighborhood $B_ r(p)\setminus \{ p\} $. If its compactly supported index there is finite, some smaller punctured ball is stable. The potential may be unbounded as $p$ is approached, provided it is locally bounded on the punctured domain. Proof Otherwise every smaller punctured ball admits a compactly supported negative test. After choosing such a test, its support stays a positive distance from $p$; choose the next ball with closure disjoint from that support. Induction produces arbitrarily many negative tests with disjoint supports in nested annuli. Their span is negative definite, contradicting finite index. This is the nested-annulus argument in [ Sharp17 ] , p. 326. It does not assert stability across $p$ when the potential or the underlying geometry is singular there. $\square$ Lemma 7.12.4 (Negative definite forms persist under matrix convergence) . DF7E085F8EF9 Let symmetric quadratic forms $Q_ j$ on $\mathbb R^ k$ converge coefficientwise to a negative definite form $Q$. Then for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $j$, \[  Q_ j(z)\leq -c|z|^2\qquad (z\in \mathbb R^ k).  \] Having $Q(e_ a)<0$ for each standard basis vector alone would not suffice. Proof The maximum of $Q$ on the compact unit sphere is strictly negative, say $-2c$. Coefficient convergence in finite dimension gives uniform convergence there, so eventually $Q_ j\leq -c$ on the sphere. Homogeneity gives the assertion. For the final warning, the symmetric matrix with diagonal entries $-1$ and off-diagonal entries $2$ is negative on both coordinate vectors, but its value on $(1,1)$ is $2>0$. Thus one must control cross terms, not just each individual direction. $\square$ Lemma 7.12.5 (Weak continuity of a finite family of ambient second variations) . C34F05CF122D Let $M$ be smooth and closed, and let stationary $n$-varifolds $V_ j	o V$ weakly. Fix smooth ambient vector fields $X_1,\ldots ,X_ k$, put $X_ z=\sum _ a z_ aX_ a$, and define \[  \varphi _ t^ z(x)=\exp _ x(tX_ z(x)),\qquad Q_{V_ j}(z)=\left. rac{d^2}{dt^2}ight|_{t=0}\| (\varphi _ t^ z)_\# V_ j\| (M).  \] These symmetric quadratic forms converge coefficientwise to $Q_ V$. For a smooth minimal hypersurface, the form is the usual second variation of its normal velocity. Compare [ Sharp17 ] , p. 324. Proof For $z$ in a fixed bounded set and $t$ sufficiently small, the maps are smooth diffeomorphisms close to the identity. CFEE9839203E Let $M^{n+1}$ be smooth and closed, $n\geq 1$. Let $\Sigma _ j$ and $\Sigma $ be smooth closed two-sided embedded minimal hypersurfaces. If \[  |\Sigma _ j|\longrightarrow m|\Sigma |\quad 	ext{as varifolds},\qquad m>0,  \] then $\operatorname {index}(\Sigma )\leq \liminf _ j\operatorname {index}(\Sigma _ j)$. u $ to smooth ambient fields $X_ a$ using a tubular neighborhood and a cutoff. At the limit varifold, Lemma 7.12.5 identifies the form on coefficient vectors with \[  Q_{m|\Sigma |}(z)=mQ_\Sigma \left(\sum _ a z_ af_ a,\sum _ a z_ af_ aight),  \] which is negative definite because $m>0$. Lemma 7.12.4 makes the corresponding forms on $\Sigma _ j$ negative definite for all large $j$. Their normal velocities are the functions $\langle X_ a,
u _ jangle $. These functions are linearly independent: a zero linear combination would have second variation zero, contradicting strict negativity for its nonzero coefficient vector. Their span therefore gives $\operatorname {index}(\Sigma _ j)\geq k$. Since every finite negative subspace of the limit can be used, the stated inequality follows, including when its index is infinite. Proof The theorem gives $\operatorname {index}(\Sigma )\leq 0$, which is stability. text: Proposition 7.12.2 (Finite index gives stability outside a compact set) . E86FC1854BD4 If the quadratic form in Definition 7.12.1 has finite index, there is a compact subset $K\subset \Sigma $ such that $Q(f,f)\geq 0$ for every $f\in C_ c^\infty (\Sigma \setminus K)$. Proof If no such $K$ existed, choose a negative test $f_1$, then a negative test $f_2$ outside a compact neighborhood of its support, and continue outside compact neighborhoods of all preceding supports. This produces arbitrarily many nonzero negative tests with pairwise disjoint supports. Every cross term vanishes, so their span is negative definite. They are linearly independent, contradicting finite index. This is the same disjoint-support mechanism as Lemma 7.3.1 ; it uses no curvature estimate and asserts no geometry of the ends. $\square$

text: Proposition 7.12.3 (Finite index gives a stable punctured neighborhood) . 7034A7DD4402 Let $p$ be an interior point of a smooth manifold, and let $Q$ be a quadratic form as in Definition 7.12.1 on a punctured neighborhood $B_ r(p)\setminus \{ p\} $. If its compactly supported index there is finite, some smaller punctured ball is stable. The potential may be unbounded as $p$ is approached, provided it is locally bounded on the punctured domain. Proof Otherwise every smaller punctured ball admits a compactly supported negative test. After choosing such a test, its support stays a positive distance from $p$; choose the next ball with closure disjoint from that support. Induction produces arbitrarily many negative tests with disjoint supports in nested annuli. Their span is negative definite, contradicting finite index. This is the nested-annulus argument in [ Sharp17 ] , p. 326. It does not assert stability across $p$ when the potential or the underlying geometry is singular there. $\square$

title: Lemma 7.12.4 (Negative definite forms persist under matrix convergence)

section: 7.12 Localization of index and weak convergence of variations
text: Lemma 7.12.4 (Negative definite forms persist under matrix convergence) . DF7E085F8EF9 Let symmetric quadratic forms $Q_ j$ on $\mathbb R^ k$ converge coefficientwise to a negative definite form $Q$. Then for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $j$, \[  Q_ j(z)\leq -c|z|^2\qquad (z\in \mathbb R^ k).  \] Having $Q(e_ a)<0$ for each standard basis vector alone would not suffice. Proof The maximum of $Q$ on the compact unit sphere is strictly negative, say $-2c$. Coefficient convergence in finite dimension gives uniform convergence there, so eventually $Q_ j\leq -c$ on the sphere. Homogeneity gives the assertion. For the final warning, the symmetric matrix with diagonal entries $-1$ and off-diagonal entries $2$ is negative on both coordinate vectors, but its value on $(1,1)$ is $2>0$. Thus one must control cross terms, not just each individual direction. $\square$

title: 7.13 Power tests and Moser iteration
search_title: Power tests and Moser iteration
text: We now prove the local-boundedness step used in elliptic regularity. Unless stated otherwise, $n\geq 2$, $A$ is measurable and symmetric, and $\lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I$ with $0<\lambda \leq \Lambda $. A weak subsolution of $\operatorname {div}(A Du)=0$ satisfies $\int A Du\cdot D\phi \leq 0$ for nonnegative compactly supported tests. There are no lower-order terms in this section. The source is [ SimonPDE ] , Lecture 17, Theorem 1 and its preparatory lemmas, printed pp. 199–205. Theorem 7.13.1 (The Sobolev gain used in iteration) . B8CE044300F3 For $n\geq 2$, put $\chi =n/(n-2)$ if $n>2$, and $\chi =2$ if $n=2$. There is $S_ n<\infty $ such that every $w\in H_0^1(B_2\subset \mathbb R^ n)$ satisfies \[  \left(\int _{B_2}|w|^{2\chi }\right)^{1/\chi } \leq S_ n\int _{B_2}|Dw|^2.  \] See [ SimonPDE ] , Lecture 17, Lemma 2, pp. 200–201, and Corollary 1, p. 202. The choice $n/(n-2)$ is not used in dimension two. Proof Corollary 7.14.6 , proved from the coordinate-projection Holder inequality and the first-power Sobolev estimate, gives the assertion with $R=2$. Its radius factor is fixed and can be included in $S_ n$. In dimension two the proof uses the finite-power inequality of Theorem 7.14.5 with $q=4$. $\square$ Lemma 7.13.2 (Positive parts preserve the subsolution inequality) . B951D0F32E6B If $v\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ is a weak subsolution for the coefficients fixed above, then $(v-k)_+$ is a weak subsolution for every constant $k$. If $v$ is a weak solution, both $v_+$ and $(-v)_+$ are nonnegative weak subsolutions. Proof Choose smooth convex nondecreasing approximations $\beta _\varepsilon $ to the positive-part function, with $0\leq \beta '_\varepsilon \leq 1$ and $\beta ''_\varepsilon \geq 0$. Test the subsolution inequality with $\eta \beta '_\varepsilon (v-k)$ for $0\leq \eta \in C_ c^\infty (U)$. This is an admissible $H_0^1$ test; approximation by nonnegative smooth tests is justified because $A Dv$ is locally square integrable. The chain rule gives \[  \int \beta '_\varepsilon (v-k)A Dv\cdot D\eta \leq -\int \eta \beta ''_\varepsilon (v-k)A Dv\cdot Dv\leq 0.  \] The Sobolev chain rule and the fact that $Dv=0$ almost everywhere on a level set give $\beta _\varepsilon (v-k)\to (v-k)_+$ in $H^1$ on compact subsets. Pass to the limit to get the required inequality. These elementary Sobolev composition and approximation facts are the functional-analytic inputs. For a solution, $-v$ is also a solution; apply the first assertion with $k=0$ to both signs. The constant shift is legitimate because the equation has no zero-order term. $\square$ Lemma 7.13.3 (Energy estimate for truncated powers) . 7066CAF042C4 Let $u\geq 0$ be an $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ weak subsolution, let $p\geq 2$, $L>0$, and set \[  u_ L=\min \{ u,L\} ,\qquad v_ L=u\, u_ L^{p/2-1}.  \] For $p=2$ interpret $v_ L=u$. For every nonnegative smooth compactly supported cutoff $\eta $, \[  \int |D(\eta v_ L)|^2 \leq C p^2(\Lambda /\lambda )^2\int v_ L^2|D\eta |^2,  \] where $C$ is an absolute constant independent of $p,L,u$. Proof For fixed $L$, the functions $s\mapsto s\min (s,L)^{p-2}$ and $s\mapsto s\min (s,L)^{p/2-1}$ are Lipschitz on $[0,\infty )$, with the $p=2$ case interpreted separately. Thus $\eta ^2u u_ L^{p-2}$ is an admissible nonnegative $H_0^1$ test, even though no boundedness of $u$ has been proved. The term obtained by differentiating $u_ L^{p-2}$ is nonnegative by ellipticity. Dropping it and using Young's inequality gives \[  \int \eta ^2 u_ L^{p-2}|Du|^2 \leq 4(\Lambda /\lambda )^2\int u^2u_ L^{p-2}|D\eta |^2.  \] On $\{ u<L\} $ the derivative of $v_ L=u^{p/2}$ is $(p/2)u^{p/2-1}Du$, whereas on $\{ u>L\} $ it is $L^{p/2-1}Du$. Consequently \[  |Dv_ L|^2\leq (p^2/4)u_ L^{p-2}|Du|^2  \] almost everywhere. Combining this with $|D(\eta v_ L)|^2\leq 2\eta ^2|Dv_ L|^2+2v_ L^2|D\eta |^2$ proves the estimate. Truncation gives an $H^1$ function with bounded value, not a claim of bounded gradient; this distinction matters in the source's power-test calculation, [ SimonPDE ] , pp. 202–203. $\square$ Lemma 7.13.4 (One step of integrability improvement) . C8B26982BF2A Let $u\geq 0$ be a weak subsolution on $B_2$, and suppose $u\in L^ p(B_ s)$ for $p\geq 2$ and $1\leq r<s\leq 2$. With $\chi $ as in Theorem 7.13.1 , \[  \| u\| _{L^{p\chi }(B_ r)} \leq \left(\frac{C p^2}{(s-r)^2}\right)^{1/p}\| u\| _{L^ p(B_ s)},  \] where $C$ depends only on $n$ and $\Lambda /\lambda $. Proof Choose $\eta =1$ on $B_ r$, supported in $B_ s$, with $|D\eta |\leq C/(s-r)$. Apply the Sobolev gain to $\eta v_ L$ and then Lemma 7.13.3 . The right side is bounded by $Cp^2(s-r)^{-2}\int _{B_ s}u^ p$, because $v_ L^2=u^2u_ L^{p-2}\leq u^ p$. As $L\to \infty $, Fatou's lemma gives \[  \left(\int _{B_ r}u^{p\chi }\right)^{1/\chi } \leq \frac{Cp^2}{(s-r)^2}\int _{B_ s}u^ p.  \] Taking the $p$th root proves the claim. In particular the higher integrability is a conclusion of the argument, not an assumption permitting an untruncated power test. $\square$ Theorem 7.13.5 (Moser local boundedness for nonnegative subsolutions) . DB183F3A4CE7 Let $n\geq 2$, let $A$ be measurable and symmetric on $B_{2R}(a)$ with $\lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I$ for $0<\lambda \leq \Lambda $, and let $u\in H^1(B_{2R}(a))$ be a nonnegative weak subsolution of $\operatorname {div}(A Du)=0$. Then \[  \operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R(a)}u \leq C(n,\Lambda /\lambda )\left(R^{-n}\int _{B_{2R}(a)}u^2\right)^{1/2}.  \] This is the zero-lower-order, $p=2$ case of [ SimonPDE ] , Lecture 17, Theorem 1, p. 200. Proof Translation and dilation reduce to $a=0,R=1$ without changing the ellipticity ratio. Let $r_ j=1+2^{-j}$ and $p_ j=2\chi ^ j$. Starting from $u\in L^2(B_2)$, Lemma 7.13.4 successively gives \[  \| u\| _{L^{p_{j+1}}(B_{r_{j+1}})} \leq \bigl (Cp_ j^2 2^{2j+2}\bigr )^{1/p_ j} \| u\| _{L^{p_ j}(B_{r_ j})}.  \] The logarithm of the product of these constants is bounded by a multiple of $\sum _ j(1+j)\chi ^{-j}$, which is finite. Thus $\| u\| _{L^{p_ j}(B_1)}\leq C\| u\| _{L^2(B_2)}$ for every $j$. If $u>A$ on a subset of $B_1$ of positive measure $m$, then $\| u\| _{L^{p_ j}(B_1)}\geq A m^{1/p_ j}$. Letting $j\to \infty $ bounds every such level $A$ by $C\| u\| _2$, and hence bounds the essential supremum. This does not assume $u\in L^\infty $ in advance. Scaling the volume integral back gives the factor $R^{-n/2}$, including in dimension two. $\square$ Proposition 7.13.6 (Local bounds from every positive integrability exponent) . 667B61D52CFD Under the hypotheses of Theorem 7.13.5 , for every $p>0$, \[  \operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R(a)}u \leq C(n,\Lambda /\lambda ,p)\left(R^{-n}\int _{B_{2R}(a)}u^ p\right)^{1/p}.  \] The right side is allowed to be infinite. For $p<1$ no norm triangle inequality is needed. Compare [ SimonPDE ] , Lecture 17, Theorem 1. Proof Work on $B_2$ by scaling. For $p\geq 2$, Holder and Theorem 7.13.5 suffice. For $0<p<2$, put $P=(\int _{B_2}u^ p)^{1/p}$ and $M(r)=\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ r}u$. Applying the half-ball estimate on small balls centered in $B_ r$ gives, for $1\leq r<s\leq 3/2$, \[  M(r)\leq C(s-r)^{-n/2}\| u\| _{L^2(B_ s)} \leq C(s-r)^{-n/2}M(s)^{1-p/2}P^{p/2}.  \] A finite covering of $B_ r$ by balls of radius comparable to $s-r$ justifies the first inequality with the same constant. Young's inequality then yields, for any fixed $0<\theta <1$, \[  M(r)\leq \theta M(s)+C_{\theta ,p}(s-r)^{-n/p}P.  \] Choose $r_ j=1+(1-2^{-j})/2$ and $\theta <2^{-n/p}$. Iteration gives a convergent geometric series for the error terms, since $r_{j+1}-r_ j=2^{-j-2}$. The remainder is at most $\theta ^ j M(3/2)$ and tends to zero; $M(3/2)<\infty $ follows from the already proved local $L^2$ bound. Thus $M(1)\leq C_ pP$. Rescaling proves the result. The argument uses interpolation of integrals and a scalar iteration, not Banach-space properties for $p<1$. $\square$ Proposition 7.13.7 (Weak maximum principle with a Sobolev boundary condition) . 3E2A4AEFD01C Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$ be bounded, $n\geq 2$, and let $u\in H^1(\Omega )$ be a weak subsolution with the ellipticity assumptions above. If $(u-k)_+\in H_0^1(\Omega )$ for a constant $k$, then $u\leq k$ almost everywhere in $\Omega $. No regularity of the boundary of $\Omega $ is assumed; its boundary condition is expressed by this Sobolev membership. Proof Set $w=(u-k)_+$. It is an admissible nonnegative $H_0^1$ test, by approximation. The Sobolev chain rule gives $Dw=Du$ on $\{ u>k\} $ and zero elsewhere, so \[  0\geq \int A Du\cdot Dw=\int A Dw\cdot Dw\geq \lambda \int |Dw|^2.  \] Extend $w$ by zero to a ball containing $\Omega $. Its extension lies in $H_0^1$ of that ball. The scaled version of Theorem 7.13.1 now forces $w=0$, which is the assertion. Unlike a pointwise boundary statement, the assumed membership has meaning on any bounded open domain. $\square$ Corollary 7.13.8 (An integrable entire subsolution vanishes) . D0D8708926B9 Let $n\geq 2$ and let $A$ be measurable and symmetric on all of $\mathbb R^ n$, with fixed global bounds $\lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I$. If $u\geq 0$ is a weak subsolution in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n)$ and $\int _{\mathbb R^ n}u^ p<\infty $ for some $p>0$, then $u=0$ almost everywhere. A signed entire weak solution with finite $\int |u|^ p$ also vanishes. Proof Proposition 7.13.6 , on balls of arbitrarily large radius, bounds $\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R}u$ by $C R^{-n/p}(\int _{\mathbb R^ n}u^ p)^{1/p}$, which tends to zero. Every fixed ball lies in these expanding balls, so $u$ vanishes on every ball. For a signed solution, its positive and negative parts are subsolutions by Lemma 7.13.2 , and each has finite $p$ integral. Apply the first assertion to both. The global ellipticity bounds and the integrability hypothesis are essential parts of this conclusion. $\square$

With $\chi $ as in Theorem 7.13.1 , \[  \| u\| _{L^{p\chi }(B_ r)} \leq \left(\frac{C p^2}{(s-r)^2}\right)^{1/p}\| u\| _{L^ p(B_ s)},  \] where $C$ depends only on $n$ and $\Lambda /\lambda $. Proof Choose $\eta =1$ on $B_ r$, supported in $B_ s$, with $|D\eta |\leq C/(s-r)$. Apply the Sobolev gain to $\eta v_ L$ and then Lemma 7.13.3 . The right side is bounded by $Cp^2(s-r)^{-2}\int _{B_ s}u^ p$, because $v_ L^2=u^2u_ L^{p-2}\leq u^ p$. As $L\to \infty $, Fatou's lemma gives \[  \left(\int _{B_ r}u^{p\chi }\right)^{1/\chi } \leq \frac{Cp^2}{(s-r)^2}\int _{B_ s}u^ p.  \] Taking the $p$th root proves the claim. In particular the higher integrability is a conclusion of the argument, not an assumption permitting an untruncated power test. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.13.5 (Moser local boundedness for nonnegative subsolutions)
search_title: Moser local boundedness for nonnegative subsolutions
text: Theorem 7.13.5 (Moser local boundedness for nonnegative subsolutions) . DB183F3A4CE7 Let $n\geq 2$, let $A$ be measurable and symmetric on $B_{2R}(a)$ with $\lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I$ for $0<\lambda \leq \Lambda $, and let $u\in H^1(B_{2R}(a))$ be a nonnegative weak subsolution of $\operatorname {div}(A Du)=0$. Then \[  \operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R(a)}u \leq C(n,\Lambda /\lambda )\left(R^{-n}\int _{B_{2R}(a)}u^2\right)^{1/2}.  \] This is the zero-lower-order, $p=2$ case of [ SimonPDE ] , Lecture 17, Theorem 1, p. 200. Proof Translation and dilation reduce to $a=0,R=1$ without changing the ellipticity ratio. Let $r_ j=1+2^{-j}$ and $p_ j=2\chi ^ j$. Starting from $u\in L^2(B_2)$, Lemma 7.13.4 successively gives \[  \| u\| _{L^{p_{j+1}}(B_{r_{j+1}})} \leq \bigl (Cp_ j^2 2^{2j+2}\bigr )^{1/p_ j} \| u\| _{L^{p_ j}(B_{r_ j})}.  \] The logarithm of the product of these constants is bounded by a multiple of $\sum _ j(1+j)\chi ^{-j}$, which is finite. Thus $\| u\| _{L^{p_ j}(B_1)}\leq C\| u\| _{L^2(B_2)}$ for every $j$. If $u>A$ on a subset of $B_1$ of positive measure $m$, then $\| u\| _{L^{p_ j}(B_1)}\geq A m^{1/p_ j}$. Letting $j\to \infty $ bounds every such level $A$ by $C\| u\| _2$, and hence bounds the essential supremum. This does not assume $u\in L^\infty $ in advance. Scaling the volume integral back gives the factor $R^{-n/2}$, including in dimension two. $\square$

title: Proposition 7.13.6 (Local bounds from every positive integrability exponent)
search_title: Local bounds from every positive integrability exponent
text: Proposition 7.13.6 (Local bounds from every positive integrability exponent) . 667B61D52CFD Under the hypotheses of Theorem 7.13.5 , for every $p>0$, \[  \operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R(a)}u \leq C(n,\Lambda /\lambda ,p)\left(R^{-n}\int _{B_{2R}(a)}u^ p\right)^{1/p}.  \] The right side is allowed to be infinite. For $p<1$ no norm triangle inequality is needed. Compare [ SimonPDE ] , Lecture 17, Theorem 1. Proof Work on $B_2$ by scaling. For $p\geq 2$, Holder and Theorem 7.13.5 suffice. For $0<p<2$, put $P=(\int _{B_2}u^ p)^{1/p}$ and $M(r)=\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ r}u$. Applying the half-ball estimate on small balls centered in $B_ r$ gives, for $1\leq r<s\leq 3/2$, \[  M(r)\leq C(s-r)^{-n/2}\| u\| _{L^2(B_ s)} \leq C(s-r)^{-n/2}M(s)^{1-p/2}P^{p/2}.  \] A finite covering of $B_ r$ by balls of radius comparable to $s-r$ justifies the first inequality with the same constant. Young's inequality then yields, for any fixed $0<\theta <1$, \[  M(r)\leq \theta M(s)+C_{\theta ,p}(s-r)^{-n/p}P.  \] Choose $r_ j=1+(1-2^{-j})/2$ and $\theta <2^{-n/p}$. Iteration gives a convergent geometric series for the error terms, since $r_{j+1}-r_ j=2^{-j-2}$. The remainder is at most $\theta ^ j M(3/2)$ and tends to zero; $M(3/2)<\infty $ follows from the already proved local $L^2$ bound. Thus $M(1)\leq C_ pP$. Rescaling proves the result. The argument uses interpolation of integrals and a scalar iteration, not Banach-space properties for $p<1$. $\square$

title: Proposition 7.13.7 (Weak maximum principle with a Sobolev boundary condition)
search_title: Weak maximum principle with a Sobolev boundary condition
text: Proposition 7.13.7 (Weak maximum principle with a Sobolev boundary condition) . 3E2A4AEFD01C Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$ be bounded, $n\geq 2$, and let $u\in H^1(\Omega )$ be a weak subsolution with the ellipticity assumptions above. If $(u-k)_+\in H_0^1(\Omega )$ for a constant $k$, then $u\leq k$ almost everywhere in $\Omega $. No regularity of the boundary of $\Omega $ is assumed; its boundary condition is expressed by this Sobolev membership. Proof Set $w=(u-k)_+$. It is an admissible nonnegative $H_0^1$ test, by approximation. The Sobolev chain rule gives $Dw=Du$ on $\{ u>k\} $ and zero elsewhere, so \[  0\geq \int A Du\cdot Dw=\int A Dw\cdot Dw\geq \lambda \int |Dw|^2.  \] Extend $w$ by zero to a ball containing $\Omega $. Its extension lies in $H_0^1$ of that ball. The scaled version of Theorem 7.13.1 now forces $w=0$, which is the assertion. Unlike a pointwise boundary statement, the assumed membership has meaning on any bounded open domain. $\square$

title: Corollary 7.13.8 (An integrable entire subsolution vanishes)
search_title: An integrable entire subsolution vanishes
text: Corollary 7.13.8 (An integrable entire subsolution vanishes) . D0D8708926B9 Let $n\geq 2$ and let $A$ be measurable and symmetric on all of $\mathbb R^ n$, with fixed global bounds $\lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I$. If $u\geq 0$ is a weak subsolution in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n)$ and $\int _{\mathbb R^ n}u^ p<\infty $ for some $p>0$, then $u=0$ almost everywhere. A signed entire weak solution with finite $\int |u|^ p$ also vanishes. Proof Proposition 7.13.6 , on balls of arbitrarily large radius, bounds $\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B_ R}u$ by $C R^{-n/p}(\int _{\mathbb R^ n}u^ p)^{1/p}$, which tends to zero. Every fixed ball lies in these expanding balls, so $u$ vanishes on every ball. For a signed solution, its positive and negative parts are subsolutions by Lemma 7.13.2 , and each has finite $p$ integral. Apply the first assertion to both. The global ellipticity bounds and the integrability hypothesis are essential parts of this conclusion. $\square$

title: 16.1 Atomic, diffuse, and singular measures
search_title: Atomic, diffuse, and singular measures
text:
These examples make the distinctions between mass, support, density, and weak convergence explicit. The conventions are Definitions 2.1.1 , 2.1.2 , and 2.2.1 . The foundational source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Sections 1–5. The Cantor constructions below are proved directly; they illustrate the covering definitions rather than invoke a structure theorem for fractals. Example 16.1.1 (A measure can be atomic and have an interval as support) . A7AFF33C67FA Enumerate the rational points of $[0,1]$ without repetitions as $q_1,q_2,\ldots $, and set \[  \mu =\sum _{j=1}^{\infty }2^{-j}\delta _{q_ j}.  \] This is a Radon probability measure on $\mathbb R$, concentrated on a countable set, with support $[0,1]$. At each $q_ j$, its one-dimensional density is infinite. In contrast, counting measure on $\mathbb Q\cap [0,1]$ is not locally finite. Proof Countable additivity follows by interchanging nonnegative sums. Finite partial sums are finite Radon measures, and their omitted tails have total mass tending to zero, which proves inner and outer regularity of $\mu $ by approximation. Every neighborhood of a point of $[0,1]$ contains some $q_ j$ and hence positive mass; outside that interval there are neighborhoods of zero mass. At $q_ j$, $\mu (B_ r(q_ j))/(2r)\geq 2^{-j}/(2r)	o \infty $. Counting measure assigns infinite mass to the compact interval $[0,1]$. Thus support alone records neither atomicity nor local finiteness. $\square$ Example 16.1.2 (Concentration of absolutely continuous measures) . 315BC1BE84A5 Let $ho \geq 0$ belong to $L^1(\mathbb R^ n)$ with $\int ho =1$, fix $a\in \mathbb R^ n$, and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Then \[  d\mu _\varepsilon (x)=\varepsilon ^{-n}ho ((x-a)/\varepsilon )\, dx \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \mu _\varepsilon ightharpoonup \delta _ a.  \] Every approximating measure is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, while the limit is singular and atomic. Proof For $\varphi \in C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)$, changing variables gives $\int \varphi \, d\mu _\varepsilon =\int \varphi (a+\varepsilon y)ho (y)\, dy$. The integrand converges pointwise to $\varphi (a)ho (y)$ and is bounded by $\| \varphi \| _\infty ho (y)$. Dominated convergence proves the claim. Local finiteness and regularity of the approximating measures follow from integration of a locally integrable density against Lebesgue measure. $\square$ Example 16.1.3 (Mass escapes through infinity or a domain boundary) . 72CA99D2039A In $\mathbb R$, $\delta _ jightharpoonup 0$ although each measure has total mass one. In the open domain $U=(0,1)$, $\delta _{1/j}ightharpoonup 0$ for $j\geq 2$, whereas the same measures viewed on $\mathbb R$ converge to $\delta _0$. Proof A compactly supported continuous test vanishes at $j$ for all sufficiently large $j$. A compact subset of $(0,1)$ has positive distance from zero, so a test supported there also eventually vanishes at $1/j$. On $\mathbb R$, continuity instead gives $\varphi (1/j)	o \varphi (0)$. The choice of the ambient open set is part of Definition 2.1.2 ; preservation of total mass does not follow from that topology. $\square$ Example 16.1.4 (Weak convergence does not imply convergence on every Borel set) . 1CE8BCF4FD05 The sequence $\delta _{1/j}ightharpoonup \delta _0$ on $\mathbb R$ has \[  \delta _{1/j}(\{ 0\} )=0,\qquad \delta _0(\{ 0\} )=1, \qquad \delta _{1/j}((0,1))=1\quad (j\geq 2),\qquad \delta _0((0,1))=0.  \] Thus both a closed set and an open set can have discontinuous masses. The open-set lower-semicontinuity inequality in Proposition 2.1.4 remains valid. Proof Evaluation of a Dirac measure at a set is its indicator function at the atom. The four values follow immediately. Here zero lies on the boundary of each of the sets at issue and carries positive limiting mass; indicators of these sets are not continuous tests at that point. $\square$ Example 16.1.5 (Oscillating densities can average without converging in norm) . 60C0FD0D3245 On $[0,1]$, put $f_ j(x)=1+\sin (2\pi jx)$ and $d\mu _ j=f_ j\, dx$. Then $\mu _ j$ are probability measures and converge weakly on $\mathbb R$ to $\mathcal L^1\llcorner [0,1]$, but \[  \int _0^1|f_ j-1|\, dx= rac2\pi  \] for every positive integer $j$. In particular weak convergence here does not imply convergence of densities in $L^1$. Proof Nonnegativity and mass one follow by direct integration. For continuous $\varphi $ on $[0,1]$, partition into the $j$ intervals $I_ k=[k/j,(k+1)/j]$. The sine has zero integral on each. Subtracting $\varphi (k/j)$ on $I_ k$ bounds the oscillating integral in absolute value by the modulus of continuity of $\varphi $ at $1/j$, which tends to zero. The displayed norm is $j$ equal copies of one period, rescaled to total length one; the integral of $|\sin |$ over a period is four. $\square$ Definition 16.1.6 (The middle-thirds Cantor set and its probability measure) . 9D0DB6B0C777 Let $C_ k$ be the union of the $2^ k$ closed intervals of length $3^{-k}$ obtained by retaining the left and right thirds at each of $k$ steps, and put $C= igcap _{k\geq 0}C_ k$. For $t\in [0,1)$ write its binary digits as $b_ j(t)\in \{ 0,1\} $, choosing the expansion eventually zero at dyadic rationals. Define \[  T(t)=\sum _{j=1}^{\infty } rac{2b_ j(t)}{3^ j}, \qquad \mu _ C=T_\# (\mathcal L^1\llcorner [0,1)).  \] The pushforward means $\mu _ C(A)=\mathcal L^1(T^{-1}(A))$ for Borel sets $A$. Each finite digit function is measurable, so the limit $T$ is measurable. This constructs the measure without presupposing a measure on an infinite product space. Proposition 16.1.7 (Cylinder masses and singular continuity) . DCBE26BC98C4 The set $C$ is compact and has Lebesgue measure zero. The measure $\mu _ C$ is a Radon probability measure supported on $C$, and every level-$k$ retained interval $I$ has mass $2^{-k}$. It has no atoms. Thus a measure may be singular with respect to Lebesgue measure without being atomic. Proof The sets $C_ k$ are nested compact sets with total length $(2/3)^ k$, so their intersection is compact and null. The ternary series defining $T$ belongs to every $C_ k$. Specifying a word of $k$ binary digits selects a half-open dyadic interval of Lebesgue measure $2^{-k}$ and the corresponding retained ternary interval; endpoint conventions affect at most a countable null set. This proves the cylinder mass. Every point of $C$ lies in a retained interval at every level; its singleton mass is therefore at most $2^{-k}$ for all $k$. These same shrinking intervals show that every neighborhood of every point of $C$ has positive mass, so the support is exactly $C$. A finite Borel measure on $\mathbb R$ is regular ( [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 1); hence this probability measure is Radon. Alternatively, regularity follows by compact cylinder approximations and finite total mass. $\square$ Proposition 16.1.8 (Power-law bounds for the Cantor measure) . 4C394463E8E0 Write $s=\log 2/\log 3$. For every $x\in C$ and $0<r<1$, \[   rac18r^ s\leq \mu _ C(B_ r(x))\leq 8r^ s.  \] In particular $\mu _ C(B_ r(x))/(2r)	o \infty $ at every $x\in C$, despite the absence of atoms. Proof Choose $k\geq 1$ with $3^{-k}\leq r<3^{-k+1}$. The level-$k+2$ interval containing $x$ has diameter strictly less than $r$ and hence lies in $B_ r(x)$. Its mass is $2^{-k-2}$. Since $r^ s<2\cdot 2^{-k}$, this is at least $r^ s/8$. Distinct level-$k$ intervals have length $L=3^{-k}$ and gaps at least $L$. An interval of length $2r<6L$ meets at most eight of them. Their total mass is at most $8\cdot 2^{-k}\leq 8r^ s$. Finally $s<1$, so the lower bound divided by $2r$ diverges. The constants are deliberately nonsharp. $\square$ Definition 16.1.9 (Hausdorff dimension via diameter covers) . 7E12771384C9 For a metric subset $E$ and $q>0$, let \[  \mathcal H^ q_{m diam}(E)=\lim _{\delta \downarrow 0} \inf \left\{ \sum _ i(\operatorname {diam}E_ i)^ q: E\subset  igcup _ iE_ i,\  \operatorname {diam}E_ i<\delta ight\} .  \] Define $\dim _ H E=\inf \{ q>0:\mathcal H^ q_{m diam}(E)=0\} $. For integer $q=m\geq 1$, this measure differs from Definition 2.2.1 by the positive constant $2^ m/\omega _ m$; this constant does not affect dimension. The covering construction for real exponents is the one in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 2. Proposition 16.1.10 (The Cantor set has a noninteger dimension) . E16EF71E7152 For $s=\log 2/\log 3$, \[  0<\mathcal H^ s_{m diam}(C)<\infty ,\qquad \dim _ H C=s.  \] Thus zero length does not imply zero Hausdorff dimension. Proof The level-$k$ cover has sum $2^ k(3^{-k})^ s=1$, and for $q>s$ its $q$-sum tends to zero. For the lower bound take any sufficiently fine countable cover. A set of diameter $d>0$ meeting $C$ is contained, on $C$, in the ball of radius $2d$ about any chosen point of its intersection. Proposition 16.1.8 bounds its $\mu _ C$ outer measure by $8(2d)^ s$. Sets of diameter zero carry no mass. Countable subadditivity gives $1\leq 8\cdot 2^ s\sum _ i d_ i^ s$, hence a uniform positive lower bound. If $0<q<s$ and $d_ i<\delta $, then $\sum _ i d_ i^ q\geq \delta ^{q-s}\sum _ i d_ i^ s$, which tends to infinity as $\delta \downarrow 0$. This also verifies the dimension assertion directly. $\square$ Example 16.1.11 (The Cantor function has a singular distributional derivative) . 2C0749FA806B Let $F(x)=\mu _ C(( -\infty ,x])$. Then $F$ is continuous, nondecreasing, equals zero for $x\leq 0$ and one for $x\geq 1$, and is constant on every component of $\mathbb R\setminus C$. It satisfies \[  F'=0\quad \mathcal L^1	ext{-almost everywhere},\qquad DF=\mu _ C  \] as distributions. In particular it is locally BV but is not absolutely continuous on $[0,1]$. Proof A distribution function jumps precisely by its singleton mass, so Proposition 16.1.7 gives continuity. An interval disjoint from the support has zero mass, giving constancy there and zero classical derivative off the null set $C$. For $\varphi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$, Fubini yields \[  -\int F(x)\varphi '(x)\, dx =-\int _ C\int _ t^\infty \varphi '(x)\, dx\, d\mu _ C(t) =\int \varphi (t)\, d\mu _ C(t).  \] The finite measure derivative proves local BV. Absolute continuity on $[0,1]$ would imply $F(1)-F(0)=\int _0^1F'=0$, contradicting the endpoint values. This is an explicit singular continuous part of a BV derivative, distinct from the jump part of a step function. $\square$ Example 16.1.12 (Diffuse approximations to a singular continuous measure) . 26512807DFDC Let $C_ k$ be the level-$k$ Cantor approximation and define \[  d
u _ k=(3/2)^ k\mathbf1_{C_ k}\, dx.  \] Then $
u _ k$ is an absolutely continuous probability measure and $
u _ kightharpoonup \mu _ C$. Each retained interval has the same mass under $
u _ k$ and $\mu _ C$, although their behavior inside it is different. Proof The total length of $C_ k$ is $(2/3)^ k$. Multiplying by $(3/2)^ k$ gives mass one, and each interval has mass $2^{-k}$. For a continuous test $\varphi $ on $[0,1]$, select one point $x_ I$ in each level-$k$ interval. The difference between either measure's integral and $\sum _ I2^{-k}\varphi (x_ I)$ is bounded by the modulus of continuity of $\varphi $ at $3^{-k}$. These two errors tend to zero, proving weak convergence. Thus concentration can produce a singular continuous limit as well as the Dirac limit in Example 16.1.2 . $\square$ Example 16.1.13 (Three mutually singular components in one measure) . 8C2551B95ECF The finite measure \[  \eta =\mathcal L^1\llcorner [0,1]+\mu _ C+\delta _0  \] has an absolutely continuous part, a singular continuous part, and an atomic part. These three summands are mutually singular even though their supports overlap. Its distribution function on $\mathbb R$ is the sum of the distribution functions of the three summands. Proof The three measures are respectively concentrated on the disjoint Borel sets $[0,1]\setminus C$, $C\setminus \{ 0\} $, and $\{ 0\} $. Removing $C$ does not change Lebesgue measure, and removing zero does not change $\mu _ C$ because it has no atoms. Each summand is therefore singular to the others, while the first two supports are $[0,1]$ and $C$. Additivity gives the distribution-function assertion. This explicit decomposition does not require the general Lebesgue decomposition theorem. $\square$

title: Definition 16.1.9 (Hausdorff dimension via diameter covers)

text: Definition 16.1.9 (Hausdorff dimension via diameter covers) . 7E12771384C9 For a metric subset $E$ and $q>0$, let \[  \mathcal H^ q_{\rm diam}(E)=\lim _{\delta \downarrow 0} \inf \left\{ \sum _ i(\operatorname {diam}E_ i)^ q: E\subset \bigcup _ iE_ i,\  \operatorname {diam}E_ i<\delta \right\} .  \] Define $\dim _ H E=\inf \{ q>0:\mathcal H^ q_{\rm diam}(E)=0\} $. For integer $q=m\geq 1$, this measure differs from Definition 2.2.1 by the positive constant $2^ m/\omega _ m$; this constant does not affect dimension. The covering construction for real exponents is the one in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 2.

title: Proposition 16.1.10 (The Cantor set has a noninteger dimension)
search_title: The Cantor set has a noninteger dimension
text: Proposition 16.1.10 (The Cantor set has a noninteger dimension) . E16EF71E7152 For $s=\log 2/\log 3$, \[  0<\mathcal H^ s_{\rm diam}(C)<\infty ,\qquad \dim _ H C=s.  \] Thus zero length does not imply zero Hausdorff dimension. Proof The level-$k$ cover has sum $2^ k(3^{-k})^ s=1$, and for $q>s$ its $q$-sum tends to zero. For the lower bound take any sufficiently fine countable cover. A set of diameter $d>0$ meeting $C$ is contained, on $C$, in the ball of radius $2d$ about any chosen point of its intersection. Proposition 16.1.8 bounds its $\mu _ C$ outer measure by $8(2d)^ s$. Sets of diameter zero carry no mass. Countable subadditivity gives $1\leq 8\cdot 2^ s\sum _ i d_ i^ s$, hence a uniform positive lower bound. If $0<q<s$ and $d_ i<\delta $, then $\sum _ i d_ i^ q\geq \delta ^{q-s}\sum _ i d_ i^ s$, which tends to infinity as $\delta \downarrow 0$. This also verifies the dimension assertion directly. $\square$

title: Example 16.1.11 (The Cantor function has a singular distributional derivative)
search_title: The Cantor function has a singular distributional derivative
text: Example 16.1.11 (The Cantor function has a singular distributional derivative) . 2C0749FA806B Let $F(x)=\mu _ C(( -\infty ,x])$. Then $F$ is continuous, nondecreasing, equals zero for $x\leq 0$ and one for $x\geq 1$, and is constant on every component of $\mathbb R\setminus C$. It satisfies \[  F'=0\quad \mathcal L^1\text{-almost everywhere},\qquad DF=\mu _ C  \] as distributions. In particular it is locally BV but is not absolutely continuous on $[0,1]$. Proof A distribution function jumps precisely by its singleton mass, so Proposition 16.1.7 gives continuity. An interval disjoint from the support has zero mass, giving constancy there and zero classical derivative off the null set $C$. For $\varphi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$, Fubini yields \[  -\int F(x)\varphi '(x)\, dx =-\int _ C\int _ t^\infty \varphi '(x)\, dx\, d\mu _ C(t) =\int \varphi (t)\, d\mu _ C(t).  \] The finite measure derivative proves local BV. Absolute continuity on $[0,1]$ would imply $F(1)-F(0)=\int _0^1F'=0$, contradicting the endpoint values. This is an explicit singular continuous part of a BV derivative, distinct from the jump part of a step function. $\square$

title: Example 16.1.12 (Diffuse approximations to a singular continuous measure)

text:
Example 16.1.12 (Diffuse approximations to a singular continuous measure) . 26512807DFDC Let $C_ k$ be the level-$k$ Cantor approximation and define \[  d
u _ k=(3/2)^ k\mathbf1_{C_ k}\, dx.  \] Then $
u _ k$ is an absolutely continuous probability measure and $
u _ kightharpoonup \mu _ C$. Each retained interval has the same mass under $
u _ k$ and $\mu _ C$, although their behavior inside it is different. Proof The total length of $C_ k$ is $(2/3)^ k$. Multiplying by $(3/2)^ k$ gives mass one, and each interval has mass $2^{-k}$. For a continuous test $\varphi $ on $[0,1]$, select one point $x_ I$ in each level-$k$ interval. The difference between either measure's integral and $\sum _ I2^{-k}\varphi (x_ I)$ is bounded by the modulus of continuity of $\varphi $ at $3^{-k}$. These two errors tend to zero, proving weak convergence. Thus concentration can produce a singular continuous limit as well as the Dirac limit in Example 16.1.2 . $\square$

title: Example 16.1.13 (Three mutually singular components in one measure)
search_title: Three mutually singular components in one measure
text: Example 16.1.13 (Three mutually singular components in one measure) . 8C2551B95ECF The finite measure \[  \eta =\mathcal L^1\llcorner [0,1]+\mu _ C+\delta _0  \] has an absolutely continuous part, a singular continuous part, and an atomic part. These three summands are mutually singular even though their supports overlap. Its distribution function on $\mathbb R$ is the sum of the distribution functions of the three summands. Proof The three measures are respectively concentrated on the disjoint Borel sets $[0,1]\setminus C$, $C\setminus \{ 0\} $, and $\{ 0\} $. Removing $C$ does not change Lebesgue measure, and removing zero does not change $\mu _ C$ because it has no atoms. Each summand is therefore singular to the others, while the first two supports are $[0,1]$ and $C$. Additivity gives the distribution-function assertion. This explicit decomposition does not require the general Lebesgue decomposition theorem. $\square$

title: 16.2 Classical minimal surfaces by calculation
search_title: Classical minimal surfaces by calculation
text: We calculate metrics, curvature, topology, and a stability distinction for explicit surfaces. The source is [ ChMin ] , Sections 13–15, pp. 35–45. Our parametrizations are fixed below, so signs and scale factors can be checked independently of source coordinates. Minimality alone will not be used to assert embeddedness, completeness, or minimizing behavior. Lemma 16.2.1 (A conformal harmonic immersion is minimal) . 7EC638CD7556 Let $X:U\subset \mathbb R^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ be a smooth immersion with $|X_ u|^2=|X_ v|^2=\lambda ^2>0$ and $\langle X_ u,X_ v\rangle =0$. Then \[  \vec H=\lambda ^{-2}(X_{uu}+X_{vv}).  \] Consequently $X$ is minimal exactly when all its coordinate functions are harmonic. Proof The induced metric is $g=\lambda ^2(du^2+dv^2)$. Its Laplace–Beltrami operator is $\Delta _ g=\lambda ^{-2}(\partial _ u^2+\partial _ v^2)$, by the coordinate divergence formula. For an immersion, tracing the normal second derivative gives $\Delta _ gX=\vec H$: the tangential Christoffel terms cancel when taking the covariant Hessian. Substitution proves the formula. This is [ ChMin ] , Lemma 15.1. Our mean curvature vector is the trace, with no factor of one half. $\square$ Example 16.2.2 (The catenoid: an embedded complete minimal annulus) . 86A763EE2A08 For $a>0$, define \[  C_ a(\theta ,v)=a(\cosh v\cos \theta ,\cosh v\sin \theta ,v), \qquad (\theta ,v)\in (\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)\times \mathbb R.  \] This is a proper embedded complete minimal surface. Its induced metric is \[  g=a^2\cosh ^2v\, (d\theta ^2+dv^2).  \] The waist is the circle $v=0$ of radius $a$. Its two open halves are graphs $z=\pm a\operatorname {arcosh}(r/a)$ over $r>a$. Proof Differentiation gives orthogonal coordinate vectors of equal squared length $a^2\cosh ^2v$. The sum of second derivatives is zero, so Lemma 16.2.1 gives minimality. The height determines $v$, and the horizontal direction determines $\theta $ modulo $2\pi $; thus the map is injective. A bounded ambient set bounds $v$, and the angular factor is compact, proving properness. The metric dominates the complete cylinder metric $a^2(d\theta ^2+dv^2)$; an intrinsic Cauchy sequence therefore converges in that cylinder, and local smooth equivalence gives convergence in $g$. Finally $r=a\cosh v$ gives the graph formulas. See [ ChMin ] , Section 14.1 and Example 15.4. $\square$ Lemma 16.2.3 (Gauss curvature in a conformal chart) . EF8AF6254F91 For a smooth surface metric $g=e^{2h}(du^2+dv^2)$, \[  K=-e^{-2h}(h_{uu}+h_{vv}).  \] Equivalently, for $\lambda =e^ h$, $K=-\lambda ^{-2}\Delta \log \lambda $, with the flat coordinate Laplacian on the right. Proof Use the orthonormal coframe $\theta ^1=e^ hdu$, $\theta ^2=e^ hdv$. The connection form $\omega =h_ vdu-h_ udv$ satisfies $d\theta ^1=-\omega \wedge \theta ^2$ and $d\theta ^2=\omega \wedge \theta ^1$. The curvature equation $d\omega =K\theta ^1\wedge \theta ^2$ now gives $-(h_{uu}+h_{vv})du\wedge dv=Ke^{2h}du\wedge dv$. This fixes the sign using the usual convention that a round sphere has positive Gauss curvature. $\square$ Proposition 16.2.4 (Curvature and total curvature of the catenoid) . CEB8A54C4892 For $C_ a$, \[  K=-\frac1{a^2\cosh ^4v},\qquad |B|^2=\frac2{a^2\cosh ^4v}, \qquad \int _{C_ a}K\, dA=-4\pi .  \] The integral counts the catenoid once, with $0\leq \theta <2\pi $. Proof Apply Lemma 16.2.3 with $\lambda =a\cosh v$ and $(\log \lambda )_{vv}=\operatorname {sech}^2v$, giving $K$. Since the surface is minimal in $\mathbb R^3$, its principal curvatures are opposite and the Gauss equation gives $|B|^2=-2K$. Multiplying $K$ by $dA=a^2\cosh ^2v\, d\theta \, dv$ leaves $-\operatorname {sech}^2v$. Its integral over $\mathbb R$ is $-2$, and the angular integral contributes $2\pi $. This also shows that total curvature is unchanged by the dilation parameter $a$. $\square$ Proposition 16.2.5 (The complete catenoid is unstable) . 4CEC3FE383CD The catenoid admits a compactly supported smooth normal variation with negative second variation. Each of its open halves $v>0$ and $v<0$, however, is stable for variations compactly supported in that half. Proof The periodic unit normal $(\operatorname {sech}v\cos \theta ,\operatorname {sech}v\sin \theta ,-\tanh v)$ makes these scalar normal variations globally defined. For an angularly constant smooth compactly supported test $f(v)$, the metric and curvature calculations give \[  Q(f,f)=2\pi \int _{\mathbb R}\bigl ((f')^2-2\operatorname {sech}^2v\, f^2\bigr )\, dv.  \] Take $f_ R$ equal to one on $[-R,R]$, zero outside $[-2R,2R]$, with $|f_ R'|\leq C/R$. The positive term is $O(R^{-1})$ and dominated convergence makes the negative integral tend to $-4$, so $Q(f_ R,f_ R)<0$ for large $R$. Each open half is a minimal graph by Example 16.2.2 ; its calibration in its graph cylinder, Proposition 7.2.13 , gives area minimization for compactly supported variations and hence nonnegative second variation. This proves instability and half-surface stability; it does not compute the full Morse index. $\square$ Proposition 16.2.6 (Rotational minimal hypersurfaces and their first integral) . 242AF4A13F4C For $n\geq 2$, let $r:I\to (0,\infty )$ be smooth and parametrize a hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ by $X(z,\omega )=(r(z)\omega ,z)$, $\omega \in S^{n-1}$. It is minimal if and only if \[  rr''=(n-1)(1+(r')^2).  \] Along any such solution, \[  \frac{r^{n-1}}{\sqrt{1+(r')^2}}=c>0  \] is constant. The constant here is the reciprocal of some source conventions for the flux parameter. Proof The area density, after integration over the unit sphere, is $r^{n-1}\sqrt{1+(r')^2}$. Its Euler–Lagrange equation simplifies to the stated ODE. To see that radial stationarity is sufficient, the normal vector is $(\omega ,-r')/\sqrt{1+(r')^2}$. A radial variation $\eta (z)\omega $ has nonzero normal factor $\eta /\sqrt{1+(r')^2}$, and the scalar mean curvature is constant on each rotational orbit. Vanishing against all $\eta $ therefore forces the scalar mean curvature to vanish. Finally direct differentiation gives \[  \left(\frac{r^{n-1}}{\sqrt{1+(r')^2}}\right)' =\frac{r^{n-2}r'}{(1+(r')^2)^{3/2}} \bigl ((n-1)(1+(r')^2)-rr''\bigr )=0.  \] This derivation fixes the constant without dividing by $r'$ at the waist. Compare [ ChMin ] , Section 14, pp. 37–40. $\square$ Example 16.2.7 (Higher-dimensional catenoids fit in a finite-height slab) . E86BB8933722 Let $r(0)=a>0$, $r'(0)=0$ in Proposition 16.2.6 . The even solution has upper half described by \[  z=\int _ a^{r(z)}\frac{d\rho }{\sqrt{(\rho /a)^{2n-2}-1}}.  \] When $n=2$, its height tends to infinity and $r(z)=a\cosh (z/a)$. When $n\geq 3$, the limiting height is finite: \[  Z_ a=a\int _1^\infty \frac{ds}{\sqrt{s^{2n-2}-1}}<\infty .  \] In every dimension the resulting hypersurface is complete and proper, with its two ends escaping horizontally; the finite height for $n\geq 3$ is not a finite intrinsic distance to an edge. Proof Smooth ODE existence and uniqueness apply near $(r,r')=(a,0)$ since $r>0$. The equation gives $r''>0$, so $r'>0$ for $z>0$, and uniqueness gives evenness. The constant is $c=a^{n-1}$. Solving the first integral for $r'$ and separating variables yields the formula. Near $s=1$ the integrand is bounded by a constant times $(s-1)^{-1/2}$, which is integrable. At infinity it is comparable to $s^{-(n-1)}$, giving divergence for $n=2$ and convergence for $n\geq 3$. The solution can continue as long as $r$ stays bounded, because its derivative is then bounded by the first integral. Thus its end has $r\to \infty $. Intrinsic lengths dominate changes in the radial coordinate, so each end has infinite distance. Properness follows from the same radial divergence and compactness of the spherical factor. Compare [ ChMin ] , Exercises 14.2–14.3. $\square$ Example 16.2.8 (The helicoid: a complete embedded minimal plane) . FEE5C0B5B785 For $a>0$, define \[  X_ a(t,\theta )=a(t\cos \theta ,t\sin \theta ,\theta ),\qquad (t,\theta )\in \mathbb R^2.  \] It is a proper embedded complete minimal surface, with \[  g=a^2\bigl (dt^2+(1+t^2)d\theta ^2\bigr ),\qquad K=-\frac1{a^2(1+t^2)^2}.  \] In particular, unlike the catenoid, it has the topology of a plane and has infinite absolute total curvature. Proof Direct differentiation gives the metric. Substitute $t=\sinh v$; the metric becomes $a^2\cosh ^2v(dv^2+d\theta ^2)$ and the three coordinate functions become harmonic, proving minimality by Lemma 16.2.1 . The conformal Gauss curvature calculation gives the displayed $K$. Height determines $\theta $ and then the horizontal coordinates determine $t$, proving injectivity. A bounded image bounds both parameters, proving properness; the metric dominates $a^2(dt^2+d\theta ^2)$, proving completeness. On $|v|<1$ the integral of $|K|dA=\operatorname {sech}^2v\, dv\, d\theta $ is infinite because $\theta $ ranges over all of $\mathbb R$. See [ ChMin ] , Section 13 and Example 15.6. $\square$ Proposition 16.2.9 (The catenoid-helicoid association and its period obstruction) . 71B33AFD8411 On the parameter plane with $z=\theta +iv$, set \[  \Phi (z)=a(\cos z,\sin z,-iz),\qquad X_\alpha =\operatorname {Re}(e^{-i\alpha }\Phi ),\quad \alpha \in \mathbb R.  \] Every $X_\alpha $ is a conformal minimal immersion with metric $a^2\cosh ^2v(d\theta ^2+dv^2)$. The choices $\alpha =0$ and $\alpha =\pi /2$ give a catenoid covering and a helicoid, up to a rigid motion. The immersion descends to the cylinder $\theta \pmod{2\pi }$ if and only if $\sin \alpha =0$. Proof The holomorphic derivative satisfies $\Phi '\cdot \Phi '=a^2(\sin ^2z+\cos ^2z-1)=0$ and $|\Phi '|^2=2a^2\cosh ^2v$. Taking real and imaginary parts therefore gives orthogonal real derivatives of equal squared norm $|\Phi '|^2/2$. Multiplication by a unit complex number preserves both identities and harmonicity. The imaginary part is $a(-\sin \theta \sinh v,\cos \theta \sinh v,-\theta )$, a rotated/reflected helicoid. Finally $\Phi (z+2\pi )-\Phi (z)=(0,0,-2\pi ia)$, whose real part after multiplication by $e^{-i\alpha }$ is $(0,0,-2\pi a\sin \alpha )$. This vanishes exactly as claimed. Local isometry does not identify the global topologies. Compare [ ChMin ] , Lemma 15.5 and Example 15.6. $\square$ Example 16.2.10 (Enneper's surface is immersed and complete but not embedded) . 6DA30A5B8CCE The polynomial map \[  E(u,v)=\left(u-\frac{u^3}{3}+uv^2, -v+\frac{v^3}{3}-u^2v,u^2-v^2\right)  \] is a proper complete conformal minimal immersion of $\mathbb R^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$, with metric $(1+u^2+v^2)^2(du^2+dv^2)$. It is not injective: $E(\sqrt3,0)=E(-\sqrt3,0)=(0,0,3)$. Proof Differentiation gives $|E_ u|^2=|E_ v|^2=(1+u^2+v^2)^2$ and $\langle E_ u,E_ v\rangle =0$; each coordinate is harmonic. The positive metric factor proves immersion and Lemma 16.2.1 proves minimality. The metric dominates the Euclidean one, giving completeness. With $z=u+iv$, the first two components satisfy $E_1+iE_2=\overline z-z^3/3$, hence $|E_1+iE_2|\geq |z|^3/3-|z|$. This tends to infinity, proving properness. The two displayed parameters prove failure of injectivity. At them, $E_ u=(-2,0,\pm 2\sqrt3)$ and $E_ v=(0,-4,0)$ span different tangent planes, so the image itself has a crossing and is not an embedded surface. This is Enneper's example from [ ChMin ] , Section 15.5, in a fixed polynomial normalization. $\square$ Proposition 16.2.11 (Total curvature counts the parameter surface) . 0E09360CBF09 For the Enneper immersion, \[  K=-\frac4{(1+u^2+v^2)^4},\qquad \int _{\mathbb R^2}K\, dA=-4\pi .  \] The integral uses the induced metric on the parameter plane; self-intersections do not cancel area or curvature contributions. Proof Put $r^2=u^2+v^2$ and $\lambda =1+r^2$. The identity $\Delta \log (1+r^2)=4/(1+r^2)^2$ and the conformal curvature formula give $K$. Multiplying by $dA=(1+r^2)^2du\, dv$ and integrating in polar coordinates yields $-8\pi \int _0^\infty r(1+r^2)^{-2}\, dr=-4\pi $. Integration over the immersion always retains parameter multiplicity. $\square$ Remark 16.2.12 (Other explicit models already developed in the project) . A15C2808E10E Example 7.2.14 computes the minimal equation for Scherk's graph and its loss of a global gradient bound. Example 5.6.4 constructs a higher-codimension calibrated minimizer, and Propositions 5.6.5 and 5.6.6 compute its density and double-plane tangent. These entries retain their original tags and locations. The present catenoid calculation shows explicitly why the words minimal, stable, and area minimizing must be distinguished.

FEE5C0B5B785 For $a>0$, define \[  X_ a(t,\theta )=a(t\cos \theta ,t\sin \theta ,\theta ),\qquad (t,\theta )\in \mathbb R^2.  \] It is a proper embedded complete minimal surface, with \[  g=a^2\bigl (dt^2+(1+t^2)d\theta ^2\bigr ),\qquad K=-\frac1{a^2(1+t^2)^2}.  \] In particular, unlike the catenoid, it has the topology of a plane and has infinite absolute total curvature. Proof Direct differentiation gives the metric. Substitute $t=\sinh v$; the metric becomes $a^2\cosh ^2v(dv^2+d\theta ^2)$ and the three coordinate functions become harmonic, proving minimality by Lemma 16.2.1 . The conformal Gauss curvature calculation gives the displayed $K$. Height determines $\theta $ and then the horizontal coordinates determine $t$, proving injectivity. A bounded image bounds both parameters, proving properness; the metric dominates $a^2(dt^2+d\theta ^2)$, proving completeness. On $|v|<1$ the integral of $|K|dA=\operatorname {sech}^2v\, dv\, d\theta $ is infinite because $\theta $ ranges over all of $\mathbb R$. See [ ChMin ] , Section 13 and Example 15.6. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.2.9 (The catenoid-helicoid association and its period obstruction)
search_title: The catenoid-helicoid association and its period obstruction
text: Proposition 16.2.9 (The catenoid-helicoid association and its period obstruction) . 71B33AFD8411 On the parameter plane with $z=\theta +iv$, set \[  \Phi (z)=a(\cos z,\sin z,-iz),\qquad X_\alpha =\operatorname {Re}(e^{-i\alpha }\Phi ),\quad \alpha \in \mathbb R.  \] Every $X_\alpha $ is a conformal minimal immersion with metric $a^2\cosh ^2v(d\theta ^2+dv^2)$. The choices $\alpha =0$ and $\alpha =\pi /2$ give a catenoid covering and a helicoid, up to a rigid motion. The immersion descends to the cylinder $\theta \pmod{2\pi }$ if and only if $\sin \alpha =0$. Proof The holomorphic derivative satisfies $\Phi '\cdot \Phi '=a^2(\sin ^2z+\cos ^2z-1)=0$ and $|\Phi '|^2=2a^2\cosh ^2v$. Taking real and imaginary parts therefore gives orthogonal real derivatives of equal squared norm $|\Phi '|^2/2$. Multiplication by a unit complex number preserves both identities and harmonicity. The imaginary part is $a(-\sin \theta \sinh v,\cos \theta \sinh v,-\theta )$, a rotated/reflected helicoid. Finally $\Phi (z+2\pi )-\Phi (z)=(0,0,-2\pi ia)$, whose real part after multiplication by $e^{-i\alpha }$ is $(0,0,-2\pi a\sin \alpha )$. This vanishes exactly as claimed. Local isometry does not identify the global topologies. Compare [ ChMin ] , Lemma 15.5 and Example 15.6. $\square$

title: Example 16.2.10 (Enneper's surface is immersed and complete but not embedded)
search_title: Enneper's surface is immersed and complete but not embedded
text: Example 16.2.10 (Enneper's surface is immersed and complete but not embedded) . 6DA30A5B8CCE The polynomial map \[  E(u,v)=\left(u-\frac{u^3}{3}+uv^2, -v+\frac{v^3}{3}-u^2v,u^2-v^2\right)  \] is a proper complete conformal minimal immersion of $\mathbb R^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$, with metric $(1+u^2+v^2)^2(du^2+dv^2)$. It is not injective: $E(\sqrt3,0)=E(-\sqrt3,0)=(0,0,3)$. Proof Differentiation gives $|E_ u|^2=|E_ v|^2=(1+u^2+v^2)^2$ and $\langle E_ u,E_ v\rangle =0$; each coordinate is harmonic. The positive metric factor proves immersion and Lemma 16.2.1 proves minimality. The metric dominates the Euclidean one, giving completeness. With $z=u+iv$, the first two components satisfy $E_1+iE_2=\overline z-z^3/3$, hence $|E_1+iE_2|\geq |z|^3/3-|z|$. This tends to infinity, proving properness. The two displayed parameters prove failure of injectivity. At them, $E_ u=(-2,0,\pm 2\sqrt3)$ and $E_ v=(0,-4,0)$ span different tangent planes, so the image itself has a crossing and is not an embedded surface. This is Enneper's example from [ ChMin ] , Section 15.5, in a fixed polynomial normalization. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.2.11 (Total curvature counts the parameter surface)
search_title: Total curvature counts the parameter surface
text: Proposition 16.2.11 (Total curvature counts the parameter surface) . 0E09360CBF09 For the Enneper immersion, \[  K=-\frac4{(1+u^2+v^2)^4},\qquad \int _{\mathbb R^2}K\, dA=-4\pi .  \] The integral uses the induced metric on the parameter plane; self-intersections do not cancel area or curvature contributions. Proof Put $r^2=u^2+v^2$ and $\lambda =1+r^2$. The identity $\Delta \log (1+r^2)=4/(1+r^2)^2$ and the conformal curvature formula give $K$. Multiplying by $dA=(1+r^2)^2du\, dv$ and integrating in polar coordinates yields $-8\pi \int _0^\infty r(1+r^2)^{-2}\, dr=-4\pi $. Integration over the immersion always retains parameter multiplicity. $\square$

title: Remark 16.2.12 (Other explicit models already developed in the project)
search_title: Other explicit models already developed in the project
text: Remark 16.2.12 (Other explicit models already developed in the project) . A15C2808E10E Example 7.2.14 computes the minimal equation for Scherk's graph and its loss of a global gradient bound. Example 5.6.4 constructs a higher-codimension calibrated minimizer, and Propositions 5.6.5 and 5.6.6 compute its density and double-plane tangent. These entries retain their original tags and locations. The present catenoid calculation shows explicitly why the words minimal, stable, and area minimizing must be distinguished.

title: 16.3 Explicit solitons and translating graphs
search_title: Explicit solitons and translating graphs
text:
We work with smooth immersed hypersurfaces $\Sigma ^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\geq 1$, and the convention $\vec H=-H
u $, $H=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma 
u $. A parametrized family is a mean curvature flow when its normal velocity is $\vec H$; tangential velocity only changes parametrization. Definitions 14.2.2 and 14.5.5 fix the scale-one shrinker and expander equations. For translators we compare with [ HIMW19 ] , Sections 3–4, converting the source's downward translation to upward translation when writing graphs. Proposition 16.3.1 (The scale and time interval of a homothetic soliton) . 9F6515E0EAAB Suppose an immersion $X:\Sigma 	o \mathbb R^{n+1}$ satisfies $\vec H=cX^\perp $ for a constant $c\in \mathbb R$. Then \[  X_ t=\sqrt{1+2ct}\, X,\qquad 1+2ct>0,  \] is a mean curvature flow in the normal-velocity sense. For $c=-1/2$ it shrinks toward time $t=1$; for $c=1/2$ it expands from time $t=-1$; for $c=0$ it is stationary. These are statements about smooth times only. Proof Under a dilation by $r>0$, the tangent and normal spaces keep their directions and the mean curvature vector becomes $r^{-1}\vec H$. The normal velocity of $r(t)X$ is $r'X^\perp $. Thus $rr'=c$ suffices. The solution with $r(0)=1$ is the displayed positive square root. This verifies the scaling and the maximal interval on which that formula is positive; it does not prescribe a weak continuation through the zero-scale time. Compare Proposition 14.3.12 . $\square$ Proposition 16.3.2 (Products preserve a soliton equation) . 2E8C324BE1EA Let $\Sigma ^ m\subset \mathbb R^{m+1}$ be smooth. For $k\geq 0$, the product $\Sigma 	imes \mathbb R^ k\subset \mathbb R^{m+k+1}$ has mean curvature vector $(\vec H_\Sigma ,0)$. It preserves a homothetic equation $\vec H=cx^\perp $. If $\Sigma $ translates with velocity $v$, the product translates with every velocity $(v,w)$, $w\in \mathbb R^ k$; the extra component is tangent. Proof Use an orthonormal tangent frame on $\Sigma $ followed by the $k$ Euclidean coordinate vectors. The second fundamental form in the new directions and mixed directions is zero. Its trace is therefore unchanged. The normal space has no component in the product factor, giving $(x,y)^\perp =(x^\perp ,0)$ and $(v,w)^\perp =(v^\perp ,0)$. This proves all the assertions. In particular a translation vector is not uniquely determined by normal motion when a Euclidean product factor is present. $\square$ Example 16.3.3 (Planes, spheres, and cylinders have different motion laws) . 094E89C237AF An affine plane is a translator with velocity $v$ exactly when $v$ is tangent to it, in which case its image is stationary. It is a scale-one shrinker or expander centered at zero exactly when it passes through zero. The round sphere of radius $\sqrt{2m}$ in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$, $m\geq 1$, satisfies the shrinker equation, and its product with $\mathbb R^ k$ gives a shrinking cylinder. No round sphere centered at zero satisfies the scale-one expander equation. Proof The mean curvature of a plane is zero. Its normal position component is its constant displacement from the parallel plane through zero, proving the plane claims. On a radius-$R$ sphere, $\vec H=-(m/R)
u $ and $x^\perp =R
u $. The shrinker equation is $m/R=R/2$, whereas the expander equation would require $-m/R=R/2$, impossible for positive $R$. Apply Proposition 16.3.2 for cylinders. The evolving sphere radius is computed in Example 14.1.3 ; the stationary plane's apparent tangential translation must not be mistaken for nonzero normal speed. $\square$ Proposition 16.3.4 (The upward translator equation for a graph) . 41D469466CE5 Let $u\in C^2(\Omega )$, $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$ open, and $c\in \mathbb R$. Its graph translates with velocity $ce_{n+1}$ if and only if \[  \operatorname {div} rac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}} = rac{c}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}, \qquad \left(\delta _{ij}- rac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}ight)u_{ij}=c.  \] With upward unit normal $
u =(-Du,1)/\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$, the scalar curvature is $H=-c/\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$. Proof The upward graph normal has tangential divergence $H=-\operatorname {div}(Du/\sqrt{1+|Du|^2})$. The normal component of the velocity is $(ce_{n+1})^\perp =(c/\sqrt{1+|Du|^2})
u $. Equating this with $-H
u $ gives the divergence equation. Expanding the divergence and multiplying by $\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$ gives the second form. Equivalently substitute $u(x,t)=u(x)+ct$ in Proposition 14.3.13 . The negative sign of $H$ here follows from the chosen upward normal. $\square$ Proposition 16.3.5 (All translating graphs of curves with nonzero vertical speed) . 05029F510E01 Let $c>0$. Every connected graph $y=u(x)$ translating upward with speed $c$ is a restriction of \[  u(x)=- rac1c\log \cos (c(x-x_0))+b, \qquad |x-x_0|< rac{\pi }{2c},  \] for constants $x_0,b$. The full graph is properly embedded and complete; a restriction to a proper open subinterval is incomplete at any new finite endpoint. Its curvature magnitude is $c\cos (c(x-x_0))$, and its total curvature is $\pi $. Proof Proposition 16.3.4 reduces to $u''=c(1+(u')^2)$. Writing $p=u'$, integration gives $\arctan p=c(x-x_0)$ after adjusting $x_0$, and a second integration yields the formula. This also identifies the maximal interval between consecutive vertical asymptotes. The arc length element is $ds=\sec (c(x-x_0))\, dx$; its integral diverges at both endpoints. Height also tends to infinity there, giving properness. At an added interior endpoint both slope and arc length density remain bounded, giving incompleteness. Finally $|\kappa |=u''/(1+(u')^2)^{3/2}=c\cos (c(x-x_0))$, so $|\kappa |ds=c\, dx$ integrates to $\pi $. The speed-one case retains its earlier entry at Example 14.5.6 ; [ HIMW19 ] , Example 1.6, uses the reflected downward version. $\square$ Example 16.3.6 (Tilted grim-reaper cylinders) . F553C58629A6 For $a\in \mathbb R$, put $A=1+a^2$ and \[  u(x,y)=-A\log \cos (x/\sqrt A)+ay, \qquad |x|< rac\pi 2\sqrt A,\quad y\in \mathbb R.  \] This is a proper complete embedded translator with velocity $e_3$. Its strip width is $\pi \sqrt{1+a^2}$. The direction $(0,1,a)$ is tangent everywhere and leaves the graph invariant under translation. Products give higher-dimensional examples. Proof Writing $\xi =x/\sqrt A$, we have $u_ x=\sqrt A	an \xi $, $u_ y=a$, $u_{xx}=\sec ^2\xi $, and the other second derivatives vanish. Since $1+|Du|^2=A\sec ^2\xi $, \[  \left(1- rac{u_ x^2}{1+|Du|^2}ight)u_{xx} = rac{1+a^2}{A\sec ^2\xi }\sec ^2\xi =1.  \] Proposition 16.3.4 proves the equation. A bounded ambient image bounds $x,y,u$; as $x$ tends to a strip endpoint with bounded $y$, the logarithmic term diverges. Thus inverse images of compact sets stay in a compact subdomain, proving properness. A proper smooth immersion into Euclidean space is complete: any intrinsic Cauchy sequence has bounded image and a convergent subsequence in its compact inverse image, and smooth local coordinates give intrinsic convergence. Graphs are embedded. The tangent-direction and product assertions follow directly. This is the upward form of [ HIMW19 ] , equation (3.2), with $a=	an 	heta $. $\square$ Proposition 16.3.7 (A translator's height is a strict elliptic test) . 8F198CC4372E Let $X:\Sigma ^ n	o \mathbb R^{n+1}$ satisfy $\vec H=v^\perp $, and put $h=\langle X,vangle $. Pointwise, \[  
abla _\Sigma h=v^ T,\qquad \Delta _\Sigma h=|v^\perp |^2, \qquad \Delta _\Sigma e^ h=|v|^2 e^ h.  \] There is no nonempty compact boundaryless translating hypersurface in Euclidean space, including the case of zero translation velocity. Proof Differentiating $h$ tangentially gives its gradient. The immersion identity $\Delta _\Sigma X=\vec H$ gives $\Delta h=\langle \vec H,vangle =|v^\perp |^2$. The exponential chain rule adds $|
abla h|^2=|v^ T|^2$, yielding the final identity. If $v
e 0$, its integral on a compact boundaryless hypersurface contradicts the divergence theorem. If $v=0$, the immersion is minimal and $\Delta _\Sigma |X|^2=2n$, again impossible after integration. Neither completeness nor properness is required for the pointwise identities. $\square$ Proposition 16.3.8 (Translation as a weighted area problem) . 65A833ADF759 A smooth immersion satisfies $\vec H=v^\perp $ if and only if it is stationary for the weighted area $\int _\Sigma e^{\langle x,vangle }\, dA$ under all compactly supported normal variations. Stationarity is understood locally even when the total weighted area is infinite. Proof For normal initial velocity $Y$, the ordinary area derivative is $-\langle \vec H,Yangle dA$ and the derivative of the weight is $e^{\langle x,vangle }\langle v,Yangle $. Therefore \[  \delta \mathcal A_ v(Y)=\int _\Sigma e^{\langle x,vangle }\langle v^\perp -\vec H,Yangle \, dA.  \] Compact support makes this expression finite and removes boundary terms. It vanishes for all normal tests precisely when the vector in parentheses is zero. In [ HIMW19 ] , Proposition 3.2, the velocity is $-e_{n+1}$ and the weight is correspondingly $e^{-x_{n+1}}$; a Gaussian weight would instead describe a shrinking soliton. $\square$ Proposition 16.3.9 (The radial equation at the tip of a bowl translator) . 728A5B325249 Let $n\geq 2$, and suppose $u(x)=f(|x|)$ is a smooth graph near zero translating with velocity $e_{n+1}$. For $r>0$ its radial equation is \[   rac{f''}{1+(f')^2}+ rac{n-1}{r}f'=1.  \] At the center, $f'(0)=0$ and $f''(0)=1/n$. If $f$ is $C^4$, then \[  f(r)=f(0)+ rac{r^2}{2n}+ rac{r^4}{4n^3(n+2)}+o(r^4).  \] These are necessary local identities; they do not by themselves prove that the solution extends to a complete entire bowl. Proof The Hessian of a radial function has eigenvalues $f''$ in the radial direction and $f'/r$ in the $n-1$ perpendicular directions. The gradient is radial, so substitution in Proposition 16.3.4 gives the ODE. Smooth radiality gives $Du(0)=0$ and $D^2u(0)=f''(0)I$; the graph equation at zero is then $nf''(0)=1$. Write $f=f(0)+Ar^2+Br^4+o(r^4)$ with the differentiated remainders furnished by $C^4$ regularity and radial symmetry. The constant equation gives $2nA=1$. The $r^2$ coefficient is $4(n+2)B-8A^3=0$, proving the formula. The complete rotational bowl is the example discussed in [ HIMW19 ] , Section 4; its global construction requires a separate ODE argument. $\square$ Example 16.3.10 (A paraboloid is not an exact bowl translator) . D5EF84E90E72 For $n\geq 2$, the function $u(x)=|x|^2/(2(n-1))$ does not solve the unit-speed translator equation, even though its growth has the quadratic scale associated with the bowl model. In fact its translator operator equals \[  \left(\delta _{ij}- rac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}ight)u_{ij} =1+ rac{1}{(n-1)(1+r^2/(n-1)^2)}>1.  \] Proof For this radial graph, $f'=r/(n-1)$ and $f''=1/(n-1)$. Substitute into the operator in Proposition 16.3.9 . The tangential term is one and the radial term is the additional positive fraction. In particular its Hessian at zero is $I/(n-1)$, whereas a smooth exact bowl tip must have Hessian $I/n$. An asymptotic shape must not be substituted for an exact solution. $\square$

Proof The Hessian of a radial function has eigenvalues $f''$ in the radial direction and $f'/r$ in the $n-1$ perpendicular directions.
