Write $f=f(0)+Ar^2+Br^4+o(r^4)$ with the differentiated remainders furnished by $C^4$ regularity and radial symmetry. The constant equation gives $2nA=1$. The $r^2$ coefficient is $4(n+2)B-8A^3=0$, proving the formula. The complete rotational bowl is the example discussed in [ HIMW19 ] , Section 4; its global construction requires a separate ODE argument. $\square$

title: Example 16.3.10 (A paraboloid is not an exact bowl translator)
search_title: A paraboloid is not an exact bowl translator
text: Example 16.3.10 (A paraboloid is not an exact bowl translator) . D5EF84E90E72 For $n\geq 2$, the function $u(x)=|x|^2/(2(n-1))$ does not solve the unit-speed translator equation, even though its growth has the quadratic scale associated with the bowl model. In fact its translator operator equals \[  \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}\right)u_{ij} =1+\frac{1}{(n-1)(1+r^2/(n-1)^2)}>1.  \] Proof For this radial graph, $f'=r/(n-1)$ and $f''=1/(n-1)$. Substitute into the operator in Proposition 16.3.9 . The tangential term is one and the radial term is the additional positive fraction. In particular its Hessian at zero is $I/(n-1)$, whereas a smooth exact bowl tip must have Hessian $I/n$. An asymptotic shape must not be substituted for an exact solution. $\square$

title: 16.4 Constructing the rotational bowl soliton
search_title: Constructing the rotational bowl soliton
text: The radial equation in Proposition 16.3.9 admits a complete solution, not just a formal series at the tip. We give the construction and its leading asymptotics in separate steps. Compare [ CSS07 ] , Section 2, equations (2.1)–(2.2) and Lemma 2.2; citations use the author-hosted September 2005 manuscript. Our local construction at the singular endpoint is supplied explicitly. Throughout this section $n\geq 2$ and the translation speed is one upward. Lemma 16.4.1 (Resolving the radial equation at zero) . DD2B8469A5C0 There is $R>0$ and a unique smooth radial solution $u(x)=f(|x|)$ on $B_ R\subset \mathbb R^ n$ of the unit-speed translator equation with $f(0)=0$. Its derivative has the form \[  p(r)=f'(r)=rq(r^2),\qquad q(0)=\frac1n,  \] where $q$ is real analytic near zero. In particular the apparent $1/r$ coefficient in the radial equation creates no singularity in the graph at its tip. Proof Put $m=n-1$ and $P(q)=q^2(1-mq)$. Multiplying $p'+mp/r=1+p^2-mp^3/r$ by $r^{n-1}$ and integrating from zero gives, after setting $p=rq(r^2)$, \[  q(z)=\frac1n+z\int _0^1t^{n+1}P(q(zt^2))\, dt.  \] To construct a smooth solution without assuming it exists, use the Banach space of functions continuous on a small closed complex disk $|z|\leq \delta $ and holomorphic in its interior, with the supremum norm. On the closed ball $\| q-1/n\| _\infty \leq 1$, the polynomial $P$ is bounded by some $M_ n$ and is Lipschitz with some $L_ n$. The right side of (*) maps this ball into itself when $\delta M_ n/(n+2)\leq 1$ and is a contraction when $\delta L_ n/(n+2)<1$. Its unique fixed point is holomorphic and real on the real axis, since iteration starting from $1/n$ preserves complex conjugation. Define \[  f(r)=\frac12\int _0^{r^2}q(s)\, ds.  \] This is analytic as a function of $|x|^2$ and satisfies the ODE away from zero by differentiation of the integral identity. At zero its Hessian is $I/n$, so the graph equation holds there as well. Conversely any smooth radial solution has $p/r\to 1/n$ by Proposition 16.3.9 , and it obeys the same integral equation on the real interval. The same contraction proof in the space of continuous real functions gives local uniqueness without assuming analyticity of the competitor. The only external analytic tools in this local construction are the contraction principle and uniform-limit closure of holomorphic functions. $\square$ Lemma 16.4.2 (Linear barriers prevent finite-radius blow-up) . 79D2E1EDDD98 The tip solution extends to all $r\geq 0$ and satisfies \[  \frac rn<p(r)<\frac r{n-1},\qquad p'(r)>0\quad (r>0).  \] Consequently its height obeys \[  \frac{r^2}{2n}<f(r)<\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}\quad (r>0).  \] Proof The tip expansion in Proposition 16.3.9 gives $p=r/n+r^3/(n^3(n+2))+o(r^3)$, so the strict barriers hold initially. At a contact with $p=r/n$, the ODE gives $p'-1/n=r^2/n^3>0$, preventing a first downward crossing. At a contact with $p=r/(n-1)$, it gives $p'-1/(n-1)=-1/(n-1)<0$, preventing a first upward crossing. Thus the two barriers persist for the whole interval of existence. Between them the factor $1-(n-1)p/r$ is positive, so $p'>0$. If a finite positive endpoint of existence existed, the barriers would bound $p$ there, and the smooth ODE away from $r=0$ would continue the solution across that endpoint. This contradiction proves global extension. Integrating the strict bounds from zero gives the height bounds. Compare the continuation and barrier argument in [ CSS07 ] , proof of Lemma 2.1. $\square$ Theorem 16.4.3 (The complete rotational bowl) . 9AE533B778E2 For every $n\geq 2$, the graph of the function $f(|x|)$ constructed above is a smooth, properly embedded, complete, strictly convex hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ translating with velocity $e_{n+1}$. It is unique among smooth rotational entire translating graphs with this speed, rotation axis, and tip height zero. Proof Lemma 16.4.1 gives smoothness at the origin, and Lemma 16.4.2 gives global continuation. The Hessian eigenvalues for $r>0$ are $p'>0$ and $p/r>0$; at zero they are all $1/n$. Thus the graph is strictly convex. The ODE and Proposition 16.3.4 give its translating equation. An entire smooth graph is embedded and proper: the base projection bounds the preimage of an ambient compact set, which is also closed. Its induced metric dominates the Euclidean base metric, proving completeness by the Cauchy-sequence argument used for the catenoid. Local uniqueness at the tip and ordinary ODE uniqueness on $r>0$ give uniqueness in the stated rotational class. This is the rotational existence result in [ CSS07 ] , Lemma 2.2; no classification of nonrotational translators is claimed. $\square$ Proposition 16.4.4 (The quadratic growth coefficient of the bowl) . 9E5E68B20123 For the normalized bowl, \[  \lim _{r\to \infty }\frac{p(r)}r=\frac1{n-1},\qquad \lim _{r\to \infty }\frac{f(r)}{r^2}=\frac1{2(n-1)}.  \] Proof Fix $b$ with $1/n<b<1/(n-1)$. If $p(r)<br$ for every sufficiently large $r$, the ODE and $p\geq r/n$ imply $p'\geq (1-(n-1)b)r^2/n^2$. Integration would force cubic growth, contradicting the linear upper bound in Lemma 16.4.2 . Therefore $p$ reaches $br$ at some arbitrarily large radius. At such a contact the derivative difference is \[  p'-b=(1+b^2r^2)(1-(n-1)b)-b>0  \] for large $r$, so it cannot subsequently cross downward. Thus $\liminf p/r\geq b$. Let $b\uparrow 1/(n-1)$ and use the upper barrier to get the first limit. Integrating $(1/(n-1)-\varepsilon )r\leq p(r)\leq r/(n-1)$ outside a fixed radius, then dividing by $r^2$, proves the second. This is the first asymptotic barrier step in [ CSS07 ] , Lemma 2.1. $\square$ Lemma 16.4.5 (The first slope correction) . E35E297F2131 Write $m=n-1$ and $w(r)=r/m-p(r)>0$. Then \[  \lim _{r\to \infty }rw(r)=1.  \] Proof The equation for the defect is \[  w'=\frac1m-a(r)w,\qquad a(r)=\frac mr(1+p(r)^2), \qquad \frac{a(r)}r\longrightarrow \frac1m.  \] Fix $0<\varepsilon <1$ and compare $w$ with $b_\pm =(1\pm \varepsilon )/r$. At $w=b_+$ the right side tends to $-\varepsilon /m$, while $b_+'\to 0$; for large radii $b_+$ is a strict supersolution. If $w>b_+$ persisted forever, then $w'\leq -\varepsilon /(2m)$ for all sufficiently large radii, contradicting $w>0$. Thus $w$ reaches this upper barrier and cannot cross it upward afterward. Similarly $b_-$ is a strict subsolution for large radii. If $w<b_-$ persisted forever, then $w'\geq \varepsilon /(2m)$, contradicting $w<b_-\to 0$. Once it crosses upward it cannot cross back. Therefore $1-\varepsilon \leq rw\leq 1+\varepsilon $ eventually. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$ Proposition 16.4.6 (A logarithmic correction to the bowl height) . 4218133DBAA6 There is a constant $C_ n$ determined by the normalization $f(0)=0$ such that \[  p(r)=\frac r{n-1}-\frac1r+O(r^{-3}),\qquad f(r)=\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}-\log r+C_ n+O(r^{-2}).  \] The constant cannot be discarded unless one changes the vertical translation of the bowl. Proof With $m=n-1$, the exact equation for $w$ from Lemma 16.4.5 is $w'=F(r,w)$, where \[  F(r,w)=\frac1m-\left(\frac rm+\frac mr\right)w+2w^2-\frac mr w^3.  \] For $b_ K(r)=r^{-1}+Kr^{-3}$, expansion gives \[  F(r,b_ K)-b_ K' =\frac{3-m-K/m}{r^2}+O_ K(r^{-4}).  \] Choose $K_+>m(3-m)$ and $K_-<m(3-m)$. Then $b_{K_+}$ is a supersolution and $b_{K_-}$ a subsolution for $r\geq R$ large. By Lemma 16.4.5 , both $w$ and these barriers lie between $0$ and $2/r$ there. Throughout this interval \[  \partial _ wF=-\frac rm-\frac mr+4w-\frac{3m}r w^2 \leq -\frac r{2m}  \] after increasing $R$. On any interval where $w-b_{K_+}>0$, the mean-value theorem gives $(w-b_{K_+})'\leq -r(w-b_{K_+})/(2m)$. At a zero this difference cannot cross from negative to positive. Hence its positive part is at most $A\exp (-(r^2-R^2)/(4m))$. Applying the same argument to $(b_{K_-}-w)_+$ gives the lower estimate. The exponentially decaying errors can be absorbed in $O(r^{-3})$, so $w=1/r+O(r^{-3})$. This proves the slope expansion. The derivative of $f-r^2/(2m)+\log r$ is consequently $O(r^{-3})$, which is integrable at infinity; its tail integral is $O(r^{-2})$. This proves the height expansion, including its additive constant. Compare [ CSS07 ] , Lemmas 2.1–2.2; the argument here uses scalar barriers rather than the longer formal series. $\square$ Corollary 16.4.7 (Translation speed and dilations of the bowl) . 69FAC94BF385 For any $c>0$, define $f_ c(r)=c^{-1}f(cr)$. Its graph translates with velocity $ce_{n+1}$ and has tip Hessian $(c/n)I$. Its large-radius expansion is \[  f_ c(r)=\frac{cr^2}{2(n-1)}-\frac1c\log r +\frac{C_ n-\log c}{c}+O_ c(r^{-2}).  \] Proof We have $f_ c'=p(cr)$ and $f_ c''=c p'(cr)$. Substitution in the radial graph operator multiplies its unit-speed value by $c$. Smoothness, completeness and properness follow by dilation. At zero the second derivative is $c/n$. Replacing $r$ by $cr$ in Proposition 16.4.6 and dividing by $c$ gives the expansion. The speed changes inversely with spatial dilation, as required by parabolic scaling. $\square$

title: 16.5 Expanding curves that smooth a corner
search_title: Expanding curves that smooth a corner
section: 16.5 Expanding curves that smooth a corner
text:
Expanding solitons give nonstationary examples defined for positive times and converging to a nonsmooth initial cone. We construct an even convex graphical family directly. The primary comparison is [ Hal12 ] , Section 6, where expanding planar curves are studied in arc-length coordinates. Here the normalization is $\vec H=x^\perp /2$, so the time family is $\sqrt t\, \Sigma $. Proposition 16.5.1 (The expander graph equation and its positive defect) . 19BF76D4A84D A graph $y=u(x)$ in $\mathbb R^2$ satisfies the scale-one expander equation exactly when \[  u''= rac12(1+(u')^2)(u-xu').  \] If $u(0)=a>0$ and $u'(0)=0$, set $p=u'$ and $q=u-xp$. On every interval of existence with $x\geq 0$, \[  p'=	frac 12(1+p^2)q,\qquad q'=-xp',\qquad q(x)=a\exp \left(- rac12\int _0^ x s(1+p(s)^2)\, dsight)>0.  \] In particular $p'>0$ and $0<q(x)\leq ae^{-x^2/4}$. Proof For the upward normal $
u =(-p,1)/\sqrt{1+p^2}$, the coefficient of the mean curvature vector along $
u $ is $u''/(1+p^2)^{3/2}$, while $\langle (x,u),
u angle =(u-xp)/\sqrt{1+p^2}$. Their equality with factor one half gives the ODE. Differentiate $q=u-xp$ to obtain $q'=-xp'=-x(1+p^2)q/2$. Solving this scalar linear equation with $q(0)=a$ gives its positive exponential expression and Gaussian upper bound. The scalar convention $H=\operatorname {div}
u $ is the negative of the coefficient of $\vec H$ here. $\square$ Lemma 16.5.2 (The expanding graph has bounded slope) . 959A9F743DAB For each $a>0$, the initial-value solution in Proposition 16.5.1 extends smoothly to all $x\geq 0$. For every $\varepsilon >0$ in its interval of existence and $x\geq \varepsilon $, \[  0<p(x)\leq p(\varepsilon )+ rac{q(\varepsilon )}\varepsilon .  \] It therefore has a finite positive limiting slope $\ell _ a=\lim _{x	o \infty }p(x)$. Proof The smooth ODE has a unique local solution for these initial data. Since $p'>0$ and $q>0$, integration of $q'=-xp'$ gives \[  q(\varepsilon )-q(x)=\int _\varepsilon ^ x s p'(s)\, ds \geq \varepsilon (p(x)-p(\varepsilon )).  \] This proves the bound. Were the maximal endpoint finite and positive, choose a fixed positive $\varepsilon $ below it. The bound controls $p$, while $0<q\leq a$ controls $u=q+xp$ on that finite interval. Smooth ODE continuation then crosses the endpoint, a contradiction. Monotonicity and boundedness of $p$ give its finite limit, which is positive since $p(x)>0$ for $x>0$. $\square$ Theorem 16.5.3 (A complete convex expander asymptotic to two rays) . 56C7AF70B331 For every $a>0$, there is a unique smooth even solution $u_ a:\mathbb R	o \mathbb R$ of the expander graph equation with $u_ a(0)=a$ and $u_ a'(0)=0$. Its graph is properly embedded, complete, and strictly convex. For a finite $\ell _ a>0$, \[  u_ a(x)-\ell _ a|x|\longrightarrow 0\quad (|x|	o \infty ), \qquad 0<u_ a(x)-\ell _ a|x|\leq a.  \] Its two asymptotic rays meet at the origin. This constructs a family; it does not assert that a prescribed cone angle determines a unique expander among arbitrary immersions. Proof The ODE is invariant under $x\mapsto -x$, so local uniqueness makes the solution even; Lemma 16.5.2 extends both halves. Positivity of $q$ gives $u_ a''>0$. As an entire smooth graph it is proper, embedded, and complete. Write $\ell =\ell _ a$. Boundedness of $p$ and the Gaussian bound for $q$ give $0<p'(x)\leq Ce^{-x^2/4}$, hence for $x\geq 1$, \[  0<\ell -p(x)\leq C\int _ x^\infty e^{-s^2/4}\, ds \leq  rac{2C}{x}e^{-x^2/4}.  \] Since $u_ a-x\ell =q-x(\ell -p)$, both terms tend to zero. Its derivative is $p-\ell <0$ for $x\geq 0$; thus it decreases from $a$ to zero and is strictly positive. Reflecting gives the negative half. These properties agree with the expanding-curve models in [ Hal12 ] , Section 6, after converting its dilation normalization. $\square$ Proposition 16.5.4 (A smooth flow converging uniformly to a corner) . 643DB83B70AB Let $u_ a$ be the expander above and define \[  U(x,t)=\sqrt t\, u_ a(x/\sqrt t),\qquad t>0.  \] Its graphs solve curve shortening flow, and for every $x\in \mathbb R$, \[  0<U(x,t)-\ell _ a|x|\leq a\sqrt t.  \] Thus the graph functions converge uniformly on all of $\mathbb R$ to the Lipschitz corner $\ell _ a|x|$ as $t\downarrow 0$. Their products with $\mathbb R^ k$ give hypersurface flows with an initial crease. Proof Put $\xi =x/\sqrt t$. Direct differentiation gives $U_ t=(u_ a-\xi u_ a')/(2\sqrt t)$, $U_ x=u_ a'$, and $U_{xx}=u_ a''/\sqrt t$. The expander equation makes $U_ t=U_{xx}/(1+U_ x^2)$. The bound follows by multiplying the height excess in Theorem 16.5.3 by $\sqrt t$. Proposition 16.3.2 handles products. This is an explicit classical solution for $t>0$ with an initial trace; no uniqueness theorem for arbitrary weak flows from that trace is used. $\square$ Proposition 16.5.5 (Total curvature and maximum curvature of the expander) . F456929A84ED The expander graph has finite total curvature \[  \int _\Sigma |\kappa |\, ds=2\arctan \ell _ a<\pi .  \] Its maximum curvature is $a/2$, attained at its tip. Along its expanding flow the maximum is $a/(2\sqrt t)$. Proof Since $u_ a''>0$, the curvature magnitude is $p'/(1+p^2)^{3/2}$ and $ds=\sqrt{1+p^2}\, dx$. Their product is $(\arctan p)'dx$. The limiting slopes are $-\ell _ a$ and $\ell _ a$, proving the integral. By the equation, $|\kappa |=q/(2\sqrt{1+p^2})$. On $x>0$, $q$ strictly decreases and $p$ strictly increases, so the curvature decreases from $q(0)/2=a/2$. Evenness handles the other half. Dilation by $\sqrt t$ divides curvature by $\sqrt t$. $\square$

Proposition 16.5.1 (The expander graph equation and its positive defect) . 19BF76D4A84D A graph $y=u(x)$ in $\mathbb R^2$ satisfies the scale-one expander equation exactly when \[  u''= rac12(1+(u')^2)(u-xu').  \] If $u(0)=a>0$ and $u'(0)=0$, set $p=u'$ and $q=u-xp$. On every interval of existence with $x\geq 0$, \[  p'=	frac 12(1+p^2)q,\qquad q'=-xp',\qquad q(x)=a\exp \left(- rac12\int _0^ x s(1+p(s)^2)\, dsight)>0.  \] In particular $p'>0$ and $0<q(x)\leq ae^{-x^2/4}$. Proof For the upward normal $
u =(-p,1)/\sqrt{1+p^2}$, the coefficient of the mean curvature vector along $
u $ is $u''/(1+p^2)^{3/2}$, while $\langle (x,u),
u angle =(u-xp)/\sqrt{1+p^2}$. Their equality with factor one half gives the ODE. Differentiate $q=u-xp$ to obtain $q'=-xp'=-x(1+p^2)q/2$. Solving this scalar linear equation with $q(0)=a$ gives its positive exponential expression and Gaussian upper bound. The scalar convention $H=\operatorname {div}
u $ is the negative of the coefficient of $\vec H$ here. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.5.2 (The expanding graph has bounded slope)
search_title: The expanding graph has bounded slope

text: Lemma 16.5.2 (The expanding graph has bounded slope) . 959A9F743DAB For each $a>0$, the initial-value solution in Proposition 16.5.1 extends smoothly to all $x\geq 0$. For every $\varepsilon >0$ in its interval of existence and $x\geq \varepsilon $, \[  0<p(x)\leq p(\varepsilon )+\frac{q(\varepsilon )}\varepsilon .  \] It therefore has a finite positive limiting slope $\ell _ a=\lim _{x\to \infty }p(x)$. Proof The smooth ODE has a unique local solution for these initial data. Since $p'>0$ and $q>0$, integration of $q'=-xp'$ gives \[  q(\varepsilon )-q(x)=\int _\varepsilon ^ x s p'(s)\, ds \geq \varepsilon (p(x)-p(\varepsilon )).  \] This proves the bound. Were the maximal endpoint finite and positive, choose a fixed positive $\varepsilon $ below it. The bound controls $p$, while $0<q\leq a$ controls $u=q+xp$ on that finite interval. Smooth ODE continuation then crosses the endpoint, a contradiction. Monotonicity and boundedness of $p$ give its finite limit, which is positive since $p(x)>0$ for $x>0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.5.3 (A complete convex expander asymptotic to two rays)
search_title: A complete convex expander asymptotic to two rays
section: 16.5 Expanding curves that smooth a corner
text: Theorem 16.5.3 (A complete convex expander asymptotic to two rays) . 56C7AF70B331 For every $a>0$, there is a unique smooth even solution $u_ a:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ of the expander graph equation with $u_ a(0)=a$ and $u_ a'(0)=0$. Its graph is properly embedded, complete, and strictly convex. For a finite $\ell _ a>0$, \[  u_ a(x)-\ell _ a|x|\longrightarrow 0\quad (|x|\to \infty ), \qquad 0<u_ a(x)-\ell _ a|x|\leq a.  \] Its two asymptotic rays meet at the origin. This constructs a family; it does not assert that a prescribed cone angle determines a unique expander among arbitrary immersions. Proof The ODE is invariant under $x\mapsto -x$, so local uniqueness makes the solution even; Lemma 16.5.2 extends both halves. Positivity of $q$ gives $u_ a''>0$. As an entire smooth graph it is proper, embedded, and complete. Write $\ell =\ell _ a$. Boundedness of $p$ and the Gaussian bound for $q$ give $0<p'(x)\leq Ce^{-x^2/4}$, hence for $x\geq 1$, \[  0<\ell -p(x)\leq C\int _ x^\infty e^{-s^2/4}\, ds \leq \frac{2C}{x}e^{-x^2/4}.  \] Since $u_ a-x\ell =q-x(\ell -p)$, both terms tend to zero. Its derivative is $p-\ell <0$ for $x\geq 0$; thus it decreases from $a$ to zero and is strictly positive. Reflecting gives the negative half. These properties agree with the expanding-curve models in [ Hal12 ] , Section 6, after converting its dilation normalization. $\square$

text: Proposition 16.5.4 (A smooth flow converging uniformly to a corner) . 643DB83B70AB Let $u_ a$ be the expander above and define \[  U(x,t)=\sqrt t\, u_ a(x/\sqrt t),\qquad t>0.  \] Its graphs solve curve shortening flow, and for every $x\in \mathbb R$, \[  0<U(x,t)-\ell _ a|x|\leq a\sqrt t.  \] Thus the graph functions converge uniformly on all of $\mathbb R$ to the Lipschitz corner $\ell _ a|x|$ as $t\downarrow 0$. Their products with $\mathbb R^ k$ give hypersurface flows with an initial crease. Proof Put $\xi =x/\sqrt t$. Direct differentiation gives $U_ t=(u_ a-\xi u_ a')/(2\sqrt t)$, $U_ x=u_ a'$, and $U_{xx}=u_ a''/\sqrt t$. The expander equation makes $U_ t=U_{xx}/(1+U_ x^2)$. The bound follows by multiplying the height excess in Theorem 16.5.3 by $\sqrt t$. Proposition 16.3.2 handles products. This is an explicit classical solution for $t>0$ with an initial trace; no uniqueness theorem for arbitrary weak flows from that trace is used. $\square$

title: 16.6 An explicit ancient oval
search_title: An explicit ancient oval
text:
An ancient solution exists for every time before some finite time. It need not preserve its shape. The explicit oval below is often called the Angenent oval or paperclip solution; [ BV11 ] , Section 3.1, equation (14), records the formula and discusses its provenance. We verify the evolution and its limiting models directly. The earlier shrinking circle and grim reaper appear here as two different limits of one solution. Theorem 16.6.1 (The implicit oval is an ancient curve-shortening flow) . 413CCED0D734 For $t<0$, the set \[  \Gamma _ t=\{ (x,y):|x|<\pi /2,\  e^ t\cosh y=\cos x\}   \] is a smooth embedded strictly convex closed curve. These curves solve curve shortening flow and shrink to the origin as $t\uparrow 0$. Their coordinate extrema are \[  |x|\leq \arccos (e^ t),\qquad |y|\leq \operatorname {arcosh}(e^{-t}).  \] Proof Set $F(x,y,t)=e^ t\cosh y-\cos x$. On the strip $|x|<\pi /2$, its spatial Hessian is positive definite. Its negative sublevel is nonempty since $F(0,0,t)<0$, and the displayed bounds show its closure stays in a compact subset of the strip. It is a strictly convex bounded domain. On its boundary, \[  |
abla F|^2=\sin ^2x+e^{2t}\sinh ^2y=1-e^{2t}>0, \qquad D^2F=\cos x\, I.  \] Thus the boundary is smooth and has outward curvature $\kappa =\operatorname {div}(
abla F/|
abla F|)=\cos x/\sqrt{1-e^{2t}}>0$. Differentiating $F=0$ in time gives outward normal velocity $-F_ t/|
abla F|=-\cos x/\sqrt{1-e^{2t}}=-\kappa $. This is curve shortening. The coordinate bounds follow by setting the other coordinate to zero and tend to zero as $t\uparrow 0$. The gradient computation avoids treating the two graph branches as separate curves at their endpoints. Compare [ BV11 ] , equation (14), p. 7. $\square$ Proposition 16.6.2 (The ancient oval changes shape) . C9B55D368ADD The extreme curvatures of $\Gamma _ t$ satisfy \[  \kappa _{\max }(t)= rac1{\sqrt{1-e^{2t}}},\qquad \kappa _{\min }(t)= rac{e^ t}{\sqrt{1-e^{2t}}},\qquad  rac{\kappa _{\max }}{\kappa _{\min }}=e^{-t}.  \] In particular this ancient solution is not a soliton moving by Euclidean similarities. Its curvature becomes asymptotically uniform as extinction approaches, but is very nonuniform far backward in time. Proof The curvature formula from Theorem 16.6.1 is proportional to $\cos x$. On the curve this ranges from $e^ t$ at the horizontal extrema to one at the vertical extrema. This proves all formulas. A Euclidean similarity changes all curvatures by the same positive scale factor, and so preserves their maximum-to-minimum ratio. Here that ratio changes strictly with time. Its limits are one as $t\uparrow 0$ and infinity as $t	o -\infty $. $\square$ Proposition 16.6.3 (Area and the shrinking-circle limit) . 453E1EC89741 The area enclosed by $\Gamma _ t$ is $-2\pi t$. The rescaled curves $(-t)^{-1/2}\Gamma _ t$ converge smoothly as $t\uparrow 0$ to the circle of radius $\sqrt2$ centered at zero. Proof The normal velocity is $-\kappa $, so the area derivative is $-\int _{\Gamma _ t}\kappa \, ds=-2\pi $, using the turning-angle formula for a smooth simple convex curve. The enclosed area tends to zero by the coordinate bounds in Theorem 16.6.1 ; integration gives $-2\pi t$. This is the area calculation in [ WhiMCF15 ] , Theorem 1.1, applied to the explicit oval. For smooth convergence put $s=-t>0$ and $(x,y)=\sqrt s(X,Y)$. On bounded sets the rescaled defining function satisfies \[   rac{e^{-s}\cosh (\sqrt sY)-\cos (\sqrt sX)}s = rac{X^2+Y^2}{2}-1+O(s)  \] with convergence of every spatial derivative, by the power series. The rescaled coordinate extrema tend to $\sqrt2$, so all curves stay in a fixed bounded set. Strict convexity and inclusion of the origin inside each oval give a single radial intersection in every direction. The limiting function has nonzero radial derivative on the radius-$\sqrt2$ circle. The implicit function theorem, uniformly over that compact circle, gives smooth convergence of the radial functions and hence of the curves. The normalization agrees with the shrinker radius in Example 16.3.3 . $\square$ Proposition 16.6.4 (The two grim-reaper limits backward in time) . 932BFFC222D3 On every compact subinterval of $(-\pi /2,\pi /2)$, the upper and lower graph branches of the ancient oval satisfy, as $t	o -\infty $, \[  y_+(x,t)+t-\log 2\longrightarrow \log \cos x, \qquad y_-(x,t)-t+\log 2\longrightarrow -\log \cos x  \] smoothly in $x$. These are the downward and upward grim-reaper profiles, respectively. The convergence is local in the horizontal strip, not uniform through its limiting endpoints. Proof The branches are $y_\pm =\pm \operatorname {arcosh}(e^{-t}\cos x)$. For large $z$, the identity $\operatorname {arcosh}z=\log (z+\sqrt{z^2-1})$ gives $\operatorname {arcosh}z=\log (2z)+O(z^{-2})$. On a compact subinterval the factor $\cos x$ stays positive, so substitution gives an $O(e^{2t})$ error with every fixed number of $x$ derivatives. This proves both limits. The signs of their vertical motions agree with Proposition 16.3.5 and reflection across the horizontal axis. This is the backward translator behavior discussed in [ BV11 ] , p. 7; the error bound here is derived from the exact inverse-hyperbolic-cosine expression. $\square$

title: 2.3 Radon representation from positive functionals
search_title: Radon representation from positive functionals
text: The examples of measures become useful in compactness arguments because one can construct a measure from limits of its integrals. We prove the positive Riesz representation theorem on an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, following [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 5, pp. 30–37. The elementary Caratheodory construction of a measure on the measurable sets of an outer measure is a background input. Metric separation and all regularity and representation steps used here are proved below. Definition 2.3.1 (A positive functional on compactly supported tests) . 9E4845BBA4ED A positive linear functional is a map $L:C_ c(U;\mathbb R)\to \mathbb R$ which is linear and satisfies $L(f)\geq 0$ whenever $f\geq 0$. Values are finite real numbers. No single bound $|L(f)|\leq C\| f\| _\infty $ for all supports is assumed. Positivity will instead give bounds on each fixed compact support. See [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 5.12 and Remark 5.13. Lemma 2.3.2 (Compact cutoffs and a finite partition of unity) . 065D9AC3265E If $K\subset U$ is compact and $O\subset U$ is open with $K\subset O$, there is $\eta \in C_ c(O)$, $0\leq \eta \leq 1$, equal to one on a neighborhood of $K$. If finitely many open sets $O_1,\ldots ,O_ N$ cover $K$, there are $\eta _ i\in C_ c(O_ i)$, $0\leq \eta _ i\leq 1$, whose sum is one on a neighborhood of $K$ and is at most one everywhere. Proof The empty-set cases are immediate. For the first assertion choose $\delta >0$ so that the closed $\delta $-neighborhood of $K$ is compact and lies in $O$. A continuous piecewise linear function of $\operatorname {dist}(x,K)$, equal to one for distance at most $\delta /2$ and zero for distance at least $\delta $, is the required cutoff. For the second assertion, cover $K$ by finitely many small balls whose closures each lie in one of the $O_ i$. Grouping their cutoffs gives nonnegative $\psi _ i\in C_ c(O_ i)$ with $S=\sum _ i\psi _ i>0$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Apply the first assertion to obtain $\chi \in C_ c(\{ S>0\} )$, equal to one near $K$ and between zero and one. Set $\eta _ i=\chi \psi _ i/S$ where $S>0$, and zero elsewhere. Its extension is continuous because $\operatorname {spt}\chi $ stays in $\{ S>0\} $. The sum equals $\chi $. This is the Euclidean version of [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 5.4 and Corollary 5.5. $\square$ Lemma 2.3.3 (Positivity gives continuity on a fixed support) . 059D87E3EFB0 If $L$ is positive, $K\subset U$ is compact, and $\eta \in C_ c(U)$ is nonnegative and at least one on $K$, then \[  |L(f)|\leq L(\eta )\| f\| _\infty \quad \text{for every }f\in C_ c(U)\text{ supported in }K.  \] Thus uniform convergence with a common compact support implies convergence of the functional values. Proof The pointwise inequalities $-\| f\| _\infty \eta \leq f\leq \| f\| _\infty \eta $ and positivity give the bound. Apply it to the difference of two functions for the continuity assertion. This is [ Sim18 ] , Remark 5.13. $\square$ Proposition 2.3.4 (The open-set mass associated with a positive functional) . D6FBFD2B5B8A For open $O\subset U$, put \[  m(O)=\sup \{ L(f):f\in C_ c(O),\  0\leq f\leq 1\} .  \] Then $m$ is monotone, $m(\varnothing )=0$, is countably subadditive on open sets, and is additive on disjoint open sets, allowing infinite values. The function \[  \mu ^*(A)=\inf \{ m(O):A\subset O\subset U,\  O\text{ open}\}   \] for arbitrary $A\subset U$ is an outer measure, equals $m$ on open sets, is finite on compact sets, and satisfies \[  \mu ^*(A\cup B)=\mu ^*(A)+\mu ^*(B) \quad \text{if }\operatorname {dist}(A,B)>0.  \] Proof Monotonicity and the empty-set assertion are immediate. If $O\subset \bigcup _ jO_ j$ and $f$ is admissible for $m(O)$, compactness of its support and Lemma 2.3.2 give a finite subordinate partition, with $f=\sum _ j\eta _ jf$. Therefore $L(f)\leq \sum _ jm(O_ j)$; take the supremum. For disjoint opens, finitely many admissible tests have sum at most one, so taking their separate suprema gives $m(\bigcup _ jO_ j)\geq \sum _{j=1}^ Nm(O_ j)$ for every finite $N$. This proves countable additivity on disjoint opens. The infimum definition is consistent on opens by monotonicity. To prove countable subadditivity of $\mu ^*$, the only nontrivial case has $\sum _ j\mu ^*(A_ j)<\infty $. Choose $O_ j\supset A_ j$ with $m(O_ j)\leq \mu ^*(A_ j)+\varepsilon 2^{-j}$, use open-set subadditivity, and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. For compact $K$, choose an open neighborhood $W$ with compact closure in $U$ and a cutoff $\eta \geq 1$ on $\overline W$. Every test for $m(W)$ is at most $\eta $, so $\mu ^*(K)\leq m(W)\leq L(\eta )<\infty $. Finally, if $A,B$ have positive distance, choose disjoint open neighborhoods $V_ A,V_ B$ of them. For every open $O\supset A\cup B$, \[  m(O)\geq m(O\cap V_ A)+m(O\cap V_ B)\geq \mu ^*(A)+\mu ^*(B).  \] Taking the infimum and using subadditivity proves the metric separation identity. This follows the construction in [ Sim18 ] , proof of Theorem 5.12. $\square$ Lemma 2.3.5 (Metric outer measures make Borel sets measurable) . 87BA9817395E Let $\mu ^*$ be an outer measure on a metric space, additive on pairs of sets at positive distance. Then every closed set, and hence every Borel set, is Caratheodory measurable. Proof Fix a closed set $F$ and a set $E$ with $\mu ^*(E)<\infty $. The empty and whole-space cases are immediate, so assume $F$ is nonempty and proper. Write $d(x)=\operatorname {dist}(x,F)$ and \[  A_ j=E\cap \{ 1/(j+1)<d\leq 1/j\} ,\qquad j\geq 1.  \] Any finite family of these annuli with indices of the same parity consists of sets separated from one another by positive distances, because $d$ is 1-Lipschitz. Their outer measures sum to at most $\mu ^*(E)$. Therefore $\sum _{j\geq 1}\mu ^*(A_ j)<\infty $, and the tails tend to zero. The part of $E\setminus F$ with $d>1/k$ is separated from $E\cap F$; hence \[  \mu ^*(E)\geq \mu ^*(E\cap F)+\mu ^*(E\cap \{ d>1/k\} ).  \] The latter set together with $\bigcup _{j\geq k}A_ j$ covers $E\setminus F$. Subadditivity and the vanishing tail now give $\mu ^*(E)\geq \mu ^*(E\cap F)+\mu ^*(E\setminus F)$. The reverse inequality is subadditivity. For $\mu ^*(E)=\infty $ the required greater-than-or-equal inequality is automatic. Thus $F$ is measurable. The Caratheodory measurable sets form a sigma algebra, so all Borel sets are measurable. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Theorem 1.15. $\square$ Proposition 2.3.6 (The constructed measure is Radon) . DCE16B3F3D66 The restriction of $\mu ^*$ from Proposition 2.3.4 to Borel sets is a Radon measure $\mu $. In particular, for every open $O\subset U$, \[  \mu (O)=\sup _{K\subset O,\  K\text{ compact}}\mu (K)=m(O).  \] Proof Lemma 2.3.5 gives a Borel measure, and Proposition 2.3.4 gives local finiteness and outer regularity. If $f\in C_ c(O)$, $0\leq f\leq 1$, with compact support $K$, then $L(f)\leq m(V)$ for every open $V\supset K$, so $L(f)\leq \mu (K)$. Taking the supremum in $f$ proves inner regularity on open sets; the opposite inequality is monotonicity. For a Borel set $A$ of finite measure, choose open $O\supset A$ with $\mu (O\setminus A)<\varepsilon $, compact $K\subset O$ with $\mu (O\setminus K)<\varepsilon $, and open $V\supset O\setminus A$ with $\mu (V)<2\varepsilon $. Then $K\setminus V$ is compact and contained in $A$, and $\mu (A\setminus (K\setminus V))<3\varepsilon $. Thus $A$ is inner regular. For arbitrary Borel $A$, exhaust $U$ by compact sets $K_ j$. The sets $A\cap K_ j$ have finite measure and increase to $A$, so their inner regularity and continuity from below give the general assertion. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Lemmas 5.7–5.9. $\square$ Theorem 2.3.7 (Positive Riesz representation on a Euclidean open set) . D8B4638B4814 For every positive linear functional $L:C_ c(U;\mathbb R)\to \mathbb R$ there is a unique Radon measure $\mu $ on $U$ such that \[  L(f)=\int _ U f\, d\mu \qquad (f\in C_ c(U;\mathbb R)).  \] Its values on open sets are given by $\mu (O)=\sup \{ L(\phi ):\phi \in C_ c(O),\  0\leq \phi \leq 1\} $. This is [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 5.12, specialized to a Euclidean open set. Proof Construct the Radon measure by Proposition 2.3.6 . First note that, for $0\leq h\leq 1$ with compact support, \[  L(h)\leq \mu (\{ h>0\} ).  \] Indeed $(h-\varepsilon )_+$ has compact support in the open set $\{ h>0\} $ and is bounded by one, while the difference from $h$ tends uniformly to zero on a common compact support. Lemma 2.3.3 gives the inequality upon taking the limit. For $f\geq 0$ with compact support, fix $\delta >0$ and an integer $N$ with $N\delta \geq \max f$. Set $h_ i=\min (1,(f-i\delta )_+/\delta )$ for $0\leq i<N$. Pointwise $f=\delta \sum _ i h_ i$. The upper bound just proved and the fact that $h_ i=1$ on $\{ f>(i+1)\delta \} $ give \[  \delta \sum _{i=0}^{N-1}\mu (\{ f>(i+1)\delta \} ) \leq L(f)\leq \delta \sum _{i=0}^{N-1}\mu (\{ f>i\delta \} ).  \] For the lower bound, every admissible test supported in that open superlevel set is at most $h_ i$. The same two sums bound $\int f\, d\mu $ by pointwise simple-function comparison. Their difference is at most $\delta \mu (\{ f>0\} )$, which tends to zero by local finiteness. Thus $L(f)=\int f\, d\mu $. Subtract positive and negative parts for signed $f$. Finally any representing Radon measure satisfies the displayed open-set formula: the upper bound is immediate, and cutoffs equal to one on compact subsets yield the reverse bound by inner regularity. Equal open-set masses and outer regularity imply equal Borel masses. This proves uniqueness. $\square$ Theorem 2.3.8 (Continuous compactly supported tests are dense in finite-power spaces) . 19396F96DC10 For any Radon measure $\mu $ on $U$ and $1\leq p<\infty $, $C_ c(U)$ is dense in $L^ p(\mu )$. The assertion concerns the completed measure as well, with functions identified almost everywhere. See [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 5.10. Proof Truncation of values and support, followed by approximation by simple functions, reduces the claim to $\mathbf1_ A$ with $\mu (A)<\infty $; a completed-measurable set can first be replaced by a Borel set modulo a null set. Choose compact $K\subset A$ and open $O\supset A$ such that $\mu (A\setminus K)<\varepsilon $ and $\mu (O\setminus A)<\varepsilon $. Lemma 2.3.2 gives $\phi \in C_ c(O)$, $0\leq \phi \leq 1$, equal to one on $K$. Then \[  \int |\mathbf1_ A-\phi |^ p\, d\mu \leq \mu (O\setminus K)<2\varepsilon .  \] Finite linear combinations approximate simple functions by the $L^ p$ triangle inequality. This proves the result. The finite-power assumption is essential to this approximation argument; no density in $L^\infty $ is asserted. $\square$

title: Definition 2.3.1 (A positive functional on compactly supported tests)
search_title: A positive functional on compactly supported tests
text: Definition 2.3.1 (A positive functional on compactly supported tests) . 9E4845BBA4ED A positive linear functional is a map $L:C_ c(U;\mathbb R)\to \mathbb R$ which is linear and satisfies $L(f)\geq 0$ whenever $f\geq 0$. Values are finite real numbers. No single bound $|L(f)|\leq C\| f\| _\infty $ for all supports is assumed. Positivity will instead give bounds on each fixed compact support. See [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 5.12 and Remark 5.13.

title: Lemma 2.3.2 (Compact cutoffs and a finite partition of unity)
search_title: Compact cutoffs and a finite partition of unity
text: Lemma 2.3.2 (Compact cutoffs and a finite partition of unity) . 065D9AC3265E If $K\subset U$ is compact and $O\subset U$ is open with $K\subset O$, there is $\eta \in C_ c(O)$, $0\leq \eta \leq 1$, equal to one on a neighborhood of $K$. If finitely many open sets $O_1,\ldots ,O_ N$ cover $K$, there are $\eta _ i\in C_ c(O_ i)$, $0\leq \eta _ i\leq 1$, whose sum is one on a neighborhood of $K$ and is at most one everywhere. Proof The empty-set cases are immediate. For the first assertion choose $\delta >0$ so that the closed $\delta $-neighborhood of $K$ is compact and lies in $O$. A continuous piecewise linear function of $\operatorname {dist}(x,K)$, equal to one for distance at most $\delta /2$ and zero for distance at least $\delta $, is the required cutoff. For the second assertion, cover $K$ by finitely many small balls whose closures each lie in one of the $O_ i$. Grouping their cutoffs gives nonnegative $\psi _ i\in C_ c(O_ i)$ with $S=\sum _ i\psi _ i>0$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Apply the first assertion to obtain $\chi \in C_ c(\{ S>0\} )$, equal to one near $K$ and between zero and one. Set $\eta _ i=\chi \psi _ i/S$ where $S>0$, and zero elsewhere. Its extension is continuous because $\operatorname {spt}\chi $ stays in $\{ S>0\} $. The sum equals $\chi $. This is the Euclidean version of [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 5.4 and Corollary 5.5. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.3.3 (Positivity gives continuity on a fixed support)
search_title: Positivity gives continuity on a fixed support
text: Lemma 2.3.3 (Positivity gives continuity on a fixed support) . 059D87E3EFB0 If $L$ is positive, $K\subset U$ is compact, and $\eta \in C_ c(U)$ is nonnegative and at least one on $K$, then \[  |L(f)|\leq L(\eta )\| f\| _\infty \quad \text{for every }f\in C_ c(U)\text{ supported in }K.  \] Thus uniform convergence with a common compact support implies convergence of the functional values. Proof The pointwise inequalities $-\| f\| _\infty \eta \leq f\leq \| f\| _\infty \eta $ and positivity give the bound. Apply it to the difference of two functions for the continuity assertion. This is [ Sim18 ] , Remark 5.13. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.3.4 (The open-set mass associated with a positive functional)
search_title: The open-set mass associated with a positive functional
text: Proposition 2.3.4 (The open-set mass associated with a positive functional) . D6FBFD2B5B8A For open $O\subset U$, put \[  m(O)=\sup \{ L(f):f\in C_ c(O),\  0\leq f\leq 1\} .  \] Then $m$ is monotone, $m(\varnothing )=0$, is countably subadditive on open sets, and is additive on disjoint open sets, allowing infinite values. The function \[  \mu ^*(A)=\inf \{ m(O):A\subset O\subset U,\  O\text{ open}\}   \] for arbitrary $A\subset U$ is an outer measure, equals $m$ on open sets, is finite on compact sets, and satisfies \[  \mu ^*(A\cup B)=\mu ^*(A)+\mu ^*(B) \quad \text{if }\operatorname {dist}(A,B)>0.  \] Proof Monotonicity and the empty-set assertion are immediate. If $O\subset \bigcup _ jO_ j$ and $f$ is admissible for $m(O)$, compactness of its support and Lemma 2.3.2 give a finite subordinate partition, with $f=\sum _ j\eta _ jf$. Therefore $L(f)\leq \sum _ jm(O_ j)$; take the supremum. For disjoint opens, finitely many admissible tests have sum at most one, so taking their separate suprema gives $m(\bigcup _ jO_ j)\geq \sum _{j=1}^ Nm(O_ j)$ for every finite $N$. This proves countable additivity on disjoint opens. The infimum definition is consistent on opens by monotonicity. To prove countable subadditivity of $\mu ^*$, the only nontrivial case has $\sum _ j\mu ^*(A_ j)<\infty $. Choose $O_ j\supset A_ j$ with $m(O_ j)\leq \mu ^*(A_ j)+\varepsilon 2^{-j}$, use open-set subadditivity, and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. For compact $K$, choose an open neighborhood $W$ with compact closure in $U$ and a cutoff $\eta \geq 1$ on $\overline W$. Every test for $m(W)$ is at most $\eta $, so $\mu ^*(K)\leq m(W)\leq L(\eta )<\infty $. Finally, if $A,B$ have positive distance, choose disjoint open neighborhoods $V_ A,V_ B$ of them. For every open $O\supset A\cup B$, \[  m(O)\geq m(O\cap V_ A)+m(O\cap V_ B)\geq \mu ^*(A)+\mu ^*(B).  \] Taking the infimum and using subadditivity proves the metric separation identity. This follows the construction in [ Sim18 ] , proof of Theorem 5.12. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.3.5 (Metric outer measures make Borel sets measurable)
search_title: Metric outer measures make Borel sets measurable
text: Lemma 2.3.5 (Metric outer measures make Borel sets measurable) . 87BA9817395E Let $\mu ^*$ be an outer measure on a metric space, additive on pairs of sets at positive distance. Then every closed set, and hence every Borel set, is Caratheodory measurable. Proof Fix a closed set $F$ and a set $E$ with $\mu ^*(E)<\infty $. The empty and whole-space cases are immediate, so assume $F$ is nonempty and proper. Write $d(x)=\operatorname {dist}(x,F)$ and \[  A_ j=E\cap \{ 1/(j+1)<d\leq 1/j\} ,\qquad j\geq 1.  \] Any finite family of these annuli with indices of the same parity consists of sets separated from one another by positive distances, because $d$ is 1-Lipschitz. Their outer measures sum to at most $\mu ^*(E)$. Therefore $\sum _{j\geq 1}\mu ^*(A_ j)<\infty $, and the tails tend to zero. The part of $E\setminus F$ with $d>1/k$ is separated from $E\cap F$; hence \[  \mu ^*(E)\geq \mu ^*(E\cap F)+\mu ^*(E\cap \{ d>1/k\} ).  \] The latter set together with $\bigcup _{j\geq k}A_ j$ covers $E\setminus F$. Subadditivity and the vanishing tail now give $\mu ^*(E)\geq \mu ^*(E\cap F)+\mu ^*(E\setminus F)$. The reverse inequality is subadditivity. For $\mu ^*(E)=\infty $ the required greater-than-or-equal inequality is automatic. Thus $F$ is measurable. The Caratheodory measurable sets form a sigma algebra, so all Borel sets are measurable. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Theorem 1.15. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.3.6 (The constructed measure is Radon)
search_title: The constructed measure is Radon
text: Proposition 2.3.6 (The constructed measure is Radon) . DCE16B3F3D66 The restriction of $\mu ^*$ from Proposition 2.3.4 to Borel sets is a Radon measure $\mu $. In particular, for every open $O\subset U$, \[  \mu (O)=\sup _{K\subset O,\  K\text{ compact}}\mu (K)=m(O).  \] Proof Lemma 2.3.5 gives a Borel measure, and Proposition 2.3.4 gives local finiteness and outer regularity. If $f\in C_ c(O)$, $0\leq f\leq 1$, with compact support $K$, then $L(f)\leq m(V)$ for every open $V\supset K$, so $L(f)\leq \mu (K)$. Taking the supremum in $f$ proves inner regularity on open sets; the opposite inequality is monotonicity. For a Borel set $A$ of finite measure, choose open $O\supset A$ with $\mu (O\setminus A)<\varepsilon $, compact $K\subset O$ with $\mu (O\setminus K)<\varepsilon $, and open $V\supset O\setminus A$ with $\mu (V)<2\varepsilon $. Then $K\setminus V$ is compact and contained in $A$, and $\mu (A\setminus (K\setminus V))<3\varepsilon $. Thus $A$ is inner regular. For arbitrary Borel $A$, exhaust $U$ by compact sets $K_ j$. The sets $A\cap K_ j$ have finite measure and increase to $A$, so their inner regularity and continuity from below give the general assertion. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Lemmas 5.7–5.9. $\square$

title: Theorem 2.3.7 (Positive Riesz representation on a Euclidean open set)
search_title: Positive Riesz representation on a Euclidean open set
text: Theorem 2.3.7 (Positive Riesz representation on a Euclidean open set) . D8B4638B4814 For every positive linear functional $L:C_ c(U;\mathbb R)\to \mathbb R$ there is a unique Radon measure $\mu $ on $U$ such that \[  L(f)=\int _ U f\, d\mu \qquad (f\in C_ c(U;\mathbb R)).  \] Its values on open sets are given by $\mu (O)=\sup \{ L(\phi ):\phi \in C_ c(O),\  0\leq \phi \leq 1\} $. This is [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 5.12, specialized to a Euclidean open set. Proof Construct the Radon measure by Proposition 2.3.6 . First note that, for $0\leq h\leq 1$ with compact support, \[  L(h)\leq \mu (\{ h>0\} ).  \] Indeed $(h-\varepsilon )_+$ has compact support in the open set $\{ h>0\} $ and is bounded by one, while the difference from $h$ tends uniformly to zero on a common compact support. Lemma 2.3.3 gives the inequality upon taking the limit. For $f\geq 0$ with compact support, fix $\delta >0$ and an integer $N$ with $N\delta \geq \max f$. Set $h_ i=\min (1,(f-i\delta )_+/\delta )$ for $0\leq i<N$. Pointwise $f=\delta \sum _ i h_ i$. The upper bound just proved and the fact that $h_ i=1$ on $\{ f>(i+1)\delta \} $ give \[  \delta \sum _{i=0}^{N-1}\mu (\{ f>(i+1)\delta \} ) \leq L(f)\leq \delta \sum _{i=0}^{N-1}\mu (\{ f>i\delta \} ).  \] For the lower bound, every admissible test supported in that open superlevel set is at most $h_ i$. The same two sums bound $\int f\, d\mu $ by pointwise simple-function comparison. Their difference is at most $\delta \mu (\{ f>0\} )$, which tends to zero by local finiteness. Thus $L(f)=\int f\, d\mu $. Subtract positive and negative parts for signed $f$. Finally any representing Radon measure satisfies the displayed open-set formula: the upper bound is immediate, and cutoffs equal to one on compact subsets yield the reverse bound by inner regularity. Equal open-set masses and outer regularity imply equal Borel masses. This proves uniqueness. $\square$

title: 2.4 Weak convergence, continuity sets, and tightness
search_title: Weak convergence, continuity sets, and tightness
section: 2.4 Weak convergence, continuity sets, and tightness
text: We now supply the compactness argument used throughout GMT and explain when weak convergence controls masses. All measures are nonnegative Radon measures on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ unless otherwise specified. The main source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 5, especially Theorem 5.15, pp. 38–39. The countable testing argument below uses the Euclidean setting explicitly. Examples 16.1.3 and 16.1.4 explain why the qualifications are needed. Lemma 2.4.1 (A countable family of compactly supported tests) . EBB2048864FA There are compact sets $K_ m\subset \operatorname {int}K_{m+1}\subset U$ exhausting $U$, and a countable family $\mathcal D\subset C_ c(U)$, such that every $f\in C_ c(U)$ supported in $K_ m$ is a uniform limit of members of $\mathcal D$ supported in $K_{m+1}$. Proof One may take $K_ m=\{ x\in U:|x|\leq m,\  \operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ n\setminus U)\geq 1/m\} $, with distance to the empty set interpreted as infinity. These are compact, lie in the interior of the next set, and their interiors cover $U$. Choose fixed cutoffs $0\leq \eta _ m\leq 1$, equal to one on $K_ m$, with support in $\operatorname {int}K_{m+1}$, using Lemma 2.3.2 . There is a countable family $\mathcal P$ of compactly supported continuous functions on $\mathbb R^ n$ dense for the uniform norm in $C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)$: use piecewise multilinear interpolation on dyadic grids, with finitely many nonzero rational vertex values. Uniform continuity controls interpolation error on sufficiently small cubes; approximation of the finitely many vertex values by rationals adds arbitrarily small uniform error. A function in $C_ c(U)$ extends continuously by zero to $\mathbb R^ n$. If its support is in $K_ m$, uniform approximants $q_ j\in \mathcal P$ give $\eta _ mq_ j\to \eta _ mf=f$, with all supports in $K_{m+1}$. The countable union $\mathcal D=\bigcup _ m\eta _ m\mathcal P$ has the asserted property. Empty initial compact sets cause no difficulty. $\square$ Lemma 2.4.2 (Diagonal extraction of a positive limit functional) . B9EF3BFBC186 Suppose $\sup _ j\mu _ j(K)<\infty $ for every compact $K\subset U$. There are a subsequence $\mu _{j_ k}$ and a positive linear functional $L:C_ c(U)\to \mathbb R$ with \[  \int f\, d\mu _{j_ k}\longrightarrow L(f)\qquad (f\in C_ c(U)).  \] Proof Enumerate the family $\mathcal D$ from Lemma 2.4.1 . For each of its functions the integrals form a bounded real sequence, because its support is compact. Successive subsequences and the diagonal construction give simultaneous convergence for every member of $\mathcal D$. For arbitrary $f$ supported in $K_ m$, approximate it uniformly by $g\in \mathcal D$ supported in $K_{m+1}$. If $M_ m=\sup _ j\mu _ j(K_{m+1})$, then \[  \left|\int f\, d\mu _{j_ k}-\int f\, d\mu _{j_\ell }\right| \leq 2M_ m\| f-g\| _\infty + \left|\int g\, d\mu _{j_ k}-\int g\, d\mu _{j_\ell }\right|.  \] First make the uniform error small and then take $k,\ell $ large. Thus the integrals of $f$ are Cauchy and define a finite limit $L(f)$. Limits preserve real linear combinations and nonnegativity. This proves the assertion. Sequential extraction here is justified by the countable tests, not merely by a compactness assertion in a possibly nonmetrizable dual space. $\square$ Proposition 2.4.3 (Upper semicontinuity on compact sets) . 5E1115A68860 If $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu $ in $U$, then \[  \limsup _ j\mu _ j(K)\leq \mu (K)  \] for every compact $K\subset U$. Proof By outer regularity and local finiteness, choose an open neighborhood $O$ of $K$ with compact closure in $U$ and $\mu (O\setminus K)<\varepsilon $. A cutoff $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ supported in $O$ and equal to one on $K$ gives \[  \limsup _ j\mu _ j(K)\leq \lim _ j\int \eta \, d\mu _ j =\int \eta \, d\mu \leq \mu (O)\leq \mu (K)+\varepsilon .  \] Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Compactness both permits the cutoff and makes all these integrals finite. Compare the open-set inequality in Proposition 2.1.4 . $\square$ Corollary 2.4.4 (Convergence of masses on continuity sets) . DDCA164F3208 If $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu $ in $U$ and $E\subset U$ is Borel with compact closure in $U$ and $\mu (\partial E)=0$, then $\mu _ j(E)\to \mu (E)$. In particular, for a fixed center $x\in U$, this holds for $E=B_ r(x)$ at all but countably many radii with $\overline B_ r(x)\subset U$. Proof Proposition 2.1.4 and Proposition 2.4.3 give \[  \mu (\operatorname {int}E)\leq \liminf _ j\mu _ j(E) \leq \limsup _ j\mu _ j(E)\leq \mu (\overline E).  \] The boundary hypothesis makes both endpoints equal to $\mu (E)$. For the ball statement, distinct centered spheres are disjoint. Inside any fixed compact ball of finite measure, only finitely many of them can have mass at least $1/k$ for a fixed positive integer $k$. Taking the union over $k$ and over a countable exhaustion of the admissible radii gives at most countably many exceptional spheres. $\square$ Definition 2.4.5 (Uniform tightness and bounded-continuous testing) . 9FBD8CC6ACC8 A sequence of finite Radon measures $\mu _ j$ on $U$ is uniformly tight if, for every $\varepsilon >0$, some compact $K\subset U$ satisfies $\sup _ j\mu _ j(U\setminus K)<\varepsilon $. Convergence against all $f\in C_ b(U)$, the bounded continuous functions, is called narrow convergence here. It is stronger than the compact-test convergence in Definition 2.1.2 ; the two agree on uniformly tight families with uniformly bounded total mass, as proved next. Theorem 2.4.6 (Tightness upgrades compact tests to bounded tests) . 51E7B8F93AB4 Suppose $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu $ in $U$, $\sup _ j\mu _ j(U)<\infty $, and the sequence is uniformly tight. Then $\mu $ is finite and $\mu _ j$ converge narrowly to $\mu $. In particular $\mu _ j(U)\to \mu (U)$; if all $\mu _ j$ are probability measures, so is $\mu $. The compact-test convention is that of [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 5.15; the additional tightness hypothesis here controls the tails, by the argument below. Proof The open-set lower-semicontinuity inequality gives $\mu (U)\leq \liminf _ j\mu _ j(U)<\infty $. Given $\varepsilon >0$, tightness supplies a compact set controlling all $\mu _ j$ tails; inner regularity of the finite measure $\mu $ supplies another compact set controlling its tail. Their union $K$ controls both. Choose $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ compactly supported and equal to one on $K$. For $f\in C_ b(U)$, the test $\eta f$ is compactly supported, while \[  \left|\int (1-\eta )f\, d\mu _ j\right| +\left|\int (1-\eta )f\, d\mu \right|\leq 2\varepsilon \| f\| _\infty .  \] Take the limit in the compactly supported part and then let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. The constant test $f=1$ gives convergence of total masses. In contrast, the escaping measures in Example 16.1.3 are not uniformly tight. $\square$ Corollary 2.4.7 (Sequential compactness for tight probability measures) . E6622953C8DE Every uniformly tight sequence of Radon probability measures on $U$ has a narrowly convergent subsequence whose limit is a Radon probability measure. Conversely, a narrowly convergent sequence of Radon probability measures is uniformly tight. Proof The local bounds required by Theorem 2.1.3 hold with upper bound one. Extract a compact-test limit and apply Theorem 2.4.6 . Conversely, suppose $\mu _ j$ converge narrowly to the probability measure $\mu $. Choose compact $K$ with $\mu (K)>1-\varepsilon $ and a cutoff $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ equal to one on $K$, with compact support $L$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $\int \eta \, d\mu _ j>1-2\varepsilon $, so $\mu _ j(U\setminus L)<2\varepsilon $. Each of the finitely many remaining probability measures has a compact set carrying all but $2\varepsilon $ of its mass by inner regularity. Adding those sets to $L$ gives a single compact set for the whole sequence. Letting the initial $\varepsilon $ be arbitrarily small proves tightness. $\square$ Proposition 2.4.8 (Smooth densities approximate any Radon measure locally) . 6D1B7D98305E Let $\mu $ be a Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ n$ and $0\leq \rho \in C_ c^\infty (B_1)$ with $\int \rho =1$. For $\varepsilon >0$ set \[  f_\varepsilon (x)=\int \varepsilon ^{-n}\rho ((x-y)/\varepsilon )\, d\mu (y), \qquad d\mu _\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon \, dx.  \] Then $f_\varepsilon $ is nonnegative and smooth, $\mu _\varepsilon $ is Radon, and $\mu _\varepsilon \rightharpoonup \mu $ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Finite total mass of $\mu $ is not required. Proof On a fixed compact set of $x$ values, every contributing $y$ lies in a fixed larger compact set. Local finiteness bounds the integrals of every derivative of the smooth kernel there, justifying differentiation under the integral and proving smoothness. For $\varphi \in C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)$, Fubini and a change of variables give \[  \int \varphi \, d\mu _\varepsilon =\int \left(\int \varphi (y+\varepsilon z)\rho (z)\, dz\right)d\mu (y).  \] The inner function converges uniformly to $\varphi (y)$ by uniform continuity. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, all these functions have support in the compact one-neighborhood of $\operatorname {spt}\varphi $, whose $\mu $ mass is finite. This proves convergence. Smooth locally bounded densities define Radon measures. The conclusion generalizes the concentration example and the diffuse Cantor approximations in Examples 16.1.2 and 16.1.12 . $\square$ Proposition 2.4.9 (Finite atomic measures also approximate locally) . EDC3E29B3DCC Every Radon measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb R^ n$ is a compact-test limit of finite nonnegative atomic measures. Consequently compact-test convergence alone preserves neither absolute continuity nor atomicity. Proof Partition the half-open cube $[-j,j)^ n$ into finitely many half-open cubes $Q$ of side $1/j$, and choose each cube center $x_ Q$. Define $\nu _ j=\sum _ Q\mu (Q)\delta _{x_ Q}$; local finiteness makes this a finite measure. For a test $\varphi $ supported in a compact $K$, sufficiently large outer cubes contain the compact one-neighborhood of $K$. Cubes contributing either to $\varphi (x_ Q)$ or to its $\mu $ integral lie in that neighborhood once $\sqrt n/j<1$. Thus \[  \left|\int \varphi \, d\nu _ j-\int \varphi \, d\mu \right| \leq \mu (K_1)\, \omega _\varphi (\sqrt n/j),  \] where $K_1=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 1\} $ and $\omega _\varphi $ is a modulus of continuity. This tends to zero. Taking Lebesgue measure as the limit gives non-atomic limits of atomic measures; Proposition 2.4.8 gives smooth-density approximations of singular limits. $\square$

section: 2.4 Weak convergence, continuity sets, and tightness
text: Corollary 2.4.4 (Convergence of masses on continuity sets) . DDCA164F3208 If $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu $ in $U$ and $E\subset U$ is Borel with compact closure in $U$ and $\mu (\partial E)=0$, then $\mu _ j(E)\to \mu (E)$. In particular, for a fixed center $x\in U$, this holds for $E=B_ r(x)$ at all but countably many radii with $\overline B_ r(x)\subset U$. Proof Proposition 2.1.4 and Proposition 2.4.3 give \[  \mu (\operatorname {int}E)\leq \liminf _ j\mu _ j(E) \leq \limsup _ j\mu _ j(E)\leq \mu (\overline E).  \] The boundary hypothesis makes both endpoints equal to $\mu (E)$. For the ball statement, distinct centered spheres are disjoint. Inside any fixed compact ball of finite measure, only finitely many of them can have mass at least $1/k$ for a fixed positive integer $k$. Taking the union over $k$ and over a countable exhaustion of the admissible radii gives at most countably many exceptional spheres. $\square$

title: Definition 2.4.5 (Uniform tightness and bounded-continuous testing)
search_title: Uniform tightness and bounded-continuous testing
section: 2.4 Weak convergence, continuity sets, and tightness
text: Definition 2.4.5 (Uniform tightness and bounded-continuous testing) . 9FBD8CC6ACC8 A sequence of finite Radon measures $\mu _ j$ on $U$ is uniformly tight if, for every $\varepsilon >0$, some compact $K\subset U$ satisfies $\sup _ j\mu _ j(U\setminus K)<\varepsilon $. Convergence against all $f\in C_ b(U)$, the bounded continuous functions, is called narrow convergence here. It is stronger than the compact-test convergence in Definition 2.1.2 ; the two agree on uniformly tight families with uniformly bounded total mass, as proved next.

title: Theorem 2.4.6 (Tightness upgrades compact tests to bounded tests)
search_title: Tightness upgrades compact tests to bounded tests
section: 2.4 Weak convergence, continuity sets, and tightness
text: Theorem 2.4.6 (Tightness upgrades compact tests to bounded tests) . 51E7B8F93AB4 Suppose $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu $ in $U$, $\sup _ j\mu _ j(U)<\infty $, and the sequence is uniformly tight. Then $\mu $ is finite and $\mu _ j$ converge narrowly to $\mu $. In particular $\mu _ j(U)\to \mu (U)$; if all $\mu _ j$ are probability measures, so is $\mu $. The compact-test convention is that of [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 5.15; the additional tightness hypothesis here controls the tails, by the argument below. Proof The open-set lower-semicontinuity inequality gives $\mu (U)\leq \liminf _ j\mu _ j(U)<\infty $. Given $\varepsilon >0$, tightness supplies a compact set controlling all $\mu _ j$ tails; inner regularity of the finite measure $\mu $ supplies another compact set controlling its tail. Their union $K$ controls both. Choose $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ compactly supported and equal to one on $K$. For $f\in C_ b(U)$, the test $\eta f$ is compactly supported, while \[  \left|\int (1-\eta )f\, d\mu _ j\right| +\left|\int (1-\eta )f\, d\mu \right|\leq 2\varepsilon \| f\| _\infty .  \] Take the limit in the compactly supported part and then let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. The constant test $f=1$ gives convergence of total masses. In contrast, the escaping measures in Example 16.1.3 are not uniformly tight. $\square$

title: Corollary 2.4.7 (Sequential compactness for tight probability measures)
search_title: Sequential compactness for tight probability measures
section: 2.4 Weak convergence, continuity sets, and tightness
text: Corollary 2.4.7 (Sequential compactness for tight probability measures) . E6622953C8DE Every uniformly tight sequence of Radon probability measures on $U$ has a narrowly convergent subsequence whose limit is a Radon probability measure. Conversely, a narrowly convergent sequence of Radon probability measures is uniformly tight. Proof The local bounds required by Theorem 2.1.3 hold with upper bound one. Extract a compact-test limit and apply Theorem 2.4.6 . Conversely, suppose $\mu _ j$ converge narrowly to the probability measure $\mu $. Choose compact $K$ with $\mu (K)>1-\varepsilon $ and a cutoff $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ equal to one on $K$, with compact support $L$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $\int \eta \, d\mu _ j>1-2\varepsilon $, so $\mu _ j(U\setminus L)<2\varepsilon $. Each of the finitely many remaining probability measures has a compact set carrying all but $2\varepsilon $ of its mass by inner regularity. Adding those sets to $L$ gives a single compact set for the whole sequence. Letting the initial $\varepsilon $ be arbitrarily small proves tightness. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.4.8 (Smooth densities approximate any Radon measure locally)
search_title: Smooth densities approximate any Radon measure locally
section: 2.4 Weak convergence, continuity sets, and tightness
text: Proposition 2.4.8 (Smooth densities approximate any Radon measure locally) . 6D1B7D98305E Let $\mu $ be a Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ n$ and $0\leq \rho \in C_ c^\infty (B_1)$ with $\int \rho =1$. For $\varepsilon >0$ set \[  f_\varepsilon (x)=\int \varepsilon ^{-n}\rho ((x-y)/\varepsilon )\, d\mu (y), \qquad d\mu _\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon \, dx.  \] Then $f_\varepsilon $ is nonnegative and smooth, $\mu _\varepsilon $ is Radon, and $\mu _\varepsilon \rightharpoonup \mu $ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Finite total mass of $\mu $ is not required. Proof On a fixed compact set of $x$ values, every contributing $y$ lies in a fixed larger compact set. Local finiteness bounds the integrals of every derivative of the smooth kernel there, justifying differentiation under the integral and proving smoothness. For $\varphi \in C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)$, Fubini and a change of variables give \[  \int \varphi \, d\mu _\varepsilon =\int \left(\int \varphi (y+\varepsilon z)\rho (z)\, dz\right)d\mu (y).  \] The inner function converges uniformly to $\varphi (y)$ by uniform continuity. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, all these functions have support in the compact one-neighborhood of $\operatorname {spt}\varphi $, whose $\mu $ mass is finite. This proves convergence. Smooth locally bounded densities define Radon measures. The conclusion generalizes the concentration example and the diffuse Cantor approximations in Examples 16.1.2 and 16.1.12 . $\square$

title: Proposition 2.4.9 (Finite atomic measures also approximate locally)
search_title: Finite atomic measures also approximate locally
section: 2.4 Weak convergence, continuity sets, and tightness
text: Proposition 2.4.9 (Finite atomic measures also approximate locally) . EDC3E29B3DCC Every Radon measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb R^ n$ is a compact-test limit of finite nonnegative atomic measures. Consequently compact-test convergence alone preserves neither absolute continuity nor atomicity. Proof Partition the half-open cube $[-j,j)^ n$ into finitely many half-open cubes $Q$ of side $1/j$, and choose each cube center $x_ Q$. Define $\nu _ j=\sum _ Q\mu (Q)\delta _{x_ Q}$; local finiteness makes this a finite measure. For a test $\varphi $ supported in a compact $K$, sufficiently large outer cubes contain the compact one-neighborhood of $K$. Cubes contributing either to $\varphi (x_ Q)$ or to its $\mu $ integral lie in that neighborhood once $\sqrt n/j<1$. Thus \[  \left|\int \varphi \, d\nu _ j-\int \varphi \, d\mu \right| \leq \mu (K_1)\, \omega _\varphi (\sqrt n/j),  \] where $K_1=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 1\} $ and $\omega _\varphi $ is a modulus of continuity. This tends to zero. Taking Lebesgue measure as the limit gives non-atomic limits of atomic measures; Proposition 2.4.8 gives smooth-density approximations of singular limits. $\square$

section: 2.5 Covering, maximal estimates, and Lebesgue points
text:
Small-ball averages recover a function almost everywhere, but can behave very differently on the support of a singular measure. We prove the Euclidean Lebesgue-measure statements directly from a covering argument. The source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Lemma 3.4 and Sections 3–4, printed pp. 15–24. Differentiation relative to an arbitrary Radon measure requires additional covering theory and is not asserted here. Balls in this section are open. Lemma 2.5.1 (Fivefold covering for a bounded family of Euclidean balls) . 9B745ADFD001 Let $\mathcal B$ be a family of balls of positive radii in $\mathbb R^ n$, with bounded centers and uniformly bounded radii. There is a finite or countable pairwise disjoint subfamily $B_ j=B_{r_ j}(x_ j)$ such that \[   igcup _{B\in \mathcal B}B\subset  igcup _ j B_{5r_ j}(x_ j).  \] Moreover every original ball intersects a selected ball whose radius is at least half its own radius. This is a bounded Euclidean version of [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 3.4. Proof If no balls remain, stop. Otherwise select a remaining ball whose radius is greater than half the supremum of the remaining radii, and discard all remaining balls intersecting it. Continue. The selected balls are disjoint and lie in a fixed bounded region. If the process is infinite, their volumes have finite sum, so their radii tend to zero. An original ball of radius $r>0$ cannot remain forever: while it remains, every selected radius is greater than $r/2$, contradicting that limit. Thus it is selected or discarded at some step. If it intersects $B_{r_ j}(x_ j)$ at that step, its radius is at most $2r_ j$, so each of its points lies within distance $r_ j+2r\leq 5r_ j$ of $x_ j$. This proves both assertions, with the open-ball inequalities giving containment in the open dilation. $\square$ Definition 2.5.2 (Centered maximal functions) . u (B_{r_ j}(x_ j)) \leq  rac{5^ n}{\lambda }
u (\mathbb R^ n).  \] Let $R	o \infty $. Letting $\lambda 	o \infty $ then shows that the infinite-value set is null. If the measure is zero, the assertions are immediate. This is the maximal-estimate application of the covering principle in [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 3.4. $\square$ Theorem 2.5.4 (A strong maximal bound above the endpoint) . 4A2AA689E78F For $1<p<\infty $ and $f\in L^ p(\mathbb R^ n)$, \[  \| Mf\| _ p^ p\leq  rac{2^ p5^ n p}{p-1}\| f\| _ p^ p.  \] This consequence of the covering estimate associated with [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 3.4, is proved here by integrating distribution functions. Proof Fix $\lambda >0$. Split $|f|$ into the part bounded by $\lambda /2$ and the tail $g_\lambda =|f|\mathbf1_{\{ |f|>\lambda /2\} }$. The first part has maximal function at most $\lambda /2$. The tail is integrable since $|f|\leq (\lambda /2)^{1-p}|f|^ p$ on its support. Subadditivity and Proposition 2.5.3 give \[  \mathcal L^ n(\{ Mf>\lambda \} ) \leq  rac{2\cdot 5^ n}{\lambda }\int _{\{ |f|>\lambda /2\} }|f|\, dx.  \] The identity $a^ p=\int _0^ a p\lambda ^{p-1}\, d\lambda $, followed by Tonelli's theorem, gives \[  \int (Mf)^ p\leq 2\cdot 5^ n p\int |f(x)| \left(\int _0^{2|f(x)|}\lambda ^{p-2}\, d\lambda ight)dx.  \] Evaluation of the inner integral proves the claim. Tonelli applies before finiteness is known because the integrands are nonnegative. Local integrability of $f$, needed to define $Mf$, follows from Holder's inequality on bounded sets. $\square$ Definition 2.5.5 (Lebesgue points) . 6B471E3298DE For a finite-valued representative of $f\in L^1_{m loc}(U)$, a point $x\in U$ is a Lebesgue point if \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{1}{\omega _ n r^ n} \int _{B_ r(x)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, dy=0,  \] with radii small enough that the ball lies in $U$. Altering values on a null set can change individual Lebesgue points but not the almost-everywhere conclusion below. This is the absolute-oscillation form of differentiation associated with [ Sim18 ] , Corollary 4.10. Theorem 2.5.6 (Lebesgue differentiation with absolute oscillation) . 2CA07074F4A7 If $f\in L^1_{m loc}(U)$, almost every point of $U$ is a Lebesgue point of any representative finite almost everywhere. Consequently \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{1}{\omega _ n r^ n}\int _{B_ r(x)}f(y)\, dy=f(x) \quad 	ext{for almost every }x\in U.  \] Compare [ Sim18 ] , Corollary 4.10. Here the proof is restricted to Lebesgue measure on a Euclidean open set. Proof First take $U=\mathbb R^ n$ and $f\in L^1$. Denote the limsup in Definition 2.5.5 by $Df(x)$. For $g\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)$, continuity gives $Dg=0$, so the triangle inequality implies \[  Df(x)\leq M(f-g)(x)+|f(x)-g(x)|.  \] The weak maximal estimate and Chebyshev's inequality yield, for $a>0$, \[  \mathcal L^ n(\{ Df>2a\} )\leq  rac{5^ n+1}{a}\| f-g\| _1.  \] These sets are measurable: for each point with finite $f(x)$ the ball integrals vary continuously with the positive radius, so the limsup can be taken over rational radii; joint measurability follows from integration of the measurable integrand. By Theorem 2.3.8 , choose $g$ with arbitrarily small $L^1$ error. Thus $\{ Df>2a\} $ is null for each $a>0$. A countable sequence $a\downarrow 0$ proves $Df=0$ almost everywhere. For the local assertion, choose compact sets $K_ m$ with $K_ m\subset \operatorname {int}K_{m+1}$ exhausting $U$. Multiply $f$ by a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $K_ m$, and extend by zero outside $U$. This gives an $L^1(\mathbb R^ n)$ function agreeing with $f$ near $K_ m$. The global result applies on each $K_ m$; their countable union gives the local assertion. Finally the absolute value of the difference between the average of $f$ and $f(x)$ is bounded by the average absolute oscillation. $\square$ Corollary 2.5.7 (The Lebesgue density theorem for measurable sets) . C69197CB30B1 For every Lebesgue measurable $E\subset \mathbb R^ n$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{\mathcal L^ n(E\cap B_ r(x))}{\omega _ n r^ n} =\mathbf1_ E(x)\quad 	ext{for almost every }x\in \mathbb R^ n.  \] Neither finite total measure nor a regular boundary is assumed. See [ Sim18 ] , Corollary 3.10. Proof The indicator belongs to $L^1_{m loc}$. Apply Theorem 2.5.6 to it. At a point in $E$, its absolute oscillation average is the complementary volume fraction; outside $E$, it is the volume fraction of $E$ itself. The conclusion is almost everywhere in ambient Lebesgue measure, and makes no assertion at every topological boundary point. $\square$ Proposition 2.5.8 (Approximate continuity at a Lebesgue point) . 6196A7F42C62 If $x$ is a Lebesgue point of $f$ and $a>0$, then \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}  rac{\mathcal L^ n(\{ y\in B_ r(x):|f(y)-f(x)|>a\} )}{\omega _ n r^ n}=0.  \] Proof Chebyshev's inequality bounds the displayed fraction by $a^{-1}$ times the average of $|f(y)-f(x)|$ over the ball. That average tends to zero. Thus values far from $f(x)$ occupy a vanishing fraction of small balls; ordinary pointwise continuity is a stronger condition. $\square$ Proposition 2.5.9 (Mollifiers converge at every Lebesgue point) . C54A732E0D36 Let $f\in L^1_{m loc}(\mathbb R^ n)$ and let $ho $ be a bounded measurable function supported in $B_1$, with $\int ho =1$. Put $ho _\varepsilon (z)=\varepsilon ^{-n}ho (z/\varepsilon )$. At every Lebesgue point $x$ of $f$, \[  (ho _\varepsilon *f)(x)\longrightarrow f(x).  \] Nonnegativity and smoothness of $ho $ are not needed for this pointwise assertion. Proof Subtract $f(x)\int ho _\varepsilon =f(x)$ from the convolution and estimate its absolute value by \[  \| ho \| _\infty \varepsilon ^{-n} \int _{B_\varepsilon (x)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, dy.  \] This is $\omega _ n\| ho \| _\infty $ times a quantity tending to zero. The smooth-density approximation of measures in Proposition 2.4.8 concerns compact-test convergence; the present assertion describes values of mollified functions at individual Lebesgue points. $\square$ Proposition 2.5.10 (A singular measure has zero ambient density almost everywhere) . 752D2F6CE2C7 Let $
u $ be a nonnegative Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ n$ singular with respect to $\mathcal L^ n$. Then \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{
u (B_ r(x))}{\omega _ n r^ n}=0 \quad 	ext{for }\mathcal L^ n	ext{-almost every }x.  \] This is a special case of the upper-density conclusions in [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 3.8 and Remark 3.9. Proof First assume $
u $ is finite, and choose a Borel null set $N$ carrying all its mass. Given $\varepsilon >0$, inner regularity gives compact $K\subset N$ with $
u (\mathbb R^ n\setminus K)<\varepsilon $. For $x
otin K$, all sufficiently small balls avoid $K$, so the upper density of $
u $ at $x$ is at most $M(
u \llcorner (\mathbb R^ n\setminus K))(x)$. Proposition 2.5.3 implies that the set where this upper density exceeds $a>0$ has Lebesgue measure at most $5^ n\varepsilon /a$, since $K$ is null. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and then take countably many $a\downarrow 0$. For locally finite $
u $, apply the finite result to its restriction to $B_{m+1}(0)$ and consider points of $B_ m(0)$. Restriction does not change sufficiently small balls there. Taking the union over positive integers $m$ proves the assertion. Restrictions to these Borel sets remain Radon measures. $\square$ Corollary 2.5.11 (Ball densities identify an absolutely continuous part) . u $ with $0\leq f\in L^1_{m loc}(\mathbb R^ n)$ and $
u \perp \mathcal L^ n$. Then \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{\mu (B_ r(x))}{\omega _ n r^ n}=f(x) \quad 	ext{for }\mathcal L^ n	ext{-almost every }x.  \] Proof Add the limits supplied by Theorem 2.5.6 and Proposition 2.5.10 , outside the union of their null exceptional sets. The decomposition is a hypothesis of this statement; existence of the Lebesgue decomposition and the Radon–Nikodym theorem are not proved by this argument. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Section 4, especially Theorem 4.18. $\square$ Example 2.5.12 (The maximal operator need not preserve integrability) . 798D622C77F0 Let $f=\mathbf1_{B_1(0)}$ on $\mathbb R^ n$. Then $f\in L^1$ but $Mf
otin L^1$. Proof For $|x|\geq 2$, the ball $B_{|x|+1}(x)$ contains $B_1(0)$, so \[  Mf(x)\geq (|x|+1)^{-n}\geq (3|x|/2)^{-n}.  \] The integral of $|x|^{-n}$ over $\{ |x|\geq 2\} $ diverges: polar coordinates reduce it to a positive constant times $\int _2^\infty r^{-1}\, dr$. This separates the weak estimate in Proposition 2.5.3 from the strong estimates for $p>1$ in Theorem 2.5.4 . $\square$

section: 2.5 Covering, maximal estimates, and Lebesgue points
text: Corollary 2.5.7 (The Lebesgue density theorem for measurable sets) . C69197CB30B1 For every Lebesgue measurable $E\subset \mathbb R^ n$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mathcal L^ n(E\cap B_ r(x))}{\omega _ n r^ n} =\mathbf1_ E(x)\quad \text{for almost every }x\in \mathbb R^ n.  \] Neither finite total measure nor a regular boundary is assumed. See [ Sim18 ] , Corollary 3.10. Proof The indicator belongs to $L^1_{\rm loc}$. Apply Theorem 2.5.6 to it. At a point in $E$, its absolute oscillation average is the complementary volume fraction; outside $E$, it is the volume fraction of $E$ itself. The conclusion is almost everywhere in ambient Lebesgue measure, and makes no assertion at every topological boundary point. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.5.8 (Approximate continuity at a Lebesgue point)
search_title: Approximate continuity at a Lebesgue point
section: 2.5 Covering, maximal estimates, and Lebesgue points
text: Proposition 2.5.8 (Approximate continuity at a Lebesgue point) . 6196A7F42C62 If $x$ is a Lebesgue point of $f$ and $a>0$, then \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} \frac{\mathcal L^ n(\{ y\in B_ r(x):|f(y)-f(x)|>a\} )}{\omega _ n r^ n}=0.  \] Proof Chebyshev's inequality bounds the displayed fraction by $a^{-1}$ times the average of $|f(y)-f(x)|$ over the ball. That average tends to zero. Thus values far from $f(x)$ occupy a vanishing fraction of small balls; ordinary pointwise continuity is a stronger condition. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.5.9 (Mollifiers converge at every Lebesgue point)
search_title: Mollifiers converge at every Lebesgue point
section: 2.5 Covering, maximal estimates, and Lebesgue points
text: Proposition 2.5.9 (Mollifiers converge at every Lebesgue point) . C54A732E0D36 Let $f\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^ n)$ and let $\rho $ be a bounded measurable function supported in $B_1$, with $\int \rho =1$. Put $\rho _\varepsilon (z)=\varepsilon ^{-n}\rho (z/\varepsilon )$. At every Lebesgue point $x$ of $f$, \[  (\rho _\varepsilon *f)(x)\longrightarrow f(x).  \] Nonnegativity and smoothness of $\rho $ are not needed for this pointwise assertion. Proof Subtract $f(x)\int \rho _\varepsilon =f(x)$ from the convolution and estimate its absolute value by \[  \| \rho \| _\infty \varepsilon ^{-n} \int _{B_\varepsilon (x)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, dy.  \] This is $\omega _ n\| \rho \| _\infty $ times a quantity tending to zero. The smooth-density approximation of measures in Proposition 2.4.8 concerns compact-test convergence; the present assertion describes values of mollified functions at individual Lebesgue points. $\square$

Proposition 2.5.10 (A singular measure has zero ambient density almost everywhere) . 752D2F6CE2C7 Let $
u $ be a nonnegative Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ n$ singular with respect to $\mathcal L^ n$. Then \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{
u (B_ r(x))}{\omega _ n r^ n}=0 \quad 	ext{for }\mathcal L^ n	ext{-almost every }x.  \] This is a special case of the upper-density conclusions in [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 3.8 and Remark 3.9. Proof First assume $
u $ is finite, and choose a Borel null set $N$ carrying all its mass. Given $\varepsilon >0$, inner regularity gives compact $K\subset N$ with $
u (\mathbb R^ n\setminus K)<\varepsilon $. For $x
otin K$, all sufficiently small balls avoid $K$, so the upper density of $
u $ at $x$ is at most $M(
u \llcorner (\mathbb R^ n\setminus K))(x)$. Proposition 2.5.3 implies that the set where this upper density exceeds $a>0$ has Lebesgue measure at most $5^ n\varepsilon /a$, since $K$ is null. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and then take countably many $a\downarrow 0$. For locally finite $
u $, apply the finite result to its restriction to $B_{m+1}(0)$ and consider points of $B_ m(0)$. Restriction does not change sufficiently small balls there. Taking the union over positive integers $m$ proves the assertion. Restrictions to these Borel sets remain Radon measures. $\square$

title: Corollary 2.5.11 (Ball densities identify an absolutely continuous part)
