text: Corollary 2.5.11 (Ball densities identify an absolutely continuous part) . E5945F5D2962 Suppose a nonnegative Radon measure is written $\mu =f\, dx+\nu $ with $0\leq f\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^ n)$ and $\nu \perp \mathcal L^ n$. Then \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mu (B_ r(x))}{\omega _ n r^ n}=f(x) \quad \text{for }\mathcal L^ n\text{-almost every }x.  \] Proof Add the limits supplied by Theorem 2.5.6 and Proposition 2.5.10 , outside the union of their null exceptional sets. The decomposition is a hypothesis of this statement; existence of the Lebesgue decomposition and the Radon–Nikodym theorem are not proved by this argument. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Section 4, especially Theorem 4.18. $\square$

title: Example 2.5.12 (The maximal operator need not preserve integrability)

section: 2.5 Covering, maximal estimates, and Lebesgue points
text: Example 2.5.12 (The maximal operator need not preserve integrability) . 798D622C77F0 Let $f=\mathbf1_{B_1(0)}$ on $\mathbb R^ n$. Then $f\in L^1$ but $Mf\notin L^1$. Proof For $|x|\geq 2$, the ball $B_{|x|+1}(x)$ contains $B_1(0)$, so \[  Mf(x)\geq (|x|+1)^{-n}\geq (3|x|/2)^{-n}.  \] The integral of $|x|^{-n}$ over $\{ |x|\geq 2\} $ diverges: polar coordinates reduce it to a positive constant times $\int _2^\infty r^{-1}\, dr$. This separates the weak estimate in Proposition 2.5.3 from the strong estimates for $p>1$ in Theorem 2.5.4 . $\square$

title: 3.4 Lipschitz extension and almost-everywhere differentiation
search_title: Lipschitz extension and almost-everywhere differentiation
text: This section develops the analytic input for rectifiable parametrizations. The source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 1, pp. 43–46. The one-variable fundamental theorem for absolutely continuous functions is a background input: such functions have an integrable derivative almost everywhere and are recovered by integrating it. Fubini and dominated convergence are also used explicitly. The many-variable differentiability argument is supplied below. Definition 3.4.1 (Lipschitz constants and local Lipschitz regularity) . 8407129C252B A map $f:X\to Y$ between metric spaces is $L$-Lipschitz if $d_ Y(f(x),f(y))\leq Ld_ X(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$. Its least such constant is $\operatorname {Lip}f$. On a Euclidean open set, locally Lipschitz means every point has a neighborhood on which some finite constant works. The local constants need not be uniformly bounded on the whole open set. See [ Sim18 ] , equation (1.1), p. 43. Proposition 3.4.2 (Scalar Lipschitz extension by cones) . B50E35CF5709 Let $A$ be a nonempty subset of a metric space $X$, and let $f:A\to \mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz. Then \[  F(x)=\inf _{a\in A}\{ f(a)+Ld(x,a)\}   \] is finite, is $L$-Lipschitz on $X$, and agrees with $f$ on $A$. If $M=\sup _ A|f|<\infty $, truncating $F$ to $[-M,M]$ gives an extension with the same Lipschitz bound and the same supremum norm as $f$. This is [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 1.2, p. 44. Proof Fix $a_0\in A$. The triangle inequality and the Lipschitz bound give \[  f(a_0)-Ld(x,a_0)\leq f(a)+Ld(x,a)  \] for every $a\in A$, while the candidate $a=a_0$ gives a finite upper bound for the infimum. If $x\in A$, every candidate is at least $f(x)$ and $a=x$ gives equality. For any $x,y$, each candidate satisfies $f(a)+Ld(x,a)\leq f(a)+Ld(y,a)+Ld(x,y)$. Take infima and exchange $x,y$ to prove the Lipschitz bound. Scalar truncation is 1-Lipschitz and fixes all values on $A$. Agreement on $A$ gives equality, rather than just an upper bound, of the supremum norms. No vector-valued extension with the identical constant is asserted by this scalar formula. $\square$ Lemma 3.4.3 (Lipschitz functions on lines are absolutely continuous) . B908FEC6A058 An $L$-Lipschitz real function on an interval is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval, is differentiable almost everywhere, and its derivative has absolute value at most $L$. A locally Lipschitz real function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^ m$ therefore has directional derivatives in any one fixed direction at almost every point locally. Proof For finitely many disjoint subintervals $(a_ j,b_ j)$, the sum of the absolute increments is at most $L\sum _ j(b_ j-a_ j)$. This is the definition of absolute continuity. The one-variable fundamental theorem gives almost-everywhere differentiability, and each difference quotient is bounded by $L$. For the higher-dimensional assertion, restrict to a box lying in a neighborhood with a fixed Lipschitz constant, rotate the box to the chosen direction, and apply the one-dimensional assertion on its parallel lines. Fubini gives a null exceptional set in the box. Countably many such local boxes cover the domain. The nondifferentiability set is measurable since the limsup and liminf of difference quotients may be taken along rational increments. This is the line argument in [ Sim18 ] , proof of Theorem 1.4, p. 45. $\square$ Lemma 3.4.4 (Vanishing distribution tests determine a locally integrable function) . 7737EDA4D935 If $h\in L^1_{\rm loc}(U)$ and $\int _ Uh\phi =0$ for every $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$, then $h=0$ almost everywhere. Proof Fix a smooth nonnegative mollifier of integral one. At a point $x$ whose distance from the complement of $U$ exceeds $\varepsilon $, the function $y\mapsto \rho _\varepsilon (x-y)$ is an admissible test, so the local mollification is zero. At almost every point, Theorem 2.5.6 and Proposition 2.5.9 , localized inside $U$, say that these mollifications tend to $h(x)$. Thus $h$ vanishes almost everywhere. $\square$ Lemma 3.4.5 (Directional derivatives are linear almost everywhere in each fixed direction) . 3FD822798C95 Suppose $f:U\to \mathbb R$ is locally Lipschitz, and put $g=(\partial _1f,\ldots ,\partial _ mf)$ where the coordinate derivatives exist, giving them arbitrary values on the null exceptional set. Then $g\in L^\infty _{\rm loc}(U;\mathbb R^ m)$. For each fixed unit vector $v$, the directional derivative $D_ vf$ exists almost everywhere and equals $v\cdot g$ almost everywhere. The exceptional set in this assertion may depend on $v$. Proof Existence and local bounds follow from Lemma 3.4.3 . If $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$, small difference quotients have a common compact support after multiplication by $\phi $ and are uniformly bounded there by local Lipschitz constants. Translation and dominated convergence give \[  \int D_ vf\, \phi =-\int f\, D_ v\phi .  \] Use the same identity for the coordinate directions and $D_ v\phi =\sum _ iv_ i\partial _ i\phi $ to obtain $\int (D_ vf-v\cdot g)\phi =0$. Lemma 3.4.4 proves the claimed equality. Localizing the test to finitely many small neighborhoods justifies the bound when no single Lipschitz constant has been specified globally. Compare [ Sim18 ] , proof of Theorem 1.4, equations (2)–(4), p. 45. $\square$ Lemma 3.4.6 (A finite angular net upgrades directional limits) . 0A24DB832853 Let $f$ be $L$-Lipschitz near $x\in \mathbb R^ m$. Suppose $a\in \mathbb R^ m$ and a dense set $D\subset S^{m-1}$ satisfy \[  \lim _{t\to 0}\frac{f(x+tv)-f(x)}t=a\cdot v\qquad (v\in D).  \] Then $f$ is differentiable at $x$ with derivative $h\mapsto a\cdot h$, and $|a|\leq L$. Proof The directional difference quotients are bounded by $L$. Taking limits on the dense set and then using continuity in $v$ gives $|a|\leq L$. Put $Q(v,t)=(f(x+tv)-f(x))/t-a\cdot v$. For fixed nonzero small $t$, \[  |Q(v,t)-Q(w,t)|\leq (L+|a|)|v-w|\leq 2L|v-w|.  \] Given $\eta >0$, compactness of the sphere supplies a finite $\eta $-net $v_1,\ldots ,v_ N$ from $D$. For all sufficiently small $|t|$, every $|Q(v_ i,t)|<\eta $. Thus $\sup _ v|Q(v,t)|\leq (2L+1)\eta $. Let $\eta \downarrow 0$ and write an arbitrary nonzero increment as $h=|h|v$. The resulting uniform estimate is exactly differentiability. This is the finite-net step in [ Sim18 ] , p. 46. $\square$ Proposition 3.4.7 (Smooth approximation preserves a scalar Lipschitz bound) . D281915E3D7D Let $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz, and let $\rho \in C_ c^\infty (B_1)$ be nonnegative with integral one. Its mollifications satisfy \[  f_\varepsilon \in C^\infty ,\qquad |f_\varepsilon -f|\leq L\varepsilon \int |z|\rho (z)\, dz, \qquad \operatorname {Lip}f_\varepsilon \leq L.  \] Moreover $Df_\varepsilon \to Df$ almost everywhere, with the derivative interpreted by Theorem 3.1.2 . Proof The kernel has compact support, so local integrability suffices for smoothness. Write $f_\varepsilon (x)=\int f(x-\varepsilon z)\rho (z)\, dz$ and apply the Lipschitz inequality, first to $x$ and $x-\varepsilon z$ and then to $x-\varepsilon z$ and $y-\varepsilon z$. This gives both bounds. The integration-by-parts identity in Lemma 3.4.5 shows that $\partial _ i f_\varepsilon =\rho _\varepsilon *\partial _ i f$. Lebesgue differentiation and convergence at Lebesgue points apply to these locally bounded weak derivatives. The coordinate limits agree with the derivative from Rademacher almost everywhere. The Lipschitz bound alone does not imply convergence of derivatives at every point. $\square$ Example 3.4.8 (All directional derivatives need not give differentiability) . DF295D29EE84 Define $f(0,0)=0$ and $f(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ away from the origin. Then $f$ is globally Lipschitz and every directional derivative at zero exists, but $f$ is not differentiable there. Proof Away from zero, \[  f_ x=\frac{x^4+3x^2y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2},\qquad f_ y=\frac{-2x^3y}{(x^2+y^2)^2}.  \] These derivatives are bounded uniformly. Integrating the gradient on a segment gives a uniform Lipschitz bound if the segment avoids zero. If it passes through zero, split the segment and use continuity at zero, which follows from $|f(x,y)|\leq \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. Homogeneity gives $D_ vf(0)=v_1^3/(v_1^2+v_2^2)$ for every nonzero direction $v$. The coordinate derivatives are 1 and 0, so a derivative would have to be $(h_1,h_2)\mapsto h_1$. At $v=(1,1)$ the directional derivative is $1/2$, not 1. The directional values fail the linearity hypothesis of Lemma 3.4.6 . $\square$

title: 7.14 Euclidean Sobolev inequalities and their endpoints
search_title: Euclidean Sobolev inequalities and their endpoints
section: 7.14 Euclidean Sobolev inequalities and their endpoints
text: The local estimates for elliptic equations use an integrability gain that comes from Euclidean geometry. We prove that input here, starting with iterated Holder inequalities. The source is [ SimonPDE ] , Lecture 17, Lemma 2 and Corollary 1, printed pp. 200–202. Throughout, $n\geq 2$ and $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega )$ denotes the closure of $C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ in the $W^{1,p}$ norm. No regularity of the open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$ is required by that definition or by the zero-boundary inequalities below. Basic completion, weak derivatives, and Holder and Tonelli inequalities are background tools. Lemma 7.14.1 (An iterated Holder inequality for coordinate projections) . 56D0A07041F8 For $i=1,\ldots ,n$, let $F_ i$ be a nonnegative integrable function of the $n-1$ coordinates $\widehat x_ i$ obtained by omitting $x_ i$. Then \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ n}\prod _{i=1}^ n F_ i(\widehat x_ i)^{1/(n-1)}\, dx \leq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left(\int _{\mathbb R^{n-1}}F_ i\right)^{1/(n-1)}.  \] Proof For $n=2$ this is the product identity from Tonelli. Suppose it is known in dimension $n-1$. Integrate in $x_ n$ first and apply Holder to the first $n-1$ factors, with all exponents equal to $n-1$. Put $G_ i(\widehat x_ i,\widehat x_ n)=\int _{\mathbb R}F_ i(\widehat x_ i)\, dx_ n$ for $i<n$, where the argument of $G_ i$ consists of the remaining $n-2$ coordinates. The integral in the statement is at most \[  \int _{\mathbb R^{n-1}}F_ n(x')^{1/(n-1)} \prod _{i<n}G_ i(\widehat x_ i,\widehat x_ n)^{1/(n-1)}\, dx'.  \] Holder with exponents $n-1$ and $(n-1)/(n-2)$ bounds this by \[  \| F_ n\| _1^{1/(n-1)} \left(\int _{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\prod _{i<n}G_ i^{1/(n-2)}\, dx'\right)^{(n-2)/(n-1)}.  \] Apply the induction hypothesis to the integral and use $\| G_ i\| _1=\| F_ i\| _1$. This gives the result. Zero factors are immediate; truncation to bounded functions on bounded boxes and monotone convergence justify the argument without any initial finiteness assumption on the product integral. $\square$ Theorem 7.14.2 (The first-power Sobolev inequality) . 3E1913FF6CC7 For every $u\in C_ c^1(\mathbb R^ n)$, \[  \| u\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}} \leq \prod _{i=1}^ n\| \partial _ i u\| _{L^1}^{1/n} \leq \| Du\| _{L^1}.  \] This is the $p=1$ input in [ SimonPDE ] , Lecture 17, Lemma 2, pp. 200–201; no sharp constant is claimed. Proof On every coordinate line, the fundamental theorem of calculus and compact support give \[  |u(x)|\leq F_ i(\widehat x_ i),\qquad F_ i(\widehat x_ i)=\int _{\mathbb R}|\partial _ i u(x)|\, dx_ i.  \] Multiply these $n$ inequalities and raise the result to the power $1/(n-1)$. Lemma 7.14.1 gives \[  \int |u|^{n/(n-1)}\leq \prod _ i\| \partial _ i u\| _1^{1/(n-1)}.  \] Taking the power $(n-1)/n$ proves the first inequality. Each $\| \partial _ i u\| _1$ is at most $\| Du\| _1$, proving the second. If one coordinate derivative vanishes identically, the same argument forces $u=0$, consistently with compact support. $\square$ Theorem 7.14.3 (Sobolev gain below the critical derivative exponent) . FB6C58CDB2CE Let $1\leq p<n$ and $p^*=np/(n-p)$. For every open $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$ and every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega )$, \[  \| u\| _{L^{p^*}(\Omega )}\leq C_{n,p}\| Du\| _{L^ p(\Omega )}.  \] One may take $C_{n,1}=1$ and $C_{n,p}=(n-1)p/(n-p)$ for $p>1$. The case $p=1$ is Theorem 7.14.2 . For $p>1$, put $\alpha =(n-1)p/(n-p)>1$ and apply that theorem to $|u|^\alpha \in C_ c^1(\mathbb R^ n)$. The chain rule and Holder give \[  \| u\| _{p^*}^{\alpha } \leq \alpha \int |u|^{\alpha -1}|Du| \leq \alpha \| u\| _{p^*}^{\alpha -1}\| Du\| _ p,  \] since $\alpha n/(n-1)=(\alpha -1)p/(p-1)=p^*$. text: Lemma 7.14.1 (An iterated Holder inequality for coordinate projections) . 56D0A07041F8 For $i=1,\ldots ,n$, let $F_ i$ be a nonnegative integrable function of the $n-1$ coordinates $\widehat x_ i$ obtained by omitting $x_ i$. Then \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ n}\prod _{i=1}^ n F_ i(\widehat x_ i)^{1/(n-1)}\, dx \leq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left(\int _{\mathbb R^{n-1}}F_ i\right)^{1/(n-1)}.  \] Proof For $n=2$ this is the product identity from Tonelli. Suppose it is known in dimension $n-1$. Integrate in $x_ n$ first and apply Holder to the first $n-1$ factors, with all exponents equal to $n-1$. Put $G_ i(\widehat x_ i,\widehat x_ n)=\int _{\mathbb R}F_ i(\widehat x_ i)\, dx_ n$ for $i<n$, where the argument of $G_ i$ consists of the remaining $n-2$ coordinates. The integral in the statement is at most \[  \int _{\mathbb R^{n-1}}F_ n(x')^{1/(n-1)} \prod _{i<n}G_ i(\widehat x_ i,\widehat x_ n)^{1/(n-1)}\, dx'.  \] Holder with exponents $n-1$ and $(n-1)/(n-2)$ bounds this by \[  \| F_ n\| _1^{1/(n-1)} \left(\int _{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\prod _{i<n}G_ i^{1/(n-2)}\, dx'\right)^{(n-2)/(n-1)}.  \] Apply the induction hypothesis to the integral and use $\| G_ i\| _1=\| F_ i\| _1$. This gives the result. Zero factors are immediate; truncation to bounded functions on bounded boxes and monotone convergence justify the argument without any initial finiteness assumption on the product integral. $\square$

text: Theorem 7.14.2 (The first-power Sobolev inequality) . 3E1913FF6CC7 For every $u\in C_ c^1(\mathbb R^ n)$, \[  \| u\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}} \leq \prod _{i=1}^ n\| \partial _ i u\| _{L^1}^{1/n} \leq \| Du\| _{L^1}.  \] This is the $p=1$ input in [ SimonPDE ] , Lecture 17, Lemma 2, pp. 200–201; no sharp constant is claimed. Proof On every coordinate line, the fundamental theorem of calculus and compact support give \[  |u(x)|\leq F_ i(\widehat x_ i),\qquad F_ i(\widehat x_ i)=\int _{\mathbb R}|\partial _ i u(x)|\, dx_ i.  \] Multiply these $n$ inequalities and raise the result to the power $1/(n-1)$. If one coordinate derivative vanishes identically, the same argument forces $u=0$, consistently with compact support. $\square$

title: 11.7 Trace-free curvature and CMC pinching
search_title: Trace-free curvature and CMC pinching
text:
The trace-free second fundamental form measures the failure to be umbilic. We derive its equation in a space form and use a sharp algebraic bound to prove a curvature gap on closed hypersurfaces. The spherical comparison source is Alencar–do Carmo [ AdC94 ] , Theorem 1.2 and Section 2. Their shape operator has the opposite sign and their mean curvature is the average of the principal curvatures. Thus their scalar mean curvature is $-H/n$ in our convention; their tensor $\phi $ agrees with the trace-free tensor used below. Their classification of all equality cases is not used in our proofs. Definition 11.7.1 (Trace-free second fundamental form) . 5CFC5E1C6CBF For a smooth two-sided hypersurface of dimension $n\geq 2$, set \[  b=h- rac Hn g,\qquad B=A- rac Hn I,\qquad s=|B|.  \] Then $\operatorname {tr}B=0$ and $|A|^2=s^2+H^2/n$. The hypersurface is totally umbilic exactly when $B=0$. The quantity $s$ does not depend on the choice of normal. Compare the tensor $\phi $ in [ AdC94 ] , Section 1. Proposition 11.7.2 (The trace-free Simons equation for CMC hypersurfaces) . CDBF4FCC1085 Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth two-sided immersed hypersurface with constant $H$ in a space form of sectional curvature $c$. With the preceding notation and $\alpha =nc+H^2/n$, \[  \Delta b=(\alpha -s^2)b+H\left(b^2- rac{s^2}{n}gight),  \] \[   rac12\Delta s^2=|
abla b|^2+\alpha s^2-s^4+H\operatorname {tr}(B^3).  \] Here $(b^2)_{ij}=b_ i{}^ kb_{kj}$. For $c=1$ the second equation is the normalization of [ AdC94 ] , equation (2.4). Proof Since $H$ is constant and $
abla g=0$, one has $\Delta b=\Delta h$. In Theorem 7.15.3 , substitute $h=b+(H/n)g$ and $|A|^2=s^2+H^2/n$. The coefficient of $b$ becomes $2H^2/n-s^2-H^2/n+nc=\alpha -s^2$. The scalar multiple of $g$ becomes $-Hs^2/n$, while the quadratic term is $Hb^2$. This proves the tensor equation. Contract it with $b$, use $\langle b,gangle =0$, and apply $ rac12\Delta |b|^2=|
abla b|^2+\langle b,\Delta bangle $ to obtain the norm equation. $\square$ Lemma 11.7.3 (The sharp cubic bound for a trace-free symmetric operator) . 71A17FBA686F For a symmetric operator $B$ on an $n$-dimensional Euclidean space, $n\geq 2$, with $\operatorname {tr}B=0$, put $ eta _ n=(n-2)/\sqrt{n(n-1)}$. Then \[  |\operatorname {tr}(B^3)|\leq  eta _ n|B|^3.  \] For $n>2$ and $B
e 0$, equality holds exactly when one eigenvalue has multiplicity one and the other has multiplicity $n-1$. For $n=2$ both sides vanish for every such $B$. This is the algebraic inequality attributed to Okumura in [ AdC94 ] , Section 2, Lemma 1; we include the optimization argument. Proof The zero operator is immediate. Divide the eigenvalues by $|B|$; they now satisfy $\sum _ i\lambda _ i=0$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ i^2=1$. For $n=2$ they are opposite, so their cubes cancel. Suppose $n>2$. The normalized constraint set is compact and its two constraint gradients are independent: otherwise all $\lambda _ i$ would be equal, contrary to the constraints. At an extremum of $\sum _ i\lambda _ i^3$, Lagrange multipliers give $3\lambda _ i^2=a+2b\lambda _ i$. There are at most two distinct eigenvalues, and the constraints rule out a single value. Let the positive value have multiplicity $p$ and the negative value multiplicity $q=n-p$. The constraints give \[  \lambda _+=\sqrt{ rac{q}{np}},\qquad \lambda _-=-\sqrt{ rac{p}{nq}},\qquad \sum _ i\lambda _ i^3= rac{q-p}{\sqrt{npq}}.  \] The square of the last expression is $n/(pq)-4/n$. Since $pq=p(n-p)\geq n-1$, its maximum is $(n-2)^2/(n(n-1))$, attained precisely when $p=1$ or $q=1$. This bounds both extrema and proves the inequality after restoring the factor $|B|^3$. It also proves the equality assertion, including its converse. $\square$ Theorem 11.7.4 (A pinching gap for closed CMC hypersurfaces) . 08262020D02C Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth connected compact two-sided immersed hypersurface without boundary in a space form of curvature $c$, with constant scalar mean curvature $H$. Assume $n\geq 2$ and $\alpha =nc+H^2/n>0$. Define \[  r= rac{\sqrt{ eta _ n^2H^2+4\alpha }- eta _ n|H|}{2}>0, \qquad  eta _ n= rac{n-2}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}.  \] If $|B|\leq r$ everywhere, then $B$ is parallel and either $B=0$ everywhere or $|B|=r$ everywhere. In particular, $\sup _\Sigma |B|<r$ forces the hypersurface to be totally umbilic. For $c=1$ this is the gap part of [ AdC94 ] , Theorem 1.2(i), in our normalization; the proof below also covers the stated values of $c$ with $\alpha >0$. Proof Proposition 11.7.2 and Lemma 11.7.3 imply \[   rac12\Delta s^2\geq |
abla b|^2+s^2(\alpha -s^2- eta _ n|H|s).  \] The polynomial $P(s)=\alpha -s^2- eta _ n|H|s$ is positive on $[0,r)$ and zero at $r$. Under the pinching hypothesis the right side is nonnegative. Integrating over the compact manifold without boundary gives zero on the left. The two continuous nonnegative terms on the right must therefore vanish everywhere. Thus $
abla b=0$, so connectedness makes $s$ constant, and $s^2P(s)=0$ forces $s=0$ or $s=r$. The strict bound excludes the latter. Compactness and absence of boundary justify this integration; the same conclusion has not been asserted for arbitrary noncompact pieces of CMC hypersurfaces. $\square$ Corollary 11.7.5 (The first curvature gap for a spherical minimal hypersurface) . 3CF4022E5000 Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth closed connected two-sided immersed minimal hypersurface in the unit sphere, $n\geq 2$. If $|A|^2\leq n$, then $A$ is parallel and either $A=0$ everywhere or $|A|^2=n$ everywhere. In particular, $|A|^2<n$ everywhere implies that the hypersurface is totally geodesic. This is the gap assertion recalled in [ AdC94 ] , Theorem 1.1(i), attributed there to Simons. Proof Here $H=0$, $c=1$, $B=A$, $\alpha =n$, and $r=\sqrt n$. Apply Theorem 11.7.4 . In the strict case compactness also gives a strict supremum bound; alternatively the constant-norm conclusion excludes the value $n$. Vanishing of the second fundamental form is exactly the totally geodesic condition. This conclusion does not require the classification of the nonzero equality case. $\square$ Example 11.7.6 (Products of spheres at and beyond the pinching threshold) . BE780D70334A For $p,q\geq 1$, $n=p+q$, and $a,b>0$ with $a^2+b^2=1$, the product \[  \Sigma =\mathbb S^ p(a)	imes \mathbb S^ q(b)\subset \mathbb S^{n+1}(1)  \] is a closed embedded CMC hypersurface with parallel second fundamental form. For a suitable normal its principal curvatures are $b/a$ with multiplicity $p$ and $-a/b$ with multiplicity $q$, and \[  H= rac{pb}{a}- rac{qa}{b},\qquad |B|^2= rac{pq}{n a^2b^2}.  \] It is minimal precisely when $a^2=p/n$, in which case $|A|^2=n$. For $n=2$ every member realizes equality in Theorem 11.7.4 . For $n>2$, $H
e 0$, equality requires one of $p,q$ to be one and additionally $H(q-p)<0$. This illustrates why not every nonminimal product is at the first pinching threshold. Compare [ AdC94 ] , Section 1 and Theorem 1.2. Proof At $(x,y)$ the vector $
u =((b/a)x,-(a/b)y)$ is unit, orthogonal to $(x,y)$, and normal to the product within the sphere. Differentiating in the two factor directions gives the displayed principal curvatures. The splitting of the product tangent bundle is parallel, and these principal curvatures are constant; hence $A$ is parallel. Their trace is $H$. For two eigenvalues $k_+,k_-$ of multiplicities $p,q$, the squared trace-free norm is $(pq/n)(k_+-k_-)^2$. Here $k_+-k_-=1/(ab)$, giving the stated formula. Solving $H=0$ yields $a^2=p/n$, and substitution gives $|A|^2=n$. For $n=2$, the identity $|B|^2=2+H^2/2$ follows either from the displayed formulas or from $k_+k_-=-1$. This is $r^2$ since $ eta _2=0$. For $n>2$, the nonzero trace-free eigenvalues are $q/(nab)$ and $-p/(nab)$, so $\operatorname {tr}(B^3)$ has sign $q-p$. The parallel norm identity gives $0=\alpha s^2-s^4+H\operatorname {tr}(B^3)$. At $s=r$, the inequality used in the gap theorem is an equality, requiring $H\operatorname {tr}(B^3)=-|H| eta _ n s^3$. For $H
e 0$, the sharp cubic equality requires $p=1$ or $q=1$, and its sign requires $H(q-p)<0$. Conversely these two conditions make the norm identity read $s^2(\alpha -s^2- eta _ n|H|s)=0$; since $s>0$, its unique positive root is $r$. No classification of other hypersurfaces is used. $\square$

title: Theorem 11.7.4 (A pinching gap for closed CMC hypersurfaces)
search_title: A pinching gap for closed CMC hypersurfaces
text: Theorem 11.7.4 (A pinching gap for closed CMC hypersurfaces) . 08262020D02C Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth connected compact two-sided immersed hypersurface without boundary in a space form of curvature $c$, with constant scalar mean curvature $H$. Assume $n\geq 2$ and $\alpha =nc+H^2/n>0$. Define \[  r=\frac{\sqrt{\beta _ n^2H^2+4\alpha }-\beta _ n|H|}{2}>0, \qquad \beta _ n=\frac{n-2}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}.  \] If $|B|\leq r$ everywhere, then $B$ is parallel and either $B=0$ everywhere or $|B|=r$ everywhere. In particular, $\sup _\Sigma |B|<r$ forces the hypersurface to be totally umbilic. For $c=1$ this is the gap part of [ AdC94 ] , Theorem 1.2(i), in our normalization; the proof below also covers the stated values of $c$ with $\alpha >0$. Proof Proposition 11.7.2 and Lemma 11.7.3 imply \[  \frac12\Delta s^2\geq |\nabla b|^2+s^2(\alpha -s^2-\beta _ n|H|s).  \] The polynomial $P(s)=\alpha -s^2-\beta _ n|H|s$ is positive on $[0,r)$ and zero at $r$. Under the pinching hypothesis the right side is nonnegative. Integrating over the compact manifold without boundary gives zero on the left. The two continuous nonnegative terms on the right must therefore vanish everywhere. Thus $\nabla b=0$, so connectedness makes $s$ constant, and $s^2P(s)=0$ forces $s=0$ or $s=r$. The strict bound excludes the latter. Compactness and absence of boundary justify this integration; the same conclusion has not been asserted for arbitrary noncompact pieces of CMC hypersurfaces. $\square$

title: Corollary 11.7.5 (The first curvature gap for a spherical minimal hypersurface)
search_title: The first curvature gap for a spherical minimal hypersurface
text: Corollary 11.7.5 (The first curvature gap for a spherical minimal hypersurface) . 3CF4022E5000 Let $\Sigma ^ n$ be a smooth closed connected two-sided immersed minimal hypersurface in the unit sphere, $n\geq 2$. If $|A|^2\leq n$, then $A$ is parallel and either $A=0$ everywhere or $|A|^2=n$ everywhere. In particular, $|A|^2<n$ everywhere implies that the hypersurface is totally geodesic. This is the gap assertion recalled in [ AdC94 ] , Theorem 1.1(i), attributed there to Simons. Proof Here $H=0$, $c=1$, $B=A$, $\alpha =n$, and $r=\sqrt n$. Apply Theorem 11.7.4 . In the strict case compactness also gives a strict supremum bound; alternatively the constant-norm conclusion excludes the value $n$. Vanishing of the second fundamental form is exactly the totally geodesic condition. This conclusion does not require the classification of the nonzero equality case. $\square$

Example 11.7.6 (Products of spheres at and beyond the pinching threshold) . BE780D70334A For $p,q\geq 1$, $n=p+q$, and $a,b>0$ with $a^2+b^2=1$, the product \[  \Sigma =\mathbb S^ p(a)	imes \mathbb S^ q(b)\subset \mathbb S^{n+1}(1)  \] is a closed embedded CMC hypersurface with parallel second fundamental form. For a suitable normal its principal curvatures are $b/a$ with multiplicity $p$ and $-a/b$ with multiplicity $q$, and \[  H= rac{pb}{a}- rac{qa}{b},\qquad |B|^2= rac{pq}{n a^2b^2}.  \] It is minimal precisely when $a^2=p/n$, in which case $|A|^2=n$. text:
Throughout this section $F:M^ n	imes [0,T)	o \mathbb R^{n+1}$ is a smooth mean curvature flow of a closed manifold, with $n\geq 2$, and with a smooth choice of unit normal. We retain $h(X,Y)=\langle D_ X
u ,Yangle $, $A=h^\sharp $, $H=\operatorname {tr}A$, and $\partial _ tF=-H
u $. Weak convexity means $A\geq 0$; strict convexity means $A>0$. Mean convexity $H\geq 0$ is a weaker condition. The source is [ Hui84 ] , Sections 3–5, pp. 242–247. We prove the preservation and quotient estimates here; convergence of a normalized convex flow to a sphere requires further estimates. Lemma 14.13.1 (Preserving a nonnegative endomorphism with scalar reaction) . F00A2BFCC2AF Let $g(t)$ be a smooth family of metrics on a closed manifold for $0\leq t\leq 	au $. Suppose $S(t)$ is a smooth endomorphism, self-adjoint with respect to $g(t)$, satisfying \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta _{g(t)})S=aS  \] for a smooth scalar function $a$. If $S(0)\geq 0$, then $S(t)\geq 0$ for every $t\leq 	au $. The Laplacian on endomorphisms uses the connection of $g(t)$. This elementary special case suffices for the tensor-preservation arguments of [ Hui84 ] , Section 4. Proof Choose $C>\sup a$ on the compact space-time interval and put $S_\delta =S+\delta e^{Ct}I$, $\delta >0$. It is positive definite initially and satisfies \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta )S_\delta =aS_\delta +\delta e^{Ct}(C-a)I.  \] If positivity first fails, compactness supplies a first time $t_0>0$, a point $x_0$, and a nonzero vector $v$ with $S_\delta v=0$. Extend $v$ smoothly near this point with spatial covariant derivative zero there, and hold its coordinate components fixed in time. Before the first failure the scalar $\psi =g(S_\delta v,v)$ is positive; at $(x_0,t_0)$ it is zero and has a spatial minimum. Thus $(\partial _ t-\Delta )\psi \leq 0$ there. At that point the derivative of the metric and the second derivatives of $v$ contribute zero, because $S_\delta v=0$ and $S_\delta $ is self-adjoint; first spatial derivatives of $v$ are zero by construction. Consequently \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta )\psi =g(((\partial _ t-\Delta )S_\delta )v,v) =\delta e^{Ct_0}(C-a)|v|^2>0,  \] a contradiction. Let $\delta \downarrow 0$. The argument treats the evolving metric explicitly and does not assume a time-independent orthonormal frame. $\square$ Proposition 14.13.2 (Preservation of convexity and linear pinching) . 483108BB132E Along the flow above, $A\geq 0$ is preserved. More generally, for any constants $\varepsilon , eta \in \mathbb R$, each inequality \[  A\geq \varepsilon H I,\qquad A\leq  eta H I  \] is preserved if it holds initially. text: Lemma 14.13.1 (Preserving a nonnegative endomorphism with scalar reaction) . F00A2BFCC2AF Let $g(t)$ be a smooth family of metrics on a closed manifold for $0\leq t\leq \tau $. Suppose $S(t)$ is a smooth endomorphism, self-adjoint with respect to $g(t)$, satisfying \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta _{g(t)})S=aS  \] for a smooth scalar function $a$. If $S(0)\geq 0$, then $S(t)\geq 0$ for every $t\leq \tau $. The Laplacian on endomorphisms uses the connection of $g(t)$. This elementary special case suffices for the tensor-preservation arguments of [ Hui84 ] , Section 4. Proof Choose $C>\sup a$ on the compact space-time interval and put $S_\delta =S+\delta e^{Ct}I$, $\delta >0$. It is positive definite initially and satisfies \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta )S_\delta =aS_\delta +\delta e^{Ct}(C-a)I.  \] If positivity first fails, compactness supplies a first time $t_0>0$, a point $x_0$, and a nonzero vector $v$ with $S_\delta v=0$. Extend $v$ smoothly near this point with spatial covariant derivative zero there, and hold its coordinate components fixed in time. Before the first failure the scalar $\psi =g(S_\delta v,v)$ is positive; at $(x_0,t_0)$ it is zero and has a spatial minimum. Thus $(\partial _ t-\Delta )\psi \leq 0$ there. At that point the derivative of the metric and the second derivatives of $v$ contribute zero, because $S_\delta v=0$ and $S_\delta $ is self-adjoint; first spatial derivatives of $v$ are zero by construction. Consequently \[  (\partial _ t-\Delta )\psi =g(((\partial _ t-\Delta )S_\delta )v,v) =\delta e^{Ct_0}(C-a)|v|^2>0,  \] a contradiction. Let $\delta \downarrow 0$. The argument treats the evolving metric explicitly and does not assume a time-independent orthonormal frame. $\square$

title: 7.17 Free-boundary geometry in the ball

text:
These local calculations connect the first variation, boundary spectra, and instability. The geometric source is Fraser's free-boundary variational paper [ Fraser00 ] , Section 2, especially Theorem 2.9, pp. 967–970. The spectral viewpoint is [ FS11 ] , Sections 1 and 3. Definition 7.17.1 (Free boundary in a Euclidean ball) . 1784BEE5B22B Let $F:\Sigma ^ n	o \overline B^ N$ be a smooth immersion of a compact manifold with nonempty boundary, where $1\leq n<N$. We require $F(\operatorname {int}\Sigma )\subset B^ N$, $F(\partial \Sigma )\subset S^{N-1}$, and that its outward unit conormal, viewed in the ambient Euclidean space, satisfies $\eta =F$ on $\partial \Sigma $. The immersion is a free-boundary minimal immersion if its mean curvature vector vanishes. The conormal condition says that the surface meets the supporting sphere orthogonally. All volumes below use the induced metric, including multiplicity for an immersion. Proposition 7.17.2 (Stationarity for boundary-preserving variations) . BB9DE49F72CD A free-boundary minimal immersion is stationary under every smooth variation whose boundary remains on the unit sphere. In particular, this holds for ambient flows generated by vector fields tangent to the sphere. Proof If $V=\partial _ tF_ t|_0$ is the variation field, differentiating the induced metric gives $A'(0)=\int _\Sigma \operatorname {div}_\Sigma V$. Decompose into tangential and normal parts and apply the divergence theorem: \[  A'(0)=-\int _\Sigma \langle \vec H,Vangle +\int _{\partial \Sigma }\langle \eta ,Vangle .  \] The interior term is zero by minimality. Differentiating $|F_ t|^2=1$ on the boundary gives $\langle F,Vangle =0$ there, and $\eta =F$ kills the boundary term. No fixed-boundary condition is imposed on $V$. $\square$ Proposition 7.17.3 (Coordinate functions and the area identity) . 07F94EB3FBAA For a free-boundary minimal immersion into the unit ball, \[  \Delta _\Sigma F=0,\qquad \partial _\eta F=F,\qquad \int _{\partial \Sigma }F=0,\qquad |\partial \Sigma |=n|\Sigma |.  \] The vector boundary integral is taken componentwise. Proof Tracing the covariant Hessian of an immersion gives $\Delta F=\vec H=0$. Since $dF(\eta )=F$ along the boundary, its coordinate functions have the displayed Robin condition. Integrating $\Delta F=0$ gives the zero boundary integral. Also $|dF|^2=n$, hence $\Delta |F|^2=2n$. Its outward derivative is $2\langle F,dF(\eta )angle =2$ on the boundary. Integration proves the area identity. These formulas use the trace convention for $\vec H$, not its average. $\square$ Definition 7.17.4 (The Steklov equation) . 69B553D39714 On a compact connected Riemannian manifold $\Sigma $ with nonempty boundary, a nonzero smooth real function $u$ is a Steklov eigenfunction with eigenvalue $\sigma $ if \[  \Delta u=0\quad \hbox{in }\Sigma ,\qquad \partial _\eta u=\sigma u\quad \hbox{on }\partial \Sigma .  \] This section uses only the displayed boundary value equation; general spectral existence and completeness are separate analytic results. Proposition 7.17.5 (Energy, sign, orthogonality, and scaling) . 8775B4161BF5 A Steklov eigenfunction satisfies \[  \int _\Sigma |
abla u|^2=\sigma \int _{\partial \Sigma }u^2.  \] Consequently $\sigma \geq 0$; the zero eigenspace consists of constants; and eigenfunctions with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal in $L^2(\partial \Sigma )$. Under $g\mapsto c^2g$ with $c>0$, every Steklov eigenvalue is divided by $c$. Proof Green's identity gives the energy formula. A harmonic function whose boundary trace is zero has zero Dirichlet energy and hence is identically zero; thus the boundary denominator is positive for a nonzero eigenfunction. If $\sigma =0$, zero energy and connectedness make $u$ constant. For eigenfunctions $u,v$ with eigenvalues $\sigma ,	au $, integration by parts in both orders gives \[  \sigma \int _{\partial \Sigma }uv=\int _\Sigma \langle 
abla u,
abla vangle =	au \int _{\partial \Sigma }uv.  \] Finally the Laplacian scales by $c^{-2}$ and the outward unit normal derivative by $c^{-1}$, proving the last assertion directly from the equation. $\square$ Corollary 7.17.6 (A geometric Steklov eigenvalue) . 42F70AD9838F Every nonzero coordinate function of a connected free-boundary minimal immersion into the unit ball is a Steklov eigenfunction of eigenvalue $1$. Their span has dimension equal to the dimension of the linear span of the image. This assertion alone does not identify the first positive eigenvalue. Proof Apply Proposition 7.17.3 . A relation $\sum a_ iF_ i=0$ is exactly a vector orthogonal to the linear span of $F(\Sigma )$, giving the dimension claim. There may be other eigenfunctions with smaller positive eigenvalues; the coordinate calculation supplies no exclusion of them. $\square$ Lemma 7.17.7 (Area acceleration under an ambient flow) . E50D256363DA Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \overline B^ N$ be free-boundary minimal and let $X$ be a smooth ambient vector field tangent to the sphere. Put $Y=D_ XX$. At $t=0$, the second derivative of area under its flow is \[  A''(0)=\int _\Sigma \left[\sum _ i|D_{e_ i}X|^2+(\operatorname {div}_\Sigma X)^2 - rac12\sum _{i,j} igl (\langle D_{e_ i}X,e_ jangle +\langle D_{e_ j}X,e_ iangle  igr )^2ight] -\int _{\partial \Sigma }|X|^2,  \] where $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ is any local orthonormal tangent frame. Proof Differentiate the pullback metric along the flow. At an orthonormal frame its first derivative is $g'_{ij}=\langle D_{e_ i}X,e_ jangle +\langle D_{e_ j}X,e_ iangle $ and $g''_{ij}=2\langle D_{e_ i}X,D_{e_ j}Xangle +\langle D_{e_ i}Y,e_ jangle +\langle D_{e_ j}Y,e_ iangle $. The second derivative of $\sqrt{\det g}$ is $	frac 12\operatorname {tr}g''-	frac 12\operatorname {tr}((g')^2)+	frac 14(\operatorname {tr}g')^2$. After substitution, the additional term is $\int _\Sigma \operatorname {div}_\Sigma Y=\int _{\partial \Sigma }\langle Y,\eta angle $ by minimality. On the sphere, differentiate $\langle X,xangle =0$ in direction $X$ to obtain $\langle D_ XX,xangle =-|X|^2$. Since $\eta =x$, this is the claimed boundary term. The flow preserves the sphere and the ball, so the variation is admissible. $\square$ Theorem 7.17.8 (Instability in every positive codimension) . 19C6839A4C10 Every nonempty compact free-boundary minimal immersion $\Sigma ^ n	o \overline B^ N$ with $1\leq n<N$ has an admissible ambient variation with strictly negative second variation of area. This is Fraser's instability theorem, [ Fraser00 ] , Theorem 2.9. Proof Write the ambient position as $x$ and its tangential projection as $x^ T$. For the standard coordinate vectors $E_ k$, set \[  X_ k=2x_ kx-(|x|^2+1)E_ k,\qquad 1\leq k\leq N.  \] These fields are tangent to $S^{N-1}$. Their derivatives satisfy $D_ vX_ k=2\langle v,E_ kangle x+2x_ kv-2\langle x,vangle E_ k$. Thus the symmetric tangential derivative is $4x_ kg$, and $\operatorname {div}_\Sigma X_ k=2nx_ k$. Summing the squared derivative over $k$ and a tangent orthonormal frame gives \[  \sum _{k,i}|D_{e_ i}X_ k|^2=8n|x|^2+4(N-2)|x^ T|^2.  \] On the boundary, $\sum _ k|X_ k|^2=4(N-1)$. Lemma 7.17.7 therefore yields \[  \sum _ k A''(X_ k)=\int _\Sigma [4(N-2)|x^ T|^2+4n^2|x|^2]-4(N-1)|\partial \Sigma |.  \] Because $\Delta |x|^4=8|x^ T|^2+4n|x|^2$ and $\partial _\eta |x|^4=4$, integration gives $|\partial \Sigma |=\int _\Sigma (2|x^ T|^2+n|x|^2)$. Substitution makes the sum equal to \[  -4N\int _\Sigma |x^ T|^2+4n(n-N+1)\int _\Sigma |x|^2<0.  \] The second coefficient is nonpositive. At the boundary $x^ T=x$ has unit length, so continuity on a boundary collar makes the first integral positive. Hence at least one summand is negative. This calculation follows the conformal fields in [ Fraser00 ] , pp. 968–970, while retaining the exact conormal equality. $\square$ Proposition 7.17.9 (Normal second variation at a free boundary) . 4E8A8B534883 Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \overline B^{n+1}$ be a smooth compact two-sided embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface, with global unit normal $
u $. For every smooth scalar function $f$ on $\Sigma $, the second variation in normal direction $f
u $ is \[  Q(f,f)=\int _\Sigma (|
abla f|^2-|A|^2f^2)-\int _{\partial \Sigma }f^2.  \] In particular $Q(1,1)<0$. The boundary is allowed to move on the sphere; this quadratic form differs from the fixed-boundary Dirichlet problem. Proof The field $f
u $ is tangent to the sphere along $\partial \Sigma $, because $\eta =x$ is tangent to $\Sigma $. It extends to a smooth ambient vector field tangent to the sphere: use boundary charts in which the transverse intersection of the hypersurface and the sphere is a coordinate intersection, extend its component functions, and combine using a partition of unity. Along $\Sigma $, $D_{e_ i}(f
u )=f_ i
u +fAe_ i$. Therefore the squared derivative sum is $|
abla f|^2+f^2|A|^2$, the tangential divergence is $fH=0$, and the symmetric derivative is $2fh$. Lemma 7.17.7 gives the formula. Its value at $f=1$ is strictly negative because $|\partial \Sigma |>0$. Compare [ Fraser00 ] , Section 2.1, p. 960. $\square$

search_title: The Steklov equation
text: Definition 7.17.4 (The Steklov equation) . 69B553D39714 On a compact connected Riemannian manifold $\Sigma $ with nonempty boundary, a nonzero smooth real function $u$ is a Steklov eigenfunction with eigenvalue $\sigma $ if \[  \Delta u=0\quad \hbox{in }\Sigma ,\qquad \partial _\eta u=\sigma u\quad \hbox{on }\partial \Sigma .  \] This section uses only the displayed boundary value equation; general spectral existence and completeness are separate analytic results.

title: Proposition 7.17.5 (Energy, sign, orthogonality, and scaling)
search_title: Energy, sign, orthogonality, and scaling
text:
Proposition 7.17.5 (Energy, sign, orthogonality, and scaling) . 8775B4161BF5 A Steklov eigenfunction satisfies \[  \int _\Sigma |
abla u|^2=\sigma \int _{\partial \Sigma }u^2.  \] Consequently $\sigma \geq 0$; the zero eigenspace consists of constants; and eigenfunctions with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal in $L^2(\partial \Sigma )$. Under $g\mapsto c^2g$ with $c>0$, every Steklov eigenvalue is divided by $c$. Proof Green's identity gives the energy formula. A harmonic function whose boundary trace is zero has zero Dirichlet energy and hence is identically zero; thus the boundary denominator is positive for a nonzero eigenfunction. If $\sigma =0$, zero energy and connectedness make $u$ constant. For eigenfunctions $u,v$ with eigenvalues $\sigma ,	au $, integration by parts in both orders gives \[  \sigma \int _{\partial \Sigma }uv=\int _\Sigma \langle 
abla u,
abla vangle =	au \int _{\partial \Sigma }uv.  \] Finally the Laplacian scales by $c^{-2}$ and the outward unit normal derivative by $c^{-1}$, proving the last assertion directly from the equation. $\square$

title: Corollary 7.17.6 (A geometric Steklov eigenvalue)
search_title: A geometric Steklov eigenvalue
text: Corollary 7.17.6 (A geometric Steklov eigenvalue) . 42F70AD9838F Every nonzero coordinate function of a connected free-boundary minimal immersion into the unit ball is a Steklov eigenfunction of eigenvalue $1$. Their span has dimension equal to the dimension of the linear span of the image. This assertion alone does not identify the first positive eigenvalue. Proof Apply Proposition 7.17.3 . A relation $\sum a_ iF_ i=0$ is exactly a vector orthogonal to the linear span of $F(\Sigma )$, giving the dimension claim. There may be other eigenfunctions with smaller positive eigenvalues; the coordinate calculation supplies no exclusion of them. $\square$

title: Lemma 7.17.7 (Area acceleration under an ambient flow)
search_title: Area acceleration under an ambient flow
text: Lemma 7.17.7 (Area acceleration under an ambient flow) . E50D256363DA Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \overline B^ N$ be free-boundary minimal and let $X$ be a smooth ambient vector field tangent to the sphere. Put $Y=D_ XX$. At $t=0$, the second derivative of area under its flow is \[  A''(0)=\int _\Sigma \left[\sum _ i|D_{e_ i}X|^2+(\operatorname {div}_\Sigma X)^2 -\frac12\sum _{i,j}\bigl (\langle D_{e_ i}X,e_ j\rangle +\langle D_{e_ j}X,e_ i\rangle \bigr )^2\right] -\int _{\partial \Sigma }|X|^2,  \] where $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ is any local orthonormal tangent frame. Proof Differentiate the pullback metric along the flow. At an orthonormal frame its first derivative is $g'_{ij}=\langle D_{e_ i}X,e_ j\rangle +\langle D_{e_ j}X,e_ i\rangle $ and $g''_{ij}=2\langle D_{e_ i}X,D_{e_ j}X\rangle +\langle D_{e_ i}Y,e_ j\rangle +\langle D_{e_ j}Y,e_ i\rangle $. The second derivative of $\sqrt{\det g}$ is $\tfrac 12\operatorname {tr}g''-\tfrac 12\operatorname {tr}((g')^2)+\tfrac 14(\operatorname {tr}g')^2$. After substitution, the additional term is $\int _\Sigma \operatorname {div}_\Sigma Y=\int _{\partial \Sigma }\langle Y,\eta \rangle $ by minimality. On the sphere, differentiate $\langle X,x\rangle =0$ in direction $X$ to obtain $\langle D_ XX,x\rangle =-|X|^2$. Since $\eta =x$, this is the claimed boundary term. The flow preserves the sphere and the ball, so the variation is admissible. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.17.8 (Instability in every positive codimension)
search_title: Instability in every positive codimension
text: Theorem 7.17.8 (Instability in every positive codimension) . 19C6839A4C10 Every nonempty compact free-boundary minimal immersion $\Sigma ^ n\to \overline B^ N$ with $1\leq n<N$ has an admissible ambient variation with strictly negative second variation of area. This is Fraser's instability theorem, [ Fraser00 ] , Theorem 2.9. Proof Write the ambient position as $x$ and its tangential projection as $x^ T$. For the standard coordinate vectors $E_ k$, set \[  X_ k=2x_ kx-(|x|^2+1)E_ k,\qquad 1\leq k\leq N.  \] These fields are tangent to $S^{N-1}$. Their derivatives satisfy $D_ vX_ k=2\langle v,E_ k\rangle x+2x_ kv-2\langle x,v\rangle E_ k$. Thus the symmetric tangential derivative is $4x_ kg$, and $\operatorname {div}_\Sigma X_ k=2nx_ k$. Summing the squared derivative over $k$ and a tangent orthonormal frame gives \[  \sum _{k,i}|D_{e_ i}X_ k|^2=8n|x|^2+4(N-2)|x^ T|^2.  \] On the boundary, $\sum _ k|X_ k|^2=4(N-1)$. Lemma 7.17.7 therefore yields \[  \sum _ k A''(X_ k)=\int _\Sigma [4(N-2)|x^ T|^2+4n^2|x|^2]-4(N-1)|\partial \Sigma |.  \] Because $\Delta |x|^4=8|x^ T|^2+4n|x|^2$ and $\partial _\eta |x|^4=4$, integration gives $|\partial \Sigma |=\int _\Sigma (2|x^ T|^2+n|x|^2)$. Substitution makes the sum equal to \[  -4N\int _\Sigma |x^ T|^2+4n(n-N+1)\int _\Sigma |x|^2<0.  \] The second coefficient is nonpositive. At the boundary $x^ T=x$ has unit length, so continuity on a boundary collar makes the first integral positive. Hence at least one summand is negative. This calculation follows the conformal fields in [ Fraser00 ] , pp. 968–970, while retaining the exact conormal equality. $\square$

title: Proposition 7.17.9 (Normal second variation at a free boundary)
search_title: Normal second variation at a free boundary
text:
Proposition 7.17.9 (Normal second variation at a free boundary) . 4E8A8B534883 Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset \overline B^{n+1}$ be a smooth compact two-sided embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface, with global unit normal $
u $. For every smooth scalar function $f$ on $\Sigma $, the second variation in normal direction $f
u $ is \[  Q(f,f)=\int _\Sigma (|
abla f|^2-|A|^2f^2)-\int _{\partial \Sigma }f^2.  \] In particular $Q(1,1)<0$. The boundary is allowed to move on the sphere; this quadratic form differs from the fixed-boundary Dirichlet problem. Proof The field $f
u $ is tangent to the sphere along $\partial \Sigma $, because $\eta =x$ is tangent to $\Sigma $. It extends to a smooth ambient vector field tangent to the sphere: use boundary charts in which the transverse intersection of the hypersurface and the sphere is a coordinate intersection, extend its component functions, and combine using a partition of unity. Along $\Sigma $, $D_{e_ i}(f
u )=f_ i
u +fAe_ i$. Therefore the squared derivative sum is $|
abla f|^2+f^2|A|^2$, the tangential divergence is $fH=0$, and the symmetric derivative is $2fh$. Lemma 7.17.7 gives the formula. Its value at $f=1$ is strictly negative because $|\partial \Sigma |>0$. Compare [ Fraser00 ] , Section 2.1, p. 960. $\square$

title: 16.7 The equatorial disk and critical catenoid
search_title: The equatorial disk and critical catenoid
section: 16.7 The equatorial disk and critical catenoid
text:
These examples connect the catenoid calculation in Example 16.2.2 to the free-boundary geometry of Section 7.17 . The critical catenoid and its Steklov spectrum are discussed in [ FS11 ] , Section 3, pp. 6–9. We derive the boundary condition and scale directly, and distinguish a negative variation from a calculation of the full Morse index. Example 16.7.1 (The equatorial ball) . 8918496434FC The flat unit ball $D^ n=\overline B^{n+1}\cap \{ x_{n+1}=0\} $ is free-boundary minimal. It has volume $\omega _ n$, boundary volume $n\omega _ n$, and $A=0$. A constant normal speed has $Q(1,1)=-n\omega _ n$. Each coordinate function $x_ i$, $1\leq i\leq n$, is a Jacobi field for the free-boundary second variation, meaning $Q(x_ i,f)=0$ for every smooth $f$. Proof Flatness gives minimality, and the outward conormal of the unit ball is its position vector. The volume formulas and Proposition 7.17.9 give the negative variation. Since $\Delta x_ i=0$ and $\partial _\eta x_ i=x_ i$, integration by parts gives $Q(x_ i,f)=\int _ D\langle 
abla x_ i,
abla fangle -\int _{\partial D}x_ if=0$. These fields arise from rotations that tilt the equatorial plane; the constant speed does not arise from such a symmetry. $\square$ Proposition 16.7.2 (The Steklov spectrum of the flat disk) . 6EFFF85D2747 For the unit disk $D^2$ with its flat metric, the Steklov eigenvalues are $0,1,2,\ldots $. The zero eigenspace is the constants; for integer $k\geq 1$, the eigenvalue $k$ has basis $r^ k\cos (k	heta )$ and $r^ k\sin (k	heta )$. Proof A smooth harmonic function on the closed disk has the harmonic Fourier expansion \[  u(r,	heta )=a_0+\sum _{k\geq 1}r^ k(a_ k\cos k	heta +b_ k\sin k	heta ).  \] This follows by taking Fourier coefficients in the harmonic equation: the radial ODE has solutions $r^{\pm k}$, of which only $r^ k$ is smooth at the origin; its zero mode is constant. The boundary condition $u_ r=\sigma u$ at $r=1$ makes $(k-\sigma )a_ k=(k-\sigma )b_ k=0$ and $\sigma a_0=0$. Fourier uniqueness proves the assertion, while each displayed function directly realizes its eigenvalue. $\square$ Proposition 16.7.3 (Index one and nullity two for the equatorial disk) . 492DCAF81B02 The equatorial unit disk in $B^3$ has free-boundary Morse index one and nullity two. Here the index is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $Q$ is negative definite, and nullity is the dimension of the bilinear kernel $\{ f:Q(f,g)=0	ext{ for every }g\} $. Proof If the boundary trace of $f$ is $a_0+\sum _{k\geq 1}(a_ k\cos k	heta +b_ k\sin k	heta )$, let $h$ be its harmonic extension. Green's identity gives $\int _ D|
abla f|^2=\int _ D|
abla h|^2+\int _ D|
abla (f-h)|^2$. Orthogonality of the trigonometric modes yields \[  Q(f,f)=\int _ D|
abla (f-h)|^2-2\pi a_0^2 +\pi \sum _{k\geq 1}(k-1)(a_ k^2+b_ k^2).  \] The codimension-one subspace of functions with zero boundary mean is nonnegative for $Q$, so a negative-definite subspace has dimension at most one. The constant function gives a negative direction, proving index one. If $Q(f,g)=0$ for all $g$, interior tests imply $\Delta f=0$ and the boundary terms give $\partial _\eta f=f$. Proposition 16.7.2 identifies its solutions as the span of $x_1,x_2$. Conversely those functions are in the kernel by Example 16.7.1 . The zero cone $Q(f,f)=0$ is not being identified with this bilinear kernel. $\square$ Lemma 16.7.4 (The critical catenoid parameter) . 9BF4DE659360 There is a unique $t_0>0$ such that $t_0	anh t_0=1$, and $t_0>1$. Put \[  a= rac1{t_0\cosh t_0}.  \] Then $a=(\cosh ^2t_0+t_0^2)^{-1/2}$, $a\cosh t_0=1/t_0$, and $at_0=\operatorname {sech}t_0$. Proof The function $t	anh t$ starts at zero, has derivative $	anh t+t\operatorname {sech}^2t>0$ for $t>0$, and tends to infinity. Its value at $1$ is less than one. The root exists uniquely and exceeds one. From $	anh t_0=1/t_0$ and $\operatorname {sech}^2t_0=1-1/t_0^2$, one gets $\cosh ^2t_0+t_0^2=t_0^2\cosh ^2t_0$, proving the scale identities. This is the centered symmetric case of [ FS11 ] , Theorem 3.1. $\square$ Example 16.7.5 (A free-boundary catenoidal annulus) . DD8FCA5146D1 With $a,t_0$ as above, the immersion \[  F(t,	heta )=a(\cosh t\cos 	heta ,\cosh t\sin 	heta ,t), \qquad -t_0\leq t\leq t_0,\quad 	heta \in \mathbb R/(2\pi \mathbb Z),  \] is a smooth embedded free-boundary minimal annulus in the unit ball. Its boundary circles have radius $1/t_0$ and heights $\pm \operatorname {sech}t_0$. Its metric is $a^2\cosh ^2t\, (dt^2+d	heta ^2)$. Proof Example 16.2.2 gives the metric, minimality, and embeddedness. Since $|F|^2=a^2(\cosh ^2t+t^2)$ is strictly increasing in $|t|>0$, the scale identity gives $|F|=1$ exactly at $t=\pm t_0$ and $|F|<1$ in the interior. At the upper circle the unit conormal is \[   rac{F_ t}{|F_ t|}=(	anh t_0\cos 	heta ,	anh t_0\sin 	heta ,\operatorname {sech}t_0)=F(t_0,	heta ).  \] At the lower circle the outward conormal is $-F_ t/|F_ t|$, which similarly equals $F(-t_0,	heta )$. The scale identities give the stated circle radii and heights. This establishes the free-boundary condition directly. $\square$ Proposition 16.7.6 (Area, boundary length, and an unstable direction) . 521D410B62DA For the critical catenoid $C$, \[  |C|= rac{2\pi }{t_0},\qquad |\partial C|= rac{4\pi }{t_0},\qquad \int _ C|A|^2= rac{8\pi }{t_0},\qquad Q(1,1)=- rac{12\pi }{t_0}.  \] These computations exhibit a negative variation but do not determine the full Morse index. Proof The area integral is $2\pi a^2\int _{-t_0}^{t_0}\cosh ^2t\, dt=2\pi a^2(t_0+\sinh t_0\cosh t_0)=2\pi /t_0$. For the simplification, use $a^2=1/(t_0^2\cosh ^2t_0)$ and $\sinh t_0=\cosh t_0/t_0$. The two boundary circles give length $4\pi /t_0$, also checking $|\partial C|=2|C|$. By Proposition 16.2.4 , $|A|^2=2/(a^2\cosh ^4t)$. Multiplication by the area element gives $2\operatorname {sech}^2t\, dt\, d	heta $, whose integral is $8\pi 	anh t_0=8\pi /t_0$. Substitute into the normal quadratic form. $\square$ Proposition 16.7.7 (First Steklov eigenspace of the critical catenoid) . 0D411F8E126C The critical catenoid has first positive Steklov eigenvalue $1$, of multiplicity three, with eigenspace spanned by its three ambient coordinate functions. In particular $\sigma _1|\partial C|=4\pi /t_0$. Proof In dimension two, the conformal factor in the metric cancels from the harmonic equation. Thus it is $u_{tt}+u_{	heta 	heta }=0$. At either boundary the unit outward derivative is $\pm t_0\partial _ t$, since $a\cosh t_0=1/t_0$. The angular zero mode is affine in $t$; its constant solution has eigenvalue zero, and its odd solution $t$ has eigenvalue one. For integer $k\geq 1$, the even modes $\cosh (kt)\cos (k	heta )$ and $\cosh (kt)\sin (k	heta )$ have eigenvalue \[  \sigma _ k^{m even}=t_0k	anh (kt_0),  \] while the analogous odd modes with $\sinh (kt)$ have eigenvalue $\sigma _ k^{m odd}=t_0k\coth (kt_0)$. Fourier decomposition and reflection into even and odd parts exhaust the smooth harmonic eigenfunctions. The function $s\mapsto s	anh (st_0)$ is strictly increasing for $s>0$. Hence its smallest integer-mode value is $\sigma _1^{m even}=t_0	anh t_0=1$; all $k\geq 2$ even values exceed one. Every odd value is greater than $t_0k>1$. Together with the zero-angular-mode function $t$, this proves precisely three eigenfunctions at one, which are multiples of $F_1,F_2,F_3$. This specializes the separation of variables in [ FS11 ] , pp. 7–9; it makes no claim about the sharp bound among all annular metrics. $\square$

title: 11.8 Gauss maps and Hopf differentials
search_title: Gauss maps and Hopf differentials
text:
Harmonic maps connect CMC surface theory to complex analysis. The sources are [ Hel01 ] , Theorem 2.1, p. 18, and Chapter 4, pp. 34–37. We use the trace $H$ and the sign $h(X,Y)=\langle D_ X
u ,Yangle $ throughout; the source uses the opposite second fundamental form and averaged mean curvature. Basic complex differentiation and Liouville's theorem are explicit complex-analytic background inputs. Global conformal parametrization of a topological sphere is not proved in this section. Definition 11.8.1 (Harmonic maps to a unit sphere) . 5F0BF2179EDD A smooth map $u:(M,g)	o S^{N-1}\subset \mathbb R^ N$ is harmonic if \[  \Delta _ gu+|du|_ g^2u=0.  \] Equivalently the Euclidean vector $\Delta _ gu$ is normal to the target sphere at $u$. Proposition 11.8.2 (The sphere-valued energy equation) . DB2FAFFE267A A smooth map $u:(M,g)	o S^{N-1}$ is harmonic precisely when it is stationary for the Dirichlet energy under all smooth target-tangent variations compactly supported in the interior. For each test variation, evaluate $E_ U(u)= rac12\int _ U|du|^2$ on a relatively compact domain $U$ containing its support; no finite total energy on a noncompact $M$ is assumed. Proof For a field $V$ along $u$ satisfying $\langle V,uangle =0$, the variation $(u+tV)/|u+tV|$ stays on the sphere and has initial velocity $V$. Differentiating the energy and integrating by parts gives $E'(0)=-\int \langle \Delta u,Vangle $. Vanishing for all such fields is exactly the vanishing of the tangential projection of $\Delta u$. Since $\Delta |u|^2=2\langle \Delta u,uangle +2|du|^2=0$, its normal component is $-|du|^2u$. This gives the displayed harmonic-map equation. Boundary values are held fixed by the compact support of the test. $\square$ Proposition 11.8.3 (The Gauss-map tension of a Euclidean hypersurface) . 70AB98B22DB0 For a smooth two-sided hypersurface immersion $F:\Sigma ^ n	o \mathbb R^{n+1}$ with global unit normal $
u $, the Gauss map satisfies \[  |d
u |^2=|A|^2,\qquad \Delta _\Sigma

title: Proposition 11.8.2 (The sphere-valued energy equation)

text: Proposition 11.8.2 (The sphere-valued energy equation) . DB2FAFFE267A A smooth map $u:(M,g)\to S^{N-1}$ is harmonic precisely when it is stationary for the Dirichlet energy under all smooth target-tangent variations compactly supported in the interior. For each test variation, evaluate $E_ U(u)=\frac12\int _ U|du|^2$ on a relatively compact domain $U$ containing its support; no finite total energy on a noncompact $M$ is assumed. Proof For a field $V$ along $u$ satisfying $\langle V,u\rangle =0$, the variation $(u+tV)/|u+tV|$ stays on the sphere and has initial velocity $V$. Differentiating the energy and integrating by parts gives $E'(0)=-\int \langle \Delta u,V\rangle $. Vanishing for all such fields is exactly the vanishing of the tangential projection of $\Delta u$. Since $\Delta |u|^2=2\langle \Delta u,u\rangle +2|du|^2=0$, its normal component is $-|du|^2u$. This gives the displayed harmonic-map equation. Boundary values are held fixed by the compact support of the test. $\square$

title: 11.9 Reconstructing CMC surfaces from harmonic maps
search_title: Reconstructing CMC surfaces from harmonic maps
section: 11.9 Reconstructing CMC surfaces from harmonic maps
text: The construction in [ Hel01 ] , Chapter 2, pp. 19–21, turns a harmonic sphere-valued map into CMC surfaces. We derive the formulas with the convention $h(X,Y)=\langle D_ X\nu ,Y\rangle $ and trace mean curvature. The period condition and the possible failure of immersion are part of the statement. Lemma 11.9.1 (The closed reconstruction form) . 28CB34BE815C Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^2$ be open and let $u:\Omega \to S^2$ be smooth and harmonic. The $\mathbb R^3$-valued one-form \[  \alpha =(u\times u_ y)\, dx-(u\times u_ x)\, dy  \] is closed. On a simply connected domain there is a smooth map $B:\Omega \to \mathbb R^3$ with $dB=\alpha $, unique up to translation. It satisfies $\Delta B=2u_ x\times u_ y$. Proof The coefficient of $dx\wedge dy$ in $d\alpha $ is $-u\times (u_{xx}+u_{yy})$, which vanishes because $\Delta u=-|Du|^2u$. On a simply connected domain a closed form has a primitive: integrate along a path from a fixed base point; Stokes' theorem applied to a homotopy shows path independence, component by component. Differentiating this integral gives the form, and any two primitives have zero derivative and differ by a constant. Finally \[  B_{xx}+B_{yy}=u_ x\times u_ y-u_ y\times u_ x+u\times (u_{yx}-u_{xy})=2u_ x\times u_ y.  \] $\square$ Proposition 11.9.2 (The global period obstruction) . 0F5256B6DCF4 On a connected, not necessarily simply connected, planar domain, the form in Lemma 11.9.1 has a single-valued primitive if and only if its integral around every closed piecewise smooth curve is zero. Without that condition the construction still works locally and on the universal cover. Proof The integral of $dB$ around a closed curve is zero by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Conversely, vanishing periods make the path integral from a base point independent of the chosen path: traverse one path and then the reverse of the other. Local differentiation produces a smooth primitive. On the universal cover, the pulled-back form is closed and the domain is simply connected, so the preceding lemma applies in local coordinates. Different lifts of a point can give values of $B$ differing by a period vector. Thus local solvability alone does not imply a single-valued map on the original domain. $\square$ Lemma 11.9.3 (The algebra of the two reconstructed maps) . 7DBEE7E31AA0 Assume $dB=\alpha $ and set $X_\varepsilon =B+\varepsilon u$ for $\varepsilon \in \{ 1,-1\} $. Write \[  E=|u_ x|^2+|u_ y|^2,\quad d=u\cdot (u_ x\times u_ y),\quad \lambda _\varepsilon ^2=E-2\varepsilon d.  \] Then $\lambda _\varepsilon ^2\ge 0$, and \[  |(X_\varepsilon )_ x|^2=|(X_\varepsilon )_ y|^2=\lambda _\varepsilon ^2,\qquad (X_\varepsilon )_ x\cdot (X_\varepsilon )_ y=0,  \] \[  (X_\varepsilon )_ x\times (X_\varepsilon )_ y=-\varepsilon \lambda _\varepsilon ^2u, \qquad \Delta X_\varepsilon =-\varepsilon \lambda _\varepsilon ^2u.  \] Proof Put $a=u_ x$, $b=u_ y$ and $Jv=u\times v$ for vectors tangent to $S^2$ at $u$. Then $J^2=-I$, $|Jv|=|v|$, and \[  (X_\varepsilon )_ x=Jb+\varepsilon a,\qquad (X_\varepsilon )_ y=-Ja+\varepsilon b=-\varepsilon J(X_\varepsilon )_ x.  \] Since $a\cdot Jb=-d$, the first squared norm is $E-2\varepsilon d$; the second and the orthogonality follow from the last relation. For a tangent vector $v$, $v\times Jv=|v|^2u$, proving the cross-product formula. The previous lemma and harmonicity give $\Delta X_\varepsilon =2a\times b-\varepsilon Eu=(2d-\varepsilon E)u$, as claimed. $\square$ Theorem 11.9.4 (CMC reconstruction on the immersion locus) . E1BAF4699366 Under the preceding hypotheses, $X_\varepsilon $ is a conformal immersion on the open set $\{ \lambda _\varepsilon ^2>0\} $. Its induced metric is $\lambda _\varepsilon ^2(dx^2+dy^2)$, and its trace scalar mean curvature relative to the chosen normal $u$ is $H=\varepsilon $. Its mean curvature vector is $-\varepsilon u$. At a point where $\lambda _\varepsilon =0$, its entire differential vanishes; no immersion assertion is made there. This is the reconstruction of [ Hel01 ] , pp. 19–21, with signs and normalization made explicit. Proof The positive conformal factor gives a rank-two differential by Lemma 11.9.3 . Since both derivatives are perpendicular to $u$, this is a unit normal. For the induced metric, $\Delta _ g X_\varepsilon =\lambda _\varepsilon ^{-2}\Delta X_\varepsilon =-\varepsilon u$. The immersion identity $\Delta _ gX=\vec H=-Hu$ yields $H=\varepsilon $. The parameter orientation instead gives unit normal $-\varepsilon u$, relative to which the scalar trace is $-1$. At a zero of the conformal factor, both coordinate derivatives have norm zero. Thus the formula can produce a degenerate map, even a constant map, as well as an immersion. $\square$ Proposition 11.9.5 (Hopf differential and degeneracy of reconstruction) . A418F2471861 Let $q=\langle u_ z,u_ z\rangle $ be the coefficient of the Hopf differential. Then \[  \lambda _+^2\lambda _-^2=16|q|^2.  \] If $\Omega $ is connected and $q$ is not identically zero, both reconstructions are immersions away from a discrete set. At a zero of $q$, at least one reconstruction has zero differential. A conformal harmonic map can therefore make one reconstruction degenerate everywhere. Proof Since $a,b$ lie in the plane perpendicular to $u$, $d^2=|a|^2|b|^2-(a\cdot b)^2$. Consequently \[  (E-2d)(E+2d)=(|a|^2-|b|^2)^2+4(a\cdot b)^2=16|q|^2.  \] Both factors are nonnegative. The Hopf coefficient is holomorphic by Proposition 11.8.5 , so its zeros are discrete unless it vanishes identically, by the identity theorem for holomorphic functions. At a zero the product vanishes, and the differential of the corresponding reconstruction is zero. The last possibility is realized explicitly in Example 16.8.3 . $\square$

section: 16.8 Cylinders, spheres and a period obstruction
text:
These calculations apply Section 11.9 to explicit harmonic maps. The construction is from [ Hel01 ] , pp. 19–21; the formulas below check its geometry, degeneracies, and global limitations directly. Example 16.8.1 (An equatorial harmonic map gives a cylinder) . 964FA842F974 For $u(x,y)=(\cos x,\sin x,0)$ on $\mathbb R^2$, a reconstruction primitive is $B=(0,0,-y)$. The two maps \[  X_\varepsilon (x,y)=(\varepsilon \cos x,\varepsilon \sin x,-y)  \] parametrize a unit circular cylinder, with induced metric $dx^2+dy^2$ and trace mean curvature $\varepsilon $ relative to $u$. They are covering immersions on $\mathbb R^2$ and descend to embedded cylinders on $(\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)	imes \mathbb R$. Proof Here $u_{xx}=-u$, $u_ y=0$, and $|Du|^2=1$, so $u$ is harmonic. Since $u	imes u_ x=(0,0,1)$, the reconstruction form is $-(0,0,1)dy=dB$. The formulas and metric follow by differentiation. The mean curvature follows from Theorem 11.9.4 ; for $\varepsilon =1$ it is the positive outward cylinder curvature. Periodicity in $x$ explains the covering, and the quotient map is injective onto the cylinder. The product metric is complete. $\square$ Example 16.8.2 (Harmonic phases and cylinder parametrizations) . 6BD94503E233 Let $\varphi $ be a smooth real harmonic function on a simply connected planar domain, and let $\psi $ be a harmonic conjugate, so $\psi _ x=-\varphi _ y$ and $\psi _ y=\varphi _ x$. Then $u=(\cos \varphi ,\sin \varphi ,0)$ is harmonic and \[  X_\varepsilon =(\varepsilon \cos \varphi ,\varepsilon \sin \varphi ,-\psi )  \] is its CMC reconstruction. Its metric is $|
abla \varphi |^2(dx^2+dy^2)$. It is an immersion exactly where $

e 0$; its image lies on the unit cylinder, but global injectivity is not implied. Proof Writing $v=(-\sin \varphi ,\cos \varphi ,0)$ gives $u_ i=v\varphi _ i$ and $\Delta u=v\Delta \varphi -u|

title: 17.1 Stationarity and harmonic-map energy
search_title: Stationarity and harmonic-map energy
text: The domain-variation calculation is the stress-energy form of Noether's theorem in [ Hel01 ] , Chapter 3, pp. 29–33. We derive its radial consequences in any domain dimension, with the energy normalization $E(u;U)=\frac12\int _ U|Du|^2$. Weak harmonicity and stationarity under domain changes are stated as separate conditions. Definition 17.1.1 (Weak harmonicity and domain stationarity) . 21BC46F055B1 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open and $u\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega ;\mathbb R^ N)$ with $|u|=1$ almost everywhere. It is weakly harmonic if \[  \int _\Omega Du:D\zeta =\int _\Omega |Du|^2u\cdot \zeta \quad (\zeta \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega ;\mathbb R^ N)).  \] It is stationary under domain variations if, in addition, \[  \int _\Omega \left(\frac12|Du|^2\operatorname {div}X -\sum _{i,j}\langle u_ i,u_ j\rangle \partial _ iX_ j\right)=0 \quad (X\in C_ c^\infty (\Omega ;\mathbb R^ m)).  \] We call a map satisfying both conditions a stationary weak harmonic map. The second identity is an additional hypothesis in the weak theory. Proposition 17.1.2 (The stress tensor and inner variations) . 33F433CCE84A For a smooth harmonic map $u:\Omega \to S^{N-1}$, set \[  S_{ij}=\tfrac 12|Du|^2\delta _{ij}-\langle u_ i,u_ j\rangle .  \] Then $\sum _ i\partial _ iS_{ij}=0$. Moreover, for the flow $\Phi _ t$ of a compactly supported domain field $X$, the derivative of the energy of $u\circ \Phi _ t^{-1}$ is $\int S_{ij}\partial _ iX_ j$. In particular every smooth harmonic map is stationary under domain variations. Compare [ Hel01 ] , Theorem 3.2; its Hamiltonian tensor is $-S$. Proof Differentiating and canceling mixed-derivative terms gives \[  \sum _ i\partial _ iS_{ij}=-\langle \Delta u,u_ j\rangle =|Du|^2\langle u,u_ j\rangle =0.  \] For the variation, change variables from $\Phi _ t(x)$ to $x$ on a relatively compact domain containing the support. The Jacobian has derivative $\operatorname {div}X$, while $D\Phi _ t^{-1}$ has derivative $-DX$. Differentiating $\frac12|Du(D\Phi _ t)^{-1}|^2\det D\Phi _ t$ gives exactly the claimed integrand. Integrating the divergence-free tensor against $DX$ gives zero by integration by parts. This smooth computation does not justify using $Du\, X$ as an admissible test in a merely weak equation; that is why Definition 17.1.1 retains domain stationarity separately. $\square$ Theorem 17.1.3 (Radial energy monotonicity) . 7B92D7E65AAC Let $m\ge 2$, let $u$ be a stationary weak harmonic map, and assume $\overline B_ R(a)\subset \Omega $. Define \[  \Theta _ u(a,r)=r^{2-m}\frac12\int _{B_ r(a)}|Du|^2.  \] For $0<\rho <R$, \[  \Theta _ u(a,R)-\Theta _ u(a,\rho ) =\int _{B_ R(a)\setminus B_\rho (a)}|x-a|^{2-m}|\partial _ r u|^2\, dx\ge 0,  \] where $\partial _ r u=Du(x)(x-a)/|x-a|$. In particular $\Theta _ u(a,r)$ is nondecreasing and has a finite nonnegative limit as $r\downarrow 0$. The proof derives the radial identity from the domain-variation framework of [ Hel01 ] , Theorem 3.2, rather than importing weak regularity results. Proof Translate $a$ to zero and write $e=|Du|^2/2$ and $E(r)=\int _{B_ r}e$. In the domain-stationarity identity use $X(x)=\eta (|x|)x$, with $\eta $ smooth and constant near zero. Since $\operatorname {tr}S=(m-2)e$ and $S(x,x)/|x|=|x|(e-|\partial _ ru|^2)$, this yields \[  0=\int \big ((m-2)\eta e+r\eta '(e-|\partial _ ru|^2)\big ).  \] Approximate the indicator of $[0,s]$ by such cutoffs. Polar integration and one-dimensional Lebesgue differentiation give, for almost every $s$, \[  (m-2)E(s)=s\int _{\partial B_ s}(e-|\partial _ ru|^2).  \] Here all surface integrals are the almost-everywhere slices given by polar integration of integrable functions. Since $E'(s)=\int _{\partial B_ s}e$ almost everywhere, \[  \frac{d}{ds}(s^{2-m}E(s))=s^{2-m}\int _{\partial B_ s}|\partial _ ru|^2.  \] Both sides are integrable on every closed radius interval away from zero, and $E$ is absolutely continuous there. Integrating and applying polar integration proves the formula for all $0<\rho <R$. Monotonicity and the finite value at $R$ give the finite limit at zero. The argument uses domain stationarity; it does not need to differentiate the weak harmonic-map equation. $\square$ Proposition 17.1.4 (Equality, homogeneity and smooth-point density) . D01FDB2147F5 Equality of $\Theta _ u(a,R)$ and $\Theta _ u(a,\rho )$ in Theorem 17.1.3 is equivalent to $\partial _ ru=0$ almost everywhere on the annulus. Equivalently $u(a+r\omega )$ is independent of $r\in (\rho ,R)$ for almost every direction $\omega $, up to Sobolev representatives. At a point where $u$ is smooth, $\lim _{r\downarrow 0}\Theta _ u(a,r)=0$. Proof The integral in the monotonicity identity is of a nonnegative function with a strictly positive weight. It is zero precisely when the radial derivative vanishes almost everywhere. On any annulus bounded away from its center, polar charts are smooth local changes of variables. The absolute continuity on almost every coordinate line of a Sobolev function, applied in these charts and then exhausted by compact subannuli, makes vanishing radial derivative equivalent to radial constancy. At a smooth point the energy density is bounded on a small ball, so $\Theta _ u(a,r)\le Cr^{2-m}|B_ r|=C\omega _ m r^2\to 0$. $\square$ Corollary 17.1.5 (Finite total energy in dimensions above two) . C271105F6A04 If $m\ge 3$ and $u:\mathbb R^ m\to S^{N-1}$ is a stationary weak harmonic map with $\int _{\mathbb R^ m}|Du|^2<\infty $, then $u$ is constant almost everywhere. The same conclusion holds for a smooth harmonic map under this energy hypothesis. Dimension two admits nonconstant finite-energy examples. Proof For any fixed $r>0$, monotonicity gives $0\le \Theta _ u(0,r)\le \Theta _ u(0,R)\le \frac12R^{2-m}\int _{\mathbb R^ m}|Du|^2\to 0$. Thus $Du=0$ almost everywhere on each centered ball and hence on all of $\mathbb R^ m$. The standard line characterization of Sobolev functions on connected domains gives an almost-everywhere constant representative. Smooth harmonic maps satisfy stationarity by Proposition 17.1.2 . Example 16.9.3 below gives the dimension-two contrast. $\square$
