title: 16.9 Harmonic-map singularities and concentration
search_title: Harmonic-map singularities and concentration
text: These examples make the scale-invariant energy in Section 17.1 concrete and connect it with weak convergence of Radon measures. The harmonic-map and stereographic framework is described in [ Hel01 ] , Chapters 2–4; the energy, weak formulation and concentration calculations are given here. Example 16.9.1 (The radial projection is a singular stationary map) . 6F437F387AA3 For $m\ge 3$, the map $u(x)=x/|x|$ on $\mathbb R^ m\setminus \{ 0\} $, with any value assigned at zero, belongs to $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ m;S^{m-1})$ and is a stationary weak harmonic map. It has \[  |Du|^2=\frac{m-1}{|x|^2},\qquad \Theta _ u(0,r)=\frac{(m-1)|S^{m-1}|}{2(m-2)}.  \] It has no continuous representative at the origin. Stationarity here does not assert energy minimization or stability. Proof For $r=|x|>0$, $Du=r^{-1}(I-u\otimes u)$, so its squared norm is $(m-1)r^{-2}$, its radial derivative is zero, and $\Delta u=-(m-1)r^{-2}u$. The energy is locally integrable precisely when $m>2$. Integration by parts for first derivatives on a punctured ball has an inner boundary term bounded by $C\varepsilon ^{m-1}$, which tends to zero; thus the displayed classical derivative is the weak derivative across zero. For the weak equation, integrate against a compactly supported smooth vector test outside $B_\varepsilon $. The normal derivative of $u$ on the inner sphere is zero, so the Laplacian integration has no inner boundary term. The integrable quantities pass to the limit and give the weak equation. For domain stationarity, the stress tensor is divergence-free away from zero. On a sphere its radial flux is $S\nu =e\nu $, with $e=(m-1)/(2\varepsilon ^2)$. In the boundary integral against $X$, the constant term $X(0)$ integrates to zero by symmetry. Since $X(x)-X(0)=O(\varepsilon )$, the remaining flux is $O(\varepsilon ^{m-2})\to 0$. This proves stationarity across zero. Polar integration gives $E(B_ r)=(m-1)|S^{m-1}|r^{m-2}/(2(m-2))$, proving the density. Distinct radial limits rule out a continuous representative. $\square$ Example 16.9.2 (The planar vortex fails the finite-energy hypothesis) . 94F25D3E2F67 The map $u(x)=x/|x|$ from a punctured planar disk to $S^1$ is smooth and harmonic there, but it is not in $W^{1,2}$ on any disk containing the origin. On $\{ \varepsilon <|x|<R\} $ its Dirichlet energy is $\pi \log (R/\varepsilon )$. Proof The same derivative formula as in Example 16.9.1 , now with $m=2$, gives $|Du|^2=r^{-2}$. Hence $E=\frac12\int _\varepsilon ^ R2\pi r^{-1}dr=\pi \log (R/\varepsilon )$, which diverges as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Altering the map at the single origin cannot change this integral. Thus the punctured-domain harmonic equation does not put this map within the finite-energy weak theory at the origin. $\square$ Example 16.9.3 (A spherical bubble concentrates its energy at one point) . F069D399A85D Let $u$ be the stereographic map in Example 16.8.3 , and put $u_\lambda (x)=u(x/\lambda )$ for $\lambda >0$. Each is smooth and harmonic on $\mathbb R^2$, and \[  e_\lambda (x)=\tfrac 12|Du_\lambda (x)|^2=\frac{4\lambda ^2}{(\lambda ^2+|x|^2)^2},\qquad \int _{\mathbb R^2}e_\lambda =4\pi .  \] As $\lambda \downarrow 0$, the maps converge strongly in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and weakly in $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to the south pole $(0,0,-1)$, whereas their energy measures converge weakly to $4\pi \delta _0$. Their gradients do not converge strongly in $L^2$ on a neighborhood of zero. Proof Scaling preserves the two-dimensional harmonic-map equation. The derivative formula in Example 16.8.3 gives the displayed density, and polar integration gives \[  \int _{B_ R}e_\lambda =8\pi \lambda ^2\int _0^ R\frac{r}{(\lambda ^2+r^2)^2}dr =4\pi \frac{R^2}{\lambda ^2+R^2}.  \] The limit as $R\to \infty $ is $4\pi $. At every nonzero point $u_\lambda $ converges to the south pole. Its norm is one, so dominated convergence gives strong local $L^2$ convergence. The total gradient norm is uniformly bounded. Any weakly convergent gradient subsequence has distributional limit zero, determined by the strong convergence of the maps; weak compactness and uniqueness of this limit give weak convergence for the entire family on each relatively compact domain. For a continuous compactly supported test function $f$, change variables $x=\lambda y$ to obtain \[  \int f(x)e_\lambda (x)dx=\int _{\mathbb R^2}f(\lambda y)\frac4{(1+|y|^2)^2}dy\longrightarrow 4\pi f(0)  \] by dominated convergence. The positive mass remaining in every $B_ R$ prevents strong gradient convergence to zero. Thus the weak limit of the energy measures differs from the energy measure of the limiting map. $\square$ Example 16.9.4 (Higher-degree spherical bubbles) . 2A3E375B030F Identify $\mathbb R^2$ with $\mathbb C$. For every integer $k\ge 1$, the smooth map $v_ k(z)=u(z^ k)$, where $u$ is the preceding stereographic map, is harmonic and has energy density \[  e_ k(z)=\frac{4k^2|z|^{2k-2}}{(1+|z|^{2k})^2},\qquad E(v_ k;\mathbb R^2)=4\pi k.  \] The rescalings $v_ k(z/\lambda )$ concentrate energy $4\pi k$ at zero. For $k>1$ the differential vanishes at zero, but the map is smooth there. Proof Away from zero, $z\mapsto z^ k$ is a local conformal coordinate change, so harmonicity follows from conformal invariance. The rational expression defining $u(z^ k)$ is smooth at zero; consequently the harmonic-map equation extends there by continuity. The derivative of $z^ k$ has conformal scale $k|z|^{k-1}$, proving the density. Polar integration and $s=r^{2k}$ give \[  E=8\pi k^2\int _0^\infty \frac{r^{2k-1}}{(1+r^{2k})^2}dr =4\pi k\int _0^\infty \frac{ds}{(1+s)^2}=4\pi k.  \] The measure-concentration argument is the same change of variables and dominated convergence as in Example 16.9.3 , using the integrable density $e_ k$. The power map has zero derivative at zero when $k>1$, which proves the last assertion. These explicit examples do not claim a general energy-quantization theorem for arbitrary weakly convergent harmonic maps. $\square$

title: Example 16.9.1 (The radial projection is a singular stationary map)
search_title: The radial projection is a singular stationary map
text: Example 16.9.1 (The radial projection is a singular stationary map) . 6F437F387AA3 For $m\ge 3$, the map $u(x)=x/|x|$ on $\mathbb R^ m\setminus \{ 0\} $, with any value assigned at zero, belongs to $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ m;S^{m-1})$ and is a stationary weak harmonic map. It has \[  |Du|^2=\frac{m-1}{|x|^2},\qquad \Theta _ u(0,r)=\frac{(m-1)|S^{m-1}|}{2(m-2)}.  \] It has no continuous representative at the origin. Stationarity here does not assert energy minimization or stability. Proof For $r=|x|>0$, $Du=r^{-1}(I-u\otimes u)$, so its squared norm is $(m-1)r^{-2}$, its radial derivative is zero, and $\Delta u=-(m-1)r^{-2}u$. The energy is locally integrable precisely when $m>2$. Integration by parts for first derivatives on a punctured ball has an inner boundary term bounded by $C\varepsilon ^{m-1}$, which tends to zero; thus the displayed classical derivative is the weak derivative across zero. For the weak equation, integrate against a compactly supported smooth vector test outside $B_\varepsilon $. The normal derivative of $u$ on the inner sphere is zero, so the Laplacian integration has no inner boundary term. The integrable quantities pass to the limit and give the weak equation. For domain stationarity, the stress tensor is divergence-free away from zero. On a sphere its radial flux is $S\nu =e\nu $, with $e=(m-1)/(2\varepsilon ^2)$. In the boundary integral against $X$, the constant term $X(0)$ integrates to zero by symmetry. Since $X(x)-X(0)=O(\varepsilon )$, the remaining flux is $O(\varepsilon ^{m-2})\to 0$. This proves stationarity across zero. Polar integration gives $E(B_ r)=(m-1)|S^{m-1}|r^{m-2}/(2(m-2))$, proving the density. Distinct radial limits rule out a continuous representative. $\square$

title: Example 16.9.2 (The planar vortex fails the finite-energy hypothesis)
search_title: The planar vortex fails the finite-energy hypothesis
text: Example 16.9.2 (The planar vortex fails the finite-energy hypothesis) . 94F25D3E2F67 The map $u(x)=x/|x|$ from a punctured planar disk to $S^1$ is smooth and harmonic there, but it is not in $W^{1,2}$ on any disk containing the origin. On $\{ \varepsilon <|x|<R\} $ its Dirichlet energy is $\pi \log (R/\varepsilon )$. Proof The same derivative formula as in Example 16.9.1 , now with $m=2$, gives $|Du|^2=r^{-2}$. Hence $E=\frac12\int _\varepsilon ^ R2\pi r^{-1}dr=\pi \log (R/\varepsilon )$, which diverges as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Altering the map at the single origin cannot change this integral. Thus the punctured-domain harmonic equation does not put this map within the finite-energy weak theory at the origin. $\square$

title: Example 16.9.3 (A spherical bubble concentrates its energy at one point)
search_title: A spherical bubble concentrates its energy at one point
text: Example 16.9.3 (A spherical bubble concentrates its energy at one point) . F069D399A85D Let $u$ be the stereographic map in Example 16.8.3 , and put $u_\lambda (x)=u(x/\lambda )$ for $\lambda >0$. Each is smooth and harmonic on $\mathbb R^2$, and \[  e_\lambda (x)=\tfrac 12|Du_\lambda (x)|^2=\frac{4\lambda ^2}{(\lambda ^2+|x|^2)^2},\qquad \int _{\mathbb R^2}e_\lambda =4\pi .  \] As $\lambda \downarrow 0$, the maps converge strongly in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and weakly in $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to the south pole $(0,0,-1)$, whereas their energy measures converge weakly to $4\pi \delta _0$. Their gradients do not converge strongly in $L^2$ on a neighborhood of zero. Proof Scaling preserves the two-dimensional harmonic-map equation. The derivative formula in Example 16.8.3 gives the displayed density, and polar integration gives \[  \int _{B_ R}e_\lambda =8\pi \lambda ^2\int _0^ R\frac{r}{(\lambda ^2+r^2)^2}dr =4\pi \frac{R^2}{\lambda ^2+R^2}.  \] The limit as $R\to \infty $ is $4\pi $. At every nonzero point $u_\lambda $ converges to the south pole. Its norm is one, so dominated convergence gives strong local $L^2$ convergence. The total gradient norm is uniformly bounded. Any weakly convergent gradient subsequence has distributional limit zero, determined by the strong convergence of the maps; weak compactness and uniqueness of this limit give weak convergence for the entire family on each relatively compact domain. For a continuous compactly supported test function $f$, change variables $x=\lambda y$ to obtain \[  \int f(x)e_\lambda (x)dx=\int _{\mathbb R^2}f(\lambda y)\frac4{(1+|y|^2)^2}dy\longrightarrow 4\pi f(0)  \] by dominated convergence. The positive mass remaining in every $B_ R$ prevents strong gradient convergence to zero. Thus the weak limit of the energy measures differs from the energy measure of the limiting map. $\square$

title: Example 16.9.4 (Higher-degree spherical bubbles)
search_title: Higher-degree spherical bubbles
text: Example 16.9.4 (Higher-degree spherical bubbles) . 2A3E375B030F Identify $\mathbb R^2$ with $\mathbb C$. For every integer $k\ge 1$, the smooth map $v_ k(z)=u(z^ k)$, where $u$ is the preceding stereographic map, is harmonic and has energy density \[  e_ k(z)=\frac{4k^2|z|^{2k-2}}{(1+|z|^{2k})^2},\qquad E(v_ k;\mathbb R^2)=4\pi k.  \] The rescalings $v_ k(z/\lambda )$ concentrate energy $4\pi k$ at zero. For $k>1$ the differential vanishes at zero, but the map is smooth there. Proof Away from zero, $z\mapsto z^ k$ is a local conformal coordinate change, so harmonicity follows from conformal invariance. The rational expression defining $u(z^ k)$ is smooth at zero; consequently the harmonic-map equation extends there by continuity. The derivative of $z^ k$ has conformal scale $k|z|^{k-1}$, proving the density. Polar integration and $s=r^{2k}$ give \[  E=8\pi k^2\int _0^\infty \frac{r^{2k-1}}{(1+r^{2k})^2}dr =4\pi k\int _0^\infty \frac{ds}{(1+s)^2}=4\pi k.  \] The measure-concentration argument is the same change of variables and dominated convergence as in Example 16.9.3 , using the integrable density $e_ k$. The power map has zero derivative at zero when $k>1$, which proves the last assertion. These explicit examples do not claim a general energy-quantization theorem for arbitrary weakly convergent harmonic maps. $\square$

The graph equation and conserved quantity are described in [ Maz02 ] , Section 2.1, p. 4. The rotational metric and curvature formulas are also in [ BBM13 ] , pp. 2–3. We use trace mean curvature with $A=D
u $ and derive the signs and arclength equations directly. Proposition 11.10.1 (Geometry of an arclength surface of revolution) . 321B1FEAB359 Let $(r(s),z(s))$ be a smooth plane curve on an interval, with $r>0$ and $(r')^2+(z')^2=1$. Write $r'=\cos \psi $, $z'=\sin \psi $ for a smooth angle lift. The immersion \[  F(s,	heta )=(r(s)\cos 	heta ,r(s)\sin 	heta ,z(s))  \] has metric $ds^2+r^2d	heta ^2$. Relative to $
u =(z'\cos 	heta ,z'\sin 	heta ,-r')$, its principal curvatures are $\psi '$ and $z'/r$. Thus its trace mean curvature is $H=\psi '+\sin \psi /r$. Proof The coordinate derivatives are orthogonal, with lengths one and $r$. The indicated normal is orthogonal to both and has length one. Differentiation gives $D_ s
u =\psi 'F_ s$ and $D_	heta 
u =(z'/r)F_	heta $. These are the two eigenvalue equations for the shape operator. A smooth angle lift exists on any interval because the tangent takes values in the circle; it may wind, so no fixed principal branch of the angle is required. $\square$ Proposition 11.10.2 (The rotational CMC system and local uniqueness) . 875DC79A9E8E A rotational arclength immersion has constant trace curvature $H$ precisely when \[  r'=\cos \psi ,\qquad z'=\sin \psi ,\qquad \psi '=H- rac{\sin \psi }{r}.  \] For any initial data with $r>0$, this system has a unique smooth local solution. Its first integral is \[  c=r\sin \psi - rac H2r^2.  \] Proof The curvature formula gives the system. Its right side is smooth for $r>0$, so the ordinary local existence and uniqueness theorem applies. Differentiation along a solution yields \[  c'=\cos \psi \sin \psi +r\cos \psi \left(H- rac{\sin \psi }{r}ight)-Hr\cos \psi =0.  \] Thus $c$ is constant throughout the interval of existence. The ODE theorem is a background analytic input; this statement gives no continuation through $r=0$. $\square$ Proposition 11.10.3 (The cylindrical graph equation) . B7727F541343 For a positive smooth function $r=r(z)$, the cylindrical graph $(r(z)\cos 	heta ,r(z)\sin 	heta ,z)$, oriented by its outward radial normal, has trace mean curvature \[  H= rac1{r\sqrt{1+r_ z^2}}- rac{r_{zz}}{(1+r_ z^2)^{3/2}}.  \] For constant $H$ its equation and first integral are \[  r_{zz}= rac{1+r_ z^2}{r}-H(1+r_ z^2)^{3/2},\qquad c= rac r{\sqrt{1+r_ z^2}}- rac H2r^2.  \] Proof Reparametrize the meridian by arclength increasing with $z$. Then $z_ s=(1+r_ z^2)^{-1/2}$, $r_ s=r_ z(1+r_ z^2)^{-1/2}$, and the tangent angle satisfies $\psi _ s=-r_{zz}(1+r_ z^2)^{-3/2}$. Substitute into Proposition 11.10.1 and solve for $r_{zz}$. The conserved quantity is the preceding first integral with $\sin \psi =z_ s$. At $H=1$, this is equation (1) in [ Maz02 ] , p. 4. The first integral used there is $-2c$. $\square$ Proposition 11.10.4 (The first integral from area minus volume) . 70AC5E706A80 For fixed endpoint radii of a cylindrical graph, critical points of area minus $H$ times enclosed volume satisfy the ODE in Proposition 11.10.3 . The translation-invariant one-dimensional integrand is \[  L(r,p)=2\pi r\sqrt{1+p^2}-H\pi r^2,  \] and its Beltrami quantity $L-pL_ p$ equals $2\pi c$. Proof The lateral area element is $r\sqrt{1+r_ z^2}\, d	heta \, dz$, and the volume between fixed axial planes is $\int \pi r^2dz$. Endpoint-fixed variations kill boundary terms. Direct differentiation gives \[  L_ r=2\pi \sqrt{1+p^2}-2\pi Hr,\qquad L_ p= rac{2\pi rp}{\sqrt{1+p^2}}.  \] The equation $(L_ p)'=L_ r$ simplifies to the stated graph ODE. Because $L$ has no explicit $z$ dependence, $(L-r_ zL_ p)'=r_ z(L_ r-(L_ p)')=0$. Evaluating $L-r_ zL_ p$ gives $2\pi [r/\sqrt{1+r_ z^2}-Hr^2/2]$. This is a stationarity calculation; it does not assert that a critical graph minimizes area under the volume constraint. $\square$ Lemma 11.10.5 (Factoring the positive-flux radius equation) . 739CD651E3E2 Fix $H>0$, $0<a<1/H$, $b=2/H-a$, and $c=Hab/2$. Then \[  r^2-\left( rac H2r^2+cight)^2 = rac{H^2}4(b^2-r^2)(r^2-a^2).  \] In an arclength solution with this flux and $z'>0$, the radius belongs to $[a,b]$ and satisfies \[  (r')^2= rac{H^2}{4r^2}(b^2-r^2)(r^2-a^2),\qquad z'= rac H2r+ rac cr.  \] Proof Use $a+b=2/H$ and $ab=2c/H$ to compare coefficients in the polynomial identity. The conserved quantity gives $z'=Hr/2+c/r>0$, and $r'^2+z'^2=1$ gives the displayed radius equation. Its left side is nonnegative and $r>0$, so the factorization forces $a\le r\le b$. The squared equation alone is not a uniqueness statement at a turning radius; the smooth second-order system in Proposition 11.10.2 retains that information. $\square$

title: 16.10 Unduloids and their geometric limits
search_title: Unduloids and their geometric limits
text: The Delaunay unduloids interpolate between cylinders and a singular chain of spheres. The underlying graph family is described in [ Maz02 ] , Section 2.1, and the roulette parametrizations in [ BBM13 ] . The arclength formula below gives direct proofs of completeness, embeddedness, and several limits without invoking a classification of arbitrary complete CMC surfaces. Theorem 16.10.1 (An explicit arclength construction of unduloids) . BE8597CDC05A Fix $H>0$ and $0<a<1/H$, put $b=2/H-a$ and $c=Hab/2$, and define for all $s\in \mathbb R$ \[  r_ a(s)=\sqrt{a^2+(b^2-a^2)\sin ^2(Hs/2)},\qquad z_ a(s)=\int _0^ s\left(\frac H2r_ a(t)+\frac c{r_ a(t)}\right)dt.  \] Then $F_ a(s,\theta )=(r_ a(s)\cos \theta ,r_ a(s)\sin \theta ,z_ a(s))$ is a smooth rotational CMC immersion of trace curvature $H$, with $s$ arclength and outward radial normal as in Proposition 11.10.1 . Its neck radius is $a$ and bulge radius $b$. These realize the unduloids of [ Maz02 ] , p. 4, after scaling its $H=1$ normalization. Proof All expressions are smooth because $r_ a\ge a>0$. With $w=r_ a^2$, differentiation gives $(w')^2=H^2(b^2-w)(w-a^2)$. Lemma 11.10.5 therefore implies $(r_ a')^2+(z_ a')^2=1$. Moreover $z_ a'>0$, so the tangent angle can be chosen smoothly with $\sin \psi >0$. The flux $r_ a z_ a'-Hr_ a^2/2$ is identically $c$. On the open intervals where $r_ a'\ne 0$, differentiation gives $\psi '=H-\sin \psi /r_ a$. The zeros of $r_ a'$ are discrete, and smoothness extends this identity across them. The curvature formula proves the assertion. The sine formula attains its minimum and maximum, giving the radii. Local uniqueness of the smooth system identifies these solutions with the graph family having the same neck data. $\square$ Proposition 16.10.2 (Periodicity, completeness, and embeddedness) . 90B100F75094 The radius in Theorem 16.10.1 has period $P=2\pi /H$, and \[  F_ a(s+P,\theta )=F_ a(s,\theta )+L_ a e_3,\qquad L_ a=\int _0^ P\left(\frac H2r_ a+\frac c{r_ a}\right)ds>0.  \] The map on $\mathbb R\times S^1$ is a complete proper embedding. In particular the surface is a global positive cylindrical graph. Proof The sine-squared formula gives the radius period and hence the periodicity of $z_ a'$, proving the translation formula. The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality and the arclength identity give $\sqrt{2Hc}\le z_ a'\le 1$. Thus $z_ a$ is strictly increasing and tends to $\pm \infty $ at the respective ends. The height recovers $s$ uniquely, and $r_ a>0$ then recovers the angular coordinate, proving injectivity. Bounded ambient sets bound the height and hence $s$; together with compactness of $S^1$, this proves properness. The induced metric $ds^2+r_ a^2d\theta ^2$ dominates the complete product metric $ds^2+a^2d\theta ^2$. An intrinsic Cauchy sequence converges for the product metric, and local smooth equivalence gives convergence in the induced metric. Finally the strictly monotone height gives the claimed global graph. $\square$ Proposition 16.10.3 (The cylinder limit) . F8523D2477AD As $a\uparrow 1/H$, the parametrizations $F_ a$ converge smoothly on compact subsets to the cylinder $(H^{-1}\cos \theta ,H^{-1}\sin \theta ,s)$. The axial translation lengths satisfy $L_ a\to 2\pi /H$. Proof Then $b\to 1/H$, $c\to 1/(2H)$, and the explicit radius converges to $1/H$ with all derivatives on compact intervals. The integrand defining $z_ a$ converges smoothly to one. Thus $z_ a\to s$ smoothly, and integration over the fixed interval $[0,2\pi /H]$ proves the period limit. The limiting cylinder has every axial translation as a symmetry; the limiting value is the limit of the chosen unduloid periods, not a smallest positive period of the cylinder. $\square$ Proposition 16.10.4 (The chain-of-spheres limit) . 05473488A6C3 As $a\downarrow 0$, $F_ a$ converges uniformly on compact parameter sets to a chain of radius-$2/H$ spheres tangent along the rotation axis. The convergence is smooth away from the neck parameters $s\in (2\pi /H)\mathbb Z$, and $L_ a\to 4/H$. The limiting image is not a smooth embedded surface at its contact points, and the displayed limiting parametrization is not an immersion there. Proof The radius converges uniformly on compact intervals to $(2/H)|\sin (Hs/2)|$, smoothly where the sine is nonzero. On such intervals $c/r_ a\to 0$ smoothly, so $z_ a'\to |\sin (Hs/2)|$. Since $0<z_ a'\le 1$, dominated convergence gives convergence in $L^1$ on compact intervals and hence uniform convergence of its primitives. On $0\le s\le 2\pi /H$ the limit is \[  r_0(s)=\frac2H\sin (Hs/2),\qquad z_0(s)=\frac2H(1-\cos (Hs/2)).  \] Consequently $r_0^2+(z_0-2/H)^2=4/H^2$, and rotation gives one sphere. Its poles are at heights zero and $4/H$. The limiting translation formula repeats it into a tangent chain. Integrating the limiting axial derivative proves $L_ a\to 4/H$. Two spherical sheets meet at each contact, so the union is not locally an embedded smooth surface; the limiting parametrization collapses an angular circle at each such point. This does not rule out representing the individual spheres by a smooth immersion from a disjoint union of spheres. $\square$ Proposition 16.10.5 (A shrinking neck converges to a catenoid after dilation) . FFB833611784 As $a\downarrow 0$, dilate the unduloid by $1/a$ about its neck at height zero and use $s=a\xi $. Then \[  a^{-1}F_ a(a\xi ,\theta )\longrightarrow \big (\sqrt{1+\xi ^2}\cos \theta ,\sqrt{1+\xi ^2}\sin \theta ,\operatorname {arsinh}\xi \big )  \] smoothly on compact subsets of $\mathbb R\times S^1$. The limit is the radius-one catenoid in arclength coordinates. The rescaled trace mean curvature is $aH\to 0$. Proof From the radius formula, \[  \frac{r_ a(a\xi )^2}{a^2}=1+(b^2-a^2)\left(\frac{\sin (Ha\xi /2)}a\right)^2\longrightarrow 1+\xi ^2.  \] The sine quotient extends smoothly to $a=0$ on compact $\xi $ intervals. Taking the positive square root preserves smooth convergence. Write this radius ratio as $R_ a$. The derivative in $\xi $ of $z_ a(a\xi )/a$ is \[  \frac{Ha}{2}R_ a+\frac{c/a}{R_ a}\longrightarrow \frac1{\sqrt{1+\xi ^2}},  \] since $c/a=Hb/2\to 1$. The primitives vanish at zero, so they converge smoothly to $\operatorname {arsinh}\xi $. Substituting $\xi =\sinh v$ gives $(\cosh v\cos \theta ,\cosh v\sin \theta ,v)$, the catenoid of Example 16.2.2 . Dilation by $1/a$ multiplies principal curvatures by $a$, proving the final assertion. $\square$ Example 16.10.6 (A round sphere is only a local positive cylindrical graph) . 217BEE2C9F5E For $H>0$, the graph $r(z)=\sqrt{4/H^2-z^2}$ on $|z|<2/H$ solves the CMC graph equation and has flux zero. It is positive on its domain but is not periodic and does not extend as a positive graph over all $\mathbb R$. Proof Its rotation is the radius-$2/H$ sphere away from its poles, with outward trace curvature $H$. Also $\sqrt{1+r_ z^2}=2/(Hr)$, so $r/\sqrt{1+r_ z^2}-Hr^2/2=0$. The radius tends to zero at the two finite endpoints. This shows why periodicity statements for positive solutions need their global-domain and flux hypotheses; positivity on an arbitrary interval is insufficient. $\square$ Proposition 16.10.7 (The stability threshold for a periodic cylinder) . 7E7A8D1960C5 In the flat three-manifold $\mathbb R^2\times (\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)$ with $L>0$, the radius-$R$ cylinder is a closed CMC boundary of trace curvature $1/R$. Its volume-constrained index and nullity are \[  \operatorname {ind}_0=2\# \{ j\in \mathbb N:j<L/(2\pi R)\} ,\qquad \operatorname {nul}_0=2+2\, \mathbf1_{\{ L/(2\pi R)\in \mathbb N\} },  \] where $\mathbb N=\{ 1,2,\ldots \} $. Its unrestricted index is $1+\operatorname {ind}_0$. It is volume-constrained stable if and only if $L\le 2\pi R$. Proof The cylinder bounds the solid torus $B_ R^2\times (\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)$, so the usual volume constraint applies in this ambient quotient. Its metric is $R^2d\theta ^2+dz^2$, its principal curvatures are $1/R$ and zero, and the ambient Ricci tensor is zero. Thus the CMC second-variation form is \[  Q(f,f)=\int \left(R^{-2}|f_\theta |^2+|f_ z|^2-R^{-2}f^2\right)dA.  \] Fourier expansion in both periodic variables diagonalizes the form. On the complex mode $e^{ik\theta }e^{2\pi ijz/L}$, the eigenvalue of $-J$ is \[  \frac{k^2-1}{R^2}+\left(\frac{2\pi j}L\right)^2,\qquad k,j\in \mathbb Z.  \] The mean-zero condition removes exactly the constant mode. Negative eigenvalues can then occur only when $k=0$ and $0<|j|<L/(2\pi R)$. Each positive $j$ contributes a real sine/cosine pair, proving the constrained index. The always-present zero modes are $\cos \theta ,\sin \theta $, induced by horizontal translations. Two further axial modes occur precisely when $j=L/(2\pi R)$ is a positive integer. No other pairs have eigenvalue zero. For the bilinear kernel on the constrained space the same computation applies, since Fourier orthogonality separates the removed constant mode. Reinstating that mode adds one negative direction. The index vanishes precisely at the stated threshold. This is a compact example in the flat quotient, not an embedded compact CMC surface in Euclidean three-space. $\square$ Example 16.10.8 (The infinite cylinder is unstable under compactly supported volume constraints) . AAED8665BA97 The round cylinder $S_ R^1\times \mathbb R\subset \mathbb R^3$ has a smooth compactly supported normal speed $f$ with $\int f\, dA=0$ and $Q(f,f)<0$. Thus even the first-order volume constraint does not make the infinite cylinder stable. Proof Choose a nonzero odd smooth function $\eta \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ and set $f_ T(\theta ,z)=\eta (z/T)$. The integral of the speed vanishes by oddness. Direct substitution into the cylinder form gives \[  Q(f_ T,f_ T)=2\pi R\left(T^{-1}\int _{\mathbb R}|\eta '|^2 -\frac T{R^2}\int _{\mathbb R}\eta ^2\right)<0  \] for sufficiently large $T$. The support is compact on the cylinder. If an exactly volume-preserving path is desired, add a second compactly supported normal variation with nonzero integral and solve for its coefficient by the same implicit-function argument as Proposition 11.3.2 . Here volume means the signed change in the bounded region affected by the compactly supported perturbation, not the infinite total volume of the solid cylinder. The zero first derivative of that correction preserves the displayed negative second variation. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.10.1 (An explicit arclength construction of unduloids)
search_title: An explicit arclength construction of unduloids
text: Theorem 16.10.1 (An explicit arclength construction of unduloids) . BE8597CDC05A Fix $H>0$ and $0<a<1/H$, put $b=2/H-a$ and $c=Hab/2$, and define for all $s\in \mathbb R$ \[  r_ a(s)=\sqrt{a^2+(b^2-a^2)\sin ^2(Hs/2)},\qquad z_ a(s)=\int _0^ s\left(\frac H2r_ a(t)+\frac c{r_ a(t)}\right)dt.  \] Then $F_ a(s,\theta )=(r_ a(s)\cos \theta ,r_ a(s)\sin \theta ,z_ a(s))$ is a smooth rotational CMC immersion of trace curvature $H$, with $s$ arclength and outward radial normal as in Proposition 11.10.1 . Its neck radius is $a$ and bulge radius $b$. These realize the unduloids of [ Maz02 ] , p. 4, after scaling its $H=1$ normalization. Proof All expressions are smooth because $r_ a\ge a>0$. With $w=r_ a^2$, differentiation gives $(w')^2=H^2(b^2-w)(w-a^2)$. Lemma 11.10.5 therefore implies $(r_ a')^2+(z_ a')^2=1$. Moreover $z_ a'>0$, so the tangent angle can be chosen smoothly with $\sin \psi >0$. The flux $r_ a z_ a'-Hr_ a^2/2$ is identically $c$. On the open intervals where $r_ a'\ne 0$, differentiation gives $\psi '=H-\sin \psi /r_ a$. The zeros of $r_ a'$ are discrete, and smoothness extends this identity across them. The curvature formula proves the assertion. The sine formula attains its minimum and maximum, giving the radii. Local uniqueness of the smooth system identifies these solutions with the graph family having the same neck data. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.10.2 (Periodicity, completeness, and embeddedness)
search_title: Periodicity, completeness, and embeddedness
text: Proposition 16.10.2 (Periodicity, completeness, and embeddedness) . 90B100F75094 The radius in Theorem 16.10.1 has period $P=2\pi /H$, and \[  F_ a(s+P,\theta )=F_ a(s,\theta )+L_ a e_3,\qquad L_ a=\int _0^ P\left(\frac H2r_ a+\frac c{r_ a}\right)ds>0.  \] The map on $\mathbb R\times S^1$ is a complete proper embedding. In particular the surface is a global positive cylindrical graph. Proof The sine-squared formula gives the radius period and hence the periodicity of $z_ a'$, proving the translation formula. The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality and the arclength identity give $\sqrt{2Hc}\le z_ a'\le 1$. Thus $z_ a$ is strictly increasing and tends to $\pm \infty $ at the respective ends. The height recovers $s$ uniquely, and $r_ a>0$ then recovers the angular coordinate, proving injectivity. Bounded ambient sets bound the height and hence $s$; together with compactness of $S^1$, this proves properness. The induced metric $ds^2+r_ a^2d\theta ^2$ dominates the complete product metric $ds^2+a^2d\theta ^2$. An intrinsic Cauchy sequence converges for the product metric, and local smooth equivalence gives convergence in the induced metric. Finally the strictly monotone height gives the claimed global graph. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.10.3 (The cylinder limit)
search_title: The cylinder limit
text: Proposition 16.10.3 (The cylinder limit) . F8523D2477AD As $a\uparrow 1/H$, the parametrizations $F_ a$ converge smoothly on compact subsets to the cylinder $(H^{-1}\cos \theta ,H^{-1}\sin \theta ,s)$. The axial translation lengths satisfy $L_ a\to 2\pi /H$. Proof Then $b\to 1/H$, $c\to 1/(2H)$, and the explicit radius converges to $1/H$ with all derivatives on compact intervals. The integrand defining $z_ a$ converges smoothly to one. Thus $z_ a\to s$ smoothly, and integration over the fixed interval $[0,2\pi /H]$ proves the period limit. The limiting cylinder has every axial translation as a symmetry; the limiting value is the limit of the chosen unduloid periods, not a smallest positive period of the cylinder. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.10.4 (The chain-of-spheres limit)
search_title: The chain-of-spheres limit
text: Proposition 16.10.4 (The chain-of-spheres limit) . 05473488A6C3 As $a\downarrow 0$, $F_ a$ converges uniformly on compact parameter sets to a chain of radius-$2/H$ spheres tangent along the rotation axis. The convergence is smooth away from the neck parameters $s\in (2\pi /H)\mathbb Z$, and $L_ a\to 4/H$. The limiting image is not a smooth embedded surface at its contact points, and the displayed limiting parametrization is not an immersion there. Proof The radius converges uniformly on compact intervals to $(2/H)|\sin (Hs/2)|$, smoothly where the sine is nonzero. On such intervals $c/r_ a\to 0$ smoothly, so $z_ a'\to |\sin (Hs/2)|$. Since $0<z_ a'\le 1$, dominated convergence gives convergence in $L^1$ on compact intervals and hence uniform convergence of its primitives. On $0\le s\le 2\pi /H$ the limit is \[  r_0(s)=\frac2H\sin (Hs/2),\qquad z_0(s)=\frac2H(1-\cos (Hs/2)).  \] Consequently $r_0^2+(z_0-2/H)^2=4/H^2$, and rotation gives one sphere. Its poles are at heights zero and $4/H$. The limiting translation formula repeats it into a tangent chain. Integrating the limiting axial derivative proves $L_ a\to 4/H$. Two spherical sheets meet at each contact, so the union is not locally an embedded smooth surface; the limiting parametrization collapses an angular circle at each such point. This does not rule out representing the individual spheres by a smooth immersion from a disjoint union of spheres. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.10.5 (A shrinking neck converges to a catenoid after dilation)
search_title: A shrinking neck converges to a catenoid after dilation
text: Proposition 16.10.5 (A shrinking neck converges to a catenoid after dilation) . FFB833611784 As $a\downarrow 0$, dilate the unduloid by $1/a$ about its neck at height zero and use $s=a\xi $. Then \[  a^{-1}F_ a(a\xi ,\theta )\longrightarrow \big (\sqrt{1+\xi ^2}\cos \theta ,\sqrt{1+\xi ^2}\sin \theta ,\operatorname {arsinh}\xi \big )  \] smoothly on compact subsets of $\mathbb R\times S^1$. The limit is the radius-one catenoid in arclength coordinates. The rescaled trace mean curvature is $aH\to 0$. Proof From the radius formula, \[  \frac{r_ a(a\xi )^2}{a^2}=1+(b^2-a^2)\left(\frac{\sin (Ha\xi /2)}a\right)^2\longrightarrow 1+\xi ^2.  \] The sine quotient extends smoothly to $a=0$ on compact $\xi $ intervals. Taking the positive square root preserves smooth convergence. Write this radius ratio as $R_ a$. The derivative in $\xi $ of $z_ a(a\xi )/a$ is \[  \frac{Ha}{2}R_ a+\frac{c/a}{R_ a}\longrightarrow \frac1{\sqrt{1+\xi ^2}},  \] since $c/a=Hb/2\to 1$. The primitives vanish at zero, so they converge smoothly to $\operatorname {arsinh}\xi $. Substituting $\xi =\sinh v$ gives $(\cosh v\cos \theta ,\cosh v\sin \theta ,v)$, the catenoid of Example 16.2.2 . Dilation by $1/a$ multiplies principal curvatures by $a$, proving the final assertion. $\square$

title: Example 16.10.6 (A round sphere is only a local positive cylindrical graph)
search_title: A round sphere is only a local positive cylindrical graph
text: Example 16.10.6 (A round sphere is only a local positive cylindrical graph) . 217BEE2C9F5E For $H>0$, the graph $r(z)=\sqrt{4/H^2-z^2}$ on $|z|<2/H$ solves the CMC graph equation and has flux zero. It is positive on its domain but is not periodic and does not extend as a positive graph over all $\mathbb R$. Proof Its rotation is the radius-$2/H$ sphere away from its poles, with outward trace curvature $H$. Also $\sqrt{1+r_ z^2}=2/(Hr)$, so $r/\sqrt{1+r_ z^2}-Hr^2/2=0$. The radius tends to zero at the two finite endpoints. This shows why periodicity statements for positive solutions need their global-domain and flux hypotheses; positivity on an arbitrary interval is insufficient. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.10.7 (The stability threshold for a periodic cylinder)
search_title: The stability threshold for a periodic cylinder
text: Proposition 16.10.7 (The stability threshold for a periodic cylinder) . 7E7A8D1960C5 In the flat three-manifold $\mathbb R^2\times (\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)$ with $L>0$, the radius-$R$ cylinder is a closed CMC boundary of trace curvature $1/R$. Its volume-constrained index and nullity are \[  \operatorname {ind}_0=2\# \{ j\in \mathbb N:j<L/(2\pi R)\} ,\qquad \operatorname {nul}_0=2+2\, \mathbf1_{\{ L/(2\pi R)\in \mathbb N\} },  \] where $\mathbb N=\{ 1,2,\ldots \} $. Its unrestricted index is $1+\operatorname {ind}_0$. It is volume-constrained stable if and only if $L\le 2\pi R$. Proof The cylinder bounds the solid torus $B_ R^2\times (\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)$, so the usual volume constraint applies in this ambient quotient. Its metric is $R^2d\theta ^2+dz^2$, its principal curvatures are $1/R$ and zero, and the ambient Ricci tensor is zero. Thus the CMC second-variation form is \[  Q(f,f)=\int \left(R^{-2}|f_\theta |^2+|f_ z|^2-R^{-2}f^2\right)dA.  \] Fourier expansion in both periodic variables diagonalizes the form. On the complex mode $e^{ik\theta }e^{2\pi ijz/L}$, the eigenvalue of $-J$ is \[  \frac{k^2-1}{R^2}+\left(\frac{2\pi j}L\right)^2,\qquad k,j\in \mathbb Z.  \] The mean-zero condition removes exactly the constant mode. Negative eigenvalues can then occur only when $k=0$ and $0<|j|<L/(2\pi R)$. Each positive $j$ contributes a real sine/cosine pair, proving the constrained index. The always-present zero modes are $\cos \theta ,\sin \theta $, induced by horizontal translations. Two further axial modes occur precisely when $j=L/(2\pi R)$ is a positive integer. No other pairs have eigenvalue zero. For the bilinear kernel on the constrained space the same computation applies, since Fourier orthogonality separates the removed constant mode. Reinstating that mode adds one negative direction. The index vanishes precisely at the stated threshold. This is a compact example in the flat quotient, not an embedded compact CMC surface in Euclidean three-space. $\square$

title: 11.11 Jacobi fields on a Delaunay unduloid
search_title: Jacobi fields on a Delaunay unduloid
section: 11.11 Jacobi fields on a Delaunay unduloid
text:
The geometric Jacobi fields and their growth are described in [ Maz02 ] , Section 2.3, pp. 8–10. For the noncylindrical unduloids of Theorem 16.10.1 , we prove a bounded-kernel statement by explicit calculations and a one-dimensional barrier. Weighted Fredholm theory and precise Floquet exponents remain outside this section. Proposition 11.11.1 (The axial period is strictly increasing with neck radius) . 00F65396A131 For fixed $H>0$ and $0<a<1/H$, the axial period $L_ a$ in Proposition 16.10.2 has $L_ a'>0$. In particular $4/H<L_ a<2\pi /H$. Proof Set $e=1-Ha\in (0,1)$ and $t=Hs$. The radius formula and $2Hc=1-e^2$ give \[  L_ a= rac1H\int _0^{2\pi } rac{1-e\cos t}{\sqrt{1+e^2-2e\cos t}}\, dt.  \] For a fixed $e<1$ the denominator is uniformly positive, so differentiation under the integral is valid. Direct differentiation of the integrand with respect to $e$ gives \[  - rac{e\sin ^2t}{(1+e^2-2e\cos t)^{3/2}}.  \] Since $de/da=-H$, it follows that \[  L_ a'=\int _0^{2\pi } rac{e\sin ^2t}{(1+e^2-2e\cos t)^{3/2}}\, dt>0.  \] Combine strict monotonicity with the two endpoint limits in Propositions 16.10.3 and 16.10.4 to get the bounds. $\square$ Proposition 11.11.2 (Six geometric Jacobi fields) . 0F900FF85ECD Write $r=r_ a$, $z=z_ a$, let primes denote arclength derivatives, and let $\partial _ a$ differentiate the fixed-$H$ family at fixed $s$. The following six functions are Jacobi fields for $J=\Delta +|A|^2$ on a noncylindrical unduloid: \[  -r',\quad z'\cos 	heta ,\quad z'\sin 	heta ,\quad (zz'+rr')\cos 	heta ,\quad (zz'+rr')\sin 	heta ,\quad f_ a=(\partial _ ar)z'-(\partial _ az)r'.  \] They are linearly independent. The first three come from translations, the next two from rotations of the axis, and the last from changing the neck radius at fixed $H$. Proof For any smooth family of immersions with the same constant $H$, the normal speed satisfies $Jf=0$ by Proposition 11.3.4 ; tangential speed differentiates a constant and contributes zero. Pair the three constant ambient vector fields with $
u =(z'\cos 	heta ,z'\sin 	heta ,-r')$ to get the translation fields. Rotation about the $y$ axis has velocity $(z,0,-r\cos 	heta )$ and hence the fourth normal component; rotation about the $x$ axis gives the fifth up to sign. Pair $\partial _ aF$ with $
u $ to get the sixth. The angular zero modes $-r'$ and $f_ a$ are independent: at the neck $s=0$, they take values zero and one respectively, while $r'$ is not identically zero. For each first angular mode, the translation coefficient $z'$ is positive and periodic. The rotational coefficient grows without bound because $z$ grows linearly, $z'$ is bounded below positively, and $rr'$ is bounded. They are therefore independent. Fourier orthogonality separates the zero, cosine and sine sectors, proving independence of all six fields. Rotation around the symmetry axis has identically zero normal speed and is not counted. $\square$ Proposition 11.11.3 (The neck Jacobi field has linear drift) . 2E8835106506 With $P=2\pi /H$ and $f_ a$ as above, \[  f_ a(s+P)=f_ a(s)-L_ a'r'(s).  \] Consequently $f_ a$ is unbounded on the complete noncylindrical unduloid, and no combination of $f_ a$ with the vertical translation field can be bounded unless the coefficient of $f_ a$ vanishes. Proof Differentiate $r_ a(s+P)=r_ a(s)$ and $z_ a(s+P)=z_ a(s)+L_ a$ with respect to $a$. The period $P$ is independent of $a$, so no derivative of the argument is introduced. Substitution into the formula for $f_ a$ proves the drift relation. At a value of $s$ where $r'(s)
e 0$, iteration gives $f_ a(s+jP)=f_ a(s)-jL_ a'r'(s)$. The coefficient is nonzero by Proposition 11.11.1 , so this grows linearly. The vertical translation field is periodic and cannot cancel this drift. $\square$ Lemma 11.11.4 (A bounded solution of a strictly positive one-dimensional potential vanishes) . 669EC3E1F072 Let $q:\mathbb R	o \mathbb R$ be continuous with $q\ge \delta >0$. If a bounded real $C^2$ function $v$ satisfies $v''=qv$ on $\mathbb R$, then $v=0$. Proof Let $M=\sup |v|$. On $[-T,T]$ define $b_ T(t)=M\cosh (\sqrt\delta \, t)/\cosh (\sqrt\delta \, T)$. For $\mathcal L=-d^2/dt^2+q$, one has $\mathcal Lb_ T=(q-\delta )b_ T\ge 0$ and $\mathcal Lv=0$. Each of $b_ T\pm v$ is nonnegative at both endpoints. If it had a negative interior minimum, its second derivative there would be nonnegative and its $q$ term strictly negative, contradicting $\mathcal L(b_ T\pm v)\ge 0$. Hence $|v(t)|\le b_ T(t)$. For fixed $t$, let $T	o \infty $ to obtain $v(t)=0$. $\square$ Proposition 11.11.5 (The conformal Jacobi potential has a uniform bound) . DF4F7144B270 Let $t$ be the global coordinate defined by $dt/ds=1/r(s)$. The unduloid metric is $r^2(dt^2+d	heta ^2)$, and \[  r^2J=\partial _ t^2+\partial _	heta ^2+V(t),\qquad V=r^2|A|^2= rac{H^2r^2}2+ rac{2c^2}{r^2}\le 2-2Hc<2.  \] In particular every bounded Jacobi field has zero Fourier coefficients in all angular frequencies $|k|\ge 2$. Proof Since $a\le r\le b$, the coordinate $t$ ranges over all of $\mathbb R$, and $ds=r\, dt$ gives the conformal metric. The flux equation yields principal curvatures $H/2+c/r^2$ and $H/2-c/r^2$, proving the formula for $|A|^2$. With $c=Hab/2$, the potential equals $H^2(r^2+a^2b^2/r^2)/2$. As a function of $r^2\in [a^2,b^2]$, this convex expression has its maximum at an endpoint, where it equals $H^2(a^2+b^2)/2=2-2Hc$. A smooth bounded Jacobi field has bounded smooth Fourier coefficients $v_ k(t)$, obtained by integrating against $e^{-ik	heta }$. Differentiating under this compact angular integral gives $v_ k''=(k^2-V)v_ k$. For $|k|\ge 2$, the coefficient is at least $2+2Hc>0$. Apply Lemma 11.11.4 to the real and imaginary parts to conclude $v_ k=0$. No Floquet asymptotic theorem is used. $\square$ Theorem 11.11.6 (Bounded Jacobi fields on a noncylindrical unduloid) . 88B3A10F8389 Every smooth bounded real Jacobi field on the complete unduloid with $0<a<1/H$ is the normal component of an ambient translation. Thus the bounded kernel is exactly three-dimensional. This is the bounded part of the geometric-field description in [ Maz02 ] , p. 9; the proof below does not claim weighted Fredholm estimates or a full classification of exponentially growing fields. Proof Proposition 11.11.5 eliminates all frequencies $|k|\ge 2$. Fourier uniqueness leaves only the angular zero, cosine and sine sectors. In each sector the Jacobi equation is a second-order linear ODE in $t$, whose solution space has dimension two by uniqueness of the initial-value problem. Proposition 11.11.2 supplies two independent solutions in each sector. In the zero sector, the neck field has nonzero linear drift by Proposition 11.11.3 , while the vertical translation field is periodic. Hence boundedness leaves only the latter. In each first angular sector the rotation coefficient $zz'+rr'$ is unbounded, while $z'$ is periodic, leaving only its translation coefficient. All three retained fields are bounded and independent, completing the proof. The cylinder endpoint is excluded: axial translation has zero normal component there and additional bounded oscillatory axial fields appear. $\square$ Proposition 11.11.7 (No square-integrable Jacobi field on a complete unduloid) . 3C28FE1AC8E1 For a noncylindrical complete unduloid with fixed $0<a<1/H$, every smooth Jacobi field $u$ satisfying $\int |u|^2\, dA<\infty $ is zero. This conclusion does not assert that the Jacobi operator has closed range on an unweighted function space. Proof In the conformal coordinates of Proposition 11.11.5 , $dA=r^2dt\, d	heta $ and $a\le r\le b$. Each angular Fourier coefficient $v_ k$ is therefore in $L^2(\mathbb R,dt)$ by Cauchy–Schwarz on the angular circle. For $|k|\ge 2$, it satisfies $v_ k''=q_ kv_ k$ with $q_ k=k^2-V\ge \delta >0$. Apply the following calculation to its real and imaginary parts. Choose $\eta _ T$ equal to one on $[-T,T]$, supported in $[-2T,2T]$, with $|\eta _ T'|\le C/T$. Integration by parts against $\eta _ T^2v_ k$ and Young's inequality give \[   rac12\int \eta _ T^2|v_ k'|^2+\int q_ k\eta _ T^2|v_ k|^2 \le 2\int |\eta _ T'|^2|v_ k|^2\le  rac{2C^2}{T^2}\| v_ k\| _2^2.  \] Letting $T	o \infty $ forces $v_ k=0$ on every bounded interval. For the remaining frequencies, the explicit bases in Proposition 11.11.2 apply. In a first angular sector, the rotational coefficient grows at least linearly at either end, while $z'$ is periodic and bounded below positively. No nonzero combination is square-integrable. In the zero sector, put $v=-r'$. The neck field obeys $f_ a(s+jP)=f_ a(s)+jL_ a'v(s)$. Choose a subinterval of one period on which $|v|$ is bounded below positively. A nonzero coefficient of $f_ a$ then makes the squared integral over its translates grow quadratically in $|j|$; a nonzero multiple of $v$ alone has the same positive squared integral on every period. Neither is square-integrable. The changes between $s$, $t$, and area measure have uniformly bounded positive weights for this fixed unduloid. Fourier uniqueness now gives $u=0$. This proof concerns the kernel only; range and weighted mapping properties require additional analysis. $\square$

text: Proposition 11.11.5 (The conformal Jacobi potential has a uniform bound) . DF4F7144B270 Let $t$ be the global coordinate defined by $dt/ds=1/r(s)$. The unduloid metric is $r^2(dt^2+d\theta ^2)$, and \[  r^2J=\partial _ t^2+\partial _\theta ^2+V(t),\qquad V=r^2|A|^2=\frac{H^2r^2}2+\frac{2c^2}{r^2}\le 2-2Hc<2.  \] In particular every bounded Jacobi field has zero Fourier coefficients in all angular frequencies $|k|\ge 2$. Proof Since $a\le r\le b$, the coordinate $t$ ranges over all of $\mathbb R$, and $ds=r\, dt$ gives the conformal metric. The flux equation yields principal curvatures $H/2+c/r^2$ and $H/2-c/r^2$, proving the formula for $|A|^2$. With $c=Hab/2$, the potential equals $H^2(r^2+a^2b^2/r^2)/2$. As a function of $r^2\in [a^2,b^2]$, this convex expression has its maximum at an endpoint, where it equals $H^2(a^2+b^2)/2=2-2Hc$. A smooth bounded Jacobi field has bounded smooth Fourier coefficients $v_ k(t)$, obtained by integrating against $e^{-ik\theta }$. Differentiating under this compact angular integral gives $v_ k''=(k^2-V)v_ k$. For $|k|\ge 2$, the coefficient is at least $2+2Hc>0$. Apply Lemma 11.11.4 to the real and imaginary parts to conclude $v_ k=0$. No Floquet asymptotic theorem is used. $\square$

title: Theorem 11.11.6 (Bounded Jacobi fields on a noncylindrical unduloid)
search_title: Bounded Jacobi fields on a noncylindrical unduloid
section: 11.11 Jacobi fields on a Delaunay unduloid
text: Theorem 11.11.6 (Bounded Jacobi fields on a noncylindrical unduloid) . 88B3A10F8389 Every smooth bounded real Jacobi field on the complete unduloid with $0<a<1/H$ is the normal component of an ambient translation. Thus the bounded kernel is exactly three-dimensional. This is the bounded part of the geometric-field description in [ Maz02 ] , p. 9; the proof below does not claim weighted Fredholm estimates or a full classification of exponentially growing fields. Proof Proposition 11.11.5 eliminates all frequencies $|k|\ge 2$. Fourier uniqueness leaves only the angular zero, cosine and sine sectors. In each sector the Jacobi equation is a second-order linear ODE in $t$, whose solution space has dimension two by uniqueness of the initial-value problem. Proposition 11.11.2 supplies two independent solutions in each sector. In the zero sector, the neck field has nonzero linear drift by Proposition 11.11.3 , while the vertical translation field is periodic. Hence boundedness leaves only the latter. In each first angular sector the rotation coefficient $zz'+rr'$ is unbounded, while $z'$ is periodic, leaving only its translation coefficient. All three retained fields are bounded and independent, completing the proof. The cylinder endpoint is excluded: axial translation has zero normal component there and additional bounded oscillatory axial fields appear. $\square$

title: Proposition 11.11.7 (No square-integrable Jacobi field on a complete unduloid)
search_title: No square-integrable Jacobi field on a complete unduloid
section: 11.11 Jacobi fields on a Delaunay unduloid
text: Proposition 11.11.7 (No square-integrable Jacobi field on a complete unduloid) . 3C28FE1AC8E1 For a noncylindrical complete unduloid with fixed $0<a<1/H$, every smooth Jacobi field $u$ satisfying $\int |u|^2\, dA<\infty $ is zero. This conclusion does not assert that the Jacobi operator has closed range on an unweighted function space. Proof In the conformal coordinates of Proposition 11.11.5 , $dA=r^2dt\, d\theta $ and $a\le r\le b$. Each angular Fourier coefficient $v_ k$ is therefore in $L^2(\mathbb R,dt)$ by Cauchy–Schwarz on the angular circle. For $|k|\ge 2$, it satisfies $v_ k''=q_ kv_ k$ with $q_ k=k^2-V\ge \delta >0$. Apply the following calculation to its real and imaginary parts. Choose $\eta _ T$ equal to one on $[-T,T]$, supported in $[-2T,2T]$, with $|\eta _ T'|\le C/T$. Integration by parts against $\eta _ T^2v_ k$ and Young's inequality give \[  \frac12\int \eta _ T^2|v_ k'|^2+\int q_ k\eta _ T^2|v_ k|^2 \le 2\int |\eta _ T'|^2|v_ k|^2\le \frac{2C^2}{T^2}\| v_ k\| _2^2.  \] Letting $T\to \infty $ forces $v_ k=0$ on every bounded interval. For the remaining frequencies, the explicit bases in Proposition 11.11.2 apply. In a first angular sector, the rotational coefficient grows at least linearly at either end, while $z'$ is periodic and bounded below positively. No nonzero combination is square-integrable. In the zero sector, put $v=-r'$. The neck field obeys $f_ a(s+jP)=f_ a(s)+jL_ a'v(s)$. Choose a subinterval of one period on which $|v|$ is bounded below positively. A nonzero coefficient of $f_ a$ then makes the squared integral over its translates grow quadratically in $|j|$; a nonzero multiple of $v$ alone has the same positive squared integral on every period. Neither is square-integrable. The changes between $s$, $t$, and area measure have uniformly bounded positive weights for this fixed unduloid. Fourier uniqueness now gives $u=0$. This proof concerns the kernel only; range and weighted mapping properties require additional analysis. $\square$

title: 16.11 Positive measure, empty interior and infinite perimeter
search_title: Positive measure, empty interior and infinite perimeter
section: 16.11 Positive measure, empty interior and infinite perimeter
text: A positive-length Cantor set separates measure from topology and rectifiability from finite boundary mass. The construction is in [ Mor16 ] , fifth edition, Example after Proposition 3.12, p. 33; the associated current is Exercise 4.17, p. 59. We give the construction and the variation argument explicitly. Definition 16.11.1 (A fat Cantor construction) . 2F0A87D1DCB7 Start with $E_0=[0,1]$. At step $n\ge 1$, remove the central open interval of length $4^{-n}$ from each of the $2^{n-1}$ closed components of $E_{n-1}$. Let $E_ n$ be the remaining union of $2^ n$ closed intervals and define $E=\bigcap _{n\ge 0}E_ n$. Proposition 16.11.2 (Length and topology of the fat Cantor set) . 51F772C179A3 The construction in Definition 16.11.1 is well defined. Every stage-$n$ component has length \[  \ell _ n=2^{-n-1}+2^{-2n-1},  \] and its intersection with $E$ has length $2^{-n-1}$. The set $E$ is compact, perfect, nowhere dense, and has Lebesgue measure $1/2$. Proof The recurrence $\ell _ n=(\ell _{n-1}-4^{-n})/2$, with $\ell _0=1$, gives the displayed formula by induction. It is positive and the removed length is smaller than its parent interval, validating every step. At step $n$ the removed total length is $2^{n-1}4^{-n}=2^{-n-1}$. These intervals are disjoint, so their total length is $1/2$, proving $|E|=1/2$ by continuity from above. Within a fixed stage-$n$ interval, the total future removed length is \[  \sum _{j\ge 1}2^{j-1}4^{-(n+j)}=\tfrac 12 4^{-n}.  \] Subtracting it from $\ell _ n$ gives $2^{-n-1}$. Compactness follows by nested closed intersections. Since $\ell _ n\to 0$, no interval can be contained in every $E_ n$, so $E$ has empty interior and, being closed, is nowhere dense. Endpoints of each component survive every later step. For any $x\in E$, choose a stage-$n$ component containing it and an endpoint different from $x$; that endpoint belongs to $E$ and is within $\ell _ n$. Hence $E$ has no isolated points. $\square$ Example 16.11.3 (Ordinary continuity and approximate continuity differ) . C6F344E46714 The function $\chi _ E$ is discontinuous at every point of $E$ and continuous at every point outside $E$. Nevertheless its approximate value is one at almost every point of $E$ and zero at almost every point outside $E$. Thus a set of positive measure can consist entirely of ordinary discontinuities of a bounded measurable function that is approximately continuous almost everywhere. Proof Every neighborhood of a point of $E$ meets its dense open complement, where the function is zero, while its value on $E$ is one. Off the closed set $E$, a small neighborhood lies in its complement and the function is constant. The approximate-value statement is the Lebesgue density theorem applied to $E$ and its complement. More explicitly, at a density-one point of $E$, for every $0<\varepsilon <1$, the set $\{ |\chi _ E-1|>\varepsilon \} $ has density zero; this is the definition of approximate convergence to one. The analogous assertion gives zero off $E$ almost everywhere. No continuity representative is claimed. $\square$ Proposition 16.11.4 (The characteristic function has infinite variation) . 203445E7552B The function $\chi _ E$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R$, does not belong to $BV(\mathbb R)$; equivalently $E$ has infinite one-dimensional perimeter. Proof Fix a positive integer $N$. Choose a stage with at least $N+1$ retained components, and select $N+1$ successive such components. Each has positive $E$ measure by Proposition 16.11.2 , so it contains a density-one point $x_ i$ of $E$, $0\le i\le N$. Between successive components choose a point $y_ i$ in a deleted open gap. In increasing order the selected points are $x_0<y_1<x_1<\cdots <y_ N<x_ N$. Let $u_\varepsilon =\rho _\varepsilon *\chi _ E$ for a nonnegative smooth compactly supported approximate identity. At the chosen density points $u_\varepsilon (x_ i)\to 1$, and at the gap points $u_\varepsilon (y_ i)\to 0$. The fundamental theorem of calculus on each consecutive interval implies \[  \int _{\mathbb R}|u_\varepsilon '|\ge \sum _{i=1}^ N\bigl (|u_\varepsilon (y_ i)-u_\varepsilon (x_{i-1})| +|u_\varepsilon (x_ i)-u_\varepsilon (y_ i)|\bigr )\longrightarrow 2N.  \] If $\chi _ E$ were BV, Lemma 4.2.3 would bound the left side by $|D\chi _ E|(\mathbb R)$ for all $\varepsilon $. Since $N$ is arbitrary this is impossible. The equivalence with perimeter is the definition of the perimeter of a measurable set via its characteristic function. $\square$ Example 16.11.5 (A finite-mass rectifiable current with infinite boundary mass) . EDA509B2D116 Define a one-dimensional current on $\mathbb R$ by $T(f\, dx)=\int _ E f(x)\, dx$. It is an integer-multiplicity rectifiable current of mass $1/2$, but its boundary has infinite mass. Consequently it is neither normal nor integral. Proof The set $E$ is a measurable subset of the oriented line, with multiplicity one and length $1/2$, giving the rectifiable representation and mass. For a smooth compactly supported function $\varphi $, $\partial T(\varphi )=T(d\varphi )=\int _ E\varphi '$. If this zero-dimensional boundary current had finite mass, then \[  \left|\int _ E\varphi '\right|\le C\| \varphi \| _\infty  \] for one finite constant $C$ and every such test. This is precisely bounded distributional variation of $\chi _ E$, contradicting Proposition 16.11.4 . A normal current must have both finite mass and finite boundary mass; an integral current has locally integral boundary and, here with compact support, finite boundary mass. Thus neither property holds. This resolves the distinction posed in [ Mor16 ] , Exercise 4.17. $\square$

title: 16.12 A one-dimensional dust without tangent lines
search_title: A one-dimensional dust without tangent lines
section: 16.12 A one-dimensional dust without tangent lines
text: The four-corner Cantor set is the example following Theorem 3.17 in [ Mor16 ] , fifth edition, pp. 36–37. We prove finite positive length, a quantitative obstruction to tangent lines, and pure unrectifiability. The last step explicitly uses the rectifiable tangent theorem, Theorem 3.1.4 ; the elementary estimates do not claim the source's exact value of the Hausdorff measure. Definition 16.12.1 (The four-corner set and cylinder measure) . F9CBD348B9C0 Let \[  C_4=\left\{ \sum _{j\ge 1}3\varepsilon _ j4^{-j}:\varepsilon _ j\in \{ 0,1\} \right\} ,\qquad K=C_4\times C_4.  \] At level $k$, the set $K$ lies in $4^ k$ disjoint corner squares of side $4^{-k}$. A cylinder is the intersection of $K$ with one such square. Let $\mu $ be the probability measure assigning mass $4^{-k}$ to each level-$k$ cylinder. Equivalently, push forward Lebesgue probability on $[0,1]^2$ by the two binary-to-base-four digit maps; the dyadic endpoint choices affect a null set only. Proposition 16.12.2 (Linear ball bounds and finite positive length) . 51869A534A53 For $x\in K$ and $0<r\le \sqrt2$, \[  \frac{r}{8\sqrt2}\le \mu (B_ r(x))\le 100r.  \] The upper bound also holds for balls centered outside $K$. Consequently $0<\mathcal H^1(K)<\infty $ and $\dim _{\rm H}K=1$; more precisely $1/100\le \mathcal H^1(K)\le \sqrt2$. Proof For $r<1$, choose $k$ with $\ell =4^{-k}\le r<4\ell $. The lower-left corners of level-$k$ squares lie on the grid $\ell \mathbb Z^2$. A square meeting a ball of radius $r$ has each lower-left coordinate in an interval of length at most $2r+\ell <9\ell $. There are at most ten grid choices per coordinate and hence at most one hundred such squares. Each has $\mu $ mass $\ell $, so $\mu (B_ r)\le 100\ell \le 100r$. For $r\ge 1$ the bound follows from total mass one. For the lower bound choose the least $k$ with $\sqrt2\, 4^{-k}\le r/2$. The level-$k$ cylinder containing $x$ lies entirely in $B_ r(x)$, and minimality gives $4^{-k}>r/(8\sqrt2)$. Thus its mass proves the lower estimate. The same cylinder masses show that every point has zero mass. The level-$k$ squares cover $K$ with total diameter $4^ k\sqrt2\, 4^{-k}=\sqrt2$, proving the Hausdorff upper bound. For any sufficiently small countable cover $K\subset \bigcup U_ i$, discard sets missing $K$ and choose $x_ i\in U_ i\cap K$. Then $U_ i\cap K\subset \overline B_{\operatorname {diam}U_ i}(x_ i)$. The ball estimate, obtained for closed balls by enlarging the radius and taking a limit, gives $1\le 100\sum _ i\operatorname {diam}U_ i$. Infimizing and shrinking the cover diameters gives the lower bound. A set of finite positive $\mathcal H^1$ measure has Hausdorff dimension one by the comparison of diameter powers in the Hausdorff definition. $\square$ Proposition 16.12.3 (The cylinder measure is normalized Hausdorff measure) . 8A4F1392293E The identity $\mu =\mathcal H^1\llcorner K/\mathcal H^1(K)$ holds. In particular a level-$k$ cylinder has $\mathcal H^1$ measure $4^{-k}\mathcal H^1(K)$. Proof Every level-$k$ cylinder is a homothetic copy of $K$ with ratio $4^{-k}$. Hausdorff one-measure scales by that ratio, directly from its definition by diameter covers. Thus normalized Hausdorff measure and $\mu $ agree on every cylinder. Finite unions of cylinders form an algebra, since the partitions refine each other, and this algebra generates the Borel sets of $K$: cylinder diameters tend to zero and every relative neighborhood contains a cylinder around each of its points. Uniqueness of finite measures on a generating algebra gives equality. All measures here are Borel measures on the compact set $K$. $\square$ Lemma 16.12.4 (Differentiation along the Cantor cylinders) . 2FE1FC9C5147 For $f\in L^1(\mu )$, let $Q_ k(x)$ be the level-$k$ cylinder containing $x$, and put \[  A_ kf(x)=\frac1{\mu (Q_ k(x))}\int _{Q_ k(x)}f\, d\mu .  \] Then $A_ kf(x)\to f(x)$ for $\mu $-almost every $x$. In particular, for a $\mu $-measurable subset $E\subset K$, at almost every point of $E$ the ratio $\mu (Q_ k(x)\setminus E)/\mu (Q_ k(x))$ tends to zero. Proof The cylinder maximal function $Mg=\sup _{k\ge 0}A_ k|g|$ satisfies \[  \mu \{ Mg>t\} \le t^{-1}\| g\| _{L^1(\mu )}.  \] For a finite range of levels, select the first cylinder in each nested chain whose average exceeds $t$. These stopping cylinders are disjoint and cover the set in question; summing $t\mu (Q)<\int _ Q|g|$ proves the inequality. Increasing the range gives the full estimate by continuity from below. For a continuous function on $K$, the averages converge uniformly to the function, because cylinder diameters tend uniformly to zero. Continuous restrictions of compactly supported ambient functions are dense in $L^1(\mu )$ by Theorem 2.3.8 . Given such an approximation $h$ to $f$, the limit superior of $|A_ kf-f|$ is at most $M(f-h)+|f-h|$. The maximal inequality and Markov's inequality bound the measure where this exceeds $2t$ by $2t^{-1}\| f-h\| _1$. Let the approximation error tend to zero and then take countably many positive rational $t$. This proves almost-everywhere convergence. Apply it to $f=\chi _ E$ for the density assertion. $\square$ Lemma 16.12.5 (Every line misses a substantial corner) . 8A401CAA49F4 Let $Q$ be a level-$k$ square of side $\ell $. For every affine line $L\subset \mathbb R^2$, one of the four child squares $Q'$ satisfies \[  \operatorname {dist}(y,L)\ge \frac{\ell }{8\sqrt2}\quad \hbox{for all }y\in Q'.  \] Its cylinder has $\mathcal H^1$ measure $\ell \mathcal H^1(K)/4$. Proof The four child centers form a square of side $3\ell /4$. Project onto a unit normal of $L$. The range of their projections is at least $3\ell /(4\sqrt2)$, so at least one center has distance at least $3\ell /(8\sqrt2)$ from $L$. Every point of its child square is within the half diagonal $\ell /(4\sqrt2)$ of that center. The triangle inequality gives the claimed distance. The measure is the cylinder formula of Proposition 16.12.3 . $\square$ Proposition 16.12.6 (No approximate tangent line at any point) . E41DED080922 For every $x\in K$ and every line $P$ through the origin, $P$ is not an approximate tangent to $K$ at $x$ in Definition 3.1.3 . More quantitatively, the measure outside a fixed narrow cone about $x+P$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of radius along the cylinder scales. Proof Take the parent square of side $\ell =4^{-k}$ containing $x$. Lemma 16.12.5 supplies a child cylinder of mass $\ell \mathcal H^1(K)/4$ at distance at least $\ell /(8\sqrt2)$ from $x+P$. All its points are within $\sqrt2\ell $ of $x$, so their angle from $P$ has sine at least $1/16$. The mass in $B_{2\sqrt2\ell }(x)$ outside the cone of sine aperture $1/32$ is therefore at least $\ell \mathcal H^1(K)/4$. This also directly contradicts the measure-limit tangent definition. After scaling by $2\sqrt2\ell $, the child lies in the fixed set $\{ |y|\le 1/2,\operatorname {dist}(y,P)\ge 1/32\} $. Choose a continuous compactly supported nonnegative test equal to one on this set and zero on $P$. Its integral against the rescaled measures has a uniform positive lower bound, whereas its integral on $P$ is zero. Hence the required convergence cannot hold. $\square$ Theorem 16.12.7 (Pure unrectifiability of the four-corner set) . 30075247956C For every countably one-rectifiable set $A\subset \mathbb R^2$, $\mathcal H^1(A\cap K)=0$. This is the example in [ Mor16 ] , pp. 36–37. The proof below uses the external rectifiable tangent theorem, Theorem 3.1.4 , and the locally proved cylinder differentiation lemma. Proof It suffices to treat the image of a Lipschitz map on a compact interval, since countably many such images cover any countably rectifiable set up to a null set. Such an image is compact and has finite length, by the elementary diameter-cover bound for a Lipschitz map. Let $E$ be its intersection with $K$ and suppose $\mathcal H^1(E)>0$. Then $E$ is rectifiable, measurable and finite in measure, so Theorem 3.1.4 gives an approximate tangent at almost every point of $E$. By Lemma 16.12.4 and Proposition 16.12.3 , choose such a point $x$ where \[  \mathcal H^1((K\cap Q_ k(x))\setminus E)=o(4^{-k}).  \] The child corner furnished by Lemma 16.12.5 for its tangent line contains $\ell \mathcal H^1(K)/4$ of $K$ measure, of which only $o(\ell )$ is missing from $E$. The same continuous test used in Proposition 16.12.6 therefore has a uniformly positive integral against the rescaled measures of $E$. This contradicts its approximate tangent. Thus the intersection with every compact Lipschitz curve has zero length; countable union and the null exceptional set prove the assertion. $\square$ Example 16.12.8 (An exceptional projection contains an interval) . 2508D7A1F8C5 Both coordinate projections of $K$ have Lebesgue measure zero. In contrast, the orthogonal projection onto the direction $(2,1)/\sqrt5$ is the interval $[0,3/\sqrt5]$. Proof A coordinate projection equals $C_4$, whose level-$k$ cover consists of $2^ k$ intervals of length $4^{-k}$; their total length tends to zero. For points of $K$, \[  2x+y=3\sum _{j\ge 1}(2\varepsilon _ j+\delta _ j)4^{-j}.  \] The digit $2\varepsilon _ j+\delta _ j$ takes each value $0,1,2,3$, independently at every level. These are exactly the base-four expansions of the interval $[0,1]$, including the endpoint expansion with every digit three. Hence $2x+y$ ranges over $[0,3]$. Division by $\sqrt5$ gives the orthogonal projection coordinate. This is a statement about particular directions; it does not purport to prove the almost-everywhere projection theorem for purely unrectifiable sets. $\square$

A square meeting a ball of radius $r$ has each lower-left coordinate in an interval of length at most $2r+\ell <9\ell $. There are at most ten grid choices per coordinate and hence at most one hundred such squares. Each has $\mu $ mass $\ell $, so $\mu (B_ r)\le 100\ell \le 100r$. For $r\ge 1$ the bound follows from total mass one. For the lower bound choose the least $k$ with $\sqrt2\, 4^{-k}\le r/2$. The level-$k$ cylinder containing $x$ lies entirely in $B_ r(x)$, and minimality gives $4^{-k}>r/(8\sqrt2)$. Thus its mass proves the lower estimate. The same cylinder masses show that every point has zero mass. The level-$k$ squares cover $K$ with total diameter $4^ k\sqrt2\, 4^{-k}=\sqrt2$, proving the Hausdorff upper bound. For any sufficiently small countable cover $K\subset \bigcup U_ i$, discard sets missing $K$ and choose $x_ i\in U_ i\cap K$. Then $U_ i\cap K\subset \overline B_{\operatorname {diam}U_ i}(x_ i)$. The ball estimate, obtained for closed balls by enlarging the radius and taking a limit, gives $1\le 100\sum _ i\operatorname {diam}U_ i$. Infimizing and shrinking the cover diameters gives the lower bound. A set of finite positive $\mathcal H^1$ measure has Hausdorff dimension one by the comparison of diameter powers in the Hausdorff definition. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.12.3 (The cylinder measure is normalized Hausdorff measure)
search_title: The cylinder measure is normalized Hausdorff measure
section: 16.12 A one-dimensional dust without tangent lines
text: Proposition 16.12.3 (The cylinder measure is normalized Hausdorff measure) . 8A4F1392293E The identity $\mu =\mathcal H^1\llcorner K/\mathcal H^1(K)$ holds. In particular a level-$k$ cylinder has $\mathcal H^1$ measure $4^{-k}\mathcal H^1(K)$. Proof Every level-$k$ cylinder is a homothetic copy of $K$ with ratio $4^{-k}$. Hausdorff one-measure scales by that ratio, directly from its definition by diameter covers. Thus normalized Hausdorff measure and $\mu $ agree on every cylinder. Finite unions of cylinders form an algebra, since the partitions refine each other, and this algebra generates the Borel sets of $K$: cylinder diameters tend to zero and every relative neighborhood contains a cylinder around each of its points. Uniqueness of finite measures on a generating algebra gives equality. All measures here are Borel measures on the compact set $K$. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.12.4 (Differentiation along the Cantor cylinders)
search_title: Differentiation along the Cantor cylinders
section: 16.12 A one-dimensional dust without tangent lines
text: Lemma 16.12.4 (Differentiation along the Cantor cylinders) . 2FE1FC9C5147 For $f\in L^1(\mu )$, let $Q_ k(x)$ be the level-$k$ cylinder containing $x$, and put \[  A_ kf(x)=\frac1{\mu (Q_ k(x))}\int _{Q_ k(x)}f\, d\mu .  \] Then $A_ kf(x)\to f(x)$ for $\mu $-almost every $x$. In particular, for a $\mu $-measurable subset $E\subset K$, at almost every point of $E$ the ratio $\mu (Q_ k(x)\setminus E)/\mu (Q_ k(x))$ tends to zero. Proof The cylinder maximal function $Mg=\sup _{k\ge 0}A_ k|g|$ satisfies \[  \mu \{ Mg>t\} \le t^{-1}\| g\| _{L^1(\mu )}.  \] For a finite range of levels, select the first cylinder in each nested chain whose average exceeds $t$. These stopping cylinders are disjoint and cover the set in question; summing $t\mu (Q)<\int _ Q|g|$ proves the inequality. Increasing the range gives the full estimate by continuity from below. For a continuous function on $K$, the averages converge uniformly to the function, because cylinder diameters tend uniformly to zero. Continuous restrictions of compactly supported ambient functions are dense in $L^1(\mu )$ by Theorem 2.3.8 . Given such an approximation $h$ to $f$, the limit superior of $|A_ kf-f|$ is at most $M(f-h)+|f-h|$. The maximal inequality and Markov's inequality bound the measure where this exceeds $2t$ by $2t^{-1}\| f-h\| _1$. Let the approximation error tend to zero and then take countably many positive rational $t$. This proves almost-everywhere convergence. Apply it to $f=\chi _ E$ for the density assertion. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.12.5 (Every line misses a substantial corner)
search_title: Every line misses a substantial corner
section: 16.12 A one-dimensional dust without tangent lines
text: Lemma 16.12.5 (Every line misses a substantial corner) . 8A401CAA49F4 Let $Q$ be a level-$k$ square of side $\ell $. For every affine line $L\subset \mathbb R^2$, one of the four child squares $Q'$ satisfies \[  \operatorname {dist}(y,L)\ge \frac{\ell }{8\sqrt2}\quad \hbox{for all }y\in Q'.  \] Its cylinder has $\mathcal H^1$ measure $\ell \mathcal H^1(K)/4$. Proof The four child centers form a square of side $3\ell /4$. Project onto a unit normal of $L$. The range of their projections is at least $3\ell /(4\sqrt2)$, so at least one center has distance at least $3\ell /(8\sqrt2)$ from $L$. Every point of its child square is within the half diagonal $\ell /(4\sqrt2)$ of that center. The triangle inequality gives the claimed distance. The measure is the cylinder formula of Proposition 16.12.3 . $\square$

title: Proposition 16.12.6 (No approximate tangent line at any point)
search_title: No approximate tangent line at any point
section: 16.12 A one-dimensional dust without tangent lines
text: Proposition 16.12.6 (No approximate tangent line at any point) . E41DED080922 For every $x\in K$ and every line $P$ through the origin, $P$ is not an approximate tangent to $K$ at $x$ in Definition 3.1.3 . More quantitatively, the measure outside a fixed narrow cone about $x+P$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of radius along the cylinder scales. Proof Take the parent square of side $\ell =4^{-k}$ containing $x$. Lemma 16.12.5 supplies a child cylinder of mass $\ell \mathcal H^1(K)/4$ at distance at least $\ell /(8\sqrt2)$ from $x+P$. All its points are within $\sqrt2\ell $ of $x$, so their angle from $P$ has sine at least $1/16$. The mass in $B_{2\sqrt2\ell }(x)$ outside the cone of sine aperture $1/32$ is therefore at least $\ell \mathcal H^1(K)/4$. This also directly contradicts the measure-limit tangent definition. After scaling by $2\sqrt2\ell $, the child lies in the fixed set $\{ |y|\le 1/2,\operatorname {dist}(y,P)\ge 1/32\} $. Choose a continuous compactly supported nonnegative test equal to one on this set and zero on $P$. Its integral against the rescaled measures has a uniform positive lower bound, whereas its integral on $P$ is zero. Hence the required convergence cannot hold. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.12.7 (Pure unrectifiability of the four-corner set)
search_title: Pure unrectifiability of the four-corner set
section: 16.12 A one-dimensional dust without tangent lines
text: Theorem 16.12.7 (Pure unrectifiability of the four-corner set) . 30075247956C For every countably one-rectifiable set $A\subset \mathbb R^2$, $\mathcal H^1(A\cap K)=0$. This is the example in [ Mor16 ] , pp. 36–37. The proof below uses the external rectifiable tangent theorem, Theorem 3.1.4 , and the locally proved cylinder differentiation lemma. Proof It suffices to treat the image of a Lipschitz map on a compact interval, since countably many such images cover any countably rectifiable set up to a null set. Such an image is compact and has finite length, by the elementary diameter-cover bound for a Lipschitz map. Let $E$ be its intersection with $K$ and suppose $\mathcal H^1(E)>0$. Then $E$ is rectifiable, measurable and finite in measure, so Theorem 3.1.4 gives an approximate tangent at almost every point of $E$. By Lemma 16.12.4 and Proposition 16.12.3 , choose such a point $x$ where \[  \mathcal H^1((K\cap Q_ k(x))\setminus E)=o(4^{-k}).  \] The child corner furnished by Lemma 16.12.5 for its tangent line contains $\ell \mathcal H^1(K)/4$ of $K$ measure, of which only $o(\ell )$ is missing from $E$. The same continuous test used in Proposition 16.12.6 therefore has a uniformly positive integral against the rescaled measures of $E$. This contradicts its approximate tangent. Thus the intersection with every compact Lipschitz curve has zero length; countable union and the null exceptional set prove the assertion. $\square$

title: Example 16.12.8 (An exceptional projection contains an interval)
search_title: An exceptional projection contains an interval
section: 16.12 A one-dimensional dust without tangent lines
text: Example 16.12.8 (An exceptional projection contains an interval) . 2508D7A1F8C5 Both coordinate projections of $K$ have Lebesgue measure zero. In contrast, the orthogonal projection onto the direction $(2,1)/\sqrt5$ is the interval $[0,3/\sqrt5]$. Proof A coordinate projection equals $C_4$, whose level-$k$ cover consists of $2^ k$ intervals of length $4^{-k}$; their total length tends to zero. For points of $K$, \[  2x+y=3\sum _{j\ge 1}(2\varepsilon _ j+\delta _ j)4^{-j}.  \] The digit $2\varepsilon _ j+\delta _ j$ takes each value $0,1,2,3$, independently at every level. These are exactly the base-four expansions of the interval $[0,1]$, including the endpoint expansion with every digit three. Hence $2x+y$ ranges over $[0,3]$. Division by $\sqrt5$ gives the orthogonal projection coordinate. This is a statement about particular directions; it does not purport to prove the almost-everywhere projection theorem for purely unrectifiable sets. $\square$
